  &\quad + \left(\frac{n}{24}+\frac{1}{12}\right)f''''(\alpha)S_{n+3}.
\end{aligned}} % source-adjudicated: faint raised mark is an ink artifact, not encoded

%% ===== canonical stable idx 62 =====
% !PRINTED 41
\weberpage{41}

We distinguish four cases:

1. $f''''(\alpha)$ and $f(\alpha)$ not $=0$ [i.\,e. $f(x)$ of the fourth degree and $\alpha$ not a root of $f(x)$].

In this case formula (2) for $n=0$ allows $S_3$ to be expressed by $S_0, S_1, S_2$, and hence $S_n$ for every positive $n$ by $S_0, S_1, S_2$. If, however, one puts $n=-1,-2,\ldots$, one obtains $S_{-2}, S_{-3}, \ldots$ expressed by $S_{-1}, S_0, S_1, S_2$. In this case, therefore, the four fundamental integrals remain
\[
S_{-1}, \quad S_0, \quad S_1, \quad S_2.
\]

2. $f''''(\alpha)$ not $=0$, $f(\alpha)=0$. In this case $S_{-1}$ can still be expressed by $S_0, S_1, S_2$, and one obtains as fundamental integrals
\[
S_0, \quad S_1, \quad S_2.
\]

3. $f''''(\alpha)=0$, $f(\alpha)$ not $=0$. Here the fundamental integrals are
\[
S_{-1}, \quad S_0, \quad S_1.
\]

4. $f''''(\alpha)=0$, $f(\alpha)=0$. Here the fundamental integrals are
\[
S_0, \quad S_1.
\]

The result of this is therefore:

I. If $f(x)$ is of the fourth degree ($a_0=1$), then all integrals $\Omega(x)$ can be expressed by integrals of the form
\[
S_0 = \int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{f(x)}}, \quad S_1 = \int \frac{x\,dx}{\sqrt{f(x)}}, \quad S_2 = \int \frac{x^2\,dx}{\sqrt{f(x)}},
\]
\[
S_{-1} = \int \frac{dx}{(x-\alpha)\sqrt{f(x)}},
\]
in which $S_{-1}$ still depends on the parameter $\alpha$.

II. If, however, $f(x)$ is of the third degree, then the three integrals suffice
\[
S_0 = \int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{f(x)}}, \quad S_1 = \int \frac{x\,dx}{\sqrt{f(x)}}, \quad S_{-1} = \int \frac{dx}{(x-\alpha)\sqrt{f(x)}}.
\]

In both cases $S_0$ is \gesperrt{of the first kind}. If $f(x)$ is of the third degree, then $S_1$ is of the second and $S_{-1}$ of the third kind. If on the other hand $f(x)$ is of the fourth degree, then $S_1$, $S_2$ and $S_{-1}$ are of the third kind. But one can compose from $S_1$ and $S_2$ an integral of the second kind. For we have
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 63 =====
% !PRINTED 42
\weberpage{42}
%<<CONT
\[
\frac{1}{\sqrt{f(x)}} = (x^4 + a_1 x^3 + a_2 x^2 + a_3 x^2 + a_4)^{-1/2} % [sic]
\]
\[
= x^{-2} - \frac{a_1}{2}x^{-3} + \cdots,
\]
and in the development of $\left(x^2 + \dfrac{a_1}{2}x\right):\sqrt{f(x)}$ in descending powers no term with $x^{-1}$ occurs. Consequently $S_2 + \dfrac{a_2}{2}S_1$ is an \gesperrt{integral of the second kind}.

By the mediation of a logarithmic function, however, the four integrals of Case I can be further reduced to three. To this end let $f(x)$ be brought into the form
\[
x^4 + a_1 x^3 + a_2 x^2 + a_3 x + a_4 = P^2 + ax + b,
\]
in which $P = x^2 + px + q$ is a quadratic function and $a$ and $b$ are constants. There results:
\[
p = \frac{a_1}{2}, \quad q = \frac{a_2}{2} - \frac{a_1^2}{8},
\]
\[
a = a_3 - \frac{a_1 a_2}{2} + \frac{a_1^3}{8}, \quad b = a_4 - \left(\frac{a_2}{2} - \frac{a_1^2}{8}\right)^2.
\]

Now:
\weq{3}{d\log\frac{\sqrt{f}-P}{\sqrt{f}+P} = \frac{f'(x)P - 2f(x)P'(x)}{f - P^2}\,\frac{dx}{\sqrt{f(x)}},}
\[
f - P^2 = ax + b,
\]
\[
f'(x) = 2PP' + a
\]
and consequently
\[
f'(x)P - 2f(x)P'(x) = a(P - 2xP') - 2bP' = Q
\]
is a quadratic function of $x$, and accordingly there results from (3)
\weq{4}{\log\frac{\sqrt{f}-P}{\sqrt{f}+P} = \int \frac{Q}{ax+b}\,\frac{dx}{\sqrt{f(x)}}.}

The right-hand side, however, is a linear function of $S_0$, $S_1$ and $S_{-1}$ (for $\alpha = -b/a$). In the particular case where $a = 0$, $Q$ becomes of the first degree, and a linear combination of $S_0$ and $S_{-1}$ can be expressed by a logarithmic function.

If we assume $a_1$ and $a_3 = 0$, to which we can reduce the general case by \S\ 4 by means of a linear transformation, we obtain as the fundamental integrals
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 64 =====
% !PRINTED 43
\weberpage{43}
%<<CONT
\[
S_0 = \int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{f(x)}}, \quad S_2 = \int \frac{x^2\,dx}{\sqrt{f(x)}}, \quad S_{-1} = \int \frac{dx}{(x-\alpha)\sqrt{f(x)}},
\]
while $S_1 = \displaystyle\int \frac{x\,dx}{\sqrt{f(x)}}$ is reduced by the substitution $x^2 = y$ to the non-elliptic integral
\[
\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{dy}{\sqrt{y^2 + a_2 y + a_4}}
\]
Here $S_0$ is of the first, $S_2$ of the second, $S_{-1}$ of the third kind. For the \gesperrt{Legendre} normal form we put $f(x) = (1-x^2)(1-\varkappa^2 x^2)$ and take as the normal integral of the second kind not $S_2$ itself, but $S_0 - \varkappa^2 S_2$. This gives the normal integrals of the three kinds:
\[
\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{(1-x^2)(1-\varkappa^2 x^2)}}, \quad \int \sqrt{\frac{1-\varkappa^2 x^2}{1-x^2}}\,dx, \quad \int \frac{dx}{(x-\alpha)\sqrt{(1-x^2)(1-\varkappa^2 x^2)}}
\]
and, if one puts $x = \sin\varphi$:
\[
\int \frac{d\varphi}{\sqrt{1-\varkappa^2\sin^2\varphi}}, \quad \int \sqrt{1-\varkappa^2\sin^2\varphi}\,d\varphi, \quad \int \frac{d\varphi}{(\sin\varphi - \alpha)\sqrt{1-\varkappa^2\sin^2\varphi}}.
\]

The same is obtained if one takes the elliptic differential in the normal form
\[
\frac{dz}{\sqrt{z(1-z)(1-\varkappa^2 z)}}
\]
and proceeds according to Case II.

\begin{center}
\textbf{\S\ 13. The \gesperrt{Addition Theorem.}}
\end{center}

The \gesperrt{addition theorem} of the elliptic integrals, discovered by \gesperrt{Euler}, consists in the theorem, of fundamental importance for the whole of the theory that follows, that if, of the three pairs of values
\[
x_1, \sqrt{f(x_1)}; \quad x_2, \sqrt{f(x_2)}; \quad x_3, \sqrt{f(x_3)}
\]
two are assumed to be given, the third can be determined by \gesperrt{algebraic means} in such a way that the differential equation
\weq{1}{\frac{dx_1}{\sqrt{f(x_1)}} + \frac{dx_2}{\sqrt{f(x_2)}} + \frac{dx_3}{\sqrt{f(x_3)}} = 0}
is satisfied. In this, $f(x)$ is a given function of the third or fourth degree. This is a special case of the great
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 65 =====
% !PRINTED 44
\weberpage{44}
%<<CONT
\gesperrt{Abel's theorem}, and it is to be conceived and derived here in this way as well\footnote{This far-reaching theorem is found derived with magnificent simplicity in an article of barely two pages in the fourth volume of \gesperrt{Crelles} Journal ``D\'emonstration d'une propri\'et\'e g\'en\'erale d'une certaine classe de fonctions transcendentes''; Oeuvres compl\`etes de N. H. \gesperrt{Abel}. Nouvelle \'edition, T.\,I, p.\,515. A detailed presentation and applications are given in the great posthumous memoir: ``M\'emoire sur une propri\'et\'e g\'en\'erale d'une classe tr\`es \'etendue de fonctions transcendentes''.}. We preface the proof with the following elementary algebraic theorem:

\gesperrt{If $F(x)$ is an integral rational function of degree $n$ without multiple factors, $F'(x)$ its derivative, if further $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ are the roots of the equation $F(x) = 0$ and $\varphi(x)$ an integral function of $x$ whose degree is at most $= n-2$, then}
\weq{2}{\frac{\varphi(x_1)}{F'(x_1)} + \frac{\varphi(x_2)}{F'(x_2)} + \cdots \frac{\varphi(x_n)}{F'(x_n)} = 0.} % [sic] no plus sign is printed after the ellipsis

The proof of this theorem follows immediately from the decomposition of the rational fraction
\[
\frac{x\,\varphi(x)}{F(x)}
\]
into partial fractions
\[
\frac{x_1\varphi(x_1)}{F'(x_1)(x-x_1)} + \frac{x_2\varphi(x_2)}{F'(x_2)(x-x_2)} + \cdots + \frac{x_n\varphi(x_n)}{F'(x_n)(x-x_n)},
\]
if we there put $x = 0$ [Bd.\,I, \S\ 15 (9)].

Now let $P$, $Q$ denote integral functions of $x$ of the degrees $m$ and $m-2$, and we ask for the values of $x$, $\sqrt{f(x)}$, for which the function
\weq{3}{P + Q\sqrt{f(x)}}
vanishes. There are $2m$ such pairs of values (points), and one finds the values of $x$ as the roots of the equation of degree $2m$:
\weq{4}{F(x) = P^2 - Q^2 f(x) = 0,}
and the corresponding values of $\sqrt{f(x)}$ from
\weq{5}{P + Q\sqrt{f(x)} = 0.}

We now assume that the coefficients in the functions $P$, $Q$ are variable, either independent variables or dependent in some way on other variables.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 66 =====
% !PRINTED 45
\weberpage{45}

The values $x$ and $\sqrt{f(x)}$ determined by (4), (5) then also
become functions of these variables, and (5) can be
differentiated.

Let us denote by $\delta$ the differentiation with respect to the
variables occurring in the coefficients of $P$, $Q$, where $x$
is regarded as constant, and by $dx$ the corresponding differential of $x$,
when $x$ is determined by (4) or (5) as a function of these
coefficients; the differentiation of (4) then gives
\[ 2P\delta P - 2Q\delta Qf(x) + F'(x)\,dx = 0, \]
from which, with the use of (5):
\weq{6}{\dfrac{Q\,\delta P - P\,\delta Q}{F'(x)} = \dfrac{dx}{2\sqrt{f(x)}},}
and since the numerator on the left side is of degree $2m-2$,
and $F(x)$ of degree $2m$, formula (2) can be applied,
and it follows that
\weq{7}{\sum \dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{f(x)}} = 0,}
when the sum is extended over all the roots of equation
 (5).

We apply this theorem to the simplest case, namely
 $m=2$, and then obtain the following theorem:

\gesperrt{If}
\weq{8}{x_1, \sqrt{f(x_1)}; \quad x_2, \sqrt{f(x_2)}; \quad x_3, \sqrt{f(x_3)}; \quad x_4, \sqrt{f(x_4)}}
\gesperrt{are four pairs of values for which some function of the
form}
\weq{9}{a + bx + cx^2 + \sqrt{f(x)}}
\gesperrt{vanishes, then these pairs of values are not entirely
independent of one another, but there subsists between
them the differential equation}
\weq{10}{\dfrac{dx_1}{\sqrt{f(x_1)}} + \dfrac{dx_2}{\sqrt{f(x_2)}} + \dfrac{dx_3}{\sqrt{f(x_3)}} + \dfrac{dx_4}{\sqrt{f(x_4)}} = 0.}

The dependence of these four pairs of values, and hence an integration
 of the differential equation (10), can however also be expressed
 in algebraic form, by setting the function
(9) equal to zero for $x = x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4$ and then eliminating
$a, b, c$. In this way one obtains the determinant equation:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 67 =====
% !PRINTED 46
\weberpage{46}
%<<CONT
\weq{11}{\begin{vmatrix} 1, & x_1, & x_1^2, & \sqrt{f(x_1)} \\ 1, & x_2, & x_2^2, & \sqrt{f(x_2)} \\ 1, & x_3, & x_3^2, & \sqrt{f(x_3)} \\ 1, & x_4, & x_4^2, & \sqrt{f(x_4)} \end{vmatrix} = 0.}

From this equation one can express $x_1$ and $\sqrt{f(x_1)}$ \gesperrt{rationally}
in terms of $x_2, \sqrt{f(x_2)}$; $x_3, \sqrt{f(x_3)}$; $x_4, \sqrt{f(x_4)}$; for
$x_1$ is the root of a biquadratic equation whose three
other roots are $x_2, x_3, x_4$, and whose coefficients depend
rationally on $x_2, \sqrt{f(x_2)}$; $x_3, \sqrt{f(x_3)}$; $x_4, \sqrt{f(x_4)}$, and $\sqrt{f(x_1)}$ can
be represented rationally in terms of $x_1$ by means of (11). If one sets $x_4$ equal to an
arbitrary constant, the differential equation
(10) passes into (1), and (11) yields its integral.

We apply this theorem first to the normal form % German source: "dies Theorem"
and set
\[ f(x) = x(1-x)(1-\varkappa^2 x). \]
If we assume $x_4 = 0$ in (11), then this
equation reduces, on division by $\sqrt{x_1 x_2 x_3}$, to:
\weq{12}{\begin{vmatrix} \sqrt{x_1}, & x_1\sqrt{x_1}, & \sqrt{(1-x_1)(1-\varkappa^2 x_1)} \\ \sqrt{x_2}, & x_2\sqrt{x_2}, & \sqrt{(1-x_2)(1-\varkappa^2 x_2)} \\ \sqrt{x_3}, & x_3\sqrt{x_3}, & \sqrt{(1-x_3)(1-\varkappa^2 x_3)} \end{vmatrix} = 0,}
or, if we develop the determinant according to the elements of the first
row:
\weq{13}{\sqrt{x_1}\,(a + bx_1) + c\sqrt{(1-x_1)(1-\varkappa^2 x_1)} = 0,}
in which, for abbreviation, we have set:
\weq{14}{\begin{aligned}
a &= x_2\sqrt{x_2}\sqrt{(1-x_3)(1-\varkappa^2 x_3)} - x_3\sqrt{x_3}\sqrt{(1-x_2)(1-\varkappa^2 x_2)}, \\
b &= -\sqrt{x_2}\sqrt{(1-x_3)(1-\varkappa^2 x_3)} + \sqrt{x_3}\sqrt{(1-x_2)(1-\varkappa^2 x_2)}, \\
c &= -(x_2-x_3)\sqrt{x_2}\sqrt{x_3}.
\end{aligned}}

If we make (13) rational, we obtain the cubic
equation:
\[ x(a+bx)^2 - c^2(1-x)(1-\varkappa^2 x) = 0, \]
whose three roots are $x_1, x_2, x_3$. Accordingly we have identically
\weq{15}{b^2(x-x_1)(x-x_2)(x-x_3) = x(a+bx)^2 - c^2(1-x)(1-\varkappa^2 x),}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 68 =====
% !PRINTED 47
\weberpage{47}
%<<CONT
and setting $x = 0, 1, 1:\varkappa^2$ in this identical equation, it
follows that:
\weq{16}{\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{x_1x_2x_3} &= -\dfrac{c}{b} \\
\sqrt{(1-x_1)(1-x_2)(1-x_3)} &= \dfrac{b+a}{b} \\
\sqrt{(1-\varkappa^2x_1)(1-\varkappa^2x_2)(1-\varkappa^2x_3)} &= \dfrac{b+\varkappa^2a}{b}.
\end{aligned}}

For the determination of the signs in these equations we obtain
further from (13), if we replace $x_1$ by $x_2$ and by $x_3$
and multiply the results:
\[ x_1x_2x_3(a+bx_1)(a+bx_2)(a+bx_3) = -c^3\sqrt{f(x_1)}\sqrt{f(x_2)}\sqrt{f(x_3)} \]
and (15) gives for $x = -a:b$
\[ (a+bx_1)(a+bx_2)(a+bx_3) = \dfrac{c^2}{b}(b+a)(b+\varkappa^2a). \]
If one uses in addition the square of the first equation (16),
there follows from this
\[ \sqrt{f(x_1)}\sqrt{f(x_2)}\sqrt{f(x_3)} = -\dfrac{c}{b^3}(b+a)(b+\varkappa^2a). \]

But the same result is given by the multiplication of the three
equations (16), and the signs in these formulae are therefore so
chosen that the product of the left-hand sides gives the value of
$\sqrt{f(x_1)}$ required by the differential equation (1). A further
determination of the signs is, from the nature of the case, not
possible in (16), and these equations serve for the unique
definition of $\sqrt{x_1}, \sqrt{1-x_1}, \sqrt{1-\varkappa^2x_1}$, when the
$\sqrt{x_2}, \sqrt{1-x_2}, \sqrt{1-\varkappa^2x_2}, \sqrt{x_3}, \sqrt{1-x_3}, \sqrt{1-\varkappa^2x_3}$ are
presupposed as given.

In order to bring the equations (16) into the customary form, we
first make the numerator of $b$ in (14) rational, and obtain
\[ b = -\dfrac{(x_2-x_3)(1-\varkappa^2x_2x_3)}{\sqrt{x_2}\sqrt{(1-x_3)(1-\varkappa^2x_3)} + \sqrt{x_3}\sqrt{(1-x_2)(1-\varkappa^2x_2)}}, \]
further, by (14):
\[ \begin{aligned}
b+a &= -\sqrt{(1-x_2)(1-x_3)}\left\{\sqrt{x_2(1-x_2)}\sqrt{1-\varkappa^2x_3} - \sqrt{x_3(1-x_3)}\sqrt{1-\varkappa^2x_2}\right\} \\
b+\varkappa^2a &= -\sqrt{(1-\varkappa^2x_2)(1-\varkappa^2x_3)}\left\{\sqrt{x_2(1-\varkappa^2x_2)}\sqrt{1-x_3} - \sqrt{x_3(1-\varkappa^2x_3)}\sqrt{1-x_2}\right\},
\end{aligned} \]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 69 =====
% !PRINTED 48
\weberpage{48}
%<<CONT
by which the equations (16) are easily brought into the form:
\weq{17}{\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{x_1} &= -\dfrac{\sqrt{x_2}\sqrt{(1-x_3)(1-\varkappa^2x_3)} + \sqrt{x_3}\sqrt{(1-x_2)(1-\varkappa^2x_2)}}{1-\varkappa^2x_2x_3}, \\
\sqrt{1-x_1} &= \dfrac{\sqrt{1-x_2}\sqrt{1-x_3} - \sqrt{x_2x_3}\sqrt{(1-\varkappa^2x_2)(1-\varkappa^2x_3)}}{1-\varkappa^2x_2x_3}, \\
\sqrt{1-\varkappa^2x_1} &= \dfrac{\sqrt{1-\varkappa^2x_2}\sqrt{1-\varkappa^2x_3} - \varkappa^2\sqrt{x_2x_3}\sqrt{(1-x_2)(1-x_3)}}{1-\varkappa^2x_2x_3},
\end{aligned}}
and our consideration teaches that, if $x_1$ and the roots
$\sqrt{x_1}, \sqrt{1-x_2}, \sqrt{1-\varkappa^2x_1}$ % [sic]
are determined by these equations as functions
of $x_2, x_3$, the differential equation (1) is identically
satisfied.

\begin{center}\rule{2cm}{0.4pt}\end{center}

In order to obtain the addition theorem in the simplest possible
 shape for the Weierstrass normal form as well, we set
\[ f(x) = 4x^3 - g_2x - g_3, \]
and let $x_4$ become infinitely great in equation (11) (after division
 by $x_4^2$). There then results the integral of the
differential equation (1)
\[ \dfrac{dx_1}{\sqrt{f(x_1)}} + \dfrac{dx_2}{\sqrt{f(x_2)}} + \dfrac{dx_3}{\sqrt{f(x_3)}} = 0 \]
in the form
\weq{18}{\begin{vmatrix} 1, & x_1, & \sqrt{f(x_1)} \\ 1, & x_2, & \sqrt{f(x_2)} \\ 1, & x_3, & \sqrt{f(x_3)} \end{vmatrix} = 0,}
or
\weq{19}{a + bx_1 + c\sqrt{f(x_1)} = 0,}
if
\weq{20}{\begin{aligned}
a &= x_2\sqrt{f(x_3)} - x_3\sqrt{f(x_2)} \\
b &= \sqrt{f(x_2)} - \sqrt{f(x_3)} \\
c &= x_3 - x_2.
\end{aligned}}
Then $x_1, x_2, x_3$ become the roots of the cubic
equation
\[ (a+bx)^2 - c^2f(x) = 0, \]
and if we here set the coefficient of $x^2$, divided by
that of $x^3$, equal to the negative sum of the roots, we
obtain
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 70 =====
% !PRINTED 49
\weberpage{49}

%<<CONT
\weq{21}{x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = \frac{1}{4}\left(\frac{\sqrt[3]{f(x_2)} - \sqrt[3]{f(x_3)}}{x_2 - x_3}\right)^2,}

and from (19)

\weq{22}{\sqrt[3]{f(x_1)} = \frac{1}{4}\left(\frac{\sqrt[3]{f(x_2)} - \sqrt[3]{f(x_3)}}{x_2 - x_3}\right)^3 - (x_2+x_3)\frac{\sqrt[3]{f(x_2)} - \sqrt[3]{f(x_3)}}{x_2 - x_3} - \frac{x_3\sqrt[3]{f(x_2)} - x_2\sqrt[3]{f(x_3)}}{x_2 - x_3}.}

§\,14. \gesperrt{Origin of the elliptic functions.}

If in the elliptic differential of the first kind in the \gesperrt{Legendre} normal form
\[
\frac{1}{2}\frac{dz}{\sqrt{z(1-z)(1-\varkappa^2 z)}}
\]
the substitution
\weq{1}{z = \sin^2\varphi}
is made, and the integration is then carried out from $\varphi = 0$ onwards, there arises the elliptic integral of the first kind
\weq{2}{\int_0^\varphi \frac{d\varphi}{\sqrt{1-\varkappa^2\sin^2\varphi}} = u.}
\gesperrt{Jacobi} calls the upper limit $\varphi$ of this integral its \gesperrt{amplitude} and writes
\weq{3}{\varphi = \mathrm{am}\,u.}
The trigonometric functions of this arc
\weq{4}{\sin\varphi,\ \cos\varphi,\ \sqrt{1-\varkappa^2\sin^2\varphi} = \Delta\varphi}
are now those which, regarded as functions of $u$, are called \gesperrt{elliptic functions} and are denoted by \gesperrt{Jacobi} with
\[
\mathrm{sinam}\,u,\quad \mathrm{cosam}\,u,\quad \Delta\,\mathrm{am}\,u,
\]
or, after \gesperrt{Gudermann}, more briefly with
\weq{5}{\mathrm{sn}\,u,\quad \mathrm{cn}\,u,\quad \mathrm{dn}\,u}
These functions depend on the two arguments $u$ and $\varkappa^2$, and when a more exact notation is necessary, one also writes
\[
\mathrm{sn}\,(u,\varkappa^2),\quad \mathrm{cn}\,(u,\varkappa^2),\quad \mathrm{dn}\,(u,\varkappa^2)
\]
instead.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 71 =====
% !PRINTED 50
\weberpage{50}

If in formula (1) $\varphi$ is changed into $-\varphi$, then $u$ passes into $-u$; thus $\mathrm{am}\,(-u) = -\mathrm{am}\,u$, and consequently
\[
\mathrm{sn}\,(-u) = -\mathrm{sn}\,u,\quad \mathrm{cn}\,(-u) = \mathrm{cn}\,u,\quad \mathrm{dn}\,(-u) = \mathrm{dn}\,u,
\]
that is, sn $u$ is an odd function, cn $u$, dn $u$ sin even functions. % [sic] \textquotedbl{}sin\textquotedbl{} printed for \textquotedbl{}sind\textquotedbl{}; the misprinted word is kept as printed, it stands for \textquotedbl{}are\textquotedbl{}
If one therefore puts
\[
\frac{d\varphi_2}{\Delta\varphi_2} = du,\quad \frac{d\varphi_3}{\Delta\varphi_3} = dv,\quad \frac{d\varphi_1}{\Delta\varphi_1} = -d(u+v),
\]
then the formulae (17), §\,13 can be applied, and one obtains the \gesperrt{addition theorems}:
\weq{6}{\begin{gathered}
\mathrm{sn}\,(u+v) = \dfrac{\mathrm{sn}\,u\,\mathrm{cn}\,v\,\mathrm{dn}\,v + \mathrm{sn}\,v\,\mathrm{cn}\,u\,\mathrm{dn}\,u}{1 - \varkappa^2\mathrm{sn}^2u\,\mathrm{sn}^2v},\\
\mathrm{cn}\,(u+v) = \dfrac{\mathrm{cn}\,u\,\mathrm{cn}\,v - \mathrm{sn}\,u\,\mathrm{sn}\,v\,\mathrm{dn}\,u\,\mathrm{dn}\,v}{1 - \varkappa^2\mathrm{sn}^2u\,\mathrm{sn}^2v},\\
\mathrm{dn}\,(u+v) = \dfrac{\mathrm{dn}\,u\,\mathrm{dn}\,v - \varkappa^2\mathrm{sn}\,u\,\mathrm{sn}\,v\,\mathrm{cn}\,u\,\mathrm{cn}\,v}{1 - \varkappa^2\mathrm{sn}^2u\,\mathrm{sn}^2v}.
\end{gathered}}
From these the three elliptic functions can be calculated \gesperrt{uniquely} for arbitrary values of the argument, provided they are determined for some region about the origin, however small. \gesperrt{Weierstrass} takes this theorem as the starting point of the theory of elliptic functions.

If one puts
\[
\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{d\varphi}{\Delta\varphi} = K,
\]
then $\mathrm{sn}\,K = 1$, $\mathrm{cn}\,K = 0$, $\mathrm{dn}\,K = \sqrt{1-\varkappa^2} = \varkappa'$, and the formulae (6) accordingly yield, on putting $v = K$:
\weq{7}{\begin{gathered}
\mathrm{sn}\,(u+K) = \dfrac{\mathrm{cn}\,u}{\mathrm{dn}\,u},\\
\mathrm{cn}\,(u+K) = \dfrac{-\varkappa'\,\mathrm{sn}\,u}{\mathrm{dn}\,u},\\
\mathrm{dn}\,(u+K) = \dfrac{\varkappa'}{\mathrm{dn}\,u},
\end{gathered}}
and if this formula is applied once more:
\weq{8}{\begin{gathered}
\mathrm{sn}\,(u+2K) = -\mathrm{sn}\,u,\\
\mathrm{cn}\,(u+2K) = -\mathrm{cn}\,u,\\
\mathrm{dn}\,(u+2K) = \mathrm{dn}\,u,
\end{gathered}}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 72 =====
% !PRINTED 51
\weberpage{51}

%<<CONT
and applied once again:
\weq{9}{\begin{gathered}
\mathrm{sn}\,(u+4K) = \mathrm{sn}\,u,\\
\mathrm{cn}\,(n+4K) = \mathrm{cn}\,u, % [sic] \textquotedbl{}n\textquotedbl{} printed for \textquotedbl{}u\textquotedbl{}
\\
\mathrm{dn}\,(u+4K) = \mathrm{dn}\,u.
\end{gathered}}
The elliptic functions therefore have the property of \gesperrt{periodicity} in common with the trigonometric functions. They have the period $4K$ (dn $u$ also the period $2K$).

In §\,3 we derived, as an example, the transformation, formula (1):
\weq{10}{\frac{dz}{\sqrt{z(1-z)(1-\varkappa^2 z)}} = \frac{dx}{i\sqrt{x(1-x)(1-\varkappa'^2 x)}},}
when
\weq{11}{z = \frac{-x}{1-x}}
held. If we therefore set
\[
\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x(1-x)(1-\varkappa'^2x)}} = i\,du,
\]
then, if $x$ and $u$ vanish together, $x = \mathrm{sn}^2(iu,\varkappa')$, $1-x = \mathrm{cn}^2(iu,\varkappa')$, and from (10) it follows that
\[
\frac{dz}{\sqrt{z(1-z)(1-\varkappa^2z)}} = du,
\]
and hence
\[
z = \mathrm{sn}^2(u,\varkappa).
\]
Accordingly (11) gives
\weq{12}{\mathrm{sn}\,(u,\varkappa) = \frac{-i\,\mathrm{sn}\,(iu,\varkappa')}{\mathrm{cn}\,(iu,\varkappa')}}
(in which the sign is to be determined from the special value $u=0$).

If we now set
\[
\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{d\varphi}{\sqrt{1-\varkappa'^2\mathrm{sn}^2\varphi}} = K',
\]
then from (8) there results
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{sn}\,(iu+2K',\varkappa') &= -\mathrm{sn}\,(iu,\varkappa'),\\
\mathrm{cn}\,(iu+2K',\varkappa') &= -\mathrm{cn}\,(iu,\varkappa'),
\end{aligned}
\]
and consequently from (12)
\[
\mathrm{sn}\,(u-2iK',\varkappa) = \mathrm{sn}\,(u,\varkappa)
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 73 =====
% !PRINTED 52
\weberpage{52}

%<<CONT
or else, if one transforms $u$ into $u+2iK'$ and again drops the notation $\varkappa$:
\weq{13}{\mathrm{sn}\,(u+2iK') = \mathrm{sn}\,u.}
The function sn $u$ therefore has a \gesperrt{double periodicity}. One of these periods, $4K$, is real the other, $2iK$, purely imaginary % [sic] German source prints K without the mathematically expected prime.
 (at least when the modulus $\varkappa$ is a positive proper fraction). This double periodicity is a property which occurs nowhere in the region of the elementary functions, and which thus showed most clearly that one has here to do with a new kind of function. At the same time it is the consequences derived from the double periodicity which, as experience has shown, lead by far the most quickly and with satisfying rigour into the interior of the theory, so that the most suitable starting point for a methodical development is to be sought here. Our next considerations will therefore be devoted to the doubly periodic functions in general.

\begin{center}
\textbf{\S\,15. \gesperrt{Assumptions from the Theory of Functions.}}
\end{center}

The concept of doubly periodic functions can be rightly grasped only if one regards them as functions of a complex argument $u = v + iw$, in which $i$ has, as usual, the meaning of $\sqrt{-1}$. The variable $u$ counts for us as an independent and unrestrictedly variable quantity, which, following the precedent of \gesperrt{Gauss}, is geometrically represented by the points of a plane in such a way that the point whose coordinates in a rectangular system are $v, w$ is regarded as the carrier of the value $u = v + iw$ and is designated briefly as the point $u$.

We here restrict our consideration to single-valued analytic functions $\varphi(u)$ which have no \gesperrt{essentially singular} points in the finite region. What happens at infinity we leave undecided. We therefore assume the following of the functions under consideration:

1. In every finite portion of surface there lies a finite number of points at which the function $\varphi(u)$ becomes infinite; these points are called \gesperrt{points of discontinuity}.

The number of points of discontinuity altogether, i.\,e. in the whole infinite plane, may of course also be infinitely great.

2. If $u_0$ is a point not belonging to the points of discontinuity, then the function is developable in a series proceeding by integral ascending positive powers of $u - u_0$, which is convergent in a circle having the point $u_0$ as its centre and reaching as far as the nearest point of discontinuity. One says that the function has, in the neighbourhood of the point $u_0$, the \gesperrt{character of an integral function}.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 75 =====
% !PRINTED 54
\weberpage{54}

3. If $u_0$ is a point of discontinuity, then there is a \gesperrt{positive integer} $m$ of such a kind that $(u-u_0)^m\varphi(u)$ remains finite, continuous and different from zero at the point $u_0$, and is therefore developable in integral positive powers of $u - u_0$. In this case the point of discontinuity is said to be \gesperrt{of the $m$th order}. From this there results a development of $\varphi(u)$ in ascending powers of $u - u_0$ which begins with $(u-u_0)^{-m}$ and converges within a circle described about $u_0$ that reaches as far as the nearest point of discontinuity. The coefficient of $(u-u_0)^{-1}$ in this development is called the \gesperrt{residue} of this function for the point $u_0$.

4. \gesperrt{Cauchy's theorem.} The integral
\[
\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int \varphi(u)\,du,
\]
extended in the positive sense over the boundary of a finite piece of surface which contains no points of discontinuity on its boundary line, is equal to the sum of the residues for the points of discontinuity lying in the interior of the piece of surface. The positive direction of integration is here to be taken as that one which lies with respect to the interior of the piece of surface as the $v$-axis lies to the $w$-axis, so that, with the usual mode of determination of these axes, the interior of the surface remains on the left when the boundary is traversed in the positive sense.

5. The function
\[
\psi(u) = \frac{d\log\varphi(u)}{du} = \frac{1}{\varphi(u)}\frac{d\varphi(u)}{du}
\]
has only points of discontinuity of the first order, and if at a point $u_0$ the product $(u-u_0)^{-m}\varphi(u)$ is finite and different from zero, then $m$ is the residue of $\psi(u)$ for this point. If $m$ is positive, then $u_0$ is called a zero point of the $m$th order of $\varphi(u)$.

Accordingly the following is an immediate consequence of \gesperrt{Cauchy's} theorem:

6. The integral
\[
\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int d\log\varphi(u),
\]
extended in the positive direction over the boundary of a piece of surface, is equal to the number of zero points, diminished by the number of points of discontinuity which lie in the interior of this
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 76 =====
% !PRINTED 55
\weberpage{55}

%<<CONT
piece of surface, where zero points and points of discontinuity of order $m$ are to be counted as $m$ such points of the first order.
From this it follows that in the interior of a finite piece of surface there also lies only a finite number of zero points.

In the same sense there results

7. The integral
\[
\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int u\,d\log\varphi(u)
\]
is equal to the sum of the values of $u$ for which $\varphi(u)$ vanishes, diminished by the sum of the values of $u$ for which $\varphi(u)$ becomes infinite.

8. A function which possesses no points of discontinuity at all in the finite region is called an \gesperrt{integral function}. \gesperrt{An integral function which also remains finite at infinity is a constant.} An integral function which also has no essentially singular point at infinity, for which there is therefore an exponent $m$ such that $u^{-m}\varphi(u)$ does not become infinite for $u = \infty$, is a rational function.

9. An integral function whose reciprocal is likewise integral is called a \gesperrt{unit function}. Such a function becomes neither infinite nor zero in the finite region. Its logarithm is therefore likewise an integral function, and from this it follows that every unit function can be represented in the form $e^{g(u)}$, in which $g(u)$ is an integral function. Conversely, every expression of this form is a unit function.

10. According to the fundamental investigations of \gesperrt{Weierstrass} on single-valued analytic functions (Abhandlungen der Berliner Akademie von 1876) there is always an integral function $G(u)$ which vanishes at the points of discontinuity of a function $\varphi(u)$ and only at these, and this function $G(u)$ is determined by the points of discontinuity of $\varphi(u)$ up to a unit function as a factor. Then $\varphi(u)G(u) = G_1(u)$ is likewise an integral function, and one can therefore represent every function $\varphi(u)$ as the quotient of two integral functions
\[
\varphi(u) = \frac{G_1(u)}{G(u)}
\]
in which $G(u)$ and $G_1(u)$ have no zero points in common.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 77 =====
% !PRINTED 56
\weberpage{56}

11. \gesperrt{Numerator and denominator of this representation are uniquely determined by $\varphi(u)$ itself, apart from unit factors.}

The functions $G(u)$, $G_1(u)$ can be decomposed into prime factors, i.e. into factors which become zero at only one point. If one pursues this path in the case of the doubly periodic functions, one arrives at the \gesperrt{Weierstrass} $\sigma$-functions. We shall, however, take another path, on which we shall not meet the $\sigma$-functions until a later place.

\begin{center}
\textbf{\S\,16. Periodicity.}
\end{center}

A function $\varphi(u)$ of $u$ which has the property that, for a constant $\omega$ and for every value of $u$,
\weq{1}{\varphi(u+\omega) = \varphi(u)}
holds, is called \gesperrt{periodic}, and $\omega$ is called the \gesperrt{period}.

The subject of our investigation is functions $\varphi(u)$ with two periods $\omega_1, \omega_2$, of which we shall presuppose once for all that their ratio $\omega_2:\omega_1$ is not real and that the imaginary part of this ratio is \gesperrt{positive}. In the latter assumption there lies only a stipulation concerning the notation $\omega_1, \omega_2$. For if $\omega_2:\omega_1$ has a negative imaginary part, then that of $\omega_1:\omega_2$ is positive.

Every combination $m_1\omega_1 + m_2\omega_2$ is likewise a period, if $m_1, m_2$ are integers.

We take an arbitrary point $u_0$ in the plane $u$ and denote the four points
\[
u_0, \quad u_0 + \omega_1, \quad u_0 + \omega_1 + \omega_2, \quad u_0 + \omega_2;
\]
if we join these four points in order by straight lines, returning from the last to the first, we obtain a parallelogram, which is called the \gesperrt{period parallelogram}. The rectilinear sides of the period parallelogram may also be replaced by curvilinear paths, provided only that the opposite ones come into coincidence by parallel displacement and that the individual paths form no loops.

If $\omega_1 = \alpha_1 + \beta_1 i$, $\omega_2 = \alpha_2 + \beta_3 i$ and $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \beta_1, \beta_3$ are real, % [sic] German source prints beta_3 twice; mathematically expected beta_2.
then by hypothesis $(\alpha_1\beta_2 - \alpha_2\beta_1)$ is positive, and the geometrical meaning of this quantity is (by known theorems
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 78 =====
% !PRINTED 57
\weberpage{57}

%<<CONT
of analytic geometry) the \gesperrt{area of the period
parallelogram}.

By ranging congruent period parallelograms one against another,
the whole $u$-plane can be covered simply and without gaps.
Corresponding points of two different ones among these parallelograms
are the representatives of $u$-values that differ by integral
multiples of the periods, and that are called \gesperrt{congruent with respect
to the modulus $(\omega_1,\omega_2)$} or, when no doubt is possible,
\gesperrt{congruent} for short. The symbol of congruence is

\[ u \equiv u' \ (\mathrm{mod}\ \omega_1,\ \omega_2)\,, \]

and it says that $u'$ has the form $u+m_1\omega_1+m_2\omega_2$, if $m_1$, $m_2$
are integers.

\weberfigure{57}{Fig. 1: Four adjoining period parallelograms in the lattice of the periods $\omega_1,\omega_2$, with corner points $u_0$, $u_0+\omega_1$, $u_0+2\omega_1$, $u_0+\omega_2$, $u_0+\omega_1+\omega_2$, $u_0+2\omega_1+\omega_2$, $u_0+2\omega_2$, $u_0+\omega_1+2\omega_2$, $u_0+2\omega_1+2\omega_2$, and the interior points (joined by dashed lines) $u_1$, $u_2$, $u_3$, $u_4$.}

Thus Fig.\,1 represents four period parallelograms laid one against
another; the points $u_1$, $u_2$, $u_3$, $u_4$ are congruent:

\[ u_2 = u_1+\omega_1\,,\quad u_3 = u_1+\omega_1+\omega_2\,,\quad u_4 = u_1+\omega_2\,, \]

and $u_1$, $u_2$, $u_3$, $u_4$ likewise form the corners of a period
parallelogram.

\gesperrt{The doubly periodic function $\varphi(u)$ has the same value at all
congruent points}, and the whole range of values of this function is
therefore exhausted \gesperrt{within a single period parallelogram}, provided
that of two opposite sides only \gesperrt{the one} is reckoned as belonging to
the parallelogram.

From our general assumptions we draw the
conclusion:

1. \gesperrt{There exists (apart from the constant) no doubly
periodic function that is free of points of discontinuity in the
period parallelogram;} for such a func-
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 79 =====
% !PRINTED 58
\weberpage{58}

%<<CONT
tion would be finite in the whole $u$-plane and would therefore, by
§\,15, 8, have to be a constant.

If $\varphi(u)$ is a doubly periodic function with the periods
$\omega_1$, $\omega_2$, then the integral taken over the boundary of the period
 parallelogram is [because of (1)]

\[
\int d\log\varphi(u) = \int\limits_{u_0}^{u_0+\omega_1} [d\log\varphi(u) - d\log\varphi(u+\omega_2)]
\]
\[
{}-\int\limits_{u_0}^{u_0+\omega_2} [d\log\varphi(u) - d\log\varphi(u+\omega_1)] = 0\,.
\]

From this there follows, by §\,15, 6., the theorem:

2. \gesperrt{A doubly periodic function becomes zero in a
period parallelogram at just as many points as it becomes
infinite.} If $m$ is this number, then $m$ is called the order
of the doubly periodic function. By 1. there are no
doubly periodic functions of order zero.

If in the proof one replaces the function $\varphi(u)$ by $\varphi(u)-c$,
it follows that a doubly periodic function of order $m$
takes any arbitrary value $c$ at equally many points.

If we take the integral of the formula in 7., §\,15 over the boundary
 of the period parallelogram, there results:

\[
\int u\, d\log\varphi(u) = \int\limits_{u_0}^{u_0+\omega_1} [u\,d\log\varphi(u) - (u+\omega_2)\,d\log\varphi(u+\omega_2)]
\]
\[
{}-\int\limits_{u_0}^{u_0+\omega_2} [u\,d\log\varphi(u) - (u+\omega_1)\,d\log\varphi(u+\omega_1)]
\]
\[
{}=\omega_1\int\limits_{u_0}^{u_0+\omega_2} d\log\varphi(u) - \omega_2\int\limits_{u_0}^{u_0+\omega_1} d\log\varphi(u)\,.
\]

Now, because of the many-valuedness of the logarithm,

\[
\int\limits_{u_0}^{u_0+\omega_2} d\log\varphi(u) = \log\varphi(u+\omega_2) - \log\varphi(u) = 2\pi i\, m_1
\]
\[
\int\limits_{u_0}^{u_0+\omega_1} d\log\varphi(u) = \log\varphi(u+\omega_1) - \log\varphi(u) = -2\pi i\, m_2\,,
\]

where $m_1$ and $m_2$ are indeterminate integers.

If therefore the function $\varphi(u)$ becomes infinite at the points $\alpha_1$, $\alpha_2$, $\dots$, $\alpha_m$
and zero at the points $\beta_1$, $\beta_2$, $\dots$, $\beta_m$, then by
§\,15, 7.:

\[ \Sigma\alpha_i \equiv \Sigma\beta_i \ (\mathrm{mod}\ \omega_1,\ \omega_2)\,. \]

%% ===== canonical stable idx 80 =====
% !PRINTED 59
\weberpage{59}

If one replaces $\varphi(u)$ by $\varphi(u)-c$, where $c$ denotes an
arbitrary value, the important theorem follows:

3. \gesperrt{The sum of the argument values at which a
doubly periodic function takes one and the same value $c$
 in the interior of a period parallelogram
is independent of $c$, or under continuous variation
 of $c$ changes at most by jumps of a period.}

4. \gesperrt{From this it follows that there is also no doubly
 periodic function of the first order.}

For such a function would have to take every value $c$ at a single
point $u$. If, then, it is equal to $c'$ at a point $u'$
and equal to $c''$ at a point $u''$ different from it, it would
follow from 3. that $u'\equiv u''$, contrary to the assumption.

By a \gesperrt{doubly periodic function of the second
kind} one understands, following \gesperrt{Hermite}, a function $\psi(u)$ which
behaves with respect to the periods $\omega_1$, $\omega_2$ according to the equations:

\[ \psi(u+\omega_1) = a_1\,\psi(u)\,, \quad \psi(u+\omega_2) = a_2\,\psi(u)\,, \]

where $a_1$, $a_2$ are constants.

5. \gesperrt{For a doubly periodic function of the
second kind also the theorem holds that it becomes zero
and infinite at equally many points of the period
 parallelogram.} If the number of these points is $m$, then here too the
function is said to be of the $m$th order.

The proof is the same as that of theorem 2. But the
extension no longer holds here, that the function $\psi(u)$ takes every
value equally often, because $\psi(u)-c$ is now no longer
 periodic.

6. \gesperrt{A doubly periodic function $\psi(u)$ of the
second kind and of order zero is necessarily a
constant or an exponential function.} For if $\psi(u)$
does not become zero, then

\[ \varphi(u) = \dfrac{\psi'(u)}{\psi(u)} \]

is a doubly periodic function of the first kind which does not
become infinite, and hence, by 1., a constant $a$. From this it follows:

\[ \psi(u) = A\,e^{a\,u}\,, \]

where $A$ is a new constant.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 81 =====
% !PRINTED 60
\weberpage{60}

\begin{center}
\textbf{§ 17. The Functions $T$.}
\end{center}

If doubly periodic functions $\varphi(u)$ of the $m$th order exist, they must be fractional functions. If we therefore set them, according to \S\,15, 10., in the form

\weq{1}{\varphi(u) = \frac{G_1(u)}{G(u)},}

where $G_1(u)$ and $G(u)$ are integral functions without a common zero point, then

\[
\frac{G_1(u+\omega_1)}{G(u+\omega_1)} = \frac{G_1(u+\omega_2)}{G(u+\omega_2)} = \frac{G_1(u)}{G(u)},
\]

and in this the three functions $G(u)$, $G(u+\omega_1)$, $G(u+\omega_2)$ have the same $m$ zero points, namely the points of discontinuity of $\varphi(u)$. Their quotients are therefore unit functions, and hence by \S\,15, 9., if $g_1(u)$, $g_2(u)$ are \gesperrt{integral functions}:

\weq{2}{\begin{aligned}
G(u+\omega_1) &= e^{g_1(u)}\,G(u),\\
G(u+\omega_2) &= e^{g_2(u)}\,G(u),
\end{aligned}}

and the function $G_1(u)$ satisfies the same equations.

If

\weq{3}{\varphi(u) = \frac{T_1(u)}{T(u)}}

is a second representation of $\varphi(u)$ of the form (1), then

\weq{4}{T(u) = e^{g(u)}\,G(u),}

where $g(u)$ is again an integral function, and if therefore, by (2),

\weq{5}{\begin{aligned}
T(u+\omega_1) &= e^{l_1(u)}\,T(u),\\
T(u+\omega_2) &= e^{l_2(u)}\,T(u)
\end{aligned}}

holds, then

\[
\begin{aligned}
g_1(u) &= l_1(u) + g(u) - g(u+\omega_1),\\
g_2(u) &= l_2(u) + g(u) - g(u+\omega_2).
\end{aligned}
\]

Everything therefore depends on our being able, under some suitable assumption about the integral functions $l_1(u)$, $l_2(u)$, to form integral functions $T(u)$ which satisfy the conditions (5) and vanish at $m$ arbitrarily given points of the period parallelogram. By the quotients of two such functions with the same $l_1(u)$, $l_2(u)$ we can then represent all doubly periodic functions $\varphi(u)$, and the more general functions $G(u)$ which accomplish the same are obtained, according to (4), by the addition of an \gesperrt{arbitrary unit factor}.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 82 =====
% !PRINTED 61
\weberpage{61}

If we wished to assume $l_1(u)$, $l_2(u)$ to be constants, then $T(u)$ would be an integral doubly periodic function of the second kind, and consequently, by \S\,16, 6., an exponential function, from which no doubly periodic functions can be formed. The simplest assumption that then remains to us is that $l_1(u)$, $l_2(u)$ are \gesperrt{linear functions} of $u$, and this includes as a special case that one of the two functions $l_1$, $l_2$ is constant.

We therefore set up the following definition:

1. \gesperrt{A $T$-function, $T(u)$, is an integral function of $u$ which satisfies the following two equations:}

\weq{6}{\begin{aligned}
T(u+\omega_1) &= e^{-\pi i [a_1(2u+\omega_1)+b_1]}\,T(u),\\
T(u+\omega_2) &= e^{-\pi i [a_2(2u+\omega_2)+b_2]}\,T(u).
\end{aligned}}

Here $a_1$, $b_1$, $a_2$, $b_2$ are constants, that is, quantities independent of $u$. The periods $\omega_1$, $\omega_2$ are here taken throughout as constants given once and for all, whose ratio $\omega_2:\omega_1$ has a positive imaginary part.

The factors

\[
\begin{aligned}
e_1 &= e_1(u) = e^{-\pi i [a_1(2u+\omega_1)+b_1]},\\
e_2 &= e_2(u) = e^{-\pi i [a_2(2a+\omega_2)+b_2]}
\end{aligned}
\]
% [sic] German source prints 2a in the second exponent; mathematically expected 2u.

are called the two \gesperrt{periodicity factors} of the function $T$.

The periodicity factors do not change when $b_1$, $b_2$ are altered by \gesperrt{even integers}. That functions of this kind really exist will appear only in the further course of the investigation.

2. \gesperrt{If the function $T(u)$ vanishes at any point, then it vanishes also at all congruent points. If it vanishes at $m$ points of the period parallelogram, it is said to be of the $m$th order.}

From this definition it follows at once:

3. \gesperrt{By multiplication of two $T$-functions $T$, $T'$ of order $m$, $m'$ one obtains a $T$-function of order $m+m'$. The periodicity factors of the product $T$, $T'$ are the products of the periodicity factors of $T$ and $T'$.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 83 =====
% !PRINTED 62
\weberpage{62}

We ask first about the possibility of $T$-functions of order zero. If $L(u)$ is such a function and $L'(u)$ its derivative, then twofold differentiation of (6) gives

\[
\frac{d}{du}\,\frac{L'(u+\omega_1)}{L(u+\omega_1)} = \frac{d}{du}\,\frac{L'(u)}{L(u)},
\]

and correspondingly from the second equation (6). Accordingly $d^2\log L(u)/du^2$, being an integral doubly periodic function, is a constant, and consequently $\log L(u)$ is an integral function of the second degree in $u$. We therefore obtain:

4. \gesperrt{A $T$-function of order zero is of the form}

\weq{7}{L(u) = C\,e^{-\pi i (\lambda u^2 + \mu u)},}

where $\lambda$, $\mu$, $C$ are constants.

That every function of this form is a $T$-function of order zero is seen at once.

The product

\weq{8}{T'(u) = L(u)\,T(u)}

is, just like $T(u)$, a $T$-function of order $m$, and vanishes at the same points.

The periodicity factors of $T'$ are obtained from those of $T$ by replacing the exponents $a_1$, $a_2$, $b_1$, $b_2$ by

\weq{9}{\begin{aligned}
a_1' &= a_1 + \lambda\omega_1, & b_1' &= b_1 + \mu\omega_1\\
a_2' &= a_2 + \lambda\omega_2, & b_2' &= b_2 + \mu\omega_2
\end{aligned}}

in which, however, the $b$, $b'$ are determined only up to additive even integers.

5. \gesperrt{By (9), $\mu$ can always be determined, and in only one way, so that $b_1'$, $b_2'$ become real.}

For if the imaginary parts of $b_1'$, $b_2'$ are set equal to zero, one obtains two linear equations for the imaginary and the real part of $\mu$, whose determinant is, by \S\,16, the area of the period parallelogram, and hence different from zero.

The periodicity factors and the zero points of a $T$-function of order $m$ stand in a certain dependence upon one another, which we obtain without difficulty from the theorems of \S\,15. First of all, the order $m$ results if one takes the integral

\[
\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int d\log T(u) = m
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 84 =====
% !PRINTED 63
\weberpage{63}
%<<CONT
extends over the boundary of the period parallelogram. If, for the sake of simplicity, we place the vertex $u_0$ (Fig. 1) at the origin of coordinates, this integral can be decomposed as follows:

\[
\begin{aligned}
2\pi i m &= \int_0^{\omega_1} d\bigl[\log T(u) - \log T(u+\omega_2)\bigr]\\
&\quad - \int_0^{\omega_2} d\bigl[\log T(u) - \log T(u+\omega_1)\bigr]
\end{aligned}
\]

and by (6) we have

\[
\begin{aligned}
d\bigl[\log T(u) - \log T(u+\omega_2)\bigr] &= 2\pi i\,a_2,\\
d\bigl[\log T(u) - \log T(u+\omega_1)\bigr] &= 2\pi i\,a_1.
\end{aligned}
\]

From this there results

\weq{10}{a_2\omega_1 - a_1\omega_2 = m.}

If we denote further by $\alpha_1$, $\alpha_2$, $\ldots$, $\alpha_m$ the zero points of a $T$-function in the interior of a period parallelogram, we obtain from \S\,15, 7.

\[
2\pi i \Sigma\alpha = \int u\,d\log Tu,
\]

if the integral is again extended over the boundary of the parallelogram. But we have

\[
\begin{aligned}
\int u\,d\log Tu &= \int_0^{\omega_1} \bigl[u\,d\log Tu - (u+\omega_2)\,d\log T(u+\omega_2)\bigr]\\
&\quad - \int_0^{\omega_2} \bigl[u\,d\log Tu - (u+\omega_1)\,d\log T(u+\omega_1)\bigr],
\end{aligned}
\]

and the first of these two integrals is, by (6),

\[
\begin{aligned}
&-\omega_2\int_0^{\omega_1} d\log T(u) + 2\pi i\,a_2\int_0^{\omega_1} (u+\omega_2)\,du\\
&= -\omega_2\bigl[\log T(\omega_1) - \log T(0)\bigr] + \pi i\,a_2\omega_1(\omega_1+2\omega_2)\\
&= \pi i\,\omega_2(a_1\omega_1+b_1) + \pi i\,a_2(\omega_1^2+2\omega_1\omega_2) + 2\pi i\,N_2\omega_2,
\end{aligned}
\]

in which $N_2$ is (because of the many-valuedness of the logarithm) an integer not more closely determined. In the same way there results for the second of the integrals:

\[
-\pi i\,\omega_1(a_2\omega_2+b_2) - \pi i\,a_1(\omega_2^2+2\omega_1\omega_2) + 2\pi i\,N_1\omega_1,
\]

and consequently (written as a congruence)

\weq{11}{\Sigma\alpha \equiv \frac{1}{2}(b_1\omega_2 - b_2\omega_1) + \frac{m}{2}(\omega_1+\omega_2).}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 85 =====
% !PRINTED 64
\weberpage{64}
This sum, or rather the totality of the numbers congruent to it with respect to the modulus $(\omega_1, \omega_2)$, is called the \gesperrt{character} of the $T$-function.

The character of the function $T$ does not change if $T$ is replaced by one of the functions $LT$ (by 8.). One can therefore, following 5., also represent the character in the form:
\weq{12}{\Sigma\alpha \equiv \frac{1}{2}(g_1\omega_2 - g_2\omega_1) + \frac{m}{2}(\omega_1+\omega_2),}
in which $g_1$, $g_2$ are \gesperrt{real}. These real numbers are determined by the character up to multiples of 2, and can take any value between 0 and 2. The symbol $(g_1, g_2)$ is called the \gesperrt{characteristic} of the $T$-function. From the characteristic the character of the $T$-function is determined by (12).

If $\gamma$ is the character of a function $T(u)$ of order $m$, and $v$ is an arbitrary constant, then $T(u+v)$ has the character
\[
\gamma' \equiv \gamma - vm.
\]
\gesperrt{Accordingly, when $m > 0$, the different characters can be reduced to one another.}

With the help of equation (10) the two equations (6) can be combined into a single general one:

If in the first equation (6) one repeatedly changes $u$ into $u + \omega_1$, one obtains the system:
\[
\begin{aligned}
T(u+\omega_1) &= e^{-\pi i[a_1(2u+\omega_1)+b_1]}T(u),\\
T(u+2\omega_1) &= e^{-\pi i[a_1(2u+3\omega_1)+b_1]}T(u+\omega_1),\\
&\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\\
T(u+n_1\omega_1) &= e^{-\pi i[a_1(2u+(2n_1-1)\omega_1)+b_1]}T[u+(n_1-1)\omega_1],
\end{aligned}
\]
and by multiplication of all these formulae:
\weq{13}{T(u+n_1\omega_1) = e^{-\pi i[a_1(2n_1u+n_1^2\omega_1)+n_1b_1]}T(u).}
This formula has been derived in the first instance for a positive integer $n_1$. But if one replaces $u$ in it by $u - n_1\omega_1$, its correctness follows for negative $n_1$ as well.

In the same way one obtains:
\weq{14}{T(u+n_2\omega_2) = e^{-\pi i[a_2(2n_2u+n_2^2\omega_2)+n_2b_2]}T(u),}
and if in this formula one changes $u$ into $u + n_1\omega_1$ and applies (13) again:
\weq{15}{\begin{aligned}
&T(u+n_1\omega_1+n_2\omega_2)\\
&= e^{-\pi i[2(a_1n_1+a_2n_2)u+2a_2n_1n_2\omega_1+a_1n_1^2\omega_1+a_2n_2^2\omega_2+n_1b_1+n_2b_2]}T(u).
\end{aligned}}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 86 =====
% !PRINTED 65
\weberpage{65}
But by (10) we have
\[
2a_2n_1n_2\omega_1 = a_1n_1n_2\omega_1 + a_2n_1n_2\omega_2 + mn_1n_2,
\]
and accordingly this last formula becomes:
\weq{16}{\begin{aligned}
&T(u+n_1\omega_1+n_2\omega_2)\\
&= e^{-\pi i[(n_1a_1+n_2a_2)(2u+n_1\omega_1+n_2\omega_2)+\pi i(b_1n_1+b_2n_2+mn_1n_2)]}T(u).
\end{aligned}}
% [sic] German source includes a nested \pi i factor in the final bracket.
And here $n_1$ and $n_2$ are arbitrary positive or negative integers.

If two $T$-functions of orders $m$ and $m'$, with the characters $\gamma$, $\gamma'$, are multiplied together, there arises a new $T$-function whose order is $m+m'$ and whose character is $\gamma+\gamma'$. If $(g_1, g_2)$ and $(g_1', g_2')$ are the characteristics of the two factors, then $(g_1+g_1', g_2+g_2')$ is the characteristic of the product.

\begin{center}
\textbf{\S\,18. \gesperrt{Relations between related $T$-Functions.}}
\end{center}

Two $T$-functions with the same periods, the same order and the same character we shall call \gesperrt{related}. If $T'(u)$ is a $T$-function related to $T(u)$, and if $a_1'$, $a_2'$, $b_1'$, $b_2'$ have the same meaning for $T'$ as $a_1$, $a_2$, $b_1$, $b_2$ have for $T$, then in consequence of the assumed relationship [§\,17, (10), (11)]:
\weq{1}{a_1'\omega_2 - a_2'\omega_1 = a_1\omega_2 - a_2\omega_1,}
\weq{2}{b_1'\omega_2 - b_2'\omega_1 = b_1\omega_2 - b_2\omega_1 + 2n_1\omega_2 - 2n_2\omega_1,}
where $n_1$, $n_2$ are integers.

Accordingly $\lambda$ and $\mu$ can be determined by § 17, (9) in such a way that the periodicity factors of the function
\[
e^{-\pi i(\lambda u^2+\mu u)}T(u)
\]
become the same as those of the function $T'(u)$, and hence we have the theorem:

1. \gesperrt{Related $T$-functions can, by the addition of a $T$-function of order zero:}
\[
L = Ce^{-\pi i(\lambda u^2+\mu u)}
\]
\gesperrt{as a factor, be given the same periodicity factors.}

Further, from the equality of the characters there follows immediately:

2. \gesperrt{If related $T$-functions of order $m$ have $m-1$ common zero points in the period parallelogram, then they have the $m$th in common as well;} and from this:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 87 =====
% !PRINTED 66
\weberpage{66}
%<<CONT
3. \gesperrt{Between at most $m+1$ related $T$-functions of order $m$, $T, T_1, \ldots, T_m$, there exists an identical equation of the form}
\[
LT + L_1T_1 + \cdots + L_mT_m = 0.
\]
For if this relation does not already hold for $L=0$, then among the constants available in $L_1, L_2, \ldots, L_m$ one can first determine $\lambda_1, \lambda_2 \ldots, \lambda_m, \mu_1, \mu_2 \ldots, \mu_m$ in such a way that all the products $L_1T_1, L_2T_2, \ldots, L_mT_m$ receive the same periodicity factors, and then the $C_1, C_2, \ldots, C_m$ in such a way that $m-1$ of the zero points of the function $L_1T_1+L_2T_2+\cdots+L_mT_m$, and consequently all of them, coincide with the zero points of the function $T$. From this, however, it follows that the ratio of $L_1T_1+L_2T_2+\cdots+L_mT_m$ to $T$ is equal to a $T^0$-function $-L$, which is what was to be proved.

4. \gesperrt{The quotients of related $T$-functions can be transformed into doubly periodic functions by the addition of a factor $L$.}

5. \gesperrt{If we assume the existence of a $T$-function of the first order $t(u)$, then every $T$-function of order $m$ can be derived from it.}

For let $\gamma$ be the character of $t(u)$, and let $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_m$ be arbitrarily given values. Then the function
\[
t(u-\alpha_i+\gamma) = t_i(u), \qquad i = 1, 2 \ldots m
\]
vanishes at the point $\alpha_i$ and at all points congruent to $\alpha_i$, but at no other.

The product
\[
T(u) = t_1(u)t_2(u) \ldots t_m(u)
\]
is therefore a $T$-function of order $m$ with the arbitrarily given zero points $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_m$.

6. \gesperrt{From this it can easily be proved that every doubly periodic function which has only a finite number of points of discontinuity in a period parallelogram can be represented as the quotient of two $T$-functions.}

For let $\varphi(u)$ be a doubly periodic function with the periods $\omega_1, \omega_2$ and the points of discontinuity $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_m$, which may also in part coincide in points of discontinuity of higher order.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 88 =====
% !PRINTED 67
\weberpage{67}
If, according to 5., one determines a function $T(u)$ with the zero points $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_m$, then:
\[
T(u)\varphi(u) = T_1(u)
\]
is a $T$-function of order $m$, and
\[
\varphi(u) = \frac{T_1(u)}{T(u)} \qquad \text{q.\,e.\,d.}
\]
The functions $T(u)$, $T_1(u)$ are \gesperrt{related}, since they have the same periodicity factors and therefore also the same characteristic.

The zero points of $T_1(u)$ are at the same time the zero points of $\varphi(u)$, and the sum of these \gesperrt{zero values} is therefore congruent with \gesperrt{the sum of the values of discontinuity}.

\begin{center}
\textbf{\S\,19. $T$-Functions of the First Order.}
\end{center}

We now proceed to determine more closely the $T$-functions of the first order, which we denote by $t(u)$, and from which, as we have seen, the remaining $T$-functions can be derived.

From 3. of the preceding section it follows that two $t$-functions of the same characteristic differ from one another only by a factor of the form
\[
Ce^{-\pi i(\lambda u^2+\mu u)}
\]
and we now wish, by an extension of the definition, to determine this factor still more closely.

This is to be done — which by § 17, (9) is possible without restriction of generality — in such a way that in the periodicity factors
\[
a_1 = 0, \quad b_1 = g_1, \quad b_2 = g_2
\]
holds, where $(g_1, g_2)$ is the characteristic; on account of the relation
\[
a_2\omega_1 - a_1\omega_2 = 1
\]
we then have
\[
a_2 = \frac{1}{\omega_1},
\]
and the conditions for this $t$-function then read (§ 17, 1.):
\weq{1}{\begin{aligned}
t(u+\omega_1) &= e^{-\pi i g_1}t(u),\\
t(u+\omega_2) &= e^{-\pi i \frac{2u+\omega_2}{\omega_1}}e^{-\pi i g_2}t(u),
\end{aligned}}
and by this the function $t(u)$ is determined up to a factor independent of $u$. In order to determine this factor still more closely, we
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 89 =====
% !PRINTED 68
\weberpage{68}
%<<CONT
determine, we take into view the dependence of the function $t$ upon
$\omega_1, \omega_2$ as well, and, regarding $g_1, g_2$ as given numbers
independent of $\omega_1, \omega_2$, we denote it by
$t(u, \omega_1, \omega_2)$. It then appears that, if $h$ is an arbitrary
factor,
\[
t(h\,u,\ h\,\omega_1,\ h\,\omega_2)
\]
likewise satisfies the conditions (1), and that accordingly

\weq{2}{\frac{t(hu,\ h\omega_1,\ h\omega_2)}{t(u,\ \omega_1,\ \omega_2)} = f(\omega_1,\ \omega_2)}

is independent of $u$.

But the function $f(\omega_1, \omega_2)$ can always be put into the
form:
\[
f(\omega_1,\ \omega_2) = \frac{\varphi(h\omega_1,\ h\omega_2)}{\varphi(\omega_1,\ \omega_2)};
\]
one has only to put, if $t(u)$ does not vanish for $u = 0$:
\[
\varphi(\omega_1,\ \omega_2) = t(0,\ \omega_1,\ \omega_2),
\]
and, if $t(0) = 0$, say
\[
\varphi(\omega_1,\ \omega_2) = \omega_1\, t'(0,\ \omega_1,\ \omega_2)
\]
where $t'$ denotes the derivative of $t$ with respect to $u$. If, then,
one now denotes

\weq{3}{\frac{t(u,\ \omega_1,\ \omega_2)}{\varphi(\omega_1,\ \omega_2)}}

again by $t(u, \omega_1, \omega_2)$, one may add to the conditions (1)
the further one that for an arbitrary $h$

\weq{4}{t(u,\ \omega_1,\ \omega_2) = t(hu,\ h\omega_1\ h\omega_2).} % [sic] -- no comma between $h\omega_1$ and $h\omega_2$, as printed in the original

The function $t$ thus depends now upon only two variables, namely upon
the ratios $u : \omega_1 : \omega_2$. In (4) we put
\[
h = \frac{1}{\omega_1},\quad \frac{u}{\omega_1} = v,\quad \frac{\omega_2}{\omega_1} = \omega,
\]
and obtain

\weq{5}{t(u,\ \omega_1,\ \omega_2) = t\left(\frac{u}{\omega_1},\ 1,\ \frac{\omega_2}{\omega_1}\right) = \vartheta(v, \omega),}

wherein $\vartheta$ is a new function symbol.

In this way, then, a new function $\vartheta(v)$ is defined, of only
two variables $v, \omega$, the first of which is unrestrictedly
variable, while $\omega$, by the assumption made in \S\,16, has a
\gesperrt{positive imaginary} part; $v$ is called the \gesperrt{argument},
$\omega$ the \gesperrt{modulus} of the $\vartheta$-function.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 90 =====
% !PRINTED 69
\weberpage{69}

\begin{center}
\S\,20. \gesperrt{The $\vartheta$-Function.}
\end{center}

The function $\vartheta(v)$ is an \gesperrt{integral} function of $v$ which
satisfies the conditions:

\weq{1}{\begin{aligned}
\vartheta(v + 1) &= e^{-\pi i g_1}\vartheta(v),\\
\vartheta(v + \omega) &= e^{-\pi i(2v+\omega)} e^{-\pi i g_2}\vartheta(v),
\end{aligned}}

\gesperrt{and it is thereby determined up to a factor independent of $v$.}
It is therefore contained among the $t$-functions as a special
case, while on the other hand the general $t$-function can be
expressed by the $\vartheta$-function in the following manner:
\[
t(u) = C\, e^{-\pi i(\lambda u^2 + \mu u)}\, \vartheta\!\left(\frac{u}{\omega_1},\ \frac{\omega_2}{\omega_1}\right),
\]
in which $C, \lambda, \mu$ are arbitrary quantities, either constant or
dependent on $\omega_1, \omega_2$.

The function $\vartheta$ depends further on the numbers $g_1, g_2$
occurring in the characteristic, and if a notation for
this dependence is required, then for $\vartheta(v, \omega)$ we shall set:
\[
\vartheta_{g_1,\, g_2}(v, \omega)
\]
where $g_1, g_2$ may be arbitrary numbers.
According to what has gone before, it suffices to assume them real and between 0
and 2.

Corresponding to the $T$-functions of higher order, we shall
also introduce $\Theta$-functions of the $m$th order, and understand
by these an integral function of $v$ which satisfies the conditions:

\weq{2}{\begin{aligned}
\Theta(v + 1) &= e^{-\pi i g_1}\Theta(v)\\
\Theta(v + \omega) &= e^{-m\pi i(2v+\omega)} e^{-\pi i g_2}\Theta(v).
\end{aligned}}

Here too the characteristic $g_1, g_2$ can be taken up into the
notation:
\[
\Theta_{g_1,\, g_2}(v, \omega).
\]

These functions are contained as special cases among the $T$-functions,
and one can form general $T$-functions in the
following manner:

\weq{3}{C\, e^{-\pi i(\lambda u^2 + \mu u)}\, \Theta\!\left(\frac{u}{\omega_1},\ \frac{\omega_2}{\omega_1}\right).}

There follows therefore from \S\,18, 3. the \gesperrt{fundamental theorem} for
the $\Theta$-functions, which we state as follows:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 91 =====
% !PRINTED 70
\weberpage{70}
%<<CONT

If we call $\Theta$-functions with the same periods, of the same
order and the same characteristic, \gesperrt{related}, and if we further
designate a system of functions as \gesperrt{linearly dependent}
or \gesperrt{independent} according as a homogeneous linear relation
with constant (not all vanishing) coefficients
does or does not subsist between these functions, then the
theorem holds:

\gesperrt{$m + 1$ related $\Theta$-functions of order $m$ are
always linearly dependent;}

or:

\gesperrt{From $m$ linearly independent related $\Theta$-functions
 of order $m$ every other related
$\Theta$-function can be composed linearly (with constant
coefficients).}

This theorem is of the most fundamental importance for the
considerations that follow; from it there results, by \S\,18, 3.,
that every $T$-function of order $m$ can be composed, with the use of formula (3),
from $m$ linearly independent $\Theta$-functions.

By \S\,17, (11), the sum of the $m$ argument values for
which the function $\Theta_{g_1,\, g_2}(v)$ vanishes in the period parallelogram
is congruent, with respect to the modulus $(1, \omega)$, to
\[
m\,\frac{1+\omega}{2} + \frac{g_1\omega - g_2}{2}.
\]

The definition of the function $\vartheta$ given up to now leaves
undetermined a factor which may be a function of $\omega$. But
by an addition to the definition we can determine this factor
still more closely.

If the defining equations (1) are differentiated twice with respect to $v$
and once with respect to $\omega$, regarding $g_1, g_2$ as constant,
then a simple calculation shows that the function
\[
\frac{\partial^2 \vartheta(v,\omega)}{\partial v^2} - 4\pi i\,\frac{\partial \vartheta(v,\omega)}{\partial \omega}
\]
itself satisfies the conditions (1) and therefore has the form
\[
\varphi(\omega)\,\vartheta(v,\omega)
\]
in which $\varphi(\omega)$ is constant with respect to $v$, and hence a function of $\omega$
alone. If one now
\[
e^{-\frac{1}{4\pi i}\int \varphi(\omega)\,d\omega}\ \vartheta(v,\omega)
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 92 =====
% !PRINTED 71
\weberpage{71}
%<<CONT
equal to a new $\vartheta$, there results for the latter the partial
differential equation

\weq{4}{\frac{\partial^2 \vartheta(v,\omega)}{\partial v^2} - 4\pi i\,\frac{\partial \vartheta(v,\omega)}{\partial \omega} = 0,}

\gesperrt{and by (1) and (4) the function $\vartheta$ is now defined up to a
factor that is independent of $v$ and $\omega$ and therefore still
depends only on $g_1, g_2$.}

\begin{center}
\S\,21.\quad\gesperrt{The Theta Functions of Different Characteristics.}

\gesperrt{Principal Characteristics.}
\end{center}

Before we go on to determine the factor in the $\vartheta$-functions
that still remains and is independent of $v$ and $\omega$, we now wish
to reduce the different characteristics to one another, which
by \S\,17 is always possible. If we denote by
$\vartheta(v)$ the $\vartheta$-function belonging to the characteristic $(0, 0)$, then
\[
\Phi(v,\omega) = e^{-\pi i g_1 v}\, \vartheta\!\left(v - \frac{g_1\omega - g_2}{2}\right)
\]
is a function satisfying the conditions (1) \S 20. But now, in
view of the differential equation (4):
\[
\frac{\partial^2 \Phi}{\partial v^2} - 4\pi i\,\frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial \omega} = -\pi^2 g_1^2\,\Phi,
\]
and so, if we put

\weq{1}{\vartheta_{g_1,\, g_2}(v) = e^{\frac{\pi i \omega g_1^2}{4} - \pi i g_1 v + \frac{g_1 g_2 \pi i}{2}}\ \vartheta\!\left(v - \frac{g_1\omega - g_2}{2}\right)}

\gesperrt{then the differential equation (4) \S 20 is satisfied by all
these functions. In this way, then, the functions
 $\vartheta_{g_1,\, g_2}$ are determined up to a numerical factor common to
them all.}

From formula (1) a more general one can be derived by
replacing $v$ by $v - \dfrac{g_1'\omega - g_2'}{2}$. One obtains in this way

\weq{2}{\vartheta_{g_1,\, g_2}\!\left(v - \frac{g_1'\omega - g_2'}{2}\right)
= e^{-\frac{\pi i \omega}{4}g_1'^2 + \pi i g_1' v - \pi i g_1 g_2' - \frac{\pi i}{2}g_1'(g_2+g_2')}\ \vartheta_{g_1+g_1',\, g_2+g_2'}(v).}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 93 =====
% !PRINTED 72
\weberpage{72}

From (2) there follows further, with the use of (1) § 20, if one
puts $g_1' = 2$, $g_2' = 0$, or $g_1' = 0$, $g_2' = 2$:

\weq{3}{
\begin{aligned}
\vartheta_{g_1+2,\,g_2}(v) &= e^{2\pi i g_2}\,\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(v),\\
\vartheta_{g_1,\,g_2+2}(v) &= e^{\pi i g_1}\,\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(v),
\end{aligned}
}

and thus by (2) the periodicity of the functions
$\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(v)$ is at the same time completely expressed. For example, if
$\mu$ and $\nu$ are integers, there follows:

\weq{4}{
\vartheta_{00}\!\left(v - \frac{(2\nu-1)\,\omega + 2\mu - 1}{2}\right)
= (-1)^{\nu+1}\, i\, e^{\frac{-\pi i \omega}{4}(2\nu-1)^2}\, e^{\pi i (2\nu-1) v}\, \vartheta_{11}(v).
}

\weq{5}{
\vartheta_{11}(v - \nu\omega - \mu) = (-1)^{\mu+\nu}\, e^{-\pi i \omega \nu^2}\, e^{2\pi i \nu v}\, \vartheta_{11}(v).
}

Formula (2) is valid for entirely arbitrary, even complex
values of $g_1, g_2$.

If in the defining formulae of the $\vartheta$-functions
[§ 20, (1)] one replaces $v$ by $-v-1$, and by $-v-\omega$, and further $g_1, g_2$ by
$-g_1, -g_2$, it appears that $\vartheta_{-g_1,-g_2}(-v)$ satisfies the same
 conditions as $\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(v)$, and that accordingly

\[
\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(v),\quad \vartheta_{-g_1,-g_2}(-v)
\]

are identical up to a constant factor; in particular, therefore, as follows from $v = 0$:

\[
\vartheta_{0,0}(v) = \vartheta_{0,0}(-v),
\]

and thereupon formula (1) yields, if one replaces $v, g_1, g_2$ by
$-v, -g_1, -g_2$:

\weq{6}{
\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(v) = \vartheta_{-g_1,-g_2}(-v).
}

If the elements $g_1, g_2$ are integers, then $(g_1, g_2)$ is called
a \gesperrt{principal characteristic}. There are four essentially
different ones, namely:

\[
(0,0),\quad (0,1),\quad (1,0),\quad (1,1),
\]

and accordingly also four essentially different principal $\vartheta$-functions:

\weq{7}{
\vartheta_{00}(v),\quad \vartheta_{01}(v),\quad \vartheta_{10}(v),\quad \vartheta_{11}(v),
}

of which the first is also denoted by $\vartheta(v)$.

\gesperrt{In what follows, by characteristics and
$\vartheta$-functions only principal characteristics and
principal functions will be understood.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 94 =====
% !PRINTED 73
\weberpage{73}

Formula (2), applied to this system of functions, yields the
following, frequently used table:

\weq{8}{
\begin{aligned}
\vartheta_{00}(v) &= \vartheta_{01}\!\left(v+\tfrac{1}{2}\right) = \varepsilon\,\vartheta_{10}\!\left(v+\tfrac{\omega}{2}\right) = \varepsilon\,\vartheta_{11}\!\left(v+\tfrac{1+\omega}{2}\right),\\
\vartheta_{01}(v) &= \vartheta_{00}\!\left(v+\tfrac{1}{2}\right) = -i\varepsilon\,\vartheta_{11}\!\left(v+\tfrac{\omega}{2}\right) = i\varepsilon\,\vartheta_{10}\!\left(v+\tfrac{1+\omega}{2}\right),\\
\vartheta_{10}(v) &= \vartheta_{11}\!\left(v+\tfrac{1}{2}\right) = \varepsilon\,\vartheta_{00}\!\left(v+\tfrac{\omega}{2}\right) = \varepsilon\,\vartheta_{01}\!\left(v+\tfrac{1+\omega}{2}\right),\\
\vartheta_{11}(v) &= -\vartheta_{10}\!\left(v+\tfrac{1}{2}\right) = -i\varepsilon\,\vartheta_{01}\!\left(v+\tfrac{\omega}{2}\right) = -i\varepsilon\,\vartheta_{11}\!\left(v+\tfrac{1+\omega}{2}\right),
\end{aligned}
}

in which, for brevity,

\[
\varepsilon = e^{\frac{\pi i \omega}{4} + \pi i v}
\]

has been set.

According to (3), (4) we have

\weq{9}{
\begin{aligned}
\vartheta_{00}(-v) &= \vartheta_{00}(v), & \vartheta_{01}(-v) &= \vartheta_{01}(v),\\
\vartheta_{10}(-v) &= \vartheta_{10}(v), & \vartheta_{11}(-v) &= -\vartheta_{11}(v),
\end{aligned}
}

that is, \gesperrt{$\vartheta_{00}(v)$, $\vartheta_{01}(v)$, $\vartheta_{10}(v)$ are even functions,
$\vartheta_{11}(v)$ is an odd function.}

According to § 17 (12) the four functions (7) vanish, respectively,
for the following values of the argument

\[
\frac{1+\omega}{2},\quad \frac{\omega}{2},\quad \frac{1}{2},\quad 0,
\]

hence for certain half periods. Of importance are the values which
all the functions (7) assume for these values of the argument, and
these can be reduced, by means of the table (8), to the three

\[
\vartheta_{00}(0) = \vartheta_{00},\quad \vartheta_{01}(0) = \vartheta_{01},\quad \vartheta_{10}(0) = \vartheta_{10}
\]

One thus obtains from (8) the following system of
formulae:

\weq{10}{
\begin{aligned}
\vartheta_{00} &= \vartheta_{01}\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right) = \varepsilon_0\,\vartheta_{10}\!\left(\tfrac{\omega}{2}\right) = \varepsilon_0\,\vartheta_{11}\!\left(\tfrac{1+\omega}{2}\right),\\
\vartheta_{01} &= \vartheta_{00}\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right) = -i\varepsilon_0\,\vartheta_{11}\!\left(\tfrac{\omega}{2}\right) = i\varepsilon_0\,\vartheta_{10}\!\left(\tfrac{1+\omega}{2}\right),\\
\vartheta_{10} &= \vartheta_{11}\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right) = \varepsilon_0\,\vartheta_{00}\!\left(\tfrac{\omega}{2}\right) = \varepsilon_0\,\vartheta_{01}\!\left(\tfrac{1+\omega}{2}\right),
\end{aligned}
}
% [sic] German source repeats theta_11 at the far right of row four in (8).
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 95 =====
% !PRINTED 74
\weberpage{74}

%<<CONT
in which

\[
\varepsilon_0 = e^{\frac{\pi i \omega}{4}}
\]

and

\weq{11}{
\vartheta_{11}(0) = 0,\quad \vartheta_{10}\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right) = 0,\quad \vartheta_{01}\!\left(\tfrac{\omega}{2}\right) = 0,\quad \vartheta_{00}\!\left(\tfrac{1+\omega}{2}\right) = 0.
}

\gesperrt{The squares of the functions (7):}

\weq{12}{
\vartheta_{00}^2(v),\quad \vartheta_{01}^2(v),\quad \vartheta_{10}^2(v),\quad \vartheta_{11}^2(v)
}

are $\Theta_{00}$-functions of the second order, and consequently there
exist two linear relations between them. If we take these relations
 in the form:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\vartheta_{10}^2(v) &= A\,\vartheta_{01}^2(v) + B\,\vartheta_{11}^2(v),\\
\vartheta_{00}^2(v) &= A'\vartheta_{01}^2(v) + B'\vartheta_{11}^2(v),
\end{aligned}
\]

then one can easily determine the coefficients on the basis of formulae (10), (11),
by setting $v = 0$ and $v = \dfrac{\omega}{2}$. In this way one
obtains

\weq{13}{
\begin{aligned}
\vartheta_{01}^2\,\vartheta_{10}^2(v) &= \vartheta_{10}^2\,\vartheta_{01}^2(v) - \vartheta_{00}^2\,\vartheta_{11}^2(v),\\
\vartheta_{01}^2\,\vartheta_{00}^2(v) &= \vartheta_{00}^2\,\vartheta_{01}^2(v) - \vartheta_{10}^2\,\vartheta_{11}^2(v),
\end{aligned}
}

and from this further, on setting $v = \tfrac{1}{2}$:

\weq{14}{
\vartheta_{00}^4 = \vartheta_{01}^4 + \vartheta_{10}^4.
}

By means of any two of the squares (12) all functions $\Theta_{00}$ of
the second order can be represented linearly; but the remaining
$\Theta$-functions of the second order can also be composed from the
functions $\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}$, for one obtains for each
characteristic two linearly independent products, of which the one is
an even and the other an odd function, namely:

\weq{15}{
\begin{aligned}
\vartheta_{00}(v)\,\vartheta_{01}(v), &\quad \vartheta_{10}(v)\,\vartheta_{11}(v) & &\text{Characteristic } (0,1)\\
\vartheta_{00}(v)\,\vartheta_{10}(v), &\quad \vartheta_{01}(v)\,\vartheta_{11}(v) & &\text{„}\quad (1,0)\\
\vartheta_{10}(v)\,\vartheta_{01}(v), &\quad \vartheta_{00}(v)\,\vartheta_{11}(v) & &\text{„}\quad (1,1)
\end{aligned}
}

According to the same principle all $\Theta$-functions of arbitrary
order and of arbitrary principal characteristic can now be formed from
the functions $\vartheta$. To establish this, we denote by
$\Theta_0, \Theta_1$ any two of the $\vartheta$-squares (12), and by $F^{(n)}(\Theta_0,\Theta_1)$ an
integral rational and homogeneous function of order $n$ of the two
arguments $\Theta_0, \Theta_1$. In accordance with this one obtains for the $\Theta$-functions
of order $m$, $\Theta^{(m)}(v)$, the following expressions:

%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 96 =====
% !PRINTED 75
\weberpage{75}
%<<CONT

$m$ even \qquad \textbf{even functions}

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Theta_{00}^{(m)}(v) &= F^{\left(\frac{m}{2}\right)}(\Theta_0,\Theta_1)\\
\Theta_{01}^{(m)}(v) &= \vartheta_{00}(v)\,\vartheta_{01}(v)\,F^{\left(\frac{m}{2}-1\right)}(\Theta_0,\Theta_1)\\
\Theta_{10}^{(m)}(v) &= \vartheta_{00}(v)\,\vartheta_{10}(v)\,F^{\left(\frac{m}{2}-1\right)}(\Theta_0,\Theta_1)\\
\Theta_{11}^{(m)}(v) &= \vartheta_{10}(v)\,\vartheta_{01}(v)\,F^{\left(\frac{m}{2}-1\right)}(\Theta_0,\Theta_1)
\end{aligned}
\]

\weq{16}{
\begin{aligned}
&\text{\textbf{odd functions}}\\
\Theta_{00}^{(m)}(v) &= \vartheta_{00}(v)\,\vartheta_{10}(v)\,\vartheta_{01}(v)\,\vartheta_{11}(v)\,F^{\left(\frac{m-4}{2}\right)}(\Theta_0,\Theta_1)\\
\Theta_{01}^{(m)}(v) &= \vartheta_{10}(v)\,\vartheta_{11}(v)\,F^{\left(\frac{m}{2}-1\right)}(\Theta_0,\Theta_1)\\
\Theta_{10}^{(m)}(v) &= \vartheta_{01}(v)\,\vartheta_{11}(v)\,F^{\left(\frac{m}{2}-1\right)}(\Theta_0,\Theta_1)\\
\Theta_{11}^{(m)}(v) &= \vartheta_{00}(v)\,\vartheta_{11}(v)\,F^{\left(\frac{m}{2}-1\right)}(\Theta_0,\Theta_1)
\end{aligned}
}

$m$ odd \qquad \textbf{even functions}

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Theta_{00}^{(m)}(v) &= \vartheta_{00}(v)\,F^{\left(\frac{m-1}{2}\right)}(\Theta_0,\Theta_1)\\
\Theta_{01}^{(m)}(v) &= \vartheta_{01}(v)\,F^{\left(\frac{m-1}{2}\right)}(\Theta_0,\Theta_1)\\
\Theta_{10}^{(m)}(v) &= \vartheta_{10}(v)\,F^{\left(\frac{m-1}{2}\right)}(\Theta_0,\Theta_1)\\
\Theta_{11}^{(m)}(v) &= \vartheta_{00}(v)\,\vartheta_{01}(v)\,\vartheta_{10}(v)\,F^{\left(\frac{m-3}{2}\right)}(\Theta_0,\Theta_1)
\end{aligned}
\]

\weq{17}{
\begin{aligned}
&\text{\textbf{odd functions}}\\
\Theta_{00}^{(m)}(v) &= \vartheta_{01}(v)\,\vartheta_{10}(v)\,\vartheta_{11}(v)\,F^{\left(\frac{m-3}{2}\right)}(\Theta_0,\Theta_1)\\
\Theta_{01}^{(m)}(v) &= \vartheta_{00}(v)\,\vartheta_{10}(v)\,\vartheta_{11}(v)\,F^{\left(\frac{m-3}{2}\right)}(\Theta_0,\Theta_1)\\
\Theta_{10}^{(m)}(v) &= \vartheta_{00}(v)\,\vartheta_{01}(v)\,\vartheta_{11}(v)\,F^{\left(\frac{m-3}{2}\right)}(\Theta_0,\Theta_1)\\
\Theta_{11}^{(m)}(v) &= \vartheta_{11}(v)\,F^{\left(\frac{m-1}{2}\right)}(\Theta_0,\Theta_1).
\end{aligned}
}

That \gesperrt{all} $\Theta$-functions are representable in this form follows,
on the basis of § 20, from the following three considerations.

1. \gesperrt{Between even and odd functions no linear dependence can
subsist unless a linear dependence already subsists among the
even functions by themselves or among the odd ones by themselves.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 97 =====
% !PRINTED 76
\weberpage{76}

2. Since two of the $\vartheta$-squares (12) do not stand in a constant ratio, there is also no equation of the form $F^{(n)}(\Theta_0,\Theta_1) = 0$.

3. The total number of the constants which, by (16), (17), occur in the even and odd functions belonging to one and the same characteristic is exactly equal to the order $m$.

\begin{center}
\textbf{\S\,22. \gesperrt{The Addition Theorem.}}
\end{center}

If $u$, $v$ are two variables, then the products
\[
\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(u+v)\,\vartheta_{g'_1,g'_2}(u-v)
\]
belong to the $\Theta$-functions of the second order, with the characteristic
\[
(g_1+g'_1,\,g_2+g'_2),
\]
and indeed for each of the two variables $u$, $v$; as functions of $v$ they can therefore be represented linearly by the functions (12) and (15) in \S\,21, so that the variable $u$ occurs in the coefficients. When the characteristic is $(0,0)$, this representation is possible in several ways, since one may choose any two of the functions (12); in the other cases it is possible in only one way. One obtains in this manner 16 formulae, of which, however, 6 are to be derived from the others by mere interchange of $v$ with $-v$, so that only 10 essentially different ones remain. These formulae are derived very easily by first setting them up with indeterminate coefficients and then determining these by putting for $v$ such special values as make one or another of the functions $\vartheta(v)$ vanish. Thus, for example:
\[
\vartheta_{00}(u+v)\,\vartheta_{00}(u-v) = A\,\vartheta_{00}^2(v) + B\,\vartheta_{11}^2(v),
\]
and if one puts $v=0$ and $v=\dfrac{1+\omega}{2}$, then, making use of the formulae of \S\,21, one obtains:
\[
A\,\vartheta_{00}^2 = \vartheta_{00}^2(u), \quad B\,\vartheta_{00}^2 = \vartheta_{11}^2(u),
\]
hence

\weq{1}{\vartheta_{00}^2\,\vartheta_{00}(u+v)\,\vartheta_{00}(u-v) = \vartheta_{00}^2(u)\,\vartheta_{00}^2(v) + \vartheta_{11}^2(u)\,\vartheta_{11}^2(v),}
and if in this one replaces $u$ by
\[
u+\frac{1}{2}, \quad u+\frac{\omega}{2}, \quad u+\frac{1+\omega}{2}
\]
then one forms three further relations, which could also have been derived directly in the same way as (1):
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 98 =====
% !PRINTED 77
\weberpage{77}
%<<CONT
\weq{2}{\vartheta_{01}^2\,\vartheta_{01}(u+v)\,\vartheta_{01}(u-v) = \vartheta_{01}^2(u)\,\vartheta_{01}^2(v) - \vartheta_{11}^2(u)\,\vartheta_{11}^2(v).}
\weq{3}{\vartheta_{10}^2\,\vartheta_{10}(u+v)\,\vartheta_{10}(u-v) = \vartheta_{10}^2(u)\,\vartheta_{10}^2(v) - \vartheta_{11}^2(u)\,\vartheta_{11}^2(v).}
\weq{4}{\vartheta_{01}^2\,\vartheta_{11}(u+v)\,\vartheta_{11}(u-v) = \vartheta_{11}^2(u)\,\vartheta_{01}^2(v) - \vartheta_{01}^2(u)\,\vartheta_{11}^2(v).}

These four equations can, as has already been mentioned, be transformed in manifold ways by applying the formulae (13) of the preceding section. The six formulae that follow have only \gesperrt{one} form. Beginning again with an arbitrary example, we have:
\[
\vartheta_{00}(u+v)\,\vartheta_{11}(u-v) = A\,\vartheta_{01}(v)\,\vartheta_{10}(v) + B\,\vartheta_{00}(v)\,\vartheta_{11}(v),
\]
and if one sets $v=0$:
\[
A\,\vartheta_{01}\vartheta_{10} = \vartheta_{00}(u)\,\vartheta_{11}(u),
\]
from which one obtains $B$ by interchanging $u$ with $v$. In this way the three following formulae are derived:

\weq{5}{\begin{aligned}\vartheta_{01}\vartheta_{10}\,\vartheta_{00}(u+v)\,\vartheta_{11}(u-v)\\ {}= \vartheta_{00}(u)\vartheta_{11}(u)\vartheta_{01}(v)\vartheta_{10}(v) - \vartheta_{01}(u)\vartheta_{10}(u)\vartheta_{00}(v)\vartheta_{11}(v),\end{aligned}}
\weq{6}{\begin{aligned}\vartheta_{00}\vartheta_{01}\,\vartheta_{10}(u+v)\,\vartheta_{11}(u-v)\\ {}= \vartheta_{10}(u)\vartheta_{11}(u)\vartheta_{00}(v)\vartheta_{01}(v) - \vartheta_{00}(u)\vartheta_{01}(u)\vartheta_{10}(v)\vartheta_{11}(v),\end{aligned}}
\weq{7}{\begin{aligned}\vartheta_{00}\vartheta_{10}\,\vartheta_{01}(u+v)\,\vartheta_{11}(u-v)\\ {}= \vartheta_{01}(u)\vartheta_{11}(u)\vartheta_{00}(v)\vartheta_{10}(v) - \vartheta_{00}(u)\vartheta_{10}(u)\vartheta_{01}(v)\vartheta_{11}(v),\end{aligned}}
which can be verified immediately by setting first $u$, then $v=0$. From these the three others follow by increasing $u$ by
\[
\frac{1}{2}, \quad \frac{\omega}{2}, \quad \frac{1}{2}:
\]
% [sic] German source repeats 1/2 as the third shift.
\weq{8}{\begin{aligned}\vartheta_{01}\vartheta_{10}\,\vartheta_{01}(u+v)\,\vartheta_{10}(u-v)\\ {}= \vartheta_{01}(u)\vartheta_{10}(u)\vartheta_{01}(v)\vartheta_{10}(v) + \vartheta_{00}(u)\vartheta_{11}(u)\vartheta_{00}(v)\vartheta_{11}(v),\end{aligned}}
\weq{9}{\begin{aligned}\vartheta_{00}\vartheta_{01}\,\vartheta_{00}(u+v)\,\vartheta_{01}(u-v)\\ {}= \vartheta_{00}(u)\vartheta_{01}(u)\vartheta_{00}(v)\vartheta_{01}(v) - \vartheta_{10}(u)\vartheta_{11}(u)\vartheta_{10}(v)\vartheta_{11}(v),\end{aligned}}
\weq{10}{\begin{aligned}\vartheta_{00}\vartheta_{10}\,\vartheta_{00}(u+v)\,\vartheta_{10}(u-v)\\ {}= \vartheta_{00}(u)\vartheta_{10}(u)\vartheta_{00}(v)\vartheta_{10}(v) + \vartheta_{01}(u)\vartheta_{11}(u)\vartheta_{01}(v)\vartheta_{11}(v).\end{aligned}}

These formulae, whose totality is designated by the name of the addition theorem, admit of generalisation in manifold ways, of which the following may serve as an example.

If $u$, $v$ are two variables, then the four products
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
\vartheta_{00}(u)\,\vartheta_{00}(u+v), & \vartheta_{01}(u)\,\vartheta_{01}(u+v), \\
\vartheta_{10}(u)\,\vartheta_{10}(u+v), & \vartheta_{11}(u)\,\vartheta_{11}(u+v),
\end{array}
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 99 =====
% !PRINTED 78
\weberpage{78}
%<<CONT
