considered as functions of $u$, related $T$-functions of the second order with the same periodicity factors, and hence any three of them are linearly dependent. We therefore have
\[
A\,\vartheta_{00}(u)\,\vartheta_{00}(u+v) + B\,\vartheta_{10}(u)\,\vartheta_{10}(u+v) + C\,\vartheta_{11}(u)\,\vartheta_{11}(u+v) = 0,
\]
from which, for $u=0$, $u=\dfrac{1}{2}$:
\[
\begin{aligned}
A\,\vartheta_{00}\vartheta_{00}(v) + B\,\vartheta_{10}\vartheta_{10}(v) &= 0,\\
A\,\vartheta_{01}\vartheta_{01}(v) + C\,\vartheta_{10}\vartheta_{10}(v) &= 0
\end{aligned}
\]
and from these:

\weq{11}{\begin{aligned}\vartheta_{10}\vartheta_{10}(v)\,\vartheta_{00}(u)\,\vartheta_{00}(u+v) - \vartheta_{00}\vartheta_{00}(v)\,\vartheta_{10}(u)\,\vartheta_{10}(u+v)\\ {}- \vartheta_{01}\vartheta_{01}(v)\,\vartheta_{11}(u)\,\vartheta_{11}(u+v) = 0.\end{aligned}}

In the same way, if $w$ is a third variable, the products contained in the form
\[
\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(u+v)\,\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(u+w), \quad \vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(u)\,\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(u+v+w)
\]
are, considered as functions of $u$, related $T$-functions of the second order with the same periodicity factors, so that between any three of them there exists a linear dependence. The coefficients are determined, as above, by special values of $u$. Thus the system of formulae follows:

\weq{12}{\begin{aligned}\vartheta_{00}\vartheta_{00}(v+w)\,\vartheta_{00}(u+v)\,\vartheta_{00}(u+w)\\ {}= \vartheta_{00}(u)\vartheta_{00}(v)\vartheta_{00}(w)\vartheta_{00}(u+v+w)\\ {}- \vartheta_{11}(u)\vartheta_{11}(v)\vartheta_{11}(w)\vartheta_{11}(u+v+w).\end{aligned}}
\weq{13}{\begin{aligned}\vartheta_{01}\vartheta_{01}(v+w)\,\vartheta_{01}(u+v)\,\vartheta_{01}(u+w)\\ {}= \vartheta_{01}(u)\vartheta_{01}(v)\vartheta_{01}(w)\vartheta_{01}(u+v+w)\\ {}+ \vartheta_{11}(u)\vartheta_{11}(v)\vartheta_{11}(w)\vartheta_{11}(u+v+w).\end{aligned}}
\weq{14}{\begin{aligned}\vartheta_{10}\vartheta_{10}(v+w)\,\vartheta_{10}(u+v)\,\vartheta_{10}(u+w)\\ {}= \vartheta_{10}(u)\vartheta_{10}(v)\vartheta_{10}(w)\vartheta_{10}(u+v+w)\\ {}+ \vartheta_{11}(u)\vartheta_{11}(v)\vartheta_{11}(w)\vartheta_{11}(u+v+w).\end{aligned}}

All these formulae can be regarded as special cases of a general formula which \gesperrt{Jacobi} derived from the series developments and employed as the foundation of the theory of elliptic functions\footnote{Theorie der elliptischen Funktionen, aus den Eigenschaften der Thetareihen abgeleitet. \gesperrt{Jacobis} gesammelte Werke, Bd.\,I, S.\,497.}. This formula can also be obtained in the following way from the concept of the theta functions.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 100 =====
% !PRINTED 79
\weberpage{79}

The four functions

\weq{15}{\vartheta_{00}(2v), \quad \vartheta_{01}(2v), \quad \vartheta_{10}(2v), \quad \vartheta_{11}(2v),}
are $\Theta_{00}$-functions of the fourth order in $v$, and since they are linearly independent, \gesperrt{all} $\Theta_{00}$-functions of the fourth order can be expressed linearly by means of them. But such a function is also the product

\weq{16}{\vartheta(v+a_1)\,\vartheta(v+a_2)\,\vartheta(v+a_3)\,\vartheta(v+a_4),}
provided that the quantities $a$ satisfy the condition

\weq{17}{a_1+a_2+a_3+a_4 = 0}
We therefore obtain, if we denote by $A_1$, $A_2$, $A_3$, $A_4$ constants (with respect to $v$):
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\vartheta(v+a_1)\,\vartheta(v+a_2)\,\vartheta(v+a_3)\,\vartheta(v+a_4) \\
&{}= A_1\,\vartheta_{00}(2v) + A_2\,\vartheta_{01}(2v) + A_3\,\vartheta_{10}(2v) + A_4\,\vartheta_{11}(2v),
\end{aligned}
\]
and from this one obtains, by increasing $v$ by $\frac{1}{2}(g_1\omega+g_2)$, four formulae:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(v+a_1)\,\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(v+a_2)\,\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(v+a_3)\,\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(v+a_4) \\
&{}= A_1\,\vartheta_{00}(2v) + (-1)^{g_2}A_2\,\vartheta_{01}(2v) + (-1)^{g_1}A_3\,\vartheta_{10}(2v) \\
&\quad{}+ (-1)^{g_1+g_2}A_4\,\vartheta_{11}(2v).
\end{aligned}
\]
If these four formulae are added, it follows that:

\weq{18}{\begin{aligned}4A_1\,\vartheta_{00}(2v)\\ {}= \sum^{g_1,g_2}\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(v+a_1)\,\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(v+a_2)\,\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(v+a_3)\,\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(v+a_4),\end{aligned}}
where in the sum all combinations of 0 and 1 are to be put for $g_1$ and $g_2$.

We now introduce a somewhat different notation, putting:
\[
v+a_1 = v'_1, \quad v+a_2 = v'_2, \quad v+a_3 = v'_3, \quad v+a_4 = v'_4,
\]
hence, on account of (17),
\[
4v = v'_1 + v'_2 + v'_3 + v'_4,
\]
and we now define the four quantities $v_1$, $v_2$, $v_3$, $v_4$ by the equations

\weq{19}{\begin{aligned}
v_1 &= \tfrac{1}{2}(v'_1+v'_2+v'_3+v'_4), \\
v_2 &= \tfrac{1}{2}(v'_1+v'_2-v'_3-v'_4), \\
v_3 &= \tfrac{1}{2}(v'_1-v'_2+v'_3-v'_4), \\
v_4 &= \tfrac{1}{2}(v'_1-v'_2-v'_3+v'_4).
\end{aligned}}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 101 =====
% !PRINTED 80
\weberpage{80}

From this, however, one obtains:

\weq{20}{
\begin{aligned}
v_1' &= \tfrac{1}{2}(v_1+v_2+v_3+v_4), & a_1 &= \tfrac{1}{2}(\phantom{-}v_2+v_3+v_4),\\
v_2' &= \tfrac{1}{2}(v_1+v_2-v_3-v_4), & a_2 &= \tfrac{1}{2}(\phantom{-}v_2-v_3-v_4),\\
v_3' &= \tfrac{1}{2}(v_1-v_2+v_3-v_4), & a_3 &= \tfrac{1}{2}(-v_2+v_3-v_4),\\
v_4' &= \tfrac{1}{2}(v_1-v_2-v_3+v_4), & a_4 &= \tfrac{1}{2}(-v_2-v_3+v_4),
\end{aligned}
}

and formula (18) then gives:
\[
4\,A_1\,\vartheta_{00}(v_1) = \sum \vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(v_1')\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(v_2')\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(v_3')\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(v_4'),
\]
in which now either the $v_i$ or the $v_i'$ may be regarded as independent variables.

If one regards the $v_i$ as independent variables, then in this formula $A_1$ is independent of $v_1$, but still depends on $v_2$, $v_3$, $v_4$. If we therefore set $4\,A_1 = c\,\vartheta_{00}(v_2)\vartheta_{00}(v_3)\vartheta_{00}(v_4)$, there results
\[
c\,\vartheta_{00}(v_1)\vartheta_{00}(v_2)\vartheta_{00}(v_3)\vartheta_{00}(v_4)
= \sum \vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(v_1')\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(v_2')\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(v_3')\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(v_4'),
\]
and in this $c$ is in any case independent of $v_1$. But since the right-hand side of this formula remains unchanged under arbitrary permutations of $v_1, v_2, v_3, v_4$, $c$ is independent of all the $v_i$, and one obtains its value by setting all $v_i = 0$:
\[
c\,\vartheta_{00}^4 = \vartheta_{00}^4 + \vartheta_{01}^4 + \vartheta_{10}^4,
\]
from which, by \S\,21, (14), it follows that $c=2$.

We thus have the formula:
\[
2\,\vartheta_{00}(v_1)\vartheta_{00}(v_2)\vartheta_{00}(v_3)\vartheta_{00}(v_4)
= \sum\limits^{g_1,g_2} \vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(v_1')\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(v_2')\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(v_3')\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(v_4').
\]

If in it each of the variables $v_1, v_2, v_3, v_4$ is increased by a half period $-\tfrac{1}{2}(g_1'\omega_1 - g_2')$, then $v_1'$ is increased by a whole period $-(g_1'\omega_1 - g_2')$, while $v_2', v_3', v_4'$ remain unchanged, and accordingly one obtains, with the help of \S\,21, (2) and (3), a system of four formulae:

\weq{21}{
\begin{aligned}
&2\,\vartheta_{g_1'g_2'}(v_1)\vartheta_{g_1',g_2'}(v_2)\vartheta_{g_1',g_2'}(v_3)\vartheta_{g_1',g_2'}(v_4)\\
&=\sum\limits^{g_1,g_2} (-1)^{g_1g_2'+g_2g_1'+g_1'g_2'}\,\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(v_1')\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(v_2')\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(v_3')\vartheta_{g_1,g_\nu}(v_4'). % [sic] German source prints g_\nu; mathematically expected g_2
\end{aligned}
}

These are the \gesperrt{Jacobi} formulae.
If one sets, for example,
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_1 &= 0, & v_2 &= v+w, & v_3 &= u+v, & v_4 &= u+w,\\
v_1' &= u+v+w, & v_2' &= -u, & v_3' &= -w, & v_4' &= -v,
\end{aligned}
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 102 =====
% !PRINTED 81
\weberpage{81}
%<<CONT
then from (21), for $g_1', g_2' = 1,1$, there results:
\[
0 = \sum\limits^{g_1,g_2} (-1)^{g_1+g_2}\,\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(u)\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(v)\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(w)\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(u+v+w),
\]
and from this one then obtains the formulae (12), (13), (14), if in (21) one puts the three other characteristics for $g_1', g_2'$.

\begin{center}
\S\,23.\\
\gesperrt{The Derivatives of the $\vartheta$-Functions.}
\end{center}

In what follows we denote by $\vartheta'_{g_1,g_2}(v)$; $\vartheta''_{g_1,g_1}(v)$ % [sic] printed subscript \textquotedbl{}g_1,g_1\textquotedbl{}, expected g_1,g_2
the derivatives of the function $\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(v)$ taken with respect to $v$, and by $\vartheta'_{g_1,g_2}$, $\vartheta''_{g_{\cdot},g_2}$ the values of this function for $v=0$. Then $\vartheta'_{01}$, $\vartheta'_{10}$, $\vartheta'_{00}$ vanish, because $\vartheta_{01}(v)$, $\vartheta_{10}(v)$, $\vartheta_{00}(v)$ are \gesperrt{even} functions of $v$, and likewise $\vartheta''_{11}$ vanishes.

The six functions
\[
\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(v)\vartheta'_{g_1',g_2'}(v) - \vartheta_{g_1',g_2'}(v)\vartheta'_{g_1,g_2}(v)
\]
are, as follows from the fundamental equations \S\,20, (1), $\vartheta$-functions of the second order with the characteristic
\[
(g_1+g_1', g_2+g_2'),
\]
and at the same time either even or odd functions, so that by \S\,21 they can be represented by $\vartheta$-functions. A constant factor is determined by a special value of $v$ ($v=0$). Thus we have
\weq{1}{\vartheta_{11}'(v)\vartheta_{01}(v) - \vartheta_{01}'(v)\vartheta_{11}(v) = A\,\vartheta_{10}(v)\vartheta_{00}(v).}
\weq{2}{A = \frac{\vartheta_{11}'\,\vartheta_{01}}{\vartheta_{10}\,\vartheta_{00}}.}

But this expression for $A$ can still be simplified.

If we differentiate (1) twice with respect to $v$ and then put $v=0$, it follows that
\[
\vartheta_{11}'''\vartheta_{01} - \vartheta_{01}''\vartheta_{11}' = A(\vartheta_{10}''\vartheta_{00} + \vartheta_{10}\vartheta_{00}''),
\]
and if one introduces for $A$ the value (2):
\weq{3}{\frac{\vartheta_{11}'''}{\vartheta_{11}'} = \frac{\vartheta_{01}''}{\vartheta_{01}} + \frac{\vartheta_{10}''}{\vartheta_{10}} + \frac{\vartheta_{00}''}{\vartheta_{00}}.}

But now the four functions $\vartheta_{11}'$, $\vartheta_{01}$, $\vartheta_{10}$, $\vartheta_{00}$ satisfy [by \S\,20, (4)] the differential equation
\weq{4}{\vartheta'' = 4\pi i\,\frac{\partial \vartheta}{\partial \omega},}
and accordingly (3) can be written thus:
\[
\frac{d\log \vartheta_{11}'}{d\omega} = \frac{d\log \vartheta_{00}\vartheta_{10}\vartheta_{01}}{d\omega},
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 103 =====
% !PRINTED 82
\weberpage{82}
%<<CONT
or by integration:
\[
\vartheta_{11}' = c\,\vartheta_{00}\vartheta_{10}\vartheta_{01},
\]
in which $c$ is independent of $\omega$. By \S\,20, 21 the $\vartheta$-functions were determined up to a factor independent of $v$, $\omega$ and common to them all. \gesperrt{This factor shall now be disposed of in such a way that the constant $c$ receives the value $\pi$,} so that the formula holds:
\weq{5}{\vartheta_{11}' = \pi\,\vartheta_{00}\vartheta_{10}\vartheta_{01},}
\gesperrt{and thereby the $\vartheta$-functions are now completely defined up to the common sign $\pm$.} By applying (5), formula (1) can be given the shape:
\weq{6}{\vartheta_{11}'(v)\vartheta_{01}(v) - \vartheta_{01}'(v)\vartheta_{11}(v) = \pi\,\vartheta_{01}^2\,\vartheta_{10}(v)\vartheta_{00}(v),}
and in the same way one obtains, using \S\,21, (8):
\weq{7}{\vartheta_{11}'(v)\vartheta_{00}(v) - \vartheta_{00}'(v)\vartheta_{11}(v) = \pi\,\vartheta_{00}^2\,\vartheta_{10}(v)\vartheta_{01}(v),}
\weq{8}{\vartheta_{11}'(v)\vartheta_{10}(v) - \vartheta_{10}'(v)\vartheta_{11}(v) = \pi\,\vartheta_{10}^2\,\vartheta_{01}(v)\vartheta_{00}(v),}
\weq{9}{\vartheta_{10}'(v)\vartheta_{01}(v) - \vartheta_{01}'(v)\vartheta_{10}(v) = -\pi\,\vartheta_{00}^2\,\vartheta_{00}(v)\vartheta_{11}(v),}
\weq{10}{\vartheta_{00}'(v)\vartheta_{01}(v) - \vartheta_{01}'(v)\vartheta_{00}(v) = -\pi\,\vartheta_{10}^2\,\vartheta_{10}(v)\vartheta_{11}(v),}
\weq{11}{\vartheta_{00}'(v)\vartheta_{10}(v) - \vartheta_{10}'(v)\vartheta_{00}(v) = \pi\,\vartheta_{01}^2\,\vartheta_{01}(v)\vartheta_{11}(v).}

If we differentiate equations (9), (10), (11) with respect to $v$ and set $v=0$, we obtain by means of (4) and (5) the relations
\weq{12}{4\,\frac{d}{d\omega}\log\frac{\vartheta_{10}}{\vartheta_{01}} = i\pi\,\vartheta_{00}^4,}
\weq{13}{4\,\frac{d}{d\omega}\log\frac{\vartheta_{00}}{\vartheta_{01}} = i\pi\,\vartheta_{10}^4,}
\weq{14}{4\,\frac{d}{d\omega}\log\frac{\vartheta_{10}}{\vartheta_{00}} = i\pi\,\vartheta_{01}^4.}

If one differentiates the fundamental formulae % [sic] printed \textquotedbl{}Fundamentformeln\textquotedbl{}, expected Fundamentalformeln
for the $\vartheta$-functions twice logarithmically, one recognises that the functions
\[
\vartheta^2(v)\,\frac{d^2\log\vartheta(v)}{dv^2} = \vartheta''(v)\vartheta(v) - \vartheta'(v)\vartheta'(v)
\]
are $\Theta$-functions of the second order with the characteristic $(0,0)$, and one can therefore express them linearly by means of the functions $\vartheta^2(v)$. In this way there results
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 104 =====
% !PRINTED 83
\weberpage{83}
%<<CONT
\weq{15}{\vartheta_{00}^2\,\vartheta_{00}^2(v)\,\frac{d^2\log\vartheta_{00}(v)}{dv^2} = \vartheta_{00}\vartheta_{00}''\vartheta_{00}^2(v) + \vartheta_{11}'^2\vartheta_{11}^2(v),}
\weq{16}{\vartheta_{01}^2\,\vartheta_{01}^2(v)\,\frac{d^2\log\vartheta_{01}(v)}{dv^2} = \vartheta_{01}\vartheta_{01}''\vartheta_{01}^2(v) - \vartheta_{11}'^2\vartheta_{11}^2(v),}
\weq{17}{\vartheta_{10}^2\,\vartheta_{10}^2(v)\,\frac{d^2\log\vartheta_{10}(v)}{dv^2} = \vartheta_{10}\vartheta_{10}''\vartheta_{10}^2(v) - \vartheta_{11}'^2\vartheta_{11}^2(v),}
\weq{18}{\vartheta_{00}^2\,\vartheta_{11}^2(v)\,\frac{d^2\log\vartheta_{11}(v)}{dv^2} = \vartheta_{00}\vartheta_{00}''\vartheta_{11}^2(v) - \vartheta_{11}'^2\vartheta_{00}^2(v).}

From these, further relations can still be derived by continued differentiation. We adduce one more of these formulae, which is obtained if one differentiates (15) twice more with respect to $v$ and then sets $v=0$. If the differentiations with respect to $v$ are expressed by those with respect to $\omega$ by means of the partial differential equation (4), it follows that:
\[
\frac{d^2\log\vartheta_{00}}{d\omega^2} - 2\left(\frac{d\log\vartheta_{00}}{d\omega}\right)^2 = -\frac{\pi^2}{8}\,\vartheta_{10}^4\vartheta_{01}^4,
\]
or
\weq{19}{\frac{d}{d\omega}\left(\frac{1}{\vartheta_{00}^4}\,\frac{d\vartheta_{00}^2}{d\omega}\right) = -\frac{\pi^2}{4}\,\frac{\vartheta_{10}^4\vartheta_{01}^4}{\vartheta_{00}^2}.}

\begin{center}
\S\,24. \gesperrt{Representation of the $\vartheta$-Functions by Infinite}\\
\gesperrt{Products.}
\end{center}

The theory of the $\vartheta$-functions has now been carried far enough for their representation to follow very easily. With this the existence of these functions is then established, and the considerations made so far first receive their secure foundation. Two ways to this goal stand open to us. The first proceeds from the zero points of the $\vartheta$-functions already known to us and composes infinite products out of them.

The function $\vartheta_{00}(v)$ vanishes, according to \S\,21, when
\[
2v = (2\nu-1)\omega + (2\mu-1)
\]
holds, where $\nu, \mu$ are integers, or when
\[
e^{\pm 2\pi i v} = -e^{\pi i \omega(2\nu-1)},
\]
where we can now restrict $\nu$ to \gesperrt{positive} numbers. If we therefore set, for brevity,
\[
e^{\pi i \omega} = q,
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 105 =====
% !PRINTED 84
\weberpage{84}
%<<CONT
then $q$ is a quantity whose absolute value is a proper fraction. The \gesperrt{convergent}
infinite product
\[
P(v) = \prod_{1,\infty}^{\nu} (1 + q^{2\nu-1}e^{2\pi i v})(1 + q^{2\nu-1}e^{-2\pi i v})
\]
therefore vanishes at \gesperrt{all and only} at those points at which $\vartheta_{00}(v)$
vanishes, and moreover
\[
\begin{gathered}
P(v+1) = P(v)\\
P(v+\omega) = \frac{1+q^{-1}e^{-2\pi i v}}{1+qe^{2\pi i v}}P(v) = q^{-1}e^{-2\pi i v}P(v).
\end{gathered}
\]
But by § 20, (1) this is the period property of the function $\vartheta_{00}(v)$, and
we therefore have:
\weq{1}{\vartheta_{00}(v) = Q\prod_{1,\infty}^{\nu}(1 + q^{2\nu-1}e^{2\pi i v})(1 + q^{2\nu-1}e^{-2\pi i v}),}
where $Q$ is a factor independent of $v$. By the formulae (8) of § 21 one obtains from
this, on putting in place of $v$
\[
v + \frac{1}{2}, \qquad v + \frac{\omega}{2}, \qquad v + \frac{1+\omega}{2}
\]
respectively:
\weq{2}{\vartheta_{01}(v) = Q\prod_{1,\infty}^{\nu}(1 - q^{2\nu-1}e^{2\pi i v})(1 - q^{2\nu-1}e^{-2\pi i v}),}
\weq{3}{\vartheta_{10}(v) = Qq^{\frac{1}{4}}(e^{\pi i v} + e^{-\pi i v})\prod_{1,\infty}^{\nu}(1 + q^{2\nu}e^{2\pi i v})(1 + q^{2\nu}e^{-2\pi i v}),}
\weq{4}{\vartheta_{11}(v) = -iQq^{\frac{1}{4}}(e^{\pi i v} - e^{-\pi i v})\prod_{1,\infty}^{\nu}(1 - q^{2\nu}e^{2\pi i v})(1 - q^{2\nu}e^{-2\pi i v}).}
If one sets $v = 0$ in these formulae, in the last one after a single differentiation,
there follows
\weq{5}{\begin{gathered}
\vartheta_{00} = Q\prod_{1,\infty}^{\nu}(1 + q^{2\nu-1})^2,\\
\vartheta_{01} = Q\prod_{1,\infty}^{\nu}(1 - q^{2\nu-1})^2,\\
\vartheta_{10} = 2Qq^{\frac{1}{4}}\prod_{1,\infty}^{\nu}(1 + q^{2\nu})^2,\\
\vartheta_{11}' = 2\pi Qq^{\frac{1}{4}}\prod_{1,\infty}^{\nu}(1 - q^{2\nu})^2.
\end{gathered}}
Accordingly, it is possible by means of (5), § 23:
\[
\vartheta_{11}' = \pi\vartheta_{00}\vartheta_{01}\vartheta_{10}
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 106 =====
% !PRINTED 85
\weberpage{85}
%<<CONT
determine the factor $Q$. One obtains first
\[
1 = Q^2\prod^{\nu}\frac{(1-q^{2\nu-1})^2(1+q^{2\nu-1})^2(1+q^{2\nu})^2}{(1-q^{2\nu})^2},
\]
or, by disposing of the still undetermined sign of $Q$ and thereby of the \gesperrt{signs} of the
$\vartheta$-functions:
\[
Q = \prod_{1,\infty}^{\nu}\frac{(1-q^{2\nu})}{(1+q^{2\nu})(1+q^{2\nu-1})(1-q^{2\nu-1})}.
\]
In the denominator one may put $\prod(1+q^{\nu})$ in place of $\prod(1+q^{2\nu})(1+q^{2\nu-1})$,
and the numerator $\prod(1-q^{2\nu})$ can be decomposed into
\[
\prod(1-q^{\nu})(1+q^{\nu}) = \prod(1-q^{2\nu})(1-q^{2\nu-1})(1+q^{\nu}).
\]
In this way there results finally
\weq{6}{Q = \prod^{\nu}(1 - q^{2\nu}).}
The expressions (1), (2), (3), (4) can be represented in real form if one carries out the
multiplication of the conjugate imaginary factors. One thus obtains:
\weq{7}{\begin{gathered}
\vartheta_{00}(v) = \prod_{1,\infty}^{\nu}(1 - q^{2\nu})(1 + 2q^{2\nu-1}\cos 2\pi v + q^{4\nu-2}),\\
\vartheta_{01}(v) = \prod_{1,\infty}^{\nu}(1 - q^{2\nu})(1 - 2q^{2\nu-1}\cos 2\pi v + q^{4\nu-1}),\\
% [sic] German source prints exponent 4\nu-1; mathematically expected 4\nu-2.
\vartheta_{10}(v) = 2q^{\frac{1}{4}}\cos\pi v\prod_{1,\infty}^{\nu}(1 - q^{2\nu})(1 + 2q^{2\nu}\cos 2\pi v + q^{4\nu}),\\
\vartheta_{11}(v) = 2q^{\frac{1}{4}}\sin\pi v\prod_{1,\infty}^{\nu}(1 - q^{2\nu})(1 - 2q^{2\nu}\cos 2\pi v + q^{4\nu}).
\end{gathered}}
If we introduce the expression (6) into the last equation (5), there results
\[
\vartheta_{11}' = 2\pi q^{\frac{1}{4}}\prod(1 - q^{2\nu})^3,
\]
and if we therefore put
\weq{8}{\eta(\omega) = q^{\frac{1}{12}}\prod(1 - q^{2\nu})}
then we have
\weq{9}{\vartheta_{11}' = 2\pi\eta(\omega)^3.}
By eliminating $Q$ with the help of the relation
\[
Q = q^{-\frac{1}{12}}\eta(\omega)
\]
from (5), we set
\weq{10}{\begin{gathered}
\vartheta_{00} = \eta(\omega)f(\omega)^2,\\
\vartheta_{01} = \eta(\omega)f_1(\omega)^2,\\
\vartheta_{10} = \eta(\omega)f_2(\omega)^2,
\end{gathered}}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 107 =====
% !PRINTED 86
\weberpage{86}

%<<CONT
in which the functions $f(\omega)$, $f_1(\omega)$, $f_2(\omega)$
are defined as follows:
\weq{11}{
\begin{aligned}
f(\omega) &= q^{-\frac{1}{24}}\prod_{1,\infty}^{\nu}(1+q^{2\nu-1}),\\
f_1(\omega) &= q^{-\frac{1}{24}}\prod_{1,\infty}^{\nu}(1-q^{2\nu-1}),\\
f_2(\omega) &= \sqrt{2}\,q^{\frac{1}{12}}\prod_{1,\infty}^{\nu}(1+q^{2\nu}).
\end{aligned}
}

The functions $\eta(\omega)$, $f(\omega)$, $f_1(\omega)$,
$f_2(\omega)$ will play an important part in our later
investigations. From § 21, (14) there follows, by (10),
the relation
\weq{12}{f(\omega)^8 = f_1(\omega)^8 + f_2(\omega)^8,}
and from § 23 (5), by (9),
\weq{13}{f(\omega)f_1(\omega)f_2(\omega) = \sqrt{2}.}
The last formula also follows from (11) by the use of the
identical relation:
\[ \prod (1+q^\nu)(1-q^{2\nu-1}) = \prod \frac{(1+q^\nu)(1-q^\nu)}{1-q^{2\nu}} = 1. \]

\begin{center}
\textbf{§ 25. Representation of the $\vartheta$-Functions by
Infinite Series.}
\end{center}

The second way of arriving at the representation of the
$\vartheta$-functions consists in seeking to form a convergent
infinite series that satisfies the fundamental equations.

Let us first observe that, on account of the condition
\[ \vartheta_{00}(v+1) = \vartheta_{00}(v) \]
the function $\vartheta_{00}(v)$ can be regarded as a one-valued
function of $e^{2\pi i v}$, and let us accordingly put
\[ \vartheta_{00}(v) = \sum_{-\infty,\infty}^{\nu} A_\nu e^{2\pi i v \nu}, \]
the differential equation § 20, (4):
\[ \frac{\partial^2 \vartheta}{\partial v^2} - 4\pi i \frac{\partial \vartheta}{\partial \omega} = 0 \]
then gives for $A_\nu$ the condition
\[ \frac{dA_\nu}{d\omega} = \pi i \nu^2 A_\nu, \qquad A_\nu = c_\nu e^{\pi i \omega \nu^2} = c_\nu q^{\nu^2}, \]
in which $c_\nu$ is constant with respect to $\omega$. Thus we obtain
\[ \vartheta_{00}(v) = \sum c_\nu q^{\nu^2} c^{2\pi i v \nu}, \]
% [sic] German source prints c as the exponential base; mathematically expected e.
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 108 =====
% !PRINTED 87
\weberpage{87}
%<<CONT
and from this:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\vartheta_{00}(v+\omega) &= \sum c_\nu q^{\nu^2+2\nu} e^{2\pi i v \nu}\\
&=q^{-1}e^{-2\pi i v}\sum c_\nu q^{(\nu+1)^2}e^{2\pi i v(\nu+1)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since $\nu$ runs from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$, it is permissible to put $\nu - 1$
in place of $\nu$ in this formula, and if one does so, there results
\[
\vartheta_{00}(v+\omega) = q^{-1}e^{-2\pi i v}\sum c_{\nu-1} q^{\nu^2}e^{2\pi i v \nu}.
\]
By the second of the fundamental equations [§ 20, (1)] the two series
\[
\sum c_\nu q^{\nu^2}e^{2\pi i v \nu} \quad \text{and} \quad \sum c_{\nu-1} q^{\nu^2}e^{2\pi i v \nu}
\]
must therefore agree with one another, that is, we must have
\[
c_{\nu-1} = c_\nu
\]
The $c_\nu$ are therefore all equal to one another; that they have the value 1 is shown by the
comparison of the two developments
\[
\sum_{-\infty,\infty}^{\nu} q^{\nu^2}e^{2\pi i v \nu}, \qquad \prod_{1,\infty}^{\nu}(1 - q^{2\nu})(1 + q^{2\nu-1}e^{2\pi i v})(1 + q^{2\nu-1}e^{-2\pi i v})
\]
for the value $q = 0$.

One may also give the development thus found for $\vartheta_{00}(v)$ the two
formulae:
\weq{1}{\begin{aligned}
\vartheta_{00}(v) &= \sum q^{\nu^2} e^{2\nu \pi i v}\\
&= 1 + 2q\cos 2\pi v + 2q^4\cos 4\pi v + 2q^9\cos 6\pi v + \cdots,
\end{aligned}}
and from this one obtains, by § 21, (8), through the increase of $v$ by $\frac{1}{2}$,
$\frac{\omega}{2}$, $\frac{1+\omega}{2}$, the developments for the three remaining
$\vartheta$-functions:
\weq{2}{\begin{aligned}
\vartheta_{01}(v) &= \sum(-1)^\nu q^{\nu^2} e^{2\nu \pi i v}\\
&= 1 - 2q\cos 2\pi v + 2q^4\cos 4\pi v - 2q^9\cos 6\pi v + \cdots
\end{aligned}}
\weq{3}{\begin{aligned}
\vartheta_{10}(v) &= \sum q^{\frac{(2\nu+1)^2}{4}} e^{(2\nu+1)\pi i v}\\
&= 2q^{\frac{1}{4}}\cos\pi v + 2q^{\frac{9}{4}}\cos 3\pi v + 2q^{\frac{25}{4}}\cos 5\pi v + \cdots
\end{aligned}}
\weq{4}{\begin{aligned}
\vartheta_{11}(v) &= -i\sum(-1)^\nu q^{\frac{(2\nu+1)^2}{4}} e^{(2\nu+1)\pi i v}\\
&= 2q^{\frac{1}{4}}\sin\pi v - 2q^{\frac{9}{4}}\sin 3\pi v + 2q^{\frac{25}{4}}\sin 5\pi v + \cdots
\end{aligned}}
For later applications we draw from these developments the conclusions:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 109 =====
% !PRINTED 88
\weberpage{88}
%<<CONT
When the imaginary part of $\omega$ grows to infinity, so
that the absolute value of $q$ vanishes, then
\[
\vartheta_{00}(v) = 1, \quad \vartheta_{01}(v) = 1, \quad q^{-\frac{1}{4}}\vartheta_{10}(v) = 2\cos\pi v,
\]
\[
q^{-\frac{1}{4}}\vartheta_{11}(v) = 2\sin\pi v.
\]
If we take $\omega$ purely imaginary, and hence $q$ real, positive and properly
fractional, then for a real $v$:

1. $\vartheta_{00}(v)$, $\vartheta_{01}(v)$, $\vartheta_{10}(v)$, $\vartheta_{11}(v)$ real, and when $v$ lies between 0
and $\frac{1}{2}$, positive [by § 24 (7)], consequently also $\vartheta_{00}$, $\vartheta_{01}$, $\vartheta_{10}$, $\vartheta'_{11}$
positive;

2. $\vartheta_{00}(iv)$, $\vartheta_{01}(iv)$, $\vartheta_{10}(iv)$, $-i\vartheta_{11}(iv)$ real, and as long as $v$
lies between 0 and $\dfrac{-i\omega}{2}$, positive; further, with the aid of the
formulae § 21, (8)

3. $\vartheta_{00}(\frac{1}{2}+iv)$, $\vartheta_{01}(\frac{1}{2}+iv)$, $i\vartheta_{10}(\frac{1}{2}+iv)$, $\vartheta_{11}(\frac{1}{2}+iv)$
real, and as long as $v$ lies between 0 and $\dfrac{-i\omega}{2}$, positive;
\[
4. \quad q^{\frac{1}{4}}e^{\pi iv}\vartheta_{00}\left(\frac{\omega}{2}+v\right), \quad -iq^{\frac{1}{4}}e^{\pi iv}\vartheta_{01}\left(\frac{\omega}{2}+v\right),
\]
\[
q^{\frac{1}{4}}e^{\pi iv}\vartheta_{10}\left(\frac{\omega}{2}+v\right), \quad -iq^{\frac{1}{4}}e^{\pi iv}\vartheta_{11}\left(\frac{\omega}{2}+v\right)
\]
real, and as long as $v$ lies between 0 and $\frac{1}{2}$, positive.

\begin{center}
§ 26. \gesperrt{Development of $\vartheta$-Quotients.}
\end{center}

If $v$ denotes a variable and $a$ an arbitrary constant, then
the quotients
\[
\frac{\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(v+a)}{\vartheta_{g'_1,g'_2}(v)}
\]
are doubly periodic functions of the second kind and of the first order,
with the periodicity factors $(-1)^{g_1+g'_1}$, $(-1)^{g_2+g'_2}e^{-2\pi ia}$; and
if one adds an exponential factor $e^{\lambda v}$, then $\lambda$
and $a$ can be so determined that the periodicity factors become arbitrarily given quantities. By choosing the principal characteristics
$(g_1,g_2), (g'_1,g'_2)$ in all possible ways, one obtains 16 such
functions. We start out from one among them, for which we
set, with the addition of a constant factor,
\weq{1}{F = \frac{\vartheta'_{11}\vartheta_{11}(v+a)}{2i\pi\vartheta_{11}(v)\vartheta_{11}(a)}}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 110 =====
% !PRINTED 89
\weberpage{89}
%<<CONT
choose. This is a single-valued function $F(z)$ of the variable
\[
z = e^{2\pi iv},
\]
and if, as before, $q = e^{\pi i\omega}$, then it has the periodicity property
:
\weq{2}{F(q^2z) = e^{-2\pi ia}F(z),}
from which, for every integer $\nu$, it follows that:
\[
F(q^{2\nu}z) = e^{-2\pi ia\nu}F(z).
\]
The function $F(z)$ becomes infinite for a finite $z$ only
when one of the factors $q^{2\nu}z - 1$ vanishes, and in
particular
\weq{3}{(z-1)F(z) = 1 \quad (\text{for } z = 1).}
But by (2)
\[
(q^{2\nu}z - 1)F(q^{2\nu}z) = e^{-2\pi ia\nu}F(z)(q^{2\nu}z - 1)
\]
and consequently, by (3),
\weq{4}{F(z)(q^{2\nu}z - 1) = e^{2\pi ia\nu} \quad (\text{for } z = q^{-2\nu}).}
If we set, under the assumption of convergence that is presently
 to be examined more closely,
\weq{5}{S(z) = \sum_{-\infty,\infty}^{\nu} \frac{e^{2\pi ia\nu}}{q^{2\nu}z - 1},}
then, replacing $z$ by $q^2z$ and $\nu$ by $\nu - 1$, we obtain
:
\weq{6}{S(q^2z) = e^{-2\pi ia}S(z),}
and the difference $F(z) - S(z)$ would therefore be, considered as a function of $v$
, by (3) and (4) an integral doubly periodic function
 of the second kind. But by § 16, 6. such a function must be an exponential
 function, and hence
\[
F(z) = S(z) + Ce^{-2\pi imv},
\]
where $m$ is an integer and $C$ a constant. But from (2) and
(6), unless $C = 0$, it follows that:
\[
e^{-2\pi im\omega} = e^{-2\pi ia};
\]
hence $a = m\omega + n$, where $m, n$ are integers. But if $a$
is a period, then $F(z)$ reduces to a constant or an
exponential function. Otherwise $C = 0$ must hold, and there follows
the development:
\weq{7}{\frac{\vartheta'_{11}\vartheta_{11}(v+a)}{2i\pi\vartheta_{11}(v)\vartheta_{11}(a)} = \sum_{-\infty,+\infty}^{\nu} \frac{e^{2\pi i\nu a}}{q^{2\nu}e^{2\pi iv} - 1}.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 111 =====
% !PRINTED 90
\weberpage{90}
We have assumed the convergence of this series for all values of $v$;
in order to judge of this, we observe that the general term of this
 series becomes
\[
\begin{array}{lccl}
\text{for} & \nu = +\infty & \text{equal to} & -e^{2\pi i\nu a}\\
\text{\textquotedbl} & \nu = -\infty & \text{\textquotedbl} & e^{-2\pi iv}e^{-2\pi i\nu(\omega-a)}
\end{array}
\]
Convergence will therefore take place if the imaginary
part of $a$ and of $\omega - a$ is positive. If we therefore set
$\omega = \omega' + i\omega''$, $a = a' + ia''$, then the condition of convergence is

\weq{8}{0 < a'' < \omega''.}
If in (7) one replaces $a$ by $a + \frac{1}{2}$, there results the
development for a second of the 16 functions:
\weq{9}{\frac{\vartheta'_{11}\vartheta_{10}(v+a)}{2\pi i\vartheta_{11}(v)\vartheta_{10}(a)} = \sum^{\nu} \frac{(-1)^\nu e^{2\pi ia\nu}}{q^{2\nu}e^{2\pi iv} - 1},}
and if in (7) and (9) one changes $a$ into $a + \frac{1}{2}\omega$:
\weq{10}{\frac{\vartheta'_{11}\vartheta_{01}(v+a)}{2\pi i\vartheta_{11}(v)\vartheta_{01}(a)} = \sum^{\nu} \frac{e^{2\pi ia\nu}q^\nu e^{\pi iv}}{q^{2\nu}e^{2\pi iv} - 1},}
\weq{11}{\frac{\vartheta'_{11}\vartheta_{00}(v+a)}{2\pi i\vartheta_{11}(v)\vartheta_{00}(a)} = \sum^{\nu} \frac{(-1)^\nu e^{2\pi ia\nu}q^\nu e^{\pi iv}}{q^{2\nu}e^{2\pi iv} - 1},}
where it is however to be noted that in the last two formulae
the condition of convergence is altered, namely:
\[
-\frac{\omega''}{2} < a'' < \frac{\omega''}{2}.
\]
From the four formulae the remaining twelve follow if we
replace $v$ by $v + \frac{1}{2}$, $v + \frac{1}{2}\omega$, $v + \frac{1}{2}(1+\omega)$, whereby the
domains of convergence are not further altered. In this way
the formulae of Table I at the end of the volume are derived.

The series so obtained do not all converge for real values
of $a$; the series (7), for example, does not, since in it the part
running towards the side of the positive $\nu$
\weq{12}{\sum_{1,\infty}^{\nu} \frac{e^{2\pi i\nu a}}{q^{2\nu}e^{2\pi iv} - 1}}
ceases to converge when the imaginary part of $a$ becomes equal
to zero, while the other part is still convergent even there
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 112 =====
% !PRINTED 91
\weberpage{91}
%<<CONT
remains. But from (12) one obtains an expression which still converges
for a real $a$ as well, if one adds the sum
\weq{13}{\sum_{1,\infty}^{\nu} e^{2\pi i\nu a} = -\frac{e^{2\pi ia}}{e^{2\pi ia} - 1}}
to it. For thereby it passes over into
\[
\sum_{1,\infty}^{\nu} \frac{e^{2\pi i\nu a}q^{2\nu}e^{2\pi iv}}{q^{2\nu}e^{2\pi iv} - 1},
\]
and this series remains convergent as long as the imaginary part $a''$
of $a$ lies between $-\omega''$ and $+\omega''$.

Accordingly there results from (7), if we separate off the term
corresponding to the value $\nu = 0$ and replace the negative $\nu$ by
$-\nu$:
\[
\frac{\vartheta'_{11}\vartheta_{11}(v+a)}{\pi\vartheta_{11}(v)\vartheta_{11}(a)} = \frac{2i}{e^{2\pi iv} - 1} + \frac{2ie^{2\pi ia}}{e^{2\pi ia} - 1}
\]
\[
+ 2i\sum_{1,\infty}^{\nu} \frac{e^{-2\pi i\nu a}}{q^{-2\nu}e^{2\pi iv} - 1} + 2i\sum_{1,\infty}^{\nu} \frac{q^{2\nu}e^{2\pi i\nu a}e^{2\pi iv}}{q^{2\nu}e^{2\pi iv} - 1}.
\]
But we have
\[
\frac{2i}{e^{2\pi iv} - 1} = \frac{e^{-\pi iv}}{\sin\pi v} = \mathrm{cotg}\,\pi v - i,
\]
\[
\frac{2ie^{2\pi ia}}{e^{2\pi ia} - 1} = \frac{e^{\pi ia}}{\sin\pi a} = \mathrm{cotg}\,\pi a + i,
\]
and accordingly this development can also be represented thus:
\weq{14}{\frac{\vartheta'_{11}\vartheta_{11}(v+a)}{\pi\vartheta_{11}(v)\vartheta_{11}(a)} = \mathrm{cotg}\,\pi v + \mathrm{cotg}\,\pi a
-2i\sum \left(\frac{q^m e^{m\pi ia}}{e^{-2\pi iv} - q^m} - \frac{q^m e^{-m\pi ia}}{e^{2\pi iv} - q^m}\right),}
in which $m$ runs through the \gesperrt{sequence of the even numbers}
\[
m = 2, 4, 6, 8, \dots
\]
The domain of validity of this development is
\[
-\omega'' < a'' < \omega''.
\]
In Table II these 16 developments are compiled.

From these formulae three others can be derived, by increasing
$v$ or $a$ or both by $\frac{1}{2}$. Three others, however, which correspond to the
increase of $v$ and $a$ by $\frac{1}{2}\omega$, must be derived directly.
They exhibit real form when $q$, $a$, $v$ are real.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 113 =====
% !PRINTED 92
\weberpage{92}
A third kind of development, in which the symmetry of the
functions with respect to the two variables $v$, $a$ finds
expression, arises if the fractions that occurred in the previous
developments are developed in powers of $q$. In this way one
obtains
\[
\begin{gathered}
\frac{q^m}{e^{-2\pi i v}-q^m} = \Sigma\, q^{m\nu} e^{2\pi i \nu v}, \\
\frac{q^m}{e^{+2\pi i v}-q^m} = \Sigma\, q^{m\nu} e^{-2\pi i \nu v}, \\
\nu = 1,\, 2,\, 3,\, \ldots
\end{gathered}
\]
and these developments hold as long as the absolute value
of $q\, e^{2\pi i v}$ is a proper fraction, hence, if we put $v = v' + i v''$,
as long as
\[
-\omega'' < v < \omega'' % [sic] German source prints v; the imaginary-part bound mathematically requires v''.
\]
holds. Accordingly there follows from (14)
\[
\begin{gathered}
\frac{\vartheta'_{11}\,\vartheta_{11}(v+a)}{\pi\,\vartheta_{11}(v)\,\vartheta_{11}(a)} = \mathrm{cotg}\,\pi v + \mathrm{cotg}\,\pi a \\
{}+ 4\Sigma\, q^{\frac{mm'}{2}} \sin(m a + m' v)\pi,
\end{gathered}
\]
in which $m$, $m'$ run, independently of one another, through the \gesperrt{even} numbers
2, 4, 6, 8, \ldots\ This formula is valid for \gesperrt{real}
$a$ and $v$, and it holds beyond that as well, as long as the imaginary
part, of $v$ as well as of $a$, is in absolute value less than $\omega''$.

In Table III the 16 formulae of this kind are collected\textsuperscript{1}).

\textsuperscript{1}) Such developments have been considered by \gesperrt{Jacobi} (sur la rotation d'un corps)
(ges. Werke Bd.\ II), thereupon by \gesperrt{Hermite} (Annales de l'école normale 1885)
and by \gesperrt{Kronecker} (Berliner Akademie 1885). Cf.\ also the
Strasbourg dissertation of L.\ \gesperrt{Vockerodt} (1905).

%% ===== canonical stable idx 114 =====
% !PRINTED none

\begin{center}
\gesperrt{Third Chapter.}

\gesperrt{Transformation of the Theta-Functions.}
\end{center}

\noindent\hrulefill

\begin{center}
§ 27. \gesperrt{The Principle of Transformation.}
\end{center}

We return to the defining equations of the $T$-functions of
order $m$ given in § 17, and there, for a reason that will be evident
at once, we furnish the letters $\omega$, $a$, $b$, $m$
with accents, so that these equations read:
\weq{1}{\begin{gathered}
T(u+\omega'_1) = e^{-\pi i [a'_1(2u+\omega'_1)+b'_1]} T(u), \\
T(u+\omega'_2) = e^{-\pi i a'_2 (2u+\omega'_2)+b'_2} T(u). % [sic] German source prints the exponent without the expected brackets.
\end{gathered}}
\weq{2}{a'_2\omega'_1 - a'_1\omega'_2 = m'.}
If $a$, $c$ are any integers whatever (positive or negative),
then, on replacing $n_1$, $n_2$ in § 17, (16) by $-c$, $a$, there results:
\weq{3}{\begin{gathered}
T(u - c\omega'_1 + a\omega'_2) \\
= e^{-\pi i(-ca'_1+aa'_2)(2u-c\omega'_1+a\omega'_2) - \pi i(-cb'_1+ab'_2-m'ac)} T(u),
\end{gathered}}
an equation which also follows from one of the equations (1)
if in it $a'$, $b'$, $\omega'$ are replaced by
\[
-ca'_1+aa'_2,\quad -cb'_1+ab'_2-m'ac,\quad -c\omega'_1+a\omega'_2
\]
respectively.

Herein is contained the principle of the transformation of the
$T$-functions.

Let $b$, $\partial$ be two other integers for which the
determinant
\weq{4}{n = a\partial - bc}
has a \gesperrt{positive} value. We put
\weq{5}{\begin{gathered}
\omega_1 = +\partial\omega'_1 - b\omega'_2, \\
\omega_2 = -c\omega'_1 + a\omega'_2,
\end{gathered}}
and consequently
\weq{6}{\begin{gathered}
n\omega'_1 = a\omega_1 + b\omega_2 \\
n\omega'_2 = c\omega_1 + \partial\omega_2.
\end{gathered}}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 115 =====
% !PRINTED 94
\weberpage{94}
Then, as one recognises from
\[
\frac{\omega'_2}{\omega'_1} = \frac{c\omega_1+\partial\omega_2}{a\omega_1+b\omega_2}
\]
by separation of the real from the imaginary part, the
imaginary part of $\omega_2:\omega_1$ has the same sign as that of
$\omega'_2:\omega'_1$ (the positive one).

If we set
\weq{7}{\begin{gathered}
a_1 = \partial a'_1 - b a'_2 \\
a_2 = -c a'_1 + a a'_2
\end{gathered}}
\weq{8}{\begin{gathered}
b_1 = \partial b'_1 - b b'_2 - m'b\partial \\
b_2 = -cb'_1 + ab'_2 - m'ac,
\end{gathered}}
then one concludes from (3) that the function $T(u)$ satisfies not only
the conditions (1), but also the equations that arise from (1) by the
interchange of $\omega'_1$, $\omega'_2$, $a'_1$, $a'_2$, $b'_1$, $b'_2$ with $\omega_1$, $\omega_2$, $a_1$, $a_2$, $b_1$, $b_2$,
that is, the equations (1), § 17. It is
therefore at the same time a $T$-function of the periods $\omega'_1$, $\omega'_2$ and of the
periods $\omega_1$, $\omega_2$, which we indicate by the following equation:
\weq{9}{T'(u,\,\omega'_1\,\omega'_2) = T(u,\,\omega_1,\,\omega_2).}
% [sic] German source omits the comma between the two primed periods.
But by (5) and (7) we have
\[
a_2\omega_1 - a_1\omega_2 = (a'_2\omega'_1 - a'_1\omega'_2)(a\partial - bc),
\]
hence, if $m$ is the order of $T$,
\weq{10}{m = m'n.}
By (8), if $(g'_1, g'_2)$ is the characteristic of $T'$ (§ 17), the
characteristic $(g_1, g_2)$ of $T$ is
\weq{11}{(g_1, g_2) = (\partial g'_1 - b g'_2 - m'b\partial,\ -c g'_1 + a g'_2 - m'ac).}
\gesperrt{By the transformation of the $T$-functions one understands
the representation of the functions $T'$ with the periods
$\omega'_1$, $\omega'_2$ by $T$-functions with the periods $\omega_1$, $\omega_2$.}

The numbers $a$, $b$, $c$, $\partial$ are called the \gesperrt{transformation numbers}
and $n = a\partial - bc$ the \gesperrt{degree of transformation}.

In order to survey the form of this representation more clearly,
we shall seek the conditions under which $T'(u, \omega_1, \omega_2)$
becomes a $\Theta$-function of the $m$th order $\Theta(u,\omega)$ (§ 20). We
take $b'_1$, $b'_2$, and consequently also $b_1$, $b_2$, to be integers, so that
$b_1$, $b_2$, $b'_1$, $b'_2$ can be replaced by $g_1$, $g_2$, $g'_1$, $g'_2$. We
then have
\[
\omega_1 = 1, \quad \omega_2 = \omega, \quad a_1 = 0, \quad a_2 = m
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 116 =====
% !PRINTED 95
\weberpage{95}
%<<CONT
to be set, and accordingly [by (6), (7), (10)] we obtain
\[
\begin{gathered}
\omega'_1 = \frac{a+b\omega}{n}, \quad \omega'_2 = \frac{c+\partial\omega}{n}, \\
a'_1 = m'b, \quad a'_2 = m'\partial.
\end{gathered}
\]
The function $T'(u, \omega'_1, \omega'_2)$ therefore satisfies the conditions (1):
\[
\begin{gathered}
T(u+\omega'_1) = (-1)^{g'_1} e^{-\pi i m'b(2u+\omega'_1)} T(u), \\
T(u+\omega'_2) = (-1)^{g'_2} e^{-\pi i m'\partial(2u+\omega'_2)} T(u),
\end{gathered}
\]
% [sic] German source prints unprimed T on both rows although the defined function is T'.
and from this it follows that the product
\[
e^{\frac{\pi i m'bu^2}{\omega'_1}} T'(u, \omega'_1, \omega'_2)
\]
is a $\Theta$-function of the order $m'$, with the arguments
\[
\frac{u}{\omega'_1}, \quad \frac{\omega'_2}{\omega'_1}
\]
and the characteristic $(g'_1, g'_2)$. We can express this in the
equation:
\weq{12}{e^{-\frac{\pi i m' n b u^2}{a+b\omega}} \Theta^{(m')}_{g'_1,g'_2}\left(\frac{nu}{a+b\omega},\ \frac{c+\partial\omega}{a+b\omega}\right) = \Theta^{(m'n)}_{g_1,g_2}(u,\omega),}
in which the characteristics are determined by (11). The means for the
representation of these functions are contained in § 21.

We denote the transformation of $T$ and $T'$ by a single
letter $S$, or by $(T', T)$, thus:
\[
S = (T', T).
\]

If $S'$ denotes a second transformation by which $T'$ passes into $T''$,
that is,
\[
S' = (T'', T'),
\]
then we can derive from these a new transformation $S''$ by which
$T$ passes into $T''$. This one is said to be composed from $S$ and $S'$,
and is denoted thus:
\[
S'' = S'S
\]
or
\[
(T'', T) = (T'', T')(T', T).
\]
In this composition the commutative law does not in general
hold; thus $SS'$ is different from $S'S$. The associative law,
however, does hold, and it is expressed in the formula:
\[
(T''', T'')\big[(T'', T')(T', T)\big] = \big[(T''', T'')(T'', T')\big](T', T) = (T''', T).
\]

%% ===== canonical stable idx 117 =====
% !PRINTED 96
\weberpage{96}

\begin{center}
\S\ 28.\quad\gesperrt{Composition of the Transformations.}
\end{center}

A transformation [\S\ 27, (9)] is completely determined by the transformation numbers $a, b, c, \partial$, and these four integers may be given arbitrarily, provided only that their determinant $n = a\partial - bc$ is \gesperrt{positive}. If one gives these four numbers the opposite sign, then $\omega_1', \omega_2'$ pass over, by \S\ 27, (6), into $-\omega_1', -\omega_2'$, and if one replaces $a, b, c, d$ by $ma, mb, mc, m\partial$, % [sic] \textquotedbl{}d\textquotedbl{} here, \textquotedbl{}\partial\textquotedbl{} a few words later — same variable printed two ways
where $m$ is an arbitrary natural number, then $\omega_1', \omega_2'$ pass over into $\omega_1'/m$, $\omega_2'/m$ and $n$ into $m^2n$. The ratio of the periods $\omega' = \omega_2'/\omega_1'$ remains unchanged in these two cases. For the present, however, we shall always regard two transformations as different when the transformation numbers are different. In accordance with this stipulation we can represent a transformation unambiguously by a matrix

\weq{1}{S = \begin{pmatrix} a, & b \\ c, & \partial \end{pmatrix}}

The determinant

\weq{2}{n = a\partial - bc}

is the degree of the transformation.

With this notation we represent the relations (6), \S\ 27 in this way as well:

\weq{3}{n(\omega_1', \omega_2') = \begin{pmatrix} a, & b \\ c, & \partial \end{pmatrix}(\omega_1, \omega_2).}

If one puts
\[
S' = \begin{pmatrix} a', & b' \\ c', & \partial' \end{pmatrix}, \quad a'\partial' - b'c' = n',
\]
then

\weq{4}{n'(\omega_1'', \omega_2'') = \begin{pmatrix} a', & b' \\ c', & \partial' \end{pmatrix}(\omega_1', \omega_2'),}

and if in (4) one expresses $\omega_1', \omega_2'$ in terms of $\omega_1, \omega_2$ according to (3), one obtains

\weq{5}{nn'(\omega_1'', \omega_2'') = \begin{pmatrix} a'a+b'c, & a'b+b'\partial \\ c'a+\partial'c, & c'b+\partial'\partial \end{pmatrix}(\omega_1, \omega_2).}

If we therefore put

\weq{6}{S'' = S'S,}

then
\[
S'' = \begin{pmatrix} a'a+b'c, & a'b+b'\partial \\ c'a+\partial'c, & c'b+\partial'\partial \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} a'', & b'' \\ c'', & \partial'' \end{pmatrix}, \quad a''\partial'' - b''c'' = n'' = nn'.
\]

%% ===== canonical stable idx 118 =====
% !PRINTED 97
\weberpage{97}

The transformations $S$ therefore compose according to the same rule as the linear substitutions and matrices which we considered in the sixth chapter of the second volume. The degree of a composed transformation is equal to the product of the degrees of the components. These matrices are here bound to the assumption that their elements are integers and their determinant is positive.

These properties are preserved under the composition of the transformations. Nevertheless the totality $\mathfrak{S}$ of the transformations $S$ forms no group, any more than the totality of the natural numbers forms a group under composition by multiplication; for when $S'$, $S''$ are given it is not always possible to determine an $S$ that satisfies condition (6), which yet (according to Bd. II, \S\ 1, 4.) would be required for a group.

By the special transformation of degree $m^2$:
\[
M = \begin{pmatrix} \pm m, & 0 \\ 0, & \pm m \end{pmatrix}
\]
the periods $\omega_1, \omega_2$ pass into $\omega_1' = \omega_1/m$, $\omega_2' = \omega_2/m$, and the period ratio $\omega = \omega_2/\omega_1$ remains unchanged. These transformations are called \gesperrt{multiplications} (similarity transformations, Bd. II, \S\ 41). Among them is contained the identical substitution
\[
1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0 \\ 0, & 1 \end{pmatrix}
\]
which leaves everything unchanged and plays the role of the unit under composition.

\gesperrt{The multiplications are permutable under composition with every transformation $S$:}

\weq{7}{SM = MS.}

If in $SM$ or $MS$ one holds the transformation $S$ fixed and lets $M$ run through the totality $\mathfrak{M}$ of the multiplications, one obtains a system $\mathfrak{M}S$, which according to Bd. II, \S\ 46 would have to be designated a collineation. If $S_1$ and $S_2$ belong to a collineation $C$, and $S_1'$ and $S_2'$ to a collineation $C'$, then $S_1'S_1$ and $S_2'S_2$ also belong to the same collineation $C''$. In this way, by setting $C'' = C'C$, one can compose the collineations. Under this composition the colli-
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 119 =====
% !PRINTED 98
\weberpage{98}
%<<CONT
neation $\mathfrak{M}$ plays the role of the unit. If $S = \begin{pmatrix} a, & b \\ c, & \partial \end{pmatrix}$ is an arbitrary transformation, then
\[
\begin{pmatrix} a, & b \\ c, & \partial \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} \partial, & -b \\ -c, & a \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} n, & 0 \\ 0, & n \end{pmatrix}
\]
is a multiplication. The two collineations
\[
C = \mathfrak{M}\begin{pmatrix} a, & b \\ c, & \partial \end{pmatrix}, \quad C^{-1} = \mathfrak{M}\begin{pmatrix} \partial, & -b \\ -c, & a \end{pmatrix}
\]
therefore give, on composition, $CC^{-1} = C^{-1}C = \mathfrak{M}$, and so are reciprocal to one another.

\begin{center}
\gesperrt{Accordingly the totality of the collineations forms a group.}
\end{center}

The transformations of degree 1 are called \gesperrt{linear transformations}. For these we denote the transformation numbers, for distinction, by the Greek letters $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta$, so that
\[
L = \begin{pmatrix} \alpha, & \beta \\ \gamma, & \delta \end{pmatrix}, \quad \alpha\delta - \beta\gamma = 1
\]
means a linear transformation. The system $\mathfrak{L}$ of the linear transformations is a group contained in $\mathfrak{S}$; for if
\[
L = \begin{pmatrix} \alpha, & \beta \\ \gamma, & \delta \end{pmatrix}, \quad L' = \begin{pmatrix} \alpha', & \beta' \\ \gamma', & \delta' \end{pmatrix},
\]
then
\[
L'' = L'L = \begin{pmatrix} \alpha'\alpha+\beta'\gamma, & \alpha'\beta+\beta'\delta \\ \gamma'\alpha+\delta'\gamma, & \gamma'\beta+\delta'\delta \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \alpha'', & \beta'' \\ \gamma'', & \delta'' \end{pmatrix}
\]
is likewise linear, and, for given $L'$, $L''$, one can determine $L$ from the equations
\[
\begin{aligned}
\alpha'\alpha+\beta'\gamma &= \alpha'', & \alpha'\beta+\beta'\delta &= \beta'', \\
\gamma'\alpha+\delta'\gamma &= \gamma'', & \gamma'\beta+\delta'\delta &= \delta''
\end{aligned}
\]
uniquely. The unit of the group $\mathfrak{L}$ is the identical substitution $\begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0 \\ 0, & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, and every substitution $L$ has its reciprocal $L^{-1}$, as the composition
\[
LL^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} \alpha, & \beta \\ \gamma, & \delta \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} \delta, & -\beta \\ -\gamma, & \alpha \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0 \\ 0, & 1 \end{pmatrix}
\]
shows. The group $\mathfrak{L}$ is infinite and is \gesperrt{not commutative}.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 120 =====
% !PRINTED 99
\weberpage{99}

From the equation

\weq{8}{\alpha\delta - \beta\gamma = 1}

it follows that neither $\alpha, \beta$ nor $\alpha, \gamma$, nor $\delta, \beta$, nor $\delta, \gamma$ can have a common factor. But if $\alpha, \beta$ have been assumed arbitrarily without a common divisor, then $\gamma, \delta$ can still be determined from (8) in infinitely many ways. If $\gamma, \delta$ is one of these determinations, then they are all contained in the form

\weq{9}{\gamma + \lambda\alpha, \quad \delta + \lambda\beta}

in which $\lambda$ is an arbitrary integer (Bd. I, \S\ 126).

\begin{center}
\S\ 29.\quad\gesperrt{Composition of the transformations from simpler ones.}
\end{center}

In the system $\mathfrak{S}$ of all transformations $S$ there is contained a system $\mathfrak{S}_0$ which consists of all those transformations $S_0$ whose second transformation number is $b = 0$, while $a$ and $\partial$ are \gesperrt{positive}:

\weq{1}{S_0 = \begin{pmatrix} a, & 0 \\ c, & \partial \end{pmatrix}.}

When two $S_0$ are composed there arises again an $S_0$; but $\mathfrak{S}_0$ is nevertheless just as little a group as $\mathfrak{S}$.

One can reduce any arbitrary transformation
\[
S = \begin{pmatrix} p, & q \\ r, & s \end{pmatrix}
\]
to an $S_0$ by a composition $LS$. For if

\weq{2}{\begin{pmatrix} \alpha, & \beta \\ \gamma, & \delta \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} p, & q \\ r, & s \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} a, & 0 \\ c, & \partial \end{pmatrix}}

is to hold, then $\alpha, \beta$ must satisfy the condition:
\[
\alpha q + \beta s = 0,
\]
and accordingly, if $\partial$ is the greatest common divisor of $q$ and $s$, one sets
\[
\partial\alpha = s, \quad \partial\beta = -q,
\]
and, after $\alpha$ and $\beta$ have hereby been ascertained as relatively prime numbers, one determines $\gamma$ and $\delta$ from formula (8), \S\ 28. Then (2) is satisfied if
\[
a\partial = n, \quad c = \gamma p + \delta r
\]
is put; $a$ and $\partial$ are hereby uniquely determined, but $c$ can, for another choice of $\gamma$ and $\delta$, be replaced by $c+\lambda a$. One can therefore dispose of $\lambda$ so that $c$ lies in the sequence
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 121 =====
% !PRINTED 100
\weberpage{100}
%<<CONT
of the numbers 0, 1, 2 \dots $a - 1$, and thereby the substitution
$S_0$ is then \gesperrt{completely determined}.

If the four transformation numbers have a common factor, then
this factor can be separated off by means of the formula
\[
\begin{pmatrix}m, & 0\\0, & m\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}a, & b\\c, & \partial\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}ma, & mb\\mc, & m\partial\end{pmatrix}
\]
through composition with the multiplication, and we accordingly
now assume that $a, b, c, \partial$ \gesperrt{have no common
divisor}. One can then always determine the two
integers $\xi, \eta$ in such a way that
\weq{3}{\begin{gathered} a\eta - c\xi = \alpha\\ b\eta - \partial\xi = \beta \end{gathered}}
are without a common divisor.

To see this, we first assume $\xi, \eta$ to be relatively prime.
Then every common divisor of $\alpha, \beta$ is necessarily a
divisor of $n$, as the solutions of (3)
\weq{4}{\begin{gathered} n\xi = b\alpha - a\beta\\ n\eta = \partial\alpha - c\beta \end{gathered}}
show. If one therefore takes $\xi$ \gesperrt{not divisible} by all the primes
that divide $a$ and $b$ at once, but $\xi$ \gesperrt{divisible} and
$\eta$ \gesperrt{indivisible} by all the other primes that divide $n$,
and moreover $\xi, \eta$ relatively prime, which is always possible, then
$\alpha$ and $\beta$ have no common divisor. Thereupon one determines $\gamma, \delta$
so that
\[
\alpha\delta - \beta\gamma = 1.
\]

By (3) it is then also the case that
\[
(a\delta - b\gamma)\eta - (c\delta - \partial\gamma)\xi = 1,
\]
and the following composition results, as is easily recognised by
use of (4):
\weq{5}{\begin{pmatrix}a, & b\\c, & \partial\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}a\delta - b\gamma, & \xi\\c\delta - \partial\gamma, & \eta\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1, & 0\\0, & n\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\alpha, & \beta\\\gamma, & \delta\end{pmatrix}.}

If we therefore call
\weq{6}{\begin{pmatrix}1, & 0\\0, & n\end{pmatrix}}
the \gesperrt{principal transformation} of degree $n$, then it is thereby proved
\gesperrt{that all transformations of degree $n$ can be composed of a
multiplication, a principal transformation and linear
transformations.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 122 =====
% !PRINTED 101
\weberpage{101}
From the composition
\weq{7}{\begin{pmatrix}1, & 0\\0, & n\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1, & 0\\0, & m\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}1, & 0\\0, & mn\end{pmatrix}, \quad \begin{pmatrix}1, & 0\\0, & n\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}n, & 0\\0, & 1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}n, & 0\\0, & n\end{pmatrix}}
we can conclude further that \gesperrt{every transformation of
degree $n$ can be composed of such transformations as have
prime degree.} If one decomposes $n = pq$ into two factors
 $p$ and $q$ that are relatively prime to one another, then,
determining the numbers $\beta, \delta$ from
\[
p\delta - q\beta = 1
\]
one obtains the composition
\[
\begin{pmatrix}p, & \beta\\q, & \delta\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1, & 0\\0, & n\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}p\delta, & -q\beta\\-1, & 1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}p, & 0\\0, & q\end{pmatrix},
\]
from which it is to be seen that in place of the principal transformation
one may also use any of these transformations $\begin{pmatrix}p, & 0\\0, & q\end{pmatrix}$ for the derivation of all
the others.

§ 30. \gesperrt{The linear fundamental transformations.}

The whole group $\mathfrak{L}$ of linear transformations can be derived
by the repetition of two among them, which we call the \gesperrt{linear
fundamental transformations}.
If
\[
L = \begin{pmatrix}\alpha, & \beta\\\gamma, & \delta\end{pmatrix}, \quad \alpha\delta - \beta\gamma = 1
\]
is an arbitrary linear transformation, then
\weq{1}{\begin{pmatrix}\alpha, & \beta\\\gamma, & \delta\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\delta, & -\beta\\-\gamma, & \alpha\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}1, & 0\\0, & 1\end{pmatrix},}
and since the identical transformation is the unit in the group $L$, % [sic] German source prints L; the group is otherwise denoted $\mathfrak{L}$.
\[
L^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}\delta, & -\beta\\-\gamma, & \alpha\end{pmatrix}
\]
is the \gesperrt{transformation reciprocal to $L$}.

By the power $L^{\pm m}$ we denote that which arises from the $m$-fold
repetition of $L$ or of $L^{-1}$, and we now wish to show
that by the powers of the \gesperrt{fundamental transformations}

\weq{2}{A = \begin{pmatrix}1, & 0\\1, & 1\end{pmatrix}, \quad B = \begin{pmatrix}0, & 1\\-1, & 0\end{pmatrix}}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 123 =====
% !PRINTED 102
\weberpage{102}
%<<CONT
every substitution $L$ of the group $\mathfrak{L}$ can be composed. First of
all we have
\weq{3}{A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}1, & 0\\-1, & 1\end{pmatrix}, \quad A^\lambda = \begin{pmatrix}1, & 0\\\lambda, & 1\end{pmatrix}}
(for every positive or negative integer $\lambda$)
\weq{4}{B^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}0, & -1\\1, & 0\end{pmatrix}, \quad B^2 = \begin{pmatrix}-1, & 0\\0, & -1\end{pmatrix}, \quad B^3 = B^{-1}.}

We further put
\weq{5}{C = \begin{pmatrix}1, & -1\\0, & 1\end{pmatrix} = B^{-1}AB, \quad C^\lambda = \begin{pmatrix}1, & -\lambda\\0, & 1\end{pmatrix},}
$C$ is therefore derivable from $A$ and $B$.

Now let $L = \begin{pmatrix}\alpha, & \beta\\\gamma, & \delta\end{pmatrix}$ be an arbitrary linear transformation.
From it we derive the sequence:
\[
L' = LA^\lambda, \quad L'' = L'C^{\lambda'}, \quad L''' = L''A^{\lambda''}, \quad L'''' = L'''C^{\lambda'''},
\]
whose first and second elements are formed thus:
\[
\begin{gathered}
\alpha' = \alpha + \lambda\beta, \quad \beta'' = \beta' - \lambda'\alpha', \quad \alpha''' = \alpha'' + \lambda''\beta'',\\
\beta'''' = \beta''' - \lambda'''\alpha''', \dots,
\end{gathered}
\]
and one may dispose of $\lambda, \lambda', \lambda'', \lambda''', \dots$ in such a way that, in
absolute value,
\[
\alpha' \leqq \tfrac{1}{2}\beta, \quad \beta'' \leqq \tfrac{1}{2}\alpha', \quad \alpha''' \leqq \tfrac{1}{2}\beta'', \quad \beta'''' \geqq \tfrac{1}{2}\alpha''' \dots, % [sic] Printed \geqq; the stated decreasing sequence requires \leqq.
\]
as long as none of these numbers vanishes. The numbers
\[
\beta, \alpha', \beta'', \alpha''', \beta'''', \dots
\]
therefore form a sequence of numbers decreasing in absolute value, and after a finite number of compositions
of this kind a number of this sequence must vanish.

If $\beta^{(\nu)} = 0$, then
\[
L^{(\nu)} = \begin{pmatrix}\pm 1, & 0\\\gamma^{(\nu)}, & \pm 1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}\pm 1, & 0\\0, & \pm 1\end{pmatrix} A^{\pm\gamma^{(\nu)}}
\]
and if $\alpha^{(\nu)} = 0$, then
\[
L^{(\nu)} = \begin{pmatrix}0, & \pm 1\\\mp 1, & \delta^{(\nu)}\end{pmatrix} = A^{\pm\delta^\nu} B^{\pm 1},
% [sic] German source prints \delta^\nu here; the parallel matrix entry has \delta^{(\nu)}.
\]
and since
\[
\begin{gathered}
L = L'A^{-\lambda} = L''C^{-\lambda'}A^{-\lambda}\\
= L'''A^{-\lambda''}C^{-\lambda'}A^{-\lambda} = L''''C^{-\lambda'''}A^{-\lambda''}C^{-\lambda'}A^{-\lambda}, \dots
\end{gathered}
\]
holds, the theorem is proved.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 124 =====
% !PRINTED 103
\weberpage{103}
§ 31. \gesperrt{The linear fundamental transformations
of the $\vartheta$-functions.}

In the application to the transformation of the $\Theta$-functions
[§ 27, (12)] the transformed modulus
\[
\omega' = \dfrac{c + \partial\omega}{a + b\omega}
\]
first comes into consideration. This does not alter if the four transformation numbers
receive a common factor $m$. The
transformation is called a \gesperrt{proper} one if $a, b, c, \partial$ have no
common factor.

The transformed argument
\[
u' = \dfrac{nu}{a + b\omega}
\]
passes over into $mu'$ if $a, b, c, \partial$ are replaced by $ma, mb, mc, m\partial$, and hence $n$
by $m^2n$. The multiplication $\begin{pmatrix}m, & 0\\0, & m\end{pmatrix}$ leaves the
modulus $\omega$ unchanged and changes $u$ into $mu$.

According to the results of the two preceding sections, the whole system of proper
transformations can be derived by repeated application of the three transformations
\[
\begin{pmatrix}1, & 0\\1, & 1\end{pmatrix}, \quad \begin{pmatrix}0, & 1\\-1, & 0\end{pmatrix}, \quad \begin{pmatrix}n, & 0\\0, & 1\end{pmatrix},
\]
and so we consider first the linear fundamental transformations
of the $\vartheta$-functions.

I. $\begin{pmatrix}1, & 0\\1, & 1\end{pmatrix}$ or $(\omega, \omega + 1)$.

By § 27, (11), (12) we have
\weq{1}{\vartheta_{11}(u, \omega + 1) = A\vartheta_{11}(u, \omega),}
in which $A$ is independent of $u$. If one replaces $u$ by
\[
u + \tfrac{1}{2}, \quad u + \tfrac{\omega}{2}, \quad u + \tfrac{1+\omega}{2},
\]
then the formulae § 21, (8) give
\weq{2}{\vartheta_{10}(u, \omega + 1) = A\vartheta_{10}(u, \omega)}
\weq{3}{e^{\frac{\pi i}{4}}\vartheta_{00}(u, \omega + 1) = A\vartheta_{01}(u, \omega)}
\weq{4}{e^{\frac{\pi i}{4}}\vartheta_{01}(u, \omega + 1) = A\vartheta_{00}(u, \omega).}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 125 =====
% !PRINTED 104
\weberpage{104}
To determine the constant $A$ we employ, as we shall often do in what follows, the device of setting $u = 0$ in (1) after the differentiation, and then, on the right and on the left, of using formula (5), § 23
\weq{5}{\vartheta'_{11} = \pi\,\vartheta_{00}\,\vartheta_{10}\,\vartheta_{01}}
; hence it follows that
\[
A^2 = e^{\frac{\pi i}{2}}, \quad A = e^{\frac{\pi i}{4}};
\]
that the positive sign stands with $A$ follows from one of the formulae (3), (4), according to the closing remark of § 25, if one lets $\omega$ become infinite.

Accordingly one obtains
\weq{6}{\begin{aligned}
\vartheta_{11}(u, \omega+1) &= e^{\frac{\pi i}{4}}\vartheta_{11}(u) \\
\vartheta_{10}(u, \omega+1) &= e^{\frac{\pi i}{4}}\vartheta_{10}(u) \\
\vartheta_{01}(u, \omega+1) &= \vartheta_{00}(u) \\
\vartheta_{00}(u, \omega+1) &= \vartheta_{01}(u).
\end{aligned}}
II. $\begin{pmatrix} 0, & 1 \\ -1, & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ or $\left(\omega, \dfrac{-1}{\omega}\right)$.

Again we have, by § 27, (12),
\weq{7}{e^{-\frac{\pi i u^2}{\omega}}\vartheta_{11}\left(\frac{u}{\omega}, -\frac{1}{\omega}\right) = A\vartheta_{11}(u, \omega),}
and, on increasing $u$ by $\dfrac{1}{2}$, $\dfrac{\omega}{2}$, $\dfrac{1+\omega}{2}$,
\weq{8}{e^{-\frac{\pi i u^2}{\omega}}\vartheta_{01}\left(\frac{u}{\omega}, -\frac{1}{\omega}\right) = iA\vartheta_{10}(u, \omega),}
\weq{9}{e^{-\frac{\pi i u^2}{\omega}}\vartheta_{10}\left(\frac{u}{\omega}, -\frac{1}{\omega}\right) = iA\vartheta_{01}(u, \omega),}
\weq{10}{e^{-\frac{\pi i u^2}{\omega}}\vartheta_{00}\left(\frac{u}{\omega}, -\frac{1}{\omega}\right) = iA\vartheta_{00}(u, \omega),}
from which one obtains, as above:
\[
A = \pm i\sqrt{-i\omega}.
\]
From $u = 0$ and a purely imaginary $\omega$ one concludes that, if $\sqrt{-i\omega}$ is taken so that \gesperrt{the real part is positive, the lower sign must stand}, and there results therefore:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 126 =====
% !PRINTED 105
\weberpage{105}
%<<CONT
\weq{11}{\begin{aligned}
e^{-\frac{\pi i u^2}{\omega}}\vartheta_{11}\left(\frac{u}{\omega}, -\frac{1}{\omega}\right) &= -i\sqrt{-i\omega}\,\vartheta_{11}(u), \\
e^{-\frac{\pi i u^2}{\omega}}\vartheta_{01}\left(\frac{u}{\omega}, -\frac{1}{\omega}\right) &= \sqrt{-i\omega}\,\vartheta_{10}(u), \\
e^{-\frac{\pi i u^2}{\omega}}\vartheta_{10}\left(\frac{u}{\omega}, -\frac{1}{\omega}\right) &= \sqrt{-i\omega}\,\vartheta_{01}(u), \\
e^{-\frac{\pi i u^2}{\omega}}\vartheta_{00}\left(\frac{u}{\omega}, -\frac{1}{\omega}\right) &= \sqrt{-i\omega}\,\vartheta_{00}(u).
\end{aligned}}

\begin{center}
§ 32. \gesperrt{The principal transformations of the second order of the $\vartheta$-functions.}
\end{center}

The two principal transformations of order $n$
\[
\begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0 \\ 0, & n \end{pmatrix}, \quad \begin{pmatrix} n, & 0 \\ 0, & 1 \end{pmatrix}
\]
transform, by § 27, (11), the characteristic $(g_1, g_2)$ into
\[
(ng_1, g_2), \quad (g_1, ng_2),
\]
that is, for odd $n$ the characteristic remains unchanged, while for even $n$ it passes over into
\weq{1}{(0, g_2) \text{ or } (g_1, 0).}
Since the transformation of even degree accordingly behaves essentially otherwise than that of odd degree, we consider first the case $n = 2$. The first and second principal transformation of the second degree are called the \gesperrt{Landen} and the \gesperrt{Gauss} transformation.

By § 27, (12),
\weq{2}{\begin{aligned}
\vartheta_{g_1, g_2}\left(u, \frac{\omega}{2}\right) &= \Theta_{g_1, 0}(u, \omega) \\
\vartheta_{g_1, g_2}(2u, 2\omega) &= \Theta_{0, g_2}(u, \omega)
\end{aligned}}
are $\Theta$-functions of the second order in $u, \omega$, which admit of representation according to § 21.

We obtain first the two pairs of formulae in which $A, B$ are independent of $u$:
\weq{3}{\begin{aligned}
A\vartheta_{11}\left(u, \frac{\omega}{2}\right) &= \vartheta_{01}(u, \omega)\vartheta_{11}(u, \omega), \\
A\vartheta_{10}\left(u, \frac{\omega}{2}\right) &= \vartheta_{00}(u, \omega)\vartheta_{10}(u, \omega),
\end{aligned}}
\weq{4}{\begin{aligned}
B\vartheta_{11}(2u, 2\omega) &= \vartheta_{10}(u, \omega)\vartheta_{11}(u, \omega), \\
B\vartheta_{01}(2u, 2\omega) &= \vartheta_{00}(u, \omega)\vartheta_{01}(u, \omega),
\end{aligned}}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 127 =====
% !PRINTED 106
\weberpage{106}
%<<CONT
of which in each case the second can be derived from the first by increasing the argument by a half period.

If one sets $u = 0$ in these equations, it follows that
\weq{5}{\begin{aligned}
A\vartheta'_{11}\left(0, \frac{\omega}{2}\right) &= \vartheta_{01}\vartheta'_{11}, & 2B\vartheta'_{11}(0, 2\omega) &= \vartheta_{10}\vartheta'_{11}, \\
A\vartheta_{10}\left(0, \frac{\omega}{2}\right) &= \vartheta_{00}\vartheta_{10}, & B\vartheta_{01}(0, 2\omega) &= \vartheta_{00}\vartheta_{01},
\end{aligned}}
from which, by division, and with the use of the relation
\[
\vartheta'_{11} = \pi\,\vartheta_{00}\,\vartheta_{11}\,\vartheta_{01},
% [sic] German source prints \vartheta_{11}; mathematically expected \vartheta_{10}.
\]
\weq{6}{\vartheta_{00}\left(0, \frac{\omega}{2}\right)\vartheta_{01}\left(0, \frac{\omega}{2}\right) = \vartheta_{01}^2,}
\weq{7}{2\vartheta_{00}(0, 2\omega)\vartheta_{10}(0, 2\omega) = \vartheta_{10}^2,}
and, if in (6) one replaces $\omega$ by $2\omega$ and in (7) $\omega$ by $\omega{:}2$:
\weq{8}{\vartheta_{01}(0, 2\omega)^2 = \vartheta_{00}\vartheta_{01},}
\weq{9}{\vartheta_{10}\left(0, \frac{\omega}{2}\right)^2 = 2\vartheta_{00}\vartheta_{10}.}
By (8) and (9) there results from the second equations (5):
\[
2A = \vartheta_{10}\left(0, \frac{\omega}{2}\right), \quad B = \vartheta_{01}(0, 2\omega),
\]
and one thus obtains for the \gesperrt{Gauss transformation}:
\weq{10}{\begin{aligned}
\vartheta_{10}\left(0, \frac{\omega}{2}\right)\vartheta_{11}\left(u, \frac{\omega}{2}\right) &= 2\vartheta_{01}(u, \omega)\vartheta_{11}(u, \omega), \\
\vartheta_{10}\left(0, \frac{\omega}{2}\right)\vartheta_{10}\left(u, \frac{\omega}{2}\right) &= 2\vartheta_{00}(u, \omega)\vartheta_{10}(u, \omega),
\end{aligned}}
and for the \gesperrt{Landen transformation}:
\weq{11}{\begin{aligned}
\vartheta_{01}(0, 2\omega)\vartheta_{11}(2u, 2\omega) &= \vartheta_{10}(u, \omega)\vartheta_{11}(u, \omega), \\
\vartheta_{01}(0, 2\omega)\vartheta_{01}(2u, 2\omega) &= \vartheta_{00}(u, \omega)\vartheta_{01}(u, \omega).
\end{aligned}}
For each of the two transformations there remain two further $\vartheta$-functions to be expressed. These expressions can be derived from (10), (11) after § 21, (13), but one also arrives at them directly in the following way. The functions
\weq{12}{\vartheta_{01}\left(u, \frac{\omega}{2}\right), \quad \vartheta_{10}(2u, 2\omega)}
vanish for
\[
w = \frac{\omega}{4}, \quad u = \frac{1}{4}.
\]
% [sic] German source prints w; the argument variable required by the formulas is u.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 128 =====
% !PRINTED 107
\weberpage{107}
On the other hand, from the formulae (8) of § 21 there follows, if we there set $v = -\dfrac{\omega}{4}$ and $= -\dfrac{1}{4}$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\vartheta_{11}\left(\frac{\omega}{4}\right) &= i\vartheta_{01}\left(\frac{\omega}{4}\right) \\
\vartheta_{11}\left(\frac{1}{4}\right) &= \vartheta_{10}\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)
\end{aligned}
\]
and accordingly the two functions (12), which are linearly expressible by two $\vartheta$-squares, agree, apart from constant factors, with
\[
\vartheta_{01}^2(u) + \vartheta_{11}^2(u), \quad \vartheta_{10}^2(u) - \vartheta_{11}^2(u).
\]
The constant factors are obtained immediately, for $u = 0$, from the relations (6), (7):
\weq{13}{\vartheta_{00}\left(0, \frac{\omega}{2}\right)\vartheta_{01}\left(u, \frac{\omega}{2}\right) = \vartheta_{01}^2(u) + \vartheta_{11}^2(u),}
\weq{14}{2\vartheta_{00}(0, 2\omega)\vartheta_{10}(2u, 2\omega) = \vartheta_{10}^2(u) - \vartheta_{11}^2(u).}
From these one obtains the last two formulae by changing $u$ into $u + \dfrac{1}{2}$ and $u + \dfrac{\omega}{2}$ [or else in the same way as (13), (14)]:
\weq{15}{\vartheta_{00}\left(0, \frac{\omega}{2}\right)\vartheta_{00}\left(u, \frac{\omega}{2}\right) = \vartheta_{00}^2(u) + \vartheta_{10}^2(u),}
\weq{16}{2\vartheta_{00}(0, 2\omega)\vartheta_{00}(2u, 2\omega) = \vartheta_{00}^2(u) + \vartheta_{01}^2(u).}
From these, manifold relations between the zero values of the $\vartheta$-functions can be derived, of which we adduce only the three following ones. The first two of them flow from (8), (9), while the last follows from the first equation (11) if one replaces $\omega$ by $\omega{:}2$, assumes $u = 1/4$, and takes into account that $\vartheta_{11}(1/4) = \vartheta_{10}(1/4)$.
\weq{17}{\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{\vartheta_{00}\vartheta_{01}} &= \vartheta_{01}(0, 2\omega), \\
\sqrt{\vartheta_{00}\vartheta_{10}} &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\vartheta_{10}\left(0, \frac{\omega}{2}\right), \\
\sqrt{\vartheta_{01}\vartheta_{10}} &= \vartheta_{10}\left(\frac{1}{4}, \frac{\omega}{2}\right).
\end{aligned}}
These formulae are of interest because they represent the square roots as single-valued functions of $\omega$.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 129 =====
% !PRINTED 108
\weberpage{108}
We make one further application of the transformation of the second order, to the proof of a formula which is necessary for the transformation of odd order.

In the second equation (10) we replace $\omega$ by $2\omega$, so that:
\[
2\vartheta_{00}(u,\,2\omega)\vartheta_{10}(u,\,2\omega) = \vartheta_{10}\vartheta_{10}(u).
\]
By this we multiply the second equation (11), so that we obtain
\[
2\vartheta_{01}(0,\,2\omega)\vartheta_{01}(2u,\,2\omega)\vartheta_{00}(u,\,2\omega)\vartheta_{10}(u,\,2\omega)
= \vartheta_{10}\vartheta_{10}(u)\vartheta_{00}(u)\vartheta_{01}(u).
\]
This we divide by the product of the two equations (7), (8):
\[
2\vartheta_{00}(0,\,2\omega)\vartheta_{10}(0,\,2\omega)\vartheta_{01}(0,\,2\omega)^2 = \vartheta_{10}^2\vartheta_{00}\vartheta_{01}
\]
and obtain

\weq{18}{\dfrac{\vartheta_{00}(u,\,2\omega)\vartheta_{10}(u,\,2\omega)\vartheta_{01}(2u,\,2\omega)}{\vartheta_{00}(0,\,2\omega)\vartheta_{10}(0,\,2\omega)\vartheta_{01}(0,\,2\omega)} = \dfrac{\vartheta_{00}(u)\vartheta_{10}(u)\vartheta_{01}(u)}{\vartheta_{00}\vartheta_{10}\vartheta_{01}}.}

If now $n$ denotes any \gesperrt{odd} integer, then the function
\[
\vartheta_{01}\left(\frac{\nu}{n}\right),
\]
remains unchanged when $\nu$ increases by a multiple of $n$, and consequently the product
\[
\overset{\nu}{\prod}\ \vartheta_{01}\left(\frac{\nu}{n}\right),
\]
when it is taken over a complete system of residues with respect to the modulus $n$, is independent of the particular choice of this system of residues. Therefore, since $2\nu$ runs through such a system of residues at the same time as $\nu$,

\weq{19}{\prod_{1,\,n-1}^{\nu} \vartheta_{01}\left(\frac{\nu}{n}\right) = \prod_{1,\,n-1}^{\nu} \vartheta_{01}\left(\frac{2\nu}{n}\right).}

If therefore we set $u = \nu:n$ in (18), form the product, and make use of formula (19) in the last factor of the left side, it follows that the product

\weq{20}{\dfrac{\displaystyle\prod_{1,\,n-1}^{\nu} \vartheta_{00}\left(\dfrac{\nu}{n}\right)\vartheta_{10}\left(\dfrac{\nu}{n}\right)\vartheta_{01}\left(\dfrac{\nu}{n}\right)}{\vartheta_{00}^{n-1}\vartheta_{10}^{n-1}\vartheta_{01}^{n-1}}}

remains unchanged when $\omega$ is replaced by $2\omega$.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 130 =====
% !PRINTED 109
\weberpage{109}
The values of $\nu$ occurring in (20) can be arranged in pairs as follows:
\[
\nu,\ n-\nu, \qquad \nu = 1,\ 2,\ \cdots\ \frac{n-1}{2},
\]
and since
\[
\begin{aligned}
\vartheta_{00}\left(\frac{\nu}{n}\right) &= \vartheta_{00}\left(\frac{n-\nu}{n}\right), \quad \vartheta_{10}\left(\frac{\nu}{n}\right) = -\vartheta_{10}\left(\frac{n-\nu}{n}\right), \\
\vartheta_{01}\left(\frac{\nu}{n}\right) &= \vartheta_{01}\left(\frac{n-\nu}{n}\right),
\end{aligned}
\]
(20) agrees, apart from the sign, with the square of

\weq{21}{\dfrac{\displaystyle\prod_{1,\,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{\nu} \vartheta_{00}\left(\dfrac{\nu}{n}\right)\vartheta_{10}\left(\dfrac{\nu}{n}\right)\vartheta_{01}\left(\dfrac{\nu}{n}\right)}{\vartheta_{00}^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\vartheta_{10}^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\vartheta_{01}^{\frac{n-1}{2}}}.}

The last quotient, which is a continuous function of $\omega$ different from zero as long as the imaginary part of $\omega$ is positive, therefore likewise remains unchanged when $\omega$ is replaced by $2\omega$, and hence also by $4\omega$, $8\omega$, $\ldots$. The value of this expression can be determined by taking the imaginary part of $\omega$ to be infinite, and hence assuming $q=0$. But for $q=0$ we have (by § 25):
\[
\vartheta_{00}(v) = 1, \quad \vartheta_{01}(v) = 1, \quad \frac{\vartheta_{10}(v)}{\vartheta_{10}} = \cos\pi v,
\]
and hence the value of (21) is:

\weq{22}{\prod_{1,\,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{\nu} \cos\frac{\nu\pi}{n}.}

Since here $\nu\pi/n$ is less than $\frac{1}{2}\pi$, this product has a positive value. But we have
\[
\cos\frac{\nu\pi}{n} = -\cos\frac{(n-\nu)\pi}{n}
\]
and by Bd. I, § 144 we have
\[
2^{\frac{n-1}{2}} \prod_{1,\,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{\nu} \cos\frac{\nu\pi}{n} = 1.
\]
This proves the formula:

\weq{23}{2^{\frac{n-1}{2}} \prod_{1,\,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{\nu} \vartheta_{00}\left(\frac{\nu}{n}\right)\vartheta_{10}\left(\frac{\nu}{n}\right)\vartheta_{01}\left(\frac{\nu}{n}\right) = \vartheta_{00}^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\vartheta_{10}^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\vartheta_{01}^{\frac{n-1}{2}}.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 131 =====
% !PRINTED 110
\weberpage{110}
With regard to the formula Bd. I, § 145, (3), one may also give this relation the form:

\weq{24}{2^{\frac{n-1}{2}} \prod_{1,\,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{\nu} \vartheta_{00}\left(\frac{2\nu}{n}\right)\vartheta_{10}\left(\frac{2\nu}{n}\right)\vartheta_{01}\left(\frac{2\nu}{n}\right) = (-1)^{\frac{n^2-1}{8}} \vartheta_{00}^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\vartheta_{10}^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\vartheta_{01}^{\frac{n-1}{2}}.}

\S\,33. \gesperrt{The Principal Transformations of Odd Order.}

The formula last proved is of use to us in carrying out the transformation of odd order $n$. We consider first the \gesperrt{first principal transformation}. By § 27, (12),

\weq{1}{\vartheta_{11}(nu,\,n\omega)}

is a $\Theta_{11}$-function of order $n$ in $u$ and $\omega$, and this can easily be formed from its zero points, of which there are $n$ in the period parallelogram. The zero points of (1) are the values
\[
u = \frac{\nu + \mu n\omega}{n} = \frac{\nu}{n} + \mu\omega,
\]
when $\nu$ and $\mu$ are integers, and one obtains all the incongruent ones among these values by holding $\mu$ fixed and letting $\nu$ run through a complete system of residues with respect to the modulus $n$. We choose the system of residues
\[
0,\ \pm 1,\ \pm 2,\ \ldots,\ \pm\frac{(n-1)}{2},
\]
and accordingly obtain, if $C$ denotes a factor independent of $u$,

\weq{2}{C\vartheta_{11}(nu,\,n\omega) = \vartheta_{11}(u) \prod_{1,\,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{\nu} \vartheta_{11}\left(\frac{\nu}{n} + u\right)\vartheta_{11}\left(\frac{\nu}{n} - u\right),}

a formula which, by § 22, (4), can also be expressed in the following way through the functions $\vartheta_{11}(u)$, $\vartheta_{01}(u)$:
\[
C\vartheta_{01}^{n-1}\vartheta_{11}(nu,\,n\omega) = \vartheta_{11}(u) \prod_{1,\,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{\nu} \left[\vartheta_{11}^2\left(\frac{\nu}{n}\right)\vartheta_{01}^2(u) - \vartheta_{01}^2\left(\frac{\nu}{n}\right)\vartheta_{11}^2(u)\right].
\]
We replace $u$ by
\[
u + \frac{1}{2}, \quad u + \frac{\omega}{2}, \quad u + \frac{1+\omega}{2}
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 132 =====
% !PRINTED 111
\weberpage{111}
%<<CONT
and obtain from (8) (§ 21):
\[
C\vartheta_{10}(nu,\,n\omega) = \vartheta_{10}(u) \prod_{1,\,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{\nu} \vartheta_{10}\left(\frac{\nu}{n} + u\right)\vartheta_{10}\left(\frac{\nu}{n} - u\right),
\]

\weq{3}{C\vartheta_{01}(nu,\,n\omega) = \vartheta_{01}(u) \prod_{1,\,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{\nu} \vartheta_{01}\left(\frac{\nu}{n} + u\right)\vartheta_{01}\left(\frac{\nu}{n} - u\right),}

\[
C\vartheta_{00}(nu,\,n\omega) = \vartheta_{00}(u) \prod_{1,\,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{\nu} \vartheta_{00}\left(\frac{\nu}{n} + u\right)\vartheta_{00}\left(\frac{\nu}{n} - u\right).
\]
But from this there follows, for $u = 0$, by the formula $\vartheta_{11}' = \pi\vartheta_{00}\vartheta_{01}\vartheta_{10}$:

% [sic] printed "4)" without an opening parenthesis, unlike the other numbered equations on this page
% [sic] German source prints \vartheta_{01} twice; the third factor is mathematically expected to be \vartheta_{10}.
\weq{4}{C \prod_{1,\,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{\nu} \vartheta_{11}\left(\frac{\nu}{n}\right) = \sqrt{n}\ \prod_{1,\,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{\nu} \vartheta_{00}\left(\frac{\nu}{n}\right)\vartheta_{01}\left(\frac{\nu}{n}\right)\vartheta_{01}\left(\frac{\nu}{n}\right),}

or, using (23) of the preceding section:

\weq{5}{C\,2^{\frac{n-1}{2}} \prod_{1,\,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{\nu} \vartheta_{11}\left(\frac{\nu}{n}\right) = \sqrt{n}\,\vartheta_{00}^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\vartheta_{10}^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\vartheta_{01}^{\frac{n-1}{2}}.}

The sign follows from the circumstance, which results from one of the formulae (3), that $C = 1$ for $q = 0$.

After this determination of $C$ the formulae (2), (3) can be written as follows:

\weq{6}{\sqrt{n}\,\vartheta_{11}(nu,\,n\omega)\vartheta_{00}^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\vartheta_{10}^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\vartheta_{01}^{\frac{n-1}{2}} = 2^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\vartheta_{11}(u) \prod_{1,\,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{\nu} \vartheta_{11}\left(\frac{\nu}{n}\right)\vartheta_{11}\left(\frac{\nu}{n}+u\right)\vartheta_{11}\left(\frac{\nu}{n}-u\right).}

% [sic] German source prints \vartheta_{01} in both product factors of (7); mathematically expected \vartheta_{10} here.
\weq{7}{\sqrt{n}\,\vartheta_{10}(nu,\,n\omega)\vartheta_{00}^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\vartheta_{10}^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\vartheta_{01}^{\frac{n-1}{2}} = 2^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\vartheta_{10}(u) \prod_{1,\,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{\nu} \vartheta_{11}\left(\frac{\nu}{n}\right)\vartheta_{01}\left(\frac{\nu}{n}+u\right)\vartheta_{01}\left(\frac{\nu}{n}-u\right).}

\weq{8}{\sqrt{n}\,\vartheta_{01}(nu,\,n\omega)\vartheta_{00}^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\vartheta_{10}^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\vartheta_{01}^{\frac{n-1}{2}} = 2^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\vartheta_{01}(u) \prod_{1,\,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{\nu} \vartheta_{11}\left(\frac{\nu}{n}\right)\vartheta_{01}\left(\frac{\nu}{n}+u\right)\vartheta_{01}\left(\frac{\nu}{n}-u\right).}

\weq{9}{\sqrt{n}\,\vartheta_{00}(nu,\,n\omega)\vartheta_{00}^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\vartheta_{10}^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\vartheta_{01}^{\frac{n-1}{2}} = 2^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\vartheta_{00}(u) \prod_{1,\,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{\nu} \vartheta_{11}\left(\frac{\nu}{n}\right)\vartheta_{00}\left(\frac{\nu}{n}+u\right)\vartheta_{00}\left(\frac{\nu}{n}-u\right).}
