\begin{center}
\S\ 34. \gesperrt{The functions $\eta(\omega)$, $f(\omega)$, $f_1(\omega)$, $f_2(\omega)$.}
\end{center}

The functions $\eta(\omega)$, $f(\omega)$, $f_1(\omega)$, $f_2(\omega)$ have already
been mentioned in § 24, where, in the representation of the $\vartheta$-functions by
infinite products, they presented themselves almost of their own accord as
single-valued functions of $\omega$, whereas they did not arise in the second
representation by infinite series. Connected with this is a remarkable circumstance:
many of our formulae, for example those belonging to the transformation of the second
order, (17), § 32, or formula (23), § 32, can easily be verified by means of the
infinite products, but with difficulty or not at all by means of the infinite series.
For that reason it was of interest to us to derive these results from the theory of
transformation without making use of either of these expressions, and in the same way
the functions $\eta(\omega)$, $f(\omega)$, $f_1(\omega)$, $f_2(\omega)$ and their
fundamental properties shall now likewise be obtained from this source.

Formula (6) of the preceding section gives for $n=3$:
\[
\sqrt{3}\,\vartheta_{11}(3u,\,3\omega)\,\vartheta_{00}\,\vartheta_{10}\,\vartheta_{01}
= 2\,\vartheta_{11}\!\left(\tfrac{1}{3}\right)\vartheta_{11}(u)\,
\vartheta_{11}\!\left(\tfrac{1}{3}+u\right)\vartheta_{11}\!\left(\tfrac{1}{3}-u\right),
\]
and if one differentiates and then sets $u=0$, one obtains by (4):
\[
3\sqrt{3}\,\vartheta'_{11}(0,\,3\omega) = 2\pi\,\vartheta_{11}\!\left(\tfrac{1}{3}\right)^3,
\]
or, replacing $\omega$ by $\dfrac{\omega}{3}$,
\[
3\sqrt{3}\,\vartheta'_{11} = 2\pi\left[\vartheta_{11}\!\left(\tfrac{1}{3},\,\tfrac{\omega}{3}\right)\right]^3.
\]
If one therefore puts
\weq{1}{\eta(\omega) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\,\vartheta_{11}\!\left(\frac{1}{3},\,\frac{\omega}{3}\right),}
then it follows, in the notation agreeing with § 24 (9):
\weq{2}{\vartheta'_{11} = \pi\,\vartheta_{00}\,\vartheta_{01}\,\vartheta_{10} = 2\pi\,\eta(\omega)^3}
and from § 25, (4) one obtains for $\eta(\omega)$ the series development
\weq{3}{\eta(\omega) = q^{\frac{1}{12}} \sum_{-\infty,\,\infty}^{\nu} (-1)^{\nu}\, q^{3\nu^2+\nu}.}

The function $\eta(\omega)$ is \gesperrt{real} for a purely imaginary $\omega$ (real $q$), and for
an infinitely large $\omega$ (i.\,e. vanishing $q$) we have
\[
q^{-\frac{1}{12}}\,\eta(\omega) = 1.
\]

%% ===== canonical stable idx 134 =====
% !PRINTED 113
\weberpage{113}

Accordingly, if one applies the formulae § 31, (6), (11) in (2), one
finds for the linear fundamental transformations of
$\eta(\omega)$
\weq{4}{\eta(\omega+1) = e^{\frac{\pi i}{12}}\eta(\omega),}
\weq{5}{\eta\left(-\frac{1}{\omega}\right) = \sqrt{-i\omega}\,\eta(\omega),}
of which the first also follows immediately from the series representation
(3), while the second cannot be proved so easily by direct
transformation of the series.

We pass on to the consideration of the two principal transformations
of the second order of the $\eta$-function.

From § 32, (11) one obtains, by differentiation and setting
$u$ equal to zero,
\[ 2\vartheta_{01}(0, 2\omega)\eta(2\omega)^3 = \vartheta_{10}\eta(\omega)^3, \]
hence, if one raises this to the square and applies § 32, (8):
\[ 4\vartheta_{00}\vartheta_{10}\vartheta_{01}\eta(2\omega)^6 = \vartheta_{10}^3\eta(\omega)^6, \]
and, with the application of (2) and extraction of the cube root:
\weq{6}{2\eta(2\omega)^2 = \vartheta_{10}\eta(\omega).}

If in (6) one replaces $\omega$ by $\dfrac{\omega}{2}$, it follows that
\[ 2\eta(\omega)^2 = \vartheta_{10}\left(0, \frac{\omega}{2}\right)\eta\left(\frac{\omega}{2}\right), \]
and if one squares and applies the formula § 32 (9):
\[ 2\eta(\omega)^4 = \eta\left(\frac{\omega}{2}\right)^2\vartheta_{00}\vartheta_{10}. \]

If one multiplies both sides by $\vartheta_{01}$, it follows
by (2):
\weq{7}{\eta\left(\frac{\omega}{2}\right)^2 = \vartheta_{01}\eta(\omega)}
and by changing $\omega$ into $\omega+1$ [(4) and § 31,
(6)]:
\weq{8}{e^{-\frac{\pi i}{12}}\eta\left(\frac{\omega+1}{2}\right)^2 = \vartheta_{00}\eta(\omega).}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 135 =====
% !PRINTED 114
\weberpage{114}

Accordingly we introduce the three functions:
\weq{9}{
\begin{aligned}
f(\omega) &= \frac{e^{-\frac{\pi i}{24}}\eta\left(\dfrac{\omega+1}{2}\right)}{\eta(\omega)},\\
f_1(\omega) &= \frac{\eta\left(\dfrac{\omega}{2}\right)}{\eta(\omega)},\\
f_2(\omega) &= \sqrt{2}\,\frac{\eta(2\omega)}{\eta(\omega)}.
\end{aligned}
}

Then by (6), (7), (8)
\weq{10}{
\begin{aligned}
\vartheta_{00} &= \eta(\omega)f(\omega)^2,\\
\vartheta_{01} &= \eta(\omega)f_1(\omega)^2,\\
\vartheta_{10} &= \eta(\omega)f_2(\omega)^2,
\end{aligned}
}
and from (8) and (9) it follows that $f(\omega)$, $f_1(\omega)$,
$f_2(\omega)$ are real and positive for a purely imaginary $\omega$.
(10) agrees with § 24, (10), and the functions $f$, $f_1$, $f_2$
introduced there are the same as these. But from (10) the relations
follow easily [(2) and § 21 (14)]:
\weq{11}{
\begin{aligned}
f(\omega)^8 &= f_1(\omega)^8 + f_2(\omega)^8,\\
\sqrt{2} &= f(\omega)f_1(\omega)f_2(\omega).
\end{aligned}
}

With the help of these formulae one can express each of the three
functions $f(\omega)^8$, $f_1(\omega)^8$, $f_2(\omega)^8$ by square
roots in terms of any other. The formula flowing from (11) leads to
this:
\weq{12}{
\begin{aligned}
{[f_1(\omega)^8 - f_2(\omega)^8]^2} &= f(\omega)^{16} - \frac{64}{f(\omega)^8},\\
{[f(\omega)^8+f_2(\omega)^8]^2} &= f_1(\omega)^{16} + \frac{64}{f_1(\omega)^8},\\
{[f(\omega)^8+f_1(\omega)^8]^2} &= f_2(\omega)^{16} + \frac{64}{f_2(\omega)^8}.
\end{aligned}
}

For the linear fundamental transformations of the functions $f$ one
obtains first of all from (4) and (9):
\weq{13}{
\begin{aligned}
f(\omega+1) &= e^{-\frac{\pi i}{24}}f_1(\omega),\\
f_1(\omega+1) &= e^{-\frac{\pi i}{24}}f(\omega),\\
f_2(\omega+1) &= e^{\frac{\pi i}{12}}f_2(\omega).
\end{aligned}
}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 136 =====
% !PRINTED 115
\weberpage{115}
Furthermore, there follows from (5) and from the last two equations (9):

\weq{14}{f_1\!\left(-\frac{1}{\omega}\right) = f_2(\omega), \qquad f_2\!\left(-\frac{1}{\omega}\right) = f_1(\omega),}
and if one makes use of this in the second equation (11):

\weq{15}{f\!\left(-\frac{1}{\omega}\right) = f(\omega).}
For the \gesperrt{transformation of the second order} there follows immediately from the last two equations (9):

\weq{16}{f_1(2\,\omega) f_2(\omega) = \sqrt{2},}
from which, by applying (12), there follows further:

\weq{17}{f_2(\omega)^4\left[f(2\,\omega)^8 + f_2(2\,\omega)^8\right] = 2\left[f(\omega)^8 + f_1(\omega)^3\right].}
% [sic] last exponent printed as 3, inconsistent with the surrounding exponents of 8
If in (16) one substitutes, in accordance with (13), (14)
\[
\begin{aligned}
f_1(2\,\omega) &= e^{-\frac{\pi i}{24}} f(2\,\omega - 1),\\
f_2(\omega) &= e^{\frac{\pi i}{24}} f\!\left(1 - \frac{1}{\omega}\right),
\end{aligned}
\]
then there follows:
\[
f\!\left(1 - \frac{1}{\omega}\right) f(2\,\omega - 1) = \sqrt{2},
\]
and on setting $2\,\omega - 1$ equal to a new $\omega$:

\weq{18}{f(\omega) f\!\left(\frac{\omega - 1}{\omega + 1}\right) = \sqrt{2}.}
If in (16) one replaces $\omega$ by $\dfrac{\omega}{2}$ and $\dfrac{\omega+1}{2}$, there follows:

\weq{19}{\begin{aligned}
f_1(\omega) f_2\!\left(\frac{\omega}{2}\right) &= \sqrt{2}, \\
f(\omega) f_2\!\left(\frac{\omega + 1}{2}\right) &= e^{\frac{\pi i}{24}} \sqrt{2}.
\end{aligned}}
Finally we also set up, for an odd $n$, the formulae for the principal transformation of order $n$ of the functions $\eta$, $f$. For $\eta(n\,\omega)$ one obtains this easily by setting $u = 0$ in the formulae (6), \S\,33 after the differentiation and extracting the third root:

\weq{20}{\sqrt{n}\,\eta(n\,\omega)\,\eta(\omega)^{\frac{n-3}{2}} = \prod_{1,\,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{\nu} \vartheta_{11}\!\left(\frac{\nu}{n}\right).}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 137 =====
% !PRINTED 116
\weberpage{116}
If one further sets $u = 0$ in (7), (8), (9), \S\,33, then uses the relations (10) and (20) and extracts the square root, one finds

\weq{21}{\begin{aligned}
f(n\,\omega)\,\eta(\omega)^{\frac{n-1}{2}} &= f(\omega) \prod_{1,\,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{\nu} \vartheta_{00}\!\left(\frac{\nu}{n}\right), \\
f_1(n\,\omega)\,\eta(\omega)^{\frac{n-1}{2}} &= f_1(\omega) \prod_{1,\,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{\nu} \vartheta_{01}\!\left(\frac{\nu}{n}\right), \\
f_2(n\,\omega)\,\eta(\omega)^{\frac{n-1}{2}} &= f_2(\omega) \prod_{1,\,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{\nu} \vartheta_{10}\!\left(\frac{\nu}{n}\right).
\end{aligned}}

The signs follow here from the assumption of an infinitely small $q$.

\begin{center}
\textbf{\S\,35. \gesperrt{The Weierstrass $\sigma$-Function.}}
\end{center}

By the general linear substitution
\[
\begin{pmatrix} \alpha, & \beta \\ \gamma, & \delta \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \alpha\delta - \beta\gamma = 1,
\]
applied to the variables $\omega_1$, $\omega_2$, every $t$-function passes again into a $t$-function % [sic] German source prints italic t twice here where \vartheta is intended., whereby the characteristic has changed. If $(g_1, g_2)$ is the characteristic of the original function and $(g_1', g_2')$ that of the transformed function, then by \S\,27, (11)
\[
(g_1, g_2) = (\delta g_1' - \beta y_2' - \beta\delta,\ -\gamma g_1' + \alpha g_2' - \alpha\gamma).
\]
% [sic] German source prints $y_2'{}$; mathematically expected $g_2'{}$.

If one solves the two linear equations contained in this for $g_1'$, $g_2'$, and observes that $\alpha\beta(\gamma+\delta+1)$, $\gamma\delta(\alpha+\beta+1)$ are necessarily even numbers, and that a characteristic does not change when its elements change by multiples of 2, then one may also write in place of it:

\weq{1}{(g_1', g_2') = (\alpha g_1 + \beta g_2 + \alpha\beta,\ \gamma g_1 + \delta g_2 + \gamma\delta).}

The $\vartheta$-functions therefore pass into one another, apart from exponential factors. It is however of importance to form a function which is \gesperrt{absolutely invariant} with respect to the linear transformations, and such a function is the $\sigma$-function introduced into the theory by \gesperrt{Weierstrass}, to whose definition we now proceed.

If we apply formula (1) to the four principal characteristics. $(0, 0)$, $(0, 1)$, $(1, 0)$, $(1, 1)$, then these pass over, in order,
% [sic] period after "principal characteristics" (German "Hauptcharakteristiken") as printed, where a colon would be expected
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 138 =====
% !PRINTED 117
\weberpage{117}
%<<CONT
successively into $(\alpha\beta, \gamma\delta)$, $[(\alpha+1)\beta, (\gamma+1)\delta]$, $[\alpha(\beta+1), \gamma(\delta+1)]$, $[(\alpha+1)(\beta+1)-1,\ (\gamma+1)(\delta+1)-1)=(1,1)]$.
% [sic] bracket shapes as printed: opens with "[", closes with ")" then "=(1,1)]"
Thus only the last characteristic $(1,1)$ remains unchanged under all linear transformations, since neither $\alpha$ and $\beta$ nor $\gamma$ and $\delta$ can be even numbers at the same time. Let $t(u, \omega_1, \omega_2)$ therefore be a $t$-function of the characteristic $(1,1)$, which by \S\,17, (12) must vanish for $u = 0$.

If
\[
(\omega_1', \omega_2') = \begin{pmatrix} \alpha, & \beta \\ \gamma, & \delta \end{pmatrix} (\omega_1, \omega_2),
\]
then, by our principle of transformation,
\[
t(u, \omega_1, \omega_2) \quad \text{and} \quad t(u, \omega_1', \omega_2')
\]
are related $T$-functions of the first order, and consequently, if $C$, $\lambda$, $\mu$ are quantities independent of $u$,

\weq{2}{t(u,\omega_1',\omega_2') = C e^{\lambda u^2 + \mu u} t(u,\omega_1.\omega_2).}
% [sic] German source prints a period between the period arguments; mathematically expected a comma.
From this there follows by logarithmic differentiation

\weq{3}{2\lambda u + \mu = \frac{d\log t(u,\omega_1',\omega_2')}{du} - \frac{d\log t(u,\omega_1,\omega_2)}{du}.}
Now if we develop in powers of $u$ by \gesperrt{Taylor's} theorem and denote by $t'$, $t''$, $t'''$ the first, second and third derivative of $t$ with respect to $u$ for $u = 0$, then
\[
\frac{d\log t(u,\omega_1,\omega_2)}{du} = \frac{1}{u} + \frac{t''}{2t'} + u\left(\frac{t'''}{3t'} - \frac{t''^2}{4t'^2}\right) + \cdots,
\]
from which it follows by comparison with (3) that $\lambda$ and $\mu$ can be put into the form:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\lambda &= \varphi(\omega_1',\omega_2') - \varphi(\omega_1,\omega_2),\\
\mu &= \psi(\omega_1',\omega_2') - \psi(\omega_1,\omega_2),
\end{aligned}
\]
in which

\weq{4}{\varphi(\omega_1,\omega_2) = \frac{t'''}{6t'} - \frac{t''^2}{8t'^2}, \qquad \psi(\omega_1,\omega_2) = \frac{t''}{2t'}.}
If one determines further the factor $C$ in (2) from the special value $u = 0$, it follows that

\weq{5}{C = \frac{t'(\omega_1',\omega_2')}{t'(\omega_1,\omega_2)}.}
Formula (2) can accordingly be expressed in the following theorem:

\gesperrt{The function}

\weq{6}{\sigma(u,\omega_1,\omega_2) = e^{-u^2\left(\frac{t'''}{6t'} - \frac{t''^2}{8t'^2}\right) - u\,\frac{t''}{2t'}} \frac{t(u,\omega_1,\omega_2)}{t'}}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 139 =====
% !PRINTED 118
\weberpage{118}
%<<CONT
\gesperrt{remains unchanged if one replaces $\omega_1$, $\omega_2$ by $\omega_1'$, $\omega_2'$, that is to say, if one applies any linear transformation whatever, or:}

\weq{7}{\sigma(u,\omega_1',\omega_2') = \sigma(u,\omega_1,\omega_2).}
The function defined by (6) remains unchanged, as a simple calculation shows, if one replaces $t$ by any related $t$-function.

The function $t(u)$ has by hypothesis the characteristic $(1,1)$, and its zero points are therefore congruent with 0. Accordingly $t(-u)$ has the same zero points, and hence also the same character as $t(u)$. The two functions therefore differ from one another only by an exponential factor, and it follows easily, if one determines a constant factor from $u = 0$:
\[
t(-u) = -e^{2\pi i \mu u} t(u),
\]
in which $\mu$ is a constant.

If one differentiates this equation twice with respect to $u$ and then sets $u = 0$, it follows that
\[
2\pi i \mu = -\frac{t''}{t'},
\]
and from this it follows by (6) that the function $\sigma(u)$ satisfies the condition

\weq{8}{\sigma(-u) = -\sigma(u)}
and is therefore an \gesperrt{odd} function of $u$.

Since $\sigma(u)$ is a $t$-function of the first order, it satisfies the two conditions:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sigma(u+\omega_1) &= c_1 e^{\eta_1(2u+\omega_1)} \sigma(u),\\
\sigma(u+\omega_2) &= c_2 e^{\eta_2(2u+\omega_2)} \sigma(u),
\end{aligned}
\]
in which $c_1$, $c_2$, $\eta_1$, $\eta_2$ are constants. The function $\sigma(u)$ vanishes for $u = 0$, but not for $u = \frac{1}{2}\omega_1$, $u = \frac{1}{2}\omega_2$; and so if one sets $u = -\frac{1}{2}\omega_1$, $-\frac{1}{2}\omega_2$ in the foregoing formulae, it follows by (8) that $c_1 = -1$, $c_2 = -1$, and hence the formulae:

\weq{9}{\begin{aligned}
\sigma(u+\omega_1) &= -e^{\eta_1(2u+\omega_1)} \sigma(u), \\
\sigma(u+\omega_2) &= -e^{\eta_2(2u+\omega_2)} \sigma(u).
\end{aligned}}
The $\eta_1$, $\eta_2$ introduced in this way are functions of $\omega_1$, $\omega_2$ which, by the relation \S\,17, (10) (in which $\pi i a_1$, $\pi i a_2$, $m$ are to be replaced by $-\eta_1$, $-\eta_2$, $1$), satisfy the equation:

\weq{10}{\eta_1 \omega_2 - \eta_2 \omega_1 = \pi i.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 140 =====
% !PRINTED 119
\weberpage{119}
By repeated application of (9) it follows, if $a$, $b$ are integers [cf. \S\,17, (16)]:

\weq{11}{\sigma(u+a\omega_1+b\omega_2) = (-1)^{a+b+ab}\,e^{(a\eta_1+b\eta_2)(2u+a\omega_1+b\omega_2)}\,\sigma(u).}
If one develops the function $\sigma(u)$, as it is given by formula (6), in powers of $u$, it is found that not only the second but also the third power of $u$ fails to occur in the development, and one has therefore:

\weq{12}{\sigma(0)=0,\quad \sigma'(0)=1,\quad \sigma''(0)=0,\quad \sigma'''(0)=0.}
If to $\omega_1, \omega_2$ a linear substitution

\weq{13}{(\omega_1', \omega_2') = \begin{pmatrix}\alpha, & \beta\\ \gamma, & \delta\end{pmatrix}(\omega_1, \omega_2)}
is applied, then the quantities $\eta_1, \eta_2$ undergo the corresponding substitution

\weq{14}{(\eta_1', \eta_2') = \begin{pmatrix}\alpha, & \beta\\ \gamma, & \delta\end{pmatrix}(\eta_1, \eta_2),}
as one infers immediately from the relations (7) and (11).

If the formulae (9) are differentiated logarithmically with respect to $u$, there follows

\weq{15}{\begin{aligned}
\frac{\sigma'(u+\omega_1)}{\sigma(u+\omega_1)} &= \frac{\sigma'(u)}{\sigma(u)} + 2\eta_1,\\
\frac{\sigma'(u+\omega_2)}{\sigma(u+\omega_2)} &= \frac{\sigma'(u)}{\sigma(u)} + 2\eta_2,
\end{aligned}}
and by setting, in the first, $u=-\dfrac{\omega_1}{2}$, in the second $u=-\dfrac{\omega_2}{2}$, and observing that $\sigma(u)$ is an odd and consequently $\sigma'(u)$ an even function of $u$:

\weq{16}{\eta_1 = \frac{\sigma'\left(\dfrac{\omega_1}{2}\right)}{\sigma\left(\dfrac{\omega_1}{2}\right)}.\quad \eta_2 = \frac{\sigma'\left(\dfrac{\omega_2}{2}\right)}{\sigma\left(\dfrac{\omega_2}{2}\right)}.}

\begin{center}
\textbf{\S\,36. \gesperrt{The Functions $\sigma_{00}, \sigma_{01}, \sigma_{10}$.}}
\end{center}

It still remains for us to obtain the analogous results for the remaining characteristics. We start from the following remark: if $x_1, x_2$; $y_1, y_2$ are any two pairs of quantities which are transformed by one and the same linear substitution $S$ into $x_1', x_2'$; $y_1', y_2'$, then we have:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 141 =====
% !PRINTED 120
\weberpage{120}
%<<CONT
\[
(x_1', x_2') = \begin{pmatrix}\alpha, & \beta\\ \gamma, & \delta\end{pmatrix}(x_1, x_2); \quad (y_1', y_2') = \begin{pmatrix}\alpha, & \beta\\ \gamma, & \delta\end{pmatrix}(y_1, y_2),
\]
then also

\[
x_1 y_2 - x_2 y_1 = x_1' y_2' - x_2' y_1',
\]
as follows from the multiplication of the determinants. Accordingly, whatever $x_1, x_2$ may be, we have by (7), \S\,35:

\weq{1}{\sigma(u + x_2\omega_1 - x_1\omega_2,\ \omega_1, \omega_2) = \sigma(u + x_2'\omega_1' - x_1'\omega_2',\ \omega_1', \omega_2').}
This function changes in accordance with formula (11) of the preceding section when $x_1, x_2$ are altered by integers. This change can, however, be avoided if instead one considers the function

\[
e^{-2(\eta_1 x_2 - \eta_2 x_1)u}\, \frac{\sigma(u + x_2\omega_1 - x_1\omega_2)}{\sigma(x_2\omega_1 - x_1\omega_2)}
\]
which we shall (for the moment) denote by $\sigma(u, x_1, x_2, \omega_1, \omega_2)$. This function satisfies the conditions:

\weq{2}{\sigma(u, x_1', x_2', \omega_1', \omega_2') = \sigma(u, x_1, x_2, \omega_1, \omega_2),}

\weq{3}{\begin{aligned}
\sigma(u, x_1+1, x_2, \omega_1, \omega_2) &= \sigma(u, x_1, x_2, \omega_1, \omega_2),\\
\sigma(u, x_1, x_2+1, \omega_1, \omega_2) &= \sigma(u, x_1, x_2, \omega_1, \omega_2),
\end{aligned}}

\weq{4}{\begin{aligned}
\sigma(u+\omega_1) &= -e^{-2\pi i x_1}\,e^{\eta_1(2u+\omega_1)}\,\sigma(u),\\
\sigma(u+\omega_2) &= -e^{-2\pi i x_2}\,e^{\eta_2(2u+\omega_2)}\,\sigma(u),
\end{aligned}}
\gesperrt{and it therefore remains unchanged when $x_1$ and $x_2$ are altered by integers.}

Restricting ourselves now once more to the principal characteristics, we set $(x_1, x_2) = \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{1}{2}\right)$, $\left(0, \dfrac{1}{2}\right)$, $\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}, 0\right)$ and obtain in this way the following three functions:

\weq{5}{\begin{aligned}
\sigma_{00}(u) &= \sigma\left(u, -\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}, \omega_1, \omega_2\right) = e^{-(\eta_1+\eta_2)u}\,\frac{\sigma\left(u+\dfrac{\omega_1+\omega_2}{2}\right)}{\sigma\left(\dfrac{\omega_1+\omega_2}{2}\right)},\\
\sigma_{10}(u) &= \sigma\left(u, 0, \frac{1}{2}, \omega_1, \omega_2\right) = e^{-\eta_1 u}\,\frac{\sigma\left(u+\dfrac{\omega_1}{2}\right)}{\sigma\left(\dfrac{\omega_1}{2}\right)},\\
\sigma_{01}(u) &= \sigma\left(u, -\frac{1}{2}, 0, \omega_1, \omega_2\right) = e^{-\eta_2 u}\,\frac{\sigma\left(u+\dfrac{\omega_2}{2}\right)}{\sigma\left(\dfrac{\omega_2}{2}\right)},
\end{aligned}}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 142 =====
% !PRINTED 121
\weberpage{121}
%<<CONT
and the function $\sigma(u)$ itself may accordingly also be denoted by $\sigma_{11}(u)$.

For these functions there follow from (4) the characteristic period equations

\weq{6}{\begin{aligned}
\sigma_{g_1,g_2}(u+\omega_1) &= (-1)^{g_1}\,e^{\eta_1(2u+\omega_1)}\,\sigma_{g_1,g_2}(u),\\
\sigma_{g_1,g_2}(u+\omega_2) &= (-1)^{g_2}\,e^{\eta_2(2u+\omega_2)}\,\sigma_{g_1,g_2}(u),\\
\sigma_{g_1,g_2}(u+a\omega_1+b\omega_2) &= (-1)^{g_1 a+g_2 b+ab}\,e^{(a\eta_1+b\eta_2)(2u+a\omega_1+b\omega_2)}\,\sigma_{g_1,g_2}(u).
\end{aligned}}

By the application of a linear transformation the three functions $\sigma_{00}, \sigma_{01}, \sigma_{10}$ are permuted among one another, as formula (2) teaches [or \S\,35, (1)]. According to this permutation the linear transformations split into \gesperrt{six classes}, the first of which comprises all those transformations that leave the functions $\sigma_{00}, \sigma_{01}, \sigma_{10}$ unchanged. These are characterized by the fact that $\alpha, \delta$ are odd and $\beta, \gamma$ even numbers, which we write briefly thus:

\[
\begin{pmatrix}\alpha, & \beta\\ \gamma, & \delta\end{pmatrix} \equiv \begin{pmatrix}1, & 0\\ 0, & 1\end{pmatrix} (\mathrm{mod}\ 2).
\]

Accordingly the six classes of linear transformations are to be characterized as follows:

\weq{7}{\begin{aligned}
&\text{I.}\quad \begin{pmatrix}\alpha, & \beta\\ \gamma, & \delta\end{pmatrix} \equiv \begin{pmatrix}1, & 0\\ 0, & 1\end{pmatrix} (\mathrm{mod}\ 2)\quad (00, 01, 10),\\
&\text{II.}\quad \text{,,} \equiv \begin{pmatrix}0, & 1\\ -1, & 0\end{pmatrix} \quad \text{,,}\quad (00, 10, 01),\\
&\text{III.}\quad \text{,,} \equiv \begin{pmatrix}1, & 1\\ -1, & 0\end{pmatrix} \quad \text{,,}\quad (10, 00, 01),\\
&\text{IV.}\quad \text{,,} \equiv \begin{pmatrix}1, & 1\\ 0, & 1\end{pmatrix} \quad \text{,,}\quad (10, 01, 00),\\
&\text{V.}\quad \text{,,} \equiv \begin{pmatrix}1, & 0\\ 1, & 1\end{pmatrix} \quad \text{,,}\quad (01, 00, 10),\\
&\text{VI.}\quad \text{,,} \equiv \begin{pmatrix}0, & 1\\ -1, & 1\end{pmatrix} \quad \text{,,}\quad (01, 10, 00),
\end{aligned}}
where in the last column the permutation of the characteristics 00, 01, 10 occurring in each case is set out.

The transformations of the first class form a group $\mathfrak{A}$ contained in the group of \gesperrt{all} linear substitutions, and hence a divisor of the group $\mathfrak{L}$ (\S\,28). If we set
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 143 =====
% !PRINTED 122
\weberpage{122}
%<<CONT
\[
\alpha_1 = \begin{pmatrix}1, & 0\\ 0, & 1\end{pmatrix}, \quad \alpha_2 = \begin{pmatrix}0, & 1\\ -1, & 0\end{pmatrix}, \quad \alpha_3 = \begin{pmatrix}1, & 1\\ -1, & 0\end{pmatrix},
\]
\[
\alpha_4 = \begin{pmatrix}1, & 1\\ 0, & 1\end{pmatrix}, \quad \alpha_5 = \begin{pmatrix}1, & 0\\ 1, & 1\end{pmatrix}, \quad \alpha_6 = \begin{pmatrix}0, & 1\\ -1, & 1\end{pmatrix},
\]
then $\alpha_1\mathfrak{A}, \alpha_2\mathfrak{A}, \alpha_3\mathfrak{A}, \alpha_4\mathfrak{A}, \alpha_5\mathfrak{A}, \alpha_6\mathfrak{A}$ are the subsidiary groups to $\mathfrak{A}$, and we have

\[
\mathfrak{L} = \alpha_1\mathfrak{A} + \alpha_2\mathfrak{A} + \alpha_3\mathfrak{A} + \alpha_4\mathfrak{A} + \alpha_5\mathfrak{A} + \alpha_6\mathfrak{A}
\]
and $\mathfrak{A}$ is a divisor of $\mathfrak{L}$ of finite index 6:

\[
(\mathfrak{L}, \mathfrak{A}) = 6 \quad (\text{Bd.\ II}, \ \S\,2).
\]
The totality $\alpha_1\mathfrak{A} + \alpha_2\mathfrak{A}$ is likewise a group $\mathfrak{A}'$, and we have

\[
\mathfrak{L} = \alpha_1\mathfrak{A}' + \alpha_3\mathfrak{A}' + \alpha_4\mathfrak{A}'
\]
and $(\mathfrak{L}, \mathfrak{A}') = 3$.

\gesperrt{Just as all the linear transformations may be derived from the two fundamental transformations, so the transformations of the first class may be derived from repeated application of}

\[
\begin{pmatrix}1, & 0\\ 2, & 1\end{pmatrix}, \quad \begin{pmatrix}1, & 2\\ 0, & 1\end{pmatrix}, \quad \begin{pmatrix}-1, & 0\\ 0, & -1\end{pmatrix}
\]
\gesperrt{which can be proved by the method of \S\,30.}

\begin{center}
\S\,37. \gesperrt{Representation of the $\sigma$-functions by $\vartheta$-functions.}
\end{center}

In order to represent the function $\sigma(u)$ as a $\vartheta$-function, one can simply apply formula (6) of \S\,35 to the function

\[
t(u) = \vartheta_{11}\left(\frac{u}{\omega_1}, \frac{\omega_2}{\omega_1}\right)
\]
and thus set

\weq{1}{\sigma(u, \omega_1, \omega_2) = \omega_1\, e^{-\dfrac{u^2}{6\omega_1^2}\,\dfrac{\vartheta_{11}'''}{\vartheta_{11}'}}\; \frac{\vartheta_{11}\left(\dfrac{u}{\omega_1}, \dfrac{\omega_2}{\omega_1}\right)}{\vartheta_{11}'}}
But in consequence of the differential equation \S\,20, (4), we have:

\[
\vartheta_{11}''' = 4\pi i\, \frac{d\vartheta_{11}'}{d\omega}
\]
and hence, by the definition of the function $\eta(\omega)$ in \S\,34, (2):

\weq{2}{\frac{\vartheta_{11}'''}{\vartheta_{11}'} = 4\pi i\, \frac{d\log \vartheta_{11}'}{d\omega} = 12\pi i\, \frac{d\log \eta(\omega)}{d\omega}.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 144 =====
% !PRINTED 123
\weberpage{123}

By logarithmic differentiation of (1) one obtains, by means of (2):
\[
\frac{d\log\sigma(u)}{du} = -\frac{4\pi i u}{\omega_1^2}\,\frac{d\log\eta(\omega)}{d\omega} + \frac{d\log\vartheta_{11}\left(\dfrac{u}{\omega_1},\dfrac{\omega_2}{\omega_1}\right)}{du},
\]
and if one here sets $u = \dfrac{\omega_1}{2}, \dfrac{\omega_2}{2}$ and applies the formulae (8) of § 21, then by § 35, (16):
\weq{3}{\begin{aligned}
\eta_1 &= -\frac{2\pi i}{\omega_1}\,\frac{d\log\eta(\omega)}{d\omega}, \\
\eta_2 &= -\frac{2\pi i \omega_2}{\omega_1^2}\,\frac{d\log\eta(\omega)}{d\omega} - \frac{\pi i}{\omega_1}.
\end{aligned}}
Accordingly one may set for $\sigma$:
\weq{4}{\sigma(u) = \omega_1\, e^{\frac{\eta_1 u^2}{\omega_1}}\,\frac{\vartheta_{11}\left(\dfrac{u}{\omega_1},\dfrac{\omega_2}{\omega_1}\right)}{\vartheta_{11}'},}
and for the three functions $\sigma_{00}, \sigma_{01}, \sigma_{10}$ one obtains by § 36, (5), when one determines a constant factor from
\weq{5}{\sigma_{00}(0) = 1, \quad \sigma_{01}(0) = 1, \quad \sigma_{10}(0) = 1}
the following:
\weq{6}{\begin{aligned}
\sigma_{00}(u) &= e^{\frac{\eta_1 u^2}{\omega_1}}\,\frac{\vartheta_{00}\left(\dfrac{u}{\omega_1},\dfrac{\omega_2}{\omega_1}\right)}{\vartheta_{00}}, \\
\sigma_{01}(u) &= e^{\frac{\eta_1 u^2}{\omega_1}}\,\frac{\vartheta_{01}\left(\dfrac{u}{\omega_1},\dfrac{\omega_2}{\omega_1}\right)}{\vartheta_{01}}, \\
\sigma_{10}(u) &= e^{\frac{\eta_1 u^2}{\omega_1}}\,\frac{\vartheta_{10}\left(\dfrac{u}{\omega_1},\dfrac{\omega_2}{\omega_1}\right)}{\vartheta_{10}}.
\end{aligned}}
The functions $\sigma_{00}(u)$, $\sigma_{01}(u)$, $\sigma_{10}(u)$ are \gesperrt{even functions} of $u$, and by twofold differentiation of the logarithms of (6) there results further [by (3) and § 34, (2)]:
\weq{7}{\sigma_{00}''(0) + \sigma_{01}''(0) + \sigma_{10}''(0) = 0.}
The expressions (4), (6) reveal at first glance an important property of the $\sigma$-functions, namely that $\sigma_{00}, \sigma_{01}, \sigma_{10}$ depend only on the \gesperrt{ratios} $u:\omega_1:\omega_2$, while for $\sigma$ the same holds apart from the factor $\omega_1$. Thus $\sigma$, $\sigma_{00}$, $\sigma_{01}$, $\sigma_{10}$ are \gesperrt{homogeneous functions of the three}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 145 =====
% !PRINTED 124
\weberpage{124}

%<<CONT
variables $u$, $\omega_1$, $\omega_2$, the former of the first order, the three others of the zeroth order, or, in symbols, if $\lambda$ denotes an arbitrary factor:
% [sic] German source prints u_1 on all four left-hand sides; mathematically expected u.
\weq{8}{\begin{aligned}
\sigma(\lambda u_1, \lambda \omega_1, \lambda \omega_2) &= \lambda \sigma(u, \omega_1, \omega_2), \\
\sigma_{00}(\lambda u_1, \lambda \omega_1, \lambda \omega_2) &= \sigma_{00}(u, \omega_1, \omega_2), \\
\sigma_{01}(\lambda u_1, \lambda \omega_1, \lambda \omega_2) &= \sigma_{01}(u, \omega_1, \omega_2), \\
\sigma_{10}(\lambda u_1, \lambda \omega_1, \lambda \omega_2) &= \sigma_{10}(u, \omega_1, \omega_2).
\end{aligned}}

\begin{center}
§ 38. \gesperrt{Linear Transformations of the Function $\eta(\omega)$.}
\end{center}

The formulae (3), § 37 lead to the linear transformation of the function $\eta(\omega)$. For if
\weq{1}{(\omega_1', \omega_2') = \begin{pmatrix}\alpha, & \beta\\ \gamma, & \delta\end{pmatrix}(\omega_1, \omega_2)}
is set, then $(\eta_1, \eta_2)$ passes over into
\weq{2}{(\eta_1', \eta_2') = \begin{pmatrix}\alpha, & \beta\\ \gamma, & \delta\end{pmatrix}(\eta_1, \eta_2)}
[§ 35, (14)], and $\omega = \omega_2 : \omega_1$ into
\weq{3}{\omega' = \frac{\gamma + \delta\omega}{\alpha + \beta\omega}.}
Now from (2), having regard to (3) of the preceding section, there follows:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\eta_1' &= -\frac{2\pi i}{\omega_1'}\,\frac{d\log\eta(\omega')}{d\omega'} = -\frac{2\pi i \omega_1'}{\omega_1^2}\,\frac{d\log\eta(\omega)}{d\omega} - \frac{\pi i \beta}{\omega_1}, \\
\eta_2' &= -\frac{2\pi i \omega_2'}{{\omega_1'}^2}\,\frac{d\log\eta(\omega')}{d\omega'} - \frac{\pi i}{\omega_1'} = -\frac{2\pi i \omega_2'}{\omega_1^2}\,\frac{d\log\eta(\omega)}{d\omega} - \frac{\pi i \delta}{\omega_1},
\end{aligned}
\]
and these two relations agree in giving
\[
\frac{d\log\eta(\omega')}{{\omega_1'}^2\,d\omega'} = \frac{d\log\eta(\omega)}{\omega_1^2\,d\omega} + \frac{\beta}{2\omega_1\omega_1'},
\]
or finally, since by (3)
\[
d\omega' = \frac{d\omega}{(\alpha+\beta\omega)^2}, \quad {\omega_1'}^2\,d\omega' = \omega_1^2\,d\omega,
\]
\[
\frac{d\log\eta(\omega')}{d\omega} = \frac{d\log\eta(\omega)}{d\omega} + \frac{\beta}{2(\alpha+\beta\omega)}.
\]
From this it follows by integration:
\weq{4}{\eta\left(\frac{\gamma+\delta\omega}{\alpha+\beta\omega}\right) = \varepsilon\sqrt{\alpha+\beta\omega}\ \eta(\omega),}
in which $\varepsilon$ is a quantity independent of $\omega$, and therefore depending only on the numbers $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$, $\delta$.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 146 =====
% !PRINTED 125
\weberpage{125}

The exact determination of this constant $\varepsilon$, especially with regard to the sign as well, is a well-known and important problem which presents peculiar difficulties; its solution, however, is indispensable for us. Solutions have been given along various routes by \gesperrt{Hermite}\footnote{Liouvilles Journal, Ser.\,II, T.\,III, 1858. Oeuvres de \gesperrt{Charles Hermite}, p.\,487.} and \gesperrt{Dedekind}\footnote{Erläuterungen zu Nr.\,XXVIII von \gesperrt{Riemanns Werken}, second edition, and \glqq{}Über die elliptischen Modulfunktionen\grqq{}, Crelles Journal, Bd.\,83, S.\,265. Cf. also the author's memoir \glqq{}Zur Theorie der elliptischen Funktionen\grqq{}, Acta Mathematica, Bd.\,6, S.\,341\,ff.}, and more recently also by \gesperrt{Mertens} and \gesperrt{Scheibner}\footnote{\gesperrt{Mertens}, Zur linearen Transformation der $\vartheta$-Reihen, Transactions of the American mathematical society. July 1901. — \gesperrt{Scheibner}, Zur linearen Transformation der Theta-Funktionen und elliptischen Modulfunktionen, Berichte der Sächs. Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften. Oktober 1906.}. We wish here to follow a route which has the advantage of great simplicity, but which for that very reason contains no derivation, but only a proof of the finished formula.

For two special cases we have already carried out this determination earlier [§ 34, (4), (5)], and it is upon this result that we shall rely here. They are the formulae:
\weq{5}{\eta(\omega \pm 1) = e^{\pm\frac{\pi i}{12}}\,\eta(\omega)}
and
\weq{6}{\eta\left(-\frac{1}{\omega}\right) = \sqrt{-i\omega}\ \eta(\omega),}
where $\sqrt{-i\omega}$ is to be taken \gesperrt{with positive real part}.

We now set
\weq{7}{\frac{\eta\left(\dfrac{\gamma+\delta\omega}{\alpha+\beta\omega}\right)}{\eta(\omega)} = E\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\alpha, & \beta\\ \gamma, & \delta\end{smallmatrix}, \omega\right),}
and have to determine the value of this symbol. By (5), (6), (7) we have:
\weq{8}{E\left(\begin{smallmatrix}-\alpha, & -\beta\\ -\gamma, & -\delta\end{smallmatrix}, \omega\right) = E\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\alpha, & \beta\\ \gamma, & \delta\end{smallmatrix}, \omega\right),}
\weq{9}{E\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1, & 0\\ 0, & 1\end{smallmatrix}, \omega\right) = 1,}
\weq{10}{E\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1, & 0\\ \pm 1, & 1\end{smallmatrix}, \omega\right) = e^{\pm\frac{\pi i}{12}},}
\weq{11}{E\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0, & 1\\ -1, & 0\end{smallmatrix}, \omega\right) = \sqrt{-i\omega}.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 147 =====
% !PRINTED 126
\weberpage{126}

We now consider two substitutions and the one composed of both, thus:
\[
\begin{pmatrix}\alpha'', & \beta''\\ \gamma'', & \delta''\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}\alpha', & \beta'\\ \gamma', & \delta'\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\alpha, & \beta\\ \gamma, & \delta\end{pmatrix}.
\]
If then
\[
\omega' = \frac{\gamma+\delta\omega}{\alpha+\beta\omega},
\]
there results from the definition (7):
\weq{12}{E\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\alpha'', & \beta''\\ \gamma'', & \delta''\end{smallmatrix}, \omega\right) = E\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\alpha', & \beta'\\ \gamma', & \delta'\end{smallmatrix}, \omega'\right) E\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\alpha, & \beta\\ \gamma, & \delta\end{smallmatrix}, \omega\right),}
and from this two special cases, by putting
\[
\begin{pmatrix}\alpha, & \beta\\ \gamma, & \delta\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}1, & 0\\ \pm 1, & 1\end{pmatrix}, \ \begin{pmatrix}0, & 1\\ -1, & 0\end{pmatrix}
\]
and writing $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$, $\delta$ again in place of $\alpha'$, $\beta'$, $\gamma'$, $\delta'$, thus
\[
\begin{pmatrix}\alpha'', & \beta''\\ \gamma'', & \delta''\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}\alpha\pm\beta, & \beta\\ \gamma\pm\delta, & \delta\end{pmatrix}, \ \begin{pmatrix}-\beta, & \alpha\\ -\delta, & \gamma\end{pmatrix}\text{:}
\]
\weq{13}{E\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\alpha\pm\beta, & \beta\\ \gamma\pm\delta, & \delta\end{smallmatrix}, \omega\right) = e^{\pm\frac{\pi i}{12}}\,E\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\alpha, & \beta\\ \gamma, & \delta\end{smallmatrix}, \omega\pm 1\right),}
\weq{14}{E\left(\begin{smallmatrix}-\beta, & \alpha\\ -\delta, & \gamma\end{smallmatrix}, \omega\right) = \sqrt{-i\omega}\ E\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\alpha, & \beta\\ \gamma, & \delta\end{smallmatrix}, \frac{-1}{\omega}\right).}
It has now been shown in § 30 that \gesperrt{all} linear transformations can be composed by repeated application of the two fundamental transformations
\[
\begin{pmatrix}1, & 0\\ 1, & 1\end{pmatrix}, \ \begin{pmatrix}0, & 1\\ -1, & 0\end{pmatrix}
\]
and of their inverse transformations, and from this it follows on the basis of (12) that the \gesperrt{symbol $E$ is completely defined by the formulae (8) to (14).}

If, then, we know an expression satisfying these conditions, it must agree with $E$. In order to set up such an expression, we distinguish two cases. Since $\alpha$, $\beta$ are relatively prime numbers, one of them is certainly odd. We put:

1. \gesperrt{$\alpha$ odd and positive:}
\weq{15}{\begin{aligned}
E\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\alpha, & \beta\\ \gamma, & \delta\end{smallmatrix}, \omega\right) &= \left(\frac{\beta}{\alpha}\right) i^{\frac{\alpha-1}{2}} e^{\frac{\pi i}{12}[\alpha(\gamma-\beta)-(\alpha^2-1)\beta\delta]}\,\sqrt{(\alpha+\beta\omega)};
\end{aligned}}
2. \gesperrt{$\beta$ odd and positive:}
\[
E\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\alpha, & \beta\\ \gamma, & \delta\end{smallmatrix}, \omega\right) = \left(\frac{\alpha}{\beta}\right) i^{\frac{1-\beta}{2}} e^{\frac{\pi i}{12}[\beta(\alpha+\delta)-(\beta^2-1)\alpha\gamma]}\,\sqrt{-i(\alpha+\beta\omega)},
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 148 =====
% !PRINTED 127
\weberpage{127}
%<<CONT
to which the following is still to be remarked: the roots $\sqrt{\alpha+\beta\omega}$,
$\sqrt{-i(\alpha+\beta\omega)}$ are to be taken with \gesperrt{positive} real part.
That one of them should be purely imaginary is excluded by the assumption
that $\omega$ has a positive imaginary part and that $\alpha$, or $\beta$
respectively, is positive; for accordingly $\alpha+\beta\omega$ or $-i(\alpha+\beta\omega)$
cannot be real and negative; $\left(\dfrac{\beta}{\alpha}\right)$ and
$\left(\dfrac{\alpha}{\beta}\right)$ is the \gesperrt{Legendre-Jacobi} symbol
from the theory of quadratic residues, with the extension that
$\left(\dfrac{\beta}{1}\right)$ and $\left(\dfrac{0}{1}\right)=1$ shall hold. If
in the first case $\alpha$, or in the second $\beta$, is negative, then on the right
all the signs of $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta$ must be reversed.
If both $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are odd, then (15), 1. as well as (15), 2.
may be applied, and both yield, as one easily proves on the basis
of the law of reciprocity for quadratic residues, the same
 result. For, if $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are odd,
$\alpha$ is taken positive, and the upper or lower sign
holds according as $\beta$ is positive or negative, we have:
\[
\left(\frac{\beta}{\alpha}\right)\left(\frac{\pm\alpha}{\pm\beta}\right)
= \pm\, e^{-\frac{\pi i}{4}(\alpha\mp1)(\beta-1)},
\]
\[
\sqrt{\mp i(\alpha+\beta\omega)} = e^{\mp\frac{\pi i}{4}}\sqrt{\alpha+\beta\omega}
\]
and the identity of (15), 1., 2. then follows from the congruences

\[
\begin{gathered}
-3\alpha\beta+\beta(\alpha+\delta)-(\beta^2-1)\alpha\gamma \equiv \alpha(\gamma-\beta)-(\alpha^2-1)\beta\delta \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 24), \\
\alpha\gamma+\alpha\beta \equiv \beta\delta \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 8),
\end{gathered}
\]
of which the second holds also for the modulus 24 whenever $\alpha$ and $\beta$
are both not divisible by 3, so that $\alpha^2\equiv\beta^2\equiv1 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 3)$.

That the formulae (8) to (11) are satisfied by (15) is
immediately evident, and it still remains to be shown that (13)
and (14) are fulfilled. We begin with (14), where it may be
assumed that $\alpha$ is odd (and positive); for if one interchanges
$\omega$ in (14) with $-1:\omega$, then $\alpha$ and $-\beta$ are interchanged, and
these cannot both be even.

We have
\[
\sqrt{-i\omega}\ \sqrt{\alpha-\frac{\beta}{\omega}} = \sqrt{-i(-\beta+\alpha\omega)};
\]
for if we set for the moment
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 149 =====
% !PRINTED 128
\weberpage{128}
%<<CONT
\[
-i\omega = r\,e^{i\varphi}, \qquad \alpha-\frac{\beta}{\omega} = \varrho\,e^{i\psi}
\]
\[
-i(-\beta+\alpha\omega) = r\varrho\,e^{i(\varphi+\psi)},
\]
then, since the real parts of $-i\omega$, $-i(-\beta+\alpha\omega)$ are positive,
\[
-\frac{\pi}{2} < \varphi < \frac{\pi}{2}, \quad -\pi < \psi < \pi, \quad
-\frac{\pi}{2} < \varphi+\psi < \frac{\pi}{2},
\]
\[
\sqrt{-i\omega} = \sqrt{r}\,e^{\frac{i\varphi}{2}}, \qquad
\sqrt{\alpha-\frac{\beta}{\omega}} = \sqrt{\varrho}\,e^{\frac{i\psi}{2}},
\]
and the real part of
\[
\sqrt{-i\omega}\ \sqrt{\alpha-\frac{\beta}{\omega}} = \sqrt{-i(-\beta+\alpha\omega)}
= \sqrt{r\varrho}\,e^{\frac{i(\varphi+\psi)}{2}}
\]
is positive. Accordingly there results from (15), 1:
\[
\sqrt{-i\omega}\, E\!\left(\begin{matrix}\alpha, & \beta \\ \gamma, & \delta\end{matrix}, \frac{-1}{\omega}\right)
= \left(\frac{\beta}{\alpha}\right) i^{\frac{\alpha-1}{2}}
e^{\frac{\pi i}{12}\left[\alpha(\gamma-\beta)-(\alpha^2-1)\beta\delta\right]}
\sqrt{-i(-\beta+\alpha\omega)}.
\]

The same formula, however, is obtained, since $\left(\dfrac{-\beta}{\alpha}\right)=i^{(\alpha-1)}\left(\dfrac{\beta}{\alpha}\right)$,
from (15), 2. for
\[
E\!\left(\begin{matrix}-\beta, & \alpha \\ -\delta, & \gamma\end{matrix}, \omega\right),
\]
and with that (14) is proved.

There still remains formula (13). It is enough to take account of the
upper signs alone, that is, to prove the formula
\[
E\!\left(\begin{matrix}\alpha+\beta, & \beta \\ \gamma+\delta, & \delta\end{matrix}, \omega\right)
= e^{\frac{\pi i}{12}} E\!\left(\begin{matrix}\alpha, & \beta \\ \gamma, & \delta\end{matrix}, \omega+1\right)
\]
since the other case reduces to this one by the interchange of $\alpha, \gamma, \omega$
with $\alpha+\beta, \gamma+\delta, \omega+1$. If in the first place
$\beta$ is odd (and positive), then (13) follows from (15), 2. on the
basis of the congruence
\[
(\beta^2-1)(1-\beta\gamma-\alpha\delta-\beta\delta) \equiv -\beta(\beta^2-1)(2\gamma+\delta) \equiv 0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 24).
\]

If $\beta$ is even, then $\alpha$ is odd. If we take $\alpha$ positive, then
$\alpha+\beta$ can be positive or negative. If in the first case the
upper signs hold, in the second the lower, then (15), 1 gives us
\weq{16}{
e^{\frac{i\pi}{12}} E\!\left(\begin{matrix}\alpha, & \beta \\ \gamma, & \delta\end{matrix}, \omega+1\right)
= \left(\frac{\beta}{\alpha}\right) i^{-\frac{1-\alpha}{2}}
e^{\frac{\pi i}{12}\left[1+\alpha(\gamma-\beta)-(\alpha^2-1)\beta\delta\right]}
\sqrt{\alpha+\beta+\beta\omega},
}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 150 =====
% !PRINTED 129
\weberpage{129}
%<<CONT
\weq{17}{
E\!\left(\begin{matrix}\alpha+\beta, & \beta \\ \gamma+\delta, & \delta\end{matrix}, \omega\right)
= \left(\frac{\pm\beta}{\pm(\alpha+\beta)}\right)
i^{-\frac{1\mp(\alpha+\beta)}{2}}
e^{\frac{\pi i}{12}\left\{(\alpha+\beta)(\gamma+\delta-\beta)-[(\alpha+\beta)^2-1]\beta\delta\right\}}
\sqrt{\pm(\alpha+\beta+\beta\omega)}.
}
Now, if the lower signs hold, $\beta$ is negative, and if accordingly
\[
-(\alpha+\beta+\beta\omega) = r\,e^{i\varphi}
\]
\[
i(\alpha+\beta+\beta\omega) = r\,e^{i\left(\varphi-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)}
\]
is set, then $\dfrac{\varphi}{2}$ and $\dfrac{\varphi}{2}-\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ lie between $-\dfrac{\pi}{2}$
and $+\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, and from this it follows that we have to set:
\[
\sqrt{-(\alpha+\beta+\beta\omega)} = i\sqrt{\alpha+\beta+\beta\omega},
\]
further, by the law of reciprocity for quadratic residues:
\[
\left(\frac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta}\right) = (-1)^{\frac{\beta(\alpha+1)}{4}}\left(\frac{\beta}{\alpha}\right),
\]
\[
\left(\frac{-\beta}{-(\alpha+\beta)}\right) = (-1)^{\frac{\alpha-1}{2}}(-1)^{\frac{\beta(\alpha-1)}{4}}\left(\frac{\beta}{\alpha}\right)\,^{1}),
\]
and from this follows the agreement of the two expressions
(16), (17), and consequently the correctness of formula (13) in accordance
with the congruence
\[
\beta(3\alpha-2\gamma+\beta-\delta+\beta^2\delta+2\alpha\beta\delta) \equiv 0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 24),
\]
which, since $\beta$ is assumed to be even, follows from $\alpha\delta-\beta\gamma=1$.

Thus the formulae (15) are proved to be correct.

\noindent\rule{4cm}{0.4pt}

\noindent $^{1})$ By the law of reciprocity we have, if $\beta=\pm2^\lambda\beta'$ is set and $\beta'$
is assumed to be odd and positive, when $\alpha+\beta$ is positive
\[
\left(\frac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta}\right) = \left(\frac{\pm2^\lambda}{\alpha+\beta}\right)\left(\frac{\alpha}{\beta'}\right)
(-1)^{\frac{(\alpha+\beta-1)(\beta'-1)}{4}},
\]
\[
\left(\frac{\beta}{\alpha}\right) = \left(\frac{\pm2^\lambda}{\alpha}\right)\left(\frac{\alpha}{\beta'}\right)
(-1)^{\frac{(\alpha-1)(\beta'-1)}{4}}.
\]
If $\lambda\geqq2$, these two values are equal to one another; if $\lambda=1$, they
differ by the factor $(-1)^{\frac{\alpha+1}{2}}$, in agreement
with the first of the formulae above. The correctness of the second formula
follows, when $\alpha+\beta$ is negative, from
\[
\left(\frac{-\beta}{-(\alpha+\beta)}\right) = \left(\frac{2^\lambda}{-(\alpha+\beta)}\right)\left(\frac{\alpha}{\beta'}\right)
(-1)^{\frac{(\alpha+\beta-1)(\beta'-1)}{4}},
\]
\[
\left(\frac{\beta}{\alpha}\right) = \left(\frac{2^\lambda}{\alpha}\right)\left(\frac{\alpha}{\beta'}\right)(-1)^{\frac{\alpha-1}{2}}
(-1)^{\frac{(\alpha-1)(\beta'-1)}{4}}.
\]

%% ===== canonical stable idx 151 =====
% !PRINTED 130
\weberpage{130}
If we set
\weq{18}{
E\!\left(\begin{matrix}\alpha, & \beta \\ \gamma, & \delta\end{matrix}, \omega\right) = \varepsilon\sqrt{\alpha+\beta\omega},
}
then $\varepsilon$ is a 24th root of unity, whose product with $\sqrt{\alpha+\beta\omega}$
is completely determined by (15), and there results the transformation
 of the $\eta$-function
\weq{19}{
\eta\!\left(\frac{\gamma+\delta\omega}{\alpha+\beta\omega}\right) = \varepsilon\sqrt{\alpha+\beta\omega}\ \eta(\omega).
}
For $\varepsilon^{12}$ one finds
\weq{20}{
\varepsilon^{12} = (-1)^{\alpha\beta+\gamma\delta+\beta\gamma}.
}

\begin{center}
§ 39. \gesperrt{Linear Transformation of the $\vartheta$-Functions.}
\end{center}

The transformation formulae of the $\vartheta$-functions are consequences
of the fundamental properties of the $\sigma$-function, namely of remaining, under the substitution
\[
(\omega_1', \omega_2') = \begin{pmatrix}\alpha, & \beta \\ \gamma, & \delta\end{pmatrix}(\omega_1, \omega_2)
\]
unchanged. From § 37, (4) there follows accordingly, if
one replaces $\omega_1, \omega_2, \eta_1$ by $\omega_1', \omega_2', \eta_1'$:
\[
\frac{\omega_1\, e^{\frac{\eta_1 u^2}{\omega_1}}\, \vartheta_{11}\!\left(\dfrac{u}{\omega_1}, \dfrac{\omega_2}{\omega_1}\right)}{\vartheta'_{11}\!\left(0, \dfrac{\omega_2}{\omega_1}\right)}
=
\frac{\omega_1'\, e^{\frac{\eta_1' u^2}{\omega_1'}}\, \vartheta_{11}\!\left(\dfrac{u}{\omega_1'}, \dfrac{\omega_2'}{\omega_1'}\right)}{\vartheta'_{11}\!\left(0, \dfrac{\omega_2'}{\omega_1'}\right)},
\]
or, since by § 35, (10), (13), (14)
\weq{1}{
\frac{\eta_1}{\omega_1} - \frac{\eta_1'}{\omega_1'}
= \frac{\omega_1'\eta_1 - \eta_1'\omega_1}{\omega_1\omega_1'}
= \beta\,\frac{\omega_2\eta_1 - \omega_1\eta_2}{\omega_1\omega_1'}
= \frac{\pi i\beta}{\omega_1\omega_1'}
}
holds, if we set:
\weq{2}{
\begin{aligned}
v &= \frac{u}{\omega_1}, & \omega &= \frac{\omega_2}{\omega_1},\\
v' &= \frac{u}{\omega_1'} = \frac{v}{\alpha+\beta\omega}, &
\omega' &= \frac{\omega_2'}{\omega_1'} = \frac{\gamma+\delta\omega}{\alpha+\beta\omega}
\end{aligned}
}
then:
\[
\frac{\vartheta_{11}(v', \omega')}{\vartheta'_{11}(0, \omega')}
= \frac{e^{\pi i\beta v v'}}{\alpha+\beta\omega}\ \frac{\vartheta_{11}(v, \omega)}{\vartheta'_{11}(0, \omega)}.
\]
Furthermore we have
\[
\vartheta'_{11}(0, \omega) = 2\pi\,\eta(\omega)^3, \qquad
\vartheta'_{11}(0, \omega') = 2\pi\,\eta(\omega')^3,
\]
from which, by § 38, (19):
\[
\vartheta'_{11}(0, \omega') = \varepsilon^3\sqrt{\alpha+\beta\omega}^{\,3}\ \vartheta'_{11}(0, \omega),
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 152 =====
% !PRINTED 131
\weberpage{131}
%<<CONT
and from this finally:
\weq{3}{e^{-\pi i \beta v v'}\vartheta_{11}(v',\omega') = \varepsilon^3\sqrt{\alpha+\beta\omega}\,\vartheta_{11}(v,\omega).}

The transformation formulae of the three remaining functions $\vartheta_{00}, \vartheta_{01}, \vartheta_{10}$ are different in the six classes of § 36, and can be derived from the formulae (5), § 36 in the same way. But the six cases can also be combined into a single system of formulae, which one obtains from (3) by replacing $v$ by
\[
v+\frac{\alpha+\beta\omega}{2}, \quad v+\frac{\gamma+\delta\omega}{2}, \quad v+\frac{\alpha+\gamma+(\beta+\delta)\omega}{2},
\]
and therefore $v'$ by
\[
v'+\frac{1}{2}, \quad v'+\frac{\omega'}{2}, \quad v' = \frac{1+\omega'}{2},
\]
% [sic] German source prints an equals sign in the third member; mathematically expected +.
and then applying the formulae (2), (3), (8) of § 21 to the right and the left side of (3). Thus one obtains:
\weq{4}{
\begin{aligned}
&e^{-\pi i \beta v v'}\vartheta_{10}(v',\omega') \\
&= i^{\beta} e^{-\frac{\pi i \alpha\beta}{4}} \varepsilon^3 \sqrt{\alpha+\beta\omega}\,\vartheta_{1+\beta,\,1-\alpha}(v,\omega),
\end{aligned}
}
\weq{5}{
\begin{aligned}
&e^{-\pi i \beta v v'}\vartheta_{01}(v',\omega') \\
&= i^{\delta-1} e^{-\frac{\pi i \gamma\delta}{4}} \varepsilon^3 \sqrt{\alpha+\beta\omega}\,\vartheta_{1+\delta,\,1-\gamma}(v,\omega),
\end{aligned}
}
\weq{6}{
\begin{aligned}
&e^{-\pi i \beta v v'}\vartheta_{00}(v',\omega') \\
&= i^{\delta+\beta-\alpha\delta} e^{-\frac{\pi i}{4}(\alpha\beta+\gamma\delta)} \varepsilon^3 \sqrt{\alpha+\beta\omega}\,\vartheta_{1+\beta+\delta,\,1-\alpha-\gamma}(v,\omega).
\end{aligned}
}

The fourth powers of these functions admit of a simpler expression by
\weq{7}{e^{-4\pi i \beta v v'}\vartheta^4_{g_1,g_2}(v',\omega') = (-1)^{g_2\alpha\beta+g_1\gamma\delta+\beta\gamma}(\alpha+\beta\omega)^2\,\vartheta^4_{g_1',g_2'}(v),}
% [sic] German source prints no second argument $\omega$; possibly an intentional abbreviation.
in which, in the six classes, the characteristics $(g_1',g_2')$ belonging to the characteristics $(g_1,g_2)=(00),(01),(10)$ are to be taken from the last column of the table in § 36.

A simpler transformation formula is obtained from the $\sigma$-functions for the product of the three $\vartheta$-functions (4), (5), (6). For if one forms the product of the three functions § 37, (6), we have:
\[
\sigma_{00}(u)\,\sigma_{01}(u)\,\sigma_{10}(u)
= e^{\frac{3\eta_1 u^2}{\omega_1}}\; \frac{\vartheta_{00}\!\left(\dfrac{u}{\omega_1}, \dfrac{\omega_2}{\omega_1}\right)\vartheta_{01}\!\left(\dfrac{u}{\omega_1}, \dfrac{\omega_2}{\omega_1}\right)\vartheta_{10}\!\left(\dfrac{u}{\omega_1}, \dfrac{\omega_2}{\omega_1}\right)}{\vartheta_{00}\,\vartheta_{01}\,\vartheta_{10}}
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 153 =====
% !PRINTED 132
\weberpage{132}
%<<CONT
a function which, by § 36, remains completely unchanged under linear transformation. If one makes further use of the relation (2):
\[
\eta_1'\omega_1 - \eta_1\omega_1' = -\pi i \beta,
\]
then it follows that
\weq{8}{
\frac{\vartheta_{00}(v,\omega)\vartheta_{01}(v,\omega)\vartheta_{10}(v,\omega)}{\vartheta_{00}\vartheta_{01}\vartheta_{10}}
= e^{-3\pi i \beta v v'}\, \frac{\vartheta_{00}(v',\omega')\vartheta_{01}(v',\omega')\vartheta_{10}(v',\omega')}{\vartheta_{00}(0,\omega')\vartheta_{01}(0,\omega')\vartheta_{10}(0,\omega')},
}
in which one may still, by (19) of the preceding section,
\[
\vartheta_{00}(0,\omega')\vartheta_{01}(0,\omega')\vartheta_{10}(0,\omega') = \varepsilon^3\sqrt{\alpha+\beta\omega}^{\,3}\,\vartheta_{00}\vartheta_{01}\vartheta_{10}
\]
set.

But we draw another conclusion from (8): namely, if one puts
\[
v' = \frac{h}{n}, \quad v = \frac{h(\alpha+\beta\omega)}{n},
\]
and takes the product for $h=1,2,\cdots,\dfrac{n-1}{2}$, then there results, by means of the known relation (Bd.\ I, § 11)
\[
\sum_{1,\ \frac{n-1}{2}}^{h} h^2 = n\,\frac{n^2-1}{24},
\]
if one applies formula (23), § 32 to the right-hand side of (8):
\weq{9}{
\begin{aligned}
&2^{\frac{n-1}{2}} \prod_{1,\ \frac{n-1}{2}}^{h} \vartheta_{00}\!\left(\frac{h(\alpha+\beta\omega)}{n}\right)\vartheta_{01}\!\left(\frac{h(\alpha+\beta\omega)}{n}\right)\vartheta_{10}\!\left(\frac{h(\alpha+\beta\omega)}{n}\right) \\
&= e^{-\frac{\pi i}{8}\frac{n^2-1}{n}\beta(\alpha+\beta\omega)}\ \vartheta_{00}^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\,\vartheta_{01}^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\,\vartheta_{01}^{\frac{n-1}{2}}, % [sic] German source prints \vartheta_{01} twice; the third factor is mathematically expected to be \vartheta_{10}.
\end{aligned}
}
in which now $\alpha, \beta$ may be any pair of relatively prime numbers.

\begin{center}
§ 40. \gesperrt{Linear Transformation of the Functions}\\
$f(\omega), f_1(\omega), f_2(\omega)$.
\end{center}

By § 34, (9), the formulae for the linear transformation of the $f$-functions are a simple consequence of the transformation of the $\eta$-function.

If we set in the linear transformation
\[
\begin{pmatrix}\alpha, & \beta\\ \gamma, & \delta\end{pmatrix}
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 154 =====
% !PRINTED 133
\weberpage{133}
%<<CONT
first that $\beta$ is \gesperrt{even} and consequently that $\alpha, \delta$ are odd, then
\weq{1}{
\begin{pmatrix}1, & 0\\ 0, & 2\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\alpha, & \beta\\ \gamma, & \delta\end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix}\alpha, & \frac{1}{2}\beta\\ 2\gamma, & \delta\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1, & 0\\ 0, & 2\end{pmatrix},
}
that is,
\[
2\,\frac{\gamma+\delta\omega}{\alpha+\beta\omega} = \frac{2\gamma+\delta.2\omega}{\alpha+\frac{1}{2}\beta.2\omega}.
\]
But by § 34, (9) we have:
\[
f_2(\omega) = \sqrt{2}\,\frac{\eta(2\omega)}{\eta(\omega)},
\]
and if we therefore carry out the substitution
\[
\omega,\ \frac{\gamma+\delta\omega}{\alpha+\beta\omega}
\]
then, using the notation of § 38, we obtain
\weq{2}{
f_2\!\left(\frac{\gamma+\delta\omega}{\alpha+\beta\omega}\right)
= \frac{E\!\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\alpha, & \frac{1}{2}\beta\\ 2\gamma, & \delta\end{smallmatrix}, 2\omega\right)}{E\!\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\alpha, & \beta\\ \gamma, & \delta\end{smallmatrix}, \omega\right)}\, f_2(\omega).
}
Here the $E$-functions are to be determined according to § 38, (15), 1., from which it follows:
\[
\frac{E\!\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\alpha, & \frac{1}{2}\beta\\ 2\gamma, & \delta\end{smallmatrix}, 2\omega\right)}{E\!\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\alpha, & \beta\\ \gamma, & \delta\end{smallmatrix}, \omega\right)}
= \left(\frac{2}{\alpha}\right) e^{\frac{\pi i}{12}\left(\alpha\gamma + \frac{\alpha\beta}{2} + (\alpha^2-1)\frac{\beta\delta}{2}\right)}.
\]
But $\dfrac{1}{24} = \dfrac{3}{8} - \dfrac{1}{3}$, and
\[
\alpha\gamma + \frac{\alpha\beta}{2} + (\alpha^2-1)\frac{\beta\delta}{2} \equiv \frac{\alpha(2\gamma+\beta)}{2} \pmod{8}
\]
\[
\equiv \alpha(\gamma-\beta) - (\alpha^2-1)\beta\delta \pmod{3},
\]
and if we therefore put, for brevity,
\weq{3}{
\varrho = e^{-\frac{2\pi i}{3}\left[\alpha(\gamma-\beta) - (\alpha^2-1)\beta\delta\right]}
}
then from (2) we obtain:
\weq{4}{
f_2\!\left(\frac{\gamma+\delta\omega}{\alpha+\beta\omega}\right) = \left(\frac{2}{\alpha}\right)\varrho\, e^{\frac{3\pi i}{8}\alpha(2\gamma+\beta)}\, f_2(\omega), \qquad \beta \equiv 0 \pmod{2}.
}
In the same way all the other formulae of this kind may be derived; but they are obtained more simply from (4) itself by using the fundamental transformations § 34, (13), (14), (15). Thus, if in (4) one replaces $\omega$ by $-1:\omega$ and then interchanges $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta$ with $\beta, -\alpha, \delta, -\gamma$ (whereby $\varrho$ remains unchanged), it follows that:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 155 =====
% !PRINTED 134
\weberpage{134}
%<<CONT
\weq{5}{
f_2\!\left(\frac{\gamma+\delta\omega}{\alpha+\beta\omega}\right) = \left(\frac{2}{\beta}\right)\varrho\, e^{\frac{3\pi i}{8}\beta(2\delta-\alpha)}\, f_1(\omega), \qquad \alpha \equiv 0 \pmod{2},
}
and if in this we replace $\omega$ by $\omega+3$ and $\gamma, \alpha$ by $\gamma-3\delta, \alpha-3\beta$, it follows that
\weq{6}{
f_2\!\left(\frac{\gamma+\delta\omega}{\alpha+\beta\omega}\right) = -\varrho\, e^{\frac{3\pi i}{8}\beta(2\delta-\alpha)}\, f(\omega), \qquad \alpha-\beta \equiv 0 \pmod{2}.
}

If in (4), (5), (6) we set
\[
f_2\!\left(\frac{\gamma+\delta\omega}{\alpha+\beta\omega}\right) = f_1\!\left(-\frac{\alpha+\beta\omega}{\gamma+\delta\omega}\right),
\]
and then interchange $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta$ with $-\gamma, -\delta, \alpha, \beta$, there results
\weq{7}{
f_1\!\left(\frac{\gamma+\delta\omega}{\alpha+\beta\omega}\right) = \left(\frac{2}{\gamma}\right)\varrho\, e^{-\frac{3\pi i}{8}\gamma(2\alpha-\delta)}\, f_2(\omega), \qquad \delta \equiv 0 \pmod{2},
}
\weq{8}{
{}= \left(\frac{2}{\delta}\right)\varrho\, e^{-\frac{3\pi i}{8}\delta(2\beta+\gamma)}\, f_1(\omega), \qquad \gamma \equiv 0 \pmod{2},
}
\weq{9}{
{}= -\varrho\, e^{-\frac{3\pi i}{8}\delta(2\beta+\gamma)}\, f(\omega), \qquad \gamma-\delta \equiv 0 \pmod{2}.
}

From (9) and (6) one obtains, on replacing $\omega$ by $\dfrac{-\gamma+\alpha\omega}{\delta-\beta\omega}$ and then $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta$ by $\delta, -\beta, -\gamma, \alpha$:
\weq{10}{
f\!\left(\frac{\gamma+\delta\omega}{\alpha+\beta\omega}\right) = -\varrho\, e^{-\frac{3\pi i}{8}\alpha(2\beta+\gamma)}\, f_1(\omega), \qquad \alpha-\gamma \equiv 0 \pmod{2},
}
\weq{11}{
f\!\left(\frac{\gamma+\delta\omega}{\alpha+\beta\omega}\right) = -\varrho\, e^{\frac{3\pi i}{8}\beta(2\alpha-\delta)}\, f_2(\omega), \qquad \beta-\delta \equiv 0 \pmod{2},
}
and if finally in (10) one replaces $\omega$ by $\omega+9$ and $\gamma, \alpha$ by $\gamma-9\delta, \alpha-9\beta$:
\weq{12}{
f\!\left(\frac{\gamma+\delta\omega}{\alpha+\beta\omega}\right) = \varrho\left(\frac{2}{\alpha-\beta}\right) e^{-\frac{3\pi i}{8}(\alpha-\beta)(\alpha+\beta+\gamma-\delta)}\, f(\omega),
}
\[
\alpha+\beta+\gamma-\delta \equiv 0 \pmod{2}.
\]
\footnote{The functions $\varphi(\omega), \psi(\omega), \chi(\omega)$ introduced by \gesperrt{Hermite} (Sur la théorie des équations modulaires, Paris 1859) are connected with the functions $f(\omega), f_1(\omega), f_2(\omega)$ by the equations
\[
f(\omega) = \frac{\sqrt[6]{2}}{\chi(\omega)}, \quad f_1(\omega) = \sqrt[6]{2}\,\frac{\psi(\omega)}{\chi(\omega)}, \quad f_2(\omega) = \sqrt[6]{2}\,\frac{\varphi(\omega)}{\chi(\omega)}
\]
The transformation formulae of the $f$-functions can be recast in manifold ways by using the relation $\alpha\delta-\beta\gamma=1$. Thus the formulae given by \gesperrt{Hermite} loc.\,cit.\ are not at once to be recognised as identical with ours. A simple calculation, however, shows their agreement. The formulae given above have the advantage that, without any loss of simplicity, they combine two of the six transformation classes at a time into a single expression.}
