\begin{center}
\gesperrt{Fourth Chapter.}

\vspace{1em}
{\Large\bfseries The Elliptic Functions.}

\vspace{0.5em}
\rule{0.3\textwidth}{0.4pt}
\end{center}

\begin{center}
\S\,41. \gesperrt{Connection of the \(\vartheta\)-functions with the elliptic\\
integrals.}
\end{center}

According to \S\,21 there exist between the squares of the four
\(\vartheta\)-functions two linear equations independent of one another, and
one can therefore express two of these squares by the other two, or indeed
all four by two independent variables \(\xi\), \(\eta\). In doing the latter,
we denote by \(\xi_1\), \(\eta_1\); \(\xi_2\), \(\eta_2\); \(\xi_3\), \(\eta_3\); \(\xi_4\), \(\eta_4\)
constants, and, connecting with the mode of notation of Bd.\,I, \S\,67, we
set:
\weq{1}{\begin{aligned}
\vartheta^2_{01}(u) &= \xi\eta_1 - \eta\xi_1 = (\xi\eta_1),\\
\vartheta^2_{11}(u) &= \xi\eta_2 - \eta\xi_2 = (\xi\eta_2),\\
\vartheta^2_{10}(u) &= \xi\eta_3 - \eta\xi_3 = (\xi\eta_3),\\
\vartheta^2_{00}(u) &= \xi\eta_4 - \eta\xi_4 = (\xi\eta_4).
\end{aligned}}
Between the constants \(\xi_i\), \(\eta_i\) and the values \(\vartheta_{01}\), \(\vartheta_{10}\),
\(\vartheta_{00}\) there exist four relations, which can be derived from the
equations (13) of \S\,21. These equations we can write, following the
notation (1), in the form:
\weq{2}{\begin{aligned}
(\xi\eta_3)\vartheta^2_{01} &= (\xi\eta_1)\vartheta^2_{10} - (\xi\eta_2)\vartheta^2_{00},\\
(\xi\eta_4)\vartheta^2_{01} &= (\xi\eta_1)\vartheta^2_{00} - (\xi\eta_2)\vartheta^2_{10}.
\end{aligned}}
By setting in (2) \(\xi\), \(\eta = \xi_1\), \(\eta_1\)
and \(= \xi_2\), \(\eta_2\), one can give these relations the form:
\weq{3}{\begin{aligned}
(\xi_1\eta_3)\vartheta^2_{01} &= (\xi_2\eta_1)\vartheta^2_{00},\\
(\xi_2\eta_3)\vartheta^2_{01} &= (\xi_2\eta_1)\vartheta^2_{10},\\
(\xi_1\eta_4)\vartheta^2_{01} &= (\xi_2\eta_1)\vartheta^2_{10},\\
(\xi_2\eta_4)\vartheta^2_{01} &= (\xi_2\eta_1)\vartheta^2_{00},
\end{aligned}}
to which one can further add, by setting in (2) \(\xi\), \(\eta = \xi_4\), \(\eta_4\)
and using (3) and \S\,21, (14):
\weq{4}{(\xi_4\eta_3) = (\xi_2\eta_1).}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 157 =====
% !PRINTED 136
\weberpage{136}

From (3) and (4) there follows for the cross ratios:
\weq{5}{\frac{(\xi_2\eta_3)(\xi_1\eta_4)}{(\xi_1\eta_3)(\xi_2\eta_4)} = \frac{\vartheta^4_{10}}{\vartheta^4_{00}},}
\weq{6}{\frac{(\xi_1\eta_2)(\xi_3\eta_4)}{(\xi_1\eta_3)(\xi_2\eta_4)} = \frac{\vartheta^4_{01}}{\vartheta^4_{00}}.}
If we now differentiate two of the equations (1), say the first
two, there follows:
\[
\begin{aligned}
2\vartheta_{01}(u)\vartheta'_{01}(u)\,du &= \eta_1\,d\xi - \xi_1\,d\eta = (\eta_1\,d\xi),\\
2\vartheta_{11}(u)\vartheta'_{11}(u)\,du &= \eta_2\,d\xi - \xi_2\,d\eta = (\eta_2\,d\xi),
\end{aligned}
\]
and from this, with the use of (1),
\[
\begin{aligned}
2\vartheta_{01}(u)\vartheta_{11}(u)\bigl[\vartheta'_{01}(u)\vartheta_{11}(u) - \vartheta'_{11}(u)\vartheta_{01}(u)\bigr]\,du \\
= (\eta_1\,d\xi)\vartheta^2_{11}(u) - (\eta_2\,d\xi)\vartheta^2_{01}(u) \\
= (\eta_1\,d\xi)(\xi\eta_2) - (\eta_2\,d\xi)(\xi\eta_1) = (\xi_2\eta_1)(\xi\,d\eta).
\end{aligned}
\]
The last expression can be derived without calculation by regarding the
next to last one as a linear function of \(d\xi\), \(d\eta\) which vanishes for
\(d\xi : d\eta = \xi : \eta\) and is therefore divisible by \((\xi\,d\eta)\). The
quotient \((\xi_2\eta_1)\) is obtained by setting \(d\xi : d\eta = \xi_2 : \eta_2\). With
the use of \S\,23, (6) one then obtains
\weq{7}{2\pi\vartheta^2_{01}\vartheta_{00}(u)\vartheta_{11}(u)\vartheta_{10}(u)\vartheta_{01}(u)\,du = (\xi_1\eta_2)(\xi\,d\eta).}
If one introduces here, according to (3) (first and last formula),
\weq{8}{(\xi_1\eta_2)\vartheta^2_{00} = \sqrt{(\xi_1\eta_3)(\xi_2\eta_4)}\ \vartheta^2_{01}}
and substitutes for the \(\vartheta\)-functions the expressions (1), there
finally follows
\weq{9}{2\pi\vartheta^2_{00}\,du = \frac{\sqrt{(\xi_1\eta_3)(\xi_2\eta_4)}\,(\xi\,d\eta)}{\sqrt{(\xi\eta_1)(\xi\eta_2)(\xi\eta_3)(\xi\eta_4)}},}
by which \(du\) is represented as an \gesperrt{elliptic differential of the first kind}
in homogeneous variables [\S\,1, (5)].

By (1) the ratio \(\xi : \eta\) is determined as a \gesperrt{doubly periodic function}
of \(u\). But likewise the ratios of the square roots
\weq{10}{\sqrt{(\xi\eta_1)},\qquad \sqrt{(\xi\eta_2)},\qquad \sqrt{(\xi\eta_3)},\qquad \sqrt{(\xi\eta_4)}}
are also defined as single-valued doubly periodic functions, and the sign
of the square roots in (9) is thereby, and by (8), likewise uniquely
determined.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 158 =====
% !PRINTED 137
\weberpage{137}

If \(\omega\) is the modulus of the \(\vartheta\)-functions, then, as follows by
(1) from the vanishing of the four \(\vartheta\)-functions, the following values
belong together:
\weq{11}{\begin{aligned}
u &= \tfrac{1}{2}\omega, & \xi : \eta &= \xi_1 : \eta_1,\\
u &= 0, & \xi : \eta &= \xi_2 : \eta_2,\\
u &= \tfrac{1}{2}, & \xi : \eta &= \xi_3 : \eta_3,\\
u &= \frac{1+\omega}{2}, & \xi : \eta &= \xi_4 : \eta_4.
\end{aligned}}

\begin{center}
\S\,42. \gesperrt{Jacobi's elliptic functions.}
\end{center}

Since the variables \(\xi\), \(\eta\) can be replaced by two new variables by
means of a linear substitution in which four coefficients are at our
disposal, one can assign arbitrary values to four of the quantities \(\xi_i\),
\(\eta_i\), or to three of their ratios, without impairing the
generality.

We shall set
\weq{1}{\xi_1 = 0,\qquad \eta_2 = 0,\qquad \xi_3 = \eta_3,}
and we further introduce \(\varkappa^2\), \(\varkappa'^2\), \(\zeta\) by the equations:
\weq{2}{\xi_4 = \varkappa^2\eta_4,\qquad \varkappa'^2 = 1 - \varkappa^2,\qquad \frac{\eta}{\xi} = \zeta.}

From \S\,41, (3), (5), (6) there then follows
\weq{3}{\begin{aligned}
\frac{\xi_2}{\eta_1} &= -\frac{\vartheta^2_{10}}{\vartheta^2_{00}}, &
\frac{\eta_3}{\eta_1} &= \frac{\vartheta^2_{10}}{\vartheta^2_{01}}, &
\frac{\eta_4}{\eta_1} &= \frac{\vartheta^2_{00}}{\vartheta^2_{01}},\\
\sqrt{\varkappa} &= \frac{\vartheta_{10}}{\vartheta_{00}}, &
\sqrt{\varkappa'} &= \frac{\vartheta_{01}}{\vartheta_{00}}, & &
\end{aligned}}
and from (1), (9), \S\,41 one finds:
\weq{4}{\begin{aligned}
\frac{\vartheta_{00}}{\vartheta_{10}}\,\frac{\vartheta_{11}(u)}{\vartheta_{01}(u)} &= \sqrt{\zeta},\\
\frac{\vartheta_{01}}{\vartheta_{10}}\,\frac{\vartheta_{10}(u)}{\vartheta_{01}(u)} &= \sqrt{1-\zeta},\\
\frac{\vartheta_{01}}{\vartheta_{00}}\,\frac{\vartheta_{00}(u)}{\vartheta_{01}(u)} &= \sqrt{1-\varkappa^2\zeta}.
\end{aligned}}
\weq{5}{2\pi\vartheta^2_{00}u = \int_0^{\zeta} \frac{d\zeta}{\sqrt{\zeta(1-\zeta)(1-\varkappa^2\zeta)}},}
in which the path of integration and the meaning of the root symbols are
determined by the formulae (4) themselves, when the transition
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 159 =====
% !PRINTED 138
\weberpage{138}
%<<CONT
from 0 to \(u\) in the \(u\)-plane is given. But the path of integration
in (5) may then also be altered, provided only that in doing so none of
the singular points \(\infty\), \(1\), \(\dfrac{1}{\varkappa^2}\) is crossed.

Equation (5) can be written in the following three forms:
\weq{6}{\begin{aligned}
d\sqrt{\zeta} &= \pi\vartheta^2_{00}\sqrt{(1-\zeta)(1-\varkappa^2\zeta)}\,du,\\
d\sqrt{1-\zeta} &= -\pi\vartheta^2_{00}\sqrt{\zeta(1-\varkappa^2\zeta)}\,du,\\
d\sqrt{1-\varkappa^2\zeta} &= -\pi\vartheta^2_{00}\varkappa^2\sqrt{\zeta(1-\zeta)}\,du.
\end{aligned}}
If we introduce a new variable \(v\) by the equation
\weq{7}{\pi\vartheta^2_{00}u = v,}
then equations (5), (6) become:
\weq{8}{v = \frac{1}{2}\int_0^{\zeta} \frac{d\zeta}{\sqrt{\zeta(1-\zeta)(1-\varkappa^2\zeta)}},}
\weq{9}{\begin{aligned}
d\sqrt{\zeta} &= \sqrt{(1-\zeta)(1-\varkappa^2\zeta)}\,dv,\\
d\sqrt{1-\zeta} &= -\sqrt{\zeta(1-\varkappa^2\zeta)}\,dv,\\
d\sqrt{1-\varkappa^2\zeta} &= -\varkappa^2\sqrt{\zeta(1-\zeta)}\,dv,
\end{aligned}}
and now we regard the three quantities \(\sqrt{\zeta} = x\), \(\sqrt{1-\zeta} = y\),
\(\sqrt{1-\varkappa^2\zeta} = z\), defined by (4) and (7), as functions of the variable
\(v\). By (4) they are \gesperrt{one-valued, doubly periodic} and, apart from isolated
points at which they become infinite, \gesperrt{continuous} functions of \(v\). After
\gesperrt{Jacobi} they are called sinus amplitudinis, cosinus amplitudinis,
\(\varDelta\) amplitudinis of \(v\), and are denoted by \(\mathrm{sinam}\,v\),
\(\mathrm{cosam}\,v\), \(\varDelta\,\mathrm{am}\,v\). Here we wish to make use of the
shorter \gesperrt{Gudermann} notation \(\mathrm{sn}\,v\), \(\mathrm{cn}\,v\),
\(\mathrm{dn}\,v\), already mentioned in \S\,14, according to which
\weq{10}{\begin{aligned}
\frac{\vartheta_{11}(u)}{\vartheta_{01}(u)} &= \sqrt{\varkappa}\,\mathrm{sn}\,v,\\
\frac{\vartheta_{10}(u)}{\vartheta_{01}(u)} &= \sqrt{\frac{\varkappa}{\varkappa'}}\,\mathrm{cn}\,v,\\
\frac{\vartheta_{00}(u)}{\vartheta_{01}(u)} &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{\varkappa'}}\,\mathrm{dn}\,v.
\end{aligned}}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 160 =====
% !PRINTED 139
\weberpage{139}

These functions satisfy, by (9), the differential equations
\weq{11}{\begin{aligned}
\frac{dx}{dv} &= yz,\\
\frac{dy}{dv} &= -zx,\\
\frac{dz}{dv} &= -\varkappa^2xy,
\end{aligned}}
and the subsidiary conditions:
\weq{12}{\operatorname{sn}0 = 0, \qquad \operatorname{cn}0 = 1, \qquad \operatorname{dn}0 = 1.}

Between them there subsist the relations
\weq{13}{y^2 = 1 - x^2, \qquad z^2 = 1 - \varkappa^2x^2.}

From the fundamental properties of the $\vartheta$-functions there follow
the first properties of the elliptic functions:
\[
\operatorname{sn}v = -\operatorname{sn}(-v), \qquad \operatorname{cn}v = \operatorname{cn}(-v), \qquad \operatorname{dn}v = \operatorname{dn}(-v),
\]
that is, $\operatorname{sn}v$ is an odd function, while $\operatorname{cn}v$, $\operatorname{dn}v$ are even functions.

If we put further
\weq{14}{\pi\vartheta_{00}^2 = 2K, \qquad \pi\vartheta_{00}^2\omega = 2iK',}
and consequently
\weq{15}{\pi\vartheta_{01}^2 = 2\varkappa'K, \qquad \pi\vartheta_{10}^2 = 2\varkappa K, \qquad \omega = \frac{iK'}{K},}
then $v$ takes the values $K$, $iK'$, $K+iK'$ when $u = \frac{1}{2}, \frac{\omega}{2}, \frac{1+\omega}{2}$, and it follows from (4), having regard to (3) and \S\,21, (10):
\weq{16}{\begin{aligned}
&\operatorname{sn}K = 1, \quad \operatorname{sn}(K+iK') = \frac{1}{\varkappa},\\
&\operatorname{cn}K = 0, \quad \operatorname{cn}(K+iK') = -\frac{i\varkappa'}{\varkappa},\\
&\operatorname{dn}K = \varkappa', \quad \operatorname{dn}(K+iK') = 0,\\
&\operatorname{sn}iK', \quad \operatorname{cn}iK', \quad \operatorname{dn}iK' = \infty.
\end{aligned}}

Now $K$, $K'$ can be expressed by means of (8) in terms of definite
integrals, and one obtains, if one displaces $v$ from one vertex of the
parallelogram $0, K, K+iK', iK'$ to the next along the periphery, and
hence $u$ along
\[
0, \qquad \frac{1}{2}, \qquad \frac{1+\omega}{2}, \qquad \frac{\omega}{2}.
\]

%% ===== canonical stable idx 161 =====
% !PRINTED 140
\weberpage{140}

\weq{17}{K = \frac{1}{2}\int_0^1 \frac{d\xi}{\sqrt{\xi(1-\xi)(1-\varkappa^2\xi)}},}
\weq{18}{iK' = \frac{1}{2}\int_1^{\frac{1}{\varkappa^2}} \frac{d\xi}{\sqrt{\xi(1-\xi)(1-\varkappa^2\xi)}},}
\weq{19}{-K = \frac{1}{2}\int_{\frac{1}{\varkappa^2}}^{\infty} \frac{d\xi}{\sqrt{\xi(1-\xi)(1-\varkappa^2\xi)}},}
\weq{20}{-iK' = \frac{1}{2}\int_{\infty}^{0} \frac{d\xi}{\sqrt{\xi(1-\xi)(1-\varkappa^2\xi)}}.}
The values of $\sqrt{\xi}$, $\sqrt{1-\xi}$, $\sqrt{1-\varkappa^2\xi}$ are determined in these
 integrations by the formulae (4). If, however, $\omega$ is purely
imaginary, and consequently $\varkappa^2$ a positive proper fraction and
$K$, $K'$ are real and positive, then the paths for $v$ run parallel to the real
and the imaginary axis, and having regard to the remarks
 at the close of \S\,25 the formulae (4) show the following:
\[
\begin{array}{lcccl}
\text{In (17) are} & \sqrt{\xi}, & \sqrt{1-\xi}, & \sqrt{1-\varkappa^2\xi} & \text{real and positive,}\\
\text{„ (18) „} & \sqrt{\xi}, & i\sqrt{1-\xi}, & \sqrt{1-\varkappa^2\xi} & \text{„ „ „}\\
\text{„ (19) „} & \sqrt{\xi}, & i\sqrt{1-\xi}, & i\sqrt{1-\varkappa^2\xi} & \text{„ „ „}\\
\text{„ (20) „} & -i\sqrt{\xi}, & \sqrt{1-\xi}, & \sqrt{1-\varkappa^2\xi} & \text{„ „ „}
\end{array}
\]
and $\sqrt{\xi}$ has on none of the paths of integration a maximum or
minimum. Hence $K$, $K'$ can be defined by the four following
\gesperrt{real integrals} with positive square root:
\[
K = \frac{1}{2}\int_0^1 \frac{d\xi}{\sqrt{\xi(1-\xi)(1-\varkappa^2\xi)}} = \frac{1}{2}\int_{\frac{1}{\varkappa^2}}^{\infty} \frac{d\xi}{\sqrt{\xi(\xi-1)(\varkappa^2\xi-1)}},
\]
\[
K' = \frac{1}{2}\int_{-\infty}^{0} \frac{d\xi}{\sqrt{-\xi(1-\xi)(1-\varkappa^2\xi)}} = \frac{1}{2}\int_1^{\frac{1}{\varkappa^2}} \frac{d\xi}{\sqrt{\xi(\xi-1)(1-\varkappa^2\xi)}}.
\]

%% ===== canonical stable idx 162 =====
% !PRINTED 141
\weberpage{141}

\begin{center}
\S\,43. \gesperrt{The Jacobian Functions} $\Theta(v)$, $H(v)$.
\end{center}

If one regards the $\vartheta$-functions of the variable $u$ as functions
of $v$, one obtains the \gesperrt{Jacobian} $\Theta$-functions.
We put
\weq{1}{\begin{aligned}
\vartheta_{01}\left(\frac{v}{2K}, \omega\right) &= \Theta(v),\\
\vartheta_{11}\left(\frac{v}{2K}, \omega\right) &= H(v).
\end{aligned}}
Then $\Theta(v)$, $H(v)$ are to be designated as functions $t(v, 2K, 2K')$, and according to \S\,25 we have
\weq{2}{\begin{aligned}
\Theta(v) &= 1 - 2q\cos\frac{\pi v}{K} + 2q^4\cos\frac{2\pi v}{K} - 2q^9\cos\frac{3\pi v}{K} + \cdots\\
H(v) &= 2q^{\frac{1}{4}}\sin\frac{\pi v}{2K} - 2q^{\frac{9}{4}}\sin\frac{3\pi v}{2K} + 2q^{\frac{25}{4}}\sin\frac{5\pi v}{2K} - \cdots\\
q &= e^{-\frac{\pi K'}{K}}.
\end{aligned}}
According to \S\,21 (8) we have
\weq{3}{\begin{aligned}
H(v) &= -ie^{-\frac{\pi K'}{4K}+\frac{\pi iv}{2K}}\Theta(v+iK'),\\
\Theta(v) &= -ie^{-\frac{\pi K'}{4K}+\frac{\pi iv}{2K}}H(v+iK').
\end{aligned}}
Further:
\weq{4}{\begin{aligned}
\vartheta_{00}\left(\frac{v}{2K}, \omega\right) &= \Theta(v+K),\\
\vartheta_{10}\left(\frac{v}{2K}, \omega\right) &= H(v+K),
\end{aligned}}
whereupon, by means of formulae (3), (10), (15) of the preceding section
and (5), \S\,23:
\[
\sqrt{\varkappa} = \frac{H(K)}{\Theta(K)}, \qquad \sqrt{\varkappa'} = \frac{\Theta(0)}{\Theta(K)},
\]
\weq{5}{\begin{aligned}
&\Theta(K) = \sqrt{\frac{2K}{\pi}}, \quad \Theta(0) = \sqrt{\frac{2\varkappa'K}{\pi}}, \quad H(K) = \sqrt{\frac{2\varkappa K}{\pi}},\\
&H'(0) = \frac{\Theta(0)H(K)}{\Theta(K)} = \sqrt{\frac{2\varkappa\varkappa'K}{\pi}};
\end{aligned}}
finally the representation of the elliptic functions:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 163 =====
% !PRINTED 142
\weberpage{142}
%<<CONT

\weq{6}{\begin{aligned}
\frac{H(v)}{\Theta(v)} &= \sqrt{\varkappa}\operatorname{sn}v,\\
\frac{H(v+K)}{\Theta(v)} &= \sqrt{\frac{\varkappa}{\varkappa'}}\operatorname{cn}v,\\
\frac{\Theta(v+K)}{\Theta(v)} &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{\varkappa'}}\operatorname{dn}v.
\end{aligned}}
The functions $\Theta$, $H$ have, as follows easily from (3), the
periodicity expressed by the following equations:
\weq{7}{\begin{aligned}
\Theta(v+2nK) &= \Theta(v),\\
\Theta(v+2niK') &= (-1)^n e^{\frac{n^2\pi K'}{K}-\frac{\pi inv}{K}}\Theta(v),
\end{aligned}}
\weq{8}{\begin{aligned}
H(v+2nK) &= (-1)^n H(v),\\
H(v+2niK') &= (-1)^n e^{\frac{n^2\pi K'}{K}-\frac{\pi inv}{K}}H(v).
\end{aligned}}
It is sometimes useful to combine the equations (3), (7), (8)
in the following way:
\weq{9}{\Phi(v+niK') = i^n e^{\frac{n^2\pi i}{4}\frac{K'}{K}-\frac{\pi inv}{2K}}\Psi(v),}
in which, if $n$ is \gesperrt{even}, $\Phi$ and $\Psi$ are both to be set equal to
$\Theta$ or both equal to $H$; if $n$ is odd, $\Phi=\Theta$, $\Psi=H$ or
$\Phi=H$, $\Psi=\Theta$.

From \S\,22 (2), (4) there result the addition formulae:
\weq{10}{\begin{aligned}
\Theta^2(0)\Theta(u+v)\Theta(u-v) &= \Theta^2(u)\Theta^2(v) - H^2(u)H^2(v),\\
\Theta^2(0)H(u+v)H(u-v) &= H^2(u)\Theta^2(v) - \Theta^2(u)H^2(v),
\end{aligned}}
for which one may also write:
\weq{11}{\begin{aligned}
\Theta^2(0)\Theta(u+v)\Theta(u-v) &= \Theta^2(u)\Theta^2(v)(1-\varkappa^2\operatorname{sn}^2u\operatorname{sn}^2v),\\
\Theta^2(0)H(u+v)H(u-v) &= \Theta^2(u)\Theta^2(v)\varkappa(\operatorname{sn}^2u-\operatorname{sn}^2v).
\end{aligned}}
We now proceed to carry over the theorems on the $\vartheta$-functions
to the elliptic functions, and we begin with
the addition theorem.

\begin{center}
\S\,44. \gesperrt{Addition theorem of the elliptic functions}.
\end{center}

From the four $\vartheta$-functions twelve quotients in all can be
formed, which by \S\,42 are expressible by elliptic functions.
If one forms these quotients for the argument
$u+v$, then by \S\,22 one can represent them by $\vartheta$-functions of $u$
and of $v$ separately, and hence also by the corresponding elliptic
 functions, and indeed always in such a way that the denominator
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 164 =====
% !PRINTED 143
\weberpage{143}
%<<CONT
contains only squares of $\vartheta$, and is therefore expressed rationally by $\mathrm{sn}^2 u$, $\mathrm{sn}^2 v$. To carry an example through, let us take formula (5), \S\,22, and divide it once by (1) and then by (4) (the first time converting $v$ into $-v$ in (5)); it then follows that:
\begin{align*}
\frac{\vartheta_{01}\vartheta_{10}}{\vartheta_{00}^2}\,\frac{\vartheta_{11}(u+v)}{\vartheta_{00}(u+v)} &= \frac{\vartheta_{00}(u)\vartheta_{11}(u)\vartheta_{01}(v)\vartheta_{10}(v) + \vartheta_{01}(u)\vartheta_{10}(u)\vartheta_{00}(v)\vartheta_{11}(v)}{\vartheta_{00}^2(u)\vartheta_{00}^2(v) + \vartheta_{11}^2(u)\vartheta_{11}^2(v)},\\
\frac{\vartheta_{10}}{\vartheta_{01}}\,\frac{\vartheta_{00}(u+v)}{\vartheta_{11}(u+v)} &= \frac{\vartheta_{00}(u)\vartheta_{11}(u)\vartheta_{01}(v)\vartheta_{10}(v) - \vartheta_{01}(u)\vartheta_{10}(u)\vartheta_{00}(v)\vartheta_{11}(v)}{\vartheta_{11}^2(u)\vartheta_{01}^2(v) - \vartheta_{01}^2(u)\vartheta_{11}^2(v)},
\end{align*}
and if $u$, $v$ are replaced by $u:2K$, $v:2K$, then according to \S\,42 (10) everything can be expressed by elliptic functions. One obtains in this way
\weq{1}{\frac{\mathrm{sn}(u+v)}{\mathrm{dn}(u+v)} = \frac{\mathrm{dn}\,u\,\mathrm{sn}\,u\,\mathrm{cn}\,v + \mathrm{dn}\,v\,\mathrm{sn}\,v\,\mathrm{cn}\,u}{\mathrm{dn}^2u\,\mathrm{dn}^2v + \varkappa^2\varkappa'^2\mathrm{sn}^2u\,\mathrm{sn}^2v},}
\weq{2}{\frac{\mathrm{dn}(u+v)}{\mathrm{sn}(u+v)} = \frac{\mathrm{dn}\,u\,\mathrm{sn}\,u\,\mathrm{cn}\,v - \mathrm{dn}\,v\,\mathrm{sn}\,v\,\mathrm{cn}\,u}{\mathrm{sn}^2u - \mathrm{sn}^2v}.}
In the same way one obtains from formulae (6), (3), (4); (7), (2), (4); (8), (2), (3); (9), (1), (2); (10), (1), (3) of \S\,22:
\weq{3}{\frac{\mathrm{sn}(u+v)}{\mathrm{cn}(u+v)} = \frac{\mathrm{cn}\,u\,\mathrm{sn}\,u\,\mathrm{dn}\,v + \mathrm{cn}\,v\,\mathrm{sn}\,v\,\mathrm{dn}\,u}{\mathrm{cn}^2u\,\mathrm{cn}^2v - \varkappa'^2\mathrm{sn}^2u\,\mathrm{sn}^2v},}
\weq{4}{\frac{\mathrm{cn}(u+v)}{\mathrm{sn}(u+v)} = \frac{\mathrm{cn}\,u\,\mathrm{sn}\,u\,\mathrm{dn}\,v - \mathrm{cn}\,v\,\mathrm{sn}\,v\,\mathrm{dn}\,u}{\mathrm{sn}^2u - \mathrm{sn}^2v},}
\weq{5}{\mathrm{sn}(u+v) = \frac{\mathrm{sn}\,u\,\mathrm{cn}\,v\,\mathrm{dn}\,v + \mathrm{sn}\,v\,\mathrm{cn}\,u\,\mathrm{dn}\,u}{1 - \varkappa^2\mathrm{sn}^2u\,\mathrm{sn}^2v},}
\weq{6}{\frac{1}{\mathrm{sn}(u+v)} = \frac{\mathrm{sn}\,u\,\mathrm{cn}\,v\,\mathrm{dn}\,v - \mathrm{sn}\,v\,\mathrm{cn}\,u\,\mathrm{dn}\,u}{\mathrm{sn}^2u - \mathrm{sn}^2v},}
\weq{7}{\mathrm{cn}(u+v) = \frac{\mathrm{cn}\,u\,\mathrm{cn}\,v - \mathrm{sn}\,u\,\mathrm{sn}\,v\,\mathrm{dn}\,u\,\mathrm{dn}\,v}{1 - \varkappa^2\mathrm{sn}^2u\,\mathrm{sn}^2v},}
\weq{8}{\frac{1}{\mathrm{cn}(u+v)} = \frac{\mathrm{cn}\,u\,\mathrm{cn}\,v + \mathrm{sn}\,u\,\mathrm{sn}\,v\,\mathrm{dn}\,u\,\mathrm{dn}\,v}{\mathrm{cn}^2u\,\mathrm{cn}^2v - \varkappa'^2\mathrm{sn}^2u\,\mathrm{sn}^2v},}
\weq{9}{\mathrm{dn}(u+v) = \frac{\mathrm{dn}\,u\,\mathrm{dn}\,v - \varkappa^2\mathrm{sn}\,u\,\mathrm{sn}\,v\,\mathrm{cn}\,u\,\mathrm{cn}\,v}{1 - \varkappa^2\mathrm{sn}^2u\,\mathrm{sn}^2v},}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 165 =====
% !PRINTED 144
\weberpage{144}
%<<CONT
\weq{10}{\frac{1}{\mathrm{dn}(u+v)} = \frac{\mathrm{dn}\,u\,\mathrm{dn}\,v + \varkappa^2\mathrm{sn}\,u\,\mathrm{sn}\,v\,\mathrm{cn}\,u\,\mathrm{cn}\,v}{\mathrm{dn}^2u\,\mathrm{dn}^2v + \varkappa^2\varkappa'^2\mathrm{sn}^2u\,\mathrm{sn}^2v},}
\weq{11}{\frac{\mathrm{dn}(u+v)}{\mathrm{cn}(u+v)} = \frac{\mathrm{dn}\,u\,\mathrm{dn}\,v\,\mathrm{cn}\,u\,\mathrm{cn}\,v + \varkappa'^2\mathrm{sn}\,u\,\mathrm{sn}\,v}{\mathrm{cn}^2u\,\mathrm{cn}^2v - \varkappa'^2\mathrm{sn}^2u\,\mathrm{sn}^2v},}
\weq{12}{\frac{\mathrm{cn}(u+v)}{\mathrm{dn}(u+v)} = \frac{\mathrm{dn}\,u\,\mathrm{dn}\,v\,\mathrm{cn}\,u\,\mathrm{cn}\,v - \varkappa'^2\mathrm{sn}\,u\,\mathrm{sn}\,v}{\mathrm{dn}^2u\,\mathrm{dn}^2v + \varkappa^2\varkappa'^2\mathrm{sn}^2u\,\mathrm{sn}^2v}.}
Many other formulae besides can be derived in the same way, among which we adduce the following three, which result from the division of \S\,22 (4), (3), (1) by (2).
\weq{13}{\mathrm{sn}(u+v)\,\mathrm{sn}(u-v) = \frac{\mathrm{sn}^2u - \mathrm{sn}^2v}{1 - \varkappa^2\mathrm{ns}^2u\,\mathrm{sn}^2v},}
% [sic] German source prints ns in the first factor; the parallel denominators (14), (15) print sn.
\weq{14}{\mathrm{cn}(u+v)\,\mathrm{cn}(u-v) = \frac{\mathrm{cn}^2u\,\mathrm{cn}^2v - \varkappa'^2\mathrm{sn}^2u\,\mathrm{sn}^2v}{1 - \varkappa^2\mathrm{sn}^2u\,\mathrm{sn}^2v},}
\weq{15}{\mathrm{dn}(u+v)\,\mathrm{dn}(u-v) = \frac{\mathrm{dn}^2u\,\mathrm{dn}^2v + \varkappa^2\varkappa'^2\mathrm{sn}^2u\,\mathrm{sn}^2v}{1 - \varkappa^2\mathrm{sn}^2u\,\mathrm{sn}^2v}.}
The most important among these formulae are (5), (7), (9), from which all the rest can be derived, even if by lengthy calculations. For the sake of a clear view we set them down here once more:
\weq{16}{\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{sn}(u+v) &= \frac{\mathrm{sn}\,u\,\mathrm{cn}\,v\,\mathrm{dn}\,v + \mathrm{sn}\,v\,\mathrm{cn}\,u\,\mathrm{dn}\,u}{1 - \varkappa^2\mathrm{sn}^2u\,\mathrm{sn}^2v},\\
\mathrm{cn}(u+v) &= \frac{\mathrm{cn}\,u\,\mathrm{cn}\,v - \mathrm{sn}\,u\,\mathrm{sn}\,v\,\mathrm{dn}\,u\,\mathrm{dn}\,v}{1 - \varkappa^2\mathrm{sn}^2u\,\mathrm{sn}^2v},\\
\mathrm{dn}(u+v) &= \frac{\mathrm{dn}\,u\,\mathrm{dn}\,v - \varkappa^2\mathrm{sn}\,u\,\mathrm{sn}\,v\,\mathrm{cn}\,u\,\mathrm{cn}\,v}{1 - \varkappa^2\mathrm{sn}^2u\,\mathrm{sn}^2v}.
\end{aligned}}
By combining these equations two at a time, one can give them, among others, the forms:
\weq{17}{\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{cn}(u+v)\,\mathrm{dn}\,u\,\mathrm{dn}\,v - \mathrm{dn}(u+v)\,\mathrm{cn}\,u\,\mathrm{cn}\,v &= -\varkappa'^2\mathrm{sn}\,u\,\mathrm{sn}\,v\\
\mathrm{dn}(u+v)\,\mathrm{sn}\,u\,\mathrm{cn}\,v - \mathrm{sn}(u+v)\,\mathrm{dn}\,u &= -\mathrm{cn}\,u\,\mathrm{sn}\,v,\\
\mathrm{sn}(u+v)\,\mathrm{cn}\,u - \mathrm{cn}(u+v)\,\mathrm{sn}\,u\,\mathrm{dn}\,v &= \mathrm{dn}\,u\,\mathrm{sn}\,v,\\
\mathrm{cn}(u+v)\,\mathrm{cn}\,u + \mathrm{sn}(u+v)\,\mathrm{sn}\,u\,\mathrm{dn}\,v &= \mathrm{cn}\,v.
\end{aligned}}

We apply the formulae (16) first of all to establish the periodicity of the elliptic functions, which can of course also be derived from \S\,21. If in (16) one puts $v = \pm K$, $v = K + iK'$, there follows from \S\,42 (16):
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 166 =====
% !PRINTED 145
\weberpage{145}
%<<CONT
\weq{18}{\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{sn}(u \pm K) &= \pm\frac{\mathrm{cn}\,u}{\mathrm{dn}\,u},\\
\mathrm{cn}(u \pm K) &= \mp\frac{\varkappa'\,\mathrm{sn}\,u}{\mathrm{dn}\,u},\\
\mathrm{dn}(u \pm K) &= \frac{\varkappa'}{\mathrm{dn}\,u},
\end{aligned}}
\weq{19}{\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{sn}(u + K + iK') &= \frac{1}{\varkappa}\,\frac{\mathrm{dn}\,u}{\mathrm{cn}\,u},\\
\mathrm{cn}(u + K + iK') &= \frac{i\varkappa'}{\varkappa}\,\frac{1}{\mathrm{cn}\,u},\\
\mathrm{dn}(u + K + iK') &= \frac{i\varkappa'\,\mathrm{sn}\,u}{\mathrm{cn}\,u},
\end{aligned}}
and if one changes $u$ into $u - K$ in (19):
\weq{20}{\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{sn}(u + iK') &= \frac{1}{\varkappa}\,\frac{1}{\mathrm{sn}\,u},\\
\mathrm{cn}(u + iK') &= -\frac{i}{\varkappa}\,\frac{\mathrm{dn}\,u}{\mathrm{sn}\,u},\\
\mathrm{dn}(u + iK') &= -i\,\frac{\mathrm{cn}\,u}{\mathrm{sn}\,u}.
\end{aligned}}

The formulae (20) show that the three functions $\mathrm{sn}\,u$, $\mathrm{cn}\,u$, $\mathrm{dn}\,u$ become infinite for $u = iK'$. If one forms the quotients of each two of them, there follows:
\weq{21}{\begin{aligned}
\lim \frac{\mathrm{sn}\,u}{\mathrm{cn}\,u} &= i\\
\lim \frac{\mathrm{sn}\,u}{\mathrm{dn}\,u} &= i % [sic] German source prints i; the relations above imply i/\varkappa.
\end{aligned}\qquad \text{for } u = iK'.}

By means of the relations (18), (19), (20) one can derive three others from every addition formula, by replacing $u$ by $u + K$, $u + K + iK'$, $u + iK'$, that is, by making the permutations that are collected in the following table:
\[
\begin{array}{ccc}
\mathrm{sn}\,u, & \mathrm{cn}\,u, & \mathrm{dn}\,u, \\ \hline
\dfrac{\mathrm{cn}\,u}{\mathrm{dn}\,u}, & \dfrac{-\varkappa'\,\mathrm{sn}\,u}{\mathrm{dn}\,u}, & \dfrac{\varkappa'}{\mathrm{dn}\,u}, \\[2ex]
\dfrac{1}{\varkappa}\dfrac{\mathrm{dn}\,u}{\mathrm{cn}\,u}, & \dfrac{i\varkappa'}{\varkappa\,\mathrm{cn}\,u}, & \dfrac{i\varkappa'\,\mathrm{sn}\,u}{\mathrm{cn}\,u}, \\[2ex]
\dfrac{1}{\varkappa\,\mathrm{sn}\,u}, & \dfrac{-i\,\mathrm{dn}\,u}{\varkappa\,\mathrm{sn}\,u}, & \dfrac{-i\,\mathrm{cn}\,u}{\mathrm{sn}\,u},
\end{array}
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 167 =====
% !PRINTED 146
\weberpage{146}
%<<CONT
and applies the same permutations to $\mathrm{sn}(u \pm v)$, $\mathrm{cn}(u \pm v)$, $\mathrm{dn}(u \pm v)$ as well. In this way, e.\,g., the twelve formulae (1) to (12) follow from the three formulae (16).

If these permutations are applied to the relations (18), (19), (20) themselves, there results:
\weq{22}{\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{sn}(u+2K) &= -\mathrm{sn}\,u, & \mathrm{sn}(u+2iK') &= \mathrm{sn}\,u,\\
\mathrm{cn}(u+2K) &= -\mathrm{cn}\,u, & \mathrm{cn}(u+2iK') &= -\mathrm{cn}\,u,\\
\mathrm{dn}(u+2K) &= \mathrm{dn}\,u, & \mathrm{dn}(u+2iK') &= -\mathrm{dn}\,u.
\end{aligned}}
The common periods of these three functions are therefore $4K$, $4iK'$; besides these, however, $\mathrm{sn}\,u$ has the period $2iK'$, $\mathrm{dn}\,u$ the period $2K$, $\mathrm{cn}\,u$ the period $2K + 2iK'$.

We give the theorem on $\Theta$-functions (\S\,21) only another expression, by stating the following theorem:

\gesperrt{Every doubly periodic function of $v$ with the periods $2K$, $2iK'$ (which everywhere has the character of a rational function) is, if it is an even function, a rational function of $\mathrm{sn}^2v$, and if it is an odd function, the product of $\mathrm{sn}\,v\,\mathrm{cn}\,v\,\mathrm{dn}\,v$ with a rational function of $\mathrm{sn}^2v$.}

In this way every theorem that refers to homogeneous functions of order zero of $\vartheta$-functions can be converted into a theorem on elliptic functions, and from this one obtains in turn the corresponding theorems on elliptic integrals. One sees at once that the addition formulae (16) are no others than the formulae (17) of \S\,13 in the first chapter. In the same way the transformation theory of the $\vartheta$-functions furnishes us a solution of the \gesperrt{Jacobi} transformation problem of the elliptic integrals, as we have set it out in \S\,8.

We will verify this for the two principal transformations of the second order, which in \S\,32, as also in \S\,9, we have designated as the \gesperrt{Gauss} and the \gesperrt{Landen} transformation. According to \S\,32, for the \gesperrt{Gauss} transformation
\weq{23}{\frac{\vartheta_{10}\left(0,\dfrac{\omega}{2}\right)\vartheta_{11}\left(u,\dfrac{\omega}{2}\right)}{\vartheta_{00}\left(0,\dfrac{\omega}{2}\right)\vartheta_{01}\left(u,\dfrac{\omega}{2}\right)} = \frac{2\,\vartheta_{01}(u)\,\vartheta_{11}(u)}{\vartheta_{01}^2(u) + \vartheta_{11}^2(u)},}
\weq{24}{\frac{\vartheta_{10}\left(0,\dfrac{\omega}{2}\right)^2}{\vartheta_{00}\left(0,\dfrac{\omega}{2}\right)^2} = \frac{2\,\vartheta_{10}\,\vartheta_{00}}{\vartheta_{00}^2 + \vartheta_{10}^2} = \frac{2\sqrt{\varkappa}}{1+\varkappa},}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 168 =====
% !PRINTED 147
\weberpage{147}
%<<CONT

\weq{25}{\vartheta_{00}\left(0,\frac{\omega}{2}\right)^{2}=\vartheta_{00}^{2}+\vartheta_{10}^{2}=(1+\varkappa)\,\vartheta_{00}^{2}.}

According to \S\,42 we thus obtain a relation between elliptic functions with two different moduli, and if $\lambda$, $L$, $L'$ arise from $\varkappa$, $K$, $K'$ by the interchange $\left(\omega,\dfrac{\omega}{2}\right)$, then by (23), (24), (25)

\weq{26}{\lambda=\frac{2\sqrt{\varkappa}}{1+\varkappa},\quad L=(1+\varkappa)\,K,\quad L'=(1+\varkappa)\,K'}

\weq{27}{\operatorname{sn}\bigl[(1+\varkappa)\,v,\ \lambda\bigr]=\frac{(1+\varkappa)\operatorname{sn}v}{1+\varkappa\operatorname{sn}^{2}v},}

if for the sake of clarity the modulus is also given as second argument under the function sign sn.

For the \gesperrt{Landen} transformation we have
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\vartheta_{11}(2u,\,2\omega)}{\vartheta_{01}(2u,\,2\omega)}&=\frac{\vartheta_{10}(u)\,\vartheta_{11}(u)}{\vartheta_{00}(u)\,\vartheta_{01}(u)},\\[4pt]
\frac{\vartheta_{01}(0,\,2\omega)^{2}}{\vartheta_{00}(0,\,2\omega)^{2}}&=\frac{2\,\vartheta_{00}\vartheta_{01}}{\vartheta_{00}^{2}+\vartheta_{01}^{2}}=\frac{2\sqrt{\varkappa'}}{1+\varkappa'},\\[4pt]
2\,\vartheta_{00}^{2}(0,\,2\omega)&=(1+\varkappa')\,\vartheta_{00}^{2},
\end{aligned}
\]
and from this, if $\lambda$, $\lambda'$, $L$, $L'$ arise by the interchange $(\omega,2\omega)$ from $\varkappa$, $\varkappa'$, $K$, $K'$:

\weq{28}{\begin{aligned}
\lambda'&=\frac{2\sqrt{\varkappa'}}{1+\varkappa'}, \qquad \sqrt{\lambda}=\frac{\varkappa}{1+\varkappa'}, \qquad \lambda=\frac{1-\varkappa'}{1+\varkappa'},\\[4pt]
2L&=(1+\varkappa')\,K, \qquad\qquad\qquad L'=(1+\varkappa')\,K',
\end{aligned}}

\weq{29}{\operatorname{sn}\bigl[(1+\varkappa')\,v,\ \lambda\bigr]=\frac{(1+\varkappa')\operatorname{sn}v\operatorname{cn}v}{\operatorname{dn}v},}

and in (26) to (29) one recognises, by \S\,42, the formulae (2) and (4) of \S\,9.

\begin{center}
\S\,45. \gesperrt{The linear transformation of the elliptic functions.}
\end{center}

The effect of the linear transformation upon the elliptic functions is best surveyed from the representation by the $\sigma$-functions. From (4) or (10), \S\,42, and the formulae (4), (6) of \S\,37 one obtains:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 169 =====
% !PRINTED 148
\weberpage{148}
%<<CONT

\weq{1}{\begin{aligned}
\frac{\omega_{1}}{2K}\operatorname{sn}\frac{2Ku}{\omega_{1}}&=\frac{\sigma(u)}{\sigma_{01}(u)},\\
\operatorname{cn}\frac{2Ku}{\omega_{1}}&=\frac{\sigma_{10}(u)}{\sigma_{01}(u)},\\
\operatorname{dn}\frac{2Ku}{\omega_{1}}&=\frac{\sigma_{00}(u)}{\sigma_{01}(u)},
\end{aligned}}

or also, by making use of the homogeneity of the $\sigma$-function [\S\,37\,(8)]:

\weq{2}{\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{sn}v&=\frac{\sigma(v,\,2K,\,2iK')}{\sigma_{01}(v,\,2K,\,2iK')},\\
\operatorname{cn}v&=\frac{\sigma_{10}(v,\,2K,\,2iK')}{\sigma_{01}(v,\,2K,\,2iK')},\\
\operatorname{dn}v&=\frac{\sigma_{00}(v,\,2K,\,2iK')}{\sigma_{01}(v,\,2K,\,2iK')}.
\end{aligned}}

The $\sigma$-functions occurring on the right-hand side of (2) depend only on the two variables $v$, $\omega$, and it is first of all the change of these functions under application of the fundamental transformations
\[
(\omega,\ \omega+1), \qquad \left(\omega,\ -\frac{1}{\omega}\right)
\]
that has to be determined. Because of
\[
\pi\,\vartheta_{00}^{2}=2K, \qquad 2iK'=2\omega K
\]
one obtains from \S\,31\,(6) and (11) the corresponding changes:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\omega, && 2K, && 2iK', && \varkappa, && \varkappa',\\
&\omega+1, && 2\varkappa'K, && 2\varkappa'(K+iK'), && \frac{i\varkappa}{\varkappa'}, && \frac{1}{\varkappa'},\\
&-\frac{1}{\omega}, && 2K', && 2iK, && \varkappa', && \varkappa.
\end{aligned}
\]
If one sets for the moment:
\[
f(v,\omega)=\sigma(v,\,2K,\,2iK'),
\]
there results:
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(v,\omega+1)&=\sigma\bigl[v,\,2\varkappa'K,\,2\varkappa'(K+iK')\bigr]\\
&=\sigma(v,\,2\varkappa'K,\,2\varkappa'iK')\ \text{[by \S\,35\,(7)]}\\
&=\varkappa'\,\sigma\!\left(\frac{v}{\varkappa'},\,2K,\,2iK'\right)\ \text{[by \S\,37\,(8)]},\\
f\!\left(v,-\frac{1}{\omega}\right)&=\sigma(v,\,2K',\,2iK)\\
&=\sigma(v,\,-2iK,\,2K')\ \text{[by \S\,35\,(7)]}\\
&=-i\,\sigma(iv,\,2K,\,2iK')\ \text{[by \S\,37\,(8)]},
\end{aligned}
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 170 =====
% !PRINTED 149
\weberpage{149}

%<<CONT
and if one does the corresponding thing for the three remaining $\sigma$-functions and takes \S\,36\,(7) into account, one obtains the following interchanges that belong together:

\weq{3}{\begin{aligned}
&\omega, && \sigma(v), && \sigma_{00}(v), && \sigma_{01}(v), && \sigma_{10}(v),\\
&\omega+1, && \varkappa'\sigma\!\left(\frac{v}{\varkappa'}\right), && \sigma_{01}\!\left(\frac{v}{\varkappa'}\right), && \sigma_{00}\!\left(\frac{v}{\varkappa'}\right), && \sigma_{10}\!\left(\frac{v}{\varkappa'}\right),\\
&-\frac{1}{\omega}, && -i\,\sigma(iv), && \sigma_{00}(iv), && \sigma_{10}(iv), && \sigma_{01}(iv),
\end{aligned}}

in which the periods are $2K$, $2iK'$. From this there follow, according to (2), the first two linear transformations of the elliptic functions:

\weq{4}{\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{sn}\left(\varkappa'v,\,\frac{i\varkappa}{\varkappa'}\right)&=\varkappa'\,\frac{\operatorname{sn}v}{\operatorname{dn}v},\\
\operatorname{cn}\left(\varkappa'v,\,\frac{i\varkappa}{\varkappa'}\right)&=\frac{\operatorname{cn}v}{\operatorname{dn}v},\\
\operatorname{dn}\left(\varkappa'v,\,\frac{i\varkappa}{\varkappa'}\right)&=\frac{1}{\operatorname{dn}v}.
\end{aligned}}

\weq{5}{\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{sn}(iv,\varkappa')&=i\,\frac{\operatorname{sn}v}{\operatorname{cn}v},\\
\operatorname{cn}(iv,\varkappa')&=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cn}v},\\
\operatorname{dn}(iv,\varkappa')&=\frac{\operatorname{dn}v}{\operatorname{cn}v}.
\end{aligned}}

The first formula (5) shows, by \S\,44\,(21), that $\operatorname{sn}(v,\varkappa')=1$ when $v=K'$. From this there results, by \S\,42\,(17), the second frequently used representation for $K'$:

\weq{6}{K'=\frac{1}{2}\int\limits_{0}^{1}\frac{d\xi}{\sqrt{\xi(1-\xi)(1-\varkappa'^{2}\xi)}}.}

From (4), (5) one obtains the remaining cases of the linear transformation by repeated application. If in (4) one puts $iv$, $\varkappa'$ in place of $v$, $\varkappa$ and applies (5), then there follows:

\weq{7}{\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{sn}\left(i\varkappa v,\,\frac{i\varkappa'}{\varkappa}\right)&=i\varkappa\,\frac{\operatorname{sn}v}{\operatorname{dn}v},\\
\operatorname{cn}\left(i\varkappa v,\,\frac{i\varkappa'}{\varkappa}\right)&=\frac{1}{\operatorname{dn}v},\\
\operatorname{dn}\left(i\varkappa v,\,\frac{i\varkappa'}{\varkappa}\right)&=\frac{\operatorname{cn}v}{\operatorname{dn}v}.
\end{aligned}}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 171 =====
% !PRINTED 150
\weberpage{150}

If, conversely, one replaces $v$, $\varkappa$, $\varkappa'$ in (5) by $\varkappa'v$, $\dfrac{i\varkappa}{\varkappa'}$, $\dfrac{1}{\varkappa'}$ and applies (4), it follows that:

\weq{8}{\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{sn}\left(i\varkappa'v,\,\frac{1}{\varkappa'}\right)&=i\varkappa'\,\frac{\operatorname{sn}v}{\operatorname{cn}v},\\
\operatorname{cn}\left(i\varkappa'v,\,\frac{1}{\varkappa'}\right)&=\frac{\operatorname{dn}v}{\operatorname{cn}v},\\
\operatorname{dn}\left(i\varkappa'v,\,\frac{1}{\varkappa'}\right)&=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cn}v}.
\end{aligned}}

If one here again replaces $v$ by $iv$, and $\varkappa$, $\varkappa'$ by $\varkappa'$, $\varkappa$, and applies (5), one finds:

\weq{9}{\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{sn}\left(\varkappa v,\,\frac{1}{\varkappa}\right)&=\varkappa\operatorname{sn}v,\\
\operatorname{cn}\left(\varkappa v,\,\frac{1}{\varkappa}\right)&=\operatorname{dn}v,\\
\operatorname{dn}\left(\varkappa v,\,\frac{1}{\varkappa}\right)&=\operatorname{cn}v,
\end{aligned}}

with which the six classes of linear transformations are exhausted, since a still more frequent repetition gives occasion to no new formulae.

\begin{center}
\S\,46. \gesperrt{The Weierstrass $\wp$-Function.}
\end{center}

The linear transformations of the elliptic functions suggest that we look for an elliptic function which, like the $\sigma$-function itself, remains unchanged under the linear transformations. In order to form such a function, we first put the equations (1) of the preceding section into the following form:

\weq{1}{\begin{aligned}
\frac{\sigma_{10}(u)}{\sigma(u)}&=\frac{2K}{\omega_{1}}\,\frac{\operatorname{cn}v}{\operatorname{sn}v},\\
\frac{\sigma_{00}(u)}{\sigma(u)}&=\frac{2K}{\omega_{1}}\,\frac{\operatorname{dn}v}{\operatorname{sn}v},\\
\frac{\sigma_{01}(u)}{\sigma(u)}&=\frac{2K}{\omega_{1}}\,\frac{1}{\operatorname{sn}v},
\end{aligned}}

in which, for brevity,

\weq{2}{v=\frac{2Ku}{\omega_{1}}}

has been set. From this one concludes, with the help of the relations
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 172 =====
% !PRINTED 151
\weberpage{151}
%<<CONT
\[ \mathrm{cn}^2v = 1-\mathrm{sn}^2v, \qquad \mathrm{dn}^2v = 1-\varkappa^2\mathrm{sn}^2v, \]
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\sigma_{01}^2(u)}{\sigma^2(u)}-\frac{\sigma_{10}^2(u)}{\sigma^2(u)} &= \frac{4K^2}{\omega_1^2}, \\
\frac{\sigma_{01}^2(u)}{\sigma^2(u)}-\frac{\sigma_{00}^2(u)}{\sigma^2(u)} &= \frac{4K^2}{\omega_1^2}\varkappa^2.
\end{aligned}
\]

Three quantities $e_1$, $e_2$, $e_3$ independent of $u$ (and therefore depending only on
$\omega_1$, $\omega_2$) can accordingly be determined in such a way that
\weq{3}{\frac{\sigma_{10}^2(u)}{\sigma^2(u)}+e_1 = \frac{\sigma_{00}^2(u)}{\sigma^2(u)}+e_2 = \frac{\sigma_{01}^2(u)}{\sigma^2(u)}+e_3 = \wp(u),}
where $\wp(u)$ is a doubly periodic function newly defined by (3). The
quantities $e_1$, $e_2$, $e_3$ may be arbitrary, provided only that they satisfy the conditions
\weq{4}{e_1-e_3 = \frac{4K^2}{\omega_1^2}, \quad e_2-e_3 = \frac{4K^2}{\omega_1^2}\varkappa^2}
We are therefore free to add, for their complete determination, the further condition
\weq{5}{e_1+e_2+e_3 = 0}
The following expressions then result for $e_1$, $e_2$, $e_3$:
\weq{6}{\begin{aligned}
e_1 &= \frac{4K^2}{\omega_1^2}\frac{1+\varkappa'^2}{3}, \\
e_2 &= -\frac{4K^2}{\omega_1^2}\frac{\varkappa'^2-\varkappa^2}{3}, \\
e_3 &= -\frac{4K^2}{\omega_1^2}\frac{1+\varkappa^2}{3}.
\end{aligned}}

The function $\wp(u)$, which possesses the periods $\omega_1$, $\omega_2$, is hereby expressed by means of (1):
\weq{7}{\wp(u) = \frac{4K^2}{\omega_1^2}\left(\frac{1}{\mathrm{sn}^2v}-\frac{1+\varkappa^2}{3}\right).}

The function $\wp(u)$ has the desired property of invariability under linear
transformations, as one recognises from the expression
\weq{8}{\wp(u) = \frac{1}{3}\frac{\sigma_{00}^2(u)+\sigma_{01}^2(u)+\sigma_{10}^2(u)}{\sigma^2(u)}}

In consequence of (3) the $e_1$, $e_2$, $e_3$ are permuted under a linear transformation
in the same way as the $\sigma_{10}$, $\sigma_{00}$, $\sigma_{01}$; a symmetric function
of them is therefore, under a linear trans-
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 173 =====
% !PRINTED 152
\weberpage{152}
%<<CONT
formation unchanged and is called an \gesperrt{invariant}. There are two fundamental ones,
which we denote by $g_2$, $g_3$:
\weq{9}{\begin{aligned}
g_2 &= -4(e_2e_3+e_3e_1+e_1e_2) = 2(e_1^2+e_2^2+e_3^2) \\
&= \frac{64}{3}\frac{K^4}{\omega_1^4}(1-\varkappa^2\varkappa'^2),
\end{aligned}}
\weq{10}{g_3 = 4e_1e_2e_3 = \frac{2^8}{27}\frac{K^6}{\omega_1^6}(2+\varkappa^2\varkappa'^2)(\varkappa'^2-\varkappa^2),}
and we add besides the function known under the name of the \gesperrt{discriminant}:
\weq{11}{\begin{aligned}
G &= (e_2-e_3)^2(e_3-e_1)^2(e_1-e_2)^2 = \frac{1}{16}(g_2^3-27g_3^2) \\
&= \frac{(2K)^{12}}{\omega_1^{12}}\varkappa^4\varkappa'^4,
\end{aligned}}
for which, by §\,43 (3), (15) and §\,34 (2), we may also put:
\weq{12}{G = \frac{2^8\pi^{12}\eta(\omega)^{24}}{\omega_1^{12}}.}
$\wp(u)$, $g_2$, $g_3$, $G$ are homogeneous functions, as the following relations show, in which
$\lambda$ is an arbitrary factor.
\weq{13}{\begin{aligned}
\wp(\lambda u, \lambda\omega_1, \lambda\omega_2) &= \lambda^{-2}\wp(u, \omega_1, \omega_2), \\
\wp'(\lambda u, \lambda\omega_1, \lambda\omega_2) &= \lambda^{-3}\wp'(u, \omega_1, \omega_2), \\
g_2(\lambda\omega_1, \lambda\omega_2) &= \lambda^{-4}g_2(\omega_1, \omega_2), \\
g_3(\lambda\omega_1, \lambda\omega_2) &= \lambda^{-6}g_3(\omega_1, \omega_2), \\
G(\lambda\omega_1, \lambda\omega_2) &= \lambda^{-12}G(\omega_1, \omega_2).
\end{aligned}}
If we put, as in §\,45 (2)
\[ \omega_1 = 2K, \qquad \omega_2 = 2iK', \]
we then have
\weq{14}{\begin{aligned}
e_1 &= \frac{1+\varkappa'^2}{3}, \quad e_2 = -\frac{\varkappa'^2-\varkappa^2}{3}, \quad e_3 = -\frac{1+\varkappa^2}{3}, \\
g_2 &= \frac{4}{3}(1-\varkappa^2\varkappa'^2), \quad g_3 = \frac{4}{27}(\varkappa'^2-\varkappa^2)(2+\varkappa^2\varkappa'^2), \\
G &= \varkappa^4\varkappa'^4.
\end{aligned}}
If we eliminate $\omega_1$ from the general expressions (9), (10), (11) for $g_2$, $g_3$, $G$,
we obtain homogeneous functions of order zero, that is, functions of $\omega$ alone, which remain
\gesperrt{unchanged under linear transformations}. Such functions are $g_2^3:G$, $g_3^2:G$. Among these
functions, which can all be reduced to one another, we single out one, which we denote by
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 174 =====
% !PRINTED 153
\weberpage{153}
%<<CONT
$j(\omega)$ and call it simply the \gesperrt{invariant}, and define it thus:
\weq{15}{j(\omega) = 2^8\frac{(1-\varkappa^2\varkappa'^2)^3}{\varkappa^4\varkappa'^4},}
from which we obtain:
\weq{16}{\begin{aligned}
\frac{4.27g_2^3}{G} &= j(\omega), \\
\frac{4.27.27g_3^2}{G} &= j(\omega)-27.64 = \frac{64.(2+\varkappa^2\varkappa'^2)^2(\varkappa'^2-\varkappa^2)^2}{\varkappa^4\varkappa'^4}.
\end{aligned}}
Regarded as a function of $\varkappa^2$, the function $j(\omega)$ has the property of
remaining unchanged if in place of $\varkappa^2$ one of the six values
\[ \varkappa^2, \quad \varkappa'^2, \quad \frac{1}{\varkappa^2}, \quad \frac{1}{\varkappa'^2}, \quad -\frac{\varkappa^2}{\varkappa'^2}, \quad -\frac{\varkappa'^2}{\varkappa^2} \]
is substituted.

If we form the differential quotient of the function $\wp(u)$ according to (7), we obtain
\weq{17}{\wp'(u) = -\frac{16K^3}{\omega_1^3}\frac{\mathrm{cn}\,v\,\mathrm{dn}\,v}{\mathrm{sn}^3v} = -2\frac{\sigma_{00}(u)\sigma_{10}(u)\sigma_{01}(u)}{\sigma(u)^3}}
and from this, by (3):
\weq{18}{\begin{aligned}
\wp'(u)^2 &= 4[\wp(u)-e_1][\wp(u)-e_2][\wp(u)-e_3] \\
&= 4\wp(u)^3-g_2\wp(u)-g_3,
\end{aligned}}
or finally
\weq{19}{du = \frac{d\wp}{\sqrt{4\wp^3-g_2\wp-g_3}},}
from which one sees that the function $\wp(u)$ stands in the same relation to the
\gesperrt{Weierstrass} normal form of the elliptic differential as the function
$\mathrm{sn}\,v$ does to the \gesperrt{Legendre} one.

\begin{center}
§\,47. \gesperrt{The elliptic transcendents of the second kind.}
\end{center}

\gesperrt{Jacobi} introduced as the transcendent of the second kind the function
\weq{1}{Z(v) = \frac{\Theta'(v)}{\Theta(v)} = \frac{d\log\Theta(v)}{dv}}
The relation of this function to the elliptic integrals of the second kind follows from
formula (16) of §\,23; and it may be remarked at once that quite similar considerations
could be attached to the formulae (15), (17), (18) there, which, however, do not lead to
essentially new results.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 175 =====
% !PRINTED 154
\weberpage{154}
If we there put $v:2K$ in place of $v$, then from §\,42 and 43 we obtain:
\weq{2}{\begin{aligned}
\frac{d^2\log\Theta(v)}{dv^2} &= \frac{1}{4K^2}\frac{\vartheta_{01}''}{\vartheta_{01}}-\varkappa^2\mathrm{sn}^2v \\
&= \frac{1}{4K^2}\frac{\vartheta_{01}''}{\vartheta_{01}}-1+\mathrm{dn}^2v.
\end{aligned}}
We set
\weq{3}{1-\frac{\vartheta_{01}''}{4K^2\vartheta_{01}} = \frac{E}{K},}
and obtain by integration of (2)
\[ \frac{d\log\Theta(v)}{dv} = Z(v) = -\frac{E}{K}v+\int_0^v \mathrm{dn}^2v\,dv, \]
or, if we set
\weq{4}{E(v) = \int_0^v \mathrm{dn}^2v\,dv}
we have:
\weq{5}{Z(v) = E(v)-\frac{E}{K}v, \qquad \frac{dZ(v)}{dv} = \mathrm{dn}^2v-\frac{E}{K}.}

The functions $\Theta(v)$ and $\Theta(v+K)$ are even functions, and therefore $\Theta'(0)$
and $\Theta'(K) = 0$. If, then, we set $v=K$ in (5), it follows that:
\weq{6}{E = \int_0^K \mathrm{dn}^2v\,dv.}

If one further introduces for $dv$ the differential
\[ \frac{1}{2}\frac{d\xi}{\sqrt{\xi(1-\xi)(1-\varkappa^2\xi)}} \]
[§\,42 (8)], one obtains for $E(v)$ an elliptic integral \gesperrt{of the second kind} (§\,11):
\weq{7}{E(v) = \frac{1}{2}\int_0^{\xi} \frac{d\xi(1-\varkappa^2\xi)}{\sqrt{\xi(1-\xi)(1-\varkappa^2\xi)}},}
\weq{8}{E = \frac{1}{2}\int_0^1 \frac{d\xi(1-\varkappa^2\xi)}{\sqrt{\xi(1-\xi)(1-\varkappa^2\xi)}},}
where the latter integral is to be taken in the same sense as §\,42 (17).

%% ===== canonical stable idx 176 =====
% !PRINTED 155
\weberpage{155}

$E(v)$ and $Z(v)$ are \gesperrt{odd functions of the argument.}

From the addition theorem of the $\Theta$-function [§ 43 (11)] there
follows, by logarithmic differentiation:

\weq{9}{Z(u+v)+Z(u-v) = 2\,Z(u) - \dfrac{2\,\varkappa^2\,\mathrm{sn}^2v\,\mathrm{sn}\,u\,\mathrm{cn}\,u\,\mathrm{dn}\,u}{1-\varkappa^2\,\mathrm{sn}^2u\,\mathrm{sn}^2v},}

\weq{10}{Z(u+v)-Z(u-v) = 2\,Z(v) - \dfrac{2\,\varkappa^2\,\mathrm{sn}^2u\,\mathrm{sn}\,v\,\mathrm{cn}\,v\,\mathrm{dn}\,v}{1-\varkappa^2\,\mathrm{sn}^2u\,\mathrm{sn}^2v}.}

In these, $Z$ may also be replaced by $E$, and by addition there
results [§ 44 (16)]:

\weq{11}{E(u)+E(v)-E(u+v) = \varkappa^2\,\mathrm{sn}\,u\,\mathrm{sn}\,v\,\mathrm{sn}(u+v).}

From this one obtains the period properties of the function
$E(u)$ by setting $v=\pm K$, $K+iK'$. But one arrives at them
in the following way as well.

From the first equation § 43 (3) it follows:

\[
\dfrac{d\log H(v)}{dv} = Z(v+iK') + \dfrac{i\pi}{2K},
\]
and accordingly, from § 43 (6) and § 42 (11):

\weq{12}{\begin{aligned}
Z(v+iK') &= Z(v)+\dfrac{\mathrm{cn}\,v\,\mathrm{dn}\,v}{\mathrm{sn}\,v}-\dfrac{i\pi}{2K},\\
Z(v+K) &= Z(v)-\dfrac{\varkappa^2\,\mathrm{sn}\,v\,\mathrm{cn}\,v}{\mathrm{dn}\,v},
\end{aligned}}
and if in the first of these formulae one sets $v=K$:

\weq{13}{Z(K+iK') = -\dfrac{i\pi}{2K}.}

By twofold application of the formulae (12) [with regard
to § 44 (18), (20)]:

\weq{14}{\begin{aligned}
Z(v+2\,iK') &= Z(v)-\dfrac{i\pi}{K},\\
Z(v+2K) &= Z(v).
\end{aligned}}

If one carries these equations over to the function $E(v)$, there
follows:

\weq{15}{\begin{aligned}
E(v+iK') &= E(v)+\dfrac{\mathrm{cn}\,v\,\mathrm{dn}\,v}{\mathrm{sn}\,v}+\dfrac{i\,E\,K'}{K}-\dfrac{i\pi}{2K},\\
E(v+K) &= E(v)+E-\dfrac{\varkappa^2\,\mathrm{sn}\,v\,\mathrm{cn}\,v}{\mathrm{dn}\,v}.
\end{aligned}}

\weq{16}{\begin{aligned}
E(v+2\,iK') &= E(v)+\dfrac{2\,i\,E\,K'}{K}-\dfrac{i\pi}{K},\\
E(v+2K) &= E(v)+2\,E.
\end{aligned}}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 177 =====
% !PRINTED 156
\weberpage{156}

If in (15) we set $v=K$ and define a quantity $E'$ by
the equation:
\weq{17}{E(K+iK') = E + i(K'-E'),}
then one obtains the formula known under the name of \gesperrt{Legendre's relation}
\weq{18}{EK' + KE' - KK' = \frac{\pi}{2}\,.}

The significance of the quantity $E'$ introduced here is recognised
if one derives \gesperrt{Legendre's relation} by a second route,
making use of one of the linear transformations.

It follows, if one sets in \S\,31 (11):
\[
u = \frac{v}{2K}, \qquad \omega = \frac{iK'}{K}, \qquad \frac{u}{\omega} = \frac{v}{2iK'},
\]
by \S\,43 (1), (4):
\weq{19}{\sqrt{K}\, e^{-\frac{\pi v^2}{4KK'}} \,\Theta(iv,\varkappa') = \sqrt{K'}\, H(v+K),}
and from this, by logarithmic differentiation,
\weq{20}{iZ(iv,\varkappa') = \frac{\pi v}{2KK'} + \frac{H'(v+K)}{H(v+K)}}
or, by \S\,43 (6),
\weq{21}{iZ(iv,\varkappa') = \frac{\pi v}{2KK'} + Z(v) + \frac{d\log \mathrm{cn}\,v}{dv}\,.}

But by (5) we have
\[
i\,\frac{dZ(iv,\varkappa')}{dv} = -\,\mathrm{dn}^2(iv,\varkappa') + \frac{E'}{K'},
\]
if $E'$ now has the meaning:
\weq{22}{E' = \int\limits_v^{K'} \mathrm{dn}^2(v,\varkappa')\, dv,}
so that it arises from $E$ by the interchange of $\varkappa$ with $\varkappa'$. But if one
sets $v=0$ in (21), after having first differentiated, the relation (18)
again results, from which it follows that $E'$ is in both
cases the same quantity.

\S\,48. \gesperrt{The elliptic transcendents of the third kind.}

If we take the formula (10) of the preceding section:
\[
\frac{\Theta'(u+v)}{\Theta(u+v)} - \frac{\Theta'(u-v)}{\Theta(u-v)} = 2Z(v) - \frac{2\varkappa^2\,\mathrm{sn}^2 u\,\mathrm{sn}\,v\,\mathrm{cn}\,v\,\mathrm{dn}\,v}{1 - \varkappa^2\,\mathrm{sn}^2 u\,\mathrm{sn}^2 v}
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 178 =====
% !PRINTED 157
\weberpage{157}

%<<CONT
and integrate it with respect to $u$, then it follows:

\weq{1}{\dfrac{1}{2}\log\dfrac{\Theta(u-v)}{\Theta(u+v)}+u\,Z(v) = \int_0^u \dfrac{\varkappa^2\,\mathrm{sn}^2u\,\mathrm{sn}\,v\,\mathrm{cn}\,v\,\mathrm{dn}\,v}{1-\varkappa^2\,\mathrm{sn}^2u\,\mathrm{sn}^2v}\,du,}

and we can further add the formula, which is to be derived in the
same way [from § 43 (11)]:

\weq{2}{\dfrac{1}{2}\log\dfrac{H(v-u)}{H(v+u)}+u\,Z(v) = \int_0^u \dfrac{\mathrm{sn}\,v\,\mathrm{cn}\,v\,\mathrm{dn}\,v\,du}{\mathrm{sn}^2u-\mathrm{sn}^2v}} % Source recheck: damaged upper-limit sort retained as u; du and the parallel formulas (1), (3) support this reading.

which, moreover, can also be derived from (1).
We now set, with \gesperrt{Jacobi},

\weq{3}{\Pi(u,v) = \int_0^u \dfrac{\varkappa^2\,\mathrm{sn}^2u\,\mathrm{sn}\,v\,\mathrm{cn}\,v\,\mathrm{dn}\,v}{1-\varkappa^2\,\mathrm{sn}^2u\,\mathrm{sn}^2v}\,du,}

and call $\Pi(u,v)$ \gesperrt{the transcendent of the third
kind} with the argument $u$ and the parameter $v$. If one
replaces $du$ by the expression:

\[
\dfrac{d\xi}{2\sqrt{\xi(1-\xi)(1-\varkappa^2\xi)}}
\]

and $\mathrm{sn}^2u$ by $\xi$, then both (1) and (2) yield an
elliptic integral of the third kind, such as we became acquainted
with in § 11.

From (1) there follows first of all

\weq{4}{\Pi(u,v)-u\,Z(v) = \Pi(v,u)-v\,Z(u),}

or \gesperrt{Jacobi's theorem} on the \gesperrt{interchange of argument
and parameter}.

The function $\Pi(u,v)$ vanishes when $v=K$ or
is $v=K+iK'$, because for the former value $\mathrm{cn}\,v$ is equal to
zero, and for the second $\mathrm{dn}\,v$. If we therefore substitute
these values for $u$ in (4), there follows

\weq{5}{\begin{aligned}
\Pi(K,v) &= K\,Z(v)\\
\Pi(K+iK',v) &= (K+iK')\,Z(v)+\dfrac{i\pi v}{2K}\ [\text{§ 47, (13)}],
\end{aligned}}

by which the complete integrals of the third kind are reduced to the
second kind.

We wish also to derive the addition theorem of the $\Pi$-function, which \gesperrt{Jacobi} gives in the Fund. nova art. 53--55\footnote{C.\,G.\,J.\ \gesperrt{Jacobis} gesammelte Werke, Berlin 1881, Bd.\,I, S.\,204.} in various
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 179 =====
% !PRINTED 158
\weberpage{158}

%<<CONT
forms that can be reduced to one another only with
 difficulty. First we obtain from the definition (1),
if we now denote the parameter by $a$:

\weq{6}{\begin{aligned}
&\Pi(u+v,a)-\Pi(u,a)-\Pi(v,a)\\
&\qquad = \dfrac{1}{2}\log\dfrac{\Theta(u+v-a)}{\Theta(u+v+a)}\,\dfrac{\Theta(u+a)\,\Theta(v+a)}{\Theta(u-a)\,\Theta(v-a)},
\end{aligned}}

and it remains only to represent the expression standing under the
logarithm by means of elliptic functions.

This is first done easily, as at the passage of the Fundamenta already
mentioned, by means of the formula [§ 43, (11)]:

\[
\Theta^2(0)\,\Theta(u+v)\,\Theta(u-v) = \Theta^2(u)\,\Theta^2(v)\,[1-\varkappa^2\,\mathrm{sn}^2u\,\mathrm{sn}^2v],
\]

if one puts therein for $u,v$ the values $u\pm a$, $v\pm a$, then $\pm a$,
$u+v\pm a$.

One thus obtains:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Theta^2(0)\,\Theta(u+v\pm 2a)\,\Theta(u-v) &= \Theta^2(u\pm a)\,\Theta^2(v\pm a)\,[1-\varkappa^2\,\mathrm{sn}^2(u\pm a)\,\mathrm{sn}^2(v\pm a)],\\
\Theta^2(0)\,\Theta(u+v\pm 2a)\,\Theta(u+v) &= \Theta^2(a)\,\Theta^2(u+v\pm a)\,[1-\varkappa^2\,\mathrm{sn}^2a\,\mathrm{sn}^2(u+v\pm a)],
\end{aligned}
\]

from which it follows:

\weq{7}{\dfrac{\Theta(u+v-a)\,\Theta(u+a)\,\Theta(v+a)}{\Theta(u+v+a)\,\Theta(u-a)\,\Theta(v-a)} = \sqrt{\dfrac{[1-\varkappa^2\,\mathrm{sn}^2(u-a)\,\mathrm{sn}^2(v-a)]\,[1-\varkappa^2\,\mathrm{sn}^2a\,\mathrm{sn}^2(u+v+a)]}{[1-\varkappa^2\,\mathrm{sn}^2(u+a)\,\mathrm{sn}^2(v+a)]\,[1-\varkappa^2\,\mathrm{sn}^2a\,\mathrm{sn}^2(u+v-a)]}}.}

A second expression is obtained from the addition formula
(13), § 22, which can be put in the form:

\[
\Theta(0)\,\Theta(u\pm a)\,\Theta(v\pm a)\,\Theta(u+v) = \Theta(u)\,\Theta(v)\,\Theta(a)\,\Theta(u+v\pm a)\,[1\pm\varkappa^2\,\mathrm{sn}\,a\,\mathrm{sn}\,u\,\mathrm{sn}\,v\,\mathrm{sn}(u+v\pm a)],
\]

from which by division:

\weq{8}{\dfrac{\Theta(u+v-a)\,\Theta(u+a)\,\Theta(v+a)}{\Theta(u+v+a)\,\Theta(u-a)\,\Theta(v-a)} = \dfrac{1+\varkappa^2\,\mathrm{sn}\,a\,\mathrm{sn}\,u\,\mathrm{sn}\,v\,\mathrm{sn}(u+v+a)}{1-\varkappa^2\,\mathrm{sn}\,a\,\mathrm{sn}\,u\,\mathrm{sn}\,v\,\mathrm{sn}(u+v-a)}.}

\gesperrt{Jacobi} gives yet a third expression for the
$\Theta$-quotients in (6):

\weq{9}{\dfrac{\left\{1-\varkappa^2\,\mathrm{sn}^2\!\left(\dfrac{u-v}{2}\right)\mathrm{sn}^2\!\left(\dfrac{u+v}{2}+a\right)\right\}\left\{1-\varkappa^2\,\mathrm{sn}^2\!\left(\dfrac{u+v}{2}\right)\mathrm{sn}^2\!\left(\dfrac{u+v}{2}-a\right)\right\}}{\left\{1-\varkappa^2\,\mathrm{sn}^2\!\left(\dfrac{u-v}{2}\right)\mathrm{sn}^2\!\left(\dfrac{u+v}{2}-a\right)\right\}\left\{1-\varkappa^2\,\mathrm{sn}^2\!\left(\dfrac{u+v}{2}\right)\mathrm{sn}^2\!\left(\dfrac{u+v}{2}+a\right)\right\}}.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 180 =====
% !PRINTED 159
\weberpage{159}

The direct transformation of the three expressions (7), (8), (9) into one
 another is most easily accomplished if one starts from the formula last
given by \gesperrt{Jacobi}:
\weq{10}{1 - \varkappa^2 \operatorname{sn}(a+u)\operatorname{sn}(a-u)\operatorname{sn}(a+v)\operatorname{sn}(a-v) = \dfrac{(1-\varkappa^2\operatorname{sn}^4 a)(1-\varkappa^2\operatorname{sn}^2u\operatorname{sn}^2v)}{(1-\varkappa^2\operatorname{sn}^2a\operatorname{sn}^2u)(1-\varkappa^2\operatorname{sn}^2a\operatorname{sn}^2v)}.}
The verification of this formula is easy for this reason, that
with the help of \S\,44, (13) one obtains on the right and on the left \gesperrt{rational functions}
of $\operatorname{sn}^2u$, $\operatorname{sn}^2v$, whose identity is immediately evident.

If in this formula one replaces
\[
\begin{array}{ccc}
u, & v, & a
\end{array}
\]
by
\[
\begin{array}{ccc}
\dfrac{u-v}{2}, & \dfrac{u+v}{2}\pm a, & \dfrac{u+v}{2},
\end{array}
\]
there results
\[
\begin{gathered}
1 \pm \varkappa^2 \operatorname{sn} u\operatorname{sn} v\operatorname{sn} a\operatorname{sn}(u+v\pm a) \\
= \dfrac{\left[1-\varkappa^2\operatorname{sn}^4\left(\dfrac{u+v}{2}\right)\right]\left[1-\varkappa^2\operatorname{sn}^2\left(\dfrac{u-v}{2}\right)\operatorname{sn}^2\left(\dfrac{u+v}{2}\pm a\right)\right]}{\left[1-\varkappa^2\operatorname{sn}^2\left(\dfrac{u+v}{2}\right)\operatorname{sn}^2\dfrac{u-v}{2}\right]\left[1-\varkappa^2\operatorname{sn}^2\left(\dfrac{u+v}{2}\right)\operatorname{sn}^2\left(\dfrac{u+v}{2}\pm a\right)\right]},
\end{gathered}
\]
and if one divides the two formulae contained herein by one
 another, there results the agreement of (8)
and (9).

If one puts $v=u$ in (10), there results:
\weq{11}{1 - \varkappa^2 \operatorname{sn}^2(a+u)\operatorname{sn}^2(a-u) = \dfrac{(1-\varkappa^2\operatorname{sn}^4a)(1-\varkappa^2\operatorname{sn}^4u)}{(1-\varkappa^2\operatorname{sn}^2a\operatorname{sn}^2u)^2}.}
If one replaces herein
\[
\begin{array}{cc}
a & u
\end{array}
\]
first by
\[
\begin{array}{cc}
\dfrac{u+v}{2}\pm a, & -\dfrac{u+v}{2},
\end{array}
\]
and then by
\[
\begin{array}{cc}
\dfrac{u+v}{2}\pm a, & \dfrac{u-v}{2},
\end{array}
\]
there result four formulae:
\[
1 - \varkappa^2\operatorname{sn}^2a\operatorname{sn}^2(u+v\pm a) = \dfrac{\left[1-\varkappa^2\operatorname{sn}^4\left(\dfrac{u+v}{2}\pm a\right)\right]\left(1-\varkappa^2\operatorname{sn}^4\dfrac{u+v}{2}\right)}{\left[1-\varkappa^2\operatorname{sn}^2\left(\dfrac{u+v}{2}\pm a\right)\operatorname{sn}^2\dfrac{u+v}{2}\right]^2},
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 181 =====
% !PRINTED 160
\weberpage{160}

%<<CONT
\[
1 - \varkappa^2\operatorname{sn}^2(u\pm a)\operatorname{sn}^2(v\pm a) = \dfrac{\left[1-\varkappa^2\operatorname{sn}^4\left(\dfrac{u+v}{2}\pm a\right)\right]\left(1-\varkappa^2\operatorname{sn}^4\dfrac{u-v}{2}\right)}{\left[1-\varkappa^2\operatorname{sn}^2\left(\dfrac{u+v}{2}\pm a\right)\operatorname{sn}^2\!\left(\dfrac{u-v}{2}\right)\right]^2},
\]
from which the agreement of (9) with (7) follows.

\begin{center}
\S\,49. \gesperrt{The transcendents of the second and third kind}\\
\gesperrt{of Weierstrass.}
\end{center}

It remains now to set up the transcendents of the second and
third kind in the \gesperrt{Weierstrass} form. We reach the
former much as in \S\,47, by twofold differentiation of
$\log \sigma(u)$. In this way there follows from
\weq{1}{\sigma(u) = \omega_1 e^{\frac{\eta_1 u^2}{\omega_1}} \dfrac{\vartheta_{11}\left(\dfrac{u}{\omega_1}\right)}{\vartheta_{11}'} \ [\S\,37,\,(4)],}
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d^2 \log \sigma(u)}{du^2} &= \frac{2\eta_1}{\omega_1} + \frac{d^2\log \vartheta_{11}\left(\dfrac{u}{\omega_1}\right)}{du^2},\\
&= \frac{2\eta_1}{\omega_1} + \frac{1}{\omega_1^2}\frac{\vartheta_{00}''}{\vartheta_{00}} - \frac{1}{\omega_1^2}\frac{\vartheta_{11}'^2}{\vartheta_{00}^2}\frac{\vartheta_{00}^2\left(\dfrac{u}{\omega_1}\right)}{\vartheta_{11}^2\left(\dfrac{u}{\omega_1}\right)} \ [\S\,23,\,(18)]
\end{aligned}
\]
and hence, if one expresses the $\vartheta$-quotient by elliptic
functions according to \S\,42, and these by the $\wp$-function according to \S\,46:
\[
\frac{d^2\log\sigma(u)}{du^2} = A - \wp(u),
\]
in which $A$ is a constant. This constant is found, however, if
one writes the equation, following \S\,46, (8), in this way:
\[
\sigma''(u)\sigma(u) - \sigma'(u)\sigma'(u) = A\sigma^2(u) - \tfrac{1}{3}\left[\sigma_{00}^2(u) + \sigma_{01}^2(u) + \sigma_{10}^2(u)\right].
\]
If one differentiates this twice and then sets $u=0$,
it follows that $A=0$ [\S\,35, (12), \S\,37, (5), (7)], and we
obtain:
\weq{2}{\frac{d^2\log\sigma(u)}{du^2} = -\wp(u),}
a formula which in \gesperrt{Weierstrass} serves as the definition of the $\wp$-function.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 182 =====
% !PRINTED 161
\weberpage{161}

If therefore we set
\weq{3}{\dfrac{\sigma'(u)}{\sigma(u)} = \zeta(u)}
then $\zeta(u)$ is a single-valued function of $u$, and indeed
an elliptic integral of the second kind:
\weq{4}{\zeta(u) = -\int \wp(u)\,du = -\int \dfrac{\wp\,d\wp}{\sqrt{4\wp^3 - g_2\wp - g_3}} \ [\S\,46,\,(19)],}
in which the additive constant is so determined that $\zeta(u)$
must be an \gesperrt{odd} function. The periodicity of the $\zeta$-function
follows from the period equations of the $\sigma$-function
[\S\,35, (9)]:
\weq{5}{\begin{aligned} \zeta(u+\omega_1) - \zeta(u) &= 2\eta_1, \\ \zeta(u+\omega_2) - \zeta(u) &= 2\eta_2. \end{aligned}}
Thus $2\eta_1$ and $2\eta_2$ are represented as complete integrals of the second
kind (analogous to the $E$, $E'$):
\weq{6}{2\eta_1 = -\int\limits_u^{u+\omega_1} \wp(u)\,du, \quad 2\eta_2 = -\int\limits_u^{u+\omega_2} \wp(u)\,du}
with the equation corresponding to the \gesperrt{Legendre} relation
\weq{7}{\eta_1\omega_2 - \eta_2\omega_1 = \pi i \ [\S\,35,\,(10)].}
In order to form the addition theorems for the \gesperrt{Weierstrass}
transcendents, we start from the $\sigma$-function.
For these we obtain from (1), using the addition formula
for $\vartheta_{11}$, \S\,22, (4):
\weq{8}{\dfrac{\sigma(u+v)\sigma(u-v)}{\sigma(u)^2\sigma(v)^2} = \wp(v) - \wp(u),}
and from this, by logarithmic differentiation:
\weq{9}{\begin{aligned} \zeta(u+v) + \zeta(u-v) - 2\zeta(u) &= \dfrac{\wp'(u)}{\wp(u) - \wp(v)}, \\ \zeta(u+v) - \zeta(u-v) - 2\zeta(v) &= \dfrac{-\wp'(v)}{\wp(u) - \wp(v)}, \end{aligned}}
\weq{10}{\zeta(u+v) = \zeta(u) + \zeta(v) + \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{\wp'(u) - \wp'(v)}{\wp(u) - \wp(v)}.}
From this one derives, by a further differentiation, the
addition theorem for the $\wp$-function. From (9) one obtains,
by differentiation with respect to $u$ and $v$:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 183 =====
% !PRINTED 162
\weberpage{162}

%<<CONT
\[
\wp(u+v) + \wp(u-v) - 2\wp(u) = -\dfrac{\wp''(u)}{\wp(u)-\wp(v)} + \dfrac{\wp'(u)^2}{[\wp(u)-\wp(v)]^2},
\]
\[
2\wp(u+v) - 2\wp(u-v) = -\dfrac{2\wp'(u)\wp'(v)}{[\wp(u)-\wp(v)]^2},
\]
\[
\wp(u+v) + \wp(u-v) - 2\wp(v) = \dfrac{\wp''(v)}{\wp(u)-\wp(v)} + \dfrac{\wp'(v)^2}{[\wp(u)-\wp(v)]^2},
\]
and on adding:
\[
4\wp(u+v) - 2\wp(u) - 2\wp(v) = \left(\dfrac{\wp'(u)-\wp'(v)}{\wp(u)-\wp(v)}\right)^2 - \dfrac{\wp''(u)-\wp''(v)}{\wp(u)-\wp(v)}.
\]
But we have
\[
\begin{aligned}
\wp'(u)^2 &= 4\wp(u)^3 - g_2\wp(u) - g_3, \\
\wp''(u) &= 6\wp(u)^2 - \tfrac{1}{2}g_2, \\
\wp''(u) - \wp''(v) &= 6\left[\wp^2(u) - \wp^2(v)\right],
\end{aligned}
\]
from which one obtains:
\weq{11}{\wp(u+v) + \wp(u) + \wp(v) = \dfrac{1}{4}\left(\dfrac{\wp'(u)-\wp'(v)}{\wp(u)-\wp(v)}\right)^2,}
in agreement with formula (21), \S\,13.

Finally, by integrating the second equation (9) with
respect to $u$, one obtains further:
\weq{12}{\dfrac{1}{2}\log\dfrac{\sigma(v-u)}{\sigma(v+u)} + u\,\zeta(v) = \dfrac{1}{2}\int\limits_0^u \dfrac{\wp'(v)\,du}{\wp(u)-\wp(v)},}
by which an \gesperrt{integral of the third kind} with argument $u$
and parameter $v$ is expressed by the $\sigma$-function.

Another form of the integral of the third kind is obtained
by integrating (10):
\weq{13}{\log\dfrac{\sigma(u+v)}{\sigma(u)\sigma(v)} - u\,\zeta(v) = \dfrac{1}{2}\int \dfrac{\wp'(u)-\wp'(v)}{\wp(u)-\wp(v)}\,du.}

\begin{center}
\S\,50. \gesperrt{Developments of the elliptic functions.}
\end{center}

If in the developments of the theta quotients that were
derived in \S\,26 and collected in Table II one sets
$a=0$, then, if one first omits the formulae that contain
$\vartheta_{11}(a)$ in the denominator, one obtains the partial fraction developments
 of twelve elliptic functions:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 184 =====
% !PRINTED 163
\weberpage{163}
%<<CONT
\[
\begin{array}{lll}
\operatorname{sn}2Ku, & \operatorname{cn}2Ku, & \operatorname{dn}2Ku, \\[2mm]
\dfrac{1}{\operatorname{sn}2Ku}, & \dfrac{\operatorname{cn}2Ku}{\operatorname{sn}2Ku}, & \dfrac{\operatorname{dn}2Ku}{\operatorname{sn}2Ku}, \\[2mm]
\dfrac{1}{\operatorname{cn}2Ku}, & \dfrac{\operatorname{sn}2Ku}{\operatorname{cn}2Ku}, & \dfrac{\operatorname{dn}2Ku}{\operatorname{cn}2Ku}, \\[2mm]
\dfrac{1}{\operatorname{dn}2Ku}, & \dfrac{\operatorname{sn}2Ku}{\operatorname{dn}2Ku}, & \dfrac{\operatorname{cn}2Ku}{\operatorname{dn}2Ku}.
\end{array}
\]

Thus there results from formula (2), Table II:
\[
\frac{\vartheta'_{11}\vartheta_{10}(u)}{\pi\vartheta_{11}(u)\vartheta_{10}} = \operatorname{cotg}\pi u - 2i\sum(-1)^{\frac{m}{2}}q^m\left(\frac{1}{e^{-2\pi iu}-q^m} - \frac{1}{e^{2\pi iu}-q^m}\right)
\]
\[
= \operatorname{cotg}\pi u + 4\sin 2\pi u\sum\frac{(-1)^{\frac{m}{2}}q^m}{1-2q^m\cos 2\pi u+q^{2m}},
\]
where $m$ runs through the sequence of positive even numbers 2, 4, 6, 8, \dots{}

But according to \S\,42, (4) we have
\[
\frac{\vartheta_{10}(u)}{\vartheta_{11}(u)} = \frac{\vartheta_{00}}{\vartheta_{01}}\frac{\operatorname{cn}2Ku}{\operatorname{sn}2Ku},
\]
and from this there results
% [sic] The source prints \cos\pi u in (1), although the preceding derivation requires \cos 2\pi u.
\weq{1}{\frac{2K}{\pi}\frac{\operatorname{cn}2Ku}{\operatorname{sn}2Ku} = \operatorname{cotg}\pi u + 4\sin 2\pi u\sum\frac{(-1)^{\frac{m}{2}}q^m}{1-2q^m\cos\pi u+q^{2m}}.}

If one applies the same procedure to formula (2) of Table III, one obtains:
\[
\frac{2K}{\pi}\frac{\operatorname{cn}2Ku}{\operatorname{sn}2Ku} = \operatorname{cotg}\pi u + 4\sum(-1)^{\frac{m'}{2}}q^{\frac{mm'}{2}}\sin\pi mu.
\]

Here $m$ and $m'$ run, independently of one another, through the sequences of positive even numbers, and the summation with respect to $m'$ can still be carried out:
\[
\sum(-1)^{\frac{m'}{2}}q^{\frac{mm'}{2}} = -\frac{q^m}{1+q^m},
\]
hence:
\weq{2}{\frac{2K}{\pi}\frac{\operatorname{cn}2Ku}{\operatorname{sn}2Ku} = \operatorname{cotg}\pi u - 4\sum\frac{q^m}{1+q^m}\sin\pi mu.}

But while the first two formulae converge for all values of $u$, the convergence of the third is restricted to the region in which the imaginary part of $u$ is absolutely smaller than the imaginary part of $\omega$. The formula is therefore in any case valid for real $u$.

If one develops these formulae in ascending powers of $a$, the developments on the right and on the left begin with $a^{-1}$, and if one sets the terms independent of $a$ equal to one another on both sides, the developments sought result.

\]

\[
= \operatorname{cotg}\pi u + 4\sum\frac{q^m}{1-q^m}\sin m\pi u.

\begin{center}
\gesperrt{Fifth Chapter.}

The Modular Functions.

\rule{2cm}{0.4pt}

\S\,51. \gesperrt{The Elliptic Differential Equations.}
\end{center}

% The source's closing predicate, omitted in the recovered German fragment, has been restored.
The elliptic functions defined so far are functions of the two variables $v$, $\omega$, and the moduli $\varkappa$, $\varkappa'$, and further $j(\omega)$, $K$, $K'$ depend on the ratio of periods $\omega$, which must have a positive imaginary part. Likewise the function $\wp(u)$ is a function of the three variables $u$, $\omega_1$, $\omega_2$, and the invariants $g_2$, $g_3$ depend on $\omega_1$, $\omega_2$. \gesperrt{The problem of the inversion of the elliptic integrals}, as we formulated it in \S\,14, presupposes however that in the elliptic functions $\varkappa^2$ (or, in the \gesperrt{Weierstrass} normal form, $g_2, g_3$) have arbitrarily given values, and the complete solution of this problem therefore requires that not $\omega$, but $\varkappa^2$ (respectively $g_2, g_3$) appear as the second independent variable, and that $\omega$ be expressed by these. The next considerations will be devoted to this problem.

We start from the problem of integrating a system of differential equations, which we call that of the \gesperrt{elliptic differential equations}:
\weq{1}{\begin{aligned}
\frac{dx}{dv} &= yz, \\
\frac{dy}{dv} &= -zx, \\
\frac{dz}{dv} &= -\varkappa^2xy,
\end{aligned}}
under the subsidiary conditions:
\weq{2}{\text{for } v=0 \text{ we are to have } x=0,\ y=1,\ z=1\text{.}}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 188 =====
% !PRINTED 167
\weberpage{167}

We saw in the previous chapter that, if

\weq{3}{\varkappa^2 = \dfrac{\vartheta_{10}^4}{\vartheta_{00}^4}}

holds, this problem is solved by the elliptic functions, and indeed in such a way that $x$, $y$, $z$ become single-valued functions of $v$ in the whole $v$-plane, continuous except where they are infinite. But if $\varkappa^2$ is now given, the question arises whether for every value of $\varkappa^2$ there is a value of $\omega$ satisfying the condition (3), and whether there are several such values.

We prove first that the functions $x$, $y$, $z$ are \gesperrt{uniquely} determined by the differential equations (1) together with the subsidiary conditions.

It follows first from (1) that $x^2+y^2$, $\varkappa^2x^2+z^2$ are constant, and from the subsidiary conditions there follows:

\weq{4}{y^2 = 1-x^2, \qquad z^2 = 1-\varkappa^2x^2.}

Suppose that a second system of functions $x_1$, $y_1$, $z_1$ satisfying the same conditions exists; then first

\[
y_1^2 = 1-x_1^2, \qquad z_1^2 = 1-\varkappa^2x_1^2,
\]

and a simple differentiation shows that

\[
\frac{x\,y_1z_1 - x_1\,yz}{1-\varkappa^2x^2x_1^2}
\]

is constant. (The addition theorem of the elliptic integrals, from which one obtains the form of this expression, is confirmed directly by differentiation.) But from the subsidiary conditions it follows that this constant vanishes, and hence:

\[
x\,y_1z_1 = x_1\,yz,
\]

from which one easily concludes, by squaring both sides:

\[
x = x_1, \qquad y=y_1, \qquad z=z_1.
\]

\begin{center}
\S\,52. \gesperrt{The independent variable $\varkappa^2$. Linear differential equation for $K$.}
\end{center}

We now show first that, and how, for an arbitrarily given value of $\varkappa^2$ one can find at least \gesperrt{one} value of $\omega$ satisfying the condition

\weq{1}{\varkappa^2 = \dfrac{\vartheta_{10}^4}{\vartheta_{00}^4}}

This question is answered most completely by reduction to a linear differential equation of the second order.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 189 =====
% !PRINTED 168
\weberpage{168}

Such a differential equation, however, is already contained in the formulae of § 23.

First of all it follows from § 23, (14):

\[
d\log \varkappa^2 = i\pi\vartheta_{01}^4\,d\omega,
\]

or, in view of

\weq{2}{\pi\vartheta_{00}^2 = 2K, \quad \pi\vartheta_{10}^2 = 2\varkappa K, \quad \pi\vartheta_{01}^2 = 2\varkappa'K\ [\S\,42,\ (3),\ (15)]:}

\weq{3}{\pi\,d(\varkappa^2) = 4i\varkappa^2\varkappa'^2K^2\,d\omega,}

and from § 23, (19):

\[
\frac{d}{d\omega}\frac{dK}{K^2d\omega} = -\frac{4}{\pi^2}\varkappa^2\varkappa'^2K^3.
\]

If by means of (3) one introduces the variable $\varkappa^2$ in place of $\omega$, there follows

\weq{4}{\frac{d}{d(\varkappa^2)}\left(\varkappa^2\varkappa'^2\frac{dK}{d(\varkappa^2)}\right) = \frac14 K,}

and this is the differential equation sought.

If we set further

\weq{5}{-i\omega = \frac{K'}{K},}

\weq{6}{-iK^2d\omega = K\,dK' - K'\,dK,}

then by (3) there results:

\weq{7}{\varkappa^2\varkappa'^2\left(K\frac{dK'}{d(\varkappa^2)} - K'\frac{dK}{d(\varkappa^2)}\right) = -\frac{\pi}{4},}

and hence, by differentiating once again:

\[
\frac1K\frac{d}{d(\varkappa^2)}\left(\varkappa^2\varkappa'^2\frac{dK}{d(\varkappa^2)}\right) = \frac{1}{K'}\frac{d}{d(\varkappa^2)}\left(\varkappa^2\varkappa'^2\frac{dK'}{d(\varkappa^2)}\right),
\]

from which it is to be seen that $K'$ is the second particular integral of the differential equation (4).

% [sic] The source prints the Latin title as “seriem infinitum” (for “seriem infinitam”) and has no comma before Werke.
This differential equation can be integrated by hypergeometric series (\gesperrt{Gauss}, Disq. circa seriem infinitum Werke, Bd. III, S. 125).

If for the moment we set $\varkappa^2 = x$, $K = y$, then the differential equation (4) reads

\weq{8}{x(1-x)\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} + (1-2x)\frac{dy}{dx} - \frac14 y = 0,}

and it arises from the general \gesperrt{Gauss} differential equation

\weq{9}{(x-x^2)\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} + [\gamma-(\alpha+\beta+1)x]\frac{dy}{dx} - \alpha\beta y = 0}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 190 =====
% !PRINTED 169
\weberpage{169}

%<<CONT
if one sets $\alpha=\beta=\frac12$, $\gamma=1$. One of its
particular integrals is therefore
\weq{10}{F(\tfrac12,\tfrac12,1,x) = 1 + \sum_{\nu=1}^{\infty} \Bigl(\frac{1.3.5\ldots 2\nu-1}{2.4\ldots 2\nu}\Bigr)^2 x^\nu}
\[
{}= \sum_{\nu=0}^{\infty} \frac{\Pi(2\nu)^2}{\Pi(\nu)^4}\Bigl(\frac{x}{16}\Bigr)^\nu,
\]
and this series is convergent as long as the absolute value of
$x$ is less than 1. As the second particular integral one may
choose
\weq{11}{F(\tfrac12,\tfrac12,1,1-x),}
which, however, has a different domain of convergence. If we think of
$x$ as a complex variable represented in a plane, then (10) converges
in a circle described about the origin with radius 1, and (11) in an
equal circle described about the point 1, so that the common domain of
convergence consists of a lune containing the part of the real
axis that lies between 0 and 1. But one can also, and this is important
for us, set up the second particular integral in a form which converges
in the same circle as the series (10). Here it is to be observed
that the second particular integral becomes infinite for $x=0$.

This second particular integral is obtained by the
following passage to the limit. If we denote the hypergeometric
series after \gesperrt{Gauss} by
\[
F(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,x) = 1 + \frac{\alpha.\beta}{1.\gamma}x + \frac{\alpha(\alpha+1)\beta(\beta+1)}{1.2.\gamma(\gamma+1)}x^2 + \cdots
\]
\[
{}= \frac{\Pi(\gamma-1)}{\Pi(\alpha-1)\Pi(\beta-1)} \sum_{\nu=0}^{\infty} \frac{\Pi(\alpha+\nu-1)\Pi(\beta+\nu-1)}{\Pi(\gamma+\nu-1)\Pi(\nu)} x^\nu,
\]
then in general one obtains the two particular integrals
of (9):
\[
\begin{aligned}
y_1 &= F_1(x) = F(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,x), \\
y_2 &= F'_2(x) = x^{1-\gamma}(1-x)^{\gamma-\alpha-\beta} F(1-\alpha,1-\beta,2-\gamma,x).
\end{aligned}
\]
But since for $\alpha=\beta=\frac12$, $\gamma=1$ these become identical
with one another, one first sets $\alpha=\beta=\frac12$, $\gamma=1+\varepsilon$, hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
y_1 &= F(\tfrac12,\tfrac12,1+\varepsilon,x), \\
y_2 &= \Bigl(\frac{1-x}{x}\Bigr)^\varepsilon F(\tfrac12,\tfrac12,1-\varepsilon,x).
\end{aligned}
\]

But we have
\[
F(\tfrac12,\tfrac12,1\pm\varepsilon,x) = \frac{\Pi(\pm\varepsilon)}{[\Pi(-\tfrac12)]^2} \sum_{\nu=0}^{\infty} \frac{\Pi(\nu-\tfrac12)^2}{\Pi(\nu\pm\varepsilon)\Pi(\nu)} x^\nu,
\]
and, with the addition of a constant factor, one may also take
the following as the second particular integral:
\[
\frac{1}{2\varepsilon}\cdot\sum_{\nu=0}^{\infty} \frac{\Pi(\nu-\tfrac12)^2}{\Pi(\nu)}\Bigl[\frac{-1}{\Pi(\nu+\varepsilon)} + \Bigl(\frac{x}{1-x}\Bigr)^{-\varepsilon}\frac{1}{\Pi(\nu-\varepsilon)}\Bigr]x^\nu.
\]
If we here develop in powers of $\varepsilon$ and then set
$\varepsilon=0$, it follows that:
\[
\sum_{\nu=0}^{\infty} \frac{\Pi(\nu-\tfrac12)^2}{\Pi(\nu)^2} x^\nu \Bigl[\frac{\Pi'(\nu)}{\Pi(\nu)} - \frac12 \log\frac{x}{1-x}\Bigr],
\]
for which, using the \gesperrt{Gauss} formula
\[
\frac{\Pi(\nu-\tfrac12)\Pi(\nu)}{\Pi(2\nu)} = \sqrt{\pi}\,2^{-2\nu}
\]
one may also write, on discarding a constant factor:
\weq{12}{\sum_{\nu=0}^{\infty} \frac{\Pi(2\nu)^2}{\Pi(\nu)^4}\Bigl(\frac{x}{16}\Bigr)^\nu \Bigl[\frac{\Pi'(\nu)}{\Pi(\nu)} - \frac12 \log\frac{x}{1-x}\Bigr]\cdot}
But for a positive integer $\nu$ we have:
\[
\frac{\Pi'(\nu)}{\Pi(\nu)} = \Pi'(0) + 1 + \frac12 + \frac13 + \cdots + \frac1\nu,
\]
and if we therefore set, for brevity:
% [sic] In the second line the source omits the plus sign between \cdots and 1/\nu.
\weq{13}{\begin{aligned}

G(x) &= 2\sum_{\nu=1}^{\infty} \frac{\Pi(2\nu)^2}{\Pi(\nu)^4}\Bigl(1+\frac12+\frac13+\cdots\frac1\nu\Bigr)\Bigl(\frac{x}{16}\Bigr)^\nu,
\end{aligned}}
then the two particular solutions of the differential equation
 (8) result, if for the second one takes a linear combination
of (10) and (12):
\weq{14}{y_1 = F(x), \qquad y_2 = \frac12 G(x) - \frac12 \log\frac{x}{16(1-x)}F(x).}
But in order now to represent the particular integrals $K$ and $K'$ by
these functions, we must investigate the behaviour of $K,K'$
for $q=0$, for which at the same time $\varkappa^2=0$.

But for $q=0$ we have, by \S\,25 and \S\,42:
\[
q^{-1}\varkappa^2 = 16, \qquad 2K = \pi,
\]
%CONT>>
