%<<CONT
thus:
\[
\mathrm{Lim}\Bigl(\log\frac{\varkappa^2}{16} - i\pi\omega\Bigr) = 0,
\]
on the other hand we have $2iK' = \pi\vartheta_{00}^2\,\omega$ (\S\,42), or:
\[
2K' + \log\frac{\varkappa^2}{16} = \Bigl(\log\frac{\varkappa^2}{16} - i\pi\omega\Bigr) + i\pi\omega(1-\vartheta_{00}^2),
\]
from which:
\weq{15}{\mathrm{Lim}_{\varkappa^2=0}\Bigl(K' + \frac12\log\frac{\varkappa^2}{16}\Bigr) = 0.}
Since $K$ and $K'$ are now particular integrals of (8) (for
$x=\varkappa^2$), both have the form:
\[
K = a_1 y_1 + a_2 y_2, \qquad K' = a_1' y_1 + a_2' y_2,
\]
in which $a_1, a_2, a_1', a_2'$ are constant. Since $K$ remains finite
for $x=0$ and takes the value $\frac12\pi$, we have $a_2=0$, $a_1=\frac12\pi$; and
in order that $K'+\frac12\log x$ remain finite and [by (15)] take the value $\log 4$,
$a_2'=1$ and $a_1'=0$ must hold. Thus there results, if
one puts $x=\varkappa^2$, $1-x=\varkappa'^2$:
\weq{16}{K = \frac{\pi}{2}F(\varkappa^2), \qquad K' = \frac12 G(\varkappa^2) - \frac12\log\frac{\varkappa^2}{16\varkappa'^2}F(\varkappa^2)}
and
\weq{17}{q = e^{-\frac{\pi K'}{K}} = \frac{\varkappa^2}{16\varkappa'^2}\,e^{-\frac{G(\varkappa^2)}{F(\varkappa^2)}},}
in which, as already remarked, the series $G(\varkappa^2)$, $F(\varkappa^2)$ are convergent
so long as the absolute value of $\varkappa^2$ is a proper fraction.
In
the differential equation (4) there lie, to be sure, the means of continuing
the expressions found for $K,K',q$ beyond this domain of convergence. % [sic] The German source prints “dies” (for “diesen”).
One reaches this more simply, however, by the
application of the \gesperrt{Landen transformation}.

We bound the plane of the complex values $\varkappa^2$ by
laying two cuts along the real axis, from 0 to $-\infty$ and
from 1 to $\infty$. In the plane so bounded all
roots of $\varkappa^2, \varkappa'^2$ are then uniquely determined by the requirement that, for
positive properly fractional $\varkappa^2$, they are to be \gesperrt{real and positive}. Now
by the formulae of the \gesperrt{Landen} transformation
[\S\,44, (28)], if we denote by $\varkappa_1,\varkappa_1',K_1,K_1'$ the functions of $\omega$
that arise from $\varkappa,\varkappa',K,K'$ when $\omega$ is replaced by $2\omega$,
we have:
\weq{18}{\begin{aligned}
\varkappa_1 &= \frac{1-\varkappa'}{1+\varkappa'}, \qquad \varkappa_1' = \frac{2\sqrt{\varkappa'}}{1+\varkappa'}, \\
2K_1 &= (1+\varkappa')K, \qquad K_1' = (1+\varkappa')K'.
\end{aligned}}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 193 =====
% !PRINTED 172
\weberpage{172}

If we therefore replace $\omega$ by $2\omega$ in (17) and extract the square root, it follows that:

\weq{19}{q = \frac{1}{4}\frac{\varkappa_1}{\varkappa_1'}\, e^{-\frac{1}{2}\frac{G(\varkappa_1{}^2)}{F(\varkappa_1{}^2)}}.}

Here the domain of convergence now extends over the unit circle lying in the plane $\varkappa_1{}^2$, and this circle corresponds to the whole plane $\varkappa^2$. For the real part of $\varkappa'$ is positive in the \gesperrt{whole plane} of the $\varkappa^2$, with the exception of the two banks of the cut running from $+1$ to $+\infty$, on which $\varkappa'$ is purely imaginary. From this it follows that the absolute value of $\varkappa_1$ is less than 1, and that the periphery of the unit circle in the plane $\varkappa_1$ corresponds to the two banks of this cut.

But one can improve the convergence of these expressions still further by a renewed application of the \gesperrt{Landen} transformation. If we denote the result of a further doubling of $\omega$ by the index 2, then it follows that:

\weq{20}{\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{\varkappa_2} &= \frac{1-\sqrt{\varkappa'}}{1+\sqrt{\varkappa'}}, \\
4K_2 &= (1+\sqrt{\varkappa'})^2 K, \quad K_2' = (1+\sqrt{\varkappa'})^2 K', \\
q &= \sqrt{\frac{\varkappa_2}{4\varkappa_2'}}\, e^{-\frac{1}{4}\frac{G(\varkappa_2{}^2)}{F(\varkappa_2{}^2)}}.
\end{aligned}}

in which the domain of convergence now covers the plane of the $\varkappa^2$ \gesperrt{twice} (with a branching at the point $\varkappa^2=1$).

This operation can be continued, by deriving from $\varkappa_2$, according to formula (17), a new quantity $\varkappa_3$ through doubling of $\omega$, and from this in the same way $\varkappa_4$, and so on. One then obtains a sequence of expressions for $q$ whose convergence becomes ever better. For an arbitrary $\nu$ we have:

\weq{21}{q = \sqrt[2^{\nu-1}]{\frac{\varkappa_\nu}{4\varkappa_\nu'}}\, e^{-\frac{G(\varkappa_\nu{}^2)}{2^\nu F(\varkappa_\nu{}^2)}}.}

The first equation (18)

\[
\varkappa_1 = \frac{\varkappa^2}{(1+\varkappa')^2}
\]

shows that, so long as the absolute value of $\varkappa^2$ is less than 1, and consequently the absolute value of $1+\varkappa'$ greater than 1, the absolute value of $\varkappa_1$ is less than that of $\varkappa^2$, and consequently
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 194 =====
% !PRINTED 173
\weberpage{173}
%<<CONT
$\varkappa_\nu$ approaches the limit zero as $\nu$ increases infinitely. From this one obtains for $q$ the representation:

\weq{22}{q = \mathop{\mathrm{Lim}}\limits_{\nu=\infty} \sqrt[2^{\nu-1}]{\frac{\varkappa_\nu}{4\varkappa_\nu'}} = \mathrm{Lim} \sqrt[2^{\nu-1}]{\frac{\varkappa_\nu}{4}},}

which is suited to computation for real values of $\varkappa$.

From each of the formulae (21) one can derive a series development of $q$ in ascending powers of $\varkappa_\nu$, whose convergence increases as $\nu$ increases. If in particular one applies formula (20), one obtains a development which was communicated by \gesperrt{Weierstrass} in the Monatsberichte der Berliner Akademie for the year 1883, and whose domain of convergence fills the plane $\varkappa^2$ twice.

The coefficients of this development are most simply computed from:

\weq{23}{\sqrt{\varkappa_2} = \frac{\vartheta_{10}(0,4\omega)}{\vartheta_{00}(0,4\omega)} = \frac{2q+2q^9+2q^{25}+\cdots}{1+2q^4+2q^{16}+\cdots},}

and one thus obtains, by the method of undetermined coefficients:

\weq{24}{q = \frac{\sqrt{\varkappa_2}}{2} + 2\left(\frac{\sqrt{\varkappa_2}}{2}\right)^5 + 15\left(\frac{\sqrt{\varkappa_2}}{2}\right)^9 + 150\left(\frac{\sqrt{\varkappa_2}}{2}\right)^{13} + 1707\left(\frac{\sqrt{\varkappa_2}}{2}\right)^{17} + \cdots}

In the same way, conversely, $\sqrt{\varkappa_2}$ can also be developed by (23) into a series proceeding in powers of $q$:

\weq{25}{\tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{\varkappa_2} = q - 2q^5 + 5q^9 - 10q^{13} + 18q^{17}\cdots,}

which one also obtains by inversion of the series (24).

With this the question posed at the beginning of this section is completely answered.

As regards the application of the formulae developed here to the numerical computation of $q$, it may still be remarked that, when $\varkappa^2$ lies nearer to 1, one obtains a better converging procedure if one interchanges $\varkappa^2$ with $\varkappa'^2$. The calculation then yields at first not $q$, but

\[
q' = e^{-\frac{\pi i}{\omega}},
\]

from which, however, one obtains $q$ from the formula:

\[
\log q \log q' = \pi^2.
\]

%% ===== canonical stable idx 195 =====
% !PRINTED 174
\weberpage{174}

\begin{center}
\textbf{\S\ 53. \gesperrt{The Solutions of the Equation} $j(\omega) = j(\omega')$.}
\end{center}

The results of \S\ 51 suffice, to begin with, to establish the relations among the various values of $\omega$ which lead to the same value of $\varkappa^2$. Let then:

\weq{1}{\frac{\vartheta_{10}^4(0,\omega')}{\vartheta_{00}^4(0,\omega')} = \frac{\vartheta_{10}^4(0,\omega)}{\vartheta_{00}^4(0,\omega)} = \varkappa^2.}

If we set

\weq{2}{v = \pi\vartheta_{00}^2(0,\omega)\,u = \pi\vartheta_{00}^2(0,\omega')\,u',}

then (by \S\ 42) both the functions

\weq{3}{\frac{\vartheta_{00}(0,\omega)\vartheta_{11}(u,\omega)}{\vartheta_{10}(0,\omega)\vartheta_{01}(u,\omega)}, \quad \frac{\vartheta_{01}(0,\omega)\vartheta_{10}(u,\omega)}{\vartheta_{10}(0,\omega)\vartheta_{01}(u,\omega)}, \quad \frac{\vartheta_{01}(0,\omega)\vartheta_{00}(u,\omega)}{\vartheta_{00}(0,\omega)\vartheta_{01}(u,\omega)},}

as well as

\weq{4}{\frac{\vartheta_{00}(0,\omega')\vartheta_{11}(u',\omega')}{\vartheta_{10}(0,\omega')\vartheta_{01}(u',\omega')}, \quad \frac{\vartheta_{01}(0,\omega')\vartheta_{10}(u',\omega')}{\vartheta_{10}(0,\omega')\vartheta_{01}(u',\omega')}, \quad \frac{\vartheta_{01}(0,\omega')\vartheta_{00}(u',\omega')}{\vartheta_{00}(0,\omega')\vartheta_{01}(u',\omega')},}

put for $x,y,z$, satisfy the differential equations (1) of the preceding section, and the corresponding ones among these functions are therefore identical. Now if $u'=\frac{1}{2}$, then $\vartheta_{10}(u',\omega')$ vanishes, and $\vartheta_{10}(u,\omega)$ must then vanish as well. Accordingly there follows from (2), with regard to \S\ 21:

\weq{5}{\vartheta_{00}^2(0,\omega') = \vartheta_{00}^2(0,\omega)(\alpha+\beta\omega),}

in which $\alpha,\beta$ are integers which satisfy the condition

\weq{6}{\alpha \equiv 1, \quad \beta \equiv 0 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 2)}

If $u'=\omega':2$, then $\vartheta_{01}(u',\omega')$ and $\vartheta_{01}(u,\omega)$ vanish, and therefore, as above,

\weq{7}{\vartheta_{00}^2(0,\omega')\,\omega' = \vartheta_{00}^2(0,\omega)(\gamma+\delta\omega),}

in which

\weq{8}{\gamma \equiv 0, \quad \delta \equiv 1 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 2).}

From this it follows:

\weq{9}{\omega' = \frac{\gamma+\delta\omega}{\alpha+\beta\omega}.}

But since one may conclude in the same way:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\vartheta_{00}^2(0,\omega) &= \vartheta_{00}^2(0,\omega')(\alpha'+\beta'\omega'),\\
\vartheta_{00}^2(0,\omega)\,\omega &= \vartheta_{00}^2(0,\omega')(\gamma'+\delta'\omega'),
\end{aligned}
\]

in which $\alpha',\beta',\gamma',\delta'$ are likewise integers, the substitution of (5) in these equations gives:

\[
\begin{aligned}
1 &= (\alpha+\beta\omega)(\alpha'+\beta'\omega'),\\
\omega &= (\alpha+\beta\omega)(\gamma'+\delta'\omega').
\end{aligned}
\]

%% ===== canonical stable idx 196 =====
% !PRINTED 175
\weberpage{175}
If in these equations one expresses $\omega'$ in terms of $\omega$ according to (9), one obtains

\[
\begin{aligned}
1 &= \alpha'(\alpha+\beta\omega) + \beta'(\gamma+\delta\omega),\\
\omega &= \gamma'(\alpha+\beta\omega) + \delta'(\gamma+\delta\omega),
\end{aligned}
\]

and since $\omega$ is not real, each of these equations splits into two others:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\alpha\alpha' + \gamma\beta' &= 1, & \beta\alpha' + \delta\beta' &= 0,\\
\alpha\gamma' + \gamma\delta' &= 0, & \beta\gamma' + \delta\delta' &= 1.
\end{aligned}
\]

Consequently

\[
(\alpha\delta - \beta\gamma)(\alpha'\delta' - \beta'\gamma') = 1,
\]

and therefore, since $\omega,\omega'$ must both have a positive imaginary part, so that by (9) the determinant $\alpha\delta-\beta\gamma$ must be positive:

\[
\alpha\delta - \beta\gamma = 1,
\]
\[
\alpha = \delta', \quad \delta = \alpha', \quad \gamma = -\gamma', \quad \beta = -\beta'.
\]

1. \gesperrt{Thus $\omega, \omega'$ are connected with one another by a linear transformation, and indeed [by (6), (8)] by one of the first class (\S\ 36). That conversely two such values $\omega, \omega'$ also give the same value $\varkappa^2$ has already been shown above.}

A similar theorem follows from this as an immediate consequence, for the invariant $j(\omega)$ (\S\ 46).

2. \gesperrt{The equation:}

\weq{10}{j(\omega') = j(\omega)}

\gesperrt{is then and} \textbf{only} \gesperrt{then satisfied, when $\omega'$ is connected with $\omega$ by some linear transformation}

\[
\begin{pmatrix} \alpha, & \beta \\ \gamma, & \delta \end{pmatrix}
\]

\gesperrt{that is, when}

\weq{11}{\omega' = \frac{\gamma+\delta\omega}{\alpha+\beta\omega}, \quad \alpha\delta-\beta\gamma = 1}

\gesperrt{holds.}

For if we denote the values of $\varkappa^2,\varkappa'^2$ belonging to $\omega'$ by $\lambda^2,\lambda'^2$, then equation (10) can be written thus:

\[
\frac{(1-\lambda^2\lambda'^2)^3}{\lambda^4\lambda'^4} = \frac{(1-\varkappa^2\varkappa'^2)^3}{\varkappa^4\varkappa'^4},
\]

and with respect to $\lambda^2$ it is an equation of the sixth degree, whose roots

\[
\varkappa^2, \quad \varkappa'^2, \quad \frac{1}{\varkappa^2}, \quad \frac{1}{\varkappa'^2}, \quad -\frac{\varkappa'^2}{\varkappa^2}, \quad -\frac{\varkappa^2}{\varkappa'^2}
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 197 =====
% !PRINTED 176
\weberpage{176}
%<<CONT
are. Consequently (having regard to \S\,45) one of the following
relations holds:
\[
\lambda^2 = \varkappa^2(\omega), \quad \varkappa^2\!\left(-\frac{1}{\omega}\right), \quad \varkappa^2(\omega+1), \quad \varkappa^2\!\left(\frac{\omega-1}{\omega}\right),
\]
\[
\varkappa^2\!\left(-\frac{1}{\omega+1}\right), \quad \varkappa^2\!\left(\frac{\omega}{1-\omega}\right),
\]
whereby the correctness of the second theorem follows from the first.

The variable $\omega$ is here always restricted to a positive
imaginary part, and if we call two numbers $\omega$, $\omega'$ that are
connected by an equation (11) \gesperrt{equivalent}, then all numbers
equivalent to $\omega$ have a positive imaginary part.
We can also state our theorem 2. in this way:

3. \gesperrt{The function $j(\omega)$ has one and the same value for all equivalent values $\omega$
and only for these}$^{1)}$.

To every value of $\omega$ there belongs a definite value of $j(\omega)$,
and to every value of $j(\omega)$ a value of $\omega$ and the totality
 of the equivalent values $\omega'$. If therefore a one-valued
function $\Phi(\omega)$ of $\omega$ satisfies the condition:
\[
\Phi\!\left(\frac{\gamma+\delta\omega}{\alpha+\beta\omega}\right) = \Phi(\omega),
\]
then $\Phi(\omega)$ is a one-valued function of $j(\omega)$, and if we
therefore assume that $\Phi(\omega)$ becomes infinite only for a finite
number of values $j(\omega)$ and only in finite order, it follows
that $\Phi(\omega)$ is a \gesperrt{rational function of $j(\omega)$}.

The assumption always holds, for example, when $\Phi(\omega)$
stands in an \gesperrt{algebraic connection} with $j(\omega)$.

\begin{center}
\S\ 54. \gesperrt{The Modular Functions.}
\end{center}

Let $\psi(\omega)$ be a single-valued function of $\omega$. If one applies
to $\omega$ a linear transformation $S = \begin{pmatrix} \alpha, & \beta \\ \gamma, & \delta \end{pmatrix}$, then $\psi(\omega)$
passes into another function
\weq{1}{\psi\!\left(\frac{\gamma+\delta\omega}{\alpha+\beta\omega}\right)}
which we shall denote by $\psi\,|\,S$.

\footnotetext{$^{1)}$ This theorem was first proved by \gesperrt{Dedekind} \gesperrt{(Crelle, Bd.\,83)}.
\gesperrt{Dedekind} accordingly calls the function $\mathrm{val}(\omega) = 3^{-3}2^{-6}j(\omega)$ the \gesperrt{valence}
of $\omega$.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 198 =====
% !PRINTED 177
\weberpage{177}
The function $\psi(\omega)$ may possibly remain unchanged under certain
 transformations $S$ (e.\,g. always under the identical
 transformation). All transformations that leave a function
 $\psi(\omega)$ unchanged form a \gesperrt{group} $\mathfrak{G}$. For if
\[
\psi\,|\,S = \psi, \qquad \psi\,|\,S_1 = \psi,
\]
then also
\[
\psi\,|\,SS_1 = \psi\,|\,S_1 = \psi.
\]
The group $\mathfrak{G}$ is a divisor of the group $\mathfrak{L}$ of all linear
transformations.

If $\mathfrak{G}$ is a divisor of $\mathfrak{L}$ of \gesperrt{finite index $(\mathfrak{L}, \mathfrak{G})$, and
$\psi(\omega)$ a function of $\omega$ with the property that
conversely}
\[
\psi(\omega') = \psi(\omega)
\]
in turn entails \gesperrt{a linear connection}
\[
\omega' = \frac{\gamma+\delta\omega}{\alpha+\beta\omega}
\]
\gesperrt{in which $\begin{pmatrix} \alpha, & \beta \\ \gamma, & \delta \end{pmatrix}$ is a transformation belonging to $\mathfrak{G}$,
 then $\psi(\omega)$ is called a modular function belonging to the group $\mathfrak{G}$}.

We restrict ourselves to the consideration of those modular functions
that stand in an \gesperrt{algebraic connection} with the modulus $\varkappa^2$, and hence also with $j(\omega)$.

Under this hypothesis the following general theorem can be
stated:

\gesperrt{If $\psi(\omega)$ belongs to the group $\mathfrak{G}$ and $\chi(\omega)$ remains unchanged under the
transformations of $\mathfrak{G}$, then $\chi(\omega)$ is}
\textbf{rationally} \gesperrt{expressible through $\psi(\omega)$.}

For in the first place $\chi(\omega)$ is an algebraic function of $\psi(\omega)$,
and $\psi(\omega)$, as an algebraic function of $j(\omega)$, can take every
value. But to each value of $\psi(\omega)$ there belongs, by \gesperrt{hypothesis,
 only one value of $\chi(\omega)$, and therefore $\chi(\omega)$, as a one-valued
 algebraic function of $\psi(\omega)$, is rational.}

The study of the groups contained in $\mathfrak{L}$ and of the modular
functions belonging to them forms the principal subject of the great
work of \gesperrt{Klein and Fricke}: \glqq Vorlesungen über die Theorie
der elliptischen Modulfunktionen\grqq{} (2 Bde., Leipzig, Teubner,
1890, 1892). Here we consider only a few quite special cases
of these groups and functions, upon which we have come in the course of our
investigations.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 199 =====
% !PRINTED 178
\weberpage{178}
A large class of divisors of the group $\mathfrak{L}$ with finite
index is formed by the so-called \gesperrt{congruence groups}, which, if
$m$ is any integer, are characterised by the four congruences
\[
\begin{pmatrix} \alpha, & \beta \\ \gamma, & \delta \end{pmatrix} \equiv \begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0 \\ 0, & 1 \end{pmatrix} (\mathrm{mod}\ m)
\]
The modular functions belonging to these groups are
 called \gesperrt{congruence moduli} of the $m$th level. For $m = 2$
this is the group $\mathfrak{A}$ (\S\ 36). We shall make use of the
following theorems:

1. \gesperrt{By \S\ 52 the modulus $\varkappa^2$ is a modular function belonging
 to this group}; and since by \S\ 36 all these transformations
can be composed from the two
\[
\begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0 \\ 2, & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \begin{pmatrix} 1, & 2 \\ 0, & 1 \end{pmatrix}
\]
we can state the theorem:

\gesperrt{Every modular function which remains unchanged under the two permutations
}
\[
(\omega,\ \omega+2), \qquad \left(\omega,\ \frac{\omega}{1+2\omega}\right)
\]
\gesperrt{is a rational function of $\varkappa^2$.}

2. The function $\varkappa^2\varkappa'^2$ belongs to the group $\mathfrak{A}'$ formed
jointly from the first and second classes of \S\ 36.
This group can be derived by repetition of the two transformations
\[
\begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0 \\ 2, & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \begin{pmatrix} 0, & 1 \\ -1, & 0 \end{pmatrix}
\]
and we can therefore state the theorem:

\gesperrt{Every modular function which remains unchanged under the two permutations
}
\[
(\omega,\ \omega+2), \qquad \left(\omega,\ -\frac{1}{\omega}\right)
\]
\gesperrt{is a rational function of $\varkappa^2\varkappa'^2$.}
From this there follows further:

3. \gesperrt{Every modular function which remains unchanged under $(\omega,\omega+2)$
and changes its sign under $\left(\omega, -\dfrac{1}{\omega}\right)$ is the
product of $(\varkappa'^2 - \varkappa^2)$ with a rational function
of $\varkappa^2\varkappa'^2$.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 200 =====
% !PRINTED 179
\weberpage{179}
4. The invariant $j(\omega)$ belongs to the group $\mathfrak{L}$ (\S\ 53), and
hence the theorem:

\gesperrt{Every modular function that remains unchanged under the two
permutations
}
\[
(\omega,\ \omega+1), \qquad \left(\omega,\ -\frac{1}{\omega}\right)
\]
\gesperrt{is a rational function of $j(\omega)$.}

Besides these we introduce two further modular
functions.

From the definition of the functions $f(\omega)$, $f_1(\omega)$, $f_2(\omega)$ [\S\,34,
(1), (10)] there follows, when the two equations \S\,42, (3) are
multiplied by one another:
\weq{2}{f(\omega) = \frac{\sqrt[6]{2}}{\sqrt[12]{\varkappa\varkappa'}}, \qquad f_1(\omega) = \sqrt[6]{2}\ \sqrt[12]{\frac{\varkappa'^2}{\varkappa}}, \qquad f_2(\omega) = \sqrt[6]{2}\ \sqrt[12]{\frac{\varkappa^2}{\varkappa'}},}
\weq{3}{\frac{f_1(\omega)}{f(\omega)} = \sqrt[4]{\varkappa'}, \qquad \frac{f_2(\omega)}{f(\omega)} = \sqrt[4]{\varkappa}.}

On the basis of \S\,46, (15), (16) we define two functions
 $\gamma_2(\omega)$, $\gamma_3(\omega)$:
\weq{4}{\begin{aligned}
\gamma_2(\omega) &= \sqrt[3]{j(\omega)} = \sqrt[3]{2^8}\ \frac{1 - \varkappa^2\varkappa'^2}{\sqrt[3]{\varkappa^4\varkappa'^4}},\\
\gamma_3(\omega) &= \sqrt{j(\omega) - 27\cdot 64} = \frac{8(2+\varkappa^2\varkappa'^2)(\varkappa'^2 - \varkappa^2)}{\varkappa^2\varkappa'^2},
\end{aligned}}
which, by (2) and (3), admit of the following representation as one-valued
 functions of $\omega$:
\weq{5}{\begin{aligned}
\gamma_2(\omega) &= \frac{f(\omega)^{24} - 16}{f(\omega)^8},\\
\gamma_3(\omega) &= \frac{[f(\omega)^{24} + 8][f_1(\omega)^8 - f_2(\omega)^8]}{f(\omega)^8},
\end{aligned}}
for which, by the fundamental formulae for the $f$-functions [\S\,34,
(11), (12)], one may also put:
\weq{6}{\gamma_2(\omega) = f(\omega)^8 f_1(\omega)^8 + f(\omega)^8 f_2(\omega)^8 - f_1(\omega)^8 f_2(\omega)^8,}
\weq{7}{\gamma_3(\omega) = \tfrac{1}{2}[f(\omega)^8 + f_1(\omega)^8][f(\omega)^8 + f_2(\omega)^8][f_1(\omega)^8 - f_2(\omega)^8].}
Thus $x = f^8,\ -f_1^8,\ -f_2^8$ are the roots of the cubic
equation
\weq{8}{x^3 - \gamma_2 x - 16 = 0,}
and $4\gamma_3^2$ is the discriminant of this equation.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 201 =====
% !PRINTED 180
\weberpage{180}
Also noteworthy are the differential equations:
\weq{9}{d\varkappa^2 = -d\varkappa'^2 = \pi i\,\vartheta_{00}^4\,\varkappa^2\varkappa'^2\,d\omega\ [\S\,52,\,(3)],}
\weq{10}{d\varkappa^2\varkappa'^2 = -\pi i\,\vartheta_{00}^4(\varkappa^2-\varkappa'^2)\varkappa^2\varkappa'^2\,d\omega,}
\weq{11}{df(\omega)^8 = \dfrac{\pi i}{3}\vartheta_{00}^4[f_2(\omega)^8 - f_1(\omega)^3]\,d\omega,}
% [sic] German source prints exponent 3 on f_1; the identity mathematically requires exponent 8.
\weq{12}{d\gamma_2(\omega) = -\dfrac{2\pi i}{3}\gamma_3(\omega)\eta(\omega)^4\,d\omega\ [\text{by}\ (5)\ \text{and}\ \S\,34,\,(10)],}
\weq{13}{dj(\omega) = -2\pi i\,\gamma_2(\omega)^2\gamma_3(\omega)\eta(\omega)^4\,d\omega.}
One then obtains for the linear fundamental transformations, from \S\,34, (13), (14), (15):
\weq{14}{\begin{array}{ll}
\gamma_2(\omega+1) = e^{-\frac{2\pi i}{3}}\gamma_2(\omega), & \gamma_2\left(-\dfrac{1}{\omega}\right) = \gamma_2(\omega),\\[6pt]
\gamma_3(\omega+1) = -\gamma_3(\omega), & \gamma_3\left(-\dfrac{1}{\omega}\right) = -\gamma_3(\omega),
\end{array}}
and from \S\,40 one finds in general:
\weq{15}{\begin{array}{l}
\gamma_2\left(\dfrac{\gamma+\delta\omega}{\alpha+\beta\omega}\right) = \varrho\,\gamma_2(\omega),\\[6pt]
\gamma_3\left(\dfrac{\gamma+\delta\omega}{\alpha+\beta\omega}\right) = (-1)^{\alpha\gamma+\beta\gamma+\beta\delta}\gamma_3(\omega),
\end{array}}
in which $\varrho$ has the meaning it has in \S\,40, (3):
\[
\varrho = e^{-\frac{2\pi i}{3}(\alpha\gamma+\beta\delta-\alpha\beta-\alpha^2\beta\delta)}.
\]
These, then, are modular functions, and the groups to which they belong are characterised by the two congruences:
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
-\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma+\beta\delta-\alpha^2\beta\gamma &\equiv 0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 3),\\
\alpha\gamma+\beta\gamma+\beta\delta &\equiv 0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 2).
\end{array}
\]
Accordingly we give our Theorem 4. the following supplement, which follows from the formulae (14).

5. \gesperrt{A modular function which changes its sign under the two substitutions}
\[
(\omega, \omega+1), \qquad \left(\omega, -\dfrac{1}{\omega}\right)
\]
\gesperrt{is the product of $\gamma_3(\omega)$ with a rational function of $j(\omega)$.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 202 =====
% !PRINTED 181
\weberpage{181}
6. \gesperrt{A modular function which remains unchanged under the substitution $\left(\omega, -\dfrac{1}{\omega}\right)$ and which under $(\omega, \omega+1)$ takes on the factor $e^{\mp\frac{2\pi i}{3}}$ is the product of $\gamma_3(\omega)^{\pm 1}$ with a rational function $j(\omega)$.} % [sic] German source prints gamma_3 although the stated cubic-root transformation requires gamma_2; it also omits \textquotedbl{}von\textquotedbl{} (English \textquotedbl{}of\textquotedbl{}) before j(\omega).

7. \gesperrt{A modular function which changes sign under the substitutions $\left(\omega, -\dfrac{1}{\omega}\right)$ and which under $(\omega, \omega+1)$ takes on the factor $-e^{\mp\frac{2\pi i}{3}}$ is the product of $\gamma_2(\omega)\gamma_3(\omega)^{\pm 1}$ with a rational function of $j(\omega)$.}

We shall occupy ourselves more thoroughly with the modular functions in the second part.

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{\S\ 55. Representation of the elliptic functions by $v$ and $\varkappa^2$.}
\medskip

If we conceive the inversion problem of the elliptic integrals, as in \S\,51, as the task of integrating the \gesperrt{elliptic differential equations}, then it demands the representation of the three functions sn\,$v$, cn\,$v$, dn\,$v$ by the two independent variables $v$, $\varkappa^2$. This task is solved by \S\,42, but with respect to the variable $\varkappa^2$ only implicitly. One can, however, also find representations in which $\varkappa^2$ occurs explicitly, namely by series which proceed in powers of $v$ and whose coefficients are \gesperrt{rational functions of $\varkappa^2$}. The coefficients of these series cannot, it is true, be represented by a general law; they can only be computed successively. These representations are owed chiefly to \gesperrt{Weierstrass}\footnote{On \gesperrt{Weierstrass}'s theory of the elliptic functions cf. especially the ``Formeln und Lehrsätze zum Gebrauch der elliptischen Funktionen'' edited by H.\,A. \gesperrt{Schwarz}. On the series developments cf. also \gesperrt{Königsberger}, ``Vorlesungen über die Theorie der elliptischen Funktionen'', 25. Vorlesung.}.

Since the $\sigma$-functions are throughout finite and continuous functions of $u$, they can be developed in unconditionally convergent power series in $u$, and if we accordingly develop the $\sigma$-functions occurring in \S\,45, (2) in this way, we obtain a solution of our task. We therefore put
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 203 =====
% !PRINTED 182
\weberpage{182}
%<<CONT
\weq{1}{\begin{array}{l}
\sigma(v,\,2K,\,2iK') = \displaystyle\sum_{0,\infty}^{\nu} A_\nu\,\dfrac{v^{2\nu+1}}{(2\nu+1)!},\\[8pt]
\sigma_{00}(v,\,2K,\,2iK') = \displaystyle\sum_{0,\infty}^{\nu} B_\nu\,\dfrac{v^{2\nu}}{(2\nu)!},\\[8pt]
\sigma_{01}(v,\,2K,\,2iK') = \displaystyle\sum_{0,\infty}^{\nu} C_\nu\,\dfrac{v^{2\nu}}{(2\nu)!},\\[8pt]
\sigma_{10}(v,\,2K,\,2iK') = \displaystyle\sum_{0,\infty}^{\nu} D_\nu\,\dfrac{v^{2\nu}}{(2\nu)!},
\end{array}}
and the $A_\nu$, $B_\nu$, $C_\nu$, $D_\nu$ are the functions of $\varkappa^2$, or of $\omega$, that are to be determined. If we regard them first as functions of $\omega$, then the linear transformations [\S\,45, (3)] give:
\weq{2}{\begin{array}{l}
A_\nu\left(-\dfrac{1}{\omega}\right) = (-1)^\nu A_\nu(\omega),\\[6pt]
B_\nu\left(-\dfrac{1}{\omega}\right) = (-1)^\nu B_\nu(\omega),\\[6pt]
C_\nu\left(-\dfrac{1}{\omega}\right) = (-1)^\nu D_\nu(\omega),\\[6pt]
D_\nu\left(-\dfrac{1}{\omega}\right) = (-1)^\nu C_\nu(\omega).
\end{array}}
\weq{3}{\begin{array}{l}
\varkappa'^{2\nu} A_\nu(\omega+1) = A_\nu(\omega),\\[4pt]
\varkappa'^{2\nu} B_\nu(\omega+1) = C_\nu(\omega),\\[4pt]
\varkappa'^{2\nu} C_\nu(\omega+1) = B_\nu(\omega),\\[4pt]
\varkappa'^{2\nu} D_\nu(\omega+1) = D_\nu(\omega).
\end{array}}
\weq{4}{\begin{array}{l}
A_\nu(\omega+2) = A_\nu(\omega),\\[4pt]
B_\nu(\omega+2) = B_\nu(\omega),\\[4pt]
C_\nu(\omega+2) = C_\nu(\omega),\\[4pt]
D_\nu(\omega+2) = D_\nu(\omega).
\end{array}}
From this we infer the characteristic properties of these coefficients as functions of $\varkappa^2$. It is evident at once from the meaning of the coefficients that, for every value of $\varkappa^2$ with the possible exception of $\varkappa^2 = 0, 1, \infty$, the coefficients $A_\nu(\varkappa^2)$, $B_\nu(\varkappa^2)$, $C_\nu(\varkappa^2)$, $D_\nu(\varkappa^2)$ are finite and continuous functions of $\varkappa^2$.

But these functions remain finite for $\varkappa^2 = 0$ as well, and their values can easily be found by letting $q$, and hence $\varkappa^2$, pass into zero in the representations of \S\,37.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 204 =====
% !PRINTED 183
\weberpage{183}
From the developments in \S\,25 one then obtains, in view of the fact that by \S\,34 and \S\,42, for a vanishing $q$,
\[
\eta(\omega) = q^{\frac{1}{12}}, \qquad 2K = \pi
\]
holds:
\weq{5}{\begin{array}{r@{}l@{\;}l}
e^{\frac{v^2}{6}} & \sin v & = \displaystyle\sum_{0,\infty}^{\nu} A_\nu(0)\,\dfrac{v^{2\nu+1}}{(2\nu+1)!},\\[8pt]
e^{\frac{v^2}{6}} & & = \displaystyle\sum_{0,\infty}^{\nu} B_\nu(0)\,\dfrac{v^{2\nu}}{(2\nu)!},\\[8pt]
e^{\frac{v^2}{6}} & & = \displaystyle\sum_{0,\infty}^{\nu} C_\nu(0)\,\dfrac{v^{2\nu}}{(2\nu)!},\\[8pt]
e^{\frac{v^2}{6}} & \cos v & = \displaystyle\sum_{0,\infty}^{\nu} D_\nu(0)\,\dfrac{v^{2\nu}}{(2\nu)!}.
\end{array}}
Formulae (2) now give:
\weq{6}{\begin{array}{l}
A_\nu(\varkappa'^2) = (-1)^\nu A_\nu(\varkappa^2),\\[4pt]
B_\nu(\varkappa'^2) = (-1)^\nu B_\nu(\varkappa^2),\\[4pt]
C_\nu(\varkappa'^2) = (-1)^\nu D_\nu(\varkappa^2),\\[4pt]
D_\nu(\varkappa'^2) = (-1)^\nu C_\nu(\varkappa^2),
\end{array}}
from which it follows that these functions remain finite for $\varkappa^2 = 1$ as well, namely:
\weq{7}{\begin{array}{l}
A_\nu(1) = (-1)^\nu A_\nu(0),\\[4pt]
B_\nu(1) = (-1)^\nu B_\nu(0),\\[4pt]
C_\nu(1) = (-1)^\nu D_\nu(0),\\[4pt]
D_\nu(1) = (-1)^\nu C_\nu(0).
\end{array}}
The system (3) can moreover be written thus:
\weq{8}{\begin{array}{l}
\varkappa'^{2\nu} A_\nu\left(\dfrac{-\varkappa^2}{\varkappa'^2}\right) = A_\nu(\varkappa^2),\\[6pt]
\varkappa'^{2\nu} B_\nu\left(\dfrac{-\varkappa^2}{\varkappa'^2}\right) = C_\nu(\varkappa^2),\\[6pt]
\varkappa'^{2\nu} C_\nu\left(\dfrac{-\varkappa^2}{\varkappa'^2}\right) = B_\nu(\varkappa^2),\\[6pt]
\varkappa'^{2\nu} D_\nu\left(\dfrac{-\varkappa^2}{\varkappa'^2}\right) = D_\nu(\varkappa^2),
\end{array}}
from which, for an infinite $\varkappa^2$:
\weq{9}{\begin{array}{l}
A_\nu(\varkappa^2) = \varkappa^{2\nu} A_\nu(0),\\[4pt]
B_\nu(\varkappa^2) = \varkappa^{2\nu} D_\nu(0),\\[4pt]
C_\nu(\varkappa^2) = \varkappa^{2\nu} B_\nu(0),\\[4pt]
D_\nu(\varkappa^2) = \varkappa^{2\nu} C_\nu(0),
\end{array}}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 205 =====
% !PRINTED 184
\weberpage{184}

%<<CONT
and from this it is concluded that the coefficients $A_\nu, B_\nu, C_\nu, D_\nu$
\gesperrt{are integral rational functions of $\varkappa^2$ of degree $\nu$}, and
from \S\,54, 2, 3, it follows moreover that $A_\nu, B_\nu$ are, for even $\nu$,
expressed rationally by $\varkappa^2\varkappa'^2$, while for odd
$\nu$ they are equal to the product of $(\varkappa'^2-\varkappa^2)$ with a rational function
 of $\varkappa^2\varkappa'^2$.

From $B_\nu$ one finds $C_\nu$ by means of the formula:

\weq{10}{C_\nu(\varkappa^2) = \varkappa'^{2\nu}B_\nu\left(\frac{-\varkappa^2}{\varkappa'^2}\right)}

and $D_\nu$ by applying (6) and (8):

\weq{11}{D_\nu(\varkappa^2) = (-1)^\nu C_\nu(\varkappa'^2) = (-1)^\nu \varkappa^{2\nu}B_\nu\left(\frac{-\varkappa'^2}{\varkappa^2}\right).}

Since the coefficients $A_\nu(0), B_\nu(0), C_\nu(0), D_\nu(0)$ can easily be
determined from (5), the system of formulae developed here yields
the coefficients $A_\nu, B_\nu, C_\nu, D_\nu$ without
further calculation up to $\nu=3$ inclusive.

One finds:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&A_0=1, \quad A_1=0, \qquad A_2=-\frac{2}{3}(1-\varkappa^2\varkappa'^2),\\
&B_0=1, \quad B_1=\frac{1}{3}(\varkappa'^2-\varkappa^2), \quad B_2=\frac{1}{3}(1+2\varkappa^2\varkappa'^2),\\
&C_0=1, \quad C_1=\frac{1}{3}(1+\varkappa^2), \quad C_2=\frac{1}{3}(\varkappa'^4-2\varkappa^2),\\
&D_0=1, \quad D_1=-\frac{1}{3}(1+\varkappa'^2), \quad D_2=\frac{1}{3}(\varkappa^4-2\varkappa'^2).\\
&A_3=-\frac{8}{9}(\varkappa'^2-\varkappa^2)(2+\varkappa^2\varkappa'^2),\\
&B_3=\frac{1}{9}(\varkappa'^2-\varkappa^2)(5-2\varkappa^2\varkappa'^2),\\
&C_3=\frac{1}{9}(1+\varkappa^2)(5\varkappa'^4+2\varkappa^2),\\
&D_3=-\frac{1}{9}(1+\varkappa'^2)(5\varkappa^4+2\varkappa'^2).
\end{aligned}
\]

Further coefficients can be calculated in the same way, though
more laboriously, by developing the expressions for the
$\sigma$-functions in \S\,32 in powers of $q$ and using the higher
powers of $q$ as the lowest one has been used here. \gesperrt{Weierstrass}
makes use, for the recurrent calculation of the coefficients,
of certain partial differential equations, similar to the one that we
shall derive in the next section for the function $\sigma$.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 206 =====
% !PRINTED 185
\weberpage{185}

\begin{center}
\textbf{\S\,56. \gesperrt{Power series for the Weierstrass functions}}\\
$\wp(u), \sigma(u)$.
\end{center}

The function $\sigma(u)$, regarded as a function of $u$, can, as has
already been remarked, be developed into a series in powers of $u$
converging in the whole $u$-plane, and by \S\,35, (8), (12)
this development has the following form:

\weq{1}{\sigma(u) = u + \alpha u^3 + \alpha_1 u^5 + \alpha_2 u^7 + \alpha_3 u^9 + \cdots}

The function

\weq{2}{\wp(u) = -\frac{d^2\log\sigma(u)}{du^2} = \frac{\sigma'(u)^2 - \sigma\sigma''(u)}{\sigma(u)^2}}

can likewise be developed in ascending powers of $u$, but no longer
into a series that is always convergent; rather, this series has a
circle of convergence. It has the form:

\weq{3}{\wp(u) = \frac{1}{u^2} + a + a_1 u^2 + a_2 u^4 + a_3 u^6 + \cdots}

and one can determine the coefficients $a, a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots$ in turn,
from the differential equation [\S\,46, (18)]

\weq{4}{\wp'(u)^2 = 4\wp(u)^3 - g_2\wp(u) - g_3}

as functions of $g_2, g_3$.
First of all we have
\[
\wp'(u) = -\frac{2}{u^3} + 2a_1 u + 4a_2 u^3 + 6a_3 u^5 + \cdots,
\]
\[
\wp'(u)^2 = \frac{4}{u^6} - \frac{8a_1}{u^2} - 16a_2 + (4a_1^2 - 24a_3)u^2 + \cdots,
\]
and since $\wp'(u)^2$ contains no term in $u^{-4}$, while in $\wp(u)^3$
the term $3au^{-4}$ occurs, $a=0$ must hold. Accordingly there
results:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\wp(u)^3 &= \frac{1}{u^6} + \frac{3a_1}{u^2} + 3a_2 + 3(a_3+a_1^2)u^2 + \cdots,\\
\wp(u) &= \frac{1}{u^2} \phantom{{}+ \frac{3a_1}{u^2} + 3a_2{}} + a_1 u^2 + \cdots
\end{aligned}
\]
And if one substitutes this into equation (4), it follows that

\weq{5}{a_1 = \frac{g_2}{20}, \quad a_2 = \frac{g_3}{28}, \quad a_3 = \frac{g_2^2}{1200}.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 207 =====
% !PRINTED 186
\weberpage{186}

By integration of (2) one finds:
\[
\sigma'(u) = \left(\frac{1}{u} - \frac{a_1 u^3}{3} - \frac{a_2 u^5}{5} - \frac{a_3 u^7}{7}\cdots\right)\sigma(u),
\]
and from this equation it follows:

\weq{6}{\alpha = 0, \quad \alpha_1 = \frac{-g_2}{240}, \quad \alpha_2 = \frac{-g_3}{840}, \quad \alpha_3 = \frac{-g_3^2}{161\,280}.}

That $\alpha=0$ follows also from the $\sigma'''(u) = 0$ proved in \S\,35;
there, however, this was proved by a rather cumbersome route. We thus have
the following beginning of the development of $\sigma(u)$, where, for the
sake of clarity, the numerical denominators are decomposed into their prime
factors:

\weq{7}{\sigma(u) = u - \frac{g_2}{2^4\cdot 3\cdot 5}u^5 - \frac{g_3}{2^3\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 7}u^7 - \frac{g_3^2}{2^9\cdot 3^2\cdot 5\cdot 7}u^9 - \cdots}

For the recurrent calculation of the coefficients in the power series for
$\sigma(u)$ there serves a partial differential equation which may be
regarded as a transformation of the partial differential equation for the
$\vartheta$-functions. We derive it in the following way.

The function $\sigma(u)$ was determined by the two period equations
\S\,35, (9)

\weq{8}{
\begin{aligned}
&\sigma(u+\omega_1) = -e^{\eta_1(2u+\omega_1)}\sigma(u),\\
&\sigma(u+\omega_2) = -e^{\eta_2(2u+\omega_2)}\sigma(u),\\
&\eta_1\omega_2 - \eta_2\omega_1 = \pi i
\end{aligned}
}

up to a factor independent of $u$. But differentiation of the last
equation (8) yields:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial \eta_1}{\partial \omega_1}\omega_2 - \frac{\partial \eta_2}{\partial \omega_1}\omega_1 - \eta_2 &= 0,\\
\frac{\partial \eta_1}{\partial \omega_2}\omega_2 - \frac{\partial \eta_2}{\partial \omega_2}\omega_1 + \eta_1 &= 0,
\end{aligned}
\]
hence:
\[
\omega_2\left(\eta_1\frac{\partial \eta_1}{\partial \omega_1} + \eta_2\frac{\partial \eta_1}{\partial \omega_2}\right) = \omega_1\left(\eta_1\frac{\partial \eta_2}{\partial \omega_1} + \eta_2\frac{\partial \eta_2}{\partial \omega_2}\right),
\]
and we therefore introduce a quantity $r$, which we define as follows:

\weq{9}{
\begin{aligned}
&\eta_1\frac{\partial \eta_1}{\partial \omega_1} + \eta_2\frac{\partial \eta_1}{\partial \omega_1} = -r\omega_1, \\ % [sic] German source repeats partial omega_1; the derivation requires partial omega_2.
&\eta_1\frac{\partial \eta_1}{\partial \omega_2} + \eta_2\frac{\partial \eta_2}{\partial \omega_2} = -r\omega_2. % [sic] German source prints partial eta_1 / partial omega_2; the derivation requires partial eta_2 / partial omega_1.
\end{aligned}
}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 208 =====
% !PRINTED 187
\weberpage{187}

Now one shows, by differentiating the period equations
(8), that the function
\[
S(u) = \frac{\partial^2 \sigma}{\partial u^2} + 4\eta_1\frac{\partial \sigma}{\partial \omega_1} + 4\eta_2\frac{\partial \sigma}{\partial \omega_2} + 4ru^2\sigma
\]
satisfies the period equations (8), and is therefore equal to $C\sigma(u)$,
where $C$ is independent of $u$. But the development of $\sigma(u)$ in % [sic] German source prints sigma(u); the argument requires S(u).
powers of $u$ begins with $u^3$, while $\sigma(u)$ begins with $u$,
and consequently we must have $C=0$.

By (7) the development of $\partial\sigma/\partial\omega_1$ and $\partial\sigma/\partial\omega_2$
begins only with $u^5$, and the first terms of $\partial^2\sigma/\partial u^2$ and $4ru^2\sigma$ are
$-g_2u^3/12$, $4ru^3$, from which $4r=g_2/12$ follows; accordingly
the differential equation for $\sigma$ takes the form:

\weq{10}{\frac{\partial^2 \sigma}{\partial u^2} + 4\eta_1\frac{\partial \sigma}{\partial \omega_1} + 4\eta_2\frac{\partial \sigma}{\partial \omega_2} + \frac{g_2}{12}u^2\sigma = 0,}

and incidentally there follow from (9) the relations:

\weq{11}{
\begin{aligned}
&\eta_1\frac{\partial \eta_1}{\partial \omega_1} + \eta_2\frac{\partial \eta_1}{\partial \omega_1} = -\frac{g_2}{48}\omega_1, \\
&\eta_1\frac{\partial \eta_1}{\partial \omega_2} + \eta_2\frac{\partial \eta_2}{\partial \omega_2} = -\frac{g_2}{48}\omega_2.
\end{aligned}
}
% [sic] In the first row the German source repeats eta_1; the derivation requires eta_2.

Now in the differential equation (10) the variables
$g_2, g_3$ are to be introduced in place of the variables $\omega_1, \omega_2$, and if we accordingly put
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{\partial \sigma}{\partial \omega_1} = \frac{\partial \sigma}{\partial g_2}\frac{\partial g_2}{\partial \omega_1} + \frac{\partial \sigma}{\partial g_3}\frac{\partial g_3}{\partial \omega_1}, \\
&\frac{\partial \sigma}{\partial \omega_2} = \frac{\partial \sigma}{\partial g_2}\frac{\partial g_2}{\partial \omega_2} + \frac{\partial \sigma}{\partial g_3}\frac{\partial g_3}{\partial \omega_2}
\end{aligned}
\]
then (10) takes the form:

\weq{12}{\frac{\partial^2 \sigma}{\partial u^2} + h_2\frac{\partial \sigma}{\partial g_2} + h_3\frac{\partial \sigma}{\partial g_3} + \frac{g_2}{12}u^2\sigma = 0,}

where
\[
\begin{aligned}
h_2 &= 4\left(\eta_1\frac{\partial g_2}{\partial \omega_1} + \eta_2\frac{\partial g_2}{\partial \omega_2}\right), \\
h_3 &= 4\left(\eta_1\frac{\partial g_3}{\partial \omega_1} + \eta_2\frac{\partial g_3}{\partial \omega_2}\right).
\end{aligned}
\]

The quantities $h_2, h_3$, expressed through $g_2, g_3$, now follow
from the differential equation itself, if one substitutes the development
(7) for $\sigma$. Accordingly, up to the 7th power of $u$:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 209 =====
% !PRINTED 188
\weberpage{188}
%<<CONT
\[
\begin{array}{r@{}c@{}r@{}r@{}r}
\displaystyle\frac{\partial^2\sigma}{\partial u^2} &{}={}& -\dfrac{g_2}{12}u^3 &{}- 12\,g_3\dfrac{u^5}{2^4\cdot3\cdot5} &{}- \dfrac{3}{8}g_2^2\dfrac{u^7}{2^3\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7},\\[2mm]
\displaystyle\frac{\partial\sigma}{\partial g_2} &{}={}& &{}- \dfrac{u^5}{2^4\cdot3\cdot5} &\\[2mm]
\displaystyle\frac{\partial\sigma}{\partial g_3} &{}={}& & &{}- \dfrac{u^7}{2^3\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7},\\[2mm]
\displaystyle\frac{g_2}{12}u^2\sigma &{}={}& \dfrac{g_2}{12}u^3 & &{}-\dfrac{7}{24}g_2^2\dfrac{u^7}{2^3\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7},
\end{array}
\]

and if we substitute this into (12) and set the coefficients of $u^5$
and $u^7$ equal to zero, we find:

\[
h_2 = -12\,g_3, \qquad h_3 = -\tfrac{2}{3}g_2^2,
\]

and we obtain the differential equation:

\weq{13}{\dfrac{\partial^2\sigma}{\partial u^2} - 12\,g_3\dfrac{\partial\sigma}{\partial g_2} - \dfrac{2}{3}g_2^2\dfrac{\partial\sigma}{\partial g_3} + \dfrac{g_2}{12}u^2\sigma = 0.}

If we set up the series development for $\sigma$ with undetermined
coefficients:

\weq{14}{\sigma = \Sigma A_\nu\dfrac{u^{2\nu+1}}{(2\nu+1)!},}

then from (13) we obtain the recursion formula:

\weq{15}{A_\nu = 12\,g_3\dfrac{\partial A_{\nu-1}}{\partial g_2} + \dfrac{2}{3}g_2^2\dfrac{\partial A_{\nu-1}}{\partial g_3} - \dfrac{(2\nu-1)(2\nu-2)}{12}g_2^2A_{\nu-2},}

from which it is to be concluded that the $A_\nu$ are \gesperrt{integral rational
functions} of $g_2$ and $g_3$, whose coefficients are rational numbers
that can have only powers of 2 and of 3 in the denominator. The series
(14) therefore consists of terms of the form

\[
a_{m,n}\left(\tfrac12 g_2\right)^m(2g_3)^n\dfrac{u^{2\nu+1}}{(2\nu+1)!},
\]

and from the homogeneity of the function $\sigma$ [§ 37, (8), § 46,
(13)] it follows that:

\weq{16}{2m+3n=\nu,}

for the coefficients $a_{m,n}$ there then results from (15):

\weq{17}{\begin{aligned}
a_{m,n} &= 3(m+1)a_{m+1,\,n-1} + \dfrac{16}{3}(n+1)a_{m-2,\,n+1}\\
&\quad{}- \dfrac{1}{3}(2m+3n-1)(4m+6n-1)a_{m-1,\,n},
\end{aligned}}

where $a_{00}=1$, and those $a$ for which one of the two indices is
negative are to be set equal to zero.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 210 =====
% !PRINTED 189
\weberpage{189}

From this $a_{m,n}$ can be found, once the earlier $a_{m,n}$, that is those
in which $2m+3n$ is smaller than $\nu$, have already been calculated.
% [sic] German source prints an ungrammatical relative construction; English conveys the intended relation.

One sees from this that the $a_{m,n}$ contain only powers of 3 in the
denominator. In the \glqq Formeln und Lehrsätzen zum Gebrauch der
elliptischen Funktionen\grqq{} edited by H. A. \gesperrt{Schwarz}, after
lectures of \gesperrt{Weierstrass} (2. Ausgabe 1893), the $a_{m,n}$ have
been calculated up to $\nu=17$. It appears thereby that these coefficients
are not only integers, but that they also contain as factors powers of 3
which increase with $\nu$. I am unable to give a proof of this.

\begin{center}
\rule{2cm}{0.4pt}
\end{center}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 211 =====
% !PRINTED none

% page (title + rule) with the § 57 heading and its opening paragraphs and formulas

\begin{center}
\gesperrt{Sixth Chapter.}

\textbf{Multiplication and Division of the Elliptic Functions.}
\end{center}

\bigskip
\begin{center}
\rule{2cm}{0.4pt}
\end{center}
\bigskip

\begin{center}
\textbf{§ 57. \gesperrt{Multiplication of the Elliptic Functions.}}
\end{center}

By the multiplication of the elliptic functions one understands the
representation of the functions $\mathrm{sn}\,nv$, $\mathrm{cn}\,nv$,
$\mathrm{dn}\,nv$ for an integer $n$ as rational functions of
$\mathrm{sn}\,v$, $\mathrm{cn}\,v$, $\mathrm{dn}\,v$ --- a problem
which, as is evident from the addition theorem, can always be solved.

The form of the solution follows easily from the consideration of the
$\vartheta$-functions.

As is to be seen immediately from § 21, the functions
$\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(nu)$ are $\Theta$-functions of order $n^2$, whose
characteristic is equal to $(0,0)$ for even $n$ and equal to
$(g_1,g_2)$ for odd $n$. Moreover $\vartheta_{11}(nu)$ is an odd
function, while $\vartheta_{00}(nu)$, $\vartheta_{10}(nu)$,
$\vartheta_{01}(nu)$ are even functions of $u$. These functions can
therefore be represented rationally by the $\vartheta$-functions, and
the theorems of § 21 yield the form of these expressions. If we again
denote by $F^{(\nu)}(x,y)$ an integral, rational, homogeneous function
of order $\nu$, we obtain:

\gesperrt{for even $n$:}

\weq{1}{\begin{aligned}
\vartheta_{11}(nu) &= \vartheta_{00}(u)\vartheta_{01}(u)\vartheta_{10}(u)\vartheta_{11}(u)\,F^{\frac{n^2-4}{2}}\bigl[\vartheta_{11}^2(u),\vartheta_{01}^2(u)\bigr],\\
\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(nu) &= F^{\frac{n^2}{2}}\bigl[\vartheta_{11}^2(u),\vartheta_{01}^2(u)\bigr], \quad (g_1,g_2)=(10),(01),(00),
\end{aligned}}

\gesperrt{for odd $n$:}

\weq{2}{\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(nu) = \vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(u)\,F^{\frac{n^2-1}{2}}\bigl[\vartheta_{11}^2(u),\vartheta_{01}^2(u)\bigr].}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 212 =====
% !PRINTED 191
\weberpage{191}

If we divide these formulae by $\vartheta_{01}(u)^{n^2}$, the
right-hand sides can be represented as integral rational functions
of the elliptic functions $\mathrm{sn}\,v$, $\mathrm{cn}\,v$,
$\mathrm{dn}\,v$ (§ 42). If, then, we set

\weq{3}{v = \pi\vartheta_{00}^2u, \quad \mathrm{sn}\,v=x, \quad \mathrm{cn}\,v=y, \quad \mathrm{dn}\,v=z}

we can write the formulae (1), (2), on determining a constant
factor suitably, as follows:

I. for even $n$:

\[
\begin{array}{ll}
\dfrac{\vartheta_{01}^{n^2}\vartheta_{00}}{\vartheta_{10}}\,\dfrac{\vartheta_{11}(nu)}{\vartheta_{01}(u)^{n^2}} = xyz\,A(x^2), & A(0)=n,\\[3mm]
\dfrac{\vartheta_{01}^{n^2}}{\vartheta_{10}}\,\dfrac{\vartheta_{10}(nu)}{\vartheta_{01}(u)^{n^2}} = B(x^2), & B(0)=1,\\[3mm]
\dfrac{\vartheta_{01}^{n^2}}{\vartheta_{00}}\,\dfrac{\vartheta_{00}(nu)}{\vartheta_{01}(u)^{n^2}} = C(x^2), & C(0)=1,\\[3mm]
\vartheta_{01}^{n^2-1}\,\dfrac{\vartheta_{01}(nu)}{\vartheta_{01}(u)^{n^2}} = D(x^2), & D(0)=1.
\end{array}
\]

II. for odd $n$:

\[
\begin{array}{ll}
\dfrac{\vartheta_{00}\vartheta_{01}^{n^2-1}}{\vartheta_{10}}\,\dfrac{\vartheta_{11}(nu)}{\vartheta_{01}(u)^{n^2}} = x\,A(x^2), & A(0)=n,\\[3mm]
\dfrac{\vartheta_{01}^{n^2}}{\vartheta_{10}}\,\dfrac{\vartheta_{10}(nu)}{\vartheta_{01}(u)^{n^2}} = y\,B(x^2), & B(0)=1,\\[3mm]
\dfrac{\vartheta_{01}^{n^2}}{\vartheta_{00}}\,\dfrac{\vartheta_{00}(nu)}{\vartheta_{01}(u)^{n^2}} = z\,C(x^2), & C(0)=1,\\[3mm]
\vartheta_{01}^{n^2-1}\,\dfrac{\vartheta_{01}(nu)}{\vartheta_{01}(u)^{n^2}} = D(x^2), & D(0)=1,
\end{array}
\]

where $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ are integral rational functions of $x^2$,
whose degrees follow from the formulae (1), (2) in this way:

\[
\begin{array}{c@{\quad}cccc@{\qquad}l}
 & A(x^2), & B(x^2), & C(x^2), & D(x^2), & \\[3mm]
\text{Degree:} & \dfrac{n^2}{2}-2, & \dfrac{n^2}{2}, & \dfrac{n^2}{2}, & \dfrac{n^2}{2} & n \text{ even,}\\[3mm]
 & \dfrac{n^2-1}{2}, & \dfrac{n^2-1}{2}, & \dfrac{n^2-1}{2}, & \dfrac{n^2-2}{2} & n \text{ odd.}
\end{array}
\]

From the definitions I., II. one obtains immediately the values of
$A(0)$, $B(0)$, $C(0)$, $D(0)$, i.\,e. the terms independent of
$n$, as they are appended.

Manifold relations among these functions are obtained further in
the following way:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 213 =====
% !PRINTED 192
\weberpage{192}
%<<CONT
If, in order to carry out an example here in fuller detail, one replaces
$v$ by $v + K$, and hence $u$ by $u + \frac{1}{2}$, then by
\S\,44, (18) $x, y, z$ pass over into $y/z$, $-\varkappa' x/z$, $\varkappa'/z$, and from
\S\,21, (8) one obtains from the first formula II, for an odd $n$:

\[
\frac{\vartheta_{00}\,\vartheta_{01}^{\,n^2-1}}{\vartheta_{10}}\,
\frac{\vartheta_{10}(nu)}{\vartheta_{01}(u)^{n^2}}
\left(\frac{\vartheta_{01}(u)}{\vartheta_{00}(u)}\right)^{n^2}
= (-1)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\,\frac{y}{z}\,A\!\left(\frac{y^2}{z^2}\right).
\]
On the other hand, by the second equation II and by \S\,42 the left
side is equal to
\[
\frac{y}{z}\left(\frac{\sqrt{\varkappa'}}{z}\right)^{n^2-1} B(x^2),
\]
and consequently:
\[
B(x^2) = (-1)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\left(\frac{z}{\sqrt{\varkappa'}}\right)^{n^2-1} A\!\left(\frac{y^2}{z^2}\right).
\]

If one puts here $x = 1$, $y = 0$, $z = \varkappa'$ or $x = 0$, $y = 1$,
$z = 1$, it follows that:
\[
B(1) = (-1)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\, n\, \sqrt{\varkappa'}^{\,n^2-1}, \qquad
A(1) = (-1)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\, \sqrt{\varkappa'}^{\,n^2-1}.
\]
A whole system of such formulae can be derived by making the
following substitutions in I and II:
% [source verified, 2026-08-22] At 300 dpi, the final-row denominators are
% varkappa y and varkappa; the adjacent x/varkappa forms are distinct.
\[
\begin{array}{cccc}
u, & x, & y, & z, \\[6pt]
u+\dfrac{1}{2}, & \dfrac{y}{z}, & \dfrac{-\varkappa' x}{z}, & \dfrac{\varkappa'}{z}, \\[10pt]
u+\dfrac{\omega}{2}, & \dfrac{1}{\varkappa x}, & \dfrac{-iz}{\varkappa x}, & \dfrac{-iy}{x}, \\[10pt]
u+\dfrac{1+\omega}{2}, & \dfrac{z}{\varkappa y}, & \dfrac{i\varkappa'}{\varkappa}\,\dfrac{1}{y}, & \dfrac{i\varkappa' x}{y}.
\end{array}
\]
In this way one obtains:
\weq{4}{
\begin{array}{ll}
\left(\dfrac{z}{\sqrt{\varkappa'}}\right)^{n^2-4}\! A\!\left(\dfrac{y^2}{z^2}\right) = (-1)^{\frac{n}{2}-1} A(x^2), & A(1) = (-1)^{\frac{n}{2}-1}\, n\, \sqrt{\varkappa'}^{\,n^2-4}, \\[8pt]
\left(\dfrac{z}{\sqrt{\varkappa'}}\right)^{n^2}\! B\!\left(\dfrac{y^2}{z^2}\right) = (-1)^{\frac{n}{2}} B(x^2), & B(1) = (-1)^{\frac{n}{2}}\, \sqrt{\varkappa'}^{\,n^2}, \\[8pt]
\left(\dfrac{z}{\sqrt{\varkappa'}}\right)^{n^2}\! C\!\left(\dfrac{y^2}{z^2}\right) = C(x^2), & C(1) = \sqrt{\varkappa'}^{\,n^2}, \\[8pt]
\left(\dfrac{z}{\sqrt{\varkappa'}}\right)^{n^2}\! D\!\left(\dfrac{y^2}{z^2}\right) = D(x^2), & D(1) = \sqrt{\varkappa'}^{\,n^2}, \\[8pt]
& n \text{ even.}
\end{array}
}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 214 =====
% !PRINTED 193
\weberpage{193}
\weq{5}{
\begin{array}{ll}
\left(\dfrac{z}{\sqrt{\varkappa'}}\right)^{n^2-1}\! A\!\left(\dfrac{y^2}{z^2}\right) = (-1)^{\frac{n-1}{2}} B(x^2), & A(1) = (-1)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\, \sqrt{\varkappa'}^{\,n^2-1}, \\[8pt]
\left(\dfrac{z}{\sqrt{\varkappa'}}\right)^{n^2-1}\! B\!\left(\dfrac{y^2}{z^2}\right) = (-1)^{\frac{n-1}{2}} A(x^2), & B(1) = (-1)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\, n\, \sqrt{\varkappa'}^{\,n^2-1}, \\[8pt]
\left(\dfrac{z}{\sqrt{\varkappa'}}\right)^{n^2-1}\! C\!\left(\dfrac{y^2}{z^2}\right) = D(x^2), & C(1) = \sqrt{\varkappa'}^{\,n^2-1}, \\[8pt]
\left(\dfrac{z}{\sqrt{\varkappa'}}\right)^{n^2-1}\! D\!\left(\dfrac{y^2}{z^2}\right) = C(x^2), & D(1) = \sqrt{\varkappa'}^{\,n^2-1}, \\[8pt]
& n \text{ odd.}
\end{array}
}
\weq{6}{
\begin{array}{ll}
(\sqrt{\varkappa}\,x)^{n^2-4}\, A\!\left(\dfrac{1}{\varkappa^2 x^2}\right) = (-1)^{\frac{n}{2}-1} A(x^2), & A(\infty) = (-1)^{\frac{n}{2}-1}\, n\, (\sqrt{\varkappa})^{n^2-4}, \\[8pt] % [sic] German source prints a positive exponent; the parallel rows suggest -(n^2-4).
(\sqrt{\varkappa}\,x)^{n^2}\, B\!\left(\dfrac{1}{\varkappa^2 x^2}\right) = B(x^2), & B(\infty) = \sqrt{\varkappa}^{\,-n^2}, \\[8pt]
(\sqrt{\varkappa}\,x)^{n^2}\, C\!\left(\dfrac{1}{\varkappa^2 x^2}\right) = C(x^2), & C(\infty) = \sqrt{\varkappa}^{\,-n^2}, \\[8pt]
(\sqrt{\varkappa}\,x)^{n^2}\, D\!\left(\dfrac{1}{\varkappa^2 x^2}\right) = (-1)^{\frac{n}{2}} D(x^2), & D(\infty) = (-1)^{\frac{n}{2}}\, \sqrt{\varkappa}^{\,-n^2}, \\[8pt]
& n \text{ even.}
\end{array}
}
\weq{7}{
\begin{array}{ll}
(\sqrt{\varkappa}\,x)^{n^2-1}\, A\!\left(\dfrac{1}{\varkappa^2 x^2}\right) = (-1)^{\frac{n-1}{2}} D(x^2), & A(\infty) = (-1)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\, \sqrt{\varkappa}^{\,-(n^2-1)}, \\[8pt]
(\sqrt{\varkappa}\,x)^{n^2-1}\, B\!\left(\dfrac{1}{\varkappa^2 x^2}\right) = C(x^2), & B(\infty) = \sqrt{\varkappa}^{\,-(n^2-1)}, \\[8pt]
(\sqrt{\varkappa}\,x)^{n^2-1}\, C\!\left(\dfrac{1}{\varkappa^2 x^2}\right) = B(x^2), & C(\infty) = \sqrt{\varkappa}^{\,-(n^2-1)}, \\[8pt]
(\sqrt{\varkappa}\,x)^{n^2-1}\, D\!\left(\dfrac{1}{\varkappa^2 x^2}\right) = (-1)^{\frac{n-1}{2}} A(x^2), & D(\infty) = (-1)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\, n\, \sqrt{\varkappa}^{\,n^2-1}, \\[8pt] % [sic] German source prints a positive exponent; the parallel rows suggest -(n^2-1).
& n \text{ odd.}
\end{array}
}

Here $A(\infty)$, $B(\infty)$, $C(\infty)$, $D(\infty)$ are in every case to be
understood as the coefficients of the highest power of $x$ in these functions. In
(7) the last two formulae can be derived from the first by the interchange of $x$
with $1/\varkappa x$.

The third system of formulae can be obtained either in the same way, or else
by replacing $x$ in the formulae (4), (5) by $1/\varkappa x$ and applying
(6), (7).
