\weberpage{194}
\weq{8}{
\begin{array}{ll}
\left(y\sqrt{\dfrac{\varkappa}{\varkappa'}}\right)^{n^2-4}\! A\!\left(\dfrac{z^2}{x^2y^2}\right) = A(x^2), & A\!\left(\dfrac{1}{x^2}\right) = n\sqrt{\dfrac{\varkappa'}{\varkappa}}^{\,n^2-4}, \\[8pt]
\left(y\sqrt{\dfrac{\varkappa}{\varkappa'}}\right)^{n^2}\! B\!\left(\dfrac{z^2}{x^2y^2}\right) = (-1)^{\frac{n}{2}} B(x^2), & B\!\left(\dfrac{1}{x^2}\right) = (-1)^{\frac{n}{2}}\sqrt{\dfrac{\varkappa'}{\varkappa}}^{\,n^2-4}, \\[8pt]
\left(y\sqrt{\dfrac{\varkappa}{\varkappa'}}\right)^{n^2}\! C\!\left(\dfrac{z^2}{x^2y^2}\right) = C(x^2), & C\!\left(\dfrac{1}{x^2}\right) = \sqrt{\dfrac{\varkappa'}{\varkappa}}^{\,n^2-4}, \\[8pt]
\left(y\sqrt{\dfrac{\varkappa}{\varkappa'}}\right)^{2}\! D\!\left(\dfrac{z^2}{x^2y^2}\right) = (-1)^{\frac{n}{2}} D(x^2), & D\!\left(\dfrac{1}{x^2}\right) = (-1)^{\frac{n}{2}}\sqrt{\dfrac{\varkappa'}{\varkappa}}^{\,n^2-4}, \\[8pt]
& n \text{ even.} % [sic] exponent printed as 2, not n^2, on the D-row of this system
\end{array}
}
\weq{9}{
\begin{array}{ll}
\left(y\sqrt{\dfrac{\varkappa}{\varkappa'}}\right)^{n^2-1}\! A\!\left(\dfrac{z^2}{x^2y^2}\right) = (-1)^{\frac{n-1}{2}} C(x^2), & A\!\left(\dfrac{1}{x^2}\right) = (-1)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\sqrt{\dfrac{\varkappa'}{\varkappa}}^{\,n^2-1}, \\[8pt]
\left(y\sqrt{\dfrac{\varkappa}{\varkappa'}}\right)^{n^2-1}\! B\!\left(\dfrac{z^2}{x^2y^2}\right) = D(x^2), & B\!\left(\dfrac{1}{x^2}\right) = \sqrt{\dfrac{\varkappa'}{\varkappa}}^{\,n^2-1}, \\[8pt]
\left(y\sqrt{\dfrac{\varkappa}{\varkappa'}}\right)^{n^2-1}\! C\!\left(\dfrac{z^2}{x^2y^2}\right) = (-1)^{\frac{n-1}{2}} A(x^2), & C\!\left(\dfrac{1}{x^2}\right) = (-1)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\, n\, \sqrt{\dfrac{\varkappa'}{\varkappa}}^{\,n^2-1}, \\[8pt]
\left(y\sqrt{\dfrac{\varkappa}{\varkappa'}}\right)^{n^2-1}\! D\!\left(\dfrac{z^2}{x^2y^2}\right) = B(x^2), & D\!\left(\dfrac{1}{x^2}\right) = \sqrt{\dfrac{\varkappa'}{\varkappa}}^{\,n^2-1}, \\[8pt]
& n \text{ odd.}
\end{array}
}

By these formulae one can, in the case of an odd $n$, reduce the four
polynomials $A(x^2)$, $B(x^2)$, $C(x^2)$, $D(x^2)$ to one of them, for example to
$A(x^2)$.

If in each of the formulae I, II one divides the first three by the last,
one obtains the multiplication formulae for the elliptic
functions (\S\,42).

\begin{center}
III. For even $n$: \qquad\qquad IV. For odd $n$:
\end{center}
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
\mathrm{sn}\,nv = \dfrac{xyzA(x^2)}{D(x^2)}, & \mathrm{sn}\,nv = \dfrac{xA(x^2)}{D(x^2)}, \\[10pt]
\mathrm{cn}\,nv = \dfrac{B(x^2)}{D(x^2)}, & \mathrm{cn}\,nv = \dfrac{yB(x^2)}{D(x^2)}, \\[10pt]
\mathrm{dn}\,nv = \dfrac{C(x^2)}{D(x^2)}, & \mathrm{dn}\,nv = \dfrac{zC(x^2)}{D(x^2)}.
\end{array}
\]

The coefficients of $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ still depend on $\omega$ or on
$\varkappa^2$. The nature of this dependence is disclosed by the recursion formulae,
which one uses for the successive calculation of
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 216 =====
% !PRINTED 195
\weberpage{195}
%<<CONT
$A, B, C, D$ from the addition theorem. If we indicate the value of the
multiplier $n$ to which these functions belong by an index, we have first
\weq{10}{A_1 = 1, \quad B_1 = 1, \quad C_1 = 1, \quad D_1 = 1;}
further, from the addition formulae [\S\,44, (16), for $u = v$]:
\weq{11}{
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{sn}\,2v &= \dfrac{2\,\mathrm{sn}\,v\,\mathrm{cn}\,v\,\mathrm{dn}\,v}{1-\varkappa^2\,\mathrm{sn}^4 v}, \\
\mathrm{cn}\,2v &= \dfrac{\mathrm{cn}^2 v - \mathrm{sn}^2 v\,\mathrm{dn}^2 v}{1-\varkappa^2\,\mathrm{sn}^4 v}, \\
\mathrm{dn}\,2v &= \dfrac{\mathrm{dn}^2 v - \varkappa^2\,\mathrm{sn}^2 v\,\mathrm{cn}^2 v}{1-\varkappa^2\,\mathrm{sn}^4 v}.
\end{aligned}
}
% [source verified, 2026-08-22] The scan distinctly prints coordinate x
% in the x^2 and x^4 factors below, beside the separate modulus \varkappa.
\weq{12}{
\begin{aligned}
A_2 &= 2, \\
B_2 &= 1 - 2x^2 + \varkappa^2x^4, \\
C_2 &= 1 - 2\varkappa^2x^2 + \varkappa^2x^4, \\
D_2 &= 1 - \varkappa^2x^4.
\end{aligned}
}
If we replace $v$ in (11) by $nv$, it follows that:
\weq{13}{
\begin{aligned}
A_{2n} &= 2A_nB_nC_nD_n, \\
B_{2n} &= B_n^2D_n^2 - x^2y^2z^2A_n^2C_n^2, & n \text{ even,} \\
&= y^2B_n^2D_n^2 - x^2z^2A_n^2C_n^2, & n \text{ odd,} \\
C_{2n} &= C_n^2D_n^2 - \varkappa^2x^2y^2z^2A_n^2B_n^2, & n \text{ even,} \\
&= z^2C_n^2D_n^2 - \varkappa^2x^2y^2A_n^2B_n^2, & n \text{ odd,} \\
D_{2n} &= D_n^4 - \varkappa^2x^4y^4z^4A_n^4, & n \text{ even,} \\
&= D_n^4 - \varkappa^2x^4A_n^4, & n \text{ odd,}
\end{aligned}
}
and if in the addition formulae of \S\,44 one sets $u = nv$, $v = (n+1)v$:
\weq{14}{
\begin{aligned}
A_{2n+1} &= y^2z^2A_nD_nB_{n+1}C_{n+1} + A_{n+1}D_{n+1}C_nB_n, & n \text{ even,} \\
&= A_nD_nB_{n+1}C_{n+1} + y^2z^2A_{n+1}D_{n+1}C_nB_n, & n \text{ odd,} \\
B_{2n+1} &= B_nB_{n+1}D_nD_{n+1} - x^2z^2A_nA_{n+1}C_nC_{n+1}, \\
C_{2n+1} &= C_nC_{n+1}D_nD_{n+1} - \varkappa^2x^2y^2A_nA_{n+1}B_nB_{n+1}, \\
D_{2n+1} &= D_n^2D_{n+1}^2 - \varkappa^2x^4y^2z^2A_n^2A_{n+1}^2.
\end{aligned}
}

From these formulae one concludes \gesperrt{that the $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ are integral
rational functions of $\varkappa^2$, and that the numerical coefficients are integral
rational numbers.}

For by (10), (12) this property holds for $n = 1, 2$, and consequently by
(13), (14) in general.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 217 =====
% !PRINTED 196
\weberpage{196}

As to the degree with respect to $\varkappa^2$ it can further be concluded that
the coefficients of $x^{2\nu}$ do not exceed the degree $\nu$ with respect to
$\varkappa^2$. For if this rule is correct for $n$ and $n+1$, its correctness
follows for $2n$ and $2n+1$, and for $n=1$, $n=2$ it holds.

From the fundamental equations between the three elliptic functions:
\[
1 = \mathrm{cn}^2 v + \mathrm{sn}^2 v = \mathrm{dn}^2 v + \varkappa^2\,\mathrm{sn}^2 x % [sic]
\]
there follow further the relations:
\weq{15}{
\begin{array}{l}
D^2 = B^2 + x^2y^2z^2A^2 = C^2 + \varkappa^2x^2y^2z^2A^2,\quad n\text{ even,}\\
D^2 = y^2B^2 + x^2A^2 = z^2C^2 + \varkappa^2x^2A^2,\quad n\text{ odd,}
\end{array}}
with whose help one can, by (14), express $B_{2n}$ and $C_{2n}$ through $A_n$
and $D_n$ alone as follows:
\weq{16}{
\begin{array}{r@{\;}c@{\;}l@{\qquad}l}
B_{2n} &=& D_n^4 - 2x^2y^2z^2A_n^2D_n^2 + \varkappa^2x^4y^4z^4A_n^4 & \\
C_{2n} &=& D_n^4 - 2\varkappa^2x^2y^2z^2A_n^2D_n^2 + \varkappa^2x^4y^4z^4A_n^4 & \left.\right\}\ n\text{ even,}\\[2mm]
B_{2n} &=& D_n^4 - 2x^2A_n^2D_n^2 + \varkappa^2x^4A_n^4 & \\
C_{2n} &=& D_n^4 - 2\varkappa^2x^2A_n^2D_n^2 + \varkappa^2x^4A_n^4 & \left.\right\}\ n\text{ odd.}
\end{array}}

\begin{center}
\textbf{\S\ 58. \gesperrt{Multiplication of the Function} $\wp(u)$.}
\end{center}

The theory of multiplication takes a very elegant form for the
\gesperrt{Weierstrass} function $\wp(u)$ with the two periods $\omega_1, \omega_2$.

Let us consider the doubly periodic function
\weq{1}{\wp(nu) - \wp(u),}
in which $n$ may be an arbitrary positive integer. This function becomes
infinite for $u=0$, and indeed in such a way that
\weq{2}{\wp(nu) - \wp(u) + \frac{n^2-1}{n^2}\,\frac{1}{u^2}}
remains finite for $u=0$. But besides this it becomes infinite for all values
$u^*$ of $u$ which satisfy the condition
\[
n\,u^* \equiv 0 \pmod{\omega_1,\omega_2}
\]
and which are therefore of the form:
\weq{3}{u^* = \frac{\nu_1\omega_1 + \nu_2\omega_2}{n},}
in which $\nu_1, \nu_2$ denote arbitrary integers. We obtain all incongruent
values contained in (3) if we let $\nu_1$ and $\nu_2$ each run through a
complete system of residues with respect to the modulus $n$.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 218 =====
% !PRINTED 197
\weberpage{197}

The function (1) vanishes for all values $u^0$ of $u$ different from zero
which satisfy the condition
\[
\pm n\,u^0 \equiv u^0 \pmod{\omega_1,\omega_2}
\]
hence for
\weq{4}{u^0 = \frac{\nu_1\omega_1 + \nu_2\omega_2}{n\pm 1},}
where again $\nu_1, \nu_2$ are arbitrary integers. The zero points are of
the first order, the points of infinity of the second.

We therefore now introduce a function $\psi_n(u)$, which we define in the
following way:
\weq{5}{\psi_n(u)^2 = n^2 \prod^{\nu_1,\nu_2}\left[\wp(u) - \wp\left(\frac{\nu_1\omega_1+\nu_2\omega_2}{n}\right)\right],}
where $\nu_1, \nu_2$ each run through a complete system of residues with
respect to the modulus $n$, with the sole exclusion of the pair of values
$0,0$; and we add the further stipulation that $\psi_1 = 1$ shall hold.

If $n$ is odd, then in the product (5) every linear factor occurs twice,
since the two incongruent values
\[
u = \pm\frac{\nu_1\omega_1 + \nu_2\omega_2}{n}
\]
give the same value of $\wp(u)$. But if $n$ is even, then again all linear
factors occur twice in (5), with the exception of the three
\[
\wp(u) - \wp\left(\frac{\omega_1}{2}\right),\quad
\wp(u) - \wp\left(\frac{\omega_2}{2}\right),\quad
\wp(u) - \wp\left(\frac{\omega_1+\omega_2}{2}\right),
\]
which occur only once. If one now observes that, according to § 41,
\[
\wp'(u)^2 = 4\left[\wp(u)-\wp\left(\frac{\omega_1}{2}\right)\right]\left[\wp(u)-\wp\left(\frac{\omega_2}{2}\right)\right]\left[\wp(u)-\wp\left(\frac{\omega_1+\omega_2}{2}\right)\right]
\]
holds, then the result follows:
\weq{6}{
\begin{array}{ll}
n\text{ odd:} & \psi_n = P_n,\\
n\text{ even:} & \psi_n = \wp'(u)\,P_n,
\end{array}}
where $P_n$ denotes an integral rational function of $\wp(u)$ which for
odd $n$ is of degree $\frac12(n^2-1)$ and for even $n$ of degree
$\frac12(n^2-4)$, and in which the term of highest order is respectively
equal to
\[
n\,\wp(u)^{\frac{n^2-1}{2}},\qquad -\frac{n}{2}\,\wp(u)^{\frac{n^2-4}{2}}
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 219 =====
% !PRINTED 198
\weberpage{198}

%<<CONT
is, by which at the same time the sign still left undetermined by (5) is
determined. With this determination of the signs, the initial term in the
development of $\psi_n(u)$ in ascending powers of $u$ is, in both cases
(§ 56):
\weq{7}{\frac{n}{u^{n^2-1}}.}

If one now considers that the points of infinity of the function (1) coincide
with the zero points of $\psi_n(u)$, and the zero points of (1) with the zero
points of $\psi_{n\pm1}(u)$, so that accordingly
\weq{8}{\frac{\psi_n(u)^2\left[\wp(nu) - \wp(u)\right]}{\psi_{n+1}(u)\,\psi_{n-1}(u)}}
is an everywhere finite doubly periodic function and therefore a constant,
whose value is found from $u=0$ to be $-1$, then it follows:
\weq{9}{\wp(nu) = \wp(u) - \frac{\psi_{n+1}(u)\,\psi_{n-1}(u)}{\psi_n(u)^2},}
from which the two following formulae result:
\weq{10}{
\begin{array}{ll}
\wp(nu) = \wp(u) - \dfrac{P_{n+1}\,P_{n-1}}{\wp'(u)^2\,P_n^2}, & n\text{ even,}\\[3mm]
\phantom{\wp(nu)}{}= \wp(u) - \dfrac{\wp'(u)^2\,P_{n+1}\,P_{n-1}}{P_n^2}, & n\text{ odd.}
\end{array}}

We determine first of all the function $P_n$ in the first cases $n=1, 2, 3,
4$. For this we form, according to the addition theorem of the $\wp$-function
[§ 49, (11)]:
\[
4\big[\wp(u) + \wp(v) + \wp(u+v)\big] = \left(\frac{\wp'(u)-\wp'(v)}{\wp(u)-\wp(v)}\right)^2,
\]
by setting $u=v$ and determining the limiting value on the right by
differentiation:
\[
\wp(2u) + 2\wp(u) = \frac14\left(\frac{\wp''(u)}{\wp'(u)}\right)^2
= \frac{\frac14\left(6\wp(u)^2 - \frac12 g_2\right)^2}{4\wp(u)^3 - g_2\wp(u) - g_3},
\]
or
\weq{11}{\wp(2u) = \wp(u) - \frac{3\wp(u)^4 - \frac32 g_2\wp(u)^2 - 3g_3\wp(u) - \frac{g_2^2}{16}}{\wp'(u)^2},}
so that
\[
\psi_1 = 1,\quad \psi_2 = -\wp'(u),\quad \psi_3 = P_3,
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 220 =====
% !PRINTED 199
\weberpage{199}

%<<CONT
\weq{12}{P_1 = 1,\quad P_2 = -1,\quad P_3 = 3\wp(u)^4 - \frac32 g_2\wp(u)^2 - 3g_3\wp(u) - \frac{g_2^2}{16}}
becomes. We obtain further, from the addition formula (§ 49):
\[
\wp(v+u) - \wp(v-u) = -\frac{\wp'(u)\,\wp'(v)}{\left[\wp(v)-\wp(u)\right]^2},
\]
on setting $v=2u$, by (9):
\[
\wp(3u) - \wp(u) = -\frac{\wp'(u)\,\wp'(2u)}{\left[\wp(2u)-\wp(u)\right]^2}
= -\frac{\wp'(u)^5\,\wp'(2u)}{\psi_3(u)^2} = -\frac{\psi_2(u)\,\psi_4(u)}{\psi_3(u)^2},
\]
hence:
\[
\psi_4(u) = \wp'(u)\,P_4 = -\wp'(u)^4\,\wp'(2u),
\]
and if one forms the value $\wp'(2u)$ from (11):
\weq{13}{P_4 = -2\wp(u)^6 + \frac52 g_2\wp(u)^4 + 10g_3\,p(u)^3 % [sic]
+ \frac58 g_2^2\wp(u)^2 + \frac12 g_2g_3\wp(u) + g_3^2 - \frac{g_2^3}{32}.}

For larger values of $n$ we derive recursion formulae. To this end we
apply formula (9) to two different numbers $m, n$ and obtain:
\[
\wp(u) - \wp(mu) = \frac{\psi_{m+1}(u)\,\psi_{m-1}(u)}{\psi_m(u)^2},
\]
\[
\wp(u) - \wp(nu) = \frac{\psi_{n+1}(u)\,\psi_{n-1}(u)}{\psi_n(u)^2},
\]
from which it is to be seen that the right-hand sides become equal to one
another for those values $u^0$ of $u$ which are different from zero and
satisfy the condition
\[
m\,u^0 \equiv \pm n\,u^0 \pmod{\omega_1,\omega_2},
\]
or
\[
(m\pm n)\,u^0 \equiv 0 \pmod{\omega_1,\omega_2};
\]
but for these same values $u^0$ the functions
\[
\psi_{m\pm n}(u),
\]
also vanish, so that the two functions:
\[
\psi_{m+1}(u)\,\psi_{m-1}(u)\,\psi_n(u)^2 - \psi_{n+1}(u)\,\psi_{n-1}(u)\,\psi_m(u)^2,
\]
\[
\psi_{m+n}(u)\,\psi_{m-n}(u),
\]
which by (6) are integral rational functions of $\wp(u)$, vanish for the
same finite values of $\wp(u)$.
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 221 =====
% !PRINTED 200
\weberpage{200}
%<<CONT
They therefore differ from one another only by a constant factor,
which by (7) turns out to be equal to 1. We therefore have
\weq{14}{\begin{aligned}
&\psi_{m+n}(u)\,\psi_{m+n}(u)\\
% [sic] The German source prints m+n in both factors; the identity mathematically requires m-n in the second.
={}&\psi_{m+1}(u)\,\psi_{m-1}(u)\,\psi_n(u)^2 - \psi_{n+1}(u)\,\psi_{n-1}(u)\,\psi_m(u)^2.
\end{aligned}}
We apply this formula to two special cases, by putting $n+1$, $n$
or $n+1$, $n-1$ in place of $m$, $n$, and so obtain:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\psi_{2n+1}(u) &= \psi_{n+2}(u)\,\psi_n(u)^3 - \psi_{n+1}(u)^3\,\psi_{n-1}(u)\\
\wp'(u)\,\psi_{2n}(u) &= -\,\psi_n(u)\,[\psi_{n+2}(u)\,\psi_{n-1}(u)^2 - \psi_{n+1}(u)^2\,\psi_{n-2}(u)],
\end{aligned}
\]
and from this one obtains, by (6), the recursion formulae for $P_n$:
\weq{15}{\begin{aligned}
P_{2n+1} &= \wp'(u)^4\,P_{n+2}\,P_n^3 - P_{n+1}^3\,P_{n-1}, &&\text{$n$ even,}\\
&= P_{n+2}\,P_n^3 - \wp'(u)^4\,P_{n+1}^3\,P_{n-1}, &&\text{$n$ odd.}
\end{aligned}}
\weq{16}{P_{2n} = -\,P_n\,(P_{n+2}\,P_{n-1}^2 - P_{n+1}^2\,P_{n-2}).}

Since in this way the functions $P_n$ can all be calculated from $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$, $P_4$,
it follows \gesperrt{that the coefficients of}
$P_n$ \gesperrt{are rationally composed of} $g_2$, $g_3$ \gesperrt{and
rational numbers}.

Our further considerations on the division, however, we attach
to the multiplication formulae of the functions $\operatorname{sn} u$, $\operatorname{cn} u$,
$\operatorname{dn} u$, whose advantages will come fully into their own only in
the fourth part.

\begin{center}
\textbf{\S~59. Division by 2.}
\end{center}

Turning first to the consideration of the simplest case, we
put $v$ in place of $2v$ in the equations (5) of \S~57. Then, if we
set
\weq{1}{x = \operatorname{sn}\frac{v}{2}, \qquad y = \operatorname{cn}\frac{v}{2}, \qquad z = \operatorname{dn}\frac{v}{2}}
we have:
\weq{2}{\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{sn} v &= \frac{2\,x\,y\,z}{1 - \varkappa^2\,x^4},\\
\operatorname{cn} v &= \frac{y^2 - x^2\,z^2}{1 - \varkappa^2\,x^4},\\
\operatorname{dn} v &= \frac{z^2 - \varkappa^2\,x^2\,y^2}{1 - \varkappa^2\,x^4}.
\end{aligned}}

The last two of these equations are quadratic with
respect to $x^2$, but they have only \gesperrt{one common}
root, for the roots of the second of the equations (2) are
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 222 =====
% !PRINTED 201
\weberpage{201}

%<<CONT
$\mathrm{sn}^2\dfrac{v}{2}$, \quad $\mathrm{sn}^2\left(\dfrac{v}{2}+K+iK'\right)$,

and those of the third

$\mathrm{sn}^2\dfrac{v}{2}$, \quad $\mathrm{sn}^2\left(\dfrac{v}{2}+K\right)$.

One now finds easily from (2):

\[
1+\mathrm{cn}\,v = \frac{2y^2}{1-\varkappa^2x^4}, \qquad 1+\mathrm{dn}\,v = \frac{2z^2}{1-\varkappa^2x^4},
\]
\[
1-\mathrm{cn}\,v = \frac{2x^2z^2}{1-\varkappa^2x^4}, \qquad 1-\mathrm{dn}\,v = \frac{2\varkappa^2x^2y^2}{1-\varkappa^2x^4},
\]
\[
\mathrm{dn}\,v+\mathrm{cn}\,v = \frac{2y^2z^2}{1-\varkappa^2x^4},
\]
hence

\weq{3}{\begin{aligned}
x &= \sqrt{\frac{1-\mathrm{cn}\,v}{1+\mathrm{dn}\,v}} = \frac{1}{\varkappa}\sqrt{\frac{1-\mathrm{dn}\,v}{1+\mathrm{cn}\,v}},\\[4pt]
y &= \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{dn}\,v+\mathrm{cn}\,v}{1+\mathrm{dn}\,v}}, \qquad z = \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{dn}\,v+\mathrm{cn}\,v}{1+\mathrm{cn}\,v}};
\end{aligned}}

between the signs of these three quantities there subsists, by the
first equation (2), a further relation, so that one obtains only four
different systems of values, which have the following meaning:

\[
\begin{array}{ccc}
\mathrm{sn}\left(\frac{v}{2}\right), & \mathrm{cn}\left(\frac{v}{2}\right), & \mathrm{dn}\left(\frac{v}{2}\right),\\
\mathrm{sn}\left(\frac{v}{2}+2K\right), & \mathrm{cn}\left(\frac{v}{2}+2K\right), & \mathrm{dn}\left(\frac{v}{2}+2K\right),\\
\mathrm{sn}\left(\frac{v}{2}+2iK'\right), & \mathrm{cn}\left(\frac{v}{2}+2iK'\right), & \mathrm{dn}\left(\frac{v}{2}+2iK'\right),\\
\mathrm{sn}\left(\frac{v}{2}+2K+2iK'\right), & \mathrm{cn}\left(\frac{v}{2}+2K+2iK'\right), & \mathrm{dn}\left(\frac{v}{2}+2K+2iK'\right).
\end{array}
\]

We further state the special cases which follow from (3):

\[
\mathrm{sn}\,\frac{K}{2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+\varkappa'}}, \qquad
\mathrm{sn}\,\frac{iK'}{2} = \frac{i}{\sqrt{\varkappa}}, \qquad
\mathrm{sn}\,\frac{K+iK'}{2} = \sqrt{\frac{\varkappa+i\varkappa'}{\varkappa}},
\]
\[
\mathrm{cn}\,\frac{K}{2} = \sqrt{\frac{\varkappa'}{1+\varkappa'}}, \qquad
\mathrm{cn}\,\frac{iK'}{2} = \sqrt{\frac{1+\varkappa}{\varkappa}}, \qquad
\mathrm{cn}\,\frac{K+iK'}{2} = \sqrt{\frac{-i\varkappa'}{\varkappa}},
\]
\[
\mathrm{dn}\,\frac{K}{2} = \sqrt{\varkappa'}, \qquad
\mathrm{dn}\,\frac{iK'}{2} = \sqrt{1+\varkappa}, \qquad
\mathrm{dn}\,\frac{K+iK'}{2} = \sqrt{\frac{\varkappa}{\varkappa+i\varkappa'}}.
\]

%% ===== canonical stable idx 223 =====
% !PRINTED 202
\weberpage{202}

From this it now follows that the division by 2, and hence also by
every power of 2, can be carried out by a chain of square roots. If we
therefore assume the problem of the division by an odd number to be
solved, then the division by an even number is reduced to
square roots. In what follows we shall occupy ourselves exclusively
with \gesperrt{the division by odd numbers}.

\begin{center}
§ 60. \gesperrt{The Division by an Odd Number.}
\end{center}

If we put, when $n$ is an odd number,

\weq{1}{x = \mathrm{sn}\,\frac{v}{n}, \qquad y = \mathrm{cn}\,\frac{v}{n}, \qquad z = \mathrm{dn}\,\frac{v}{n},}

then from the equations IV, \S\ 57 we obtain:

\weq{2}{\begin{aligned}
D(x^2)\,\mathrm{sn}\,v - x\,A(x^2) &= 0,\\
D(x^2)\,\mathrm{cn}\,v - y\,B(x^2) &= 0,\\
D(x^2)\,\mathrm{dn}\,v - z\,C(x^2) &= 0.
\end{aligned}}

The first of these equations is of degree $n^2$ with respect to the
unknown $x$; by the second and the third, $y$ and $z$ are expressed
\gesperrt{rationally} in terms of $x$ (and of cn\,$v$, dn\,$v$). There result,
then, $n^2$ systems of values for the three unknowns $x, y, z$, whose
meaning is:

\weq{3}{\begin{aligned}
x_{\mu,\mu'} &= \mathrm{sn}\left(\frac{v}{n} + \frac{4\mu K+4\mu' iK'}{n}\right),\\
y_{\mu,\mu'} &= \mathrm{cn}\left(\frac{v}{n} + \frac{4\mu K+4\mu' iK'}{n}\right),\\
z_{\mu,\mu'} &= \mathrm{dn}\left(\frac{v}{n} + \frac{4\mu K+4\mu' iK'}{n}\right),
\end{aligned}}

in which $\mu, \mu'$ each run through a complete system of residues
$(\mathrm{mod}\ n)$.

The first equation (2):

\weq{4}{D(x^2)\,\mathrm{sn}\,v - x\,A(x^2) = 0,}

of degree $n^2$, is called the \gesperrt{general division equation}. It
is irreducible in the sense that it is not decomposable into factors
which are rational with respect to sn\,$v$, cn\,$v$, dn\,$v$ and have
arbitrary coefficients independent of $v$.

For, in the first place, the $n^2$ values $x_{\mu,\mu'}$ are all
different from one another, and if any rational equation:

\[
F\left(\mathrm{sn}\,\frac{v}{n},\ \mathrm{sn}\,v,\ \mathrm{cn}\,v,\ \mathrm{dn}\,v\right) = 0
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 224 =====
% !PRINTED 203
\weberpage{203}

%<<CONT
holds, then in it the variable $v$ may be replaced by $v + 4\mu K + 4\mu' iK'$.
On account of the periodicity of sn\,$v$, cn\,$v$, dn\,$v$ it follows from this,
however, that the equation

\[
F(x,\ \mathrm{sn}\,v,\ \mathrm{cn}\,v,\ \mathrm{dn}\,v) = 0
\]

is satisfied for \gesperrt{all} roots of equation (4). In order to determine its \gesperrt{Galois}
group, we first fix the \gesperrt{domain of rationality}. It is to comprise the
following quantities:

\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] rational numbers,
\item[2.] rational functions of $\varkappa^2$,
\item[3.] the three functions sn\,$v$, cn\,$v$, dn\,$v$,
\item[4.] the quantities $\mathrm{sn}\left(\dfrac{4\mu K' + 4\mu' iK'}{n}\right)$. % [sic]
\end{enumerate}

From (2) it then follows that

\[
\mathrm{cn}\left(\frac{4\mu K + 4\mu' iK'}{n}\right), \qquad \mathrm{dn}\left(\frac{4\mu K + 4\mu' iK'}{n}\right)
\]

also belong to the domain of rationality.

We now remark that, by the addition theorem, each of the quantities
$x_{\mu,\mu'}$ is rationally expressible through every other one among
them. If in particular

\weq{5}{x_{\mu,\mu'} = F_{\mu,\mu'}(x_{0,0})}

holds, then

\weq{6}{x_{\mu+\nu,\mu'+\nu'} = F_{\mu,\mu'}(x_{\nu,\nu'}) = F_{\mu+\nu,\mu'+\nu'}(x_{0,0}).}

From this it follows that the \gesperrt{Galois} group of our equation consists of the
$n^2$ permutations $S_{\nu,\nu'}$ which one obtains by increasing, in the
roots $x_{\mu,\mu'}$, the indices $\mu, \mu'$ all by the same pair of
numbers $\nu, \nu'$ (where each index is to be taken according to the
modulus $n$).

For by (5) every rational function of the roots
$x_{\mu,\mu'}$ can be expressed rationally through $x_{0,0}$ in the form

\[
\Phi(x_{0,0})
\]

and therefore passes over, by (6), under the substitution
$S_{\nu,\nu'}$ into $\Phi(x_{\nu,\nu'})$; if it thus remains unchanged under this
substitution, then \gesperrt{it} is \gesperrt{rational}. Conversely it follows from the
irreducibility that every rational equation between the roots,
since it can be put into the form:

\[
\psi(x_{0,0}) = 0,
\]

and thus

\[
\psi(x_{\nu,\nu'}) = 0
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 225 =====
% !PRINTED 204
\weberpage{204}
%<<CONT

has as a consequence, \gesperrt{admits the substitution $S_{\nu,\nu'}$.} But the group
of the $S_{\nu,\nu'}$ is, on account of

\[
S_{\nu,\nu'} S_{\mu,\mu'} = S_{\nu+\mu,\nu'+\mu'}
\]

an Abelian one, which by the formula

\[
S_{\nu,\nu'} = S_{1,0}^{\nu} S_{0,1}^{\nu'}
\]

is representable by the basis $S_{1,0}$, $S_{0,1}$; and so the \gesperrt{general division equation is an Abelian equation and hence algebraically solvable} (Bd. I, § 169\,f.).

\begin{center}
\S\ 61. \quad \gesperrt{The Division of the Periods.}
\end{center}

The problem that still remains to be solved now consists in determining by
algebraic means the quantities

\weq{1}{x_{\mu,\mu'} = \operatorname{sn}\left(\frac{4\mu K + 4\mu' iK'}{n}\right)}

One obtains all values of this quantity by letting $\mu$, $\mu'$, independently
of one another, each run through a complete system of residues
with respect to the modulus $n$. But these values are also
all \gesperrt{different from one another}, for $\operatorname{sn} v$ can be
$= \operatorname{sn} v'$ only if $v'$ is congruent to $v$ or congruent to $2K - v$
modulo $4K$, $2iK'$, and neither of these can occur for two different ones
among the arguments of (1).

The $n^2$ quantities (1) are the roots of the equation

\weq{2}{xA(x^2) = 0,}

and by the formulae

\weq{3}{y = \frac{D(x^2)}{B(x^2)}, \qquad z = \frac{D(x^2)}{C(x^2)}}

one can also express

\[
\begin{aligned}
y_{\mu,\mu'} &= \operatorname{cn}\left(\frac{4\mu K + 4\mu' iK'}{n}\right),\\
z_{\mu,\mu'} &= \operatorname{dn}\left(\frac{4\mu K + 4\mu' iK'}{n}\right)
\end{aligned}
\]

rationally in terms of $x_{\mu,\mu'}$, if the \gesperrt{domain of rationality consists of rational numbers and rational
functions of $x^2$}.

From the roots $x^2$ of the equation $A = 0$ the roots of $B = 0$,
$C = 0$, $D = 0$ can be derived rationally by
§ 60, (2) and § 44, (18), (19), (20); for if $x^2$ is a root
of $A = 0$, then
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 226 =====
% !PRINTED 205
\weberpage{205}

%<<CONT
\[
\frac{1-x^2}{1-\varkappa^2 x^2}, \qquad \frac{1-\varkappa^2 x^2}{\varkappa^2(1-x^2)}, \qquad \frac{1}{\varkappa^2 x^2}
\]

the roots of $B = 0$, $C = 0$, $D = 0$. The meaning of this latter
root, however, is % [sic] The German source prints the singular although three roots precede.

\[
\operatorname{sn}\left(\frac{(4\mu+1)K + 4\mu' iK'}{n}\right)^2,
\]
\[
\operatorname{sn}\left(\frac{(4\mu+1)K + (4\mu'+1)iK'}{n}\right)^2,
\]
\[
\operatorname{sn}\left(\frac{4\mu K + (4\mu'+1)iK'}{n}\right)^2,
\]

and accordingly, by the solution of the equation $A = 0$, all
quantities of the form

\[
\operatorname{sn}\left(\frac{\mu K + \mu' iK'}{n}\right)^2,
\]

in which $\mu$, $\mu'$ are arbitrary integers, are \gesperrt{rationally determined}.

\begin{center}
\S\ 62. \quad \gesperrt{The Abelian Relations.}
\end{center}

For a closer investigation of the algebraic nature of the equation of
the division of the periods, a system of relations among its roots is
of great importance, and we now pass on to the derivation of that
system \textsuperscript{1}).

We consider the sum:

\weq{1}{\sum^{\nu} e^{\frac{8\nu\nu'\pi i}{n}} \frac{\vartheta_{11}\left(u + \frac{2\nu}{n}\right)}{\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}\left(u + \frac{2\nu}{n}\right)},}

taken over $\nu$ through a complete system of residues for the (odd)
modulus $n$. $\nu'$ is an arbitrary integer, and $g_1$, $g_2$ is one of
the three even characteristics $(0,0)$, $(0,1)$, $(1,0)$. This sum
is independent of the particular system of residues that has been
taken for $\nu$.

\begingroup
\footnotesize
\textsuperscript{1}) These relations are due to \gesperrt{Abel} (Oeuvres complètes, Bd. I,
S. 523; Bd. II, S. 251 der neuen Ausgabe). The proof of these relations
given above follows \gesperrt{Hermite} (Crelles Journal, Bd. 32,
S. 283). Also to be mentioned is \gesperrt{Sylow}, Christiania Videnskabsselskabs
Forhandlinger 1864 und 1871. \gesperrt{Kronecker}, Berichte der Berliner Akademie,
19. Juli 1875. \gesperrt{Engel}, Berichte der Sächsischen Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften, 31. Juli 1884.
\endgroup

%% ===== canonical stable idx 227 =====
% !PRINTED 206
\weberpage{206}

The common denominator of the fractions occurring in (1):

\[
\prod^{\nu} \vartheta_{g_1,g_2}\left(u + \frac{2\nu}{n}\right) = \pm \prod^{\nu} \vartheta_{g_1,g_2}\left(u + \frac{\nu}{n}\right)
\]

is, by the last formulae of § 33, equal, apart from a constant
factor, to

\[
\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(nu, n\omega),
\]

and if we therefore set the sum (1) equal to

\weq{2}{\frac{\Phi(u)}{\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(nu, n\omega)}}

then $\Phi(u)$ is an \gesperrt{integral} transcendental function of $u$.
Now we have

\[
\frac{\vartheta_{11}\left(u + \frac{2\nu+1}{u}\right)}{\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}\left(u + \frac{2\nu+1}{u}\right)} = (-1)^{g_1+1} \frac{\vartheta_{11}\left(u + \frac{2\nu+n+1}{n}\right)}{\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}\left(u + \frac{2\nu+n+1}{n}\right)}
\]
% [sic] The German source prints u in both left-hand inner denominators; n is intended.

and $\nu$ runs, simultaneously with $\nu + \frac{1}{2}(n+1)$, through a complete system of residues with respect to $n$. From this it follows by (1) and (2) that

\weq{3}{\Phi\left(u + \frac{1}{n}\right) = -e^{-\frac{4\nu'\pi i}{n}} \Phi(u)}

and similarly

\weq{4}{\Phi(u + \omega) = -e^{-n\pi i(2u+\omega)} \Phi(u).}

From this it follows that the function $\Phi(u)$ is a $t$-function % [sic] The German source prints t; theta is intended.
with the periods $1/n$, $\omega$, one that is determined by the conditions (3), (4)
up to a factor independent of $u$ and can be expressed by
a $\vartheta$-function (§ 19). One sees easily that
the conditions (3), (4) are satisfied by the function

\[
e^{-4\pi i\nu' u} \vartheta_{11}(nu - 4\nu'\omega, n\omega)
\]
% [sic] The German source prints 4 here but 2 in the corresponding argument in (5).

so that there results:

\weq{5}{\sum^{\nu} e^{\frac{8\nu\nu'\pi i}{n}} \frac{\vartheta_{11}\left(u + \frac{2\nu}{n}\right)}{\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}\left(u + \frac{2\nu}{n}\right)} = Ce^{-4\pi i\nu' u} \frac{\vartheta_{11}(nu - 2\nu'\omega, n\omega)}{\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(nu, n\omega)}.}

The determination of the constant $C$ can easily be carried out if one multiplies on the right and on the left by

\[
\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(u)
\]

and then

\[
u = \frac{(1-g_2) + (1-g_1)\omega}{2}
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 228 =====
% !PRINTED 207
\weberpage{207}

%<<CONT
sets. Formula (2) of § 21 then gives:

\weq{6}{C = (-1)^{(g_1+1)(g_2+1)\frac{n-1}{2}} n \frac{\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(0,\omega)}{\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}(2\nu'\omega, n\omega)} \frac{\vartheta_{11}'(0, n\omega)}{\vartheta_{11}'(0, \omega)}.}

One obtains the \gesperrt{Abelian} relations quite simply by setting
$nu = 2\nu'\omega$ in (5), whereby the right-hand side vanishes:

\weq{7}{\sum^{\nu} e^{\frac{2\nu\nu'\pi i}{n}} \frac{\vartheta_{11}\left(\frac{2\nu'\omega + 2\nu}{n}\right)}{\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}\left(\frac{2\nu'\omega + 2\nu}{n}\right)} = 0.}

If one applies to the $\vartheta$-functions occurring here a
linear transformation

\[
\begin{pmatrix} \alpha, & \beta \\ \gamma, & \delta \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \alpha\delta - \beta\gamma = 1

then by § 39 one obtains the general formula:

\weq{8}{\sum^{\nu} e^{\frac{8\nu\nu'\pi i}{n}} \frac{\vartheta_{11}\left(\frac{2(\nu\alpha+\nu'\gamma) + 2(\nu\beta+\nu'\delta)\omega}{n}\right)}{\vartheta_{g_1,g_2}\left(\frac{2(\nu\alpha+\nu'\gamma) + 2(\nu\beta+\nu'\delta)\omega}{n}\right)} = 0.}

These equations now pass over, when one sets $g_1, g_2 = 0, 1$
and introduces the notation of § 42, directly into relations between the roots $x_{\nu,\nu'}$ (§ 61):

\weq{9}{\sum^{\nu} e^{\frac{8\nu\nu'\pi i}{n}} x_{\nu\alpha+\nu'\gamma,\ \nu\beta+\nu'\delta} = 0,}

and to the two special cases:

\[
\begin{pmatrix} \alpha, & \beta \\ \gamma, & \delta \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0 \\ 0, & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \begin{pmatrix} 0, & 1 \\ -1, & 0 \end{pmatrix}

correspondingly:

\weq{10}{\sum^{\nu} e^{\frac{8\nu\nu'\pi i}{n}} x_{\nu,\nu'} = 0,}

\weq{11}{\sum^{\nu'} e^{-\frac{8\nu\nu'\pi i}{n}} x_{\nu,\nu'} = 0.}

By (5), (6) one can also determine the value of these sums, if in them the $n$th root of unity

e^{\frac{8\pi i}{n}}
\]

\weberpage{208}
%<<CONT
is replaced by another, by replacing $\nu'$ in (5) by another symbol, $m$, and then setting $nu = 2\nu'\omega$. If we restrict ourselves to the case $(g_1, g_2) = (0, 1)$, and (5) is further multiplied by $\vartheta_{00} : \vartheta_{10}$, there follows:

\medskip

\begin{center}
\textbf{\S\,63. The \gesperrt{Galois Group} of the Division Equation.}
\end{center}

In the thirteenth chapter of the first volume it was shown how the algebraic nature of an equation finds its simplest expression in the \gesperrt{Galois group} of the equation.

Let the definition of the \gesperrt{Galois group} be briefly recalled here.

Once the domain of rationality $\Omega$ has been fixed, the \gesperrt{Galois group} of an equation $F(x) = 0$, of which it is assumed only that it has no equal roots, is defined as the group $G$ of the permutations among the roots of this equation to which the twofold property belongs:

a) Every rational equation in $\Omega$ which subsists among the roots of $F(x)$ remains correct when the roots are subjected to any permutation of this group.

b) Every rational function in $\Omega$ of the roots of $F(x)$ which admits all the permutations of the group is contained in $\Omega$.

Now, as we seek to determine the group $G$ of the division equation, we assume as domain of rationality in the first place the \gesperrt{totality of all rational numbers and rational functions of $\varkappa^2$}.

By the addition and multiplication theorem (cf. \S\, 57, 61), if $f$ and $\varphi_m$ denote rational functions which are independent of $\mu, \mu' \nu, \nu'$, then % [sic] The German source omits the comma between \mu' and \nu.

\weq{1}{x_{\mu+\nu,\,\mu'+\nu'} = f(x_{\mu,\mu'}, x_{\nu,\nu'}),}

\weq{2}{x_{m\mu,\,m\mu'} = \varphi_m(x_{\mu,\mu'}).}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 230 =====
% !PRINTED 209
\weberpage{209}
Now if $S$ is any substitution of the group $\mathfrak{G}$ through which, when $a, b, c, \partial$ denote integers taken with respect to the modulus $n$, the passage

\[
x_{1,0}, x_{0,1} \quad \text{into} \quad x_{\partial,-c}, x_{-b,a}
\]

takes place, then we can apply $S$ to each of the formulae (1), (2). But by (2):

\[
x_{\mu,0} = \varphi_\mu(x_{1,0}),
\]

from which it is to be concluded that through the substitution $S$ the passage

\[
x_{\mu,0} \quad \text{into} \quad \varphi_\mu(x_{\partial,-c}) = x_{\partial\mu,\,-c\mu}
\]

takes place. Likewise one finds that through $S$ the passage

\[
x_{0,\mu'} \quad \text{into} \quad \varphi_{\mu'}(x_{-b,a}) = x_{-b\mu',\,a\mu'}
\]

takes place.

If we apply this to the equation resulting from (1)

\[
x_{\mu,\mu'} = f(x_{\mu,0}, x_{0,\mu'})
\]

then it follows that through $S$ the passage

\weq{3}{x_{\mu,\mu'} \quad \text{into} \quad x_{\partial\mu - b\mu',\,-c\mu + a\mu'}}

takes place.

From this we conclude first of all that the numbers $a, b, c, \partial$ must be so constituted that their determinant

\weq{4}{m = a\partial - bc}

has no divisor in common with $n$. For if such a divisor were present, then $\mu, \mu'$ could be so determined, without both being divisible by $n$, that

\[
\partial\mu - b\mu' \equiv 0, \quad -c\mu + a\mu' \equiv 0 \pmod{n},
\]

and several roots $x_{\mu,\mu'}$ distinct from one another would pass through $S$ into one and the same root, which is impossible. For, to begin with, neither $a$ and $b$ nor $c$ and $\partial$ can have a divisor in common with $n$, since otherwise, if $a\mu'$, $b\mu'$ or $c\mu$, $\partial\mu$ are taken divisible by $n$, all the $x_{\mu',0}$ or all the $x_{0,\mu}$ would pass into $x_{0,0}$. If one then puts $m\mu = n(ha + h'b)$, $m\mu' = n(hc + h'\partial)$, and determines $h$ and $h'$ so that $ha + h'b$ has no divisors in common with $n$, then, if $n$ and $m$ have a common divisor, $\mu, \mu'$ need not both be divisible by $n$, and not only $x_{0,0}$ but also $x_{\mu,\mu'}$ passes into $x_{0,0}$ by (3).

If we denote the permutation (3) briefly by

\[
(x_{\mu,\mu'}, x_{\nu,\nu'}),
\]

then

\[
\begin{aligned}
\nu &\equiv \partial\mu - b\mu' \\
\nu' &\equiv -c\mu + a\mu'
\end{aligned}
\pmod{n},
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 231 =====
% !PRINTED 210
\weberpage{210}
%<<CONT
and from this, by solving, using the notation of \S\, 28, (4):

\weq{5}{m(\mu, \mu') \equiv \begin{pmatrix} a, & b \\ c, & \partial \end{pmatrix} (\nu, \nu').}

Therefore

\weq{6}{\begin{pmatrix} a, & b \\ c, & \partial \end{pmatrix}}

is a suitable symbol for the permutation $S$, and from (5) one sees that two such permutations:

\[
S = \begin{pmatrix} a, & b \\ c, & \partial \end{pmatrix}, \qquad S' = \begin{pmatrix} a', & b' \\ c', & \partial' \end{pmatrix}
\]

compose exactly according to the rule given in \S\, 28:

\weq{7}{S S' = S'' = \begin{pmatrix} a a' + b c', & a b' + b \partial' \\ c a' + \partial c', & c b' + \partial \partial' \end{pmatrix}}

so that the permutation $S''$ of the roots arises when \gesperrt{first} the permutation $S$, and \gesperrt{then} the permutation $S'$, is carried out among the roots of the division equation. It must always be observed, however, that here only the residues of the numbers $a, b, c, \partial$ taken with respect to the modulus $n$ come into consideration, so that the number of permutations $S$ is always finite\footnote{If one wished to choose the notation $S = \begin{pmatrix} \partial, & -b \\ -c, & a \end{pmatrix}$, which at first sight seems to lie nearer, then the composition would have to be denoted by the formula $S'S = S''$, that is, in the reverse sense from the usual composition of permentations % [sic]
.}.

1. \gesperrt{The totality of all substitutions $\begin{pmatrix} a, & b \\ c, & \partial \end{pmatrix}$ forms a group, which we denote by $\mathfrak{A}$, and in it, as we have proved, the group $\mathfrak{G}$ of the division equation is contained.}

In $\mathfrak{A}$ there is contained as a divisor a group $\mathfrak{B}$ which consists of all substitutions (5) % [sic] The German source's cross-reference appears to require (8) or (6).

\weq{8}{T = \begin{pmatrix} \alpha, & \beta \\ \gamma, & \delta \end{pmatrix}}

for which the condition

\weq{9}{\alpha\delta - \beta\gamma \equiv 1 \pmod{n}}

holds.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 232 =====
% !PRINTED 211
\weberpage{211}
Every substitution $S$ can be derived by composition of

\[
\begin{pmatrix} m, & 0 \\ 0, & 1 \end{pmatrix}
\]

with a substitution $T$; in order that

\[
S = \begin{pmatrix} m, & 0 \\ 0, & 1 \end{pmatrix} T
\]

hold, one has simply to determine $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta$ from the congruences

\[
a \equiv \alpha m, \quad b \equiv \beta m, \quad c \equiv \gamma, \quad d \equiv \delta \pmod{n}
\]

We now consider

\weq{10}{x_{\mu,\mu'} = \mathrm{sn}\left(\frac{4\mu K + 4\mu' i K'}{n}\right) = \frac{\vartheta_{00}\,\vartheta_{11}\left(\dfrac{2\mu + 2\mu'\omega}{n}\right)}{\vartheta_{10}\,\vartheta_{01}\left(\dfrac{2\mu + 2\mu'\omega}{n}\right)},}

\[
\varkappa^2 = \frac{\vartheta_{10}^4}{\vartheta_{00}^4}
\]

as functions of $\omega$, and apply to them a linear transformation

\[
\begin{pmatrix} \alpha, & \beta \\ \gamma, & \delta \end{pmatrix} \equiv \begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0 \\ 0, & 1 \end{pmatrix} \pmod{8}
\]

in which we replace $\omega$ by

\weq{11}{\omega' = \frac{\gamma + \delta\omega}{\alpha + \beta\omega}}

Then, by the formulae (3), (5) and (6), \S\, 39, it follows that

\[
x_{\mu,\mu'} \quad \text{into} \quad x_{\alpha\mu + \gamma\mu',\,\beta\mu + \delta\mu'}
\]

passes over; that is, the $x_{\mu,\mu'}$ undergo a substitution which, by (3), (6), is to be denoted by

\[
T = \begin{pmatrix} \delta, & -\gamma \\ -\beta, & \alpha \end{pmatrix}
\]

while $\varkappa^2$ remains unchanged.

Conversely, every one of the substitutions $T$ can arise in this way as well; for if any substitution $T$ whatever is given, then by adding suitable multiples of the (odd) number $n$ to the numbers $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta$ the conditions

\[
\alpha \equiv 1, \quad \delta \equiv 1, \quad \beta \equiv 0, \quad \gamma \equiv 0 \pmod{8}
\]

can always be satisfied.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 233 =====
% !PRINTED 212
\weberpage{212}
Any rational equation between the roots $x_{\mu,\mu'}$ and $\varkappa^2$ passes by (10) into an identity, even when arbitrary constant numerical coefficients, i.\,e. coefficients independent of $\omega$, occur in it, and one may therefore substitute for $\omega$

\[
\frac{\gamma + \delta\omega}{\alpha + \beta\omega}
\]

i.\,e. one may apply every substitution $T$ to the rational equation between the $x_{\mu,\mu'}$. From this it follows \gesperrt{that the whole group $\mathfrak{B}$ is contained in $\mathfrak{G}$ (Bd.\,I, § 156), and indeed in the group $\mathfrak{G}'$, which arises from the group $\mathfrak{G}$ of the division equation by the adjunction of arbitrary numbers.}

If we extend the domain of rationality of the rational numbers by the adjunction of $n$th roots of unity, then the \gesperrt{Abelian} relations of the preceding section also belong among the rational equations. To these relations, say to

\[
\overset{\nu}{\Sigma} e^{\frac{8\nu\nu'\pi i}{n}} x_{\nu,\nu'} = 0
\]

however, \gesperrt{none} of the substitutions

\[
M = \begin{pmatrix} m, & 0 \\ 0, & 1 \end{pmatrix},
\]

in which $m$ vanishes from 1, % [sic] the page prints \textquotedbl{}verschwindet\textquotedbl{} (vanishes); the sense required is \textquotedbl{}verschieden ist\textquotedbl{} (differs from 1)
is applicable; for by this substitution, if $mm' \equiv 1 \pmod{n}$, there passes

\[
\overset{\nu}{\Sigma} e^{\frac{8\nu\nu'\pi i}{n}} x_{\nu,\nu'} \ \text{into} \ \overset{\nu}{\Sigma} e^{\frac{8\nu m'\nu'\pi i}{n}} x_{\nu,\nu'}
\]

which by (12), § 62 is different from zero unless $m'$ and hence also $m \equiv 1 \pmod{n}$. From this follows the theorem:

2. \gesperrt{After adjunction of the $n$th roots of unity (and of arbitrary other constants), $\mathfrak{B}$ is the Galois group of the division equation. $\mathfrak{B}$ is also called the monodromy group of the division equation.}

3. We now prove further that in the original domain of rationality, that is, without adjunction of the $n$th roots of unity or of other irrational numbers, \gesperrt{the group of the division equation is identical with the group $\mathfrak{A}$.}

It is shown in Bd.\,I, § 174 that the primitive $n$th roots of unity $\varrho$ are roots of an irreducible equation

\weq{12}{\Phi(\varrho) = 0}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 234 =====
% !PRINTED 213
\weberpage{213}
%<<CONT
are, and this equation also cannot split when the independent variable $\varkappa^2$ is extended by adjunction of the domain of rationality of the rational numbers. % [sic] word order as printed; expected sense \textquotedbl{}when the domain of rationality ... is extended by adjunction of the independent variable ...\textquotedbl{}

The degree of this equation is $\varphi(n)$, i.\,e. equal to the number of the numbers $m$ incongruent modulo $n$ that are relatively prime to $n$.

Now let

\weq{13}{F'(r) = 0} % [sic] The German source prints F' here; the subsequent argument consistently uses F.

be a \gesperrt{Galois} resolvent of degree $\mu$ of the division equation in the original domain of rationality (so that all roots $x_{\nu,\nu'}$ can be represented rationally by $r$, Bd.\,I, § 152). This equation must \gesperrt{split} after the adjunction of a root of (12); for if it did not, then every rational relation

\weq{14}{\psi(r,\varrho) = 0}

would be satisfied for \gesperrt{all} roots of (13), and $\psi(t,\varrho)$ would be divisible by $F(t)$ (for a variable $t$). Hence (14) would still continue to hold if $\varrho$ were replaced by another root $\varrho^m$ of (12). But by § 62, (12) this is not the case when one puts one of the \gesperrt{Abelian} relations in place of (14).

Now let, \gesperrt{after the adjunction of} $\varrho$,

\weq{15}{F(r,\varrho) = 0}

be the \gesperrt{Galois} resolvent of degree $\nu$ of the division equation, so that, by 2., $\nu$ is equal to the degree of the group $\mathfrak{B}$. Then $F(t)$ is algebraically divisible by $F(t,\varrho)$, and hence, because of the irreducibility of (12), also by each of the functions $F(t,\varrho^m)$. Since the functions $F(t,\varrho^m)$ are irreducible, two of them can have a common divisor only when they are entirely identical. But if

\[
F(t,\varrho) = F(t,\varrho^m)
\]

were the case, then from every equation of the form (14) it would follow that $\psi(t,\varrho)$ is divisible by $F(t,\varrho) = F(t,\varrho^m)$, and it would follow that in (14) the \gesperrt{interchange} $(\varrho,\varrho^m)$ is admitted, which again is not the case for the \gesperrt{Abelian} relations. Consequently the $\varphi(n)$ functions $F(t,\varrho^m)$ are all different from one another, and $F(t)$ is divisible by their product. The degree $\mu$ of $F(t)$ is therefore at least $= \nu\varphi(n)$. But it also cannot be higher than $\nu\varphi(n)$, since $\nu\varphi(n)$ is the degree of the group $\mathfrak{A}$, and the
%CONT>>

% !PRINTED 214
\weberpage{214}
%<<CONT
group $\mathfrak{G}$ of degree $\mu$ is certainly contained in $\mathfrak{A}$. From this there results

\weq{16}{\mu = \nu\varphi(n)}

and at the same time the identity of $\mathfrak{G}$ with $\mathfrak{A}$.

But it also follows from this that $F(t)$ is equal to the product of all the factors $F(t,\varrho^m)$, so that

\weq{17}{F(t) = \overset{m}{\varPi} F(t, \varrho^m),}

and, since $F(t) = 0$ has no equal roots, that $F(r,\varrho)$ does indeed vanish, but that none of the other factors $F(r,\varrho^m)$ does. The equations

\weq{18}{F(r,t) = 0, \quad \varPhi(t) = 0}

have therefore only the single root $t = \varrho$ in common with one another, and by seeking out their greatest common divisor \gesperrt{one finds $\varrho$ expressed rationally by $r$, that is, by the roots of the division equation.}

These expressions for $\varrho$ do not change their value when a substitution of the group $\mathfrak{B}$ is applied to $r$, while [according to (12)] $\varrho$ passes over into a power of $\varrho$ under a substitution of the group $\mathfrak{A}$.

The \gesperrt{Abelian} relations show that under the substitution contained in $\mathfrak{A}$

\weq{19}{\begin{pmatrix} m, & 0 \\ 0, & 1 \end{pmatrix}}

$\varrho$ passes over into $\varrho^m$; for if we set

\[
e^{\frac{8\pi i}{n}} = \varrho^\lambda,
\]

then one of the \gesperrt{Abelian} relations reads

\weq{20}{\overset{\nu}{\Sigma} \varrho^{\lambda\nu\nu'} x_{\nu,\nu'} = 0,}

to which, when the expression in terms of $r$ is put in place of $\varrho$, \gesperrt{all} substitutions of $\mathfrak{A}$, and hence (19) as well, are applicable. But by § 62, (12), equation (20) remains correct under this substitution \gesperrt{only} if $\varrho$ passes over into $\varrho^m$.

Since $\varrho$ is not changed by the substitutions in $\mathfrak{B}$, and since the group $\mathfrak{A}$ arises from $\mathfrak{B}$ by composition with (19), it follows that under any substitution in $\mathfrak{A}$

\[
\begin{pmatrix} a, & b \\ c, & \partial \end{pmatrix}
\]

% !PRINTED 215
\weberpage{215}
%<<CONT
$\varrho$ passes into $\varrho^m$ if $m$ is congruent to the determinant $(a\partial - bc)$ with respect to the modulus $n$. % [sic] see note on preceding page: entry printed as \partial, likely \delta

4. \gesperrt{We wish finally to determine the number $\nu$, that is, the degree of the group $\mathfrak{B}$.}

$\varphi(n)$ has, as is well known, the expression (Bd.\,I, § 140)

\weq{21}{\varphi(n) = n\varPi\left(1 - \frac{1}{p}\right),}

where the product sign $\varPi$ extends over all the primes $p$ dividing $n$ that are distinct from one another.

The number $\nu$ is equal to the number of systems of numbers $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta$ incongruent with respect to $n$ which satisfy the condition

\weq{22}{\alpha\delta - \beta\gamma \equiv 1 \pmod{n}}

We ask first for the number of pairs $\alpha, \beta$ which have no common divisor with $n$, and denote it by $\chi(n)$.

If $n = n'n''$ and $n'$ is relatively prime to $n''$, then out of every combination of a pair of numbers $\alpha', \beta'$ belonging to $n'$ with a pair of numbers $\alpha'', \beta''$ belonging to $n''$ one can derive a pair belonging to $n$,

\[
\alpha = n''\alpha' + n'\alpha'', \quad \beta = n''\beta' + n'\beta''
\]

and one obtains in this way all the pairs of numbers $\alpha, \beta$, and each only once. From this it follows:

\weq{23}{\chi(n) = \chi(n')\chi(n'').}

It remains therefore to determine $\chi(p^\pi)$, that is, $\chi(n)$ for a prime power $n = p^\pi$.

If we first put for $\alpha, \beta$ all the numbers distinct modulo $p^\pi$, this number is $p^{2\pi}$. From these, however, all those pairs are to be omitted in which $\alpha$ \gesperrt{and} $\beta$ are divisible by $p$, whose number amounts to $p^{2\pi-2}$, so that

\[
\chi(p^\pi) = p^{2\pi} - p^{2\pi-2},
\]

and consequently, by (23), there follows in general

\weq{24}{\chi(n) = n^2\varPi\left(1 - \frac{1}{p^2}\right)}

where $p$ runs through the primes dividing $n$.

Every pair of numbers $\alpha, \beta$ can be changed, by increase through multiples of $n$, into one whose numbers are relatively prime to one another, and then $\gamma, \delta$ can be so determined that

\[
\alpha\delta - \beta\gamma = 1
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 237 =====
% !PRINTED 216
\weberpage{216}
%<<CONT
in it $\gamma, \delta$ can be replaced by $\gamma + h\alpha$, $\delta + h\beta$,
and by letting $h$ run through a complete system of residues modulo $n$,
one recognises that to every pair of numbers $\alpha, \beta$ there belong $n$
pairs of numbers $\gamma, \delta$ satisfying condition (23). Accordingly the
order of the group $\mathfrak{B}$ is:
\[
\nu = n^3 \Pi\left(1 - \frac{1}{p^2}\right),
\]
or, if we further introduce the numerical function

\weq{25}{\psi(n) = n\Pi\left(1 + \frac{1}{p}\right)}
then:

\weq{26}{\nu = n\varphi(n)\psi(n)}
and the order of the group $\mathfrak{A}$:

\weq{27}{\mu = n\varphi(n)^2\psi(n).}

\begin{center}
\S\,64. \gesperrt{The irreducible factors of the division equation.}
\end{center}
If
\[
\begin{aligned}
\nu &= \partial\mu - b\mu'\\
\nu' &= -c\mu + a\mu'
\end{aligned}
\]
and $a\partial - bc$ is relatively prime to $n$, then the greatest common
divisor of $\mu, \mu', n$ is at the same time the greatest common
divisor of $\nu, \nu', n$. The roots $x_{\mu,\mu'}$ of the division equation
therefore split, according to the greatest common divisor of
$\mu, \mu', n$, into systems which under the substitutions of the group $\mathfrak{A}$
always pass only into one another, that is, the group $\mathfrak{G}$ is \gesperrt{intransitive}, % Source verified: the group letter is Fraktur G.
and the systems of \gesperrt{intransitivity} are the
systems $x_{\mu,\mu'}$ in which $\mu, \mu', n$ have one and the same greatest
common divisor. The division equation is therefore
reducible (except when $n$ is a prime) and the roots
of one of these systems of imprimitivity % [sic] The German source changes from systems of intransitivity to imprimitivity here.
satisfy a rational
equation (Bd.\,I, \S\,157).

According to the preceding section there are $\varphi(n)\psi(n)$
pairs of numbers $\mu, \mu'$ whose greatest common divisor with $n$
is equal to 1, and the roots corresponding to these pairs of numbers
$x_{\mu,\mu'}$ therefore satisfy a rational equation of degree $\varphi(n)\psi(n)$.
This equation we call the \gesperrt{proper division equation}
for the divisor $n$, because only when $\mu, \mu', n$ are without a common
divisor is $x_{\mu,\mu'}$ not at the same time a root of a division
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 238 =====
% !PRINTED 217
\weberpage{217}
%<<CONT
equation for a smaller divisor. In contrast to this we call the
equation whose roots \gesperrt{are all} the $x_{\mu,\mu'}$ % [sic]
the \gesperrt{general division equation} for the divisor $n$.

By any substitution of the group $\mathfrak{A}$
\[
S = \begin{pmatrix} a, & b\\ c, & \partial \end{pmatrix}
\]
$(1,0)$, $(0,1)$ pass over into $(\partial, -c)$, $(-b, a)$, and so if $S$ is not
the identical substitution, then certainly at least one of the
two roots $x_{1,0}$, $x_{0,1}$ is altered by $S$. From this it results
\gesperrt{that the Galois group of the proper division equation
is exactly the same as that of the general one,}
only applied to the case in which $\mu, \mu', n$ have no common
divisor, namely, according as the $n$th roots of unity
are adjoined or not, $\mathfrak{B}$ or $\mathfrak{A}$.

From this it follows further \gesperrt{that the proper division equation
is irreducible, even after the adjunction of arbitrary constants.}

For if $\gamma, \delta$ are any two numbers having no common divisor
with $n$, then one can determine $\alpha, \beta$ in accordance with the congruence
\[
\alpha\delta - \beta\gamma \equiv 1 \pmod{n}
\]
and apply the substitution contained in $\mathfrak{B}$
\[
T = \begin{pmatrix} \alpha, & \beta\\ \gamma, & \delta \end{pmatrix}
\]
to every rational equation between the roots $x_{\mu,\mu'}$.
If then $x_{1,0}$ satisfies a rational equation (with arbitrary constant
coefficients)
\[
\Phi(x_{1,0}) = 0
\]
then every other root $x_{\delta,-\gamma}$ of the proper division equation
satisfies the same equation, from which the irreducibility of the
latter follows.

\begin{center}
\S\,65. \gesperrt{Reduction of the division equation}\\
\gesperrt{to transformation equations.}
\end{center}
The roots of the proper division equation can be arranged
in \gesperrt{rows} in the following way. Choose at will
one of the roots:
\[
x_{\mu_1,\mu'_1} = \mathrm{sn}\left(\frac{4\mu_1 K + 4\mu'_1 iK'}{n}\right) = \mathrm{sn}\,\Omega_1.
\]

%% ===== canonical stable idx 239 =====
% !PRINTED 218
\weberpage{218}
Among the roots of the division equation there occur also the
$\varphi(n)$ quantities

\weq{$R_1$}{\mathrm{sn}\,h\,\Omega_1}
which, when $h$ runs through a complete system of numbers incongruent
and coprime to $n$, are all different from one another. The system
$(R_1)$ we shall call the \gesperrt{first row of the roots}.

If now $\mathrm{sn}\,\Omega_2$ is a root not contained in $(R_1)$, then the
$\varphi(n)$ quantities

\weq{$R_2$}{\mathrm{sn}\,h\,\Omega_2,}
which are different both among themselves and from the roots $(R_1)$,
form a second row; and in this way one can proceed until all the
$\varphi(n)\psi(n)$ roots of the proper division equation are distributed
into $\psi(n)$ rows of $\varphi(n)$ terms each.

By the multiplication theorem, every other root of the same row can be
expressed \gesperrt{rationally} by means of one root, in the form:

\weq{1}{\mathrm{sn}\,h\,\Omega = f_h(\mathrm{sn}\,\Omega),}
where $f_h$ is a rational function depending only on the multiplier $h$,
not on the choice of $\Omega$.

If the two roots $x_{\mu,\mu'}$, $x_{\nu,\nu'}$ belong to the same row, then the number $h$ must admit of being so determined that

\weq{2}{h\mu \equiv \nu, \quad h\mu' \equiv \nu' \pmod{n},}
and conversely, if this is the case, then the two roots belong to the
same row. From (2), however, there follows the congruence

\weq{3}{\mu\nu' - \nu\mu' \equiv 0 \pmod{n},}
and from this, conversely, the congruences (2) can be derived again.

For since $\mu, \mu', n$ are relatively prime, one can determine the
numbers $\alpha, \beta$ so that
\[
\alpha\mu - \beta\mu' \equiv 1 \pmod{n}
\]
holds, and from this there follows by means of (3):
\[
\nu \equiv (\alpha\nu - \beta\nu')\mu, \quad \nu' \equiv (\alpha\nu - \beta\nu')\mu' \pmod{n},
\]
hence, if $\alpha\nu - \beta\nu' = h$ is put, the congruences (2).

\gesperrt{The congruence (3) is therefore the necessary and sufficient
condition that the two roots of the proper
division equation $x_{\mu,\mu'}$, $x_{\nu,\nu'}$ belong to the same
row.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 240 =====
% !PRINTED 219
\weberpage{219}
From this it follows that the division into rows is entirely independent
of the arbitrariness in the assumption about the
roots $\mathrm{sn}\,\Omega_1, \mathrm{sn}\,\Omega_2 \ldots$

\gesperrt{It follows further, however, that under the
substitutions of the group $\mathfrak{A}$ the rows are not torn apart,
but are only interchanged with one another.}
The group of the division equation is therefore imprimitive, and the
individual rows are the systems of imprimitivity (Bd.\,I, \S\,158).

For if one applies to $(\mu,\mu')$ and $(\nu,\nu')$ simultaneously the
substitution
\[
\begin{pmatrix} a, & b\\ c, & \partial \end{pmatrix}
\]
the congruence (3) remains preserved.

If one selects, among the substitutions of the group $\mathfrak{A}$, those substitutions
which interchange the roots of one row only among themselves, one obtains a group, and indeed a divisor
of $\mathfrak{A}$. To every row there thus belongs such a divisor of $\mathfrak{A}$.
If we denote by $R_{\mu,\mu'}$ the row in which the root $x_{\mu,\mu'}$ occurs,
and by $\mathfrak{A}_{\mu,\mu'}$ the divisor of $\mathfrak{A}$ belonging to this row,
then by (3) [cf. \S\,63, (3)] the substitutions
\[
\begin{pmatrix} a, & b\\ c, & \partial \end{pmatrix}
\]
of $\mathfrak{A}_{\mu,\mu'}$ are characterized by the congruence

\weq{4}{(\partial\mu - b\mu')\mu' + (c\mu - a\mu')\mu \equiv 0 \pmod{n}}

In the same way one obtains a group $\mathfrak{B}_{\mu,\mu'}$ if one seeks out the substitutions
in $\mathfrak{B}$ which interchange the roots of the row $R_{\mu,\mu'}$ only
among themselves; their substitutions:
\[
\begin{pmatrix} \alpha, & \beta\\ \gamma, & \delta \end{pmatrix}
\]
are characterized by the two congruences:

\weq{5}{\begin{aligned}
(\delta\mu - \beta\mu')\mu' + (\gamma\mu - \alpha\mu')\mu &\equiv 0\\
\alpha\delta - \beta\gamma &\equiv 1
\end{aligned}\ \ (\mathrm{mod}\ n)}

For example, the groups $\mathfrak{A}_{1,0}$, $\mathfrak{B}_{1,0}$ consist of the substitutions
\[
\begin{pmatrix} a, & b\\ 0, & \partial \end{pmatrix}, \quad
\begin{pmatrix} \alpha, & \beta\\ 0, & \delta \end{pmatrix}, \quad \alpha\delta \equiv 1 \pmod{n}.
\]

%% ===== canonical stable idx 241 =====
% !PRINTED 220
\weberpage{220}

The groups $\mathfrak{A}_{\mu,\mu'}$ are \gesperrt{conjugate divisors} of $\mathfrak{A}$
(Bd.\ II, § 3); for if $x_{1,0}$ passes by $S$ into $x_{\mu,\mu'}$, and hence $R_{1,0}$ into $R_{\mu,\mu'}$,
then by the group
\[
S^{-1}\mathfrak{A}_{1,0}S
\]
the roots of $R_{\mu,\mu'}$ are permuted only among themselves, and therefore
\weq{6}{S^{-1}\mathfrak{A}_{1,0}S = \mathfrak{A}_{\mu,\mu'}.}

Likewise, if $T$ is a substitution in $\mathfrak{B}$ by which
$x_{1,0}$ passes into $x_{\mu,\mu'}$:
\weq{7}{T^{-1}\mathfrak{B}_{1,0}T = \mathfrak{B}_{\mu,\mu'}.}

The greatest common divisor $\mathfrak{A}_0$ of all the groups $\mathfrak{A}_{\mu,\mu'}$
is determined, according to (4), by
\[
b \equiv 0, \quad c \equiv 0, \quad a \equiv \partial \ (\mathrm{mod}\ n)
\]
and consists therefore of the substitutions:
\[
\begin{pmatrix} a, & 0 \\ 0, & a \end{pmatrix},
\]
in which $a$ is an arbitrary number coprime to $n$. $\mathfrak{A}_0$ is identical
with the greatest common divisor of three of the groups $\mathfrak{A}_{\mu,\mu'}$
that belong to different rows. For $\mathfrak{A}_0$ is then
the greatest common divisor of $\mathfrak{A}_{\mu,\mu'}$, $\mathfrak{A}_{\nu,\nu'}$, $\mathfrak{A}_{\varrho,\varrho'}$ if
the three congruences
\[
\begin{aligned}
c\mu^2 - (\partial - a)\mu\mu' - b\mu'^2 &\equiv 0 \\
c\nu^2 - (\partial - a)\nu\nu' - b\nu'^2 &\equiv 0 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ n) \\
c\varrho^2 - (\partial - a)\varrho\varrho' - b\varrho'^2 &\equiv 0
\end{aligned}
\]
are satisfied \gesperrt{only} under the assumption
\[
\partial \equiv a, \quad b \equiv 0, \quad c \equiv 0 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ n)
\]
This takes place when the determinant
\[
\begin{vmatrix} \mu^2, & \mu\mu', & \mu'^2 \\ \nu^2, & \nu\nu', & \nu'^2 \\ \varrho^2, & \varrho\varrho', & \varrho'^2 \end{vmatrix}
= -(\nu\varrho' - \varrho\nu')(\varrho\mu' - \mu\varrho')(\mu\nu' - \nu\mu')
\]
is relatively prime to $n$.

Likewise, by (5), the greatest common divisor $\mathfrak{B}_0$
of all the $\mathfrak{B}_{\mu,\mu'}$ is the totality of the substitutions:
\weq{8}{\begin{pmatrix} \alpha, & 0 \\ 0, & \alpha \end{pmatrix}}
with the condition:
\weq{9}{\alpha^2 \equiv 1 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ n).}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 242 =====
% !PRINTED 221
\weberpage{221}

The congruence (9) possesses, if $k$ is the number of the mutually distinct primes dividing $n$,
$2^k$ incongruent solutions, and this is therefore the degree of the group
$\mathfrak{B}_0$\footnote{Cf. \gesperrt{Dirichlet-Dedekind}, Vorlesungen über Zahlentheorie, 4.\ Aufl., § 37.}.

A rational function $\xi$ of the roots of \gesperrt{one row}, say of the row $R_{1,0}$, can by (1) be
represented rationally by \gesperrt{one of these} roots. If this function has the property of remaining
unchanged when this one root is replaced by another of the same row, that is, if for example
$\xi$ is a \gesperrt{symmetric function of the roots of one row}, then $\xi$ takes, through application of
the substitutions of $\mathfrak{A}$ (or also of $\mathfrak{B}$), only
\weq{10}{\nu = \psi(n)}
different values
\weq{11}{\xi_1, \xi_2, \ldots, \xi_\nu,}
% Source reading \xi_\nu retained: the damaged subscript is fixed by the immediately following count of \nu quantities.
\gesperrt{and if these values are all different from one another, then $\xi$ belongs to the group
$\mathfrak{A}_{1,0}$, and all other symmetric functions of the roots of $R_{1,0}$ can be
represented rationally by $\xi$} (Bd.\ I, § 162).

The $\nu$ quantities (11) are the roots of an irreducible rational equation of degree $\nu$,
which we call a \gesperrt{transformation equation}.

The transformation equation itself has rational numerical coefficients, provided that only
rational numerical coefficients occur in $\xi$. \gesperrt{But it remains irreducible even when $n$th roots
of unity, or indeed any constants whatever, are adjoined}, as follows from the fact that by
substitutions of the group $\mathfrak{B}$ every root of the division equation can be carried
over into every other, and hence also every row into every other row.

By the adjunction of a root $\xi$ of the transformation equation, say of the one belonging to
the group $\mathfrak{A}_{1,0}$, the group of the division equation reduces to
$\mathfrak{A}_{1,0}$; but this latter group is no longer transitive, and instead permutes among
themselves the $\varphi(n)$ roots $x_{h,0}$, in which $h$ runs through a complete system of
incongruent numbers coprime to $n$. The division equation therefore becomes reducible and has a
factor of degree $\varphi(n)$,
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 243 =====
% !PRINTED 222
\weberpage{222}

%<<CONT
whose roots are the $x_{h,0}$. The influence of a substitution of the group
$\mathfrak{A}_{1,0}$
\[
\begin{pmatrix} a, & b \\ 0, & \partial \end{pmatrix}
\]
upon $x_{h,0}$ consists in this, that $x_{h,0}$ passes over into $x_{\partial h,0}$, and the
group of this equation of degree $\varphi(n)$ therefore consists of the permutations
\[
(x_{h,0},\ x_{\partial h,0}),
\]
in which $\partial$ may be any number whatever coprime to $n$. This group is
an \gesperrt{Abelian} one, and therefore the roots $x_{h,0}$ are, \gesperrt{after the adjunction of $\xi$,
to be determined algebraically by radicals.}

If, however, we adjoin not merely one, but all the roots $\xi$ of the
transformation equation, or, what comes to the same thing, the three belonging to
$R_{1,0}$, $R_{0,1}$, $R_{1,1}$, then the group of the
division equation reduces to $\mathfrak{A}_0$, and if we adjoin in addition $n$th roots of unity,
to $\mathfrak{B}_0$. The group $\mathfrak{B}_0$ is an \gesperrt{Abelian} one of
degree $2^k$ which contains only such elements as have degree $= 2$. In consequence the
\gesperrt{division equation is solvable by square roots.}

In order to find the form of this solution, let one put
\[
n = p^\pi p'^{\pi'} \ldots,
\]
in which $p, p', \ldots$ are primes different from one another, and $\pi, \pi', \ldots$
are positive exponents. Let the numbers $c, c', \ldots$ be determined from the congruences
\[
\begin{aligned}
c &\equiv -1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ p^\pi), & c' &\equiv -1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ p'^{\pi'}) \ldots \\
c &\equiv +1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ np^{-\pi}), & c' &\equiv +1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ np'^{-\pi'}) \ldots
\end{aligned}
\]
then one obtains every solution $\alpha$ of the congruence
\[
\alpha^2 \equiv 1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ n),
\]
and each only once, in the form
\weq{12}{\alpha \equiv c^\varepsilon c'^{\varepsilon'} \ldots \ (\mathrm{mod}\ n),}
when $\varepsilon, \varepsilon', \ldots$ take the values 0, 1.

Now if $\Omega$ is any one of the values
\[
\frac{4\mu K + 4\mu' i K'}{n},
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 244 =====
% !PRINTED 223
\weberpage{223}

%<<CONT
and thus $\mathrm{sn}\,\Omega$ any root of the proper division equation, then the sum, to be
extended over all $\alpha$,
\weq{13}{\Sigma(\pm 1)^\varepsilon(\pm 1)^{\varepsilon'}\ldots\, \mathrm{sn}\,\alpha\Omega = \psi(\Omega),}
in which the $k$ signs of $\pm 1$ may be chosen arbitrarily, has the property that for every
$\alpha$ determined according to (12)
\weq{14}{\psi(\alpha\Omega) = (\pm 1)^\varepsilon(\pm 1)^{\varepsilon'}\ldots \psi(\Omega)}
holds; and the square of $\psi(\Omega)$ remains unchanged under the substitutions of the group
$\mathfrak{B}_0$, and is therefore rationally expressible by $n$th roots of unity and the roots
of a transformation equation. $\psi(\Omega)$ is therefore the square root $\sqrt{A}$ of such an
expression $A$. But the number of the expressions (13) amounts to $2^k$, and by addition of all
the equations so formed we obtain
\weq{15}{2^k\,\mathrm{sn}\,\Omega = \Sigma\sqrt{A}.}

It is still to be remarked that of the quantities $\psi$, and hence also of the $A$, half
vanish. For we have
\[
-1 \equiv cc' \ldots \ (\mathrm{mod}\ n),
\]
and if we therefore set $\alpha \equiv -1$ in (14), it follows that:
\[
\psi(-\Omega) = (\pm 1)(\pm 1)\ldots\psi(\Omega);
\]
but on the other hand
\[
\psi(-\Omega) = -\psi(\Omega),
\]
and consequently $\psi(\Omega)$ always vanishes when among the $k$ quantities $\pm 1$ occurring
in (14) an even number of negative units is contained.

The roots $x_{\mu,\mu'}$ can therefore be expressed linearly by $2^{k-1}$ square roots.

\gesperrt{If $n$ is a prime or a power of a prime, then the squares of the roots of the division equation
are rationally expressible by the roots of the transformation equation}\footnote{Cf. on this
theorem \gesperrt{Kronecker}, Monatsbericht der Berliner Akademie, 19.\ Juli 1875. There \gesperrt{Kronecker} draws
attention to an oversight which occurs in a memoir of \gesperrt{Jacobi} bearing on this subject (Crelle,
Bd.\ 47 and Bd.\ 50).}.

If $n$ is a composite number, the classification of the roots $x_{\mu,\mu'}$ into rows can be
carried still further. If $p$ is a prime divisor of
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 245 =====
% !PRINTED 224
\weberpage{224}
%<<CONT
$n$, then one takes two roots $x_{\mu,\mu'}$, $x_{\nu,\nu'}$
into the same row or into different rows, according as

\[
\mu\nu' - \nu\mu' \equiv 0 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ p)
\]

or not; if accordingly $x_{\nu,\nu'}$ and $x_{\nu_1,\nu_1'}$ belong to one row with
$x_{\mu,\mu'}$, then they belong to the same row with one another as well. The
number of the rows so formed is, as is easily shown,
$p + 1$, and in this way one obtains, as the first resolvent of the
division equation, a transformation equation belonging to the divisor $p$.
We shall show later, by another route, how the
transformation equations for composite divisors can be reduced to
those for prime divisors.

\begin{center}
\rule{3cm}{0.4pt}
\end{center}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 246 =====
% !PRINTED none
\begin{center}
\gesperrt{Seventh Chapter.}

\medskip
{\Large\textbf{Theory of the Transformation Equations.}}

\medskip
\rule{3cm}{0.4pt}
\end{center}

\begin{center}
\textbf{\S\,66. Formation of Transformation Equations.}
\end{center}

Now that the division equations have been reduced to transformation equations, we proceed to a more exact study of these latter equations.

We assume $n$ to be odd, understand by $p$ the primes that divide $n$, and put

\weq{1}{\nu = \psi(n) = n\,\Pi\left(1+\frac{1}{p}\right),}

and denote the $\nu$ rows of the roots of the division equation by $R_1, R_2, \ldots, R_\nu$.

From each of these rows we take, for

\weq{2}{\Omega_{\mu,\mu'} = \frac{4\mu K + 4\mu' i K'}{n}}

a representative $\Omega_1, \Omega_2, \ldots, \Omega_\nu$, and we obtain the $\varphi(n)$ roots of one row if in

\[
\mathrm{sn}\, m\,\Omega
\]

we let $m$ run through a complete system of incongruent numbers coprime to $n$.

The simplest expressions that can be introduced as roots of transformation equations are the products

\weq{3}{\mathop{\Pi}\limits_{1,\,n-1}^{n} \Phi(\mathrm{sn}\,h\,\Omega),}

where $\Phi$ is an arbitrary rational function, and $h$ runs through the sequence of numbers $1, 2, \ldots, n-1$.

Every such function is rationally expressible by $\mathrm{sn}\,\Omega$, and evidently remains unchanged when $\Omega$ is replaced by any $m\,\Omega$
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 247 =====
% !PRINTED 226
\weberpage{226}
%<<CONT
is replaced; one has therefore only to see to it that the $\nu$ values of (3), which correspond to the $\nu$ rows, are distinct from one another, \gesperrt{so that (3) becomes the root of an (irreducible) transformation equation}\textsuperscript{1)}.

We assume that the function $\Phi(x)$ is either an \gesperrt{even} or an \gesperrt{odd} function of $x$, and accordingly make the following distinction.

If $\Phi(x)$ is an even function, then among the factors of the product (3) two at a time, namely

\weq{4}{\Phi(\mathrm{sn}\,h\,\Omega), \quad \Phi[\mathrm{sn}\,(n-h)\,\Omega]}

are equal to one another. If we therefore set

\weq{5}{\Pi(\Omega) = \prod_{1,\,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{h} \Phi(\mathrm{sn}\,h\,\Omega),}

then, if $m$ is any number coprime to $n$,

\weq{6}{\Pi(m\,\Omega) = \Pi(\Omega)}

[because among the $\frac{1}{2}(n-1)$ numbers $h\,m$ no two have a sum or a difference divisible by $n$, so that, apart from sign, the $\mathrm{sn}\,h\,\Omega$ are the same as the $\mathrm{sn}\,h\,m\,\Omega$]. Thus $\Pi(\Omega)$ is the root of a transformation equation. This class of transformation equations we call \gesperrt{modular equations}.

If $\Phi(x)$ is an odd function, then the two quantities (4) are opposite to one another and (6) is no longer generally correct; instead we have

\weq{7}{\Pi(m\,\Omega) = \pm\,\Pi(\Omega).}

Hence, at least in general, it is no longer $\Pi(\Omega)$, but only $\Pi(\Omega)^2$, that is a root of a transformation equation. This kind of transformation equations we call \gesperrt{multiplier equations}. In order to learn the cases in which $\Pi(\Omega)$ itself is a root of a transformation, the sign in (7) must be determined.

This is achieved by means of a theorem of number theory which is derived in Bd.\ I, \S\,145.

The theorem runs:
%CONT>>

\textsuperscript{1)}~Expressions like (3) are still roots of transformation equations even when $h$ takes only values coprime to $n$. Such a transformation equation % [sic] The German source prints the plural determiner with a singular noun.
has hitherto been little used. We shall become acquainted with an example further on.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 248 =====
% !PRINTED 227
\weberpage{227}
%<<CONT
If $m, n$ are any two coprime numbers, the latter odd, and if $\mu$ further denotes the number of those among the numbers

\[
m,\ 2m,\ 3m \cdots \frac{n-1}{2}\,m,
\]

whose absolutely least residues $(\mathrm{mod}\ n)$ are negative, then

\weq{8}{(-1)^\mu = \left(\frac{m}{n}\right),}

where $\left(\dfrac{m}{n}\right)$ is the \gesperrt{Legendre-Jacobi} symbol from the theory of quadratic residues\textsuperscript{1)}.

This theorem now leads immediately to the determination of the sign in (7). For if the function $\Phi(x)$ in (5) is odd, then in the passage from $\Omega$ to $m\,\Omega$ exactly $\mu$ factors in (5) change their sign, and we conclude

\weq{9}{\Pi(m\,\Omega) = \left(\frac{m}{n}\right) \Pi(\Omega).}

If $n$ is not a square number, then $m$ can always be assumed such that $\left(\dfrac{m}{n}\right) = -1$. For if $n = p^\lambda n'$, with $\lambda$ odd, $n'$ not divisible by $p$, and $\beta$ a quadratic non-residue of $p$, then one need only determine $m$ from the congruences

\[
m \equiv \beta \pmod{p^\lambda}, \quad m \equiv 1 \pmod{n'}
\]

in order to find such a number $m$. And then $\Pi(m\,\Omega) = -\Pi(\Omega)$, and not $\Pi(\Omega)$, but only $\Pi(\Omega)^2$ is a root of a transformation equation. But if $n$ is a square number, then $\Pi(m\,\Omega) = \Pi(\Omega)$ for every $m$, and consequently $\Pi(\Omega)$ itself is a root of a transformation equation. Hence the theorem follows:

\begin{quote}
\gesperrt{For an odd function $\Phi$ it is $\Pi(\Omega)^2$, and only when $n$ is a square number $\Pi(\Omega)$ itself, that is a root of a transformation equation\textsuperscript{2)}.}
\end{quote}

\textsuperscript{1)}~Cf.\ on this theorem: \gesperrt{Schering} and \gesperrt{Kronecker} in the Monatsbericht der Berliner Akademie of 22 June 1876. \gesperrt{Schering}, Acta mathematica I.

\textsuperscript{2)}~This simplification of the multiplier equation in the case where $n$ is a square was discovered by \gesperrt{Joubert}, but was demonstrated by a path entirely different from ours. ``Sur les équations, qui se rencontrent dans la théorie de la transformation des fonctions elliptiques.'' Paris 1876.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 249 =====
% !PRINTED 228
\weberpage{228}
\begin{center}
\S\,67. \textbf{\gesperrt{Special Transformation Equations.}}
\end{center}

The roots of the transformation equations are now to be represented by $\vartheta$-functions. For this purpose we set:

\weq{1}{
\begin{aligned}
\Omega &= \frac{4\mu K + 4\mu' i K'}{n}, \quad iK' = K\omega,\\
\varpi &= \frac{\mu+\mu'\omega}{n}, \quad \Omega = 4K\varpi
\end{aligned}
}

and consider the products

\[
\prod_{1,\,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{h} \vartheta_{00}(2h\varpi), \quad
\prod_{1,\,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{h} \vartheta_{01}(2h\varpi), \quad
\prod_{1,\,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{h} \vartheta_{10}(2h\varpi), \quad
\prod_{1,\,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{h} \vartheta_{11}(2h\varpi).
\]

The following notation is recommended:

\weq{2}{
\begin{aligned}
P_{00}\,\vartheta_{00}^{\frac{n-1}{2}} &= e^{\frac{\pi i}{6}\mu'(\mu+\mu'\omega)\frac{n^2-1}{n}} \prod_{1,\,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{h} \vartheta_{00}(2h\varpi),\\
P_{10}\,\vartheta_{10}^{\frac{n-1}{2}} &= e^{\frac{\pi i}{6}\mu'(\mu+\mu'\omega)\frac{n^2-1}{n}} \prod_{1,\,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{h} \vartheta_{10}(2h\varpi),\\
P_{01}\,\vartheta_{01}^{\frac{n-1}{2}} &= e^{\frac{\pi i}{6}\mu'(\mu+\mu'\omega)\frac{n^2-1}{n}} \prod_{1,\,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{h} \vartheta_{01}(2h\varpi).
\end{aligned}
}

Formula \S\,39, (9) is now to be applied, but for the present purpose it is presented somewhat differently.

If one sets $v' = 2h/n$, $v = 2h(\alpha+\beta\omega)/n$ in \S\,39, (8) and again takes the product over $h = 1, 2, \ldots (n-1)/2$, then, with the application of \S\,32, (24), it follows that:

\[
\begin{aligned}
&2^{\frac{n-1}{2}} \prod_{1,\,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{h} \vartheta_{00}\!\left(\frac{2h(\alpha+\beta\omega)}{n}\right) \vartheta_{01}\!\left(\frac{2h(\alpha+\beta\omega)}{n}\right) \vartheta_{10}\!\left(\frac{2h(\alpha+\beta\omega)}{n}\right)\\
&= (-1)^{\frac{n^2-1}{8}} e^{-\frac{\pi i}{2}\frac{n^2-1}{n}\beta(\alpha+\beta\omega)} \vartheta_{00}^{\frac{n-1}{2}} \vartheta_{10}^{\frac{n-1}{2}} \vartheta_{01}^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\textsuperscript{1)}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Accordingly, by multiplication of the three equations (2), one obtains:

\weq{3}{(-1)^{\frac{n^2-1}{8}} 2^{\frac{n-1}{2}} P_{00} P_{10} P_{01} = 1.}

\textsuperscript{1)}~In \S\,34, (9) of the first edition the formula in question is given at once in this form, which can also be derived, though somewhat more circumstantially, from \S\,39, (9).

%% ===== canonical stable idx 250 =====
% !PRINTED 229
\weberpage{229}
Besides this we further set:
\weq{4}{P_{11}\,\eta(\omega)^{\frac{n-1}{2}} = e^{\frac{\pi i}{6}\mu'(\mu+\mu'\omega)\frac{n^2-1}{n}}\;\mathop{\Pi}\limits_{1,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{h}\vartheta_{11}(2h\varpi).}

These quantities $P$ can be expressed by the roots of the division equation if, applying (3), one forms the quotients
\[
\frac{P_{00}^2}{P_{01}P_{10}},\quad \frac{P_{10}^2}{P_{01}P_{00}},\quad \frac{P_{01}^2}{P_{10}P_{00}},\quad \frac{P_{11}^3}{P_{00}P_{01}P_{10}}
\]
and by means of the formulae of § 42 introduces elliptic functions.

One obtains in this way
\weq{5}{\begin{aligned}
(-1)^{\frac{n^2-1}{8}}\,2^{\frac{n-1}{2}}P_{00}^3 &= \mathop{\Pi}\limits_{1,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{h}\frac{\operatorname{dn}^2h\Omega}{\operatorname{cn}h\Omega},\\
(-1)^{\frac{n^2-1}{8}}\,2^{\frac{n-1}{2}}P_{10}^3 &= \mathop{\Pi}\limits_{1,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{h}\frac{\operatorname{cn}^2h\Omega}{\operatorname{dn}h\Omega},\\
(-1)^{\frac{n^2-1}{8}}\,2^{\frac{n-1}{2}}P_{01}^3 &= \mathop{\Pi}\limits_{1,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{h}\frac{1}{\operatorname{cn}h\Omega\,\operatorname{dn}h\Omega},
\end{aligned}}
\weq{6}{(-1)^{\frac{n^2-1}{8}}P_{11}^3 = (\varkappa\varkappa')^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\mathop{\Pi}\limits_{1,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{h}\frac{\operatorname{sn}^3h\Omega}{\operatorname{cn}h\Omega\,\operatorname{dn}h\Omega}.}

These expressions now show that $P_{00}^3$, $P_{10}^3$, $P_{01}^3$ \gesperrt{are the roots of transformation equations (modular equations)}. $P_{11}^6$ is the root of a multiplier equation, and if $n$ is a square number, then $P_{11}^3$ too is \gesperrt{the root of a multiplier equation}.

One can combine the functions $P$ with one another in manifold ways in order to obtain new transformation equations. We adduce the following:
\weq{7}{\begin{aligned}
\frac{P_{10}}{P_{00}} &= \mathop{\Pi}\limits_{1,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{h}\frac{\operatorname{cn}h\Omega}{\operatorname{dn}h\Omega},\\
\frac{P_{01}}{P_{00}} &= \mathop{\Pi}\limits_{1,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{h}\frac{1}{\operatorname{dn}h\Omega},
\end{aligned}}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 251 =====
% !PRINTED 230
\weberpage{230}
%<<CONT
\weq{8}{\begin{aligned}
(-1)^{\frac{n^2-1}{8}}\frac{2^{\frac{n-1}{3}}P_{00}^2P_{11}}{\sqrt{\varkappa\varkappa'}^{\frac{n-1}{3}}} &= \mathop{\Pi}\limits_{1,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{h}\frac{\operatorname{sn}h\Omega\,\operatorname{dn}h\Omega}{\operatorname{cn}h\Omega},\\
(-1)^{\frac{n^2-1}{8}}\frac{2^{\frac{n-1}{3}}P_{10}^2P_{11}}{\sqrt{\varkappa\varkappa'}^{\frac{n-1}{3}}} &= \mathop{\Pi}\limits_{1,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{h}\frac{\operatorname{sn}h\Omega\,\operatorname{cn}h\Omega}{\operatorname{dn}k\Omega},\\ % [sic] printed \textquotedbl{}dn k Omega\textquotedbl{} for \textquotedbl{}dn h Omega\textquotedbl{}
(-1)^{\frac{n^2-1}{8}}\frac{2^{\frac{n-1}{3}}P_{01}^2P_{11}}{\sqrt{\varkappa\varkappa'}^{\frac{n-1}{3}}} &= \mathop{\Pi}\limits_{1,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{h}\frac{\operatorname{sn}h\Omega}{\operatorname{cn}h\Omega\,\operatorname{dn}h\Omega}.
\end{aligned}}

One further important result, however, is obtained by applying the multiplication theorem. If in the last formula II of § 57 one sets $u = 2h\varpi$, one finds
\weq{9}{e^{4\pi i\omega h^2\mu'^2}\vartheta_{01}(2h\varpi)^{n^2} = \frac{\vartheta_{01}^{n^2}}{D(\operatorname{sn}^2h\Omega)},}
in which, as we recall, $D$ is an integral rational function whose coefficients are formed rationally from $\varkappa^2$ and integers.

If we take the product of these expressions, for $h = 1, 2, \ldots, \frac{n-1}{2}$, then from the last equation (2) it follows (because, as is well known, $\Sigma h^2 = \frac{n(n^2-1)}{24}$):
\weq{10}{P_{01}^{n^2} = \mathop{\Pi}\limits_{1,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{h}\frac{1}{D(\operatorname{sn}^2h\Omega)}.}

We conclude from this that $P_{01}^{n^2}$ too is a root of a transformation equation. This is nothing new when $n$ is divisible by 3, but it is new when $n$ is not divisible by 3, so that $n^2 - 1$ is divisible by 3. For in that case we obtain from (10), with the use of (5), (7), (8):
\weq{11}{\begin{aligned}
