P_{01} &= 2^{\frac{(n-1)(n^2-1)}{6}}\mathop{\Pi}\limits_{1,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{h}\frac{(\operatorname{cn}h\Omega)^{\frac{n^2-1}{3}}(\operatorname{dn}h\Omega)^{\frac{n^2-1}{3}}}{D(\operatorname{sn}^2h\Omega)},\\
P_{00} &= 2^{\frac{(n-1)(n^2-1)}{6}}\mathop{\Pi}\limits_{1,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{h}\frac{(\operatorname{cn}h\Omega)^{\frac{n^2-1}{3}}(\operatorname{dn}h\Omega)^{\frac{n^2+2}{3}}}{D(\operatorname{sn}^2h\Omega)},\\
P_{10} &= 2^{\frac{(n-1)(n^2-1)}{6}}\mathop{\Pi}\limits_{1,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{h}\frac{(\operatorname{cn}h\Omega)^{\frac{n^2+2}{3}}(\operatorname{dn}h\Omega)^{\frac{n^2-1}{3}}}{D(\operatorname{sn}^2h\Omega)},
\end{aligned}}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 252 =====
% !PRINTED 231
\weberpage{231}
%<<CONT
\weq{12}{(-1)^{\frac{n^2-1}{8}}\,2^{\frac{n^2(n-1)}{3}}P_{11} = \sqrt{\varkappa\varkappa'}^{\frac{n-1}{3}}\mathop{\Pi}\limits_{1,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{h}\frac{\operatorname{sn}h\Omega\,D(\operatorname{sn}^2h\Omega)^2}{(\operatorname{cn}h\Omega)^{\frac{2n^2+1}{3}}(\operatorname{dn}h\Omega)^{\frac{2n^2+1}{3}}}.}

If the domain of rationality is to be maintained as that of the rational numbers and rational functions of $\varkappa^2$, then the last equation is better written in the form [cf. § 54, (4)]:
\weq{13}{\begin{aligned}
P_{11}\gamma_2(\omega)^{\frac{n-1}{2}} &= (-1)^{\frac{n^2-1}{8}}\,2^{-\frac{(n^2-4)(n-1)}{3}}(\varkappa\varkappa')^{-\frac{n-1}{2}}(1-\varkappa^2\varkappa'^2)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\\
&\quad\times \mathop{\Pi}\limits_{1,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{h}\frac{\operatorname{sn}h\Omega\,D(\operatorname{sn}^2h\Omega)^2}{(\operatorname{cn}h\Omega)^{\frac{2n^2+1}{3}}(\operatorname{dn}h\Omega)^{\frac{2n^2+1}{3}}},
\end{aligned}}
and from this one infers the following theorem:

\gesperrt{If $n$ is not divisible by 3, then $P_{00}$, $P_{01}$, $P_{10}$, $P_{11}^2\gamma_2(\omega)^{n-1}$, and, when $n$ is a square, also $P_{11}\gamma_2(\omega)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}$, are roots of transformation equations.}

\begin{center}
\textbf{§ 68.} \textbf{\gesperrt{Second Representation of the Roots of the Transformation Equations.}}
\end{center}

If we first fix our attention on one of the rows, namely the one to which the root $x_{1,0}$ belongs, and accordingly put $\mu = 1$, $\mu' = 0$, then we may apply to (2), (3) of the preceding section the formulae (20), (21), (10), § 34. If there, when $\nu$ is odd, one puts $n - \nu$ in place of $\nu$ and uses the formula
\[
\vartheta_{g_1g_2}\left(\frac{n-\nu}{n}\right) = (-1)^{g_1(g_2+1)}\vartheta_{g_1g_2}\left(\frac{\nu}{n}\right),
\]
then only the even $\nu$ occur in these formulae, and if one accordingly puts $\nu = 2h$, then the formulae (20), (21) there may also be written thus:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{n}\,\eta(n\omega)\eta(\omega)^{\frac{n-3}{2}} &= \mathop{\Pi}\limits_{1,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{h}\vartheta_{11}\!\left(\frac{2h}{n}\right),\\
f(n\omega)\eta(\omega)^{\frac{n-1}{2}} &= f(\omega)\mathop{\Pi}\limits_{1,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{h}\vartheta_{00}\!\left(\frac{2h}{n}\right),\\
f_1(n\omega)\eta(\omega)^{\frac{n-1}{2}} &= f_1(\omega)\mathop{\Pi}\limits_{1,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{h}\vartheta_{01}\!\left(\frac{2h}{n}\right),\\
f_2(n\omega)\eta(\omega)^{\frac{n-1}{2}} &= \left(\frac{2}{n}\right)f_2(\omega)\mathop{\Pi}\limits_{1,\frac{n-1}{2}}^{h}\vartheta_{10}\!\left(\frac{2h}{n}\right),
\end{aligned}
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 253 =====
% !PRINTED 232
\weberpage{232}
%<<CONT
in which $\left(\frac{2}{n}\right) = (-1)^{\frac{n^2-1}{8}}$, and if we accordingly denote by $P^0$ the functions $P$ that correspond to the case $\mu = 1$, $\mu' = 0$, then from § 67, (2) and (4), with regard to § 34, (10), there follows:
\weq{1}{\begin{aligned}
P_{00}^0 &= \frac{f(n\omega)}{f(\omega)^n},\\
P_{01}^0 &= \frac{f_1(n\omega)}{f_1(\omega)^n},\\
P_{10}^0 &= \left(\frac{2}{n}\right)\frac{f_2(n\omega)}{f_2(\omega)^n},
\end{aligned}}
\weq{2}{P_{11}^0 = \sqrt{n}\,\frac{\eta(n\omega)}{\eta(\omega)}.}

In order to represent all the roots of the transformation equations by such formulae, we determine a linear transformation as follows:
\weq{3}{\begin{pmatrix}\alpha, & \beta\\ \gamma, & \delta\end{pmatrix} \equiv \begin{pmatrix}1, & 0\\ 0, & 1\end{pmatrix} \pmod{16},}
\weq{4}{\alpha \equiv \mu, \qquad \beta \equiv \mu' \pmod{n},}
and replace $\omega$ in (1), (2) by
\weq{5}{\omega' = \frac{\gamma + \delta\omega}{\alpha + \beta\omega};}
to the left side the formulae (3) to (6) § 39 and (19), § 38 can then be applied, and they give:
\weq{6}{\begin{aligned}
P_{00} &= \frac{f(n\omega')}{f(\omega')^n},\\
P_{01} &= \frac{f_1(n\omega')}{f_1(\omega')^n},\\
P_{10} &= \left(\frac{2}{n}\right)\frac{f_2(n\omega')}{f_2(\omega')^n},\\
P_{11} &= \varepsilon^{1-n}\sqrt{n}\,\frac{\eta(n\omega')}{\eta(\omega')},
\end{aligned}}
in which $\varepsilon$ is the 24th root of unity exactly defined in § 33, (15), (18).

Now two transformations
\[
% [sic] The source prints a semicolon after \alpha' in the first matrix.
\begin{pmatrix}\alpha'; & \beta'\\ \gamma', & \delta'\end{pmatrix}, \quad \begin{pmatrix}a, & 0\\ c, & \partial\end{pmatrix}, \quad a\partial = n,
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 254 =====
% !PRINTED 233
\weberpage{233}
%<<CONT
of which the first is linear, the other of the $n$th order,
in such a way that

\weq{7}{\begin{pmatrix} \alpha', & \beta' \\ \gamma', & \delta' \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} a, & 0 \\ c, & \partial \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0 \\ 0, & n \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} \alpha, & \beta \\ \gamma, & \delta \end{pmatrix}.}

For if we write the relation (7) thus:
\[
\begin{pmatrix} \delta', & -\beta' \\ -\gamma', & \alpha' \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0 \\ 0, & n \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} a, & 0 \\ c, & \partial \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} \delta, & -\beta \\ -\gamma, & \alpha \end{pmatrix},
\]
then one derives from it simply:

\weq{8}{\begin{aligned}
\delta' &= a\delta, & \gamma' &= \partial\gamma - c\delta,\\
\partial\beta' &= \beta, & n\alpha' &= \partial\alpha - c\beta, & a\alpha' &= \alpha - c\beta'.
\end{aligned}}

By this $\partial$ is first of all determined as the \gesperrt{greatest common
divisor} of $\beta$ and $n$, or [because of (4)] of $\mu'$ and $n$. For if
$\partial$ were not the greatest common divisor of $n=\partial a$ and
$\beta=\partial\beta'$, then $a$ and $\beta'$ would have to have a common
% [sic] The source prints \alpha=\alpha a'+c\beta, contrary to (8).
divisor, and consequently so would $\beta$ and $\alpha=\alpha a'+c\beta$, which
cannot be. At the same time $a=n/\partial$ is thereby determined, and $c$ must
satisfy the congruence

\weq{9}{\partial\alpha - c\beta \equiv 0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ n)}

by which, however, $c$ is determined not absolutely, but only to the modulus
$a$. One can therefore attach to $c$ the further condition, e.\,g., that it
shall be divisible by some power of 2, or, if $a$ is not divisible by 3, by
some power of 3, as we shall sometimes do later.

The three numbers $a$, $\partial$, $c$ can have no common divisor,
for such a one would [by (8)] also be a divisor of $\alpha$ and $\beta$, which
is impossible. If we therefore denote the greatest common divisor of $a$
and $\partial$ by $e$, then $c$ must be \gesperrt{relatively prime} to $e$.

The numbers $a$, $\partial$, $c$, the last modulo $a$, are, on account of (4)
and (8), completely determined by the two numbers $\mu$, $\mu'$, and do not
change when $\mu$, $\mu'$ are multiplied by a common factor coprime to $n$,
i.\,e. are replaced by another pair of the same \gesperrt{row}.
If one decomposes $n$ in any way into two factors $a$, $\partial$, then for
$c$ one can still take
\[
\frac{a}{e}\varphi(e)
\]
values to the modulus $a$ that are distinct and coprime to $e$. Each
of these assumptions leads to a pair of numbers $\mu$, $\mu'$ through the
congruences
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 255 =====
% !PRINTED 234
\weberpage{234}
%<<CONT
\weq{10}{\begin{aligned}
\mu &\equiv \alpha = a\alpha' + c\beta'\\
\mu' &\equiv \beta = \partial\beta'
\end{aligned}\ (\mathrm{mod}\ n),}

where $\beta'$ denotes an arbitrary number coprime to $a$, and $\alpha'$ is so
determined that $\alpha$, $\beta$ become relatively prime; and it is also easy
to see [by §\,65, (3)] that, so long as $a$, $\partial$, $c$ remain the same,
the pairs of numbers $\mu$, $\mu'$ determined by (10) belong to the same
row.

We call the numbers $a$, $c$, $\partial$ (as in §\,27) the \gesperrt{transformation
numbers}, and $n$ the \gesperrt{degree of transformation}.

\gesperrt{The system of numbers $a$, $c$, $\partial$ is therefore completely
characteristic for a row}, and the number of rows is equal to the
number of these systems of numbers, from which there follows for the number
$\psi(n)$, (§\,63):

\weq{11}{\psi(n) = \Sigma \frac{a}{e}\varphi(e),}

when the sum is extended over all divisors $a$ of $n$.

It is of interest to prove this relation directly as well, in which case the
restriction to an odd $n$ can be dropped. If we now regard $\psi(n)$ as a
symbol for the sum (11), then, when $n'$, $n''$ are relatively prime, we
obtain first
\[
\psi(n')\psi(n'') = \psi(n'n''),
\]
and it thus only remains to determine the sum $\psi(n)$ for the case in which
$n=p^\pi$ is a power of a prime. In this case $e$ is equal to the smaller of
the two divisors $a$, $\partial$, and when $a=\partial$, $e=a$. If, then, we
separate off the first and last term of the sum $\psi(n)$, we obtain
\[
\psi(p^\pi) = 1 + p^\pi + \sum_{1<a\leqq\sqrt{n}}\varphi(a) + \sum_{\sqrt{n}<a<n}\frac{a}{\partial}\varphi(\partial).
\]
But we have
\[
\varphi(a) = a\frac{p-1}{p}, \qquad \varphi(\partial) = \partial\frac{p-1}{p},
\]
hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
\psi(p^\pi) &= 1 + p^\pi + \frac{p-1}{p}\sum_{1<a<n} a\\
&= 1 + p^\pi + (p-1)(1+p+p^2+\cdots p^{\pi-2}) = p^\pi\Bigl(1+\frac{1}{p}\Bigr),
\end{aligned}
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 256 =====
% !PRINTED 235
\weberpage{235}
%<<CONT
from which, for $\psi(n)$, the expression
\[
\psi(n) = n\,\Pi\Bigl(1+\frac{1}{p}\Bigr)
\]
results, as in §\,63\footnote{Cf. \gesperrt{Dedekind}: Über die
elliptischen Modulfunktionen. Journal f. Mathematik, Bd.\ 83.}.

By (7) we must now put in the formulae (6) for $n\omega'$:
\[
\frac{\displaystyle \gamma' + \delta'\frac{c+\partial\omega}{a}}{\displaystyle \alpha' + \beta'\frac{c+\partial\omega}{a}},
\]
and the linear transformations of the $f$-functions
[§\,40, (4), (8), (11)] can be applied. In doing so we take

\weq{12}{c \equiv 0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 16),}

so that, by (3) and (8):
\[
\begin{pmatrix} \alpha', & \beta' \\ \gamma', & \delta' \end{pmatrix} \equiv \begin{pmatrix} a^3, & 0 \\ 0, & a \end{pmatrix}\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 16).
\]

If we denote by $\varrho$ the third root of unity

\weq{13}{\varrho = e^{-\frac{2\pi i}{3}[\alpha'(\gamma'-\beta')-(\alpha'^2-1)\beta'\delta']}\, e^{\frac{2n\pi i}{3}[\alpha(\gamma-\beta)-(\alpha^2-1)\beta\delta]},}

then we obtain
\weq{14}{\begin{aligned}
P_{00} &= \varrho\,\frac{f\left(\dfrac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right)}{f(\omega)^n},\\
P_{01} &= \varrho\left(\frac{2}{a}\right)\frac{f_1\!\left(\dfrac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right)}{f_1(\omega)^n},\\
P_{10} &= \varrho\left(\frac{2}{\partial}\right)\frac{f_2\!\left(\dfrac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right)}{f_2(\omega)^n}.
\end{aligned}}

The quotient

\weq{15}{\frac{P_{10}}{P_{00}} = \left(\frac{2}{\partial}\right)\frac{f_2\left(\dfrac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right)}{f\left(\dfrac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right)}\left(\frac{f\omega}{f_2\omega}\right)^n}

gives, by §\,54, (3), if one puts
\[
u(\omega) = \sqrt[4]{k}
\]
the quantities
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 257 =====
% !PRINTED 236
\weberpage{236}
%<<CONT
\weq{16}{\left(\frac{2}{\partial}\right)\frac{u\left(\dfrac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right)}{u(\omega)^n}}

as roots of a modular equation, and this is the \gesperrt{Jacobi} modular
equation\footnote{If $M$ is the \gesperrt{Jacobi} multiplier, then
\[
\frac{(kk')^{\frac{n-1}{3}}}{M} = 4^{\frac{n-1}{3}} P_{11}^2 P_{00}^4.
\]}.

If $n$ is not divisible by 3, we assume

\weq{17}{c \equiv 0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 3)}

whereby $\varrho$ takes the value 1.

In the same way one can apply the transformation of the $\eta$-function
[§\,38, (15), (18), (19)] to the last of the equations (6), and one
obtains:

\weq{18}{P_{11} = \left(\frac{\beta}{\alpha}\right)\left(\frac{\beta'}{\alpha'}\right)\varrho\, i^{\frac{a-1}{2}}\sqrt{\partial}\,\frac{\eta\left(\dfrac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right)}{\eta(\omega)}}

(where it would already suffice if $c$ is divisible by 8). If $n$ is not
divisible by 3 and $c$ is divisible by 3, then here too one must set
$\varrho=1$. The determination of the sign in (18) is of interest to us
only in the case where $n$ is a square. But we have [by (8)]
\[
\left(\frac{\beta}{\alpha}\right)\left(\frac{\beta'}{\alpha'}\right) = \left(\frac{\partial}{\alpha}\right)\left(\frac{\beta'}{\alpha\alpha'}\right) = \left(\frac{\partial}{\alpha}\right)\left(\frac{\beta'}{a}\right) = \left(\frac{\alpha}{\partial}\right)\left(\frac{\beta'}{a}\right)
\]
[the latter by the law of reciprocity of the quadratic residues, because
$\alpha \equiv 1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 4)$]. If now $n$ is a square, then
$a\!:\!e$, $\partial\!:\!e$ are squares as well, and there results:
\[
\left(\frac{\alpha}{\partial}\right)\left(\frac{\beta'}{a}\right) = \left(\frac{\alpha\beta'}{e}\right) = \left(\frac{c}{e}\right),
\]
thus in this case
\[
P_{11} = \varrho\, i^{\frac{a-1}{2}}\left(\frac{c}{e}\right)\sqrt{\partial}\,\frac{\eta\left(\dfrac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right)}{\eta(\omega)}.
\]

The formulae (10) set up for the characterization of a row are a
special case of a more general system, which one obtains by applying a
linear transformation to $\alpha'$, $\beta'$ in (10). One then obtains the
following:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 258 =====
% !PRINTED 237
\weberpage{237}
%<<CONT
If $a$, $b$, $c$, $\partial$ are four integers without a common divisor
satisfying the condition:
\[
a\partial - bc = n
\]
then one obtains the pairs of numbers $\mu$, $\mu'$ corresponding to one
row by letting, in
\weq{19}{\begin{gathered}
\mu \equiv a\alpha' + c\beta' \\
\mu' \equiv b\alpha' + \partial\beta' \ (\mathrm{mod}\ n)
\end{gathered}}
$\alpha'$, $\beta'$ run through all those values, and only those, for which
$\mu$, $\mu'$ have no common divisor with $n$.

That two pairs of values $\mu$, $\mu'$ corresponding to the congruences (19)
really do belong to the same row follows immediately
from § 65 (3), and it is likewise self-evident that \gesperrt{all pairs of numbers}
of one row are contained in this form, since $\alpha'$, $\beta'$
may be replaced by $h\alpha'$, $h\beta'$ when $h$ is relatively prime to $n$. That
one obtains \gesperrt{all the rows} in this way is shown by
the formulae (10).

\begin{center}
\textbf{§ 69.} \textbf{\gesperrt{The Invariant Equation.}}
\end{center}

Among the transformation equations one deserves particular
interest, namely the one whose roots are the $\psi(n)$ quantities
\weq{1}{j\left(\frac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right)}
or, by the determination (19), § 68, the quantities identical with
them
\weq{2}{j\left(\frac{c+\partial\omega}{a+b\omega}\right)}
where $j(\omega)$ is the invariant defined in § 46.

This equation is called the \gesperrt{invariant equation.}

The function $j(\omega)$ can, by § 54, be represented rationally by $f(\omega)^{24}$,
namely
\weq{3}{j(\omega) = \frac{[f(\omega)^{24} - 16]^3}{f(\omega)^{24}},}
so that, by the results of the preceding section, the
quantities (1) are the roots of an equation whose coefficients
are rational functions of $\varkappa^2$.

But if for $f(\omega)$ in (3) one substitutes one of the developments
found earlier, e.g. § 24, (11):
\[
% [sic] The source prints a stray comma after the lower limit 1.
f(\omega) = q^{-\frac{1}{24}} \prod_{1,}^{\nu} (1+q^{2\nu-1}),
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 259 =====
% !PRINTED 238
\weberpage{238}
%<<CONT
one recognises that $j(\omega)$ can be developed into a series
progressing according to powers of $q^2$, which has the form
\weq{4}{j(\omega) = q^{-2} + a_1 + a_2 q^2 + a_3 q^4 + \cdots,}
in which the $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3 \ldots$ are \gesperrt{integral rational numbers} which
can be calculated successively (there results, for example, $a_1 = 744$,
$a_2 = 196\,884$). The developments of the quantities (1) therefore
begin with
\weq{5}{e^{-\frac{2\pi i c}{a}} e^{-\frac{2\pi i \partial}{a}\omega}}
\gesperrt{and are therefore all different from one another. The
invariant equation is therefore, by § 65, irreducible.}

There is, however, a second way of arriving at this equation, and at
the transformation equations generally, which we shall now first
become acquainted with in the case of the invariant equation.
This derivation rests upon the theorems of § 54 on modular functions
and holds also for an \gesperrt{even} $n$. Here it is
Theorem 4, § 54, that comes into application:

I. \gesperrt{Every modular function which under the two transformations}
\weq{6}{\begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0 \\ 1, & 1 \end{pmatrix},}
\weq{7}{\begin{pmatrix} 0, & 1 \\ -1, & 0 \end{pmatrix}}
\gesperrt{remains unchanged is a rational function of $j(\omega)$.}

We first show that by application of the substitutions
(6), (7) the $\nu$ quantities (1) are permuted among one another.
We have the composition
\weq{8}{\begin{pmatrix} a, & 0 \\ c, & \partial \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0 \\ 1, & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0 \\ \lambda, & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} a, & 0 \\ c_1, & \partial \end{pmatrix},}
when
\weq{9}{c_1 = c + \partial - \lambda a}
is set, and by the transformation (6), since $j(\omega)$
remains unchanged under every linear transformation, there passes
\[
j\left(\frac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right) \text{ into } j\left(\frac{c_1+\partial\omega}{a}\right)
\]
over.

Further we determine $a_2$, $\partial_2$, $c_2$ so that
\weq{10}{\begin{gathered}
\begin{pmatrix} a, & 0 \\ c, & \partial \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 0, & 1 \\ -1, & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \alpha, & \beta \\ \gamma, & \delta \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} a_2, & 0 \\ c_2, & \partial_2 \end{pmatrix}, \\
\alpha\delta - \beta\gamma = 1.
\end{gathered}}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 260 =====
% !PRINTED 239
\weberpage{239}
For this it is required that
\weq{11}{\begin{gathered}
\alpha a_2 + \beta c_2 = 0 \\
\gamma a_2 + \delta c_2 = -\partial,
\end{gathered}}
\weq{12}{\begin{gathered}
\beta \partial_2 = a \\
\delta \partial_2 = c.
\end{gathered}}
Thus $\partial_2$ is determined as the greatest common
divisor of $a$ and $c$, and with it at the same time, because of $a_2\partial_2 = n$, also $a_2$.

By the two equations (12) one now knows $\beta$, $\delta$
as relatively prime numbers, and can determine $\alpha$, $\gamma$ from the Diophantine
equation
\[
\alpha\delta - \beta\gamma = 1
\]
% ["bestimmen." closes the German sentence after the display; English requires the verb before it]
When this has been done, there follows from the two
equations (11)
\weq{13}{\begin{gathered}
a_2 = \partial\beta, \\
c_2 = -\partial\alpha,
\end{gathered}}
whereby $c_2$ also is determined, and it appears at the same time that $\partial$
is the greatest common divisor of $a_2$, $c_2$. If one replaces
$\alpha$, $\gamma$ by another solution $\alpha + h\beta$, $\gamma + h\delta$, then only
$c_2$ is altered, by a multiple of $a_2$.

Through the transformation (7), therefore,
\[
j\left(\frac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right) \text{ goes over into } j\left(\frac{c_2+\partial_2\omega}{a_2}\right)
\]
% ["über." — the separable prefix that closes the German sentence is carried into the display's \text{}]

Let us now form a \gesperrt{symmetric} function of all the
quantities (1), say, for an indeterminate $x$, the product
\[
\Pi\left[x - j\left(\frac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right)\right],
\]
then this function is not altered by the transformations
(6), (7), and is therefore, by the theorem mentioned above, a \gesperrt{rational
function} of $j(\omega)$. Moreover it is an integral rational
function of $x$ of degree $\nu$ with the initial term $x^{\nu}$, and
we denote it by $F_n[x, j(\omega)]$. The equation
\weq{14}{F_n[x, j(\omega)] = 0}
has the quantities $j\left(\dfrac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right)$ as roots, and is the \gesperrt{invariant equation},
whose most important properties we now propose to derive.

1. The invariant equation is \gesperrt{irreducible} when, as domain of rationality, the totality of all rational functions of
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 261 =====
% !PRINTED 240
\weberpage{240}
%<<CONT
$j(\omega)$ is considered with arbitrary numerical coefficients. For if
there exists any rational equation
\weq{15}{\Phi[j(n\omega),\ j(\omega)] = 0,}
then any arbitrary linear transformation
\[
\begin{pmatrix} \alpha, & \beta \\ \gamma, & \delta \end{pmatrix}
\]
may be applied to it, and by § 29, (5), if
\[
\begin{pmatrix} a, & b \\ c, & \partial \end{pmatrix}
\]
is an arbitrary transformation of order $n$, the linear
transformations
\[
\begin{pmatrix} \alpha, & \beta \\ \gamma, & \delta \end{pmatrix}, \quad
\begin{pmatrix} \alpha', & \beta' \\ \gamma', & \delta' \end{pmatrix}
\]
can always be determined so that
\weq{16}{\begin{pmatrix} \alpha', & \beta' \\ \gamma', & \delta' \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} a, & b \\ c, & \partial \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0 \\ 0, & n \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} \alpha, & \beta \\ \gamma, & \delta \end{pmatrix}.}
But from this it follows that equation (9) is satisfied by \gesperrt{each} of the
quantities
\[
j\left(\frac{c+\partial\omega}{a+b\omega}\right)
\]
and hence also by each of the quantities (1), from which
[because of the distinctness of the quantities (1)] the irreducibility
of (14) follows.

2. The function
\weq{17}{F_n[x, j(\omega)] = \Pi\left[x - j\left(\frac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right)\right]}
has a finite value for every finite value of $\omega$ with positive imaginary part, and hence also for every \gesperrt{finite value} of $j(\omega)$, and is accordingly an \gesperrt{integral} rational function of $j(\omega)$.

If we next seek, by (3), the initial term of the development
of the function (17) in powers of $q$, we obtain
\[
(-1)^{\nu} e^{-2\pi i \Sigma \frac{c}{a}} e^{-2\pi i \omega \Sigma \frac{\partial}{e}\varphi(e)} = C q^{-2\nu},
\]
where $C$ is a finite constant. Therefore
\[
j(\omega)^{-\nu} F_n[x, j(\omega)]
\]
is finite for an infinite $j(\omega)$, that is, the degree of $F_n[x, j(\omega)]$
with respect to $j(\omega)$ is likewise the $\nu$th.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 262 =====
% !PRINTED 241
\weberpage{241}
3. We have
\[
F_n[j(n\omega), j(\omega)] = 0
\]
and if we replace $n\omega$ by $\omega$:
\[
F_n\Bigl[j(\omega), j\Bigl(\frac{\omega}{n}\Bigr)\Bigr] = 0.
\]
Since now $j\left(\dfrac{\omega}{n}\right)$ is likewise a root of the invariant equation, it follows that the two equations of degree $\nu$
\[
F_n[x, j(\omega)] = 0, \quad F_n[j(\omega), x] = 0
\]
have one root in common, and consequently, because of the irreducibility of the former and the equality of the degree, all of them. Therefore
\[
F_n(x, y) = C F_n(y, x)
\]
for indeterminate values of the variables $x$, $y$ and a constant $C$.
Hence also, by interchange of $x$ with $y$:
\[
F_n(y, x) = C F_n(x, y),
\]
and so $C^2 = 1$ or
\[
F_n(x, y) = \pm F_n(y, x).
\]
If we now set $x = y$, it follows that:
\[
F_n(y, y) = \pm F_n(y, y),
\]
and so, if the lower sign holds,
\[
F_n(y, y) = 0.
\]
But this is possible only when $n = 1$ [where $F_1(x, y) = x - y$], since otherwise $F_n(x, y)$ would have to be divisible by $x - y$, which contradicts the irreducibility. Therefore we always have, as soon as $n > 1$:
\weq{18}{F_n(x, y) = F_n(y, x).}

4. Let
\[
n = n' n'', \quad \nu' = \psi(n'), \quad \nu'' = \psi(n''),
\]
and let $n'$, $n''$ be \gesperrt{without common divisor}, and let $x_1, x_2, \dots x_{\nu''}$ be the roots of the equation
\weq{19}{F_{n''}[x, j(\omega)] = 0.}
The product
\weq{20}{F_{n'}(x, x_1)\, F_{n'}(x, x_2) \dots F_{n'}(x, x_{\nu''}),}
whose degree with respect to $x$ is equal to
\[
\nu = \psi(n) = \psi(n') \psi(n'')
\]
depends, as a symmetric function of the roots of (19), rationally on $j(\omega)$, and vanishes for
\[
x = j\left(\frac{\omega}{n' n''}\right),
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 263 =====
% !PRINTED 242
\weberpage{242}
%<<CONT
i.e. for a root of the equation $F_n[x, j(\omega)] = 0$. In view of the irreducibility of the latter equation, and of the equality of the degree and of the coefficient of $x^{\nu}$, we therefore have
\weq{21}{F_n[x, j(\omega)] = F_{n'}(x, x_1)\, F_{n'}(x, x_2) \dots F_{n'}(x, x_{\nu''}).}
5. If $n = p^{\pi}$ is a power of a prime, then the degree of the function $F_n[x, j(\omega)]$ is equal to $p^{\pi-1}(p+1)$, and the equation
\weq{22}{F_{p^{\pi-1}}[x, j(\omega)] = 0}
is of degree
\[
\nu' = p^{\pi-2}(p+1).
\]
We denote its roots by $x_1, x_2, \dots x_{\nu'}$.
The product
\[
P = F_p(x, x_1)\, F_p(x, x_2) \dots F_p(x, x_{\nu'})
\]
is, with respect to $x$, of degree $\nu'(p+1) = p^{\pi-2}(p+1)^2$; it depends symmetrically on the roots of (22), and hence rationally on $j(\omega)$, and vanishes for
\[
x = j\left(\frac{\omega}{p^{\pi}}\right).
\]
Therefore $P$ is divisible by $F_n[x, j(\omega)]$.
But the degree of $P$ is higher than that of $F_n$. If we take
\[
x_1 = j\left(\frac{p^{\pi-2}c + \omega}{p^{\pi-1}}\right),
\]
where $c$ may have any of the values $0, 1, 2, \dots p-1$, then $F_p(x, x_1)$ vanishes for
\[
x = j\left(\frac{\omega}{p^{\pi-2}}\right),
\]
i.e. $p$ of the factors of $P$ have a definite factor in common with $F_{p^{\pi-2}}[x, j(\omega)]$; from this it follows that $P$ is divisible by
\[
\{F_{p^{\pi-2}}[x, j(\omega)]\}^p
\]
and hence, as the comparison of the degrees and of the highest terms shows:
\weq{23}{F_{p^{\pi}}[x, j(\omega)] = \dfrac{F_p(x, x_1)\, F_p(x, x_2) \dots F_p(x, x_{\nu'})}{\{F_{p^{\pi-2}}[x, j(\omega)]\}^p}.}
This formula is subject to an exception for $\pi = 2$, because in this case the degree of the function on the right-hand side is still too high. For this case, however, \gesperrt{each} of the $p+1$ factors of the product $P$ has the divisor $x - j(\omega)$, precisely because every $x_i$ is a root of the equation $F_p[x, j(\omega)]$, and in place of (23) there appears the formula
\weq{24}{F_{p^2}[x, j(\omega)] = \dfrac{F_p(x, x_1)\, F_p(x, x_2) \dots F_p(x, x_{p+1})}{[x - j(\omega)]^{p+1}}.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 264 =====
% !PRINTED 243
\weberpage{243}
In this way the solution of the invariant equation $F_n = 0$ is reduced to the successive solution of those cases in which $n$ is a \gesperrt{prime}.

6. In the derivation of the transformation equations from the division equations it is settled from the outset that the numerical coefficients in these equations are rational numbers; the second derivation, however, teaches us nothing at first about the numerical coefficients. But we can prove afterwards that these coefficients are not only \gesperrt{rational} numbers but \gesperrt{integers}, and we arrive at the same time at an important theorem on the divisibility of these coefficients.

If we can prove that, when $p$ is a prime, the coefficients in $F_p(x, y)$ are integers, then the same follows from 4. and 5. for every composite $n$.

By (4), $j(\omega)$ can be developed in a series of the form
\weq{25}{j(\omega) = q^{-2} \sum_{0,\infty}^{h} a_h q^{2h},}
whose coefficients $a_h$ are integers, and indeed $a_0 = 1$.
If from this we form, when $p$ is a prime, the $p$th power, and observe \gesperrt{Fermat's} theorem, valid for every integer:
\[
a^p \equiv a\ (\mathrm{mod}\ p),
\]
then it follows
\weq{26}{j(\omega)^p = q^{-2p} \sum_{0,\infty}^{h} a_h q^{2hp} + p\, q^{-2(p-1)} \sum_{0,\infty}^{h} b_h q^{2h},}
in which $b_h$ are likewise integers. On the other hand, if one replaces $\omega$ by $p\omega$ in (25), then:
\weq{27}{j(p\omega) = q^{-2p} \sum_{0,\infty}^{h} a_h q^{2hp}}
and from this, if one puts
\[
j(\omega) = u, \quad j(p\omega) = v
\]
one obtains:
\[
u^p - v = p\, q^{-2(p-1)} \sum_{0,\infty}^{h} b_h q^{2h},
\]
for which we may also write:
\weq{28}{(u^p - v)(u - v^p) = p\, q^{-2(p^2+p-1)} \sum_{0,\infty}^{h} c_h q^{2h},}
if $c_h$ denotes a third system of integers.
Now in $F_p(x, y)$ there occur the terms $x^{p+1} + y^{p+1}$, the highest with respect to $x, y$, and we accordingly put
\weq{29}{F_p(x, y) = (x^p - y)(x - y^p) - \sum_{0,p}^{h,k} c_{h,k} x^h y^k,}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 265 =====
% !PRINTED 244
\weberpage{244}
%<<CONT
where $c_{h,k}$ are the coefficients to be determined, which by 3. satisfy the condition
\[
c_{h,k} = c_{k,h}
\]
To determine them, we set in (29)
\[
x = u, \quad y = v,
\]
whereby $F_p$ vanishes, and obtain
\weq{30}{(u^p - v)(u - v^p) = \sum^{h,k} c_{h,k} u^h v^k.}
From this it follows first of all that
\[
c_{p,p} = 0
\]
must hold, since by (28), in the development (of the left side) in powers of $q$, the power $q^{-2(p^2+p)}$ cannot occur, and we can now put (29) into the form:
\weq{31}{(u^p - v)(u - v^p) = \sum_{0,p}^{h} \sum_{0,h-1}^{k} c_{h,k}(u^h v^k + u^k v^h) + \sum_{0,p-1}^{h} c_{h,h} u^h v^h.}
In this there are to be inserted the developments, resulting from (25) and (27), of
\[
u^h v^k + u^k v^h, \quad u^h v^h
\]
in powers of $q$, whose initial terms
\[
q^{-2(hp+k)}, \quad q^{-2h(p+1)}
\]
have the coefficients 1.
On the right side of (31) no two terms occur whose development begins with the same power of $q$; for from
\[
hp + k = h'p + k'
\]
it follows that $k \equiv k'\ (\mathrm{mod}\ p)$, and hence, since $k$ and $k' < p$, that $k = k'$, $h = h'$.
If one therefore arranges the sequences which represent the two sides of (31) according to ascending powers of $q$, and then sets equal to one another the coefficients of equally high powers, one obtains a sequence of linear equations for the unknowns $c_{h,k}$, of which each succeeding one contains only \gesperrt{one} new unknown, and this with the coefficient 1. The known terms of these equations which arise from the left side are, by (28), all \gesperrt{integers divisible by $p$}, and hence for the $c_{h,k}$ there likewise result integral numerical values divisible by $p$. Accordingly we have
\weq{32}{F_p(x, y) = (x^p - y)(x - y^p) - p \sum_{0,p}^{h,k} a_{h,k} x^h y^k,}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 266 =====
% !PRINTED 245
\weberpage{245}
%<<CONT
in which the $a_{h,k}$ are integers, and the conditions
\[
a_{h,k} = a_{k,h}, \quad a_{p,p} = 0
\]
are satisfied.

\begin{center}
\textbf{§ 70.\quad \gesperrt{Transformation Equations of the First Level.}}
\end{center}

The invariant equation is of great theoretical importance, partly because
of its general validity (for even $n$ as well), partly because of the ease
with which the linear transformations can be applied to $j(\omega)$. The
actual computation of this equation, however, proves so complicated, and
the numerical coefficients are so large, that the computation has so far
been carried out only in the simplest case $p=2$. On the other hand, by
making use of other modular functions, one can obtain far simpler
transformation equations.

Concerning the principle to be applied here we remark the following:

If there is given any system of $\nu$ functions of $\omega$, corresponding
to the $\nu$ systems of transformation numbers $a$, $c$, $\partial$, which
we shall denote by
\weq{1}{\Phi_{a,c,\partial}}
and which are permuted among one another \gesperrt{isomorphically} with the functions
\weq{2}{j\left(\frac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right)}
by the substitutions
\weq{3}{\left(\omega, -\frac{1}{\omega}\right), \quad (\omega, \omega+1)}
then (1) is expressible \gesperrt{rationally} through (2) and through $j(\omega)$; for
the function

\weq{4}{F_n[x,j(\omega)] \sum^{a,c,\partial} \frac{\Phi_{a,c,\partial}}{x-j\left(\frac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right)} = \Psi[x,j(\omega)]}

remains unaltered under the substitutions (3), and is therefore (for an
indeterminate $x$) a \gesperrt{rational function} of $j(\omega)$, and moreover an
integral rational function of $x$, of degree at most $\nu-1$;
$F_n[x,j(\omega)]$ has the same meaning as in (17) of the preceding
section, and $\nu=\psi(n)$ is the degree of this function with respect to
$x$. From (4), however, on setting
\[
x = j\left(\frac{c+\hat{\partial}\,\omega}{a}\right)
\]
one obtains:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 267 =====
% !PRINTED 246
\weberpage{246}
%<<CONT
\weq{5}{\Phi_{a,c,\partial} = \frac{\Psi\left[j\left(\frac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right), j(\omega)\right]}{F'\left[j\left(\frac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right)\right]}.}

Thus $\Phi_{a,c,\partial}$ belongs to the algebraic field which consists
of the rational functions of $j\left(\frac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right)$
and $j(\omega)$, and we can apply the theorems of Bd. I, § 151. From
these it follows that the $\nu$ quantities $\Phi_{a,c,\partial}$ are
the roots of an equation of degree $\nu$ whose coefficients depend
rationally on $j(\omega)$. If the $\nu$ quantities
$\Phi_{a,c,\partial}$ are different from one another, then this
equation is \gesperrt{irreducible}. Such an equation we call a \gesperrt{transformation
equation of the first stage belonging to the transformation degree
$n$}\footnote{In the first edition I called these equations
``\gesperrt{invariant transformation equations}''. This expression has
been objected to by \gesperrt{Klein} (Vorlesungen über ausgewählte
Kapitel der Zahlentheorie, autographiertes Heft, Göttingen 1897). I
adopt \gesperrt{Klein's} proposal, in that I now call these equations
``\gesperrt{transformation equations of the first stage}'', without
entering here more closely into the justification of this
expression.}. Every other quantity of the field can be rationally
expressed by such a $\Phi_{a,c,\partial}$ and by $j(\omega)$.

If the functions $\Phi_{a,c,\partial}$ have the property of remaining
finite for every finite value of $\omega$ with positive imaginary
part, and hence for every finite $j(\omega)$, then the function
$\Psi[x,j(\omega)]$ in (4) is also an \gesperrt{integral function}
with respect to $j(\omega)$. Formula (5) could therefore fail only for
those \gesperrt{particular values} of $\omega$ for which two roots of the
invariant equation become equal to one another.

If the $\nu$ quantities $\Phi_{a,c,\partial}$ are not all different
from one another, then they split into rows of equally many mutually
equal ones, and the equation of degree $\nu$ to be derived from (5) is
a power of an irreducible equation, which we shall occasionally also
designate as a transformation equation (Bd. I, § 151, 2).

If the quantities $\Phi_{a,c,\partial}$ are so chosen that they become
infinite for no finite $\omega$ with positive imaginary part, then
they remain finite for every finite $j(\omega)$, from which it follows
that the coefficients in the function of degree $\nu$
\weq{6}{\Pi(x-\Phi_{a,c,\partial})}
are \gesperrt{integral rational functions of $j(\omega)$}, i.e. the
$\Phi_{a,c,\partial}$ are \gesperrt{integral algebraic functions of
$j(\omega)$}.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 268 =====
% !PRINTED 247
\weberpage{247}
If the functions $\Phi_{a,c,\partial}$ are so arranged, say by a
suitable determination of the constants that are still at our disposal
in them, that they remain finite for an infinite imaginary $\omega$ as
well, i.e. for $q=0$, then these functions are finite for an infinite
$j(\omega)$ as well, and the coefficients in (6) are constant. But
this is possible only if the $\Phi_{a,c,\partial}$ are \gesperrt{all equal to
one and the same constant $C$}. If one knows $\Phi_{a,c,\partial}$ as a
rational function of another quantity $\Psi_{a,c,\partial}$, then
$\Phi_{a,c,\partial} = C$ is either an \gesperrt{identity} or a \gesperrt{transformation
equation}
for $\Psi_{a,c,\partial}$.

\begin{center}
\textbf{§ 71. \gesperrt{The Transformation Equations for $\gamma_2$ and $\gamma_3$.}}
\end{center}

Transformation equations of the first level are obtained first of all
from the consideration of the functions § 54, (4), (5):
\[
\gamma_2(\omega) = \sqrt[3]{j(\omega)}, \quad \gamma_3(\omega) = \sqrt{j(\omega)-1728}.
\]
If $n$ is not divisible by 3, we can choose the numbers $a$, $c$,
$\partial$ in such a way that \gesperrt{$c$ always becomes divisible
by 3}.

Now, by § 54, (15), a linear transformation
$\begin{pmatrix} \alpha, & \beta \\ \gamma, & \delta \end{pmatrix}$
exerts upon the function $\gamma_2(\omega)$ the influence:
\[
\gamma_2\left(\frac{\gamma+\delta\omega}{\alpha+\beta\omega}\right) = e^{-\frac{2\pi i}{3}(\alpha\gamma+\beta\delta-\alpha\beta-\alpha^2\beta\delta)} \gamma_2(\omega).
\]
In the compositions (8), (10) of § 69 we obtain
\[
\lambda \equiv n, \quad \delta \equiv 0 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 3),
\]
and then $\alpha$ can be further determined in such a way that
$\alpha$ also, and consequently $c_2$, become divisible by 3.

From this it follows that by the two substitutions
\[
(\omega, \omega+1), \quad \left(\omega, -\frac{1}{\omega}\right)
\]
the $\nu$ functions
\weq{1}{\gamma_2\left(\frac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right) \gamma_2(\omega)^{-n}}
are only permuted among one another, and hence are the roots of a
transformation equation of the first level.

If, secondly, $n$ is an \gesperrt{odd} number, let $c$ be assumed
\gesperrt{even}.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 269 =====
% !PRINTED 248
\weberpage{248}
For the function $\gamma_3(\omega)$ we have [by § 54, (15)]:
\[
\gamma_3\left(\frac{\gamma+\delta\omega}{\alpha+\beta\omega}\right) = (-1)^{\alpha\gamma+\beta\gamma+\beta\delta} \gamma_3(\omega),
\]
and in the compositions (8), (10), § 69 we have
\[
\lambda \equiv 1, \quad \alpha \equiv \delta \equiv 0 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 2).
\]
The $\nu$ quantities
\weq{2}{\gamma_3\left(\frac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right) \gamma_3(\omega)}
are therefore permuted among themselves, and are accordingly likewise the
roots of a transformation equation of the first level.

In order to form the former of these equations for the simplest case
$n=2$, note the relation [§ 54, (5)]:
\weq{3}{\gamma_2(\omega) = \frac{f(\omega)^{24}-16}{f(\omega)^8} = \frac{f_1(\omega)^{24}+16}{f_1(\omega)^8} = \frac{f_2(\omega)^{24}+16}{f_2(\omega)^8},}
from which, in virtue of
\[
f_1(2\omega) f_2(\omega) = \sqrt{2} \qquad [\S\ 34, (16)]
\]
there follows:
\weq{4}{
\begin{gathered}
\gamma_2(2\omega) = \frac{2^8+f_2(\omega)^{24}}{f_2(\omega)^{16}} \\[4pt]
\gamma_2\left(\frac{\omega}{2}\right) = \frac{2^8+f_1(\omega)^{24}}{f_1(\omega)^{16}} \\[4pt]
\gamma_2\left(\frac{\omega+3}{2}\right) = \frac{2^8-f(\omega)^{24}}{f(\omega)^{16}}. \qquad [\S\ 34, (13)]
\end{gathered}
}

If we denote these three quantities by $x$, $x_0$, $x_1$, then from the
relations (6), (8), § 54 there results:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x + x_0 + x_1 &= \gamma_2(\omega)^2 \\
xx_0 + xx_1 + x_0x_1 &= 495\,\gamma_2(\omega) \\
xx_0x_1 &= -j(\omega) + 2^4.3^3.5^3,
\end{aligned}
\]
so that $x$, $x_0$, $x_1$ are the roots of the equation
\weq{5}{x^3 - \gamma_2(\omega)^2 x^2 + 5.9.11.\gamma_2(\omega) x + j(\omega) - 2^4.3^3.5^3 = 0.}
The equation whose roots are the cubes of the roots of (5) is the
invariant equation for $n=2$, and it can be computed from this without
difficulty.

\begin{center}
\textbf{§ 72. Multiplier Equations of the First Level.}
\end{center}

Among the multiplier equations, those will be considered here whose roots
are the various powers of $P_{11}$, multiplied by powers of
$\gamma_2(\omega)$, $\gamma_3(\omega)$, whose coefficients
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 270 =====
% !PRINTED 249
\weberpage{249}
%<<CONT
depend rationally on $j(\omega)$. These equations we call
\gesperrt{multiplier equations of the first level}\footnote{These equations have been investigated in particular detail by \gesperrt{Kiepert}, first in several memoirs in Crelles Journal, Bd.~87, 88, 95, and most fully in the memoirs in the Mathematischen Annalen, Bd.~26, 33. Cf. also F. \gesperrt{Klein}, Mathematische Annalen, Bd.~14, 15 and the autographed lectures mentioned above.}.

We consider the quantities [§\,68, (16)]:

\weq{1}{P_{c,\eth,a} = i^{\frac{a-1}{2}}\left(\frac{c}{e}\right)\sqrt{\eth}\,\frac{\eta\left(\dfrac{c+\eth\,\omega}{a}\right)}{\eta(\omega)},}

and the influence which the transformations
\[
\begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0 \\ 1, & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad
\begin{pmatrix} 0, & 1 \\ -1, & 0 \end{pmatrix}
\]
exert upon them. This influence is determined by the formulae
(8) to (13), §\,69, according to which [because $c_1 \equiv c \pmod{e}$]
\[
P_{c,\eth,a} \text{ by } (\omega, \omega+1) \text{ into } e^{\frac{\pi i(\lambda-1)}{12}} P_{c_1,\eth,a}
\]

% Source scan confirms that the matrix and following fraction share one E(...) delimiter pair.
\weq{2}{\text{by } \left(\omega, -\frac{1}{\omega}\right) \text{ into } \sqrt{\frac{\eth}{\eth_2}}\,\frac{i^{\frac{a-a_2}{2}}}{\sqrt{-i\omega}}\left(\frac{c}{e}\right)\left(\frac{c_2}{e_2}\right) E\!\left(\begin{matrix}\alpha, & \beta \\ \gamma, & \delta' \end{matrix}\ \frac{c_2+\eth_2\,\omega}{a_2}\right) P_{c_2,\eth_2,a_2}}

goes over, in which $E$ has the meaning given in §\,38, (15).
But we have [§\,69, (11), (12)]
\[
\sqrt{\eth}\,\sqrt{\alpha+\beta\,\frac{c_2+\eth_2\,\omega}{a_2}} = \sqrt{\eth_2\,\omega},
\]
and consequently, if we set
\[
E\!\left(\begin{matrix}\alpha, & \beta \\ \gamma, & \delta' \end{matrix}\ \frac{c_2+\eth_2\,\omega}{a_2}\right) = r\,\sqrt{-i\omega}\,\sqrt{\frac{\eth_2}{\eth}}
\]
then
\[
r = \left(\frac{\alpha}{\beta}\right) i^{\frac{1-\beta}{2}} e^{\frac{\pi i}{12}\left[\beta(\alpha+\delta)-(\beta^2-1)\alpha\gamma\right]}
\]
is \gesperrt{a 24th root of unity}, and by the interchange
\[
\left(\omega, -\frac{1}{\omega}\right)
\]
the quantity
\[
P_{c,\eth,a} \text{ into } r\,i^{\frac{a-a_2}{2}}\left(\frac{c}{e}\right)\left(\frac{c_2}{e_2}\right) P_{c_2,\eth_2,a_2}
\]
goes over.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 271 =====
% !PRINTED 250
\weberpage{250}
From this there follows, as above, the conclusion:

1. \gesperrt{For every arbitrary $n$ the quantities}
\[
P^{24}_{c,\eth,a}
\]
\gesperrt{are the roots of a transformation equation.}

If $n$ is not divisible by 3, one may assume the $c, c_2, c_1$ to be
divisible by 3. Then
\[
\lambda \equiv n, \quad \alpha \equiv 0, \quad \delta \equiv 0 \pmod{3}.
\]
Thus, as follows from §\,38, (15), $r$ is an \gesperrt{eighth root of unity};
if we therefore also observe
\[
\gamma_2(\omega+1) = e^{-\frac{2\pi i}{3}}\gamma_2(\omega), \quad
\gamma_2\left(-\frac{1}{\omega}\right) = \gamma_2(\omega), \quad \text{[§\,54, (14)]}
\]
we have the theorem:

2. \gesperrt{If $n$ is not divisible by 3 and $c$ is divisible by 3,
then the quantities}
\[
P^{8}_{c,\eth,a}\,\gamma_2(\omega)^{n-1}
\]
\gesperrt{are roots of a transformation equation.}

To make the application to the simplest case $n=2$, we set

\weq{3}{x = 16\,\frac{\eta(2\omega)^8}{\eta(\omega)^8}, \quad
x_0 = \frac{\eta\left(\dfrac{\omega}{2}\right)^8}{\eta(\omega)^8}, \quad
x_1 = \frac{\eta\left(\dfrac{\omega+3}{2}\right)^8}{\eta(\omega)^8},}

and then $x, x_0, x_1$ are nothing other than our functions
\[
f_2(\omega)^8, \quad f_1(\omega)^8, \quad -f(\omega)^8. \qquad \text{[§\,34, (9)]}
\]
These are, as we have already seen earlier [§\,54, (8)], the
roots of the cubic equation
\weq{4}{x^3 - x\,\gamma_2(\omega) + 16 = 0.}
The circumstance that $f_2^8, f_1^8, -f^8$ are themselves roots of a transformation equation for the transformation degree 2 explains the
phenomenon that on the adjunction of these quantities, and hence also on
the adjunction of $x^2$, the transformation equations belonging to an even $n$ become reducible.

If $n$ is an odd number, one takes $c$ to be \gesperrt{divisible by 4}; then
it follows that [§\,69, (9), (11), (12)]
\[
\lambda \equiv n \pmod{4},
\]
\[
\alpha \equiv 0, \quad \delta \equiv 0, \quad \beta \equiv a\,\eth_2, \quad \gamma \equiv -\eth\,a_2 \pmod{4},
\]
and hence there results
\[
r^6 = (-1)^{\frac{\beta-1}{2}} = (-1)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}(-1)^{\frac{a-a_2}{2}}
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 272 =====
% !PRINTED 251
\weberpage{251}
%<<CONT
and from this there follows, having regard to
\[
\gamma_3(\omega+1) = -\gamma_3(\omega), \quad
\gamma_3\left(-\frac{1}{\omega}\right) = -\gamma_3(\omega): \qquad \text{[§\,54, (14)]}
\]

3. \gesperrt{If $n$ is odd and $c$ divisible by 4, then the
quantities}
\[
P^{6}_{c,\eth,a}\,\gamma_3(\omega)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}
\]
\gesperrt{are roots of a multiplier equation.} If $n \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$, the same holds of $P^{6}_{c,\eth,a}$.

As an example we choose $n=3$ and set

\weq{5}{x = 27\left(\frac{\eta(3\omega)}{\eta(\omega)}\right)^6, \quad
x_0 = -\left(\frac{\eta\left(\dfrac{\omega}{3}\right)}{\eta(\omega)}\right)^6, \quad
x_1 = -\left(\frac{\eta\left(\dfrac{4+\omega}{3}\right)}{\eta(\omega)}\right)^6, \quad
x_2 = -\left(\frac{\eta\left(\dfrac{8+\omega}{3}\right)}{\eta(\omega)}\right)^6.}

The coefficients of the equation which has these quantities for its
roots are rational functions of $\gamma_3(\omega)$, and since none of
the quantities (5) becomes infinite for a finite value of $\gamma_3$,
they are \gesperrt{integral} functions of $\gamma_3$. According to 3. we may
therefore set this equation up in the form:
\[
x^4 + A_1\gamma_3 x^3 + A_2 x^2 + A_3 \gamma_3 x + A_4 = 0,
\]
in which $A_1, A_2, A_3, A_4$ are integral rational functions of
$j(\omega)$. First of all one obtains $A_4$ as the product $x x_0 x_1 x_2$,
which can vanish for no value of $j(\omega)$ and must therefore be
constant. From the beginnings of the development [§\,24]

\weq{6}{\begin{aligned}
x &= 27\,q\dots,\\
x_0 &= -q^{-\frac{1}{3}}\dots,\\
x_1 &= -e^{\frac{2\pi i}{3}}q^{-\frac{1}{3}}\dots,\\
x_2 &= -e^{-\frac{2\pi i}{3}}q^{-\frac{1}{3}}\dots,\\
\gamma_3 &= q^{-1}\dots
\end{aligned}}

one therefore finds
\[
A_4 = -27.
\]
Further we have
\[
-A_1\gamma_3 = x + x_0 + x_1 + x_2.
\]
Since the right-hand side does not become infinite even in the first
order for an infinite $\gamma_3$, that is, for $q=0$, $A_1$ must
vanish.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 273 =====
% !PRINTED 252
\weberpage{252}
From
\[
-A_3\gamma_3 = x x_0 x_1 x_2\left(\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{x_0}+\frac{1}{x_1}+\frac{1}{x_2}\right)
\]
there results by (6) the constant value 1 for $A_3$. But in order to
determine $A_2$, we must go one term further in the development. In
\[
x_0^4 + \gamma_3 x_0 - 27 = -A_2 x_0^2
\]
we substitute for $x_0$ the development
\[
x_0 = -q^{-\frac{1}{3}} + 6\,q^{\frac{1}{3}} + \cdots,
\]
and find $A_2 = 18$, so that the equation sought for reads:
\weq{7}{x^4 + 18\,x^2 + \gamma_3\,x - 27 = 0.}

If $n$ is odd and not divisible by 3, let $c$ be assumed \gesperrt{divisible
by 12}.

It is then
\[
\lambda \equiv n, \quad \alpha \equiv 0, \quad \delta \equiv 0, \quad
\beta \equiv a\,\eth_2, \quad \gamma \equiv -\eth\,a_2 \pmod{12}
\]
and there results
\[
r^2 = (-1)^{\frac{\beta-1}{2}} = (-1)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}(-1)^{\frac{a-a'}{2}}, % [sic] printed a' here, not a_2 as in the parallel formulas above
\]
hence the theorem

4. \gesperrt{If $n$ is relatively prime to 6 and $c$ divisible by 12,
then the quantities}
\[
P^{2}_{c,\eth,a}\,\gamma_2(\omega)^{n-1}\,\gamma_3(\omega)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}
\]
\gesperrt{are roots of a multiplier equation of the first level.}

Since the functions $P^2$ become infinite or zero for no finite value
of $j(\omega)$, we conclude that the coefficients of the equation
whose roots are the $P^2$ are \gesperrt{integral rational functions of
$\gamma_2, \gamma_3$, and that the last coefficient is a constant.}

If $n$ is a prime $p$, the roots of this equation are
\[
x = p\left(\frac{\eta(p\omega)}{\eta(\omega)}\right)^2, \quad
x_h = (-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2}}\left(\frac{\eta\left(\dfrac{12h+\omega}{p}\right)}{\eta(\omega)}\right)^2
\quad h=0,1,\dots,p-1
\]
and the initial terms of the developments are the following:
\[
x = p\,q^{\frac{p-1}{6}}\dots, \quad
x_h = (-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2}}e^{\frac{2\pi i h}{p}}q^{-\frac{p-1}{6p}}\dots,
\]
whereby the value $(-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2}}p$ results for the last
coefficient. From the fact that the first term in the development of
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 274 =====
% !PRINTED 253
\weberpage{253}
%<<CONT
$j(\omega)$ in powers of $q$ has the coefficient 1, one concludes
easily that the numerical coefficients in these equations are
\gesperrt{integral rational numbers}.

For $p=5$ the equation in question has the form:
\[
x^6 + A_1\gamma_2^2x^5 + A_2\gamma_2x^4 + A_3x^3 + A_4\gamma_2x + 5 = 0,
\]
in which $A_1$, $A_2$, $A_3$, $A_4$ are integral rational functions of
$j(\omega)$ and, as is easily seen, constants.

From the initial terms there follows at once
\[
A_1 = 0, \quad A_2 = 0, \quad A_4 = -1.
\]

But in order to determine $A_3$, one carries the development of $x_0$
as far as the next following term:
\[
x_0 = q^{-\frac{7}{15}}\Bigl(1 - 2q^{\frac{2}{5}}\dots\Bigr),
\]
from which one obtains $A_3 = 10$; thus for $n=5$ the multiplier
equation reads
\weq{8}{x^6 + 10x^3 - \gamma_2x + 5 = 0.}

In the same way one computes the equations for $p=7$, $p=11$, by using
the developments of $x_0$:
\[
p=7:\ x_0 = -q^{-\frac{1}{7}}\Bigl(1 - 2q^{\frac{2}{7}} - q^{\frac{4}{7}} + 2q^{\frac{6}{7}}\dots\Bigr),
\]
\[
p=11:\ x_0 = -q^{-\frac{5}{33}}\Bigl(1 - 2q^{\frac{2}{11}} - q^{\frac{4}{11}} + 2q^{\frac{6}{11}} + q^{\frac{8}{11}} + 2q^{\frac{10}{11}} + \dots\Bigr),
\]
while of $\gamma_2(\omega)$, $\gamma_3(\omega)$ only the first terms
are ever needed. Thus one finds
\weq{9}{p=7:\quad x^8 + 7.2x^6 + 7.9x^4 + 7.10x^2 + \gamma_3x - 7 = 0,}
\weq{10}{p=11:\quad x^{12} - 11.90x^6 + 11.40\gamma_2x^4 + 11.15\gamma_3x^3 + 11.2\gamma_2^2x^2 + \gamma_2\gamma_3x - 11 = 0.}

If $n$ is an odd square number, we assume $c$ to be \gesperrt{divisible by 8}.
Then $a:e$ and $\partial:e$ are likewise square numbers. Further we
have
\weq{11}{\alpha \equiv \delta \equiv 0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 8), \quad \lambda \equiv 1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 8)}
\weq{12}{\left.
\begin{aligned}
a &= \beta\partial_2, & a_2 &= \beta\partial, & a &\equiv \partial \equiv e \equiv 1\\
c &= \delta\partial_2, & c_2 &= -\alpha\partial, & a_2 &\equiv \partial_2 \equiv e_2 \equiv 1
\end{aligned}
\right\}\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 8).}

The root of unity $r$ in (2) takes the value
\weq{13}{r = \left(\frac{\alpha}{\beta}\right) i^{\frac{1-\beta}{2}} e^{\frac{2\pi i}{3}\frac{\beta(\alpha+\delta) - (\beta^2-1)\alpha\gamma}{8}}.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 275 =====
% !PRINTED 254
\weberpage{254}
But by (12) $\beta$ is divisible both by $e$ and by $e_2$, and
$\beta e e_2$ is a square; hence
\[
\left(\frac{\alpha}{\beta}\right) = \left(\frac{\alpha}{ee_2}\right) = \left(\frac{\alpha}{e}\right)\left(\frac{\alpha}{e_2}\right) = \left(\frac{\delta}{e}\right)\left(\frac{\alpha}{e_2}\right) \ (\text{since}\ \alpha\delta \equiv 1\ \mathrm{mod}\ e);
\]
furthermore, by (12),
\[
\left(\frac{\delta}{e}\right) = \left(\frac{c}{e}\right)\left(\frac{\partial_2}{e}\right), \quad \left(\frac{\alpha}{e_2}\right) = \left(\frac{c_2}{e_2}\right)\left(\frac{-\partial}{e_2}\right),
\]
and
\[
\left(\frac{\partial_2}{e}\right) = \left(\frac{e_2}{e}\right), \quad \left(\frac{-\partial}{e_2}\right) = \left(\frac{-e}{e_2}\right), \quad \left(\frac{e_2}{e}\right)\left(\frac{-e}{e_2}\right) = (-1)^{\frac{(e+1)(e_2-1)}{4}},
\]
hence
\[
\left(\frac{\alpha}{\beta}\right) = (-1)^{\frac{(e+1)(e_2-1)}{4}}\left(\frac{c}{e}\right)\left(\frac{c_2}{e_2}\right)
\]
\[
i^{\frac{1-\beta}{2}} = i^{\frac{1-ee_2}{2}}; \quad i^{\frac{a-a_2}{2}} = i^{\frac{e-e_2}{2}}.
\]

Thus by the permutations (2) there passes over
\weq{14}{P_{c,\partial,a}\ \text{into}\ e^{\frac{2\pi i}{3}\frac{\lambda-1}{8}}P_{c_1,\partial,a}\ \text{and into}\ e^{\frac{2\pi i}{3}\frac{\beta(\alpha+\delta)-(\beta^2-1)\alpha\gamma}{8}}P_{c_2,\partial_2,a_2}.}

If $n$ is moreover not divisible by 3, then let $c$ be assumed
divisible by 3, whereby
\[
\lambda \equiv 1, \quad \alpha \equiv \delta \equiv 0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 3)
\]
result, and the third roots of unity occurring in (14) receive the
value 1.

From this there result the theorems:

5. \gesperrt{If $n$ is an odd square number, $c$ divisible by 8, then
the quantities}
\[
P^3_{c,\partial,a},
\]
\gesperrt{and if $n$ is an odd square number not divisible by 3, $c$
divisible by 24, then the quantities}
\[
P_{c,\partial,a}
\]
\gesperrt{are roots of multiplier equations of the first stage.}

The first examples are $n=9$, $n=25$.

One can arrive at the formation of these equations in various ways.
We wish here [after \gesperrt{Kiepert}$^1$)] to take the path in
which, according to § 69, we consider the roots of an equation
belonging to the degree $p$
%CONT>>

\footnotetext{$^1$) Zur Transformationstheorie der elliptischen
Funktionen. Crelles Journal, Bd. 87, 88, 95.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 276 =====
% !PRINTED 255
\weberpage{255}
%<<CONT
corresponding transformation equation rationally in terms of that for
the degree $p^2$, and substitute this expression into the transformation
equation belonging to $p$.

According to 3., formula (7), the equation
\weq{15}{x^4 + 18x^2 + \gamma_3(\omega)x - 27 = 0}
is satisfied by the two functions
\weq{16}{-\left(\frac{\eta\left(\frac{\omega}{3}\right)}{\eta(\omega)}\right)^6, \quad 27\left(\frac{\eta(3\omega)}{\eta(\omega)}\right)^6}
Denoting the first of these values by $x$, the second passes under the
substitution $\left(\omega,\frac{\omega}{3}\right)$ into $\dfrac{-27}{x}$,
and consequently the equation
\weq{17}{27^3 + 18.27x^2 - \gamma_3\left(\frac{\omega}{3}\right)x^3 - x^4 = 0}
is also satisfied by $x$. If we now set
\weq{18}{y = \left(\frac{\eta\left(\frac{\omega}{9}\right)}{\eta(\omega)}\right)^3,}
then $x$ passes under the substitution $\left(\omega,\frac{\omega}{3}\right)$
into $\dfrac{y^2}{x}$, so that one also obtains the equation:
\weq{19}{y^8 + 18y^4x^2 + \gamma_3\left(\frac{\omega}{3}\right)y^2x^3 - 27x^4 = 0,}
and by elimination of $\gamma_3\left(\frac{\omega}{3}\right)$ from
(17) and (19) one obtains, after cancellation of the factor $y^2+27$,
\weq{20}{x^4 - 18x^2y^2 - y^2(y^4 - 27y^2 + 27^2) = 0.}

If this quadratic equation is solved for $x^2$, it follows that:
\weq{21}{x^2 = y^3 + 9y^2 + 27y = (y+3)^3 - 27,}
where the sign is decided by substituting the initial terms of the
developments, most simply, no doubt, since this equation (by § 69) is
also satisfied for
\[
x = 27\left(\frac{\eta(3\omega)}{\eta(\omega)}\right)^6, \quad y = 27\left(\frac{\eta(9\omega)}{\eta(\omega)}\right)^3
\]
when one sets
\[
x = 27q + \cdots, \quad y = 27q^2 + \cdots
\]
in it.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 277 =====
% !PRINTED 256
\weberpage{256}
If in (15) one separates off the first power of $x$ and squares, one
obtains, by substituting (21), the multiplier equation sought for the
9th degree of transformation. It takes a simpler shape if one sets
\weq{22}{(y+3)^3 = t}
it then becomes:
\weq{23}{[j(\omega) - 27\cdot64](t-27) = (t^2 - 36t + 27\cdot8)^2}
or
\weq{24}{j(\omega)(t-27) = t(t-24)^3.}

One can proceed in quite a similar way with the 25th degree of transformation.

If we set
\weq{25}{x = \left(\frac{\eta\left(\frac{\omega}{5}\right)}{\eta(\omega)}\right)^2, \quad y = \frac{\eta\left(\frac{\omega}{25}\right)}{\eta(\omega)}}
then we have first of all, by 4. (8):
\weq{26}{x^6 + 10x^3 - \gamma_2(\omega)x + 5 = 0,}
from which, as above, the two equations
\[
5^5 + 10\cdot5^2x^3 - \gamma_2\left(\frac{\omega}{5}\right)x^5 + x^6 = 0,
\]
\[
y^{12} + 10y^6x^3 - \gamma_2\left(\frac{\omega}{5}\right)y^2x^5 + 5x^6 = 0,
\]
and, by elimination of $\gamma_2\left(\frac{\omega}{5}\right)$,
\[
x^6 - 10x^3y^2(5+y^2) = y^2(y^8 + 5y^6 + 5^2y^4 + 5^3y^2 + 5^4).
\]
This equation, solved for $x^3$, gives:
\weq{27}{x^3 = y^5 + 5y^4 + 15y^3 + 25y^2 + 25y,}
and if for brevity we denote the right-hand side of this equation by
$\chi(y)$, then by (26)
\weq{28}{j(\omega)\chi(y) = [\chi(y)^2 + 10\chi(y) + 5]^3.}
This is the equation of degree 30 for $y$ that was sought.

\begin{center}
§ 73.\quad \gesperrt{The Schlaefli Modular Equations.}
\end{center}

One arrives at simpler transformation equations by adjoining to the
domain of rationality, which up to now consisted of the rational
functions of $j(\omega)$, the quantity $f(\omega)^{24}$. To this
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 278 =====
% !PRINTED 257
\weberpage{257}
%<<CONT
domain of rationality belong the functions of $\omega$ which, under
the two substitutions

\weq{1}{\left(\omega, -\frac{1}{\omega}\right), \quad (\omega, \omega+2)}

remain unchanged (\S\,54, 2). If, then, a system of $\nu$
functions $\Phi_{a,c,\partial}$ is permuted by the substitutions (1) only among
themselves, these functions are the roots of a
transformation equation whose coefficients depend rationally on
$f(\omega)^{24}$. To these belong (as we have already shown earlier by another
route), for an \gesperrt{odd} $n$, which we shall
now always assume, certain powers of the quantities

\[
f\left(\frac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right),
\]

in which, as may be remarked once and for all, $c$ is assumed divisible by 16, and,
when $n$ is not divisible by 3, divisible by 48.

The somewhat extended principles of \S\,70 lead comparatively
simply to the calculation of these equations.

An extension is, however, necessary for the following reason:

In the considerations hitherto we were able to draw the
conclusion: if a \gesperrt{rational} function of $j(\omega)$ remains finite for every
finite $\omega$ with positive imaginary part, then it is
an \gesperrt{integral} function of $j(\omega)$, because to every \gesperrt{finite} $j(\omega)$
there belongs also a finite, non-real $\omega$ (\S\,52). In the case of the
rational functions of $f(\omega)$, however, from the finiteness
for every finite imaginary $\omega$ we can only conclude that they are integral
functions of $f(\omega)$ and $1:f(\omega)$, because only to every finite
$f(\omega)$, with the exception of $f(\omega) = 0$, does there belong a finite
imaginary $\omega$.

But to the substitution

\weq{2}{\left(\omega, \frac{\omega-1}{\omega+1}\right)}

there corresponds the interchange

\[
\left(f(\omega), \frac{\sqrt{2}}{f(\omega)}\right), \qquad [\S\,34, (18)]
\]

and if, then, the functions $\Phi_{a,c,\partial}$ are so chosen that they
are permuted only among one another by the substitution (2) as well,
then the coefficients of the equation of which they are the roots will
depend rationally on
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 279 =====
% !PRINTED 258
\weberpage{258}
%<<CONT

\[
f(\omega) + \frac{\sqrt{2}}{f(\omega)}
\]

depend. They are \gesperrt{integral} functions of these combinations
if the $\Phi_{a,c,\partial}$ remain finite for every finite, non-real $\omega$,
and they are \gesperrt{constant} if all the $\Phi_{a,c,\partial}$ remain finite for $q = 0$ as well, that is,
for $f(\omega) = 0$ and $f(\omega) = \infty$. In this case
\gesperrt{all the $\Phi_{a,c,\partial}$ are equal to one and the same constant}
(\S\,70).

From this the theorem follows:

\gesperrt{If one forms integral rational functions $\Phi_{a,c,\partial}$ from}

\[
f\left(\frac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right), \quad f(\omega), \quad \frac{1}{f\left(\dfrac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right)}, \quad \frac{1}{f(\omega)},
\]

\gesperrt{which have the property:}

1. \gesperrt{by the substitutions}

\[
\left(\omega, -\frac{1}{\omega}\right), \quad (\omega, \omega+2), \quad \left(\omega, \frac{\omega-1}{\omega+1}\right)
\]

\gesperrt{of being only permuted among one another,}

2. \gesperrt{of not becoming infinite for $q = 0$, then}

\[
\Phi_{a,c,\partial} = \text{constans}
\]

\gesperrt{is a transformation equation.}

In order to satisfy these conditions, the influence
of the substitutions (1) upon the functions $f$ must first be investigated.
This follows from the compositions \S\,69, (8) to (13)
and from the transformation formulae for the $f$-functions \S\,40.

For brevity we introduce the notation:

\weq{3}{\begin{aligned}
f(\omega) &= u, & f\left(\frac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right) &= v, \\[4pt]
f_1(\omega) &= u_1, & \left(\frac{2}{a}\right) f_1\left(\frac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right) &= v_1, \\[4pt]
f_2(\omega) &= u_2, & \left(\frac{2}{\partial}\right) f_2\left(\frac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right) &= v_2.
\end{aligned}}

There then result the following corresponding changes, if in the
notation no account is taken of the conversion of the
numbers $a, c, \partial$ into $a, c_1, \partial$ or $a_2, c_2, \partial_2$, as it has just been
characterised by the cited formulae of \S\,69:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 280 =====
% !PRINTED 259
\weberpage{259}
%<<CONT

\weq{4}{\begin{array}{cccc}
\omega, & u, & u_1, & u_2, \\
-\dfrac{1}{\omega}, & u, & u_2, & u_1, \\
\omega+1, & e^{-\frac{\pi i}{24}}u_1, & e^{-\frac{\pi i}{24}}u, & e^{\frac{\pi i}{12}}u_2, \\
\omega+2, & e^{-\frac{\pi i}{12}}u, & e^{-\frac{\pi i}{12}}u_1, & e^{\frac{\pi i}{6}}u_2, \\
\hline
\omega, & v, & v_1, & v_2, \\
-\dfrac{1}{\omega}, & \varrho v, & \varrho v_2, & \varrho v_1, \\
\omega+1, & \sigma e^{-\frac{n\pi i}{24}}v_1, & \sigma e^{-\frac{n\pi i}{24}}v, & \sigma e^{\frac{n\pi i}{12}}v_2, \\
\omega+2, & \sigma^2 e^{-\frac{n\pi i}{12}}v, & \sigma^2 e^{-\frac{n\pi i}{12}}v_1, & \sigma^2 e^{\frac{n\pi i}{6}}v_2,
\end{array}}

where

\[
\varrho = e^{-\frac{2\pi i}{3}\left[\alpha(\gamma-\beta)+(\alpha^2-1)\beta^3\delta\right]}, \qquad \sigma = \left(\frac{2}{a}\right) e^{\frac{(n-\lambda)\pi i}{24}} % Source confirms \beta^3\delta.
\]

are two third roots of unity, which, if $n$ is not divisible by 3,
have the value 1.

In order to determine further the effect of the substitution (2),
which arises from the transformation of the second degree

\[
\begin{pmatrix} 1, & 1 \\ -1, & 1 \end{pmatrix}
\]

upon the functions $u$, $v$, we must determine the transformations
of the first and $n$th order

\[
\begin{pmatrix} \alpha, & \beta \\ \gamma, & \delta \end{pmatrix}, \quad \begin{pmatrix} a', & 0 \\ c', & \partial' \end{pmatrix}
\]

in such a way that

\weq{5}{\begin{pmatrix} a, & 0 \\ c, & \partial \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1, & 1 \\ -1, & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \alpha, & \beta \\ \gamma, & \delta \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1, & 1 \\ -1, & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} a', & 0 \\ c', & \partial' \end{pmatrix}}

holds. This approach leads to the equations

\weq{6}{\begin{aligned}
a &= a'(\alpha-\beta)+c'(\alpha+\beta), & a &= \partial'(\alpha+\beta), \\
c-\partial &= a'(\gamma-\delta)+c'(\gamma+\delta), & c+\partial &= \partial'(\gamma+\delta).
\end{aligned}}

With this, since $\alpha+\beta$ and $\gamma+\delta$ are relatively prime in
consequence of $\alpha\delta-\beta\gamma = 1$, $\partial'$ is first determined as the
greatest common divisor of $a$ and $c+\partial$, and $a'$ results from
$n = a'\partial'$. Then, by equations (6):

\[
\alpha+\beta = \frac{a}{\partial'}, \qquad \gamma+\delta = \frac{c+\partial}{\beta'}, % [sic] German source prints \beta'; equations (6) imply \partial'.
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 281 =====
% !PRINTED 260
\weberpage{260}
%<<CONT
and $\delta$ and $\beta$ can be so determined that

\weq{7}{\delta(\alpha+\beta) - \beta(\gamma+\delta) = \alpha\delta - \beta\gamma = 1.}

From the equations (6) for $a$ and $c-\partial$ there is then found

\weq{8}{c'+a' = a\delta - (c-\partial)\beta.}

Since $\alpha+\beta$ and $\gamma+\delta$ are both odd, $\delta$ and $\beta$
cannot, by (7), both be odd; consequently $c'$ turns out even by (8).
If one replaces $\delta$, $\beta$, which by (7) is permitted, by
$\delta+h(\gamma+\delta)$, $\beta+h(\alpha+\beta)$, for an arbitrary $h$, then
$c'$ changes by $2ha'$ according to (6) and (8), and $h$ can be so disposed
of that $c'$ becomes divisible by 16 or 48.

Then, by (6), $\alpha+\beta+\gamma-\delta$ is even, and therefore
formula (12), \S\,40 is to be applied. In it the following is now to be taken into account


\[
\begin{aligned}
a'(\alpha-\beta) &\equiv a, & \partial(\alpha-\beta) &\equiv \partial' \\
\partial'(\alpha+\beta) &\equiv a, & a'(\gamma-\delta) &\equiv -\partial
\end{aligned} \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ 16),
\]

from which it follows:

\[
n(\alpha-\beta)(\alpha+\beta+\gamma-\delta) \equiv a^2 - \partial'^2 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 16),
\]

hence

\[
\left(\frac{2}{\alpha-\beta}\right) e^{-\frac{3\pi i}{8}(\alpha-\beta)(\alpha+\beta+\gamma-\delta)} = \left(\frac{2}{a}\right)\left(\frac{2}{a'}\right)\left(\frac{2}{a}\right)\left(\frac{2}{\partial'}\right) = \left(\frac{2}{n}\right)
\]

and

\[
\varrho = e^{-\frac{2\pi i}{3}\left[\alpha(\gamma-\beta)-(\alpha^2-1)\beta\delta\right]}.
\]

If $n$ is not divisible by 3, then

\[
\begin{aligned}
2\alpha &\equiv a(a'+\partial'), & 2\delta &\equiv \partial(a'+\partial'), \\
2\beta &\equiv a(\partial'-a'), & 2\gamma &\equiv \partial(\partial'-a')
\end{aligned} \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ 3),
\]

hence either $\alpha$ and $\delta$ or $\beta$ and $\gamma$ are divisible by 3, and therefore
$\varrho = 1$.

From this there result the following interchanges belonging together
 (where the change of $a, c, \partial$ into $a', c', \partial'$ is determined by (6)):

\weq{9}{\begin{array}{ccc}
\omega, & u, & v \\[4pt]
\dfrac{\omega-1}{\omega+1}, & \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{u}, & \varrho\left(\dfrac{2}{n}\right)\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{v}.
\end{array}}

We apply the interchanges (4), (5), (9) to the following
functions:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 282 =====
% !PRINTED 261
\weberpage{261}
%<<CONT
\weq{10}{\begin{aligned} A &= \left(\frac{u}{v}\right)^r + \left(\frac{v}{u}\right)^r \\ B &= (uv)^s + \left(\frac{2}{n}\right)^{r+s} \frac{2^s}{(uv)^s} , \end{aligned}}
in which $r$, $s$ are two integers that satisfy the conditions
\weq{11}{(n-1)r \equiv 0, \quad (n+1)s \equiv 0 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 12)}
and which therefore, if $n$ is divisible by 3, are both divisible
by 3, and where
\[ \left(\frac{2}{n}\right) = (-1)^{\frac{n^2-1}{8}} \]
holds.

There then result the following mutually corresponding permutations:
\weq{12}{\begin{aligned}
&\omega, & & A, & & B, \\
&-\frac{1}{\omega}, & & A, & & B, \\
&\omega+2, & & (-1)^{\frac{(n-1)r}{12}} A, & & (-1)^{\frac{(n+1)s}{12}} B, \\
&\frac{\omega-1}{\omega+1}, & & \left(\frac{2}{n}\right)^r A, & & \left(\frac{2}{n}\right)^r B.
\end{aligned}}

If we now form from $A$, $B$ an integral rational function with
numerical coefficients
\weq{13}{\Phi_{a,c,\partial} = \Sigma\, M_{h,k}\, A^h B^k,}
in which, should changes of sign occur in (12), the exponents
$h$, $k$ are to be so arranged that in all terms of (13)
the same alterations of sign take place, then the system
of functions $\Phi_{a,c,\partial}$, or at least $\Phi^2_{a,c,\partial}$, will satisfy requirement 1.
of the theorem set up above; and in order to satisfy
requirement 2. as well, and so to obtain a transformation equation, we have to determine the coefficients $M_{h,k}$ in such a way
that all the $\nu$ values of $\Phi_{a,c,\partial}$ remain finite for $q=0$.
This problem is simplified essentially if $n$ has no square divisor, and still more if $n$ is a prime.

For if $n$ has no square divisor, one can derive all the
values $\Phi_{a,c,\partial}$ from $\Phi_{a,0,\partial}$ by increasing
$\omega$ by certain integers; if therefore, as is our requirement, no negative powers occur in the development of $\Phi_{a,0,\partial}$ % [sic] German source prints a period after 0 here; parallel occurrences have a comma.
in ascending powers
of $q$, then the same holds
of all the $\Phi_{a,c,\partial}$.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 283 =====
% !PRINTED 262
\weberpage{262}
But if $n$ is a prime, it is enough to show that $\Phi_{1,0,n}$
contains no negative powers of $q$, since the same follows for
$\Phi_{n,0,1}$ by the interchange of $\omega$ with $\omega:n$.

The constant value which the function $\Phi_{a,c,\partial}$ takes is
determined from \gesperrt{one} term of the development.

In carrying out these calculations the developments § 24, (11), are of use,
\weq{14}{\begin{aligned}
A &= q^{-\frac{n-1}{24}r} \prod_{1,\infty}^{h} \left(\frac{1+q^{n(2h-1)}}{1+q^{2h-1}}\right)^r \\
&\quad + q^{\frac{n-1}{24}r} \prod_{1,\infty}^{h} \left(\frac{1+q^{2h-1}}{1+q^{n(2h-1)}}\right)^r \\
B &= q^{-\frac{n+1}{24}s} \prod_{1,\infty}^{h} (1+q^{2h-1})^s (1+q^{n(2h-1)})^s \\
&\quad + \left(\frac{2}{n}\right)^{r+s} q^{\frac{n+1}{24}s} 2^s \prod_{1,\infty}^{h} \frac{1}{(1+q^{2h-1})^s (1+q^{n(2h-1)})^s} .
\end{aligned}}
The formulae do not always come out simplest when $r$, $s$ are
assumed as small as possible; rather it proves most expedient to add
the further condition
\weq{15}{\frac{(n-1)r}{12} \equiv \frac{(n+1)s}{12} \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 2)}
as well.

In this way we obtain, for the first seven odd primes, the
following determination of $A$ and $B$:
\[
\begin{aligned}
n &= 3, & A &= \left(\frac{u}{v}\right)^6 + \left(\frac{v}{u}\right)^6, & B &= (uv)^3 - \frac{8}{(uv)^3}, \\
n &= 5, & A &= \left(\frac{u}{v}\right)^3 + \left(\frac{v}{u}\right)^3, & B &= (uv)^2 - \frac{4}{(uv)^2}, \\
n &= 7, & A &= \left(\frac{u}{v}\right)^4 + \left(\frac{v}{u}\right)^4, & B &= (uv)^3 + \frac{8}{(uv)^3}, \\
n &= 11, & A &= \left(\frac{u}{v}\right)^6 + \left(\frac{v}{u}\right)^6, & B &= uv - \frac{2}{vu}, \\
n &= 13, & A &= \frac{u}{v} + \frac{v}{u}, & B &= (uv)^6 - \frac{64}{(uv)^6}, \\
n &= 17, & A &= \left(\frac{u}{v}\right)^3 + \left(\frac{v}{u}\right)^3, & B &= (uv)^4 + \frac{16}{(uv)^4}, \\
n &= 19, & A &= \left(\frac{u}{v}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{v}{u}\right)^2, & B &= (uv)^3 - \frac{8}{(uv)^3}.
\end{aligned}
\]

%% ===== canonical stable idx 284 =====
% !PRINTED 263
\weberpage{263}
The developments in powers of $q$ for $A$ and $B$ result
from (14), so far as they are needed for the calculation,
as follows:
\[
\begin{aligned}
n &= 3, & A &= q^{-\frac{1}{2}}(1 - 5q \dots), \\
& & B &= q^{-\frac{1}{2}}(1 - 5q \dots), \\
n &= 5, & A &= q^{-\frac{1}{2}}(1 - 2q \dots), \\
& & B &= q^{-\frac{1}{2}}(1 - 2q \dots), \\
n &= 7, & A &= q^{-1}(1 - 4q \dots), \\
& & B &= q^{-1}(1 + 3q \dots), \\
n &= 11, & A &= q^{-\frac{5}{2}}(1 - 6q + 21q^2 \dots), \\
& & B &= q^{-\frac{1}{2}}(1 - q + 2q^2 \dots), \\
n &= 13, & A &= q^{-\frac{1}{2}}(1 + 2q^2 - 2q^3 \dots), \\
& & B &= q^{-\frac{7}{2}}(1 + 6q + 15q^2 + 26q^3 \dots), \\
n &= 17, & A &= q^{-2}(1 - 3q + 6q^2 - 13q^3 + 25q^4 - 39q^5 + 76q^6 \dots), \\
& & B &= q^{-3}(1 + 4q + 6q^2 + 8q^3 + 17q^4 + 28q^5 + 54q^6 \dots), \\
n &= 19, & A &= q^{-\frac{3}{2}}(1 - 2q + 3q^2 - 5q^3 + 11q^4 - 13q^5 + 24q^6 - 28q^7 \dots), \\
& & B &= q^{-\frac{5}{2}}(1 + 3q + 3q^2 + 4q^3 + 9q^4 + 4q^5 + 39q^6 - 27q^7 \dots),
\end{aligned}
\]
and from these one obtains, by elimination of the negative powers,
the required equations between $A$ and $B$:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{I.}\quad n &= 3, & A - B &= 0, \\
n &= 5, & A - B &= 0, \\
n &= 7, & A - B + 7 &= 0, \\
n &= 11, & A - B^5 + B^3 + 2B &= 0, \\
n &= 13, & A^7 + 6A^5 + A^3 - 20A - B &= 0, \\
n &= 17, & A^3 - B^2 + 17AB - 34A^2 + 34B + 116A \\
& & + 440 &= 0, \\
n &= 19, & A^5 - B^3 + 19AB^2 - 95A^2B + 109A^3 \\
& & + 128B - 128A &= 0\ ^{1}).
\end{aligned}
\]
$^{1}$) These equations were first set up by \gesperrt{Schlaefli} (Journal für
Mathematik, Bd. 72).

%% ===== canonical stable idx 285 =====
% !PRINTED 264
\weberpage{264}
From this system of equations one derives a second and a
third for the functions $f_1$, $f_2$, by replacing $\omega$ by
$\omega + 1$ and thereupon $\omega$ by $-1:\omega$. These two systems
have the same form; only that in the one case
\[
u_1 = f_1(\omega), \qquad v_1 = \left(\frac{2}{a}\right) f_1\left(\frac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right),
\]
and in the other case
\[
u_1 = f_2(\omega), \qquad v_1 = \left(\frac{2}{\partial}\right) f_2\left(\frac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right)
\]
is to be set. From the interchanges (4) there results in this way:
{\small
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{II.}\quad n &= 3, & A_1 &= \left(\frac{u_1}{v_1}\right)^6 - \left(\frac{v_1}{u_1}\right)^6, & B_1 &= (u_1v_1)^3 + \frac{8}{(u_1v_1)^3}, \\
& & A_1 + B_1 &= 0, \\
n &= 5, & A_1 &= \left(\frac{u_1}{v_1}\right)^3 - \left(\frac{v_1}{u_1}\right)^3, & B_1 &= (u_1v_1)^2 + \frac{4}{(u_1v_1)^2}, \\
& & A_1 + B_1 &= 0, \\
n &= 7, & A_1 &= \left(\frac{u_1}{v_1}\right)^4 + \left(\frac{v_1}{u_1}\right)^4, & B_1 &= (u_1v_1)^3 + \frac{8}{(u_1v_1)^3}, \\
& & A_1 - B_1 - 7 &= 0, \\
n &= 11, & A_1 &= \left(\frac{u_1}{v_1}\right)^6 - \left(\frac{v_1}{u_1}\right)^6, & B_1 &= u_1v_1 + \frac{2}{u_1v_1}, \\
& & A_1 + B_1^5 + B_1^3 - 2B_1 &= 0, \\
n &= 13, & A_1 &= \frac{u_1}{v_1} - \frac{v_1}{u_1}, & B_1 &= (u_1v_1)^6 + \frac{64}{(u_1v_1)^6}, \\
& & A_1^7 - 6A_1^5 + A_1^3 + 20A_1 + B_1 &= 0, \\
n &= 17, & A_1 &= \left(\frac{u_1}{v_1}\right)^3 + \left(\frac{v_1}{u_1}\right)^3, & B_1 &= (u_1v_1)^4 + \frac{16}{(u_1v_1)^4}, \\
& & A_1^3 - B_1^2 - 17A_1B_1 - 34A_1^2 - 34B_1 + 116A_1 \\
& & + 440 &= 0, \\
n &= 19, & A_1 &= \left(\frac{u_1}{v_1}\right)^2 - \left(\frac{v_1}{u_1}\right)^2, & B_1 &= (u_1v_1)^3 + \frac{8}{(u_1v_1)^3}, \\
& & A_1^5 + B_1^3 - 19A_1B_1^2 + 95A_1^2B_1 - 109A_1^3 \\
& & + 128B_1 - 128A_1 &= 0.
\end{aligned}
\]
}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 286 =====
% !PRINTED 265
\weberpage{265}

\begin{center}
\textbf{\S\,74. The \gesperrt{Form} of the \gesperrt{Schlaefli} Modular Equations}\\
\textbf{for a Prime Degree.}
\end{center}

The form which we have found in the preceding section for the relations
subsisting between
\weq{1}{u=f(\omega),\qquad v=f\Bigl(\frac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\Bigr)}
% German source confirms the printed partial-shaped d glyph, transcribed as \partial.
can easily be brought under a general law, at least when the degree of
transformation is a prime $p$. Since much depends on this form in what
follows, we enter here somewhat more closely into it.

The determination of the numbers $r, s$ by (11) and (15) of the
preceding section depends on the behaviour of $p$ with respect to the
modulus 24, and since we may exclude the case $p=3$, we have the
following cases:
\weq{2}{\begin{array}{lll}
p\equiv 1 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 24) & r=1 & s=12\\
p\equiv 5 & r=3 & s=2\\
p\equiv 7 & r=4 & s=3\\
p\equiv 11 & r=6 & s=1\\
p\equiv 13 & r=1 & s=6\\
p\equiv 17 & r=3 & s=4\\
p\equiv 19 & r=2 & s=3\\
p\equiv 23 & r=12 & s=1,
\end{array}}
so that $r+s$ is always odd, and $p+1$ is divisible by $2r$, $p-1$
by $2s$. Accordingly we obtain
\weq{3}{\begin{aligned}
A &= \Bigl(\frac{u}{v}\Bigr)^r+\Bigl(\frac{v}{u}\Bigr)^r,\\
B &= (uv)^s+\Bigl(\frac{2}{p}\Bigr)\frac{2^s}{(uv)^s}.
\end{aligned}}
Now we know that the $p+1$ quantities $v$ are the roots of an
irreducible transformation equation
\weq{4}{\Phi_p(v,u)=v^{p+1}+U_1v^p+\cdots U_{p+1}=0}
in which the coefficients $U_1\ldots, U_{p+1}$ are rational
functions of $u$.

We conclude at once that they are \gesperrt{integral} rational functions
of $u$. For in the \gesperrt{first place}, all the roots of (4) become
infinite for $u=\infty$, as one recognises on letting $\omega=i\infty$,
and therefore $q=0$. In the second place, by (9) of the preceding
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 287 =====
% !PRINTED 266
\weberpage{266}
%<<CONT
section, the interchange $\Bigl(u,\dfrac{\sqrt2}{u}\Bigr)$ carries the
totality of the roots $v$ over into
\[
\Bigl(\frac{2}{p}\Bigr)\frac{\sqrt2}{v}
\]
From this it follows that for $u=0$ all the roots $v$ pass over into
zero, so that none of them becomes infinite; and from this we must
conclude that the $U_1, U_2, \ldots U_{p+1}$ are not only
\gesperrt{integral} functions of $u$, but that each of them must also
contain the factor $u$.

We now conclude first of all, exactly as with the invariant equation
(\S\ 69, 2., 3. and 6.), that
\weq{5}{\Phi_p(v,u)=\Phi_p(u,v),}
and that
\weq{6}{\Phi_p(v,u)=(v^p-u)(v-u^p)+p\sum_{1,p-1}^{h,k}c_{h,k}u^hv^k,}
where $c_{h,k}=c_{k,h}$ are \gesperrt{integers}.
We wish to represent this function in the form
\weq{7}{\Phi_p(v,u)=v^{p+1}+u^{p+1}+\sum_{1,p}^{h,k}a_{h,k}u^hv^k,}
where accordingly $a_{h,k}=a_{k,h}$ are likewise integers, upon whose
divisibility by $p$ nothing further now depends, and in particular
$a_{p,p}=-1$. If in the equation
\[
\Phi_p[f(p\,\omega), f(\omega)]=0
\]
we replace $\omega$ by $\omega+2$, then, on account of the
irreducibility, it results from the relation
\[
f(\omega+2)=e^{-\frac{\pi i}{12}}f(\omega),
\]
that in (7) not \gesperrt{all} terms occur, but only those in which the exponents
$h, k$ satisfy the congruence
\weq{8}{hp+k\equiv p+1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 24)}

Now we know yet a further property of the functions
$\Phi_p(v,u)$, one which follows from the interchange (9) of the
preceding section already used, where $\varrho=1$ is to be put, and
which, if for brevity we set
\[
\varepsilon=\Bigl(\frac{2}{p}\Bigr)=(-1)^{\frac{p^2-1}{8}}
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 288 =====
% !PRINTED 267
\weberpage{267}
%<<CONT
set, it can be represented as follows:
\weq{9}{\Phi_p(v,u)=\Bigl(\frac{uv}{\sqrt2}\Bigr)^{p+1}\Phi_p\Bigl(\frac{\varepsilon\sqrt2}{v},\frac{\sqrt2}{u}\Bigr).}
From this one infers the relations
\weq{10}{\varepsilon^h2^{\frac{h+k-p-1}{2}}a_{p+1-h,\,p+1-k}=a_{h,k}, \qquad a_{h,k}=a_{k,h}.}
If, therefore, we collect together in (7) the terms with equal
coefficients $a_{h,k}$, we may restrict ourselves to the assumption
that $h\geqq k$, $h+k\geqq p+1$; and, apart from the two terms
$v^{p+1}, u^{p+1}$, $\Phi_p$ presents itself as an aggregate of
terms of the two following forms (if it is further taken into
account that, on account of (8), $\varepsilon^h=\varepsilon^k$):
\weq{11}{\begin{aligned}
&v^hu^k+v^ku^h+\varepsilon^h2^{\frac{h+k-p-1}{2}}\bigl(u^{p+1-h}v^{p+1-k}+u^{p+1-k}v^{p+1-h}\bigr)=\\
&\underset{h>k}{(uv)^{\frac{p+1}{2}}}\left[\Bigl(\frac{v}{u}\Bigr)^{\frac{h-k}{2}}+\Bigl(\frac{u}{v}\Bigr)^{\frac{h-k}{2}}\right]\left[(uv)^{\frac{h+k-p-1}{2}}+\frac{\varepsilon^h2^{\frac{h+k-p-1}{2}}}{(uv)^{\frac{h+k-p-1}{2}}}\right].
\end{aligned}}
\weq{12}{\begin{aligned}
&v^hu^h+\varepsilon^h2^{h-\frac{p+1}{2}}(uv)^{p+1-h}\\
&=(uv)^{\frac{p+1}{2}}\left[(uv)^{h-\frac{p+1}{2}}+\frac{\varepsilon^h2^{h-\frac{p+1}{2}}}{(uv)^{h-\frac{p+1}{2}}}\right].
\end{aligned}}
The coefficients of these terms in $\Phi_p$ are integers.
Now from (8) there results:
\[
\begin{aligned}
(h-k)&\equiv (h-1)(p+1)\\
h+k-p-1&\equiv -h(p-1)
\end{aligned}
\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 24),
\]
and therefore $h-k$ is divisible by $2r$, and $h+k-p-1$ (in which
$h$ may also be $=k$) by $2s$ [\S\ 74, (2)].

If we therefore set
\[
\frac{h-k}{2}=r\alpha, \qquad \frac{h+k-p-1}{2}=s\beta,
\]
then $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are positive integers which lie between
the limits
\weq{13}{0\leqq\alpha<\frac{p+1}{2r}, \qquad 0\leqq\beta\leqq\frac{p+1}{2s},}
and moreover the congruence $-h(p-1)\equiv 2s\beta\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 24)$,
which follows from (8), shows that at least in the cases where
