$\varepsilon=-1$, $h\equiv\beta\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 2)$
[\S\ 74, (2)], and hence always $\varepsilon^h=\varepsilon^\beta$.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 289 =====
% !PRINTED 268
\weberpage{268}
Accordingly (11) becomes
\[
(uv)^{\frac{p+1}{2}}\left[\Bigl(\frac{v}{u}\Bigr)^{r\alpha}+\Bigl(\frac{u}{v}\Bigr)^{r\alpha}\right]\left[(uv)^{s\beta}+\frac{\varepsilon^\beta2^{s\beta}}{(uv)^{s\beta}}\right],
\]
and (12)
\[
(uv)^{\frac{p+1}{2}}\left[(uv)^{s\beta}+\frac{\varepsilon^\beta2^{s\beta}}{(uv)^{s\beta}}\right].
\]
Now the well-known formulae hold, when $x, \gamma$ are arbitrary
quantities and
\[
x+\frac{\gamma}{x}=y
\]
is put,
\[
x^2+\frac{\gamma^2}{x^2}=y^2-2\gamma, \qquad x^3+\frac{\gamma^3}{x^3}=y^3-3\gamma y,\ \ldots,
\]
\[
\Bigl(x^n+\frac{\gamma^n}{x^n}\Bigr)\Bigl(x+\frac{\gamma}{x}\Bigr)=x^{n+1}+\frac{\gamma^{n+1}}{x^{n+1}}+\gamma\Bigl(x^{n-1}+\frac{\gamma^{n-1}}{x^{n-1}}\Bigr),
\]
from which one recognises, by the inference from $n$ to $n+1$, that
\[
x^n+\frac{\gamma^n}{x^n}
\]
can be represented, for every arbitrary $n$, as an integral rational
function of degree $n$ in $y$, which, when $\gamma$ is an integer, has
integral coefficients, of which the highest $=1$.

The two quantities
\[
\Bigl(\frac{v}{u}\Bigr)^{r\alpha}+\Bigl(\frac{u}{v}\Bigr)^{r\alpha} \qquad \text{and} \qquad (uv)^{s\beta}+\frac{\varepsilon^\beta2^{s\beta}}{(uv)^{s\beta}}
\]
can therefore be represented in this way as integral rational functions
of $A$ and $B$, of degrees $\alpha$ and $\beta$, and we find, if we
further separate off the term corresponding to the value
$\beta=\dfrac{p-1}{2s}$, which has the coefficient $-1$, and denote
integral coefficients by $c_{\alpha,\beta}$:
\weq{14}{\frac{\Phi_p(u,v)}{(uv)^{\frac{p+1}{2}}}=A^{\frac{p+1}{2r}}-B^{\frac{p-1}{2s}}+\sum^{\alpha,\beta}c_{\alpha,\beta}A^\alpha B^\beta,}
in which $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are bound to the limits
\[
0\leqq\alpha<\frac{p+1}{2r}, \qquad 0\leqq\beta<\frac{p-1}{2s}
\]
This is the form which we gave to the modular equations up to $p=19$
in the preceding section.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 290 =====
% !PRINTED 269
\weberpage{269}
It should still be mentioned that the discussion carried out in §\,69, 4., 5. for the invariant equation in the case of a composite degree of transformation holds unchanged for the \gesperrt{Schlaefli} modular equations as well, from which we may conclude that all these equations have rational numerical coefficients.

\begin{center}
\textbf{§\,75.\quad \gesperrt{The Irrational Forms of the Modular Equations.}}
\end{center}

By applying the same procedure, far simpler forms can be given to the transformation equations. The forms of equation with which we shall now occupy ourselves contain the three functions $f$, $f_1$, $f_2$ at once; but since, by §\,34, (11), (12), two of these functions can be expressed by the third, two of them can be eliminated, and in this way one can arrive at the equations of the preceding section. If one substitutes for $f_1$, $f_2$ the expressions in terms of $f$, or for the three functions $f$, $f_1$, $f_2$ the expressions in terms of $k^2$, then radical signs occur, and this explains the name of these equations.

We set, as above,
\weq{1}{\begin{aligned}
u &= f(\omega), & v &= f\Bigl(\frac{c+\partial\,\omega}{a}\Bigr),\\
u_1 &= f_1(\omega), & v_1 &= \Bigl(\frac{2}{a}\Bigr) f_1\Bigl(\frac{c+\partial\,\omega}{a}\Bigr),\\
u_2 &= f_2(\omega), & v_2 &= \Bigl(\frac{2}{\partial}\Bigr) f_2\Bigl(\frac{c+\partial\,\omega}{a}\Bigr),\\
u\,u_1\,u_2 &= \sqrt{2}, & v\,v_1\,v_2 &= \Bigl(\frac{2}{n}\Bigr)\sqrt{2},
\end{aligned}}
and obtain the following corresponding permutations:
\weq{2}{\begin{array}{llll}
\omega, & uv, & u_1v_1, & u_2v_2,\\
-\dfrac{1}{\omega}, & \varrho\,uv, & \varrho\,u_2v_2, & \varrho\,u_1v_1,\\
\omega+1, & e^{-\frac{(n+1)\pi i}{24}}\sigma\,u_1v_1, & e^{-\frac{(n+1)\pi i}{24}}\sigma\,uv, & e^{\frac{(n+1)\pi i}{12}}\sigma\,u_2v_2,
\end{array}}
% Source scan and the row pattern confirm the exponent numerator (n+1).
where $\varrho$, $\sigma$ are the third roots of unity defined above [§\,73, (4)].

We distinguish three different cases according to the behaviour of $n$ with respect to the modulus 8.

1. $n+1\equiv 0$, (mod 8).

%% ===== canonical stable idx 291 =====
% !PRINTED 270
\weberpage{270}
We set
\weq{3}{\begin{aligned}
2A &= uv + (-1)^{\frac{n+1}{8}}(u_1v_1+u_2v_2),\\
B &= uvu_1v_1 + uvu_2v_2 + (-1)^{\frac{n+1}{8}}u_1v_1u_2v_2\\
&= \frac{2}{u_1v_1} + \frac{2}{u_2v_2} + (-1)^{\frac{n+1}{8}}\frac{2}{uv},
\end{aligned}}
so that the interchanges that belong together come out as
\weq{4}{\begin{array}{lll}
\omega, & A, & B,\\
-\dfrac{1}{\omega}, & \varrho\,A, & \varrho^2 B,\\
\omega+1, & e^{\frac{\pi i(n+1)}{12}}\sigma\,A, & e^{-\frac{\pi i(n+1)}{12}}\sigma^2 B.
\end{array}}

A product of the form $A^h B^k$ therefore takes on, through the two interchanges
\[
\Bigl(\omega, -\frac{1}{\omega}\Bigr), \quad (\omega, \omega+1)
\]
the factors
\[
\varrho^{h-k}, \quad e^{(h-k)\frac{(n+1)\pi i}{12}}\sigma^{h-k},
\]
which are $=1$ when $n+1$ is divisible by 3. We therefore now form, with numerical coefficients $M_{h,k}$, functions of the form
\weq{5}{\Phi_{a,c,\partial} = \Sigma\,M_{h,k}A^h B^k,}
in which, if $n \equiv 0$ or $\equiv 1$ (mod 3), $h$ and $k$ may take only such (integral) values whose differences $h-k$ leave the same residue on division by 3, while if $n \equiv -1$ (mod 3) they are not subject to this restriction. Such a function itself, or at least its third power, therefore satisfies a transformation equation of the first level. It remains finite, moreover, for all finite values of $j(\omega)$, and is consequently an \gesperrt{integral} algebraic function of $j(\omega)$. [The transformation of the second order $\begin{pmatrix} 1, & 1\\ -1, & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ need not be brought in here, since the totality of the $\Phi_{a,c,\partial}$ remains unchanged already under the substitution $(\omega, \omega+1)$, and not only under $(\omega, \omega+2)$. Cf. the remark at the beginning of §\,73.]

If, then, we determine the constants in $\Phi_{a,c,\partial}$ so that no negative powers of $q$ occur in the developments of these functions, then all the $\Phi_{a,c,\partial}$ must be equal to one and the same constant.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 292 =====
% !PRINTED 271
\weberpage{271}
To attain this goal it suffices here too that, when $n$ has no square divisor, $\Phi_{a,0,\partial}$, and when $n$ is a prime, $\Phi_{1,0,n}$ remain finite for $q=0$.

In these calculations we make use of the developments:
\weq{6}{\begin{aligned}
uv &= q^{-\frac{n+1}{24}}\Pi(1+q^{n(2h+1)})(1+q^{2h+1}),\\
u_1v_1 &= q^{-\frac{n+1}{24}}\Pi(1-q^{n(2h+1)})(1-q^{2h+1}),\\
u_2v_2 &= 2q^{\frac{n+1}{12}}\Pi(1+q^{2hn})(1+q^{2h}),
\end{aligned}}
from which, by development in powers of $q$:
\weq{7}{\begin{aligned}
uv &= q^{-\frac{n+1}{24}}(1+q+q^3+q^4+q^5+q^6+q^7+2q^8\dots),\\
u_1v_1 &= q^{-\frac{n+1}{24}}(1-q-q^3+q^4-q^5+q^6-q^7+2q^8\dots),\\
u_2v_2 &= 2q^{\frac{n+1}{12}}(1+q^2+q^4+2q^6+2q^8+\cdots).
\end{aligned}}
The latter formulae are correct for $n>7$ (for $n=3,5,7$ the terms from $q^3, q^5, q^7$ on are to be modified). For $n=7$, $n=23$ these expressions show that $A$ itself remains finite for $q=0$, from which the equations follow for these cases:
\weq{8}{\begin{aligned}
n&=7, & A&=0,\\
n&=23, & A&=1.
\end{aligned}}
By a simple calculation one finds further still:
\weq{9}{\begin{aligned}
n&=31, & (A^2-B)^2-A&=0,\\
n&=47, & A^2-A-B&=2,\\
n&=71, & A^3-4A^2+2A-B&=1.
\end{aligned}}
The calculation turns out not quite so simple for a composite $n$. Thus for $n=15$, for example, one must take account of the condition of finiteness for $q=0$ not only for $\Phi_{1,0,15}$, but also for $\Phi_{3,0,5}$. These two, however, suffice. One obtains in this way:
\weq{10}{n=15, \quad A^3-AB+1=0.}
2. If $n \equiv 3$ (mod 8), the same conclusions are to be drawn, if we set:
\weq{11}{\begin{aligned}
4A &= u^2v^2 - u_1^2v_1^2 - u_2^2v_2^2,\\
B &= u^2v^2u_1^2v_1^2 + u^2v^2u_2^2v_2^2 - u_1^2v_1^2u_2^2v_2^2,
\end{aligned}}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 293 =====
% !PRINTED 272
\weberpage{272}
%<<CONT
for which one obtains from (2) the corresponding permutations:
\weq{12}{\begin{array}{lll}
\omega, & A, & B,\\
-\dfrac{1}{\omega}, & \varrho^2 A, & \varrho B,\\
\omega+1, & e^{\frac{(n+1)\pi i}{6}}\sigma^2 A, & e^{-\frac{(n+1)\pi i}{6}}\sigma B,
\end{array}}
and from this one derives in the same way the equations:
\weq{13}{\begin{aligned}
n&=3, & A&=0,\\
n&=11, & A&=1,\\
n&=19, & A^5-7A^2-B&=0.
\end{aligned}}
3. If $n \equiv 1$ (mod 4), one can proceed in the same way with the functions
\weq{14}{\begin{aligned}
8A &= u^4v^4 - u_1^4v_1^4 - u_2^4v_2^4,\\
B &= u^4v^4u_1^4v_1^4 + u^4v^4u_2^4v_2^4 - u_1^4v_1^4u_2^4v_2^4,
\end{aligned}}
for which one obtains the corresponding permutations:
\weq{15}{\begin{array}{lll}
\omega, & A, & B,\\
-\dfrac{1}{\omega}, & \varrho\,A, & \varrho^2 B,\\
\omega+1, & e^{\frac{(n+1)\pi i}{3}}\sigma\,A, & e^{-\frac{(n+1)\pi i}{3}}\sigma^2 B.
\end{array}}
Only the first case $n=5$ leads here to a simple result:
\weq{16}{n=5, \quad A=1.}
For $n=5$ a still simpler form of the transformation equation can be obtained.

For if we apply to the three functions
\weq{17}{w = \frac{u_1^2v_2^2+u_2^2v_1^2}{uv}, \quad w_1 = \frac{u_2^2v^2-v_2^2u^2}{u_1v_1}, \quad w_2 = \frac{u_1^2v^2-v_1^2u}{u_2v_2}} % [sic] German source prints u without the square in the w_2 numerator.
the substitutions $\bigl(\omega, -\frac{1}{\omega}\bigr)$, $(\omega, \omega+1)$, then under the assumption $n \equiv 5$ (mod 8) the corresponding permutations result:
\[
\begin{array}{llll}
\omega, & w, & w_1, & w_2,\\
-\dfrac{1}{\omega}, & w, & w_2, & w_1,\\
\omega+1, & e^{-\frac{\pi i}{24}(n-5)}w_1, & e^{-\frac{\pi i}{24}(n-5)}w, & e^{\frac{\pi i}{12}(n-5)}w_2.
\end{array}
\]

%% ===== canonical stable idx 294 =====
% !PRINTED 273
\weberpage{273}
If we therefore set
\[
\begin{aligned}
A &= w^2 + w_1^2 + w_2^2,\\
B &= w^2w_1^2 + w^2w_2^2 + w_1^2w_2^2,\\
C &= w\,w_1\,w_2,
\end{aligned}
\]
we obtain
\[
\begin{array}{cccc}
\omega, & A, & B, & C, \\
-\dfrac{1}{\omega}, & A, & B, & C, \\
\omega+1, & e^{-\frac{\pi i}{12}(n-5)}A, & e^{-\frac{\pi i}{6}(n-5)}B, & C,
\end{array}
\]
so that two of these functions can be used just as $A$ and $B$ were used
above. For $n=5$ it appears, however, that in the developments of $w$,
$w_1$, $w_2$ in powers of $q$ no negative powers occur, and that therefore
$A$, $B$, $C$, and hence also $w$, $w_1$, $w_2$ themselves, are constant.

The modular equation for $n=5$ can therefore be set up in each of the
three forms:
\weq{18}{
\begin{aligned}
u_1^2v_2^2 + u_2^2v_1^2 &= 2uv,\\
u_2^2v^2 - v_2^2u^2 &= 2u_1v_1,\\
u_1^2v^2 - v_1^2u^2 &= 2u_2v_2.
\end{aligned}
}

These equations can also be derived from the one given by \gesperrt{Jacobi}
(Fund. art. 30, gesammelte Werke, Bd. 1, S. 123).

We close these considerations by deriving, in the simplest cases, the
\gesperrt{Jacobi modular equations} from these irrational forms.

We set [cf. \S 54, (3)]:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{u_2}{u} = x = \sqrt[4]{\varkappa}, &\qquad \frac{u_1}{u} = x' = \sqrt[4]{\varkappa'},\\[6pt]
\frac{v_2}{v} = y = \sqrt[4]{\lambda}, &\qquad \frac{v_1}{v} = y' = \sqrt[4]{\lambda'},
\end{aligned}
\]
% Source scan confirms the radicands \varkappa and \varkappa'.
and eliminate, by means of the relations
\weq{19}{
\begin{aligned}
x^8 + x'^8 &= 1, & xx' &= \frac{\sqrt{2}}{u^3}\\
y^8 + y'^8 &= 1, & yy' &= \frac{\sqrt{2}}{v^3}
\end{aligned}
}
% Source scan confirms the denominator v^3, parallel to u^3 above.
the quantities $u$ and $v$.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 295 =====
% !PRINTED 274
\weberpage{274}
For $n=3$ one obtains from (13):
\weq{20}{
x^2y^2 + x'^2y'^2 = 1,
}
a form of the modular equation which goes back to \gesperrt{Legendre}.

From this, by substituting for $x'$, $y'$ the values from (19),
\[
x^8 + y^8 = 4x^2y^2 - 6x^4y^4 + 4x^6y^6,
\]
or
\[
(x^4 - y^4)^2 = 4(xy - x^3y^3)^2
\]
and by extracting the root from this and determining the sign
by $q=0$, one finds:
\weq{21}{
x^4 - y^4 = 2xy - 2x^3y^3, \qquad (n=3),
}
which, apart from the sign of $\sqrt[4]{\lambda}$ that is not further
explained there, agrees with \S 10, (12).

For $n=5$ there follows from the second equation (18):
\[
(x^2 - y^2)^3 = 4xy\,x'^4y'^4,
\]
and from this by squaring
\[
(x^2 - y^2)^6 = 16x^2y^2(1 - x^8 - y^8 + x^8y^8),
\]
which is easily brought into the form
\[
(x^2 - y^2)^2\bigl[(x^2 - y^2)^2 + 8x^2y^2\bigr]^2 = 16x^2y^2(1 - x^4y^4)^2.
\]
If one extracts the root from this, it follows, as above:
\weq{22}{
x^6 - y^6 - 4xy(1 - x^4y^4) + 5x^2y^2(x^2 - y^2) = 0 \quad (n=5).
}
For $n=7$ one obtains, without extraction of roots, from (8):
\weq{23}{
xy + x'y' = 1,
}
and from this:
\weq{24}{
\begin{aligned}
x^8 + y^8 - 8xy(1 + x^6y^6) &+ 28x^2y^2(1 + x^4y^4)\\
- 56x^3y^3(1 + x^2y^2) &+ 70x^4y^4 = 0 \qquad (n=7).
\end{aligned}
}

\begin{center}
\S\ 76.\quad \gesperrt{Composite Degrees of Transformation.}
\end{center}

If the degree of transformation is a composite number, one can
set up still simpler transformation equations than those which are
obtained by the method of the preceding section.

We carry out these considerations here only in the simplest
cases.

Let the odd degree of transformation $n$ be decomposed into two
factors
\weq{1}{
n = n'n'',
}
which are relatively prime to each other.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 296 =====
% !PRINTED 275
\weberpage{275}
To each transformation of degree $n$ of the
form
\weq{2}{
\begin{pmatrix} a, & 0\\ c, & \partial \end{pmatrix}
}
there can then be assigned one and only one transformation of each of the degrees $n'$, $n''$:
\weq{3}{
\begin{pmatrix} a', & 0\\ c', & \partial' \end{pmatrix}, \quad
\begin{pmatrix} a'', & 0\\ c'', & \partial'' \end{pmatrix}
}
and these are determined by the following conditions:
\weq{4}{
\begin{aligned}
a &= a'a'', & \partial &= \partial'\partial'',\\
\partial''c' &\equiv c \pmod{a'}, & \partial'c'' &\equiv c \pmod{a''},
\end{aligned}
}
and conversely, from every pair of transformations of the
form (3) there follows, by (4), one and only one transformation (2). For by
(4) the quantities $\partial'$, $\partial''$ are first determined as the greatest common
divisors of $\partial$ with $n'$ and $n''$, and thereupon $c'$ is determined with
respect to the modulus $a'$, and $c''$ with respect to the modulus $a''$, from the two
last congruences (4).

What now matters above all is to show that the
congruences (4) are preserved when the transformations (2)
and (3), in accordance with \S 69, (8) to (12), by means of the two linear transformations
\[
(\omega, \omega+1), \quad \left(\omega, -\frac{1}{\omega}\right)
\]
are transformed.

Following the formulae mentioned, we set:
\weq{5}{
\begin{aligned}
\begin{pmatrix} a, & 0\\ c, & \partial \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0\\ 1, & 1 \end{pmatrix}
&=
\begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0\\ \lambda, & 1 \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} a, & 0\\ c_1, & \partial \end{pmatrix}\\
\begin{pmatrix} a', & 0\\ c', & \partial' \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0\\ 1, & 1 \end{pmatrix}
&=
\begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0\\ \lambda', & 1 \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} a', & 0\\ c_1', & \partial' \end{pmatrix}\\
\begin{pmatrix} a'', & 0\\ c'', & \partial'' \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0\\ 1, & 1 \end{pmatrix}
&=
\begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0\\ \lambda'', & 1 \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} a'', & 0\\ c_2'', & \partial'' \end{pmatrix}. % [sic] German source prints c_2''; parallelism suggests c_1''.
\end{aligned}
}
\weq{6}{
\begin{aligned}
\begin{pmatrix} a, & 0\\ c, & \partial \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} 0, & 1\\ -1, & 0 \end{pmatrix}
&=
\begin{pmatrix} \alpha, & \beta\\ \gamma, & \delta \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} a_2, & 0\\ c_2, & \partial_2 \end{pmatrix}\\
\begin{pmatrix} a', & 0\\ c', & \partial' \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} 0, & 1\\ -1, & 0 \end{pmatrix}
&=
\begin{pmatrix} \alpha', & \beta'\\ \gamma', & \delta' \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} a_2', & 0\\ c_2', & \partial_2' \end{pmatrix}\\
\begin{pmatrix} a'', & 0\\ c'', & \partial'' \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} 0, & 1\\ -1, & 0 \end{pmatrix}
&=
\begin{pmatrix} \alpha'', & \beta''\\ \gamma'', & \delta'' \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} a_2'', & 0\\ c_2'', & \partial_2'' \end{pmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 297 =====
% !PRINTED 276
\weberpage{276}
It follows first of all from \S 69, (9):
\[
c_1 \equiv c+\partial \pmod{a}, \quad c_1' \equiv c'+\partial' \pmod{a'}, \quad c_1'' \equiv c''+\partial'' \pmod{a''},
\]
from which, by (4),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\partial''c_1' &\equiv \partial''c' + \partial \equiv c_1 \pmod{a'}\\
\partial'c_1'' &\equiv \partial'c'' + \partial \equiv c_1 \pmod{a''}
\end{aligned}
\]
in agreement with the congruences (4).

For the composition (6) it follows, by \S 69, (12), that
$\partial_2$, $\partial_2'$, $\partial_2''$ are the greatest common divisors of $a,c$;
$a',c'$; $a'',c''$; but since $\partial''$ is relatively prime to $a'$, and
$\partial''c' \equiv c \pmod{a'}$, $\partial_2'$ is also the greatest common
divisor of $a'$ and $c$, and for the same reasons $\partial_2''$ the greatest
common divisor of $a''$ and $c$. From this one concludes, since
$a'$, $a''$ are relatively prime:
\[
\partial_2 = \partial_2'\partial_2'', \qquad a_2 = a_2'a_2''.
\]
Further, by \S 69, (11), (12), (13):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\partial_2 &= \alpha c - \gamma a, & c_2 &= -\partial\alpha,\\
\partial_2' &= \alpha'c' - \gamma'a', & c_2' &= -\partial'\alpha',
\end{aligned}
\]
hence, by (4):
\[
\partial_2c_2' - c_2\partial_2' \equiv \alpha\alpha'(\partial c' - c\partial') \equiv 0 \pmod{n'},
\]
and consequently also
\[
\partial_2''c_2' - c_2 \equiv 0 \pmod{a_2'},
\]
in agreement with (4), and in the same way it follows that:
\[
\partial_2'c_2'' - c_2 \equiv 0 \pmod{a_2''},
\]
whereby the proof is furnished that the belonging together of the
transformations expressed by (4)
\[
\begin{pmatrix} a, & 0\\ c, & \partial \end{pmatrix}, \quad
\begin{pmatrix} a', & 0\\ c', & \partial' \end{pmatrix}, \quad
\begin{pmatrix} a'', & 0\\ c'', & \partial'' \end{pmatrix}
\]
is not disturbed by the application of any \gesperrt{linear} transformation to $\omega$.
Since we here assume $n$ to be odd, we may always take $c$, $c'$, $c''$
to be divisible by 16; and if $n$, and consequently also $n'$, $n''$, are
indivisible by 3, then $c$, $c'$, $c''$ may also be assumed divisible by 3.
But if $n$ is divisible by 3, then of the two factors $n'$, $n''$ one, say
$n''$, will be divisible by 3, and the other, $n'$, not. It may then still
be assumed that $c'$ is divisible by 3, but not $c$ and $c''$.
In this case the dependence of $c''$ upon $c$ shall be determined
more closely by the congruence
\weq{7}{
\partial'c'' \equiv c \pmod{3a''}.
}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 298 =====
% !PRINTED 277
\weberpage{277}
A solution of this congruence can always be derived from a solution of the
congruence (4) $\partial' c'' \equiv c \ (\mathrm{mod}\ a'')$ by adding to
$c''$ a multiple of $a''$.

By § 69, (9) to (13), the congruence (7) then has as a consequence:
\weq{8}{\lambda \equiv n'\lambda'' \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 3),}
\weq{9}{
\begin{array}{ll}
\alpha \equiv \alpha''\partial'\partial_2', & \beta \equiv \beta''a'\partial_2' \\
\gamma \equiv \gamma''a'\partial_2', & \delta \equiv \delta''\partial'\partial_2'
\end{array}
\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 3).}

Now let $v', v_1', v_2'; v'', v_1'', v_2''$ have for the numbers
$n', n''$ the same meaning that was given to $v, v_1, v_2$ in § 73, (3) for
the number $n$, namely:
\[
v' = f\left(\frac{c' + \partial'\omega}{a'}\right), \qquad
v'' = f\left(\frac{c'' + \partial''\omega}{a''}\right),
\]
\weq{10}{
\begin{array}{ll}
v_1' = \left(\dfrac{2}{a'}\right) f_1\left(\dfrac{c' + \partial'\omega}{a'}\right), &
v_1'' = \left(\dfrac{2}{a''}\right) f_1\left(\dfrac{c'' + \partial''\omega}{a''}\right), \\[2ex]
v_2' = \left(\dfrac{2}{\partial'}\right) f_2\left(\dfrac{c' + \partial'\omega}{a'}\right), &
v_2'' = \left(\dfrac{2}{\partial''}\right) f_2\left(\dfrac{c'' + \partial''\omega}{a''}\right).
\end{array}
}

We apply the table of permutations (4), § 73 to these functions. Since $n'$
is under all circumstances indivisible by 3, the cubic roots of unity are to
be set equal to $\varrho', \sigma' = 1$, while in consequence of the
congruences (8), (9):
\weq{11}{\varrho'' = \varrho^{n'}, \quad \sigma'' = \sigma^{n'}}
results. We accordingly obtain the following permutations that belong together:
\weq{12}{
\begin{array}{llll}
\omega, & v', & v_1', & v_2', \\
-\dfrac{1}{\omega}, & v', & v_2', & v_1', \\
\omega+1, & e^{-\frac{n'\pi i}{24}}v_1', & e^{-\frac{n'\pi i}{24}}v', & e^{\frac{n'\pi i}{12}}v_2', \\
\hline
\omega, & v'', & v_1'', & v_2'', \\
-\dfrac{1}{\omega}, & \varrho^{n'}v'', & \varrho^{n'}v_2'', & \varrho^{n'}v_1'', \\
\omega+1, & \sigma^{n'}e^{-\frac{n''\pi i}{24}}v_1'', & \sigma^{n'}e^{-\frac{n''\pi i}{24}}v'', & \sigma^{n'}e^{\frac{n''\pi i}{12}}v_2'',
\end{array}
}
which hold together with the permutations (4), § 73.

We now distinguish two cases.

1. If
\weq{13}{(n'+1)(n''+1) = 8\mu \equiv 0 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 8)}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 299 =====
% !PRINTED 278
\weberpage{278}
%<<CONT
is, we set
\weq{14}{U = uvv'v'', \quad U_1 = u_1v_1v_1'v_1'', \quad U_2 = u_2v_2v_2'v_2'',}
\weq{15}{
\begin{array}{rl}
2A & = U + (-1)^\mu(U_1+U_2), \\
B & = UU_1 + UU_2 + (-1)^\mu U_1U_2, \\
& = \dfrac{4}{U_1} + \dfrac{4}{U_2} + (-1)^\mu\dfrac{4}{U}.
\end{array}
}

From (12) and § 73, (4) we then obtain the following associated
permutations:
\weq{16}{
\begin{array}{lll}
\omega, & A, & B, \\
-\dfrac{1}{\omega}, & \varrho^{n'+1}A, & \varrho^{-(n'+1)}B, \\
\omega+1, & \sigma^{n'+1}e^{\frac{2\mu\pi i}{3}}A, & \sigma^{-(n'+1)}e^{-\frac{2\mu\pi i}{3}}B.
\end{array}
}

We apply our principle for the derivation of modular equations to these
functions, and remark in addition the following:

The third roots of unity occurring in (16) are $=1$ if either $n$ is
indivisible by 3 and $\mu$ is divisible by 3, or $n''$ is divisible by 3
and $n'$ leaves the residue 2. In these cases every rational function of
$A$ and $B$ is a root of a transformation equation. In the other cases
this property belongs to the cube of such a rational function of $A$ and
$B$, for which the differences of the exponents of all the terms are
congruent to one another with respect to the modulus 3.

If these rational functions are \gesperrt{integral} functions and if
moreover all their values for $q = 0$ are finite, then they must be equal
to a constant, and thereby we obtain transformation equations.

If $n', n''$ are primes, then here too it suffices (cf. § 72) that the
negative powers of $q$ in the development of such a function in ascending
powers of $q$ drop out in the one principal case, namely in that where
\[
\begin{pmatrix} a, & 0 \\ c, & \partial \end{pmatrix}, \quad
\begin{pmatrix} a', & 0 \\ c', & \partial' \end{pmatrix}, \quad
\begin{pmatrix} a'', & 0 \\ c'', & \partial'' \end{pmatrix}
\]
are equal to
\[
\begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0 \\ 0, & n \end{pmatrix}, \quad
\begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0 \\ 0, & n' \end{pmatrix}, \quad
\begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0 \\ 0, & n'' \end{pmatrix},
\]
thus
\[
U = f(\omega)f(n'\omega)f(n''\omega)f(n'n''\omega);
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 300 =====
% !PRINTED 279
\weberpage{279}
%<<CONT
for from the development for this one case one can derive the
developments for the remaining cases, by replacing $\omega$
by
\weq{17}{\dfrac{\omega}{n}, \quad \dfrac{\omega}{n'}, \quad \dfrac{\omega}{n''}}
and then further increasing $\omega$ by integers, whereby no negative
powers of $q$ can be newly introduced.

For carrying out the calculation one makes use of the developments
\weq{18}{
\begin{array}{l}
U = q^{-\frac{(n'+1)(n''+1)}{24}} \times
\Pi(1+q^{2h-1})(1+q^{(2h-1)n'})(1+q^{(2h-1)n''})(1+q^{(2h-1)n}) \\
U_1 = q^{-\frac{(n'+1)(n''+1)}{24}} \times
\Pi(1-q^{2h-1})(1-q^{(2h-1)n'})(1-q^{(2h-1)n''})(1-q^{(2h-1)n}) \\
U_2 = 4q^{\frac{(n'+1)(n''+1)}{12}} \times
\Pi(1+q^{2h})(1+q^{2hn'})(1+q^{2hn''})(1+q^{2hn}),
\end{array}
}
which in the individual cases furnish the power developments of $A$, $B$,
from which the negative powers of $q$ are to be eliminated. In this way
one computes very simply the following equations:
\weq{19}{
\begin{array}{l}
n = 15, \quad A = 1, \\
n = 21, \quad (A^2-B)^2-A = 0, \\
n = 33, \quad A^2-B-A = 4, \\
n = 35, \quad A^2-B-A = 2, \\
n = 55, \quad A^3-B-4A^2-A+4 = 0.
\end{array}
}

2. If
\[
(n'-1)(n''-1) = 8\mu \equiv 0 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 8),
\]
then we set
\weq{20}{
\begin{array}{l}
A = \dfrac{uv}{v'v''} + (-1)^u\left(\dfrac{u_1v_1}{v_1'v_1''} + \dfrac{u_2v_2}{v_2'v_2''}\right), \\[2ex]
B = \dfrac{v'v''}{uv} + (-1)^u\left(\dfrac{v_1'v_1''}{u_1v_1} + \dfrac{v_2'v_2''}{u_2v_2}\right),
\end{array}
}
and obtain, according to (12), the permutations belonging together:
\weq{21}{
\begin{array}{lll}
\omega, & A, & B, \\
-\dfrac{1}{\omega}, & \varrho^{1-n'}A, & \varrho^{n'-1}B, \\
\omega+1, & \sigma^{1-n'}e^{\frac{2u\pi i}{3}}A, & \sigma^{n'-1}e^{-\frac{2u\pi i}{3}}B.
\end{array}
}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 301 =====
% !PRINTED 280
\weberpage{280}
We can therefore apply the same procedure as above if we add the further
restriction that only \gesperrt{symmetric} functions of $A$ and $B$, that
is, rational functions of $AB$, $A+B$, are used, because \gesperrt{only} under this
assumption do all the others follow from one of the values of such a
function by the permutations (17). The following examples are easily
computed:
\weq{22}{
\begin{array}{l}
n = 15, \quad AB+1 = 0, \\
n = 35, \quad 2(A+B)-AB = 5 \\
n = 39, \quad 2(A+B)-AB = 3.
\end{array}
}

The computation presents no insurmountable difficulties even in still
more complicated cases. Thus in the memoir Acta mathematica Bd. II,
S. 359 I have communicated the following formula for the case $n = 105$:
\[
\begin{array}{l}
A = \sum \dfrac{f(3\omega)f(5\omega)f(7\omega)f(105\omega)}{f(\omega)f(15\omega)f(21\omega)f(35\omega)}, \\[2ex]
B = \sum \dfrac{f(\omega)f(15\omega)f(21\omega)f(35\omega)}{f(3\omega)f(5\omega)f(7\omega)f(105\omega)}, \\[2ex]
A^2+B^2-4(A+B)^3+10AB(A+B) \\
\quad{}+4(A+B)^2+10AB+14(A+B)+5 = 0,
\end{array}
\]
if the sums $\Sigma$ in $A$ and $B$ refer to the three functions
$f, f_1, f_2$.

\begin{center}
§ 77.\quad \gesperrt{Geometric interpretation of the irrational modular equations as}\\
\gesperrt{modular correspondences.}
\end{center}

We make the content of the irrational forms of the modular equations
more intuitive by means of a geometric interpretation. Let us first
consider the case $n \equiv -1 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 8)$ and put
\weq{1}{x = f(\omega), \quad y = f_1(\omega), \quad z = f_2(\omega),}
so that, if we regard $x, y, z$ as Cartesian coordinates of a point
$P$, a space curve is thereby represented, which we can also express
by the two equations:
\weq{2}{
\begin{array}{c}
x^8 - y^8 - z^8 = 0 \\
xyz = \sqrt{2}
\end{array}
}
and which we shall call the \gesperrt{fundamental curve}. This curve is
therefore of the 24th order. One can
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 302 =====
% !PRINTED 281
\weberpage{281}
%<<CONT
a plane curve of the third order, if one sets $x^8=X$,
$y^8=Y$:

\weq{3}{X\,Y(X-Y)=16.}

If we set [§ 75, (1)]

\weq{4}{\xi=f\left(\dfrac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right),\ \eta=\left(\dfrac{2}{a}\right)f_1\left(\dfrac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right),\ \zeta=\left(\dfrac{2}{\partial}\right)f_2\left(\dfrac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right),}

then the quantity $\xi, \eta, \zeta$ likewise satisfies the equations (2), since % [sic] German source prints the singular noun and verb for three quantities.
\[
\left(\dfrac{2}{a}\right)\left(\dfrac{2}{\partial}\right)=\left(\dfrac{2}{n}\right)=+1
\]
holds, and the point $\Pi$, whose coordinates are $\xi, \eta, \zeta$, therefore also lies
on the fundamental curve.

An equation
\[
\Phi\,(x,\,y,\,z,\,\xi,\,\eta,\,\zeta)=0
\]
% [sic] The German source calls this equation (5), but prints no number here and assigns (5) to the following display.
denotes, when the point $P$ is held fixed, a \gesperrt{surface} on
which $\Pi$ is to lie, and the intersection of this surface with the
fundamental curve gives a certain number of points $\Pi$ that correspond to the
point $P$. In the same way, to a fixed point $\Pi$ there corresponds
a certain number of points $P$, and this assignment is called
a \gesperrt{correspondence on the fundamental curve.} If the point $P$
coincides with one of the points $\Pi$ corresponding to it, we obtain a \gesperrt{double point or coincidence of the correspondence.}

If equation (5) is not altered by the interchange of $P$ with $\Pi$,
the correspondence is a \gesperrt{mutual one}.
Such correspondences are given by equations (8), (9),
(10), § 75.

By § 75, (3) we have then to set

\weq{5}{\begin{aligned} 2A &= x\xi+(-1)^{\frac{n+1}{8}}(y\eta+z\zeta)\\ B &= x\xi y\eta+x\xi z\zeta+(-1)^{\frac{n+1}{8}}y\eta z\zeta \end{aligned}}

$A$ is of the first, $B$ of the second degree with respect to
the coordinates of each of the two points $P$ and $\Pi$.

We wish to determine the degree of these correspondences, that is, the
number of points $\Pi$ corresponding to a point $P$. In doing so we have to multiply the degree of the equation $\Phi=0$ with
respect to $\xi, \eta, \zeta$ by the degree of the fundamental curve, that is, by 24,
and there results:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 303 =====
% !PRINTED 282
\weberpage{282}
%<<CONT
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
\text{for } n=7, & m=24,\\
\textquotedblbase\quad n=23, & m=24,\\
\textquotedblbase\quad n=31, & m=96,\\
\textquotedblbase\quad n=47, & m=48,\\
\textquotedblbase\quad n=71, & m=72,\\
\textquotedblbase\quad n=15, & m=72.
\end{array}
\]

In the cases 23, 47, 71 the degree of the correspondence is therefore
equal to the degree of the corresponding modular equation, that is,
equal to the number of the transformations in question; in the cases
$n=7, 31, 15$ the degree is \gesperrt{three times} the degree of the
modular equations.

What do these supernumerary points signify? They are explained by
the fact that in these cases, in which $n\equiv 0, 1$
$\pmod 3$, the exponents $h+2k$ in the function $\Phi_{a,c,\partial}$ [§ 75, (5)], which by the
above equation (5) is equal to a constant, leave the same residue
with respect to the modulus 3 in all terms, and
that accordingly the equation $\Phi=0$, and likewise the equations (2),
remain satisfied if $\xi, \eta, \zeta$ are multiplied by an arbitrary third root of unity. Any three points of the
correspondence therefore give the same transformation.

We could also, if $x, y, z$ are determined by (1), have put,
in place of (4),

\weq{6}{\xi=f\left(\dfrac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right),\ \eta=\left(\dfrac{2}{\partial}\right)f_2\left(\dfrac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right),\ \zeta=\left(\dfrac{2}{a}\right)f_1\left(\dfrac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right)}

and consequently for $A, B$:

\weq{7}{\begin{aligned} 2A &= x\xi+(-1)^{\frac{n+1}{8}}(y\zeta+z\xi),\\ B &= x\xi y\zeta+x\xi z\eta+(-1)^{\frac{n+1}{8}}y\eta z\zeta \end{aligned}} % [sic] German source prints z\xi in 2A; the symmetric pattern suggests z\eta.

The fundamental curve and the degree of the correspondence
would then have remained the same, but the coincidences would have
acquired a different and indeed simpler meaning. In
both cases the coincidences belong to the singular values
of the modular functions, in which $\omega$ is an imaginary quadratic
irrationality, as we shall see more precisely in
what follows.

In the case $n\equiv 3 \pmod 8$ we set
\[
x=f^2(\omega),\ y=f_1^2(\omega),\ z=f_2^2(\omega),
\]
\weq{8}{\xi=f^2\left(\dfrac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right),\ \eta=f_1^2\left(\dfrac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right),\ \varrho=f_2^2\left(\dfrac{c+\partial\omega}{a}\right),}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 304 =====
% !PRINTED 283
\weberpage{283}
%<<CONT
and obtain a fundamental curve

\weq{9}{\begin{aligned} x^4-y^4-z^4 &= 0,\\ x\,y\,z &= 2, \end{aligned}}

which is only of degree 12. We then have further, according to § 75:

\weq{10}{\begin{aligned} 4A &= x\xi-y\eta-z\varrho,\\ B &= x\xi y\eta+x\xi z\varrho-y\eta z\varrho, \end{aligned}}

and for the degree $m$ of the correspondence one obtains, according to
§ 75 (13):
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
n=3, & m=12,\\
n=11, & m=12,\\
n=19, & m=60,
\end{array}
\]
and so again, as in the previous case, when $n\equiv 0, 1 \pmod 3$,
a number three times too large.

If finally $n\equiv 1 \pmod 4$, then one sets
\[
x=f^4(\omega),\ y=f_1^4(\omega),\ z=f_2^4(\omega)
\]
and obtains a fundamental curve of the sixth degree.

For $n=5$ the correct number $m=6$ results.

\noindent\rule{0.3\textwidth}{0.4pt}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 305 =====
% !PRINTED none
% Part-title / section-opening page: no running head / page number visible
% in any of the three bands (top band is essentially blank). Content:
% the "Achter Abschnitt." part title with its descriptive subtitle, a
% dividing rule, then the "§ 78." section heading and the opening of its
% body text.
\begin{center}
\gesperrt{Eighth Chapter.}

\gesperrt{The Group of the Transformation Equations and the Equation of Degree 5.}
\end{center}

\noindent\rule{0.3\textwidth}{0.4pt}

\begin{center}
§ 78.

\gesperrt{The Galois Group of the Transformation Equations for a Prime Degree.}
\end{center}

A more thorough algebraic study of the transformation equations requires a
knowledge of their \gesperrt{Galois} group. Since we have derived the transformation
equations from the division equations, whose group is known to us (§ 63), we
can form the group of the transformation equations as well.

The transformation equations arose (§ 65) from the fact that the roots of the
division equations admitted of a partition into rows which are not torn apart
by the permutations of the group of the division equation, but are only
interchanged among one another.

To each of these rows there corresponds a definite root of a transformation
equation, and the \gesperrt{group of the latter
therefore consists of the totality of the permutations that are produced among the rows by the group of the division equation.}

If the degree of transformation $n$ is \gesperrt{an odd prime $p$}, this group admits a
very elegant representation which is suited to further investigations, and we
now hold fast to this assumption.

In § 65, (3) the necessary and sufficient condition was already determined for
two roots of the division equation

\weq{1}{x_{\mu,\mu'},\quad x_{\nu,\nu'}}

to belong to the same row $R$, namely the congruence

\weq{2}{\mu\,\nu'-\nu\,\mu' \equiv 0 \pmod{p}.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 306 =====
% !PRINTED 285
\weberpage{285}

If we now, as is customary in number theory (\gesperrt{Gauss}, Disquisitiones arithmeticae, art. 31), understand by the symbol
\[
\frac{a}{b} \ (\mathrm{mod}\ p)
\]
an \gesperrt{integer} [or class of numbers (mod $p$)] which, multiplied by $b$, leaves the residue $a$ on division by $p$, then, provided that $\mu'$ $\nu'$ are not divisible by $p$, we can also write the congruence (2) that defines a sequence as follows:
\weq{3}{\frac{\mu}{\mu'} \equiv \frac{\nu}{\nu'} \ (\mathrm{mod}\ p),}
and we are thus naturally led to denote this sequence $R$ by the value of the ratio
\weq{4}{\frac{\mu}{\mu'} \equiv z \ (\mathrm{mod}\ p),}
which can be congruent to any one of the numbers $0, 1, \ldots, p-1$ and which is invariable for a whole sequence. At first one sequence here remains undesignated, namely that in which $\mu'$, and consequently all $\nu'$, are divisible by $p$; but this sequence too is subsumed very well under the general designation if, in the case $\mu' \equiv 0 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ p)$, we put
\weq{5}{\frac{\mu}{\mu'} \equiv \infty \ (\mathrm{mod}\ p)}
so that we thus obtain a further $(p+1)$th sequence $R_\infty$. The totality of the sequences, whose number amounts to $p+1$, is accordingly to be denoted by
\weq{6}{R_\infty, R_0, R_1, \ldots, R_{p-1}.}

Correspondingly, for the associated roots of a transformation equation the designations
\weq{7}{v_\infty, v_0, v_1, \ldots, v_{p-1}}
will have to be used.

If, for example, we take the invariant equation (§ 69) as our basis, then [according to the determinations of § 68, (10) concerning the numbers $a$, $c$, $\partial$] we must put
\weq{8}{v_\infty = j(p\,\omega), \quad v_z = j\left(\frac{z+\omega}{p}\right)}
and likewise, if any other transformation equation is chosen.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 307 =====
% !PRINTED 286
\weberpage{286}

By this mode of notation we are in a position to derive the group of the transformation equation at once from that of the division equation.

We first fix as domain of rationality the totality of the rational functions of $\varkappa^2$ with \gesperrt{rational numerical coefficients}.

By § 63, 3. the group of the division equation consists, in this domain of rationality, of all substitutions by which $\mu$, $\mu'$ are carried over into
\[
\begin{array}{c} \partial \mu - b \mu' \\ -c \mu + a \mu' \end{array}
\]
where $a$, $b$, $c$, $\partial$ are arbitrary integers taken according to the modulus $p$, whose determinant
\weq{9}{\Delta = a\partial - bc}
is not divisible by $p$; and the number of all these substitutions amounts to
\weq{10}{p(p-1)(p^2-1) \qquad [\S\ 63,\,(27)]}

But from this there results, by the mode of notation (4), (5), \gesperrt{the group of the transformation equation as consisting of all} the permutations which the symbol
\weq{11}{\left(z, \frac{\partial z - b}{-cz+a}\right) \ (\mathrm{mod}\ p)}
\gesperrt{expresses.}

We denote a substitution $(z, z')$, when
\weq{12}{z \equiv \frac{c+\partial z'}{a+bz'} \ (\mathrm{mod}\ p)}
holds, similarly as before by
\weq{13}{\begin{pmatrix} a, & b \\ c, & \partial \end{pmatrix},}
and obtain for the composition of two such substitutions, when
\[
z' \equiv \frac{c'+\partial' z''}{a'+b'z''} \ (\mathrm{mod}\ p)
\]
holds, the rule:
\weq{14}{(z,z')(z'z'') \equiv \begin{pmatrix} a, & b \\ c, & \partial \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} a', & b' \\ c', & \partial' \end{pmatrix} \equiv \begin{pmatrix} aa'+bc', & ab'+b\partial' \\ ca'+\partial c', & cb'+\partial\partial' \end{pmatrix} \ (\mathrm{mod}\ p),}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 308 =====
% !PRINTED 287
\weberpage{287}
%<<CONT
in agreement with the rule for the composition of two transformations in § 28. The substitution (11) is accordingly to be denoted by
\[
\begin{pmatrix} \partial, & c \\ b, & a \end{pmatrix}.
\]
The group formed by all substitutions of this form [according to (14)] we denote by $\mathfrak{L}$ (group of linear substitutions).

The functions (12) of $z'$, and therefore also the substitutions (13), remain unchanged if the four numbers $a$, $b$, $c$, $\partial$ are multiplied by one and the same factor not divisible by $p$, and from this there follows, by (10), the number of these functions, or the degree of the group $\mathfrak{L}$
\weq{15}{p(p^2-1),}
which one also finds easily by direct enumeration.

If in one of the substitutions (13) the four numbers $a$, $b$, $c$, $\partial$ are multiplied by a common factor indivisible by $p$, then the determinant $\Delta$ is multiplied by the \gesperrt{square} of this factor. Hence it is not the determinant $\Delta$, but rather its quadratic character, that is, the value of the symbol
\[
\left(\frac{\Delta}{p}\right)
\]
that is preserved under this multiplication.

If we compose two of the substitutions (13), their determinants are multiplied together, and from this it follows that \gesperrt{all substitutions of the group $\mathfrak{L}$ in which $\Delta$ is a quadratic residue of $p$ form a group among themselves, which we shall denote by $\mathfrak{L}_0$.}

The group $\mathfrak{L}_0$ is a (proper) divisor of the group $\mathfrak{L}$ of index 2.

If one composes the substitutions of $\mathfrak{L}_0$ with any substitution $(z, \beta z) = \begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0 \\ 0, & \beta^{-1} \end{pmatrix}$, where $\beta$, and therefore also $\beta^{-1}$, is a quadratic non-residue of $p$, then one obtains the whole group $\mathfrak{L}$.

If $\Delta$ is a quadratic residue of $p$, then one can choose the common factor to be attached to $a$, $b$, $c$, $\partial$ in such a way that $\Delta \equiv 1 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ p)$, so that we can also represent the group $\mathfrak{L}_0$ by
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 309 =====
% !PRINTED 288
\weberpage{288}
%<<CONT
\weq{16}{\begin{pmatrix} \alpha, & \beta \\ \gamma, & \delta \end{pmatrix}, \quad \alpha\delta - \beta\gamma \equiv 1 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ p).}
In one of these substitutions the numbers $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$, $\delta$ are determined, with respect to the modulus $p$, up to the common sign. The degree of the group $\mathfrak{L}_0$ is
\weq{17}{\frac{1}{2}p(p^2-1).}

One arrives at the form (16) directly, however, if one takes as the group of the division equation not the group $\mathfrak{A}$ but the group $\mathfrak{B}$ of § 63, that is, if one adjoins \gesperrt{the $p$th roots of unity to the domain of rationality}; from which the theorem flows:

\gesperrt{The group $\mathfrak{L}_0$ is the group of the transformation equation when the $p$th roots of unity are adjoined to the domain of rationality.}

For the reduction of the group $\mathfrak{L}$ to the group $\mathfrak{L}_0$, however, the adjunction of a two-valued function already suffices, and with the adjunction of the $p$th roots of unity too much has therefore been done. To recognise which irrationality it is \gesperrt{necessary} to adjoin, the theorems of §§ 63, 65 serve.

In § 63, 3. we have seen that the $p$th root of unity $\varrho$ is rationally representable by the roots of the division equation, and that by a substitution of the group $\mathfrak{A}$ whose determinant is congruent to $m$, $\varrho$ passes over into $\varrho^m$; further, we proved in § 65 that by the adjunction of all the roots of a transformation equation the group of the division equation is reduced to the group $\mathfrak{A}_0$, which consists of all substitutions of the form
\weq{18}{\begin{pmatrix} a, & 0 \\ 0, & a \end{pmatrix}}
where $a$ is an arbitrary number not divisible by $p$. The determinants of the substitutions of $\mathfrak{A}_0$ are therefore squares, and are consequently congruent, with respect to the modulus $p$, each with one of the $\frac{1}{2}(p-1)$ \gesperrt{quadratic residues} of $p$.

The sum
\weq{19}{A = \overset{a}{\Sigma}\varrho^a,}
in which all the \gesperrt{quadratic residues} of $p$ are to be put for $a$, therefore remains unchanged by the substitutions
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 310 =====
% !PRINTED 289
\weberpage{289}
%<<CONT
of $\mathfrak{A}_0$ and is consequently expressible rationally through
the roots of the transformation equation. The sum $A$ remains
unchanged under the substitutions of the group $\mathfrak{B}$, and hence
also under $\mathfrak{L}_0$, while under the substitutions of $\mathfrak{A}$, and
therefore also of $\mathfrak{L}$, it takes two different values, namely,
when $b$ runs through the sequence of non-residues,
\[
A = \overset{a}{\Sigma}\varrho^a, \qquad B = \overset{b}{\Sigma}\varrho^b.
\]

$A$ is therefore a function belonging to the group $\mathfrak{L}_0$, and
by its adjunction $\mathfrak{L}$ is reduced to $\mathfrak{L}_0$.

The values of the sums $A$, $B$ are, however, known (Bd. I, \S\,179):
\[
A = \frac{-1 \pm \sqrt{(-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2}}\,p}}{2}, \qquad
B = \frac{-1 \mp \sqrt{(-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2}}\,p}}{2}.
\]

The sign of the root depends on the choice of the root $\varrho$
and can be determined, but does not come into consideration here.
We have therefore the theorem:

\gesperrt{The group of the transformation equation is $\mathfrak{L}_0$,
when $\sqrt{(-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2}}\,p}$ is adjoined to the domain of
rationality.}

The group of the invariant equation can also be derived, without
the division of the elliptic functions, in the following simple
way; in doing so one obtains, however, only the monodromy
group, i.\,e. the group in the field of the rational
functions of $j(\omega)$, without regard to the constants to be
adjoined. We restrict ourselves to the case of a prime degree
$p$ of the transformation, and set
\weq{20}{v_c = j\!\left(\frac{c+\omega}{p}\right), \qquad v_\infty = j(p\omega), \qquad u = j(\omega),}
where $c$ is to be taken with respect to the modulus $p$.

If one applies to $\omega$ a linear substitution $S = \begin{pmatrix}\alpha, & \beta \\ \gamma, & \delta\end{pmatrix}$,
then $j(\omega)$ remains unchanged, and $v_c$ passes into $v_{c'}$. To
find $c'$, one has to seek a second linear substitution
$S' = \begin{pmatrix}\alpha', & \beta' \\ \gamma', & \delta'\end{pmatrix}$, so that
\[
\begin{pmatrix}\alpha', & \beta' \\ \gamma', & \delta'\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}p, & 0 \\ c', & 1\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}p, & 0 \\ c, & 1\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}\alpha, & \beta \\ \gamma, & \delta\end{pmatrix}
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 311 =====
% !PRINTED 290
\weberpage{290}
%<<CONT
or
\[
\begin{aligned}
p\alpha' + c'\beta' &= p\alpha, & \beta' &= p\beta\\
p\gamma' + c'\delta' &= c\alpha+\gamma, & \delta' &= c\beta+\delta.
\end{aligned}
\]
From this there follows, by the third equation: $c'\delta' \equiv
c\alpha+\gamma$, and with the help of the fourth:
\[
c' \equiv \frac{c\alpha+\gamma}{c\beta+\delta} \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ p).
\]

If $c\beta+\delta \equiv 0$, then $c' \equiv \infty$, and if
$c \equiv \infty$, then $c' \equiv \alpha/\beta$.

In the application to the determination of $c$, $c'$ one may
replace the $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$, $\delta$ by congruent numbers $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$
whose determinant $ad-bc$ is a quadratic residue of $c$, % [sic] German source prints c; mathematically p is expected.
and it can
also be shown that in this way every substitution of the group
$\mathfrak{L}_0$ can be obtained. Every function of $v_c$, then, which
remains unchanged under the substitutions of the group $\mathfrak{L}_0$,
remains unchanged also when a linear substitution is applied to
$\omega$, and is consequently a rational function of $j(\omega)$. But of
the nature of the coefficients in this function this consideration teaches
us nothing, and therefore $\mathfrak{L}_0$ is recognised only as the monodromy
group of the invariant equation.

\begin{center}
\S\,79. \gesperrt{Investigation of the Group $\mathfrak{L}_0$}\textsuperscript{1}).
\end{center}

In the 10th chapter of Band II we investigated the congruence group
and its divisors quite generally. We carry this investigation through
here once more in a special form, so far as it bears on the transformation
problem.

The substitutions contained in $\mathfrak{L}_0$
\weq{1}{\begin{pmatrix}a, & b \\ c, & \partial\end{pmatrix} = \left(z, \frac{-c+az}{\partial-bz}\right),}
in which
\weq{2}{\varDelta = a\partial - bc}
is a quadratic residue of $p$, can, as already remarked above,
be brought into the form:
\weq{3}{\begin{pmatrix}\alpha, & \beta \\ \gamma, & \delta\end{pmatrix} = \left(z, \frac{-\gamma+\alpha z}{\delta-\beta z}\right),}
%CONT>>

\footnotetext{$^{1}$) On the group of linear substitutions $\mathfrak{L}_0$ cf.:
\gesperrt{Galois}, Liouvilles Journal, Bd.\,XI. \gesperrt{Serret},
Algèbre supérieure, Section IV, Chapitre IV. C. \gesperrt{Jordan}, Traité des
Substitutions. \gesperrt{Gierster}, Gruppe der Modulargleichungen.
Mathematische Annalen, Bd.\,18.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 312 =====
% !PRINTED 291
\weberpage{291}
%<<CONT
in which
\weq{4}{\alpha\delta - \beta\gamma \equiv 1 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ p),}
and if by $\sqrt{\varDelta}$ $(\mathrm{mod}\ p)$ we understand an integer
whose square is congruent with $\varDelta$ with respect to the modulus
$p$, we have only to set:
\[
\begin{aligned}
a &\equiv \alpha\sqrt{\varDelta}, & b &\equiv \beta\sqrt{\varDelta}\\
c &\equiv \gamma\sqrt{\varDelta}, & \partial &\equiv \delta\sqrt{\varDelta}
\end{aligned}
\quad (\mathrm{mod}\ p)
\]
In the form (3) the signs of $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$, $\delta$ can
still be changed simultaneously.

We ask for those elements $z$ which remain unchanged under a substitution
of the form (3). These are determined by the congruence
\[
z \equiv \frac{\gamma+\delta z}{\alpha+\beta z} \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ p),
\]
or
\weq{5}{\beta z^2 + (\alpha-\delta) z - \gamma \equiv 0 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ p),}
a congruence which, if it is not identical, has at most two incongruent
roots. To obtain these we write the congruence (5), first under the
assumption that $\beta$ is not divisible by $p$, thus:
\[
\left(\beta z + \frac{\alpha-\delta}{2}\right)^2 \equiv \left(\frac{\alpha-\delta}{2}\right)^2 + \beta\gamma \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ p),
\]
or with the help of (4):
\weq{6}{\left(\beta z + \frac{\alpha-\delta}{2}\right)^2 \equiv \left(\frac{\alpha+\delta}{2}\right)^2 - 1 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ p).}
Accordingly three different cases are to be distinguished:
\[
\mathrm{I.} \qquad \left(\frac{\alpha+\delta}{2}\right)^2 - 1 \equiv 0 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ p);
\]
then the congruence (5) has one root; there is one and
only one element $z$ that remains unchanged.
\[
\mathrm{II.} \qquad \left(\frac{\alpha+\delta}{2}\right)^2 - 1 \ \text{\gesperrt{quadratic residue of $p$}};
\]
the congruence (5) has two different roots; there are two
elements $z$ that remain unchanged.
\[
\mathrm{III.} \qquad \left(\frac{\alpha+\delta}{2}\right)^2 - 1 \ \text{\gesperrt{quadratic non-residue of $p$}};
\]
the congruence (5) has no root at all, and all elements $z$
\gesperrt{are displaced.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 313 =====
% !PRINTED 292
\weberpage{292}
If $\beta \equiv 0$, then (5) always has the one root $z = \infty$; if
moreover $\delta \equiv \alpha$, and $\gamma$ not $\equiv 0$ $(\mathrm{mod}\ p)$, then there is only this
one; in this case, however,
\[
\alpha\delta \equiv 1, \qquad \alpha \equiv \delta, \qquad \left(\frac{\alpha+\delta}{2}\right)^2 \equiv 1 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ p),
\]
and condition I. is satisfied. But if at the same time $\gamma \equiv 0$ $(\mathrm{mod}\ p)$,
then the substitution is the \gesperrt{identical one}.

If $\beta \equiv 0$, but $\alpha-\delta$ not $\equiv 0$ $(\mathrm{mod}\ p)$, then (5) has yet
a second root; since now $\alpha\delta \equiv 1$ $(\mathrm{mod}\ p)$, we have:
\[
\left(\frac{\alpha+\delta}{2}\right)^2 - 1 \equiv \left(\frac{\alpha-\delta}{2}\right)^2 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ p),
\]
hence a quadratic residue, and condition II. is satisfied. We
summarise these theorems as follows:

\gesperrt{In case I. one element or all elements remain
unchanged, in case II. two elements remain unchanged
 and in case III. all elements are
changed.}

When we repeat one and the same substitution
\weq{7}{A = \begin{pmatrix}\alpha, & \beta \\ \gamma, & \delta\end{pmatrix}}
several times, the substitutions
\[
A, \ A^2, \ A^3 \dots,
\]
arise, in whose sequence the identical substitution $\begin{pmatrix}1, & 0 \\ 0, & 1\end{pmatrix}$
must once occur. If $n$ is the least positive number for which
\[
A^n = \begin{pmatrix}1, & 0 \\ 0, & 1\end{pmatrix}
\]
holds, then $n$ is called the degree of $A$ (Bd. II, \S\,2).

If we set, for an arbitrary $m$,
\[
A^m = \begin{pmatrix}\alpha_m, & \beta_m \\ \gamma_m, & \delta_m\end{pmatrix},
\]
then for the computation of the numbers $\alpha_m$, $\beta_m$, $\gamma_m$,
$\delta_m$ we obtain the following system of recurrent formulae:
\weq{8}{\begin{aligned}
\alpha_{m+1} &= \alpha\alpha_m+\beta\gamma_m, & \beta_{m+1} &= \alpha\beta_m+\beta\delta_m,\\
\gamma'_{m+1} &= \gamma\alpha_m+\delta\gamma_m, & \delta_{m+1} &= \gamma\beta_m+\delta\delta_m.
\end{aligned}} % [sic] printed with a prime on \gamma'_{m+1}, inconsistent with the other three terms

From these the numbers $\alpha_m$, $\beta_m$,
$\gamma_m$, $\delta_m$ can be computed with particular ease in case I.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 314 =====
% !PRINTED 293
\weberpage{293}

In this case, since the signs of $\alpha$, $\beta$,
$\gamma$, $\delta$ may all be reversed at the same time, we may assume:
\[
\alpha+\delta\equiv 2, \quad \alpha\delta-\beta\gamma\equiv 1 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ p),
\]
and thus we obtain from (8):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\alpha_2 &\equiv -1+2\alpha, & \beta_2 &\equiv 2\beta\\
\delta_2 &\equiv -1+2\delta, & \gamma_2 &\equiv 2\gamma\\
\alpha_3 &\equiv -2+3\alpha, & \beta_3 &\equiv 3\beta\\
\delta_3 &\equiv -2+3\delta, & \gamma_3 &\equiv 3\gamma
\end{aligned}\ \ (\mathrm{mod}\ p),
\]
from which, by the inference from $m$ to $m+1$, it follows that:
\weq{9}{\begin{aligned}
\alpha_m &\equiv -(m-1)+m\alpha, & \beta_m &\equiv m\beta\\
\delta_m &\equiv -(m-1)+m\delta, & \gamma_m &\equiv m\gamma
\end{aligned}\ \ (\mathrm{mod}\ p).}
\gesperrt{From this one sees that all the $A^m$ again
belong to Case I., and that $p$ is the degree of $A$.}

The analogous consideration of the two other cases has been carried out by
\gesperrt{Serret}, but appears dispensable for our purpose.

On the other hand, we wish to add here the further theorem, \gesperrt{that
the whole group $\mathfrak{L}_0$ can be composed out of the
two following special substitutions}
\weq{10}{A=\begin{pmatrix}1, & 0\\ 1, & 1\end{pmatrix}, \quad B=\begin{pmatrix}0, & 1\\ -1, & 0\end{pmatrix}.}
The proof follows from \S\,30, if one observes that
for every system of numbers $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$, $\delta$ satisfying the condition $\alpha\delta-\beta\gamma\equiv 1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ p)$
the system of numbers $\alpha'$, $\beta'$, $\gamma'$, $\delta'$ can be
chosen so that
\[
\begin{pmatrix}\alpha', & \beta'\\ \gamma', & \delta'\end{pmatrix} \equiv \begin{pmatrix}\alpha, & \beta\\ \gamma, & \delta\end{pmatrix}\ (\mathrm{mod}\ p) \ \text{and}\ \alpha'\delta'-\beta'\gamma'=1
\]
holds. All substitutions of $\mathfrak{L}_0$ are therefore contained among those considered in \S\,30.
But here we can also easily exhibit the actual
composition of an arbitrary substitution in $\mathfrak{L}_0$ out of $A$ and
$B$, and so carry out the proof independently of \S\,30.

For if in the first place $c$ is an arbitrary number not divisible by $p$,
then actual calculation easily gives
\weq{11}{A^c=\begin{pmatrix}1, & 0\\ c, & 1\end{pmatrix}, \quad C=\begin{pmatrix}c, & 0\\ 0, & c^{-1}\end{pmatrix}=A^{-c^{-1}}BA^{-c}BA^{-c^{-1}}B,}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 315 =====
% !PRINTED 294
\weberpage{294}
%<<CONT
and then, if $\begin{pmatrix}\alpha, & \beta\\ \gamma, & \delta\end{pmatrix}$ is an arbitrary substitution in $\mathfrak{L}_0$ and
$\beta$ is different from $0$:
\weq{12}{\begin{pmatrix}\alpha, & \beta\\ \gamma, & \delta\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1, & 0\\ \delta\beta^{-1}, & 1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\beta, & 0\\ 0, & \beta^{-1}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0, & 1\\ -1, & 0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1, & 0\\ \alpha\beta^{-1}, & 1\end{pmatrix},}
and if $\beta=0$:
\weq{13}{\begin{pmatrix}\alpha, & 0\\ \gamma, & \alpha^{-1}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha, & 0\\ 0, & \alpha^{-1}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1, & 0\\ \gamma\alpha, & 1\end{pmatrix}.}
\gesperrt{From this theorem it is to be concluded that a group contained
 in $\mathfrak{L}_0$ which contains the two substitutions $A, B$
must necessarily be identical with $\mathfrak{L}_0$.}

\begin{center}
\S\,80. \gesperrt{Normal divisors of the group $\mathfrak{L}_0$.}
\end{center}

In order to learn the reductions of the transformation equation
 that may perhaps be possible, it is above all necessary to investigate the divisors
 of the group $\mathfrak{L}_0$. We ask first after
the existence of a \gesperrt{normal divisor} $\mathfrak{R}$ of $\mathfrak{L}_0$ (Bd. II, \S\,3)\footnote{After \gesperrt{Galois}: \glqq Proper divisors\grqq{}.}.

If
\weq{1}{S=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha, & \beta\\ \gamma, & \delta\end{pmatrix}}
is any substitution in $\mathfrak{R}$ different from the identical substitution,
 then, by the nature of the normal divisor, every
substitution
\weq{2}{U=TST^{-1}}
is likewise contained in $\mathfrak{R}$, if
\weq{3}{T=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha', & \beta'\\ \gamma', & \delta'\end{pmatrix}}
is an \gesperrt{arbitrary} substitution in $\mathfrak{L}_0$.
We set ourselves the task of determining $T$ and $\xi$ in such a way that
\weq{4}{U=\begin{pmatrix}0, & 1\\ -1, & \xi\end{pmatrix}}
results. This condition can also be written thus:
\[
\begin{pmatrix}\alpha', & \beta'\\ \gamma', & \delta'\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\alpha, & \beta\\ \gamma, & \delta\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0, & 1\\ -1, & \xi\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\alpha', & \beta'\\ \gamma', & \delta'\end{pmatrix},
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 316 =====
% !PRINTED 295
\weberpage{295}
%<<CONT
and leads to the congruences:
\weq{5}{\begin{aligned}
1.&\quad \alpha'\alpha+\beta'\gamma \equiv \gamma'\\
2.&\quad \alpha'\beta+\beta'\delta \equiv \delta'\\
3.&\quad \gamma'\alpha+\delta'\gamma \equiv -\alpha'+\gamma'\xi\\
4.&\quad \gamma'\beta+\delta'\delta \equiv -\beta'+\delta'\xi
\end{aligned}\ \ (\mathrm{mod}\ p),}
and from 1. and 2. there follows further:
\weq{6}{\begin{aligned}
5.&\quad \alpha' \equiv \gamma'\delta-\delta'\gamma\\
6.&\quad \beta' \equiv -\gamma'\beta+\delta'\alpha
\end{aligned}\ \ (\mathrm{mod}\ p).}
If these values are substituted in (5) 3. and 4., it follows that:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\gamma'(\alpha+\delta-\xi) &\equiv 0\\
\delta'(\alpha+\delta-\xi) &\equiv 0
\end{aligned}\ \ (\mathrm{mod}\ p),
\]
from which, since $\gamma'$, $\delta'$ cannot both be divisible by $p$, it follows that:
\weq{7}{\xi \equiv \alpha+\delta \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ p);}
if $\xi$ is determined in this way, then in (5) the congruences 3., 4. follow
from 1., 2. But if one substitutes $\gamma'$, $\delta'$ from 1., 2. in
\weq{8}{\alpha'\delta'-\beta'\gamma' \equiv 1 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ p)}
then one obtains
\weq{9}{\alpha'^2\beta+\alpha'\beta'(\delta-\alpha)-\beta'^2\gamma \equiv 1 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ p).}
If $\alpha'$, $\beta'$ are determined from this, then all the requirements stated
in (5), and hence also in (2), (4), are satisfied.

It therefore remains only to show that the congruence (9) is always
solvable.

This possibility is evident if $\beta$ or $-\gamma$ is a quadratic
residue of $p$; for then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\alpha' &\equiv \sqrt{\beta^{-1}}, & \beta' &\equiv 0\\
\text{or}\quad \alpha' &\equiv 0, & \beta' &\equiv \sqrt{-\gamma^{-1}}
\end{aligned}\ \ (\mathrm{mod}\ p)
\]
satisfies the requirement laid down.

In what follows we must now distinguish whether the substitution $S$
belongs to class I, II, III of the preceding section.

If first
\[
\text{I.} \qquad \left(\frac{\alpha+\delta}{2}\right)^2 \equiv 1 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ p),
\]
then, if we put $S^m$ in place of $S$, by \S\,79, (9),
$\beta$ passes into $m\beta$, $\gamma$ into $m\gamma$, and $m$ can always be so determined
that $m\beta$ or $-m\gamma$ becomes a quadratic residue of $p$.

Here belongs also the case that $\beta \equiv 0$ or $\gamma \equiv 0$ and
$\alpha \equiv \delta \ (\mathrm{mod}\ p)$.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 317 =====
% !PRINTED 296
\weberpage{296}

If, on the other hand, $\beta \equiv 0$ and $\alpha-\delta$ is not divisible by $p$, then
one may choose $\beta'$ in (9) arbitrarily and then determine $\alpha'$ from a congruence
 of the first degree.

If $\beta$ is not divisible by $p$, then (9) may be put into the form
\weq{10}{\left[\alpha'\beta+\beta'\left(\frac{\delta-\alpha}{2}\right)\right]^2 \equiv \beta+\beta'^2\left[\left(\frac{\alpha+\delta}{2}\right)^2-1\right] \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ p),}
and if now
\[
\text{II.} \qquad \left(\frac{\alpha+\delta}{2}\right)^2-1 \ \text{is a quadratic residue of}\ p\text{, then determine}
\]
$\beta'$ from the congruence:
\[
\beta'^2\left[\left(\frac{\alpha+\delta}{2}\right)^2-1\right] \equiv \left(\frac{\beta-1}{2}\right)^2,
\]
whereby (10) passes into
\[
\alpha'\beta+\beta'\left(\frac{\delta-\alpha}{2}\right) \equiv \pm \frac{\beta+1}{2} \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ p),
\]
and from this $\alpha'$ can be determined, whichever sign be
chosen.

If
\[
\text{III.} \qquad \left(\frac{\alpha+\delta}{2}\right)^2-1 \ \text{is a quadratic non-residue of}\ p \ \text{and at the}
\]
same time $\beta$ is a quadratic non-residue, then a non-residue
 $\nu$ can always be determined such that $\beta+\nu$ becomes a quadratic residue; for if
one lets $\nu$ run through the sequence of non-residues in $\beta+\nu$, then
the results cannot be \gesperrt{nothing but} non-residues, since among them
$\beta$ too would have to occur.

Then $\beta'$ can be determined so that
\[
\beta'^2\left[\left(\frac{\alpha+\delta}{2}\right)^2-1\right] \equiv \nu \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ p),
\]
and then $\alpha'$ from
\[
\alpha'\beta+\beta'\left(\frac{\delta-\alpha}{2}\right) \equiv \pm\sqrt{\beta+\nu} \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ p).
\]
From this it follows:

\gesperrt{In a normal divisor $\mathfrak{R}$ of the group $\mathfrak{L}_0$ a substitution
$U$ of the form}
\weq{11}{\begin{pmatrix}0, & 1\\ -1, & \xi\end{pmatrix}}
\gesperrt{must certainly occur.}

\gesperrt{Let $\xi$ first be different from zero $(\mathrm{mod}\ p)$.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 318 =====
% !PRINTED 297
\weberpage{297}
By the concept of the normal divisor, $\mathfrak{N}$ also contains the substitution
\weq{12}{\begin{pmatrix} 0, & -1 \\ 1, & 0 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 0, & 1 \\ -1, & \xi \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 0, & 1 \\ -1, & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \xi, & 1 \\ -1, & 0 \end{pmatrix}}
and consequently also
\weq{13}{\begin{pmatrix} 0, & 1 \\ -1, & \xi \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} \xi, & 1 \\ -1, & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0 \\ 2\xi, & 1 \end{pmatrix} \equiv A^{2\xi}\ [\S\ 79,\ (11)],}
hence also $A$ and all its powers. Therefore $\mathfrak{N}$ also contains
\weq{14}{\begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0 \\ \eta, & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 0, & 1 \\ -1, & \xi \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0, & 1 \\ -1, & \xi+\eta \end{pmatrix}}
for an arbitrary $\eta$, that is, the substitution (11) for \gesperrt{every arbitrary} $\xi$, and consequently also
\[
B = \begin{pmatrix} 0, & 1 \\ -1, & 0 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
Accordingly, by the theorem of the preceding section, the group $\mathfrak{N}$ is identical with $\mathfrak{L}_0$.

It still remains to discuss the possibility that in (11) $\xi \equiv 0$.

In this case, then, the group $\mathfrak{N}$ contains the substitution
\[
B = \begin{pmatrix} 0, & 1 \\ -1, & 0 \end{pmatrix},
\]
and consequently also, for an arbitrary $\alpha$ not divisible by $p$,
\[
V = \begin{pmatrix} 0, & \alpha \\ -\alpha^{-1}, & 0 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 0, & 1 \\ -1, & 0 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 0, & -\alpha \\ \alpha^{-1}, & 0 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 0, & -1 \\ 1, & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \alpha^2, & 0 \\ 0, & \alpha^{-2} \end{pmatrix}.
\]
From this one derives further, as contained in $\mathfrak{N}$:
\[
W = \begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0 \\ -1, & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} \alpha^{-2}, & 0 \\ 0, & \alpha^2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0 \\ 1, & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} \alpha^2, & 0 \\ 0, & \alpha^{-2} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0 \\ \alpha^4-1, & 1 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
If now $p$ is greater than 5, then $\alpha$ can be so assumed that $\alpha^4 - 1$ is not divisible by $p$; then $\mathfrak{N}$ also contains the substitution $A$ and its powers, and consequently $\mathfrak{N}$ is identical with $\mathfrak{L}_0$.

If $p = 5$, then $\alpha^4 - 1$ is always divisible by $p$, so this conclusion is not applicable.

In this case, however, it follows from the concept of the normal divisor, as contained in $\mathfrak{N}$:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 319 =====
% !PRINTED 298
\weberpage{298}
%<<CONT
\[
\begin{pmatrix} 1, & 1 \\ 2, & -2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 0, & 1 \\ -1, & 0 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} -2, & -1 \\ -2, & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 0, & 1 \\ -1, & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -2, & 0 \\ 0, & 2 \end{pmatrix},
\]
\[
\begin{pmatrix} -2, & 0 \\ 0, & 2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0 \\ -1, & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 2, & 0 \\ 0, & -2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0 \\ 1, & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0 \\ 2, & 1 \end{pmatrix},
\]
i.\,e. $A^2$, and hence all powers of $A$, from which it is to be concluded, as above, that $\mathfrak{N}$ is identical with $\mathfrak{L}_0$. We have therefore the theorem:

\gesperrt{If $p > 3$, then the group $\mathfrak{L}_0$ has no normal divisor.}

In the case $p = 3$, $\mathfrak{N}$ likewise contains
\[
\begin{pmatrix} 0, & 1 \\ -1, & 0 \end{pmatrix},
\]
and therefore also
\[
\begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0 \\ \pm1, & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 0, & 1 \\ -1, & 0 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0 \\ \mp1, & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \mp1, & 1 \\ 1, & \pm1 \end{pmatrix},
\]
and in fact the four substitutions
\weq{15}{\begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0 \\ 0, & 1 \end{pmatrix},\ \begin{pmatrix} 0, & 1 \\ -1, & 0 \end{pmatrix},\ \begin{pmatrix} -1, & 1 \\ 1, & 1 \end{pmatrix},\ \begin{pmatrix} 1, & 1 \\ 1, & -1 \end{pmatrix}}
do form a normal divisor of $\mathfrak{L}_0$ of index 3.

In the case $p = 3$ the group $\mathfrak{L}_0$ is isomorphic with the alternating group of the permutations of four elements. This is the group of an \gesperrt{arbitrary} equation of the fourth degree, when the square root of the discriminant is adjoined to the domain of rationality. The divisor (15) of this group, of index 3, then furnishes the cubic resolvent of the biquadratic equation that is known in algebra.

A function \gesperrt{belonging} to the group (15), formed from the roots $v_\infty, v_0, v_1, v_2$ of the transformation equation for the third degree of transformation, is for example
\[
v_\infty v_0 + v_1 v_2
\]
or
\[
(v_\infty - v_0)(v_1 - v_2).
\]
The difference between these two functions is this, that the first remains unchanged under the substitution of determinant $-1$
\[
\begin{pmatrix} -1, & 0 \\ 0, & 1 \end{pmatrix}
\]
while the second thereby changes its sign. The first will therefore lead to an equation of the third degree with \gesperrt{rational} coefficients, while in the cubic equation for the second $\sqrt{-3}$ still occurs (§ 78).

%% ===== canonical stable idx 320 =====
% !PRINTED 299
\weberpage{299}
\begin{center}
\textbf{\S\ 81. \gesperrt{Non-normal divisors of $\mathfrak{L}_0$.}}
\end{center}

We now inquire, leaving aside the case $p = 3$, after the non-normal divisors of the group $\mathfrak{L}_0$ whose index is smaller than $p+1$; upon the existence of such divisors depends the possibility of forming resolvents of the transformation equation \gesperrt{whose degree is lower than $p+1$.}

First of all it can be shown that the index of a divisor $\mathfrak{K}$ of $\mathfrak{L}_0$ can never be smaller than $p$.

Let
\weq{1}{\mathfrak{K} = S_0,\ S_1,\ \ldots,\ S_{\nu-1}}
be any divisor whatever of $\mathfrak{L}_0$ of degree $\nu$, and, if it is possible, let
\weq{2}{T = \begin{pmatrix} \alpha, & \beta \\ \gamma, & \delta \end{pmatrix}}
be a substitution of degree $p$ which occurs in $\mathfrak{L}_0$ but not in $\mathfrak{K}$. Then too, since $p$ is a prime, no power of $T$ lower than the $p$th can occur in $\mathfrak{K}$. The subsidiary groups
\weq{3}{\mathfrak{K},\ T\mathfrak{K},\ T^2\mathfrak{K},\ \ldots,\ T^{p-1}\mathfrak{K}}
contain none but \gesperrt{mutually distinct elements} $T^i S_k$, and accordingly $\nu p$ is at most equal to the degree of the group $\mathfrak{L}_0$, that is:
\[
\nu p \leqq p\,\frac{p^2-1}{2}.
\]
Thus the index of $\mathfrak{K}$, that is the quotient
\[
p\,\frac{p^2-1}{2} : \nu
\]
\gesperrt{is equal to $p$ or greater than $p$.}

A divisor $\mathfrak{K}$ of $\mathfrak{L}_0$ whose index is smaller than $p$ must therefore contain all substitutions of degree $p$, and hence also (§ 79, I.) all substitutions $T$ in which
\weq{4}{\alpha + \delta \equiv 2 \pmod{p}}
holds. Accordingly such a group $\mathfrak{K}$ contains in the first place the substitution
\weq{5}{A = \begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0 \\ 1, & 1 \end{pmatrix}}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 321 =====
% !PRINTED 300
\weberpage{300}
%<<CONT
and their powers; likewise the substitutions
\[
\begin{pmatrix} 1, & 2 \\ 0, & 1 \end{pmatrix},\quad \begin{pmatrix} 2, & 1 \\ -1, & 0 \end{pmatrix},
\]
and consequently also
\weq{6}{B = \begin{pmatrix} 0, & 1 \\ -1, & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1, & 2 \\ 0, & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 2, & 1 \\ -1, & 0 \end{pmatrix}.}
But if the substitutions $A$, $B$ are contained in $\mathfrak{K}$, then by § 79 $\mathfrak{K}$ must be identical with $\mathfrak{L}_0$. We have therefore the theorem:

\gesperrt{The index of a divisor of $\mathfrak{L}_0$ cannot be smaller than $p$.}

Our problem is thus restricted to the question of the divisors of $\mathfrak{L}_0$ of index $p$, or of degree $\dfrac{p^2-1}{2}$.

Let $\mathfrak{K}$ be such a divisor, and let $S_0, S_1, \ldots, S_{\nu-1}$ be its elements, so that the number $\nu$ has the value
\weq{7}{\nu = \frac{p^2-1}{2}}
.

Since the degree of every element of a group is always a divisor of the degree of the group, and since $\nu$ is not divisible by $p$, \gesperrt{no} element of degree $p$ can occur in $\mathfrak{K}$; if we therefore take for $T$ the substitution of degree $p$:
\weq{8}{A = \begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0 \\ 1, & 1 \end{pmatrix},}
then the group $\mathfrak{L}_0$ can be decomposed into the $p$ subsidiary groups:
\weq{9}{\mathfrak{L}_0 = \mathfrak{K},\ A\mathfrak{K},\ A^2\mathfrak{K}\ \ldots,\ A^{p-1}\mathfrak{K}.}
Of the same degree as $\mathfrak{K}$, and hence also of the same index, are all its conjugate divisors
\[
T\mathfrak{K}T^{-1}.
\]
Now let $g$ be a primitive root of the prime $p$, and
\weq{10}{C = \begin{pmatrix} g, & 0 \\ 0, & g^{-1} \end{pmatrix},}
a substitution which is evidently of degree $\dfrac{p-1}{2}$. Like every substitution of $\mathfrak{L}_0$, it must occur in one of the rows (9); that is, there is a substitution $S$ in $\mathfrak{K}$ and an exponent $\lambda$ for which
\weq{11}{C = A^\lambda S,\quad S = A^{-\lambda} C.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 322 =====
% !PRINTED 301
\weberpage{301}

But $\gamma$ can be further determined so that

\weq{12}{A^{\gamma-\lambda}CA^{-\gamma}=C,}

and for this one obtains the condition

\[ \gamma(g-g^{-1})\equiv\lambda g\quad(\mathrm{mod}\ p), \]

which, since $p>3$, can always be satisfied; but then, on account of (11),

\[ C=A^{\gamma}SA^{-\gamma}. \]

Thus $C$ occurs in the divisor $A^{\gamma}\mathfrak{K} A^{-\gamma}$ conjugate to $\mathfrak{K}$, and we may therefore, by putting this group in place of $\mathfrak{K}$, assume without loss of generality that $\mathfrak{K}$ itself contains the substitution $C$.

Now the substitution

\[ B=\begin{pmatrix}0, & 1\\ -1, & 0\end{pmatrix} \]

may either occur in $\mathfrak{K}$ or not occur. In the first case $\mathfrak{K}$ also contains all the substitutions composed of $B$ and $C$, which are all of one of the two forms:

\weq{13}{\begin{pmatrix}g^{r}, & 0\\ 0, & g^{-r}\end{pmatrix},\qquad r=0,1,\dots\frac{p-3}{2},}

\weq{14}{\begin{pmatrix}0, & g^{-r}\\ -g^{r}, & 0\end{pmatrix},}

and whose number amounts to $p-1$. In the first case, then, $\mathfrak{K}$ contains all substitutions of the form (13), (14), in the second all substitutions of the form (13) and \gesperrt{none} of the form (14).

Now let

\weq{15}{V=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha, & \beta\\ \gamma, & \delta\end{pmatrix}}

be a substitution contained in $\mathfrak{K}$ which is contained neither in the form (13) nor in the form (14), and for which therefore neither $\alpha$ and $\delta$, nor $\beta$ and $\gamma$, are simultaneously congruent to $0$. Then all the substitutions of the form

\weq{16}{C^{r}VC^{s}=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha g^{r+s}, & \beta g^{r-s}\\ \gamma g^{-r+s}, & \delta g^{-r-s}\end{pmatrix},}

when $r,s$ both run through the sequence of numbers:

\[ 0,1,2,\dots\frac{p-3}{2} \]

are contained in $\mathfrak{K}$ and are all \gesperrt{different from one another}. For if two among the substitutions (16) are equal to one another, then we must have
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 323 =====
% !PRINTED 302
\weberpage{302}

%<<CONT
there would also be one among them which, without $r, s$ vanishing, becomes identical with $V$. But this requires

\begin{align*}
\alpha\equiv\pm\alpha g^{r+s}, &\qquad \beta\equiv\pm\beta g^{r-s}\\
\gamma\equiv\pm\gamma g^{-r+s}, &\qquad \delta\equiv\pm\delta g^{-r-s}\quad(\mathrm{mod}\ p),
\end{align*}

where in all four formulae the upper or the lower signs hold, and hence, since neither $\alpha$ and $\delta$ nor $\beta$ and $\gamma$ vanish simultaneously,

\[ r+s\equiv 0,\qquad r-s\equiv 0\qquad(\mathrm{mod}\ p-1), \]
or
\[ r+s\equiv\frac{p-1}{2},\qquad r-s\equiv\frac{p-1}{2}\qquad(\mathrm{mod}\ p-1), \]

and so in both cases

\[ r\equiv 0,\qquad s\equiv 0\ \left(\mathrm{mod}\ \frac{p-1}{2}\right),\qquad\text{q. e. d.} \]

In the form (16) there are therefore contained $\left(\dfrac{p-1}{2}\right)^2$ \gesperrt{different substitutions}. If the group $\mathfrak{K}$ is not yet exhausted by them, one chooses a substitution $V'$ not contained in (13), (14), (16) and forms in the same way the sequence

\weq{17}{C^{r}V'C^{s},}

whose substitutions are different both among themselves and from those contained in (13), (14), (16); and one proceeds in this way until the whole group $\mathfrak{K}$ is exhausted.

If we denote by $q$ the number of the sequences (16), (17), $\dots$ so formed, then the degree of the group $\mathfrak{K}$ comes out:

1. if $B$ does not occur in $\mathfrak{K}$:

\[ =\frac{p-1}{2}+q\left(\frac{p-1}{2}\right)^2; \]

2. if $B$ occurs in $\mathfrak{K}$:

\[ =p-1+q\left(\frac{p-1}{2}\right)^2, \]

and by the requirement of our problem this number is to be

\[ =\frac{(p-1)(p+1)}{2} \]

From this, however, it follows that case 1. is impossible, for in this case we should necessarily have

\[ q\left(\frac{p-1}{2}\right)=p, \]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 324 =====
% !PRINTED 303
\weberpage{303}

%<<CONT
so that
\[
q=p,\qquad p=3
\]
would have to hold, which we have excluded.

In case 2., however, it follows for every arbitrary $p$:

\[ q=2. \]

Hence the substitution $B$ must in any case occur in $\mathfrak{K}$, and the group sought is exhausted by (13), (14), (16), (17).

We show first that in the two substitutions $V, V'$ of the group $\mathfrak{K}$ none of the numbers $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta,\alpha',\beta',\gamma',\delta'$ can be congruent to $0$.

For, as we have already seen, there does not occur in $\mathfrak{K}$

\[ \begin{pmatrix}1, & 0\\ \gamma, & 1\end{pmatrix}, \]

if $\gamma$ is different from $0$, and hence neither

\[ \begin{pmatrix}\alpha, & 0\\ 0, & \alpha^{-1}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1, & 0\\ \alpha\gamma, & 1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha, & 0\\ \gamma, & \alpha^{-1}\end{pmatrix}, \]

where $\alpha$ is arbitrary; and consequently neither

\begin{align*}
\begin{pmatrix}\alpha, & 0\\ \gamma, & \alpha^{-1}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0, & 1\\ -1, & 0\end{pmatrix} &=\begin{pmatrix}0, & \alpha\\ -\alpha^{-1}, & \gamma\end{pmatrix}\\
\begin{pmatrix}0, & 1\\ -1, & 0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\alpha, & 0\\ \gamma, & \alpha^{-1}\end{pmatrix} &=\begin{pmatrix}\gamma, & \alpha^{-1}\\ -\alpha, & 0\end{pmatrix}\\
\begin{pmatrix}0, & -1\\ 1, & 0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0, & \alpha\\ -\alpha^{-1}, & -\gamma\end{pmatrix} &=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha^{-1}, & \gamma\\ 0, & \alpha\end{pmatrix},
\end{align*}

in which are contained all substitutions $\begin{pmatrix}\alpha, & \beta\\ \gamma, & \delta\end{pmatrix}$ in which one of the four numbers $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta$ is congruent with $0$.

We now denote the substitutions of the system (16) by

\[ W=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha g^{r+s}, & \beta g^{r-s}\\ \gamma g^{-r+s}, & \delta g^{-r-s}\end{pmatrix}, \]

and set

\weq{18}{\xi\equiv\alpha g^{r+s},\qquad \varrho\equiv\alpha^{-1}\beta g^{-2s}}

\weq{19}{\alpha\delta\equiv m,\qquad \beta\gamma\equiv m-1\quad(\mathrm{mod}\ p).}

$m$ does not change when $V$ is replaced by an arbitrary substitution of the system (16). The number $m'$ shall have the corresponding meaning for the system (17); in each of these two systems $\xi$ can assume any of the values

\weq{20}{1,2,\dots p-1}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 325 =====
% !PRINTED 304
\weberpage{304}

%<<CONT
\gesperrt{assume, and $\varrho$ runs, according as $\alpha^{-1}\beta$ is a quadratic residue or a non-residue, in one system through the sequence of the residues or of the non-residues.} The change of the sign of $\xi$ gives no new substitution $W$. Accordingly we can represent $W$ in this way:

\weq{21}{W=\begin{pmatrix}\xi, & \xi\varrho\\ \xi^{-1}\varrho^{-1}(m-1), & \xi^{-1}m\end{pmatrix}.}

Now since the square of $W$

\[ W^2=\begin{pmatrix}\xi^2+m-1, & (\xi^2+m)\varrho\\ \xi^{-2}\varrho^{-1}(m-1)(\xi^2+m), & [(m-1)\xi^2+m^2]\xi^{-2}\end{pmatrix} \]

must belong to $\mathfrak{K}$, it is contained under one of the systems (13), (14), (16), (17), from which the following four possibilities result:

\weq{22}{\begin{aligned}
1.&\quad \xi^2+m\equiv 0,\\
2.&\quad \xi^2+m-1\equiv 0,\quad (m-1)\xi^2+m^2\equiv 0,\\
3.&\quad (\xi^2+m-1)[(m-1)\xi^2+m^2]\equiv m\xi^2,\\
4.&\quad (\xi^2+m-1)[(m-1)\xi^2+m^2]\equiv m'\xi^2,
\end{aligned}}

and each of the $p-1$ values (20), put for $\xi$, must satisfy one of these four cases. If one of the congruences (22), 2. is fulfilled, then the other must follow from it, which is possible only if

\weq{23}{2m\equiv 1,\qquad \xi^2\equiv m\quad(\mathrm{mod}\ p).}

Now a congruence with respect to a prime modulus has \gesperrt{at most} as many incongruent roots as the degree of the congruence amounts to; 1. and 2. can therefore be satisfied for at most two values each, 3. and 4. for at most four values each of $\xi$; there are therefore in all at most twelve values of $\xi$ which satisfy \gesperrt{one} of the four congruences (22).

From this it follows:

\[ p-1\leqq 12,\qquad p\leqq 13. \]

But if $p=13$, then each of the congruences (22) must have the maximum number of roots; 2. must therefore also be satisfied for two values of $\xi$; then by (23) we should have $m\equiv 7$, $\xi^2\equiv 7\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 13)$, which is impossible, since $7$ is a quadratic non-residue of $13$.

\gesperrt{A divisor of $\mathfrak{L}_0$ of index $p$ therefore does not exist} when $p>11$.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 326 =====
% !PRINTED 305
\weberpage{305}

\begin{center}
\textbf{§ 82. \gesperrt{Divisors of $\mathfrak{L}_0$ of index $p$ for $p = 5, 7, 11$.}}
\end{center}

There remains the possibility that for $p = 5, 7, 11$ divisors of $\mathfrak{L}_0$ of index $p$ exist.
