1. $p = 5$. We investigate first the case $p = 5$. Since $m$ and $m - 1$ cannot be congruent to 0, there remain for $m$ the assumptions
\[
m \equiv 2, 3, 4 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ p).
\]
If, however, we replace the substitution $W$ § 81, (21) by
\weq{1}{WB = \begin{pmatrix} -\xi\varrho, & \xi \\ -\xi^{-1}m, & \xi^{-1}\varrho^{-1}(m-1) \end{pmatrix},}
whereby $m$ passes into $1 - m$, then the case $m \equiv 4$ is brought back to the case $m \equiv 2$.

For $m \equiv 2$, however, (23), § 81 is not satisfied, and of the congruences (22) none is possible, since $\pm 2$ are non-residues of 5 and the left sides of (22), 3., 4. reduce for $m = 2$ to $\xi^4 - 1$, which for every $\xi$ different from zero is divisible by 5. It therefore only remains that
\weq{2}{m \equiv 3, \quad m' \equiv 3 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ 5)}
and the two systems $W, W'$ [§ 81, (16), (17)] can differ from one another only in this, that $\alpha^{-1}\beta$, and hence also $\varrho$, is in the one a quadratic residue, in the other a quadratic non-residue of 5. The group sought therefore consists, if it exists, of the 12 substitutions contained in the three forms
\weq{3}{\begin{pmatrix} \xi, & 0 \\ 0, & \xi^{-1} \end{pmatrix}, \quad \begin{pmatrix} 0, & \xi \\ -\xi^{-1}, & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \begin{pmatrix} \xi, & \eta \\ 2\eta^{-1}, & 3\xi^{-1} \end{pmatrix}}
in which
\[
\xi \equiv 1, 2, \quad \eta \equiv \pm 1, \pm 2 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ 5)
\]
is to be set.

2. $p = 7, 11$.

Since $-1$ is to be found among the quadratic non-residues for $p = 7, 11$, the composed substitution $WB$, (1), belongs to the $W'$ [because the quadratic character of the quantity denoted by $\varrho$ in (18), § 81 is the opposite one in $W$ and in $WB$]. Accordingly, by (1) and § 81, (19), (21), $\beta'\gamma' \equiv -m \equiv m' - 1$, hence:
\weq{4}{m + m' \equiv 1 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ p).}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 327 =====
% !PRINTED 306
\weberpage{306}

For $p = 7$, since the interchange of $m$ with $m'$ yields nothing new, the following three possibilities remain: 1. $m \equiv 2$, $m' \equiv 6$. 2. $m \equiv 3$, $m' \equiv 5$. 3. $m \equiv 4$, $m' \equiv 4$.

In case 1., of the congruences § 81, (22), numbers 1. and 2. are impossible; hence for every $\xi$ one of the two congruences 3., 4. would have to be satisfied, which here read:
\[
(\xi^2 + 1)(\xi^2 + 4) \equiv 2\xi^2, 6\xi^2 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ 7),
\]
\gesperrt{none of which is satisfied for $\xi \equiv 1$.}

In case 3., (22), 1. cannot be satisfied, and (22), 2. is satisfied for $\xi^2 \equiv 4$; hence for $\xi^2 \equiv 1, 2$ the congruence (22) 3. or 4.:
\[
(\xi^2 + 3)(3\xi^2 + 2) \equiv 4\xi^2 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ 7)
\]
must be satisfied, which again is not the case. Thus for $p = 7$ there remains only:
\weq{5}{m \equiv 3, \quad m' \equiv 5 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ 7).}

For $p = 11$ the possibility that the congruences (22), 2. be satisfied is to be excluded from the outset, because in that case, in consequence of (4) and § 81, (23):
\[
m \equiv m'
\]
would have to hold; then (22), 3., 4. would not be distinct, and the congruences (22) could together have at most eight roots and not ten, as they nevertheless must.

Accordingly the congruences (22), 1., 3., 4 must each have the maximal number of roots, and in order that 1. be satisfied, $m$, and for the same reasons $m'$, must be a quadratic non-residue of 11. But this condition, and at the same time the condition (4), is satisfied only by the two numbers
\weq{6}{m, m' \equiv 2, -1 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ 11).}

The groups sought therefore consist, in these two cases, if they exist, of the following substitutions:

$p = 7$
\weq{7}{\begin{pmatrix} \xi, & 0 \\ 0, & \xi^{-1} \end{pmatrix}, \ \begin{pmatrix} 0, & \xi \\ \xi^{-1}, & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \ \begin{pmatrix} \xi & \xi\varrho \\ 2\xi^{-1}\varrho^{-1}, & 3\xi^{-1} \end{pmatrix}, \ \begin{pmatrix} -\xi\varrho, & \xi \\ -3\xi^{-1}, & 2\xi^{-1}\varrho^{-1} \end{pmatrix}}
\[
\xi \equiv 1, 2, 3 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ 7),
\]

$p = 11$
\weq{8}{\begin{pmatrix} \xi, & 0 \\ 0, & \xi^{-1} \end{pmatrix}, \ \begin{pmatrix} 0, & \xi \\ -\xi^{-1}, & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \ \begin{pmatrix} \xi, & \xi\varrho \\ \xi^{-1}\varrho^{-1}, & 2\xi^{-1} \end{pmatrix}, \ \begin{pmatrix} -\xi\varrho, & \xi \\ -2\xi^{-1}, & \xi^{-1}\varrho^{-1} \end{pmatrix}}
\[
\xi \equiv 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ 11);
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 328 =====
% !PRINTED 307
\weberpage{307}

%<<CONT
$\varrho$ runs in (7) and (8) through either the sequence of the quadratic residues or that of the non-residues, so that for $p = 7$ or 11 one obtains \gesperrt{in each case two groups of index $p$.}

That the systems of substitutions collected in (3), (7), (8) really constitute groups can be shown by direct composition in various ways. One reaches this proof more simply, however, by forming functions of the $v_z$, § 78, (7), which remain unchanged under the substitutions of these systems, and which under the substitutions of $\mathfrak{L}_0$ take only $p$ different values in all.

The systems (3), (7), (8) can, as follows from their mode of origin, be composed by repeated application of $B, C, U, U'$, if $U, U'$ are any two special substitutions $W, W'$. For $p = 5$ the substitution $U^2$, and for $p = 7, 11$ the substitution $UB$, belongs to the $W'$, so that $U'$ can then be omitted. If we choose $U$ quite arbitrarily, and take for the primitive root $g$ in $C$, for $p = 5, 7, 11$ respectively, $2, -2, 2$, then we can compose the group (3) from:
\[
B = \begin{pmatrix} 0, & 1 \\ -1, & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad C = \begin{pmatrix} 2, & 0 \\ 0, & 3 \end{pmatrix}, \quad U = \begin{pmatrix} 1, & 1 \\ 2, & 3 \end{pmatrix} \quad (p = 5),
\]
the group (7) from:
\[
B = \begin{pmatrix} 0, & 1 \\ -1, & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad C = \begin{pmatrix} 2, & 0 \\ 0, & 4 \end{pmatrix}, \quad U = \begin{pmatrix} 1, & \pm 1 \\ \pm 2, & 3 \end{pmatrix} \quad (p = 7),
\]
the group (8) from:
\[
B = \begin{pmatrix} 0, & 1 \\ -1, & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad C = \begin{pmatrix} 2, & 0 \\ 0, & 6 \end{pmatrix}, \quad U = \begin{pmatrix} 1, & \pm 1 \\ \pm 1, & 2 \end{pmatrix} \quad (p = 11),
\]
where in the two last cases the two different groups mentioned above arise from the double signs.

We now collect the permutations of the indices $z$ that correspond to these substitutions [§ 79, (3)].

$p = 5$:
\[
\begin{array}{ccccccl}
z = \infty, & 0, & 1, & 2, & 3, & 4 & \\
0, & \infty, & 4, & 2, & 3, & 1 & (B)\\
\infty, & 0, & 4, & 3, & 2, & 1 & (C)\\
4, & 1, & 2, & 0, & \infty, & 3 & (U).
\end{array}
\]
Thus by $B, C, U$ the index pairs
\[
(\infty, 0), \quad (1, 4), \quad (2, 3)
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 329 =====
% !PRINTED 308
\weberpage{308}

%<<CONT
not torn apart, but only interchanged among one another. Moreover, in two of these pairs the elements are interchanged each time. If we therefore form a function like
\weq{9}{V = (v_\infty - v_0)(v_1 - v_4)(v_2 - v_3),}
then it remains unchanged under $B, C, U$, and hence under the whole system (3), while by repeated application of the cyclic permutation $(0, 1, 2, 3, 4)$, that is, of the substitution
\[
A = \begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0 \\ 1, & 1 \end{pmatrix}
\]
it takes \gesperrt{five} different values. But the whole group $\mathfrak{L}_0$ can be composed from $A$ and $B$ [§ 79, (10)], and $V$ therefore takes no more than five values under the application of $\mathfrak{L}_0$.

The five values of $V$ are the roots of an equation of the fifth degree.

For $p = 7$ we have
\[
B = \left(z, -\frac{1}{z}\right), \quad C = (z, 4z), \quad U = \left(z, \frac{\mp 2 + z}{3 \mp z}\right).
\]

For a better survey we also represent $B, C, U$ by the \gesperrt{cyclic permutations} which they produce among the eight values of $z$:
\[
\begin{aligned}
B &= (0, \infty)(1, -1)(2, 3)(-2, -3), \\
C &= (1, -3, 2)(-1, 3, -2), \\
U &= (\infty, \mp 1, \pm 1, \pm 3)(0, \mp 3, \mp 2, \pm 2),
\end{aligned}
\]
and from this one obtains the \gesperrt{seven-valued function}
\weq{10}{V = (v_\infty - v_0)(v_{\mp 1} - v_{\mp 3})(v_{\pm 1} - v_{\mp 2})(v_{\pm 3} - v_{\pm 2}),}
in which the one or the other sign may be taken.

For $p = 11$ we have
\[
B = \left(z, -\frac{1}{z}\right), \quad C = (z, 4z), \quad U = \left(z, \frac{\mp 1 + z}{2 \mp z}\right),
\]
or, represented by the cycles:
\[
\begin{aligned}
B &= (0, \infty)(1, -1)(2, 5)(-2, -5)(3, -4)(-3, 4), \\
C &= (1, 4, 5, -2, 3)(-1, -4, -5, 2, -3), \\
U &= (\infty, \mp 1, \pm 3, \mp 2, \pm 2)(0, \pm 5, \mp 5, \mp 4, \pm 1),
\end{aligned}
\]
from which the two 11-valued functions
\weq{11}{V = (v_\infty - v_0)(v_{\mp 1} - v_{\pm 5})(v_{\pm 3} - v_{\mp 5})(v_{\mp 2} - v_{\mp 4})(v_{\pm 2} - v_{\pm 1})(v_{\pm 4} - v_{\mp 3}).}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 330 =====
% !PRINTED 309
\weberpage{309}
The following remark is still of interest here. The resolvents of degree $p$, whose roots are the quantities (9), (10), (11), still contain $\sqrt{\pm p}$ in their coefficients, according to §\,78.

But the group $\mathfrak{L}_0$ is extended to the group $\mathfrak{L}$ if we add \gesperrt{a} linear substitution of the form §\,78, (13) in which $ad - bc$ is a quadratic non-residue, thus for instance: % Source scan clearly prints ad - bc.
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{for } p&=5 & &(z,\,2z)\\
\text{for } p&=7,\,11 & &(z,\,-z).
\end{aligned}
\]
By applying this substitution, however, the value (9)
\[
V = (v_\infty - v_0)(v_1 - v_4)(v_2 - v_3)
\]
passes into its opposite, and from this it follows that, when $p=5$, $V^2$ satisfies an equation of degree 5 with \gesperrt{rational} numerical coefficients. From this one concludes that in the equation for $V$ the coefficients of the odd powers have the factor $\sqrt5$, while the others are rational; or that for the unknown $\sqrt5\,V$ one obtains an equation with \gesperrt{rational coefficients}.

For $p=7,\,11$ the expressions corresponding to the two signs in (10) or (11) pass into one another through the interchange $(z,-z)$. The resolvents of degree 7 or 11, which one of the two expressions (10) or (11) respectively satisfies, therefore pass into one another through a change of the sign of $\sqrt{-7}$, $\sqrt{-11}$.

§\,83. \gesperrt{Various Resolvents of Degree 5 for the 5th Degree of Transformation.}

In the formation of the resolvents of degree $p$ we restrict ourselves here to the case $p=5$.

These resolvents can be given very manifold forms; for one may not only choose, in the function $V$, (9) of the preceding section, the roots of an \gesperrt{arbitrary} transformation equation for the quantities $v$, but may also replace $V$ by various other functions, for example by
\[
(v_\infty + v_0)(v_1+v_4)(v_2+v_3),
\]
or by
\[
v_\infty v_0 + v_1 v_4 + v_2 v_3.
\]

%% ===== canonical stable idx 331 =====
% !PRINTED 310
\weberpage{310}

We wish first to apply the transformation equation \S\,72, (8)',
in which now, in agreement with the preceding section,
$v$ is put for $x$:
\weq{1}{v^6 + 10\,v^3 - \gamma_2 v + 5 = 0}
Here, if
\[
c \equiv 0 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 12), \quad z \equiv c \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 5)
\]
then
\weq{2}{v_\infty = 5\left(\frac{\eta(5\omega)}{\eta\,\omega}\right)^2, \quad v_z = \left(\frac{\eta\left(\dfrac{\omega+c}{5}\right)}{\eta(\omega)}\right)^2.}
If we then take
\weq{3}{\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{5}\,w_z &= (v_\infty - v_z)(v_{z+1} - v_{z-1})(v_{z-2} - v_{z+2}) \\
&= (v_\infty - v_c)(v_{c+12} - v_{c-12})(v_{c+24} - v_{c-24}), \\
z &= 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, \quad c = 0, \pm 12, \pm 24,
\end{aligned}}
then, by the concluding remark of the preceding section, the
$w_0$, $w_1$, $w_2$, $w_3$, $w_4$ are the roots of an equation of degree 5,
whose coefficients are formed rationally from $\gamma_2$ and rational
numbers.

If, however, we observe the relations [\S\,54, (14)]:
\[
\gamma_2(\omega+1) = e^{-\frac{2\pi i}{3}} \gamma_2(\omega), \quad \gamma_2\left(-\frac{1}{\omega}\right) = \gamma_2(\omega),
\]
it follows from the form of (1) that under the interchange
$(\omega, \omega+1)$ the roots $v$, apart from a rearrangement, take on the
factor $e^{\frac{2\pi i}{3}}$, while under $\left(\omega, -\dfrac{1}{\omega}\right)$ they remain
unchanged.

The $w_z$ are therefore interchanged only among themselves, and
their symmetric functions remain \gesperrt{unchanged} and depend
therefore rationally only on the invariant $j(\omega)$. The coefficients
in the equation for $w$ can moreover become infinite for no finite $j(\omega)$,
and they are accordingly \gesperrt{integral functions}
of $j(\omega)$.

Further information about these coefficients results
from the development in ascending powers of $q$. By (2) the
developments of the $v$ have the beginnings
\[
v_\infty = 5\,q^{\frac{2}{3}} + \cdots, \quad v_z = e^{\frac{c}{12}\frac{2\pi i}{5}} q^{-\frac{2}{15}} + \cdots,
\]
and from this it follows, with the use of the well-known equation
\[
4\sin\frac{2\pi}{5}\cdot\sin\frac{4\pi}{5} = \sqrt{5}
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 332 =====
% !PRINTED 311
\weberpage{311}
%<<CONT
the beginning of the development for $w_z$:
\weq{4}{w_z = q^{-\frac{2}{5}} e^{\frac{c}{2}\frac{\pi i}{5}} + \cdots}
From this it follows that the power sums of the $w_z$, up to the fourth inclusive, are constants, since they cannot contain even the first power of $j(\omega)$, and that the product of the $w_z$ must be a \gesperrt{linear} function of $j(w)$, % [sic] German source prints w here, but omega four words later.
in which $j(\omega)$ has the coefficient 1.

The equation of the $w$ therefore has the form:
\weq{5}{w^5 + b_1 w^4 + b_2 w^3 + b_3 w^2 + b_4 w + b_5 = j(\omega),}
where the $b$ are rational numbers. These coefficients can be calculated by carrying the development (4) further. Here we take another route, which, strictly speaking, belongs to the complex multiplication treated in the next part, but which, being so simple, may nevertheless quite well find its place here.

If we set $\omega = i = \sqrt{-1}$, then
\[ \omega = -\frac{1}{\omega} \]
and consequently [§ 34, (11), (12), (14)]:
\[ f_1(i) = f_2(i) = \sqrt[8]{2}, \quad f(i) = \sqrt[4]{2}, \]
hence [§ 54, (5)]:
\weq{6}{\gamma_3(i) = 0, \quad \gamma_2(i) = 12, \quad j(i) = 12^3.}
But one finds further, from the transformation formulae for $\eta(\omega)$ [§ 34, (4), (5)]:
\[ \eta(\omega+1) = e^{\frac{\pi i}{12}} \eta(\omega), \quad \eta\left(-\frac{1}{\omega}\right) = \sqrt{-i\omega}\,\eta(\omega), \]
if the decomposition
\[ 5 = (2+i)(2-i) \]
is taken into account:
\[ \eta\left(\frac{12+i}{5}\right) = e^{\frac{\pi i}{6}} \eta\left(\frac{2+i}{5}\right) = e^{\frac{\pi i}{6}} \eta\left(\frac{1}{2-i}\right) = \sqrt{1+2i}\,\eta(i), \]
hence
\[ v_2 = 1+2i, \quad v_3 = 1-2i, \]
and now, since for $\gamma_2 = 12$ two roots of equation (1) are known, one can easily decompose the left part of this equation into factors for this particular value of $\gamma_2$:
\[ v^6 + 10v^3 - 12v + 5 = (v^2+2v+5)(v^2+v-1)^2, \]
%CONT>>

\weberpage{312}

from which it is to be concluded:
\weq{7}{\begin{aligned} v_\infty &= v_0 = \frac{-1+\sqrt5}{2}, \\ v_1 &= v_4 = \frac{-1-\sqrt5}{2}. \end{aligned}}
($v_0$, $v_\infty$ must be positive, since $q$ is real in them.)

From (3) there then results:
\weq{8}{\begin{aligned} w_0 &= 0, \quad w_1 = w_3 = -5-2i\sqrt5, \\ w_2 &= w_4 = -5+2i\sqrt5. \end{aligned}}
These must be the roots of (5) for $j=12^3$, and from this one obtains the resolvent sought in the form:
\weq{9}{w(w^2+10w+45)^2 = j(\omega) - 12^3 = \gamma_3^2.}
This equation can also be brought into the form:
\weq{10}{(w+3)^3(w^2+11w+64) = j(\omega) = \gamma_2^3,}
which one also reaches directly if, in place of setting $\omega=i$,
\[ \omega = \frac{-1+i\sqrt3}{2} \]
is assumed.

The resolvent found simplifies still further if [according to (9)]:

is set:
\weq{11}{z^5+10z^3+45z = \gamma_3,}
or if [according to (10)]

\weq{13}{y^5 - 40y^2 - 5\gamma_2 y - \gamma_2^2 = 0,}
an equation which also results if one makes the assumption from the outset:
\[ 2y = v_\infty v_0 + v_1 v_4 + v_2 v_3. \]

In equation (13), as one sees, the third and the fourth power of the unknown are missing. The same property belongs also, as is easily shown, to the equation whose roots

\weq{14}{x = y(\lambda+\mu z) = \frac{(\lambda+\mu z)\gamma_2}{z^2+3}}%

then, after some calculations making use of the particular values of $x$ for

a &= 8\lambda^3 - 72\lambda\mu^2 + \gamma_3(\lambda^2\mu - \mu^3),\\

\par\noindent\rule{0.3\linewidth}{0.4pt}\par

One more resolvent of degree 5 is to be formed, making use of the function
$f(\omega)$.

We put:

\weq{17}{\begin{gathered}
u = f(\omega), \quad v_\infty = f(5\omega), \quad v_z = f\left(\frac{\omega+c}{5}\right)\\
c \equiv 0 \pmod{48}, \quad z \equiv c \pmod{5},
\end{gathered}}

and by §\,73 we have between $u$ and $v$ the equation of degree 6:

\weq{18}{u^6 + v^6 - u^5v^5 + 4uv = 0.}

We investigate the influence which the three permutations

\[
(\omega, \omega+2), \quad \left(\omega, -\frac{1}{\omega}\right), \quad
\left(\omega, \frac{\omega-1}{\omega+1}\right)
\]

have on the quantities $v_z$. By these permutations $c$ passes over into
$c_1, c_2, c'$, which by §\,69, (9), (11) and §\,73, (6) are determined by the
congruences

\weq{19}{c_1 \equiv c+2, \quad c_2 \equiv -\frac{1}{c}, \quad c' \equiv \frac{c-1}{c+1} \pmod{5}}

Apart from this change of the index, by §\,73, (4) and (9) the $v$ pass over
into

\weq{20}{e^{-\frac{5\pi i}{12}}v, \quad v, \quad -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{v}.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 335 =====

Thus, if we set $e^{-\frac{5\pi i}{12}} = \varepsilon$ for brevity, we have the
following permutations belonging together:

\weq{21}{\begin{array}{cccccccc}
\omega, & u, & v_\infty, & v_0, & v_1, & v_2, & v_3, & v_4,\\
\omega+2, & e^{-\frac{\pi i}{12}}u, & \varepsilon v_\infty, & \varepsilon v_2, & \varepsilon v_3, & \varepsilon v_4, & \varepsilon v_0, & \varepsilon v_1,\\
-\dfrac{1}{\omega}, & u, & v_0, & v_\infty, & v_4, & v_2, & v_3, & v_1,\\
\dfrac{\omega-1}{\omega+1}, & \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{u}, & -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{v_1}, & -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{v_4}, & -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{v_0}, & -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{v_2}, & -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{v_3}, & -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{v_\infty}.
\end{array}}

We now introduce the five quantities $w_z$ by the equation:

\weq{22}{w_z = \frac{(v_\infty - v_z)(v_{z+1}-v_{z-1})(v_{z+2}-v_{z-2})}{\sqrt{5}\,u^3},}

that is:

\[
\begin{aligned}
w_0 &= \frac{(v_\infty - v_0)(v_1-v_4)(v_2-v_3)}{\sqrt{5}\,u^3},\\
w_1 &= \frac{(v_\infty - v_1)(v_2-v_0)(v_3-v_4)}{\sqrt{5}\,u^3},\\
w_2 &= \frac{(v_\infty - v_2)(v_3-v_1)(v_4-v_0)}{\sqrt{5}\,u^3},\\
w_3 &= \frac{(v_\infty - v_3)(v_4-v_2)(v_0-v_1)}{\sqrt{5}\,u^3},\\
w_4 &= \frac{(v_\infty - v_4)(v_0-v_3)(v_1-v_2)}{\sqrt{5}\,u^3},
\end{aligned}
\]

so that, if one makes use in the last row of the fact that by (18) the product
of the six quantities $v_z$ has the value $u^6$, there follow from (21) these
permutations of the $w$ belonging together:

\weq{23}{\begin{array}{cccccc}
\omega, & w_0, & w_1, & w_2, & w_3, & w_4,\\
\omega+2, & -w_2, & -w_3, & -w_4, & -w_0, & -w_1,\\
-\dfrac{1}{\omega}, & w_0, & w_2, & w_1, & w_4, & w_3,\\
\dfrac{\omega-1}{\omega+1}, & -w_0, & -w_3, & -w_4, & -w_2, & -w_1.
\end{array}}

The functions $w$ cannot become infinite for any value of $u$ different from 0
and $\infty$. Let us therefore assume the equation whose roots are the five
quantities $w_z$ in the form:

\[
w^5 + A_1w^4 + A_2w^3 + A_3w^2 + A_4w + A_5 = 0,
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 336 =====
% !PRINTED 315
\weberpage{315}
%<<CONT
then, by the principles of §\,73, $A_1^2, A_2, A_3^2, A_4, A_5^2$ are
\gesperrt{integral rational functions} of

\weq{24}{u^{24} + \frac{2^{12}}{u^{24}}.}

The development of (24) in ascending powers of $q$ begins with
$q^{-1}$, while the beginning of the development of $w_z$ is

\[
q^{-\frac{1}{10}}e^{-\frac{c\pi i}{60}}
\]

The quantities $A_1^2, A_2, A_3^3, A_4$ can % [sic] German source prints A_3^3 here; above it prints A_3^2.
 therefore not contain even
the first power of (24), and are accordingly constant, while $A_5^2$
has the form:

\[
A_5^2 = u^{24} + \frac{2^{12}}{u_{24}} + C,
\]

in which $C$ is a constant. The values of the constants can be
determined if one knows the values of the $w_z$ for $\omega = i$. But
for $\omega = i$ we have [cf. above (6), (7)]:

\[
\begin{aligned}
u &= f(i) = \sqrt[4]{2},\\
v_3 &= f\left(\frac{i+48}{5}\right) = f\left(\frac{i-2}{5}+10\right) = e^{-\frac{10\pi i}{24}}f\left(\frac{i-2}{5}\right),\\
&= e^{-\frac{10\pi i}{24}}f(i+2) = -i\sqrt[4]{2},\\
v_2 &= i\sqrt[4]{2}
\end{aligned}
\]

and hence, by (18):

\[
\begin{aligned}
v_\infty &= v_0 = \sqrt[4]{2}\,\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2},\\
v_1 &= v_4 = \sqrt[4]{2}\,\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}. % [sic] Both printed rows have the same plus sign.
\end{aligned}
\]

Consequently:

\[
w_0 = 0, \quad w_1 = w_2 = i\sqrt{5}, \quad w_3 = w_4 = -i\sqrt{5}.
\]

Accordingly we obtain first of all $C = -2^7$, and so

\[
A_5^2 = \left(u^{12} - \frac{64}{u^{12}}\right)^2,
\]

and from this, by comparison of the beginnings of the development,

\[
A_5 = -u^{12} + \frac{64}{u^{12}},
\]

and the equation for $w$ takes the form:

\weq{25}{w(w^2+5)^2 = u^{12} - \frac{64}{u^{12}}.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 337 =====
% !PRINTED 316
\weberpage{316}

But one can give it yet another, very remarkable form.

By the relations that subsist between the functions $f(\omega), f_1(\omega), f_2(\omega)$
[§\,34, (11), (12)] we have:

\[
\frac{f(\omega)^{24} - 64}{f(\omega)^{12}} = \frac{[f_1(\omega)^8 - f_2(\omega)^8]^2}{f(\omega)^4}.
\]

If, therefore, for $w$ we introduce the new unknown

\weq{26}{y = \sqrt{w} = \frac{f_1(\omega)^8 - f_2(\omega)^8}{f(\omega)^2(w^2+5)}}

then we obtain the form:

\weq{27}{y^5 + 5y = \frac{f_1(\omega)^8 - f_2(\omega)^8}{f(\omega)^2}.}

On these formulae rests the solution of the equation of the fifth degree by
elliptic functions created by \gesperrt{Hermite} and \gesperrt{Kronecker}, to
which we have referred in the 14th chapter of Band II.

By Bd.\,I, §\,60 the general equation of the fifth degree can be reduced to the
form:

\weq{28}{z^5 + 5z = a,}

and this equation becomes identical with (27) if one sets:

\[
f_1(\omega)^8 - f_2(\omega)^8 = af^2(\omega).
\]

If one adds to this the equations:

\[
f_1^8 = f_2^8 = f^8, \quad ff_1f_2 = \sqrt{2}, % [sic] German source prints both equals signs.
\]

one obtains

\weq{29}{f^{24} - a^2f^{12} - 64 = 0.}

By this quadratic equation $f^{12}$ is determined as a function of $a$.

The roots of equation (28) are then represented by the square roots of the
expressions (22). The double sign of these square roots is explained by the
fact that two opposite values of $a$ lead to the same equation (29). But the
roots can also be determined uniquely by formula (26):

\weq{30}{z = \frac{a}{w^2+5}.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 338 =====
% !PRINTED 317
\weberpage{317}

In the paper of \gesperrt{Kiepert} mentioned above the general equation of the fifth degree is transformed into the form (15), for which only the solution of a quadratic equation is required. If one regards $a, b, c$ therein as arbitrarily given, then the equations (16) serve for the determination of $\lambda, \mu, \gamma_3$. This likewise is done with the help of a quadratic equation, though this is not to be seen at first glance. (Cf. F. \gesperrt{Klein}, Vorlesungen über das Ikosa\"eder, S. 191 f.)

We shall return further on to the formation of resolvents for the seventh transformation degree, when we have at our disposal the means which complex multiplication offers us.

\begin{center}
\gesperrt{Ninth Chapter.}

\textbf{\Large Discriminant.}

\rule{0.3\linewidth}{0.4pt}
\end{center}

\begin{center}
\textbf{§ 84. \gesperrt{Definition of the Discriminants.}}
\end{center}

In the theory of quadratic fields there occur as discriminants certain integral rational (positive or negative) numbers which, if they are even, are divisible by 4, and which, if they are odd, leave the residue 1 on division by 4.

\gesperrt{Kronecker} has called such numbers \glqq \gesperrt{numbers of discriminant form}\grqq{}. We shall here call them briefly discriminants, and shall not take offence at the fact that this word has still various other meanings in algebra. We therefore define:

1. \gesperrt{An integer, positive or negative and different from zero, which satisfies one of the two congruences}
\weq{1}{D\equiv 0,\quad D\equiv 1 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ 4)}
\gesperrt{is called a discriminant.}

By this definition every square number is a discriminant. But since these occupy a certain exceptional position, we shall call them \gesperrt{improper discriminants whenever the distinction is necessary.}

2. \gesperrt{The product of two, and consequently of arbitrarily many, discriminants is again a discriminant.}

3. \gesperrt{A discriminant which contains (apart from 1) no square divisor after the separation of which a discriminant remains is called a stem discriminant.}

In what follows, stem discriminants shall be denoted by $\Delta$, to distinguish them from others. If $D$ is not a stem discriminant, then there is one and only one square number $Q^2$ and one stem discriminant $\Delta$ such that
\weq{2}{D = \Delta Q^2}
holds; $\Delta$ is then called the \gesperrt{stem of} $D$.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 343 =====
% !PRINTED 322
\weberpage{322}

A stem discriminant is divisible by no odd square number. If, however, $\Delta$ is divisible by 4, then
\weq{3}{\Delta \equiv 8,\ 12 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ 16)}
must hold. For were $\Delta \equiv 0, 4$ $(\mathrm{mod}\ 16)$, then after cancellation of the factor 4 a discriminant would remain.

In order, then, to find the stem for a given $D$, one has first to separate off the greatest odd square number, and then in addition so high a power of 4 that $\Delta$ becomes either odd and $\equiv 1$ (mod 4), or $\equiv 8$, or $\equiv 12$ (mod 16).

4. \gesperrt{A proper discriminant which is not decomposable into factors that are themselves again discriminants is called a prime discriminant.}

If $p$ is a natural odd prime, and if the sign $\pm$ is so determined that $\pm p \equiv 1$ (mod 4), then the prime discriminants are the following:
\weq{4}{\pm p,\quad -4,\quad +8,\quad -8.}

5. \gesperrt{Every stem discriminant can be decomposed in one and only one way into prime discriminants.}

For if one first separates off from $\Delta$ all the factors $\pm p$, there remains only one of the numbers 1, $-4$, $+8$, $-8$.

\begin{center}
\textbf{§ 85. The extended \gesperrt{Legendre-Jacobi} symbol.}
\end{center}

\gesperrt{The Legendre symbol} $\left(\dfrac{m}{p}\right)$ has, when $m$ is an arbitrary positive or negative number different from zero and $p$ is a natural prime not dividing $m$, the value $+1$ if $m$ is a quadratic residue, and the value $-1$ if $m$ is a quadratic non-residue of $p$ (Bd. I, § 145).

The meaning of the symbol has been extended by \gesperrt{Jacobi} in such a way that a composite number may also be put for $p$. If, however, $m$ is a discriminant, then a still further reaching generalization is sometimes to be recommended, and this we must now set forth\footnote{\gesperrt{Kronecker}, Berliner Sitzungsberichte, 30. Juli 1885. \gesperrt{Dirichlet-Dedekind}, Vorlesungen über Zahlentheorie, 4. Aufl., § 186. H.\ \gesperrt{Weber}, Göttinger Nachrichten, Januar 1893.}.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 344 =====
% !PRINTED 323
\weberpage{323}

If $D$ is a discriminant and $n$ an integral rational number, then we define a symbol $(D,n)$ by the following stipulations:
\weq{1}{(D,0)=0.}
\weq{2}{(D,1)=1.}
\weq{3}{\begin{aligned} (D,-1) &= +1, & D>0.\\ &= -1, & D<0. \end{aligned}}
\weq{4}{(D,p)=0,}
if $p$ is a prime divisor of $D$.
\weq{5}{(D,2)=(-1)^{\frac{D^2-1}{8}},\quad D\ \text{odd}.}
\weq{6}{(D,p)=\left(\dfrac{D}{p}\right),}
if $p$ is an odd prime that does not divide $D$.

If one decomposes $\pm n$ into its prime factors
\[
n = \pm p,\ p',\ p'',\ \dots,
\]
then
\weq{7}{(D,n) = (D,\pm 1)(D,p)(D,p')(D,p'')\dots}

By (1) to (7) the symbol $(D,n)$ is evidently defined without contradiction for all numbers $n$, and can have only one of the values $-1$, $0$, $+1$. It is always $=0$ then and only then, when $D$ and $n$ are not relatively prime to one another. From (7) there follows further:
\weq{8}{(D,n)(D,n') = (D,nn'),}
and if $Q^2$ is a square number that has no common divisor with $n$,
\weq{9}{(Q^2D,n) = (D,n).}

The formulae relating to the law of reciprocity take a particular form in this notation. We consider first the \gesperrt{prime discriminants}.

If $\pm p \equiv 1$ (mod 4), then by (3), (5), (6):
\[
(\pm p, -1) = (-1)^{\frac{p-1}{4}} = \left(\dfrac{-1}{p}\right),
\]
\[
(\pm p, 2) = (-1)^{\frac{p^2-1}{8}} = \left(\dfrac{2}{p}\right),
\]
\[
(\pm p, n) = \left(\dfrac{\pm p}{n}\right) = \left(\dfrac{n}{p}\right),
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 345 =====
% !PRINTED 324
\weberpage{324}

%<<CONT
when $n$ is an odd prime (by the law of reciprocity and its supplementary theorems [Bd. I, § 145, 9.]), and these formulae can be summarised in
\weq{10}{(\pm p, n) = \left(\dfrac{n}{p}\right).}
But by (7) this formula holds for \gesperrt{every arbitrary $n$ that is not divisible by $p$.}

In the same way one finds, for an odd $n$:
\weq{11}{\begin{aligned} (-4,n) &= (-1)^{\frac{n-1}{2}},\\ (8,n) &= (-1)^{\frac{n^2-1}{8}},\\ (-8,n) &= (-1)^{\frac{n-1}{2}+\frac{n^2-1}{8}}. \end{aligned}}
Further, in general, if $D$, $D'$ are two discriminants:
\weq{12}{(D,n)(D',n) = (DD',n).}
This formula holds in the first place when $DD'$ and $n$ are not relatively prime, because then both sides are $=0$. It holds further for $n=-1$ [by (3)], for $n=2$ [by (5) and the congruence $\dfrac{D^2-1}{8}+\dfrac{D'^2-1}{8} \equiv \dfrac{D^2D'^2-1}{8}$ (mod 2)] and for an odd prime $n$ [by (6)]. Hence by (7) it holds in general.

We can now summarise the law of reciprocity together with its supplementary theorems for discriminants in the following way:
\weq{13}{(D,D') = \pm(D',D),}
\gesperrt{in which the upper sign holds when at least one of the two discriminants $D$, $D'$ is positive, the lower when both are negative.}

In order to derive this formula from the usual form of the law of reciprocity, we assume first that the two formulae hold:
\[
(D,D') = \pm(D',D),
\]
\[
(D_1,D') = \pm(D',D_1).
\]
Then from (8) and (12) it follows that
\[
(DD_1,D') = \pm(D',DD_1),
\]
in which again the lower sign holds only when $D'$ and $DD_1$ are both negative. By a repeated application there results
\[
(DD_1,D'D_1') = \pm(D'D_1',DD_1)
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 346 =====
% !PRINTED 325
\weberpage{325}
%<<CONT
and consequently formula (12) is proved if it holds for any two prime discriminants.

But by (10), if $p$ and $p'$ are odd primes:
\[
(\pm p, \pm p') = \pm\left(\frac{p'}{p}\right), \quad (\pm p', \pm p) = \pm\left(\frac{p'}{p}\right), % [sic] The source prints p'/p in both members; the following prose requires p/p' in the second.
\]
in which the negative sign stands on the right only when \gesperrt{both signs on the left are negative}, that is, when $p$ as well as $p' \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$. In this case, and only in this case, $\left(\dfrac{p'}{p}\right) = -\left(\dfrac{p}{p'}\right)$, otherwise $\left(\dfrac{p'}{p}\right) = \left(\dfrac{p}{p'}\right)$. Thus formula (13) proves to be correct for this case.

Further, by (11) and (3), (5)
\[
(-4, \pm p) = +1, \quad (\pm p, -4) = \pm 1,
\]
\[
(p, \pm 8) = (p, \pm 2) = (p, 2) = (-1)^{\frac{p^2-1}{8}},
\]
\[
(\pm 8, p) = \left(\frac{\pm 8}{p}\right) = (-1)^{\frac{p^2-1}{8}},
\]
\[
[p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}],
\]
\[
(-p, \pm 8) = (-p, \pm 2) = \pm(-p, 2) = -1,
\]
\[
(\pm 8, -p) = \pm\left(\frac{\pm 8}{p}\right) = -1,
\]
\[
[p \equiv 3 \pmod{8}],
\]
from which formula (13) follows for these cases, and it is thereby proved in general.

From (13) it follows further, since every square number is a positive discriminant, that if $m$ is \gesperrt{relatively prime} to $D$,
\weq{14}{(D, m^2) = 1}
and consequently, by (8):
\weq{15}{(D, m^2 n) = (D, n),}
if $m$ and $D$ have no common divisor.

We have further the theorem:
\weq{16}{(D, n) = (D, n'),}
if $n \equiv n' \pmod{D}$.

The theorem is correct when $n$ and $D$ have a common divisor, and by (12) it is proved in general if it holds for every prime discriminant $D$. For these, however, it follows at once from (10), (11).

%% ===== canonical stable idx 347 =====
% !PRINTED 326
\weberpage{326}
Let us assume that in (16) $n$, $n'$ are themselves discriminants:
\[
n = D_1, \quad n' = D_2, \quad D_1 \equiv D_2 \pmod{D},
\]
then
\[
(D, D_1) = (D, D_2)
\]
and from (13) it follows that
\[
\begin{aligned}
(D, D_1) &= \pm(D_1, D) \\
(D, D_2) &= \pm(D_2, D),
\end{aligned}
\]
in which the upper signs hold when $D$ is positive, the lower ones when $D$, $D_1$, $D_2$ are all three negative, and different signs when $D$ is negative and $D_1$, $D_2$ are of different signs. Accordingly, by (16):
\weq{17}{(D_1, D) = \pm(D_2, D),}
in which the lower sign holds only when the \gesperrt{two numbers} $D$ and $D_1 D_2$ are both negative.

If $D_1$, $D_2$ are odd, we may set $D = 4m$, where $m$ is an arbitrary integer, and we obtain from (17)
\weq{18}{(D_1, m) = \pm(D_2, m),}
provided that
\weq{19}{D_1 \equiv D_2 \pmod{4m}}
\gesperrt{holds, the lower sign holding only when $m$ and $D_1 D_2$ are both negative.}

This theorem has so far been proved under the assumption that $D_1$ and $D_2$ are odd. But it holds in general. For the congruence (19) requires in the first place that $D_1$ and $D_2$ be at the same time even or at the same time odd. If they are both even, and $m$ is then even, (18) is correct, because both sides vanish. But if $m$ is odd and $D_1$, $D_2$ are even, then in (17) let us set $D = \pm m \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$, where $m$ is a positive odd number. Then from $D_1 \equiv D_2 \pmod{D}$ the congruence (19) follows, and by (17) we have
\[
(D_1, m) = (D_2, m),
\]
\weq{20}{\begin{aligned}
(D_1, m) &= (D_2, m),\\
(D_1, -m) &= \pm(D_2, -m), \\
(D_1, -1) &= \pm(D_2, -1),
\end{aligned}}
and consequently again
\[
(D_1, m) = (D_2, m).
\]
This formula therefore holds for every positive odd $m$, and by (20) then (18) is proved for a negative $m$ as well. The formulae (16) and (18) can be used for the calculation of the symbol $(D, n)$
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 348 =====
% !PRINTED 327
\weberpage{327}
%<<CONT
according to the algorithm of the greatest common divisor. For from the congruences
\[
\begin{aligned}
D &\equiv D' \pmod{4n}, \\
n &\equiv n' \pmod{D'}, \\
D' &\equiv D'' \pmod{4n'}, \\
n' &\equiv n'' \pmod{D''}, \\
&\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots
\end{aligned}
\]
one can determine the sequence of numbers
\[
D', \quad 2n', \quad D'', \quad 2n'', \quad \dots
\]
in such a way that each following one is smaller in absolute value than the preceding one, so long as none of the numbers $n'$, $n''$, $n'''$, $\dots$ has become equal to $\pm 1$.

If $D$ is not a square number, then a number $\beta$ can always be determined so that
\weq{21}{(D, \beta) = -1.}

For if $\varDelta$ is the stem of $D$ and $\beta$ is relatively prime to $D$, then (by 9)
\[
(D, \beta) = (\varDelta, \beta).
\]

If $\varDelta = \delta \varDelta'$ and $\delta$ is a prime discriminant, and therefore relatively prime to $\varDelta'$, then $\beta_0$ can be assumed in such a way that
\[
(\delta, \beta_0) = -1
\]
holds [by (10) and (11)], and $\beta$ can be determined from the two congruences
\[
\begin{aligned}
\beta &\equiv \beta_0 \pmod{\delta}, \\
&\equiv 1 \pmod{\varDelta'}
\end{aligned}
\]
Then one obtains, by (12),
\[
(D, \beta) = (\delta, \beta_0) = -1.
\]

If one lets $s$ run through a complete system of residues with respect to the modulus $D$ and sets
\[
S = \overset{s}{\Sigma}(D, s), % Source scan confirms s as the upper index on Sigma.
\]
then multiplication by $(D, \beta)$ gives
\[
-S = \overset{s}{\Sigma}(D, \beta s),
\]
and since $\beta s$ runs through a system of residues at the same time as $s$, it follows that
\weq{22}{S = 0.}

From this it follows:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 349 =====
% !PRINTED 328
\weberpage{328}
%<<CONT
In a complete system of numbers $s$ incongruent and coprime to $D$ there are just as many numbers $\alpha$ for which $(D, \alpha) = +1$ as there are numbers $\beta$ for which $(D, \beta) = -1$, and we have
\[
\begin{aligned}
(D,n) &= +1, \quad \text{if } n \equiv \alpha \\
&= -1, \quad \text{\textquotedbl} \quad n \equiv \beta \pmod{D}.
\end{aligned}
\]

\begin{center}
\S\,86. The \gesperrt{Gauss} Sums.
\end{center}

In the first volume we became acquainted with the \gesperrt{Gauss} sums from the theory of the division of the circle. These expressions admit of generalisation, and through the use of the symbol $(D, n)$ they take on a simple shape.

We had [Bd.\,I, \S\,179, (16)], when $n$ denotes an odd prime, $s$ a number not divisible by $n$, and $k$ runs through a system of residues with respect to the modulus $n$:
\weq{1}{\sum \left(\frac{k}{n}\right) e^{\frac{2\pi i s k}{n}} = \left(\frac{s}{n}\right) i^{\left(\frac{n-1}{2}\right)^2} \sqrt{n}.}

If we put $\pm n = \varDelta \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$, then $\varDelta$ is a prime discriminant, and by \S\,85, (10) we have
\[
\left(\frac{k}{n}\right) = (\varDelta, k), \quad \left(\frac{\mp s}{n}\right) = (\varDelta, \mp s) = (\varDelta, s)
\]
[the latter by \S\,85, (3), since the upper signs hold for positive and the lower for negative $\varDelta$], further:
\[
i^{\left(\frac{n-1}{2}\right)^2} \sqrt{n} = \sqrt{\varDelta},
\]
where $\sqrt{\varDelta}$ is positive real or positive imaginary according as $n \equiv 1$ or $\equiv 3 \pmod{4}$, and we can write (1) in the form:
\weq{2}{\overset{k}{\Sigma}(\varDelta, k) e^{-\frac{2\pi i k s}{\varDelta}} = (\varDelta, s) \sqrt{\varDelta}, % Source scan confirms k as the upper index on Sigma.
}
provided that in the case where $\varDelta$ is positive we replace $s$ by $-s$. This formula has so far been proved only for an odd prime discriminant. But it holds also, as direct calculation shows, for
\[
\varDelta = -4, \quad 8, \quad -8,
\]
and therefore for every prime discriminant.

If we assume the correctness of formula (2) for $\varDelta = \varDelta'$ and for $\varDelta = \varDelta''$, then, provided $\varDelta'$ and $\varDelta''$ have no common divisor, its correctness follows for $\varDelta = \varDelta' \varDelta''$.

For we have
\weq{3}{\sqrt{\varDelta'}\sqrt{\varDelta''} = \pm\sqrt{\varDelta' \varDelta''},}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 350 =====
% !PRINTED 329
\weberpage{329}

%<<CONT
when the upper sign holds, provided that at least one of the two fundamental discriminants $\Delta'$, $\Delta''$ is positive, and the lower one when both are negative.

If we set
\[
k = k'\Delta'' + k''\Delta',
\]
and let $k'$, $k''$ run through systems of residues with respect to $\Delta'$, $\Delta''$, then $k$ runs through a system of residues with respect to $\Delta = \Delta'\Delta''$.

The multiplication of the two sums
\weq{4}{\overset{k'}{\Sigma}(\Delta',k')\,e^{-\frac{2s\pi ik'}{\Delta'}}, \quad \overset{k''}{\Sigma}(\Delta'',k'')\,e^{-\frac{2s\pi ik''}{\Delta''}}}
gives
\weq{5}{\overset{k'k''}{\Sigma}(\Delta',k')(\Delta'',k'')\,e^{-\frac{2s\pi ik}{\Delta}}.}

But by \S\,85, (16) we have
\[
(\Delta',k) = (\Delta',\Delta'')(\Delta',k'),
\]
\[
(\Delta'',k) = (\Delta'',\Delta')(\Delta'',k''),
\]
and consequently, by \S\,85, (13),
\[
(\Delta,k) = \pm(\Delta',k')(\Delta'',k''),
\]
and accordingly the general validity of formula (2) for every fundamental discriminant $\Delta$ follows from (3), (4) and (5).

\begin{center}\rule{0.2\linewidth}{0.4pt}\end{center}
