\begin{center}
\gesperrt{Tenth Chapter.}\\[4pt]
\textbf{Algebraic Numbers and Forms.}
\end{center}

\begin{center}
\rule{0.25\textwidth}{0.4pt}
\end{center}

\begin{center}
\S\,87. \gesperrt{Ideals and Forms in Algebraic Fields.}
\end{center}

The interest which the theory of elliptic functions has for the algebraist springs from its application to the theory of quadratic irrational numbers, to which these functions stand in a relation analogous to that of the roots of unity to the rational numbers. They offer us the first and hitherto only example, more exactly known in its laws, of a region of algebraic numbers going beyond the cyclotomic numbers. In order to be able to present the theory of these numbers more fully, we must first premise some theorems from the theory of forms and of algebraic fields, and especially of quadratic forms.

In Bd. II, \S\,163, 169 a connection was found between the ideals of an algebraic field $\Omega$ of the $n$th degree and certain homogeneous functions of the $n$th degree of $n$ variables. Before we apply this to quadratic fields, let the general theorems be briefly recalled.

Let $\mathfrak{a}$ be an ideal of a field $\Omega$ and let $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n$ be a basis of this ideal. Further, let $\omega_1, \omega_2, \ldots, \omega_n$ be a minimal basis of $\Omega$. Then
\weq{1}{(\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n) = (A)(\omega_1, \omega_2, \ldots, \omega_n),}
if $(A)$ denotes a \gesperrt{linear substitution with integral coefficients}. In order to pass over to another basis $\alpha_1', \alpha_2', \ldots, \alpha_n'$ of $\mathfrak{a}$, one makes a linear substitution $L$ with the determinant $\pm 1$,
\weq{2}{(\alpha_1', \alpha_2', \ldots, \alpha_n') = (L)(\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n),}
from which there results
\weq{3}{(\alpha_1', \alpha_2', \ldots, \alpha_n') = (L)(A)(\omega_1, \omega, \ldots, \omega_n)^{\text{1)}}.} % [sic] printed \textquotedbl{}$\omega$\textquotedbl{} without subscript 2 in the second entry

\medskip
\noindent\rule{0.3\textwidth}{0.4pt}\\
$^{1}$) On linear substitutions and their composition cf. the sixth chapter of the second volume.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 352 =====
% !PRINTED 331
\weberpage{331}

\gesperrt{By the norm} $N(\mathfrak{a})$ of the ideal $\mathfrak{a}$ one understands the
\gesperrt{absolute value} of the determinant $A$ of the substitution $(A)$:
\[
A = \Sigma \pm a_{1,1}\,a_{2,2}\ldots a_{n,n},
\]
and by (3) the norm is independent of the choice of the basis.

1. \gesperrt{We shall call the basis $(\alpha_\nu)$ positive if
the determinant $A$ is positive, and so equal to the norm of $\mathfrak{a}$.
If $(\alpha_\nu)$ is positive, then $(\alpha'_\nu)$ is always
positive when the substitution determinant $L = +1$.}

From every basis one can derive a positive basis by a substitution with
determinant $-1$, for example by an interchange of two of the $\alpha_\nu$, and
in what follows we shall for the most part use only
positive bases.

The basis determined in Bd. II, \S\ 163, (3) \gesperrt{is positive}.

If now $t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_n$ denotes a system of independent variables and
\weq{4}{\lambda = \sum_\nu \alpha_\nu t_\nu}
% Source scan confirms nu as the lower summation index in (4).
is a basis form with positive basis, then there results (Bd. II, \S\ 164)
\weq{5}{N(\lambda) = N(\mathfrak{a})\,T,}
in which
\weq{6}{T = \Sigma \pm t_{1,1}\,t_{2,2}\ldots t_{n,n}}
is a \gesperrt{primitive homogeneous form with integral coefficients}, of degree $n$, in the
variables $t_\nu$. The $t_{r,s}$ are \gesperrt{linear functions} of the $t_\nu$.

If the substitution (2) is applied to (4), there results
\weq{7}{\lambda = \lambda' = \sum \alpha'_\nu t'_\nu,}
if
\weq{8}{(t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_n) = L'(t'_1, t'_2, \ldots, t'_n),}
in which $L'$ is the \gesperrt{transposed substitution} of $L$; and if
$(\alpha'_\nu)$ is likewise a positive basis, then $L'$ has the
determinant $+1$, and formula (5) gives
\weq{9}{N(\lambda) = N(\mathfrak{a})\,T',}
in which $T'$ is a homogeneous function of degree $n$ in the variables $t'$
which arises from $T$ by the substitution (8).

Two forms which arise from one another by a linear substitution with integral
coefficients of determinant $+1$ are called \gesperrt{equivalent}. Sometimes the forms are also
called equivalent when the substitution determinant is $-1$, but then
with the addition ``\gesperrt{improperly}''. It is then proved by (8):
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 353 =====
% !PRINTED 332
\weberpage{332}
%<<CONT
2. \gesperrt{If we call the form $T$ the form belonging to the basis $(\alpha_\nu)$ of $\mathfrak{a}$, then the forms belonging to different positive bases of the same ideal are equivalent.}

Let us denote the conjugate values of $\alpha_s, \omega_s$ by

\[
\alpha_{s,1},\ \alpha_{s,2},\ \dots,\ \alpha_{s,n};\quad \omega_{s,1},\ \omega_{s,2},\ \dots,\ \omega_{s,n}
\]

and set

\weq{10}{\alpha_{s,r} = \overset{\nu}{\Sigma}\, a_{s,\nu}\,\omega_{\nu,r},}

then there results

\weq{11}{(\Sigma \pm \alpha_{1,1}\,\alpha_{2,2}\,\dots\,\alpha_{n,n})^2 = N(\mathfrak{a})^2 \varDelta,}

where $\varDelta$ is the fundamental number of the field $\Omega$, namely the determinant square:

\[
\varDelta = (\Sigma \pm \omega_{1,1}\,\omega_{2,2}\,\dots\,\omega_{n,n})^2
\]

(Bd.\,II, \S\,162).

If $\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \dots, \lambda_n$ are the conjugate values of $\lambda$, then by (4)

\weq{12}{\lambda_r = \overset{\nu}{\Sigma}\, \alpha_{\nu,r}\, t_\nu}

is a linear substitution for the variables $t_\nu$ with the substitution determinant

\weq{13}{r = N(\mathfrak{a})\,\sqrt{\varDelta},}

and through this the form $T$ passes, by (5), into the product

\weq{14}{T' = [N(\mathfrak{a})]^{-1}\,\lambda_1\,\lambda_2\,\dots\,\lambda_n}

since $N(\lambda)$ is the product of the conjugate values of $\lambda$ (Bd.\,II, \S\,151). We can apply invariant theory (Bd.\,I, \S\,65) to this, and if we form the \gesperrt{Hesse} determinant:

\weq{15}{H = \Sigma \pm \frac{\partial^2 T}{\partial t_1 \partial t_1}\,\frac{\partial^2 T}{\partial t_2 \partial t_2}\cdots\frac{\partial^2 T}{\partial t_n \partial t_n},}

then

\weq{16}{H' = r^{-2}\,H.}

If, however, we form $H'$ by (14) in the variables $\lambda_\nu$, and observe that an $n$-rowed determinant in which the diagonal terms are $=0$ and all the other terms are $=1$ has the value $(-1)^{n-1}(n-1)$\footnote{One can easily prove this theorem by extending the determinant through the addition of an $(n+1)$th row and an $(n+1)$th column, in which the added row contains only \gesperrt{ones}, and the column contains zeros with the exception of the last element.}, then it follows:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 354 =====
% !PRINTED 333
\weberpage{333}
%<<CONT
\[
\begin{aligned}
H' &= (-1)^{n-1}(n-1)\,N(\mathfrak{a})^{-n}(\lambda_1\lambda_2\ldots\lambda_n)^{n-2}, \\
&= (-1)^{n-1}(n-1)\,N(\mathfrak{a})^{-2}\,T^{n-2}
\end{aligned}
\]
and consequently, by (13) and (16),
\weq{17}{H = (-1)^{n-1}(n-1)\,T^{n-2}\Delta.}

\begin{center}
§ 88. \gesperrt{Ideal Classes and Classes of Forms.}
\end{center}

In Bd. II, § 170 we explained the \gesperrt{equivalence} of ideals and the \gesperrt{ideal classes}. According to this, two ideals $\mathfrak{a}$, $\mathfrak{b}$ were equivalent. If there is an integral or fractional \gesperrt{number} of the field $\Omega$ which is the quotient of $\mathfrak{b}$ and $\mathfrak{a}$, that is:
\weq{1}{\eta\,\mathfrak{a} = \mathfrak{b},}
and it has been shown that the ideals are thereby divided into classes, and that the \gesperrt{number of these classes is finite}. In some cases it is expedient to take the concept of equivalence somewhat more narrowly and to call $\mathfrak{a}$ and $\mathfrak{b}$ equivalent only if there is a number $\eta$ with \gesperrt{positive norm} that satisfies condition (1). This difference naturally does not come into consideration when the norms of all numbers are positive, as for example in the imaginary quadratic field. Neither does it come into consideration when there are \gesperrt{units with the norm} $-1$, because, if $\varepsilon$ is such a unit, either $N(\eta)$ or $N(\varepsilon\eta)$ is positive, and $\varepsilon$ and $\varepsilon\eta$ satisfy condition (1) at the same time.

But if there are no units whose norm $=-1$, while there are other numbers in $\Omega$ with negative norm, then under the narrower definition of equivalence every ideal class divides once again into two classes. We wish to hold here to the narrower concept of equivalence, which comes into force, for example, for some \gesperrt{real quadratic fields}\footnote{Namely, when the \gesperrt{Pell} equation $t^2 - D\,u^2 = -4$ has no solution.}.

In (1) $\eta$ may be fractional. But if $\alpha$ is an integer divisible by $\mathfrak{a}$, then $\eta\alpha$ is an \gesperrt{integer divisible by $\mathfrak{b}$}, and from this it follows: If
\weq{2}{(\alpha_1,\ \alpha_2,\ \ldots,\ \alpha_n)}
is a basis of $\mathfrak{a}$, then
\[
(\beta_1,\ \beta_2,\ \ldots,\ \beta_n) = (\alpha_1\eta,\ \alpha_2\eta,\ \ldots,\ \alpha_n\eta)
\]
is a basis of $\mathfrak{b}$, and if the first basis is positive, then (under the narrower concept of equivalence) so is the second.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 355 =====
% !PRINTED 334
\weberpage{334}
For the necessary and sufficient condition that (2) be a basis of $\mathfrak{a}$ consists in this, that every integer $\alpha$ divisible by $\mathfrak{a}$, and only such, is contained in the form:
\weq{3}{\alpha = x_1\alpha_1 + x_2\alpha_2 + \cdots + x_n\alpha_n}
with integer $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$. Consequently all numbers
\weq{4}{\beta = x_1\alpha_1\eta + x_2\alpha_2\eta + \cdots + x_n\alpha_n\eta}
are divisible by $\mathfrak{b}$. If, conversely, $\beta$ is an integer divisible by $\mathfrak{b}$, then $\beta/\eta$ is divisible by $\mathfrak{a}$ and consequently representable in the form (3). Hence $\beta$ is representable by (4).

Further, in the notation of (9) and (10), § 87, if $\alpha$ is a positive basis:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Sigma \pm \alpha_{1,1}\alpha_{2,2}\ldots\alpha_{n,n} &= N(\mathfrak{a})\, \Sigma \pm \omega_{1,1}\omega_{2,2}\ldots\omega_{n,n}, \\
\Sigma \pm \beta_{1,1}\beta_{2,2}\ldots\beta_{n,n} &= N(\eta)\, \Sigma \pm \alpha_{1,1}\alpha_{2,2}\ldots\alpha_{n,n}, \\
&= N(\eta)N(\mathfrak{a})\, \Sigma \pm \omega_{1,1}\omega_{2,2}\ldots\omega_{n,n}, \\
&= \pm N(\mathfrak{b})\, \Sigma \pm \omega_{1,1}\omega_{2,2}\ldots\omega_{n,n},
\end{aligned}
\]
and since by (1)
\weq{5}{N(\mathfrak{b}) = N(\eta)N(\mathfrak{a})}
holds, the positive sign must stand in $\pm N(\mathfrak{b})$.

If $\lambda$ is a basis form of $\mathfrak{a}$, then $\eta\lambda$ is a basis form of $\mathfrak{b}$, and
\weq{6}{\begin{aligned} N(\lambda) &= N(\mathfrak{a})T, \\ N(\eta\lambda) &= N(\mathfrak{b})T, \end{aligned}}
and thus the same form $T$ belongs to the two ideals $\mathfrak{a}$, $\mathfrak{b}$. If we unite equivalent forms $T$ into one class, then by 2. we can say:

3. \gesperrt{To every ideal class there belongs a definite class of forms.}

In answering the question whether different ideal classes can belong to one and the same class of forms, we make the assumption that $\Omega$ is a \gesperrt{normal field}: let us assume, then, that equivalent forms $T$ and $T'$ belong to two ideals $\mathfrak{a}$ and $\mathfrak{a}'$; then, if $\lambda$ is a basis form of $\mathfrak{a}$,
\weq{7}{N(\lambda) = N(\mathfrak{a})T,}
and if we carry $T'$ over into $T$ by a linear substitution, and understand by $\lambda'$ a basis form of $\mathfrak{a}'$ (with the same variables $t$ as $\lambda$), then
\weq{8}{N(\lambda') = N(\mathfrak{a}')T.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 356 =====
% !PRINTED 335
\weberpage{335}
The linear factors of $N(\lambda)$ and $N(\lambda')$ must therefore agree with one another, apart from a constant factor, because an integral function of arbitrary variables can be decomposed into irreducible (here linear) factors in only one way (Bd.\,I, § 20, Bd.\,II, § 152); and since all these factors belong to the same field $\Omega$, there is among the conjugate factors $\lambda'$ one that satisfies the condition:
\[
\lambda = \eta\lambda',
\]
in which $\eta$ is a number in $\Omega$. The functionals $\lambda$ and $\lambda'$, and accordingly the corresponding ideals, are therefore equivalent.

4. \gesperrt{If in a normal field the same class of forms belongs to the two ideals $\mathfrak{a}$ and $\mathfrak{a}'$, then among the ideals conjugate to $\mathfrak{a}'$ there is one that is equivalent to $\mathfrak{a}$.}

\begin{center}
\textbf{§ 89. Composition of forms and multiplication of ideals.}
\end{center}

Let $\mathfrak{a}$ and $\mathfrak{b}$ now be two ideals in $\Omega$, and let
\weq{1}{\mathfrak{c} = \mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}}
be the product formed from them both. Let further
\weq{2}{\begin{aligned}
\mathfrak{a} &= (\alpha_1,\ \alpha_2,\ \ldots,\ \alpha_n), \\
\mathfrak{b} &= (\beta_1,\ \beta_2,\ \ldots,\ \beta_n), \\
\mathfrak{c} &= (\gamma_1,\ \gamma_2,\ \ldots,\ \gamma_n)
\end{aligned}}
be bases of these ideals. Since every number $\alpha_h\beta_k$ belongs to $\mathfrak{c}$, there is a system of integral rational numbers $c^{(r)}_{hk}$ such that
\weq{3}{\alpha_h\beta_k = \overset{r}{\Sigma}\, c^{(r)}_{h,k}\,\gamma_r}
holds; and since every number in $\mathfrak{c}$ arises by the multiplication of one number from $\mathfrak{a}$ and one from $\mathfrak{b}$ and the addition of these products (Bd.\,II, § 169), conversely also
\weq{4}{\gamma_s = \overset{h,k}{\Sigma}\, a^{(s)}_{h,k}\,\alpha_h\beta_k,}
in which the $a^{(s)}_{h,k}$ are likewise integral rational numbers.

If one substitutes (3) into (4), it follows that
\weq{5}{\gamma_s = \overset{r}{\Sigma}\,\gamma_r \overset{h,k}{\Sigma}\, a^{(s)}_{h,k}\,c^{(r)}_{h,k},}
and from this
\weq{6}{\overset{h,k}{\Sigma}\, a^{(s)}_{h,k}\,c^{(r)}_{h,k} = (r,s),}
in which
\[
(r,r) = 1, \quad (r,s) = 0, \quad r \neq s.
\]

%% ===== canonical stable idx 357 =====
% !PRINTED 336
\weberpage{336}
If, then, we denote variables by $x_r$ and set
\weq{7}{\overset{r}{\Sigma}\, x_r\, c^{(r)}_{h,k} = y_{h,k},}
it follows that:
\weq{8}{x_s = \overset{h,k}{\Sigma}\, a^{(s)}_{h,k}\, y_{h,k}.}
Now let $u_r$, $v_r$, $t_r$ denote three systems of variables, and let
\weq{9}{\begin{aligned}
\mu &= \Sigma\, \alpha_r\, u_r, \\
\nu &= \Sigma\, \beta_r\, v_r, \\
\lambda &= \Sigma\, \gamma_r\, t_r
\end{aligned}}
be basis forms of $\mathfrak{a}$, $\mathfrak{b}$, $\mathfrak{c}$, and further let $U$, $V$, $T$ be the forms belonging to $\mathfrak{a}$, $\mathfrak{b}$, $\mathfrak{c}$, written in the variables $u,v,t$. Then
\weq{10}{\begin{aligned}
N(\mu) &= N(\mathfrak{a})\,U, \\
N(\nu) &= N(\mathfrak{b})\,V, \\
N(\lambda) &= N(\mathfrak{c})\,T.
\end{aligned}}
From (3) there follows therefore, by multiplication with $u_h v_k$ and summation according to (9):
\weq{11}{\mu\nu = \overset{r}{\Sigma}\, \gamma_r \overset{h,k}{\Sigma}\, c^{(r)}_{h,k}\, u_h v_k,}
hence, if one sets
\weq{12}{t_r = \overset{h,k}{\Sigma}\, c^{(r)}_{h,k}\, u_h v_k}
then:
\weq{13}{\mu\nu = \lambda,}
and from this, since $N(\mathfrak{a})N(\mathfrak{b}) = N(\mathfrak{c})$, there follows by (10)
\weq{14}{T = UV.}
In this, however, the $t_r$ are no longer independent variables; rather, they arise from $u_h$, $v_k$ through the \gesperrt{bilinear substitution} (12).

5. \gesperrt{The form $T$ passes, through the bilinear substitution (12), into the product of the two forms $U, V$.}

But this substitution has still one essential peculiarity. We call the functions $t_r$ determined by (12) \gesperrt{linearly independent} with respect to a prime modulus $p$ if from the congruence
\weq{15}{\Sigma\, x_r t_r \equiv 0 \pmod{p},}
in which the $x_r$ are integral rational numbers, it follows that all these numbers are divisible by $p$. If this holds for every arbitrary prime $p$, the $t_r$ are called \gesperrt{simply linearly independent}.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 358 =====
% !PRINTED 337
\weberpage{337}

By (12) and (7) the congruence (15) is equivalent
to the $n^2$ congruences

\[
y_{h,k}=\overset{r}{\Sigma}\,x_{r}\,c_{h,k}^{(r)}\equiv 0\pmod{p} % Source scan prints r above Sigma and no lower index.
\]
and from (6) there then follows:
\[
x_s\equiv 0\pmod{p},
\]
and this says that the substitutions (17) are linearly
independent for every modulus $p$.

\gesperrt{According to Gauss (Disq. aritm. art. 235) a form $T$
is said to be compounded or composed of the two forms $U, V$ when $T$ passes over,
by a bilinear substitution for the variable $t$ whose equations are
linearly independent for every modulus, into the product $UV$.}

Accordingly we have the theorem:

6. \gesperrt{The form that belongs to the product of two ideals $\mathfrak{a}, \mathfrak{b}$
is compounded from the forms of the ideals $\mathfrak{a}$ and $\mathfrak{b}$}\footnote{The theorems that \gesperrt{Gauss} proves at the passage mentioned by a very
lengthy calculation for binary quadratic forms are here derived in the greatest
generality by simple considerations. Cf. \gesperrt{Dirichlet-Dedekind}, Vorlesungen \"uber Zahlentheorie, \S 182. For binary quadratic
forms: \gesperrt{Dedekind}, Crelles Journal, Bd. 129; \gesperrt{H. Weber}, G\"ottinger Nachrichten 1907.}.

\begin{center}\rule{0.2\linewidth}{0.4pt}\end{center}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 359 =====
% !PRINTED 338
\weberpage{338}

\begin{center}
\gesperrt{Eleventh Chapter.}

\textbf{\Large Ideals in Quadratic Fields.}

\rule{3cm}{0.4pt}
\end{center}

\begin{center}
\textbf{\S\ 90. \gesperrt{Discriminant of the Quadratic Field.}}
\end{center}

A quadratic field arises when a square root $\sqrt{d}$ is \gesperrt{adjoined} to the
field of rational numbers; here $d$ may be assumed to be \gesperrt{an integer without
a square divisor}. The field is real or imaginary according as $d$ is positive or negative. If we denote the field of
rational numbers, the absolute domain of rationality, by $\mathfrak{R}$, and
by $\mathfrak{R}(x,x',\dots)$ the field which arises from $\mathfrak{R}$ by the adjunction of $x,x',\dots$,
then the quadratic field $\Omega$ is to be denoted thus:
\weq{1}{\Omega=\mathfrak{R}(\sqrt{d}).}

Every number of the field $\Omega$ can be put into the form:
\weq{2}{\omega=\frac{x+y\sqrt{d}}{2},}
in which $x, y$ are rational integral or fractional numbers.

The number \gesperrt{conjugate} to $\omega$
\weq{3}{\omega'=\frac{x-y\sqrt{d}}{2}}
is likewise contained in the field $\Omega$, and consequently $\Omega$ is a
\gesperrt{normal field.}

In order that $\omega$ be \gesperrt{an integer}, it is necessary that
\[
\omega+\omega'=x,\quad(\omega-\omega')^2=y^2 d
\]
be integral rational numbers, and since $d$ is to have no square divisor,
$x$ and $y$ must be integers. But in order that $\omega$ should really be an
integer, the norm $\frac{1}{4}(x^2-y^2 d)$ must also be an integral rational number, i.\,e.
\weq{4}{x^2-y^2 d\equiv 0\pmod{4}}
must hold. If $d\equiv 2$ or $\equiv 3\pmod 4$, this condition can only be
satisfied if $x$ and $y$ are even numbers, and hence, if we replace
$x, y$ by $2x, 2y$, it follows:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 360 =====
% !PRINTED 339
\weberpage{339}
%<<CONT

1. \gesperrt{If $d\equiv 2, 3\pmod 4$, then all and only those
numbers of the field $\Omega$ are integral which are contained in the form}
\[
x+y\sqrt{d}
\]
\gesperrt{with integral rational $x, y$.}

But if $d\equiv 1\pmod 4$, then (3) is satisfied when $x$ and $y$
are both even or both odd, that is, when $x$ has the form
$2x_1-y$. If one then again replaces $x_1$ by $x$, it follows:

2. \gesperrt{If $d\equiv 1\pmod 4$, then all and only those numbers
in $\Omega$ are integral which are contained in the form}
\[
x+y\,\frac{-1+\sqrt{d}}{2}
\]
\gesperrt{with integral rational $x, y$.}

Thus in case 1. $(1,\sqrt{d})$, in case 2. $\left(1,\dfrac{-1+\sqrt{d}}{2}\right)$
is \gesperrt{a minimal basis of the field $\Omega$. The fundamental number or discriminant of the field $\Omega$} is therefore, in case 1.:
\weq{5}{\varDelta=\begin{vmatrix}1, & \sqrt{d}\\ 1, & -\sqrt{d}\end{vmatrix}^{2}=4d,}
in case 2.:
\weq{6}{\varDelta=\begin{vmatrix}1, & \dfrac{-1+\sqrt{d}}{2}\\[6pt] 1, & \dfrac{-1-\sqrt{d}}{2}\end{vmatrix}^{2}=d.}
In both cases one can therefore put the integer $\omega$ into the
form:
\weq{7}{\omega=\frac{x+y\sqrt{\varDelta}}{2},}
with the condition that
\weq{8}{4N(\omega)=x^2-\varDelta y^2\equiv 0\pmod 4}
shall hold.

The two forms of the minimal basis which we have obtained,
namely $(1,\sqrt{d})$ and $\left(1,\dfrac{-1+\sqrt{d}}{2}\right)$, are therefore:
\weq{9}{\begin{aligned}(1,0)&=\left(1,\tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{\varDelta}\right), & \varDelta&\equiv 0,\\ &=\left(1,\frac{-1+\sqrt{\varDelta}}{2}\right), & \varDelta&\equiv 1.\end{aligned}\quad(\mathrm{mod}\ 4).}
Here the sign of $\sqrt{\varDelta}$ may be fixed in any manner whatever, but it must then be kept fixed throughout the same discussion. We will assume once and for all:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 361 =====
% !PRINTED 340
\weberpage{340}
%<<CONT

3. \gesperrt{If $\varDelta$ is positive, $\sqrt{\varDelta}$ shall likewise be
positive, and if $\varDelta$ is negative, $-i\sqrt{\varDelta}$ shall be positive, or
$\sqrt{\varDelta}$ positive imaginary.}

From (1), (2) there follows further:

4. \gesperrt{The fundamental number of a quadratic field is
always $\equiv 0$ or $\equiv 1$ with respect to the modulus 4, and has, apart from 4,
no quadratic divisor. It is therefore a discriminant,
and indeed a stem discriminant.}

\textbf{\S\ 91. \gesperrt{Ideals and Forms in Quadratic Fields.}}

If $\mathfrak{a}$ is an ideal of the quadratic field $\Omega$, $\alpha_1, \alpha_2$ a
positive basis, and
\weq{1}{\lambda=\alpha_1 t_1+\alpha_2 t_2}
a basis form of $\mathfrak{a}$, then
\weq{2}{N(\lambda)=(\alpha_1 t_1+\alpha_2 t_2)(\alpha_1' t_1+\alpha_2' t_2)=N(\mathfrak{a})\,T,}
and $N(\mathfrak{a})$ is the greatest common divisor of the three integral
rational numbers
\[
\alpha_1\alpha_1', \quad \alpha_1\alpha_2'+\alpha_2\alpha_1', \quad \alpha_2\alpha_2'.
\]
If we therefore set
\weq{3}{\begin{aligned}
\alpha_1\alpha_1' &= a\,N(\mathfrak{a}),\\
\alpha_1\alpha_2'+\alpha_2\alpha_1' &= b\,N(\mathfrak{a}),\\
\alpha_2\alpha_2' &= c\,N(\mathfrak{a}),
\end{aligned}}
then
\weq{4}{T=a t_1^2+b t_1 t_2+c t_2^2}
is the form belonging to the basis $\alpha_1, \alpha_2$. We denote it, when
the notation for the variables is of no consequence, by
\weq{5}{\varphi=(a, b, c).}
It is a primitive quadratic form whose discriminant
\weq{6}{\varDelta=b^2-4ac}
is equal to the fundamental number of the field $\Omega$ (\S\ 87). In order to form
the basis $\alpha_1, \alpha_2$ according to Bd.\,II, \S\ 163, one seeks first the least
natural number $a_{11}$ divisible by $\mathfrak{a}$, and then the least
natural number $a_{12}$ for which a rational number $a_{12}$ satisfying the condition % [sic] German source prints a_{12} in both occurrences.

\weq{7}{a_{12}+a_{22}\theta\equiv 0\pmod{\mathfrak{a}}}
can be determined. Since the congruence (7) can be satisfied for
$a_{22}=a_{11}$, namely by $a_{12}=0$, then
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 362 =====
% !PRINTED 341
\weberpage{341}
%<<CONT
it follows that $a_{11}$ is divisible by $a_{22}$, and we set $a_{11} = a_{22}a$.
Then we have the basis of $\mathfrak{a}$:
\weq{8}{\begin{aligned} \alpha_1 &= a_{22}a,\\ \alpha_2 &= a_{12} + a_{22}\theta. \end{aligned}}
Then, by Bd.\,II, §\,164, (12):
\weq{9}{N(\mathfrak{a}) = a_{22}^2\,a,}
and if for $(1, \theta)$ we take the basis §\,90, (9), then
\[
\theta + \theta' = 0 \text{ or } = -1,
\]
\weq{10}{\theta\theta' = -\tfrac14\Delta \text{ or } = \frac{1-\Delta}{4}.}
According as $\Delta \equiv 0$, or $\equiv 1 \pmod 4$, and
\[
(\theta - \theta')^2 = \Delta.
\]
In these two cases there then results, when one substitutes (8) in (3)
and takes account of (9):
\[
a_{22}b = 2a_{12} \text{ or } = 2a_{12} - a_{22},
\]
and consequently in both cases:
\weq{11}{\alpha_1 = a_{22}a, \quad \alpha_2 = a_{22}\,\frac{b+\sqrt{\Delta}}{2},}
and the form
\[
T = (a,\,b,\,c)
\]
here has a \gesperrt{positive first coefficient}.

If we set
\weq{12}{\omega = -\frac{\alpha_2}{\alpha_1} = -\frac{b+\sqrt{\Delta}}{2a},}
then $\omega$ is a root of the quadratic equation:
\weq{13}{a\omega^2 + b\omega + c = 0}
and
\weq{14}{\lambda = a_{22}a(x-\omega y)}
is a functional corresponding to the ideal $\mathfrak{a}$, and at the same time a
basis form of $\mathfrak{a}$. $a$ is the least positive integer for which
$a\omega$ becomes an integer.

The necessary and sufficient condition for two
integers $\alpha_1, \alpha_2$ of the field $\Omega$ to form the basis of an ideal
consists in this, that first of all $\alpha_1, \alpha_2$ is a basis of the field $\Omega$,
and that, if $\omega_1, \omega_2$ is a minimal basis of this field,
\[
\alpha_1\omega_1,\quad \alpha_2\omega_1,\quad \alpha_1\omega_2,\quad \alpha_2\omega_2
\]
by the linear form
\[
\lambda = \alpha_1 t_1 + \alpha_2 t_2
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 363 =====
% !PRINTED 342
\weberpage{342}
%<<CONT
are representable with integral $t_1, t_2$ (Bd.\,II, §\,163, 164). For
then, if $\alpha$ is representable by $\lambda$, every product $\omega\alpha$ is
also representable by $\lambda$. In our case this condition reduces to the requirement that $\alpha_1\theta, \alpha_2\theta$ must be representable by $\lambda$. But if
$(a, b, c)$ is any quadratic form of the discriminant $\Delta$
with \gesperrt{positive first} coefficient $a$, then we may also take
$\tfrac12(b+\sqrt{\Delta})$ for $\theta$, and since
\[
\left(\frac{b+\sqrt{\Delta}}{2}\right)^2 = -ac + b\,\frac{b+\sqrt{\Delta}}{2}
\]
holds, (11) is always the basis of an ideal in $\Omega$. Here
the positive number $a_{22}$ may be assumed arbitrarily. If we set
$a_{22} = 1$, then
\weq{15}{\lambda = a(x-\omega y)}
is the basis form of an ideal $\mathfrak{a}$ completely determined by $(a, b, c)$, whose
norm is equal to $a$, and a basis of this ideal is
\weq{16}{(a,\ a\omega).}

\begin{center}
§ 92. \gesperrt{Prime Ideals in the Quadratic Field.}
\end{center}

A prime $p$ is in the quadratic field $\Omega$ either
still indecomposable itself, and is then a prime ideal of the second
degree, or $p$ splits into two prime ideals of the first degree $\mathfrak{p}, \mathfrak{p}'$.
We have accordingly two cases to distinguish:
\[
\text{a)}\quad p = \mathfrak{p} \text{ in } \Omega \text{ indecomposable:}\quad N(\mathfrak{p}) = p^2,
\]
\[
\text{b)}\quad p = \mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{p}' \qquad\qquad N(\mathfrak{p}) = N(\mathfrak{p}') = p,
\]
and in the latter case the two prime ideals $\mathfrak{p}, \mathfrak{p}'$ may be either
different from one another or else equal, so that we can distinguish
yet a third case:
\[
\text{c)}\quad p = \mathfrak{p}^2,\quad N(\mathfrak{p}) = p.
\]
It is now a question of ascertaining the conditions
under which the one or the other of these cases occurs.

If $N(\mathfrak{p}) = p$, then $p$ is the number of incongruent
numbers $(\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak{p})$ in $\Omega$, and consequently in this case \gesperrt{every number}
in $\Omega$ is congruent to one of the rational numbers $r$:
\weq{1}{0,\ 1,\ 2,\ \ldots,\ p-1}

If on the other hand $N(\mathfrak{p}) = p^2$, then there are also numbers which,
with respect to $\mathfrak{p}$, are not congruent to any rational number.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 364 =====
% !PRINTED 343
\weberpage{343}
If, however, $(1, \theta)$ is a basis of $\Omega$ and if, in order to comprise
both cases of §\,90, (9),
\weq{2}{\theta = \frac{-\Delta+\sqrt{\Delta}}{2}}
is assumed, then in case a)
\[
\theta \text{ not congruent with a number } r,
\]
in case b) or c)
\[
\theta \equiv r \pmod{\mathfrak{p}},
\]
so that, if one sets $-x = 2r + \Delta$, it follows:

1. \gesperrt{The necessary and sufficient condition for
the occurrence of one of the cases b), c) is this, that
there is an integral rational number which is at once
even or odd with $\Delta$, and for which}
\weq{3}{\frac{x+\sqrt{\Delta}}{2} \equiv 0 \pmod{\mathfrak{p}}.}
If $\mathfrak{p}'$ is the ideal conjugate to $\mathfrak{p}$, then
\weq{4}{\frac{-x+\sqrt{\Delta}}{2} \equiv 0 \pmod{\mathfrak{p}'},}
and from this it follows
\weq{5}{x^2 \equiv \Delta \pmod{4p}.}
If conversely the congruence (5) is satisfied by $x = r$, then
\[
\frac{r+\sqrt{\Delta}}{2}\cdot\frac{-r+\sqrt{\Delta}}{2} \equiv 0 \pmod{\mathfrak{p}},
\]
and consequently either $x = r$ or $x = -r$ satisfies condition (3).

The two ideals $\mathfrak{p}, \mathfrak{p}'$ will be identical with one another
when the two numbers (3) and (4), and consequently their
sum $\sqrt{\Delta}$ as well, are divisible by $\mathfrak{p}$, and hence $\Delta$ by $p$. Then
$x \equiv 0$ or $x \equiv p \pmod{2p}$ is the only root of (5).

We thus have the result:

2. \gesperrt{The prime factor $\mathfrak{p}$ of the natural prime $p$ is
of the second degree when the congruence (5) has no
solution, of the first degree when (5) has a solution,
and $p$ is the square of $\mathfrak{p}$ when (5) has only
one solution, that is, when $p$ divides $\Delta$.}

The latter is in agreement with the general
theorem Bd.\,II, §\,174.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 365 =====
% !PRINTED 344
\weberpage{344}
With the use of the symbol $(\Delta, p)$, which we introduced in §\,85, we can also give these theorems the form:
\[
\begin{array}{@{}l@{\enspace}l@{}}
\text{3.} & \gesperrt{\text{If } \ensuremath{(\Delta, p) = -1} \text{, then } \ensuremath{p} \text{ is indecomposable in } \ensuremath{\Omega}\text{.}} \\
 & \gesperrt{\text{„} \ \ensuremath{(\Delta, p) = +1} \text{, then } \ensuremath{p} \text{ splits into two different conjugate prime ideals.}} \\
 & \gesperrt{\text{„} \ \ensuremath{(\Delta, p) = 0} \text{, then } \ensuremath{p} \text{ is the square of a prime ideal.}}
\end{array}
\]

\begin{center}
§ 93. \gesperrt{Representation of Numbers as Ideal Norms.}
\end{center}

A prime $p$ is the norm of an ideal only when
$(\Delta, p) = +1$ or $= 0$, but not when $(\Delta, p) = -1$.
In the last case it is only $p^2$ that is a norm, namely that of $p$. In
general a positive integral rational number $m$ can be represented \gesperrt{as a norm in more than one way}. We will denote the number of
these representations for the moment by $\psi(m)$
and determine it more closely.

We first take $m$ to be a prime power $p^k$. If then
$(\Delta, p) = +1$ and $p = \mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{p}'$, one can represent $p^k$ in the following way:
\weq{1}{p^k = N(\mathfrak{p}^k),\ N(\mathfrak{p}^{k-1}\mathfrak{p}'),\ N(\mathfrak{p}^{k-2}\mathfrak{p}'^2),\ \ldots,\ N(\mathfrak{p}'^k),}
and therefore
\weq{2}{(\Delta, p) = +1:\quad \psi(p^k) = k+1.}
But if $(\Delta, p) = -1$, then, when $k$ is even, $p^k = N(p^{1/2\,k})$,
and when $k$ is odd, $p$ is not representable as a norm. Thus
\weq{3}{(\Delta, p) = -1:\quad \psi(p^k) = 0 \text{ or } = 1,}
according as $k$ is odd or even.

If finally $(\Delta, p) = 0$, so that $p$ is contained in $\Delta$, then $p = \mathfrak{p}^2$
and $p^k = N(\mathfrak{p}^k)$; hence:
\weq{4}{(\Delta, p) = 0:\quad \psi(p^k) = 1.}
These three cases can be combined into a single formula:
for the number $p^k$ has the following $k+1$ divisors:
\weq{5}{1,\ p,\ p^2,\ \ldots,\ p^k.}
And therefore the formulae (2), (3), (4) give, when $m = p^k$,
and $n$ runs through the divisors of $m$,
\weq{6}{\psi(m) = \overset{n}{\Sigma}(\Delta, n).}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 366 =====
% !PRINTED 345
\weberpage{345}

This expression, however, holds generally. For if $m_1$ and $m_2$ are
relatively prime and if
\[
m_1 = N(\mathfrak{m}_1), \quad m_2 = N(\mathfrak{m}_2),
\]
then
\[
m = m_1 m_2 = N(\mathfrak{m}_1 \mathfrak{m}_2).
\]

From a representation of $m_1$, $m_2$ as norms one can therefore derive
a representation of $m$ as a norm.

If conversely
\[
m_1 m_2 = N(\mathfrak{m}) = \mathfrak{m}\,\mathfrak{m}',
\]
where $\mathfrak{m}$, $\mathfrak{m}'$ are conjugate ideals, then, if $m_1$ and $m$ are divisible by
a prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}$, $m_1$ must also be divisible by $\mathfrak{p}\,\mathfrak{p}'$, and hence
$m_1 = N(\mathfrak{m}_1)$ as well, and likewise $m_2 = N(\mathfrak{m}_2)$.

Accordingly, if $m_1$ and $m_2$ are relatively prime:
\weq{7}{\psi(m_1)\,\psi(m_2) = \psi(m_1 m_2).}
On the other hand, if $n_1$ and $n_2$ run through the divisors of $m_1$ and $m_2$,
\[
\Sigma(\Delta,\, n_1)\, \Sigma(\Delta,\, n_2) = \Sigma(\Delta,\, n_1 n_2),
\]
and with this formula (6) is established in general. We
state this as a theorem:

4. \gesperrt{A natural number $m$ can be represented in the quadratic
field $\Omega$ with the fundamental number $\Delta$ in}
\[
\Sigma(\Delta,\, n)
\]
\gesperrt{different ways as the norm of an ideal,
when $n$ runs through all the divisors of $m$.}

\S\,94. \gesperrt{The quadratic law of reciprocity.}

From the decomposition of the primes in the quadratic field
\gesperrt{Dedekind} derives a new proof of the law of reciprocity
of quadratic residues\footnote{\gesperrt{Dirichlet-Dedekind}, Zahlentheorie, 4. Aufl. (S. 636, Anm.).}.

By Bd.\ II, \S\,167, 3. the necessary and sufficient
condition that the prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}$ dividing the prime $p$
(in any field $\Omega$) be of the first degree is this,
that for \gesperrt{every} integer $\omega$ of the field $\Omega$
\weq{1}{\omega^p \equiv \omega \ (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak{p}),}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 367 =====
% !PRINTED 346
\weberpage{346}

%<<CONT
and in our case of the quadratic field this reduces to the requirement
that
\weq{2}{\theta^p \equiv \theta \ (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak{p})}
must hold.

If we take $\Delta = -4$, then $\theta = i = \sqrt{-1}$, and the congruence
 (2) becomes
\[
i^{p-1} \equiv 1 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak{p}).
\]

Now since $(1+i)(1-i) = 2$, so that for an odd $p$ neither 2 nor
$(1 \pm i)$ can be divisible by $\mathfrak{p}$, we must have $i^{p-1} = 1$,
and hence $p - 1$ must be divisible by 4.

Accordingly there follows from \S\,92, 2.:

1) \gesperrt{The congruence}
\[
x^2 \equiv -4 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 4p),
\]
\gesperrt{or, what is the same thing,}
\[
x^2 \equiv -1 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ p)
\]
\gesperrt{has solutions then and only then, when $p \equiv 1 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 4)$.}

If we take, secondly, $\Delta = 8$, then $\theta = \sqrt{2}$, or, if
$r = \sqrt{i}$ is an 8th root of unity,
\[
\theta = r + r^{-1},
\]
and by the binomial theorem the condition (2) can be represented
thus:
\[
r^p + r^{-p} \equiv r + r^{-1} \ (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak{p}).
\]

This requires:
\[
(r^p - r)(r^p - r^{-1})\, r^{-p} \equiv 0 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak{p}),
\]
hence:
\[
r^p \equiv r \ \text{or} \ r^p \equiv r^{-1} \ (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak{p}),
\]
\[
r^{p \pm 1} \equiv 1, \quad i^{\frac{p \pm 1}{2}} - 1 \equiv 0 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak{p}),
\]
and from this it follows as above, for an odd $p$:
\[
p \equiv \pm 1 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 8).
\]

2) \gesperrt{The congruence}
\[
x^2 \equiv 2 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ p)
\]
\gesperrt{is therefore solvable then and only then, when $p \equiv 1$ or
$p \equiv -1 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 8)$.}

Finally we set, if $q$ is an odd prime,
\weq{3}{\Delta = \pm q}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 368 =====
% !PRINTED 347
\weberpage{347}

%<<CONT
and determine the sign so that $\pm q \equiv 1 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 4)$.
In this case
\[
\theta = \frac{-1 + \sqrt{\pm q}}{2},
\]
and we can represent this expression by $q$th roots of unity.
Let $r$ denote an imaginary $q$th root of unity, and let
$a$ run through the quadratic residues, $b$ through the non-residues of $q$.
We set, as in Bd.\ I, \S\,179
\weq{4}{A = \overset{a}{\Sigma}\, r^a, \quad B = \overset{b}{\Sigma}\, r^b}
and have, by the formulas (3) given there, which are derived without the use
of the law of reciprocity:
\weq{5}{\theta = A, \quad \theta' = B.}
The sign of $\sqrt{+q}$ depends on the choice of $r$,
but does not come into consideration here. Now, by the polynomial
 theorem:
\[
A^p \equiv \Sigma r^{pa}, \quad B^p \equiv \Sigma r^{pb},
\]
hence
\[
A^p \equiv A, \quad B^p \equiv B, \quad \text{if} \ \left(\frac{p}{q}\right) = +1,
\]
and
\[
A^p \equiv B, \quad B^p \equiv A, \quad \text{if} \ \left(\frac{p}{q}\right) = -1.
\]

Since $A$ is not congruent to $B$ when $p$ is different from $q$,
it follows from this and from 2. of the preceding section:

3) \gesperrt{The congruence}
\[
x^2 \equiv \pm q \ (\mathrm{mod}\ p)
\]
\gesperrt{has solutions then and only then, when $p$ is a quadratic
residue of $q$.}

And this is the law of reciprocity with its supplementary theorems.

\S\,95. \gesperrt{Equivalent Forms and Ideals in the Quadratic Field.}

If the two ideals [\S\,91, (16)]
\weq{1}{\mathfrak{a} = (a,\, a\,\omega), \quad \mathfrak{a}' = (a',\, a'\,\omega')}
are equivalent, then there is an (integral or non-integral) number $\eta$
in $\Omega$ for which $\eta\, \mathfrak{a}' = \mathfrak{a}$, and this number $\eta$ is determined by the ideals
$\mathfrak{a}$, $\mathfrak{a}'$ themselves up to a factor which is a \gesperrt{numerical unit}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 369 =====
% !PRINTED 348
\weberpage{348}

%<<CONT
\gesperrt{is determined.} There must therefore be four integral rational numbers
$\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$, $\delta$ which satisfy the condition
\weq{2}{\begin{aligned}\eta\, \mathfrak{a}' &= \mathfrak{a}\,(\alpha - \gamma\,\omega),\\ \eta\, \mathfrak{a}'\,\omega' &= \mathfrak{a}\,(-\beta + \delta\,\omega)\end{aligned}}
If we denote for the moment by $\eta_1$, $\omega_1$, $\omega_1'$ the numbers
conjugate to $\eta$, $\omega$, $\omega'$, then accordingly
\[
\mathfrak{a}'^2\, \eta\, \eta_1
\begin{vmatrix} 1, & \omega' \\ 1, & \omega_1' \end{vmatrix}
= \mathfrak{a}^2
\begin{vmatrix} \alpha, & -\gamma \\ -\beta, & \delta \end{vmatrix}
\begin{vmatrix} 1, & \omega \\ 1, & \omega_1 \end{vmatrix},
\]
hence:
\[
\mathfrak{a}'^2\, \eta\, \eta_1\,(\omega' - \omega_1') = \mathfrak{a}^2\,(\alpha\delta - \beta\gamma)\,(\omega - \omega_1),
\]
and since, by \S\,91, (12):
\[
\mathfrak{a}\,(\omega - \omega_1) = \mathfrak{a}'\,(\omega' - \omega_1') = -\sqrt{\Delta}
\]
holds, there follows from this, if
\[
\varepsilon = \alpha\delta - \beta\gamma
\]
is put,
\weq{3}{\mathfrak{a}\,\varepsilon = \mathfrak{a}'\,\eta\,\eta_1;}
if therefore, as we have already assumed, $\mathfrak{a}$ and $\mathfrak{a}'$ are positive
and (according to the sharpened concept of equivalence) $\eta\eta_1$ is
positive, then $\varepsilon$ is positive as well.

But if we interchange $\mathfrak{a}$ with $\mathfrak{a}'$, then $\eta$ passes into $1 : \eta$, and
$\varepsilon$ may pass into $\varepsilon'$. Accordingly there follows also
\weq{4}{\mathfrak{a}'\,\varepsilon' = \frac{\mathfrak{a}}{\eta\,\eta_1},}
and consequently $\varepsilon \varepsilon' = 1$. But since $\varepsilon$ and $\varepsilon'$ are positive integral
rational numbers, it follows from this that $\varepsilon = \varepsilon' = 1$. Hence by (2)
\weq{5}{\omega' = \frac{-\beta - \delta\,\omega}{\alpha - \gamma\,\omega}, \qquad \omega = \frac{\alpha\,\omega' + \beta}{\gamma\,\omega' + \delta},}
\[
\alpha\delta - \beta\gamma = 1.
\]

Now $\omega$ and $\omega'$ are the roots of the two forms
\[
(a,\, b,\, c), \quad (a',\, b',\, c') \qquad [\S\,91,\ (13)],
\]
and the equivalence of these forms is expressed by (5).
We therefore have, in agreement with the general theory
(\S\,88), the theorem:

5. \gesperrt{The quadratic forms belonging to equivalent ideals
are equivalent.}

From this one recognises the significance of the sharpened concept of
equivalence: for if one wished to admit negative values of
$N(\eta)$ as well, then $\varepsilon = -1$ would also be possible, and the
corresponding forms could be \gesperrt{improperly} equivalent.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 370 =====
% !PRINTED 349
\weberpage{349}

%% [running head, not body text -- commented out 2026-08-07] Page furniture (running
%% head, folio, signature) is excluded from this edition by standing policy.
%% \noindent\S\ 95.\hfill Equivalent forms and ideals in the quadratic field.\hfill 349

Now let $\varphi = (a, b, c)$, $\varphi' = (a', b', c')$ be, conversely, two
\gesperrt{equivalent forms with positive first coefficients} $a, a'$, and
\weq{6}{\omega = -\frac{b+\sqrt{\Delta}}{2a}, \quad \omega' = -\frac{b'+\sqrt{\Delta}}{2a'}\,.}
Then there is a linear substitution $\begin{pmatrix} \alpha, & \beta \\ \gamma, & \delta \end{pmatrix}$ with determinant $+1$ by which $(a, b, c)$ passes into $(a', b', c')$.

We then have
\weq{7}{
\begin{aligned}
a' &= a\alpha^2 + b\alpha\gamma + c\gamma^2,\\
b' &= 2a\alpha\beta + b(\alpha\delta + \beta\gamma) + c\gamma\delta,\\
c' &= a\beta^2 + b\beta\delta + c\delta^2,
\end{aligned}
}
\weq{8}{
\omega = \frac{\alpha\omega' + \beta}{\gamma\omega' + \delta}, \quad \omega' = \frac{\delta\omega - \beta}{-\gamma\omega + \alpha}\,,
}
and a short calculation shows that $\omega$ and $\omega'$ are corresponding roots, i.\,e. roots with the same sign of $\sqrt{\Delta}$.

Accordingly, for the ideals $\mathfrak{a}, \mathfrak{a}'$ belonging to $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ we obtain two basis forms:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\lambda &= a(x - \omega y),\\
\lambda' &= a'(x' - \omega'y'),
\end{aligned}
\]
and by (8) we have
\[
\lambda = \frac{a[(\delta x - \beta y) + (\gamma x - \alpha y)\omega']}{\gamma\omega' + \delta}\,.
\]

If we therefore set
\[
x' = \delta x - \beta y, \quad y' = -\gamma x + \alpha y,
\]
it follows that
\[
\lambda = \frac{a}{a'(\gamma\omega' + \delta)}\,\lambda',
\]
and since $a : a'(\gamma\omega' + \delta)$ is a number in $\Omega$, it follows that $\mathfrak{a}$ and $\mathfrak{a}'$ are equivalent.

We thus have once more, in agreement with the general theorem \S\ 88, 4. and at the same time in closer determination:

6. \gesperrt{If $(a, b, c)$ $(a', b', c')$ are two equivalent forms with positive first coefficients, and if $\omega, \omega'$ are corresponding roots of these forms, then the ideals $(a, a\omega)$ and $(a', a'\omega')$ are equivalent.}

For a negative discriminant the first coefficients of equivalent forms always have the same sign, and one considers only those forms in which this sign is positive.
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 371 =====
% !PRINTED 350
\weberpage{350}
%<<CONT

%% [running head, not body text -- commented out 2026-08-07] Page furniture (running
%% head, folio, signature) is excluded from this edition by standing policy.
%% \noindent 350\hfill Eleventh Chapter.\hfill \S\ 95.

With a positive discriminant there exist in every class of forms forms with positive first coefficients, and therefore classes of forms and classes of ideals correspond to one another in a one-to-one manner.

A basis of the principal ideal $\eta$ is $(\eta, \eta\theta)$ and
\[
\left.\begin{aligned}
\theta &= \frac{\sqrt{\Delta}}{2}, & \theta^2 &= \frac{\Delta}{4}, & \Delta &\equiv 0\\
\theta &= \frac{-1+\sqrt{\Delta}}{2}, & \theta^2 &= \frac{\Delta-1}{4} - \theta, & \Delta &\equiv 1
\end{aligned}\right\}\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 4).
\]
If $x, y$ are integral rational numbers and
\[
\eta = x + y\theta,
\]
then this basis is, in the two cases:
\[
\begin{aligned}
(\alpha_1, \alpha_2) &= \left(x + y\theta,\ \frac{\Delta y}{4} + \theta x\right),\\
&= \left(x + y\theta,\ y\,\frac{\Delta-1}{4} + (x-y)\theta\right)
\end{aligned}
\]
and the substitution determinant $A$ [\S\ 87, (1)] is
\[
x^2 - \frac{\Delta}{4}y^2, \quad x^2 - xy + \frac{1-\Delta}{4}y^2 = N(\eta).
\]
The basis $(\alpha_1, \alpha_2)$ is therefore positive if the norm of $\eta$ is positive (otherwise $\alpha_1$ would have to be interchanged with $\alpha_2$). From the basis form
\[
\lambda = \alpha_1 t_1 + \alpha_2 t_2 = \eta(t_1 + \theta t_2)
\]
one obtains
\[
N(\lambda) = N(\eta)\,T,
\]
and thereupon $T$ becomes the \gesperrt{principal form}
\weq{9}{
(1,\,0,\,\tfrac{\Delta}{4}), \quad \left(1,\,-1,\,\frac{+1-\Delta}{4}\right).
}
If $N(\eta)$ were negative, one would have obtained for $T$ the forms
\[
\left(-1,\,0,\,\frac{-\Delta}{4}\right), \quad \left(-1,\,+1\ \frac{-1-\Delta}{4}\right) % [sic] -- no comma printed before the fraction
\]
and these are equivalent to (9) only if the \gesperrt{Pell} equation $t^2 - \Delta u^2 = -4$ is solvable.

\rule{4cm}{0.4pt}

% Part-title / section-opening page: no folio printed. Centred divider "Twelfth
% Chapter. / Orders in the quadratic field" with a footnote marker, a rule,
% then the "§ 96. Discriminants of the orders." heading and the start of running

\begin{center}
\gesperrt{Twelfth Chapter.}

Orders in the quadratic field\textsuperscript{1}).
\end{center}

\rule{3cm}{0.4pt}

\begin{center}
\textbf{\S\ 96. \gesperrt{Discriminants of the orders.}}
\end{center}

1. \gesperrt{Definition. If $Q$ is a natural number, then the totality of the integers of the quadratic field $\Omega$ that are congruent to a rational number with respect to the modulus $Q$ is called an order, and $Q$ is called the conductor of this order.} The order with the conductor $Q$ is denoted by $[Q]$. From this definition it follows:

1. \gesperrt{All rational integral numbers belong to every order;}

2. \gesperrt{Sum, difference and product of two numbers of the order belong to the same order;}

i.\,e. within the order one can carry out addition, subtraction and multiplication unconditionally, but not division in general.

Let the totality of all \gesperrt{integers} of the field $\Omega$ likewise form an order (of conductor 1), the \gesperrt{principal order}, which would accordingly be denoted by $[1]$.

\rule{4cm}{0.4pt}

\textsuperscript{1}) \gesperrt{Dedekind} introduced the expression order in the general theory of algebraic numbers, because in the special case of the quadratic field they correspond to the \gesperrt{Gauss} orders of quadratic forms. \gesperrt{Hilbert} uses for it the expression \glqq Ring\grqq{} or \glqq Zahlring\grqq{}. Cf. \gesperrt{Dirichlet-Dedekind}, Vorlesungen über Zahlentheorie (\S\ 172 of the third, \S\ 170 of the fourth edition). \gesperrt{Dedekind}: Über die Anzahl der Idealklassen in den verschiedenen Ordnungen eines endlichen Körpers, Festschrift zur Säkularfeier von \gesperrt{Gauss'} Geburtstag, Braunschweig 1877. \gesperrt{Hilbert}: Die Theorie der algebraischen Zahlen, Bericht der Deutschen Mathematischen Vereinigung von 1894/95, Kap. IX.

\weberpage{352}

If $\Delta$ is the fundamental number of the field $\Omega$, we put, according as $\Delta$ is even or odd:
\weq{1}{
\begin{aligned}
\theta_0 &= \tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{\Delta}, & &\text{or}\\
\theta_0 &= \frac{-1+\sqrt{\Delta}}{2}\,.
\end{aligned}
}

Then by \S\ 90 every integer of the field $\Omega$ is representable in the form
\weq{2}{
\omega = x + y\theta_0
}
where $x$ and $y$ are integers, and this number is then and only then congruent to a rational number $a$ with respect to the modulus $Q$, when $y$ is divisible by $Q$, because then
\[
\frac{x - a + y\theta_0}{Q}
\]
must be an integer. Accordingly all numbers of the order $[Q]$ are contained in the form:
\[
\omega = x + yQ\theta_0,
\]
or, in the two cases distinguished in (1), if
\weq{3}{
D = Q^2\Delta
}
is put:
\weq{4}{
\begin{aligned}
&x - y\,\frac{\sqrt{D}}{2}, & &\Delta \text{ even},\\
&x - \frac{Q}{2}y + y\,\frac{\sqrt{D}}{2}, & &\Delta \text{ odd}, D \text{ even},\\
&x - \frac{Q-1}{2}y + y\,\frac{-1+\sqrt{D}}{2}, & &D \text{ odd}.
\end{aligned}
}

If we therefore put
\weq{5}{
\begin{aligned}
\theta &= \frac{\sqrt{D}}{2}, & D &\equiv 0 \pmod{4}\\
\theta &= \frac{-1+\sqrt{D}}{2}, & D &\equiv 1 \pmod{4}
\end{aligned}
}
and in the last two formulae (4) replace the arbitrary integers
\[
x - \frac{Q}{2}y, \quad x - \frac{Q-1}{2}y
\]
by $x$, we obtain the result:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 374 =====
% !PRINTED 353
\weberpage{353}
%<<CONT

2. Theorem. \gesperrt{Every number of the order $[Q]$, and only these, are contained in the form}
\weq{6}{\omega = x + y\theta,}
\gesperrt{in which $x, y$ are arbitrary integral rational numbers.}

We call the system
\weq{7}{(1, \theta)}
a basis of the order $[Q]$.

By substituting (5) one can also represent the numbers (6) in the form:
\weq{8}{\omega = \dfrac{x + y\sqrt{D}}{2},}
where the $x, y$ are integers which satisfy the condition
\weq{9}{x^2 - y^2 D \equiv 0 \pmod{4}.}
The number $D$ is a discriminant whose stem is $\Delta$. We call it the \gesperrt{discriminant of the order $[Q]$}.

\begin{center}
\S\ 97. \gesperrt{Orders and Ideals.}
\end{center}

Let $\mathfrak{m}$ be an ideal of the quadratic field $\Omega$. If all integers divisible by $\mathfrak{a}$ are divisible by a rational number $m$, then the ideal $\mathfrak{a} = m\mathfrak{m}$ is divisible by $m$; we have
\[ N(\mathfrak{a}) = m^2 N(\mathfrak{m}), \]
and the rational number $m N(\mathfrak{m})$, which is less than $N(\mathfrak{a})$, is divisible by $\mathfrak{a}$.

If $m$ is the greatest natural number by which $\mathfrak{a}$ is divisible, we shall call $m$ \gesperrt{the divisor of $\mathfrak{a}$}. If the divisor $= 1$, the ideal is called \gesperrt{primary}, otherwise \gesperrt{derived}. One obtains all ideals derived from a primary ideal $\mathfrak{m}$ by multiplying $\mathfrak{m}$ by arbitrary natural numbers, and all ideals derived from a primary ideal are \gesperrt{equivalent} to one another.

3. Theorem. \gesperrt{If $\mathfrak{a}$ is a primary ideal, then the norm of $\mathfrak{a}$ is at the same time the least natural number divisible by $\mathfrak{a}$.}

For let us denote by $a$ the least natural number divisible by $\mathfrak{a}$; the norm of $\mathfrak{a}$ is then in any case divisible by $a$. We put
\[ N(\mathfrak{a}) = ma, \]
and if $\mathfrak{a}'$ is the ideal conjugate to $\mathfrak{a}$, then, since by Bd.\ II, \S\ 164 the norm of an ideal is equal to the product of the conjugate ideals, it follows that
\weq{1}{N(\mathfrak{a}) = \mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{a}' = ma.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 375 =====
% !PRINTED 354
\weberpage{354}

Since $a$ is to be divisible by $\mathfrak{a}$, we set
\[ a = \mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{m}' = \mathfrak{a}'\mathfrak{m} \]
and obtain from (1):
\weq{2}{\mathfrak{a} = m\mathfrak{m}.}
Thus $m$ divides the divisor of the ideal $\mathfrak{a}$, and with this Theorem 3. is proved, since, if $\mathfrak{a}$ is primary, its divisor must be $= 1$.

4. \gesperrt{Theorem. If $\mathfrak{m}$ is a primary ideal of the field $\Omega$, then every integer in $\Omega$ is congruent to a rational number with respect to the modulus $\mathfrak{m}$.}

For by Bd.\ II, \S\ 165, $N(\mathfrak{m})$ is in general the number of the numbers in $\Omega$ that are incongruent with respect to $\mathfrak{m}$. If now $N(\mathfrak{m}) = a$ is at the same time the least \gesperrt{natural} number divisible by $\mathfrak{m}$, then the $a$ numbers
\[ 0, 1, 2, \ldots, a - 1 \]
are all incongruent, and among them all classes of numbers modulo $\mathfrak{m}$ are represented.

Let now $[Q]$ be an order with the conductor $Q$ and the discriminant $D$, and $(1, \theta)$ the basis of this order. Further let $\mathfrak{m}$ be a \gesperrt{primary} ideal coprime to $Q$. By Theorem 4. there is then an integral rational number $t$ which satisfies the condition
\[ \theta + t \equiv 0 \pmod{\mathfrak{m}} \]
We set
\weq{3}{\begin{aligned}
t &= \frac{b}{2}, && \text{if } D \equiv 0 \\
t &= \frac{1+b}{2}, && \text{„} \quad D \equiv 1
\end{aligned}
\qquad \text{(mod 4)}}
and obtain from \S\ 96, (5):
\weq{4}{\theta + t = \frac{b + \sqrt{D}}{2} \equiv 0 \pmod{\mathfrak{m}},}
wherein $b$ is an integral rational number which by (3) satisfies the condition
\[ b \equiv D \pmod{2} \]
Moreover let
\weq{5}{N(\mathfrak{m}) = a,}
so that $a$ is the least natural number divisible by $\mathfrak{m}$.

By the congruence (4) the number $b$ is determined only with respect to the modulus $2a$. For if $b, b'$ are two numbers which satisfy the condition (4), then $\frac{1}{2}(b' - b)$ is divisible by $a$.

Since further
\[ N\left(\frac{b + \sqrt{D}}{2}\right) = \frac{b^2 - D}{4} \]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 376 =====
% !PRINTED 355
\weberpage{355}

%<<CONT
is an integral rational number divisible by $\mathfrak{m}$, then it must be divisible by $a$; if we set it $= ac$, then $c$ is an integral rational number and
\weq{6}{D = b^2 - 4ac,}
\weq{7}{b^2 \equiv D \pmod{4a},}
and if the congruence (7) is satisfied, then every number $b'$ congruent to $b$ with respect to the modulus $2a$ satisfies the same congruence.

From this we conclude:

5. \gesperrt{Theorem. Every primary ideal $\mathfrak{m}$ coprime to $Q$ whose norm $= a$ yields us, through (4), one and only one root $b$ of the congruence (7), provided that not individual numbers, but classes of numbers with respect to the modulus $2a$, are regarded as roots.}

The two numbers
\weq{8}{a, \quad \frac{b + \sqrt{D}}{2}}
cannot, if $a$ is relatively prime to $Q$, both be divisible by one and the same rational prime; for otherwise
\[ \frac{b + \sqrt{D}}{2} - \frac{b - \sqrt{D}}{2} = \sqrt{D} \]
would have to be divisible by $p$; hence $D$ would be divisible by $p^2$, and $p$ would have to be a divisor of $Q$, contrary to the assumption.

For an odd $p$ this is evident, but for $p = 2$ it would follow:
\[ b \equiv 0 \pmod{2}, \quad b^2 - D \equiv 0 \pmod{16}, \]
and hence
\[ D \equiv 0, 4 \pmod{16}. \]
Thus $D/4$ would still be a discriminant and 2 would have to divide $Q$. With this it is proved:

6. Theorem. \gesperrt{If $a$ is a natural number coprime to $Q$ and $b$ is a root of (7), then one obtains a definite primary ideal $\mathfrak{m}$ as the greatest common divisor of the two numbers (8).}

Now we prove:

7. \gesperrt{Theorem. Every number $\mu$ of the order $[Q]$ that is divisible by the primary ideal $\mathfrak{m}$ and coprime to $Q$ is representable in the form}
\weq{9}{\mu = ax + \frac{b + \sqrt{D}}{2} y}
\gesperrt{once and only once, if $x, y$ are integral rational numbers. If $x, y$ are regarded as vari-}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 377 =====
% !PRINTED 356
\weberpage{356}

%<<CONT
\gesperrt{considered, then $\mu$ is called a basis form of the ideal $\mathfrak{m}$ in the order $[Q]$.}

For the proof we observe that, by (4), every number of the order $[Q]$ is contained in the form
\weq{10}{\omega = z + \frac{b + \sqrt{D}}{2} y,}
where $y$ and $z$ are integral rational numbers. Now if $\mathfrak{m}$ is primary, then
\weq{11}{N(\mathfrak{m}) = a}
is the least natural number divisible by $\mathfrak{m}$, and hence if $\omega$ is to be divisible by $\mathfrak{m}$, then $z$ must be divisible by $a$. If therefore we set $z = ax$, we obtain the form (9). Conversely it is evident that every number of this form is divisible by $\mathfrak{m}$.

That the representation of a number $\mu$ in this form is possible in only one way follows from the fact that $\sqrt{D}$ is irrational.

The form $\mu$ is therefore called a \gesperrt{basis form of the ideal $\mathfrak{m}$ in the order $Q$}. From it one obtains a basis form of the same ideal in the field $\Omega$:
\[ \lambda = ax + \frac{b' + \sqrt{\Delta}}{2} y, \]
if $b'$ is determined from the congruence
\[ b'Q \equiv b \pmod{2a} \]
which is always solvable, since $Q$ is relatively prime to $a$, and for even $Q$ also $b$ is even.

From (9) there results
\weq{12}{N(\mu) = a(ax^2 + bxy + cy^2).}
The number $\mu$ which one obtains when definite numbers are put in (9) for $x, y$ we can decompose into ideal factors:
\[ \mu = \mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{m}, \]
if
\weq{13}{N(\mathfrak{a}) = ax^2 + bxy + cy^2}
holds, and the following theorem is valid:

8. Theorem. \gesperrt{If $\mu$ is relatively prime to $Q$, and $x, y$ have no common divisors, then the ideal $\mathfrak{a}$ is primary.}

We prove it thus: Let $p$ be a rational prime dividing $\mathfrak{a}$; then $\mu$ is divisible by $p$, and from this it follows first of all that $y$ must be divisible by $p$; for a number $\omega$ of the form (10) can be divisible by a prime $p$ that does not divide $Q$ only if both $y$ and $z = ax$ are divisible by $p$. Accordingly, since by assumption $x$ and $y$
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 378 =====
% !PRINTED 357
\weberpage{357}
%<<CONT
are relatively prime, $x$ cannot be divisible by $p$, and $\mathfrak{a}$
must be divisible by $p$.

If we put $\mathfrak{a} = p^k \mathfrak{a}_1$, where $\mathfrak{a}_1$ is no longer divisible by $p$,
and denote by $\mathfrak{p}$ a prime ideal dividing $p$, then by
(11) $\mathfrak{p}$ must divide $\mathfrak{m}$ or $\mathfrak{m}'$, and since $\mathfrak{m}$ was assumed to be primary, $\mathfrak{p}$ cannot be $= p$. Therefore $N(\mathfrak{p}) = p = \mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{p}'$,
and if $\mathfrak{m}$ is divisible by $\mathfrak{p}$, it cannot at the same time be divisible by $\mathfrak{p}'$.
Consequently $\mathfrak{m}$ is divisible by $\mathfrak{p}^k$. Hence, by
the definition of $\mathfrak{m}$ (Theorem 6), $\dfrac{b+\sqrt D}{2}$ is also divisible by $\mathfrak{p}^k$,
and consequently $\dfrac{b+\sqrt D}{2} y$ at least by $\mathfrak{p}^{k+1}$, while $ax$ and consequently $\mu$
exactly by $\mathfrak{p}^k$, whereas on the other hand $\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{m} = \mu$ is likewise divisible at least by $\mathfrak{p}^{k+1}$, in which lies a contradiction. The like holds also when $p = \mathfrak{p}^2$, that is, in $\Delta$ (but not in $Q$).
Consequently no rational prime can be contained in $\mathfrak{a}$,
and $\mathfrak{a}$ is primary.

From what has been proved so far we can formulate the following
theorem:

9. \gesperrt{Theorem. If}
\[
\mu = ax + \frac{b+\sqrt D}{2} y = \mathfrak{m}\mathfrak{a},
\]
\[
\mu' = ax' + \frac{b+\sqrt D}{2} y' = \mathfrak{m}\mathfrak{a}'
\]
% Source scan supports b before \sqrt D, matching the parallel line above.
\gesperrt{are two numbers coprime to $Q$, if neither $x$ and $y$
nor $x'$ and $y'$ have a common divisor, if}
\[
N(\mathfrak{a}) = N(\mathfrak{a}') = A,
\]
\gesperrt{and if for one and the same number $B$}
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{B+\sqrt D}{2}&\equiv 0 \pmod{\mathfrak{a}}\\
&\equiv 0 \pmod{\mathfrak{a}'},
\end{aligned}
\]

\begin{center}\rule{0.2\linewidth}{0.4pt}\end{center}
\gesperrt{then the two ideals $\mathfrak{a}$ and $\mathfrak{a}'$ are identical, and the
numbers $\mu$, $\mu'$ differ only by a unit factor.}

For $\mathfrak{a}$ as well as $\mathfrak{a}'$ are primary by 8., and by 6. are
defined as the greatest common divisor of
\[
A \text{ and } \frac{B+\sqrt D}{2}.
\]

% !PRINTED none
% Part-title (Abschnitt-opening) page: "Thirteenth Chapter. Equivalence with
