\begin{center}
\gesperrt{Thirteenth Chapter.}

Equivalence with respect to Number Groups.
\end{center}

\rule{0.3\textwidth}{0.4pt}

\begin{center}
\textbf{§ 98. \gesperrt{Number groups in the orders.}}
\end{center}

In order to investigate more closely the relations of the quadratic
irrational numbers to the orders of the quadratic forms, we derive
from the numbers of the field $\Omega$ \gesperrt{number groups} according to
the following points of view.

1. We take an arbitrary natural number $Q$ and exclude from the
integers in $\Omega$ in the first place all those that are not coprime
to $Q$. From the remaining ones we also take arbitrary
quotients.

The integral and fractional numbers $\eta$ so obtained we call
\gesperrt{foreign to $Q$}. Let their totality be denoted by $O$. They
form a \gesperrt{group} in so far as multiplication and division
of two of these numbers always yield numbers of the same system.

2. We now proceed in the same way with the numbers of the order $[Q]$,
that is, we exclude all numbers of this order that are not
relatively prime to $Q$, and we also form the quotients
of any two of the numbers that remain. We denote
these numbers in $\eta'$ % [sic] German source prints in, where mit is expected. and their totality by $O'$, and call them
integral and fractional numbers of the order $[Q]$. The numbers $O'$
are all contained in $O$ and likewise form a \gesperrt{group} with respect to
multiplication and division. We call it the
\gesperrt{group of the order $[Q]$}, or briefly an \gesperrt{order group}.

Every number $\eta$ in $O$ can, by multiplication by an integral
rational number $n$ \gesperrt{coprime to $Q$}, be transformed into an integer $\omega$.

If $\eta'$ is a number in $O'$, one can make the denominator
rational and finds that $n\eta'$ is an integer of the order
$[Q]$, and consequently is congruent to a rational number with respect to
the modulus $Q$.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 380 =====
% !PRINTED 359
\weberpage{359}
Since $n$ is coprime to $Q$, one can set this number $= nr$,
where $r$ is a rational number coprime to $Q$. Accordingly every number $\eta'$ has the property
\weq{1}{\eta' \equiv r \pmod{Q},}
where $r$ is an integral rational number and the congruence is to be
understood in the sense $n\eta' \equiv nr$.

The congruences (1) can be multiplied and divided
if by $r^{-1}$ one understands the integer satisfying the condition $r \cdot r^{-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{Q}$.

Conversely, an integral or fractional number $\eta'$ which
satisfies a condition (1) belongs to the group $O'$. For if
$n\eta' = \omega \equiv nr$ is a number in $[Q]$, then $\eta' = \omega : n$ is a quotient
of two such numbers.

3. In $O'$ there is now again contained a group $O_0$, which consists
of all numbers $\eta_0$ that satisfy the condition
\weq{2}{\eta_0 \equiv 1 \pmod{Q}}
and the numbers of $O_0$ likewise yield again, through multiplication
and division, numbers of $O_0$.

We thus have three kinds of number groups, each of which is contained
in the preceding one:

1. $O$ \gesperrt{contains all numbers in $\Omega$ prime to $Q$.}

2. $O'$ \gesperrt{contains the integral and fractional numbers of the order $[Q]$ prime to $Q$.}

3. $O_0$ \gesperrt{contains the number classes in $O'$ that are congruent to unity with respect to the modulus $Q$.}

The groups $O$, $O'$, $O_0$ are infinite \gesperrt{Abelian} groups.
But if one takes a complete system of residues of rational numbers coprime
 to $Q$, $r_1, r_2, \ldots, r_\mu$, then every number in $O'$ can be represented as the product
of one of these $r_i$ with a number in $O_0$, and one
can therefore set, in the mode of expression used in Bd.\,II, § 2:
\weq{3}{O' = r_1 O_0 + r_2 O_0 + \cdots + r_\mu O_0,}
and $\mu$ is the \gesperrt{index} of the divisor $O_0$ of $O$: % [sic] German source prints unprimed O.
\weq{4}{\mu = (O', O_0),}
hence a finite number, namely:
\weq{5}{\mu = \varphi(Q) = Q\, \Pi\left(1 - \frac{1}{q}\right),}
where $\varphi(Q)$ is the symbol customary in number theory for
the number of number classes with respect to the modulus $Q$ with numbers coprime to $Q$,
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 381 =====
% !PRINTED 360
\weberpage{360}
%<<CONT
and $q$ in the product $\Pi$ runs through the primes,
 distinct from one another, that divide $Q$.

If we denote by
\[
\varrho_1, \varrho_2, \ldots, \varrho_\nu
\]
a complete system of representatives of the numbers coprime to $Q$
in $\Omega$, taken to the modulus $Q$, then in the same way
\weq{6}{O = \varrho_1 O_0 + \varrho_2 O_0 \cdots + \varrho_\nu O_0}
and
\weq{7}{\nu = \psi(Q) = (O, O_0)}
is the index of the divisor $O_0$ with respect to $O$.

The number $\psi(Q)$ we have determined in general in § 168, (3) of Band II,
 and also for the case in which an ideal takes
the place of $Q$. Since here $N(Q) = Q^2$, we have:
\weq{8}{\psi(Q) = Q^2\, \Pi\left(1 - \frac{1}{N(\mathfrak{q})}\right),}
when $\mathfrak{q}$ runs through the ideal prime divisors of $Q$ that are distinct
from one another.

Now (§ 92)
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{1. } N(\mathfrak{q}) = q, \quad \text{when } (\Delta,q) = 0,\\
&\text{2. } N(\mathfrak{q}) = q, \quad \text{when } (\Delta,q) = +1,\\
&\text{3. } N(\mathfrak{q}) = q^2, \quad \text{when } (\Delta,q) = -1.
\end{aligned}
\]
We shall denote these three kinds of primes by $q_1$, $q_2$, $q_3$,
 and observe that every prime $q_2$ is the norm of
two different prime ideals $q$. Accordingly there follows from (8)
\weq{9}{\psi(Q) = Q^2\, \Pi\left(1 - \frac{1}{q_1}\right) \Pi\left(1 - \frac{1}{q_2}\right)^2 \Pi\left(1 - \frac{1}{q_3^2}\right).}

Now the index of $O'$ with respect to $O$ is, by Bd.\,II, § 2 (4):
\[
j = \frac{\nu}{\mu} = (O, O') = \frac{(O, O_0)}{(O', O_0)} = \frac{\psi(Q)}{\varphi(Q)}
\]
and
\[
\varphi(Q) = Q\, \Pi\left(1 - \frac{1}{q_1}\right) \Pi\left(1 - \frac{1}{q_2}\right) \Pi\left(1 - \frac{1}{q_3}\right);
\]
consequently there results:
\[
(O, O') = Q\, \Pi\left(1 - \frac{1}{q_2}\right) \Pi\left(1 + \frac{1}{q_3}\right),
\]
for which one may then also put (according to 1., 2., 3.):
\weq{10}{j = (O, O') = Q\, \Pi\left(1 - \frac{(\Delta,q)}{q}\right).}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 382 =====
% !PRINTED 361
\weberpage{361}

In this the product $\Pi$ refers to all primes $q$ that divide $Q$.

We can therefore select a system of representatives
\[
\sigma_1,\ \sigma_2,\ \dots,\ \sigma_j
\]
in $O$ in such a way that
\weq{11}{O = \sigma_1 O' + \sigma_2 O' + \cdots \sigma_j O'} % [sic] German source omits the plus sign before the final summand.
holds.

\begin{center}
\S\,99. \gesperrt{Equivalence in the Orders.}
\end{center}

10. \gesperrt{Definition. We will now call two ideals $\mathfrak{a}$, $\mathfrak{a}'$ equivalent with respect to the order $[Q]$ if}
\weq{1}{\mathfrak{a}' = \eta' \mathfrak{a}}
\gesperrt{holds, and $\eta'$ denotes a number in $O'$. $\mathfrak{a}$ and $\mathfrak{a}'$ are here always assumed to be coprime to $Q$.}

If one takes a number $\mu = \mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{m}$ in $[Q]$ divisible by $\mathfrak{a}$ in such a way that $\mathfrak{m}$ becomes a primary ideal, and sets $\mu' = \eta'\mu$, then we have:
\weq{2}{\begin{aligned}\mu&=\mathfrak{m}\mathfrak{a},\\ \mu'&=\mathfrak{m}\mathfrak{a}',\end{aligned}}
\gesperrt{and we can also explain the equivalence of $\mathfrak{a}$ and $\mathfrak{a}'$ with respect to $[Q]$ by the fact that $\mathfrak{a}$ and $\mathfrak{a}'$ are transformed into numbers of the order $[Q]$ by multiplication with one and the same ideal $\mathfrak{m}$.}

By the ideal $\mathfrak{m}$ there is determined, according to \S\,97, a family of parallel quadratic forms $(a,b,c)$\footnote{By a family of parallel forms one understands the system \[ (a,\ b+2la,\ c+lb+l^2a), \] when $l$ runs through all integral rational numbers.}, in which $a$ and $b$ are determined from % [sic] German source prints singular wird with plural a und b.

\weq{3}{a = N(\mathfrak{m}),\quad \frac{b+\sqrt{D}}{2} \equiv 0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak{m})}
And so this family of forms does not change, by (2), when $a$ is replaced by an equivalent ideal $a'$.

But if in (2) one takes another ideal $\mathfrak{m}_1$ in place of the ideal $\mathfrak{m}$ and sets
\weq{4}{\mu_1 = \mathfrak{m}_1\mathfrak{a},}
then
\[
\frac{\mu}{\mu_1} = \frac{\mathfrak{m}}{\mathfrak{m}_1} = \eta
\]
is a number in $[O']$, and hence $\mathfrak{m}_1$ is equivalent to $\mathfrak{m}$.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 383 =====
% !PRINTED 362
\weberpage{362}

If therefore one puts
\weq{5}{a_1 = N(\mathfrak{m}_1) = \mathfrak{m}_1\mathfrak{m}_1',\quad \frac{b_1+\sqrt{D}}{2} \equiv 0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak{m}_1),}
then one obtains another quadratic form $(a_1,b_1,c_1)$, of which we can show that it is equivalent to $(a,b,c)$.

We put, for brevity:
\[
\omega = \frac{b+\sqrt{D}}{2a},\quad \omega_1 = \frac{b_1+\sqrt{D}}{2a_1}
\]
and remark that
\[
\eta a_1 = \eta \mathfrak{m}_1\mathfrak{m}_1' = \mathfrak{m}\mathfrak{m}_1',
\]
\[
\eta \omega_1 a_1 = \frac{\mathfrak{m}}{\mathfrak{m}_1}\,\frac{b_1+\sqrt{D}}{2}
\]
are numbers in $[Q]$ divisible by $\mathfrak{m}$ [by (5)]. Accordingly, by \S\,97, 7., the integral rational numbers $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$, $\delta$ can be so determined that:
\weq{6}{\begin{aligned}\eta a_1&=a(\alpha-\gamma\omega),\\ \eta a_1\omega_1&=a(-\beta+\delta\omega),\end{aligned}}
and one proves exactly as in \S\,95 that
\[
\alpha\delta - \beta\gamma = 1
\]
must hold, and hence that the two forms
\[
(a,b,c),\quad (a_1,b_1,c_1)
\]
are equivalent. We have therefore:

11. \gesperrt{Theorem. Every ideal class with respect to $[Q]$ that is represented by an ideal $\mathfrak{a}$ corresponds to a class of forms $A$ represented by the form $(a,b,c)$, and conversely.}

In order to obtain the class of forms $A$, one takes a primary ideal $\mathfrak{m}$ of the class $A^{-1}$ reciprocal to $A$ and puts $a = N(\mathfrak{m})$,
$\frac{b+\sqrt{D}}{2} \equiv 0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak{m})$. And if conversely the form $(a,b,c)$ is given, then the greatest common divisor $\mathfrak{m}$ of
\[
a,\quad \frac{b+\sqrt{D}}{2}
\]
is an ideal of the class $A^{-1}$.

\begin{center}
\S\,100. \gesperrt{Ideal classes with respect to the orders.}
\end{center}

The concept of the equivalence of ideals, and the theorems on class numbers, can be presented most clearly if
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 384 =====
% !PRINTED 363
\weberpage{363}

%<<CONT
one represents the ideals, according to Bd.~II, \S\,169, by the \gesperrt{functionals} discussed in Bd.~II, \S\,153\,ff., because in doing so one can make use of the ordinary rules of multiplication and division\footnote{Cf. also the author's memoir \glqq Über Zahlengruppen in algebraischen Körpern\grqq{}, first communication, Mathematische Annalen 48, 438.}.

\gesperrt{We restrict ourselves here once and for all, in the field $\Omega$, to numbers and ideals that are coprime to an arbitrarily assumed integral rational number $Q$} (the conductor of an order)\gesperrt{.}

Under this supposition the integral and fractional numbers of the field $\Omega$ form the group previously denoted by $O$. We extend this group by the addition of the \gesperrt{functionals} and denote the \gesperrt{group} so extended by $\overline{O}$. To every element of $\overline{O}$ there then corresponds an integral or fractional ideal, and to those elements whose quotient is a functional unit \gesperrt{there corresponds the same ideal.}

If $\eta$ is a number in $O$ and $\varepsilon$ is any functional unit, then a \gesperrt{principal ideal} corresponds to the product $\varepsilon\eta$. Accordingly we denote
\begin{quote}
\gesperrt{by $\overline{E}$ the group of functional units,}\\
\gesperrt{\glqq\ $E$\ \glqq\ \glqq\ \glqq\ numerical units,}
\end{quote}
and by
\begin{quote}
\gesperrt{$\overline{E}O$ the principal class of the functionals.}
\end{quote}
\gesperrt{If we take a system of representatives}
\weq{1}{\varphi_1,\ \varphi_2,\ \dots,\ \varphi_h}
of non-equivalent integral functionals in $\Omega$, then every integral or fractional functional $\Phi$ will be representable in the form:
\[
\Phi = \varphi_i \overline{\omega},
\]
where $\overline{\omega}$ is a functional from $\overline{E}O$, and the classes of ideals in $\Omega$ are the subsidiary groups of $\overline{E}O$ in $\overline{O}$. Accordingly the class number $h$ is the index of the divisor $\overline{E}O$ of $\overline{O}$:
\weq{2}{h = (\overline{O},\ EO).} % [sic] German source prints E here without an overbar.
Here, in the sharper division into classes, one has to restrict oneself in the case of $O$ to the numbers with positive norm.

If we now consider the division of the ideals into classes according to the order $[Q]$, then we have to take the functional group $\overline{E}O'$ as the \gesperrt{principal class}, and the class number is
\[
h' = (\overline{O},\ \overline{E}O').
\]

%% ===== canonical stable idx 385 =====
% !PRINTED 364
\weberpage{364}

In order to derive from this the relation between $h$ and $h'$, we make use of the general group theorems of Bd.~II, \S\,2, which we formulate and supplement as follows:

12. \gesperrt{Theorem. If $A$ is a group and $B$ a divisor of $A$ of finite index $(A,B)$, and further $C$ a divisor of $B$ of finite index $(B,C)$, then, by Bd.~II, \S\,2, (4):}
\weq{4}{(A,C) = (A,B)(B,C).}
If $A$ is again a group with the divisor $B$ of index $\mu$, we set
\weq{5}{A = a_1 B + a_2 B + \cdots + a_\mu B,}
where $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_\mu$ is a complete system of representatives of $A$ with respect to $B$.

Now let $C$ be a group of elements which are composable with the elements of $A$ (e.\,g. in our case simply by multiplication); then from (5) there follows:
\weq{6}{AC = a_1 BC + a_2 BC + \cdots + a_u BC.} % [sic] German source prints u instead of \mu.
Now one and the same element can occur in the two subsidiary groups $a_1BC$, $a_2BC$ only if $a_1a_2^{-1}$ is contained in $BC$, but not in $B$.

From this we formulate the theorem:

13. \gesperrt{Theorem. If $A$ is a group, $B$ a divisor of $A$ of finite index $(A,B)$, and further $C$ a group composable with $A$ of such a kind that $A$ and $BC$ contain no common elements apart from those of $B$, then}
\weq{7}{(AC,\ BC) = (A,B).}
The assumption of this theorem can also be expressed thus:

\begin{center}\gesperrt{$B$ is the intersection of $A$ and $BC$,}\end{center}

and it is satisfied, e.\,g., when $C$ is contained in $B$, that is, when $B = BC$, and also when $C$ has no element in common with $A$.

14. \gesperrt{Theorem. If $A$ is a group composed of the two groups $A'$ and $B$}
\weq{8}{A = A'B}
\gesperrt{and $B'$ the intersection of $A'$ and $B$, then}
\weq{9}{(A,B) = (A',B'),}
\gesperrt{provided that these indices are finite.}

For by (8), in every subsidiary group $aB$ to $B$ in $A$ an element $a'$ from $A'$ is contained, and one can therefore represent these subsidiary
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 386 =====
% !PRINTED 365
\weberpage{365}
%<<CONT
groups also by $a'B$, where $a'$ is contained in $A'$. If then $a_1'B, a_2'B$ are \gesperrt{different} subsidiary groups to $B$ in $A$, then $a_1'B', a_2'B'$ are \gesperrt{different} subsidiary groups to $B'$ in $A'$, and conversely; for $a_1'a_2'^{-1}$ is contained in $B'$ then and only then, when it is at the same time contained in $B$, and from this follows formula (9).

We now apply these theorems to the expressions (2) and (3) for $h$ and $h'$. By (4) we have
\weq{10}{(\overline{O}, \overline{E}O') = (\overline{O}, \overline{E}O)(\overline{E}O, \overline{E}O'),}
hence
\weq{11}{h' = h(\overline{E}O, \overline{E}O').}

We now denote, as already above, by $E$ the group of the numerical units in $O$. Then $\overline{E}E = \overline{E}$, since the numerical units are contained among the functional ones, and every \gesperrt{number} that is contained in $\overline{E}O'$ is contained in $EO'$. Consequently $EO'$ is the intersection of $O$ and $\overline{E}O'$. If we therefore apply (7), putting $O, EO', \overline{E}$ in place of $A, B, C$, then $B$ is the intersection of $A$ and $BC$, and we obtain:
\weq{12}{(\overline{E}O, \overline{E}O') = (\overline{E}O, \overline{E}EO') = (O, EO').}

Further, by (4):
\weq{13}{(O, EO')(EO', O') = (O, O'),}
and if we denote by $E'$ the group of the numerical unit in $O'$ % [sic] German source prints the singular Einheit., that is, the intersection of $E$ with $O'$, so that $E'O' = O'$:
\[
(EO', O') = (EO', E'O') = (E, E')
\]
(by 2), for $E'$ is the intersection of $E'O'$ and $E$.

Thus by (13) we have
\[
(O, EO')(E, E') = (O, O')
\]
and by (12)
\[
(\overline{E}O, \overline{E}O')(EE') = (O, O'), % [sic] German source prints no comma between E and E'.
\]
hence finally by (11):
\weq{14}{(E, E')h' = (O, O')h.}

15. \gesperrt{Theorem. Formula (14) holds unchanged if $O'$ denotes not precisely the order group, but any number group of finite index $(O, O')$ contained in $O$, provided we call two ideals $\mathfrak{a}, \mathfrak{a}'$ equivalent according to $O'$ if their quotient $\mathfrak{a}'/\mathfrak{a} = \eta'$ is a number in $O'$.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 387 =====
% !PRINTED 366
\weberpage{366}
\gesperrt{If $E'$ is the group of the units contained in $O'$, and if $(E, E')$ has a finite value, then the class number $h'$ is finite and determined by the formula (12).}

If, for example, $O$ is the group of all numbers in $\Omega$ (apart from 0), and $O'$ the group of the numbers with positive norm, then, provided there are any numbers with negative norm at all, $(O, O') = 2$. If there are then units with negative norm, $(E, E') = 2$ as well. But if all units have positive norm, then $(E, E') = 1$, and we obtain $h' = h$ in the first case, $2h' = h$ in the second case.

\gesperrt{The equivalence with respect to $O$ is then the general equivalence, that with respect to $O'$ the sharpened one.}

Let us return to the orders $[Q]$ and understand by $O$ the numbers coprime to $Q$ (if necessary only those with positive norm); then we have determined $(O, O')$ in the preceding section.

If the discriminant $D$ and its stem $\Delta$ are negative, then in general, both in $E$ and in $E'$, there are only the two units $\pm 1$. In the two exceptional cases $\Delta = -3, -4$, $E$ contains six and four units, but $E'$, if $Q > 1$, only two, and thus $(E, E') = 1$ in general, $(E, E') = 3$ in the case $\Delta = -3$, $(E, E') = 2$ in the case $\Delta = -4$. Hence in these cases we have, by \S\,98, (10):
\weq{15}{\lambda h' = Q\varPi\left(1 - \frac{(\Delta, q)}{q}\right)h,}
in which:
\weq{16}{
\begin{aligned}
\lambda &= 2, & &\text{for } \Delta = -4 \\
\lambda &= 3, & &\text{\glqq} \ \Delta = -3 \\
\lambda &= 1, & &\text{\glqq} \ \Delta < -4
\end{aligned}
}
This is the relation which was first derived by \gesperrt{Gauss} and later confirmed by \gesperrt{Dirichlet} in another way.

If, for example, $\Delta \equiv 1 \, (\mathrm{mod}\ 4)$, $Q = 2$, then in \gesperrt{Gaussian} notation $h$ is the class number for the forms of the second kind, $h'$ that for the forms of the first kind. We have
\[
\begin{aligned}
Q\left(1 - \frac{(\Delta, q)}{2}\right) &= 1, & \Delta &\equiv 1 \, (\mathrm{mod}\ 8), \\
&= 3, & \Delta &\equiv 5 \, (\mathrm{mod}\ 8).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus
\[
\begin{aligned}
h' &= h, & \Delta &\equiv 1 \\
&= 3h, & \Delta &\equiv 5
\end{aligned}
\qquad (\mathrm{mod}\ 8),
\]
and only in the exceptional case $\Delta = -3$ does $h' = h$ occur.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 388 =====
% !PRINTED 367
\weberpage{367}
If $D$ is positive, then $(E, E')$ still has to be determined.

Let
\[
\varepsilon = \frac{t + u\sqrt{D}}{2}
\]
be the fundamental unit in $O$, and $\lambda$ the smallest positive exponent for which
\[\varepsilon^{\lambda} = \frac{t + u\sqrt{D}}{2}\]
is contained in $O'$. Then $E$ consists of the powers $\pm \varepsilon^{\nu}$, and $E'$ of the powers $\pm \varepsilon^{\lambda\nu}$, and we have
\[
(E, E') = \lambda,
\]
and formula (15) gives the class number $h'$. In general no further determination can be given for $\lambda$.

If again $\Delta \equiv 1 \, (\mathrm{mod}\ 4)$ and $Q = 2$, then $\lambda = 1$ or $= 3$; namely $= 1$ if $u$ is even in (17), and $= 3$ if $u$ is odd. The latter can occur only when $\Delta \equiv 5 \, (\mathrm{mod}\ 8)$, and consequently for $\Delta \equiv 1 \, (\mathrm{mod}\ 8)$ we always have $\lambda = 1$, while for $\Delta \equiv 1 \, (\mathrm{mod}\ 8)$ % [sic]
$\lambda$ can be either $= 1$ or $= 3$.

\begin{center}\rule{0.32\linewidth}{0.4pt}\end{center}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 389 =====
% !PRINTED none
% Abschnitt-opening page: no running page number visible in any of the three bands
% (top band is blank page-top whitespace; the title block sits lower on the page).
\begin{center}
\gesperrt{Fourteenth Chapter.}

\textbf{Composition of Forms and Ideals.}

\rule{0.2\linewidth}{0.4pt}

\S\,101. \gesperrt{Composition in the Orders.}
\end{center}

Let $\Delta$ be the field discriminant and $D = Q^2\Delta$ the discriminant of the order $[Q]$.

If $T = (a, b, c)$ is a primitive quadratic form of the discriminant $D$ % [sic] German source prints plural Diskriminanten.
 with $a$ positive and coprime to $Q$, then from it we can determine a basis form $\lambda$ in $O$ of an ideal $\mathfrak{a}$ coprime to $Q$, in the following way:

We set
\weq{1}{\lambda = a t_1 + \frac{b + \sqrt{D}}{2} t_2,}
\weq{2}{N(\lambda) = a(a t_1^2 + b t_1 t_2 + c t_2^2).}
If we denote the ideal determined by the functional $\lambda$, that is, the greatest common divisor of
\weq{3}{a, \frac{b + \sqrt{D}}{2}}
by $\mathfrak{a}$, then from (2) it follows that
\weq{4}{N(\mathfrak{a}) = a.}
Here $a$ is the least natural number divisible by $\mathfrak{a}$. For if this least number is $a_1$, then $a_1$ must be a divisor of $a$, say $a = a_1 a_2$. Here $a_1, a_2, b$ can have no common divisor; for, in the first place, they cannot all three be even, since otherwise we should have $a = 4a'$, $b = 2b'$, $c = c'$,
\[
D = 4(b'^2 - 4a'c)
\]
and 4 would have to divide $Q$, contrary to the assumption that $a$ is coprime to $Q$; and likewise an odd common prime divisor of $a_1, b, a_2$ would divide $Q$.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 390 =====
% !PRINTED 369
\weberpage{369}
If we therefore set
\[
\lambda_1 = a_1 t_1 + \frac{b+\sqrt D}{2}\,t_2,
\]
then
\[
N(\lambda_1) = a_1 (a_1 t_1^2 + b\,t_1 t_2 + a_2 c\,t_2^2),
\]
and $(a_1,\ b,\ a_2 c)$ is likewise primitive. Since $\lambda_1$ is now divisible by $\mathfrak{a}$, $a_1$ must be divisible by $N(\mathfrak{a})$, i.\,e. by $a$, and must therefore be $=a$. Hence $\mathfrak{a}$ is primary.

If in (1) we fix the $\sqrt D$ once and for all, e.\,g. as positively real or positively imaginary, then the linear form $\lambda$ is \gesperrt{uniquely determined} by the quadratic form $T$. The form of the conjugate ideal would be obtained not by changing the sign of $\sqrt D$, but that of $b$.

Let $\mathfrak{a}$ and $\mathfrak{b}$ be any two ideals coprime to the conductor $Q$ of the order $[Q]$, which we shall now denote by $O$, and let
\weq{5}{
\begin{aligned}
\mu &= \alpha_1 u_1 + \alpha_2 u_2,\\
\nu &= \beta_1 v_1 + \beta_2 v_2
\end{aligned}
}
be basis forms of $\mathfrak{a}$ and $\mathfrak{b}$ in $O$. From $\mathfrak{a}$ and $\mathfrak{b}$ we form the product
\[
\mathfrak{a}\,\mathfrak{b} = \mathfrak{c}
\]
with the basis form in $O$:
\weq{6}{\lambda = \gamma_1 t_1 + \gamma_2 t_2.}
The quadratic forms belonging to $\mu$, $\nu$, $\lambda$ shall be denoted by $U$, $V$, $T$.

1. \gesperrt{We call $\lambda$ composed or compounded out of $\mu$ and $\nu$, and $T$ out of $U$ and $V$.}

We set:
\weq{7}{
\begin{aligned}
T &= (a,\ b,\ c),\\
U &= (a_1,\ b_1,\ c_1),\\
V &= (a_2,\ b_2,\ c_2),
\end{aligned}
}
and our problem is solved if $T$ can be derived from $U$ and $V$.

If
\[
\begin{array}{lcl}
\mathfrak{a} & \text{equivalent to} & \mathfrak{a}', \\
\mathfrak{b} & \text{\textquotedbl}\quad\text{\textquotedbl} & \mathfrak{b}',
\end{array}
\]
then also
\[
\mathfrak{a}\,\mathfrak{b} \quad \text{\textquotedbl}\quad\text{\textquotedbl} \quad \mathfrak{a}'\mathfrak{b}',
\]
hence
\[
\mathfrak{c} \quad \text{\textquotedbl}\quad\text{\textquotedbl} \quad \mathfrak{c}',
\]
and if therefore $U$, $V$ are replaced by equivalent forms $U'$, $V'$, then an equivalent form $T'$ also takes the place of $T$.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 391 =====
% !PRINTED 370
\weberpage{370}
If we denote by $A$, $B$, $C$ the classes in $O$ to which $\lambda$, $\mu$, $\nu$ belong, and likewise denote the classes of the quadratic forms $U$, $V$, $T$, then $C$ is also said to be \gesperrt{compounded} from $A$ and $B$, and one sets symbolically
\weq{8}{C = AB.}
\gesperrt{This composition of the classes} is uniquely determined once any three representatives $U$, $V$, $T$ of them are given, and it is therefore enough if we choose $U$, $V$ in their classes in any suitable way.

In every ideal class there are ideals that are relatively prime to any given ideal. We therefore first take $\mathfrak{a}$ in $A$ primary, but otherwise arbitrary, then $\mathfrak{b}$ likewise primary and relatively prime, not only to $\mathfrak{a}$, but to $a_1$. Then $a_1$ and $a_2$ are relatively prime (for the greatest common divisor $d$ of $a_1$ and $a_2$ would be relatively prime to $\mathfrak{b}$, and consequently $a_2 : d$ would be divisible by $\mathfrak{b}$). But from this it follows that $d=1$, because $a_2$ was to be the least natural number divisible by $\mathfrak{b}$.

Once $a_1$, $a_2$ have been determined in this way, one can determine $b$ in accordance with the two congruences
\[
\begin{aligned}
b &\equiv b_1 \pmod{2 a_1}, \\
&\equiv b_2 \pmod{2 a_2}
\end{aligned}
\]
and then
\[
b^2 - D = 4\,a_1 a_2 c
\]
is divisible by $4 a_1 a_2$. We therefore set
\weq{9}{
\begin{aligned}
U &= (a_1,\ b,\ a_2 c), \\
V &= (a_2,\ b,\ a_1 c).
\end{aligned}
}
Now $a_1 a_2$ is the least integral rational number divisible by $\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}$, and $\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}$ is the greatest common divisor of
\[
a_1 a_2, \quad \frac{b-\sqrt D}{2};
\]
consequently
\weq{10}{T = (a_1 a_2,\ b,\ c)}
is the form compounded from $U$ and $V$, and the linear forms $\lambda$, $\mu$, $\nu$ corresponding to the quadratic forms $T$, $U$, $V$ are:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\lambda &= a_1 a_2\,t_1 + \frac{b-\sqrt D}{2}\,t_2, \\
\mu &= a_1\,u_1 + \frac{b-\sqrt D}{2}\,u_2, \\
\nu &= a_2\,v_1 + \frac{b-\sqrt D}{2}\,v_2.
\end{aligned}
\]

%% ===== canonical stable idx 392 =====
% !PRINTED 371
\weberpage{371}
From this it follows, with regard to
\[
\left(\frac{b-\sqrt D}{2}\right)^2 = a_1 a_2 c + b\,\frac{b-\sqrt D}{2}:
\]
\weq{11}{
\mu\nu = a_1 a_2 (u_1 v_1 - c\,u_2 v_2) + \frac{b-\sqrt D}{2}\,(a_1 u_1 v_2 + a_2 u_2 v_1 + b\,u_2 v_2).
}
If, then, one makes the bilinear substitution:
\weq{12}{
\begin{aligned}
t_1 &= u_1 v_1 - c\,u_2 v_2, \\
t_2 &= a_1 u_1 v_2 + a_2 u_2 v_1 + b\,u_2 v_2,
\end{aligned}
}
there results
\weq{13}{\lambda = \mu\nu,}
and consequently
\weq{14}{T = UV.}
In the requirement that $a_1$ and $a_2$ are to be relatively prime there lies at times a certain inconvenience, e.\,g. when it is a question of the composition of a form with itself.

Let us then drop the hypothesis that $\mathfrak{a}$ is relatively prime to $\mathfrak{b}$, and $a_1$ to $a_2$, but hold fast to the assumption that
\weq{15}{b^2 - D = 4\,a_1 a_2 c}
is divisible by $4 a_1 a_2$; then relation (11) still holds, and it follows that $\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}$ is the greatest common divisor of
\[
a_1 a_2, \quad a_1\,\frac{b-\sqrt D}{2}, \quad a_2\,\frac{b-\sqrt D}{2}, \quad b\,\frac{b-\sqrt D}{2}
\]
(Bd.\,II, §~160, 2).

If now $a_1$, $a_2$, $b$ have no common divisor, then the equation $k_1 a_1 + k_2 a_2 + kb = 1$ can be satisfied by integral rational $k$, and accordingly $\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}$ is likewise the greatest common divisor of
\weq{16}{a_1 a_2, \quad \frac{b-\sqrt D}{2}.}

2. \gesperrt{It is to be proved that $a_1 a_2$ is the smallest natural number divisible by $\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}$.}

For if we set this smallest number $=a$, then $a_1 a_2$ is divisible by $a$, say
\[
a_1 a_2 = a\,a'.
\]

%% ===== canonical stable idx 393 =====
% !PRINTED 372
\weberpage{372}
If we form the two forms
\[
\begin{aligned}
\lambda &= a_1 a_2\,t_1 + \frac{b-\sqrt D}{2}\,t_2, \\
\lambda' &= a\,t_1 + \frac{b-\sqrt D}{2}\,t_2,
\end{aligned}
\]
then it follows that:
\[
\begin{aligned}
N(\lambda) &= a_1 a_2 (a_1 a_2\,t_1^2 + b\,t_1 t_2 + c\,t_2^2), \\
N(\lambda') &= a (a\,t_1^2 + b\,t_1 t_2 + a'c\,t_2^2).
\end{aligned}
\]
The two forms $(a_1 a_2,\ b,\ c)$, $(a,\ b,\ a'c)$ are primitive (because a common prime divisor of $a_1 a_2$, $b$, $c$ would, on account of (15), have to divide $Q$), and for the absolute norm it follows that:
\[
\begin{aligned}
N_a(\lambda) &= a_1 a_2 = N(\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}), \\
N_a(\lambda') &= a;
\end{aligned}
\]
but since $\lambda'$ is divisible by $\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}$, $a$ must be divisible by $a_1 a_2$, and consequently $a'=1$.

From this it follows:

3. \gesperrt{If $a_1$, $a_2$, $b$ are without common divisor and}
\[
D = b^2 - 4\,a_1 a_2 c,
\]
\gesperrt{then the form}
\[
T = (a_1 a_2,\ b,\ c)
\]
\gesperrt{is compounded from the two forms}
\[
U = (a_1,\ b,\ c\,a_2), \quad V = (a_2,\ b,\ c\,a_1)
\]
\gesperrt{compounded.}

Applying this to two opposite forms
\[
U = (a,\ b,\ c), \quad V = (c,\ b,\ a)
\]
there results
\[
T = (ac,\ b,\ 1),
\]
and this is equivalent to the principal form $\left(1,\ 0,\ \dfrac{-D}{4}\right)$ or $\left(1,\ 1,\ \dfrac{1-D}{4}\right)$.

4. \gesperrt{Two opposite classes, compounded, give the principal class.}

In order to compose a class $A$ repeatedly with itself, one chooses $\mathfrak{a}$ in $A$ so that it is relatively prime to $D$, and denotes by $(a,\ b,\ c)$ the corresponding form. Then $a$ is relatively prime to $b$. For if $d$ were a divisor of $a$ and $b$, then $d$ would also be contained in $D$, hence relatively prime to $\mathfrak{a}$. Then $a:d$ too would be divisible by $a$, which, if $d>1$, contradicts the definition of $a$.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 394 =====
% !PRINTED 373
\weberpage{373}
Now one can, however, choose $b$ so that
\weq{17}{b^2 \equiv D \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 4a^n)}
holds, for an arbitrarily large $n$. For one can alter $b$ by an arbitrary multiple of $2a$. If we therefore assume (17) to be satisfied for an exponent $n$, and accordingly put
\weq{18}{b^2 = D + 4a^n c,}
then it follows that:
\[
(b + 2ha^n)^2 - D \equiv 4a^n(c+hb) \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 4a^{n+1}),
\]
and hence, if one determines $h$ from the congruence $c + hb \equiv 0 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ a)$, there results a $b$ satisfying the congruence (17) for $n+1$.

Since now $b$ is relatively prime to $a$, it follows by 2. that, if $n \geqq m$, then $a^m$ is the least natural number divisible by $\mathfrak{a}^m$, and from this there results the following rule of composition:

5. \gesperrt{If the form $(a, b, a^n c) = U$ satisfies the condition (18), and if $m \leqq n$, then}
\[
U^m = (a^m, b, a^{n-m}c).
\]
With this the classes of quadratic forms of the discriminant $\Delta$ are united into an \gesperrt{Abelian group} which is \gesperrt{isomorphic with the group of ideal classes}, and at the same time a way has been indicated by which one can actually carry out the composition in these groups by means of suitably chosen representatives\footnotemark).

\begin{center}
\S\,102. \gesperrt{Composition of the Orders.}
\end{center}

An order $O = [Q]$ in the field $\Omega$ is completely determined by the conductor $Q$. Let $O_1$, $O_2$ be two orders with the conductors $Q_1$, $Q_2$, and let the greatest common divisor of $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ be $Q$. If then $M$ is the least common multiplum of $Q_1$ and $Q_2$, then
\weq{1}{Q_1 Q_2 = QM.}

\footnotetext{$^1$) The \gesperrt{unit} in the group of classes is formed by the \gesperrt{principal class}. Concerning the composition of quadratic forms the following are to be mentioned: \gesperrt{Gauss}, \glqq Disquisitiones arithmeticae\grqq{}, Art. 235\,ff. \gesperrt{Dirichlet}, De formarum binariarum secundi gradus compositione (1851), Werke Bd. II, S. 105. \gesperrt{Dirichlet-Dedekind}, Vorlesungen über Zahlentheorie, 4. Aufl., \S\,145\,f. \gesperrt{Dedekind}, Crelles Journal, Bd. 129. \gesperrt{H. Weber}, Göttinger Nachrichten, 9. Februar 1907.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 395 =====
% !PRINTED 374
\weberpage{374}
6. \gesperrt{The order $O$ belonging to the conductor $Q$ is called composed or compounded from $O_1$ and $O_2$.}

We set symbolically
\weq{2}{O = O_1 O_2.}
The discriminants of these three orders are
\weq{3}{D = Q^2 \Delta, \quad D_1 = Q_1^2 \Delta, \quad D_2 = Q_2^2 \Delta.}
If $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ are relatively prime, then the order composed from the two is the principal order $O_0$.

To carry out the composition of the orders one can proceed just as in the preceding section. We set
\weq{4}{Q_1 = Qm_1, \quad Q_2 = Qm_2,}
and then $m_1$, $m_2$ are relatively prime to one another.

Let $\mathfrak{a}$ and $\mathfrak{b}$ then denote two ideals which are relatively prime to $Q_1 Q_2$.

If then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathfrak{a}&\ \text{equivalent}\ \mathfrak{a}'&&\ \text{with respect to}\ O_1,\\
\mathfrak{b}&\ \text{\glqq}\ \mathfrak{b}'&&\ \text{\glqq}\ O_2,
\end{aligned}
\]
then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathfrak{a}}{\mathfrak{a}'}&=\eta_1\ \text{a number in}\ O_1,\\
\frac{\mathfrak{b}}{\mathfrak{b}'}&=\eta_2\ \text{\glqq}\ \text{\glqq}\ \text{\glqq}\ O_2,
\end{aligned}
\]
i.\,e. $\eta_1$ is congruent to a rational number with respect to the modulus $Q_1$, and $\eta_2$ with respect to the modulus $Q_2$. Hence both, and consequently their product, are congruent to a rational number with respect to the modulus $Q$ and belong to the order $Q$. % [sic] German source prints Q instead of O.
Accordingly we have also
\[
\mathfrak{c} = \mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b} \ \text{equivalent to} \ \mathfrak{c}' = \mathfrak{a}'\mathfrak{b}' \ \text{with respect to} \ O.
\]
Let $a_1$ be the least natural number divisible by $\mathfrak{a}$, and let $\mathfrak{b}$ be relatively prime to $a_1$ (and consequently also to $\mathfrak{a}$); and if $a_2$ is the least natural number divisible by $b$, then $a_1$ and $a_2$ are also relatively prime. One can then always, whatever $b_1$, $b_2$ may be, satisfy the congruences
\[
b_1 \equiv m_1 b \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 2a_1),
\]
\[
b_2 \equiv m_2 b \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 2a_2)
\]
and accordingly assume the basis forms of $\mathfrak{a}$ and $\mathfrak{b}$ in the shape:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 396 =====
% !PRINTED 375
\weberpage{375}
%<<CONT
\[
\mu = a_1 u_1 + m_1 \frac{b - \sqrt{D}}{2} u_2,
\]
\[
\nu = a_2 v_1 + m_2 \frac{b - \sqrt{D}}{2} v_2,
\]
and
\[
b^2 - D = 4a_1 a_2 c
\]
is divisible by $4a_1 a_2$. Then $a_1 a_2$ is the least natural number divisible by $\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}$, and
\[
\lambda = a_1 a_2 t_1 + \frac{b - \sqrt{D}}{2} t_2
\]
is a basis form of $\mathfrak{c}$.

Accordingly, the composition of the corresponding quadratic forms of the discriminants $D_1$, $D_2$:
\weq{5}{\begin{aligned} U &= (a_1, m_1 b, m_1^2 a_2 c), \\ V &= (a_2, m_2 b, m_2^2 a_1 c), \end{aligned}}
gives the form $T$ of the discriminant $D$:
\weq{6}{T = (a_1 a_2, b, c).}

\begin{center}\rule{0.32\linewidth}{0.4pt}\end{center}
