\begin{center}
\gesperrt{Seventeenth Chapter.}

\textbf{\Large Elliptic Functions and Quadratic Forms.}

\rule{0.12\linewidth}{0.4pt}
\end{center}

\textbf{§ 114. Singular periods of the doubly periodic functions.}

If we denote by $\varphi(u)$ a doubly periodic function with the periods $\omega_1$, $\omega_2$, then, if $n$ denotes an integer, $\varphi(nu)$ has the same periods, and upon this rests the multiplication of the elliptic functions which was considered in the sixth chapter. The question now arises whether a multiplier $\mu$ cannot be determined in yet another way, so that $\varphi(\mu u)$ has the periods $\omega_1$, $\omega_2$; that is, whether a multiplication exists also with a non-integer multiplier. This will be the case then and only then, when for a system of integers $a$, $b$, $c$, $\partial$ the equations hold:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mu\,\omega_1 &= a\,\omega_1 + b\,\omega_2,\\
\mu\,\omega_2 &= c\,\omega_1 + \partial\,\omega_2.
\end{aligned}
\]
If, in order to explore more closely the requirement contained in them, we put:
\[
\omega = \dfrac{\omega_2}{\omega_1}
\]
and assume that $\omega$ has a positive imaginary part, then it follows:
\[\mu=a+b\omega,\]
\weq{1}{\omega=\dfrac{c+\partial\omega}{a+b\omega}.}
So long as $\omega$ is regarded as variable, this equation is only possible if $b=c=0$, $a=\partial$, and $\mu$ is therefore an integer.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 445 =====
% !PRINTED 414
\weberpage{414}
If, on the other hand, equation (1) is not an identity, then $\omega$ is
the root of a quadratic equation with integral coefficients:
\weq{2}{b\,\omega^2 + (a-\partial)\,\omega - c = 0,}
hence, if we put
\[
a\,\partial - b\,c = n
\]
\[
m = -4\,b\,c - (a-\partial)^2 = 4\,n - (a+\partial)^2
\]
then we have
\[
m \equiv 0 \ \text{ or } \ \equiv -1 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 4),
\]
and we obtain:
\[
\omega = \frac{-a+\partial+\sqrt{-m}}{2\,b},
\]
\[
\mu = \frac{a+\partial+\sqrt{-m}}{2},
\]
\[
n = \frac{a+\partial+\sqrt{-m}}{2}\cdot\frac{a+\partial-\sqrt{-m}}{2}, % Source scan shows a minus; the mark above it is a scan/print speck.
\]
\[
\mu^2 - (a+\partial)\,\mu + n = 0.
\]

In order that $\omega$ may have a positive imaginary part, $m$, and all
the more therefore $n$, must be \gesperrt{positive}, and $\mu$ is a complex,
integral, algebraic number. This explains the designation
\gesperrt{complex multiplication}.

If now, conversely, $\omega$ satisfies a quadratic equation
\weq{3}{A\,\omega^2 + B\,\omega + C = 0}
in which $A$, $B$, $C$ are integers, and the discriminant
\weq{4}{D = B^2 - 4\,A\,C}
is negative, then $\omega$ is not real, and in one of the two roots
of (3) the imaginary part is positive. This one shall be taken for
$\omega$. Then $\omega$ is called a root of the quadratic form
$(A, B, C)$.

Without prejudice to generality, $A$, $B$, $C$ may be assumed to be
without a common divisor and $A$, $C$ positive. Infinitely many
relations of the form (1) [or (2)] can then be set up for $\omega$. One
has only to put, when $x$ is an integer different from zero:
\weq{5}{\begin{aligned}
b &= A\,x,\\
c &= -\,C\,x,\\
a-\partial &= B\,x.
\end{aligned}}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 446 =====
% !PRINTED 415
\weberpage{415}
If one further sets
\weq{6}{a+\partial = y,}
then it follows:
\weq{7}{\begin{aligned}
a&=\frac{y+B\,x}{2},\\
b&=A\,x,\\
c&=-C\,x,\\
\partial&=\frac{y-B\,x}{2},
\end{aligned}}
from which, if
\[
a\,\partial - b\,c = n
\]
is set, there results:
\weq{8}{4\,n = y^2 - D\,x^2.}
The number $n$ is thus decomposed into the two complex integer factors
\[
n = \frac{y+x\sqrt{D}}{2}\cdot\frac{y-x\sqrt{D}}{2}
\]
For $\omega$ and $\mu$ there is found further:
\[
\omega = \frac{-B+\sqrt{D}}{2\,A} = \frac{2\,C}{-B-\sqrt{D}},
\]
\[
\mu = a+b\,\omega = \frac{y+\sqrt{D}\,x}{2}.
\]

The numbers $x$, $y$ introduced here are bound to the single condition
that $y+B\,x$, and consequently $y-B\,x$ as well, be even numbers, so
that $a$, $\partial$ become integers according to (7). If therefore $B$
is even, then $y$ must be even, while $x$ is arbitrary; if $B$ is odd,
then $x$ and $y$ are to be assumed both even or both odd. By (4) this
distinction can also be expressed thus:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{1) If }D&\equiv0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 4), &\text{then }y&\equiv0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 2),\\
\text{2) If }D&\equiv1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 4), &\text{then }y&\equiv x\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 2).
\end{aligned}
\]

If, for given $A$, $B$, $C$, the numbers $a$, $b$, $c$, $\partial$ are to
be without a common divisor, then still other conditions come in:

From (5), (6) it follows that every common divisor of $a$, $b$, $c$,
$\partial$ is also a divisor of $x$ and $y$; conversely every common
divisor of $x$ and $y$ is also a divisor of $b$, $c$, $2\,a$,
$2\,\partial$. If therefore $a$, $b$, $c$, $\partial$ are to be without a
common divisor, then $x$ and $y$
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 447 =====
% !PRINTED 416
\weberpage{416}
%<<CONT
no greater common divisor than 2. If $x$ and $y$ have the greatest
common divisor 2, then $b$ and $c$ are even, and $a$, $b$, $c$,
$\partial$ are then and only then relatively prime, when $a$ and
$\partial$, and hence also $n = a\,\partial - b\,c$, are \gesperrt{odd}.

If we disregard the uninteresting case $n=1$, equation (8) has no
solution satisfying these conditions in which $x=0$. But if we change
the signs of $x$, $y$ at the same time, then by (10) $a$, $b$, $c$, % [sic] German source reference (10); (7) is mathematically expected.
$\partial$ pass over into $-a$, $-b$, $-c$, $-\partial$, and equation
(1) is not altered. The transformation
$\begin{pmatrix} a, & b\\ c, & \partial \end{pmatrix}$ therefore
remains unchanged.

For brevity we now call a solution of equation (8) a
proper solution, and $n = \frac{1}{4}(y^2-D\,x^2)$ a
\gesperrt{proper representation} of $n$, if $x$ and $y$ satisfy the
following conditions:

\gesperrt{$x$ is positive.}

\gesperrt{The greatest common divisor of $x$ and $y$ is 1 or 2.}

\gesperrt{If it is $=2$, then $n$ is odd.}

If now $\omega$ satisfies a given equation (3), then by every system
$\begin{pmatrix} a, & b\\ c, & \partial \end{pmatrix}$ a proper
solution of (8) is uniquely determined. For by (5) $x$ is the greatest
common divisor of $b$, $c$, $a-\partial$, and $y$ is determined by
(6); and conversely, from a proper solution of (8) the system $a$,
$b$, $c$, $\partial$ is completely determined by (7). But the question
is still to be decided whether two \gesperrt{different} proper solutions $x$, $y$
and $x'$, $y'$ can lead to equivalent systems
$\begin{pmatrix} a, & b\\ c, & \partial \end{pmatrix}$,
$\begin{pmatrix} a', & b'\\ c', & \partial'
\end{pmatrix}$. By equivalent systems are here to be understood,
according to \S\,28, \S\,53, two such for which
\weq{9}{\begin{pmatrix} a', & b'\\ c', & \partial' \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \alpha, & \beta\\ \gamma, & \delta \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} a. & b\\ c, & \partial \end{pmatrix}} % [sic] source prints a full stop after a in the rightmost matrix.
holds, when $\begin{pmatrix} \alpha, & \beta\\ \gamma, & \delta
\end{pmatrix}$ is a \gesperrt{linear} transformation, and hence
\weq{10}{\alpha\,\delta - \beta\,\gamma = 1.}
If we compose both sides of equation (9) on the right with
$\begin{pmatrix} \partial, & -b\\ -c, & a \end{pmatrix}$, there
results:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 448 =====
% !PRINTED 417
\weberpage{417}
%<<CONT
\[
\begin{pmatrix} a'\,\partial - b'\,c, & -a'\,b + b'\,a\\ c'\,\partial - \partial'\,c, & -c'\,b + \partial'\,a \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} n\,\alpha, & n\,\beta\\ n\,\gamma, & n\,\delta \end{pmatrix},
\]
or, if for $a$, $b$, $c$, $\partial$ we put the expressions (7) and for
$a'$, $b'$, $c'$, $\partial'$ the corresponding ones
\[
a' = \frac{y'+B\,x'}{2}, \quad b' = A\,x',
\]
\[
c' = -\,C\,x', \qquad \partial' = \frac{y'-B\,x'}{2}
\]
we obtain:
\[
\begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{y\,y'-D\,x\,x'+B(x'y-y'x)}{4}, & A\,\dfrac{x'y-y'x}{2}\\[2ex] -\,C\,\dfrac{x'y-y'x}{2}, & \dfrac{y\,y'-D\,x\,x'-B(x'y-y'x)}{4} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} n\,\alpha, & n\,\beta\\ n\,\gamma, & n\,\delta \end{pmatrix}.
\]
From this it follows:
\[
\begin{aligned}
4\,n\,\alpha &= y\,y' - D\,x\,x' + B(x'y-y'x),\\
2\,n\,\beta &= A(x'y-y'x),\\
2\,n\,\gamma &= -\,C(x'y-y'x),\\
4\,n\,\delta &= y\,y' - D\,x\,x' - B(x'y-y'x),
\end{aligned}
\]
\begin{center}\rule{0.32\linewidth}{0.4pt}\end{center}
\[
\begin{aligned}
2\,n(\alpha-\delta) &= B(x'y-y'x),\\
2\,n(\alpha+\delta) &= y\,y' - D\,x\,x'.
\end{aligned}
\]
Now since $A$, $B$, $C$ have no common divisor, it follows that $x'y -
y'x$ must be divisible by $2n$, and by the last equation
$y\,y' - D\,x\,x'$ is divisible by $2n$ as well. We therefore set
\weq{11}{\begin{aligned}
x'y - y'x &= 2\,n\,\xi,\\
y\,y' - D\,x\,x' &= 2\,n\,\eta
\end{aligned}}
and obtain:
\[
\alpha = \frac{\eta+B\,\xi}{2}, \qquad \beta = A\,\xi,
\]
\[
\gamma = -\,C\,\xi, \qquad \delta = \frac{\eta-B\,\xi}{2},
\]
from which, by (10), it follows:
\weq{12}{\eta^2 - D\,\xi^2 = 4.}
If we solve the equations (11) for $x'$ and $y'$, it follows:
\weq{13}{\begin{aligned}
2\,x' &= \xi\,y + \eta\,x,\\
2\,y' &= \eta\,y + D\,\xi\,x.
\end{aligned}}
If $-D > 4$, then (12) has only the two solutions
\weq{14}{\xi = 0, \qquad \eta = \pm 2,}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 449 =====
% !PRINTED 418
\weberpage{418}
%<<CONT
and from this it follows, since $x$ and $x'$ are to be positive:
\[
x' = x, \quad y' = y, \quad (\eta = + 2).
\]
But if $-D = 4$, then (12) has in addition the solution
\[
\xi = \pm 1, \quad \eta = 0,
\]
and from (13) it follows:
\[
\begin{aligned}
y' &= \mp 2\,x, \\
x' &= \pm \frac{y}{2},
\end{aligned}
\]
and the sign of $\eta$ is to be determined so that $x'$ becomes positive.
If finally $-D = 3$, then besides (14) we have the solutions
\[
\xi = \pm 1, \quad \eta = \pm 1,
\]
in which at first both signs are arbitrary.
But then from (13) it follows:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\pm 2\,x' &= x \pm y, \\
\pm 2\,y' &= y \mp 3\,x,
\end{aligned}
\]
and one can choose the signs in two ways so that $x'$ becomes positive. We thus have the theorem:

I. \gesperrt{For a given equation (3), every proper solution of the equation (8) leads to a transformation $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a, & b\\ c, & \partial\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ of the $n$th order. Different solutions of (8) lead in general to non-equivalent systems $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a, & b\\ c, & \partial\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. In the two exceptional cases $D = -4$ and $D = -3$, in each case two or three different solutions of (8) lead to equivalent systems.}

If we denote by $k$ a number which is in general equal to the number of proper solutions of (8), but for $D = -4$ and $D = -3$ is half or a third of the number of these solutions, then we can state Theorem I. as follows:

II. \gesperrt{From an equation (3) we can derive $k$ non-equivalent systems $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a, & b\\ c, & \partial\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ which satisfy the equation (1).}

\begin{center}
\textbf{\S\,115. The singular values of the invariant $j(\omega)$.}
\end{center}

The question that first claims our interest is that of the values of the modular functions of $\omega$ for the
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 450 =====
% !PRINTED 419
\weberpage{419}
%<<CONT
particular values of the argument $\omega$ that we considered in the preceding section. On these depend the moduli of the elliptic functions which admit a complex multiplication. After \gesperrt{Kronecker} they are called \gesperrt{singular moduli}. Accordingly we shall speak also of the \gesperrt{singular values of the modular functions}, and in particular of the \gesperrt{singular invariants} $j(\omega)$, and we understand by these the values that these functions take when $\omega$ is the \gesperrt{root} (with positive imaginary part) \gesperrt{of a quadratic form with negative discriminant}.

If $\omega$ satisfies equation (3), § 114, and $a, b, c, \partial, n$ are determined as in the preceding section, then there follows first of all:

\weq{1}{j(\omega) = j\left(\frac{c + \partial\,\omega}{a + b\,\omega}\right),}

and if therefore

\weq{2}{F_n(u, v) = 0}

is the invariant equation belonging to the degree of transformation $n$ (§ 69), then (2) is satisfied if $a, b, c, \partial$ are without a common divisor and

\weq{3}{u = j(\omega), \quad v = j\left(\frac{c + \partial\,\omega}{a + b\,\omega}\right) = u}

is set. Thereupon we arrive at the first principal theorem of this theory:

III. \gesperrt{The singular value}
\[
u = j(\omega)
\]
\gesperrt{is a root of the algebraic equation:}

\weq{4}{F_n(u, u) = 0.}

If conversely $u$ is a root of equation (4), then, when $\omega$ is determined from the equation $j(\omega) = u$, one of the values of $v$ that satisfy equation (2) is likewise $= u$, and there subsists therefore an equation of the form (1); by § 53 this has the consequence that $\omega$ is equivalent to $\dfrac{c + \partial\,\omega}{a + b\,\omega}$, and from this there results an equation of the form § 114, (3). Thus we have the complement to III.:

IV. \gesperrt{Every root of (4) is a singular invariant.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 451 =====
% !PRINTED 420
\weberpage{420}
If $\tau$ is a variable with positive imaginary part, and $v$ likewise a variable, then by § 69 $F_n[v, j(\tau)]$ splits into the linear factors

\[
v - j\left(\frac{c + \partial\,\tau}{a + b\,\tau}\right),
\]

in which $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a, & b\\ c, & \partial\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ runs through a complete system of representatives of non-equivalent transformations of degree $n$, and consequently $F_n(u, u)$ can be decomposed into the factors

\weq{5}{j(\tau) - j\left(\frac{c + \partial\,\tau}{a + b\,\tau}\right)}

when $u = j(\tau)$ is set.

But from Theorem II., § 114, it follows that, if we set $\tau = \omega$, $k$ of the factors (5) vanish. We can, however, conclude still further that the quotient

\weq{6}{\dfrac{j(\tau) - j\left(\dfrac{c + \partial\,\tau}{a + b\,\tau}\right)}{j(\tau) - j(\omega)}}

remains finite and different from zero for $j(\tau) = j(\omega)$. For if numerator and denominator are differentiated with respect to $\tau$, and $\tau = \omega$ is then set, the limiting value results:

\[
1 - \frac{n}{(a + b\,\omega)^2} = \frac{2\sqrt{D}\,x}{y + \sqrt{D}\,x},
\]

which is different from zero.

The invariant $j(\omega)$ remains unchanged when $\omega$ is replaced by an equivalent number, but it has a different value for every other number $\omega$. It therefore belongs not to the individual form $(A, B, C)$, but to the whole \gesperrt{class} of equivalent forms, and is for that reason called the \gesperrt{class invariant}.

Further, the number $k$ depends not on the coefficients $A, B, C$, but only on $D$ and $n$, and is therefore the same for all primitive forms of discriminant $D$. We now introduce the following function of the variable $u$: let $\omega_1, \omega_2, \ldots, \omega_h$ denote a complete system of non-equivalent numbers of discriminant $D$, that is, the system of the roots of a system of non-equivalent forms $(A, B, C)$ of discriminant $D$. We set

\weq{7}{H_m(u) = [u - j(\omega_1)]\,[u - j(\omega_2)]\,\ldots\,[u - j(\omega_h)],}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 452 =====
% !PRINTED 421
\weberpage{421}
%<<CONT
in which, as we shall now often do,

\weq{8}{m = -D}

has been set, so that $m$ denotes a positive integer.

This function, which is very important for what follows, is called the \gesperrt{class function}. The roots of the equation

\weq{9}{H_m(u) = 0}

are the class invariants of the discriminant $D = -m$, and this equation is therefore called the \gesperrt{class equation}.

The degree $h$ of the class equation is equal to the number of primitive classes of the quadratic forms of the discriminant $D$. If we now consider the quotients (6), then from all this there results:

V. \gesperrt{The function $F_n(u, u)$ is divisible by $[H_m(u)]^k$, and the quotient is relatively prime to $H_m(u)$.}

Accordingly the function $F_n(u, u)$ can be decomposed into factors, and it follows, if $C$ is a constant equal to the coefficient of the highest power $u^N$ of $u$:

\weq{10}{F_n(u, u) = C\,H_m^k(u)\,H_{m'}^{k'}(u)\,H_{m''}^{k''}(u) \ \ldots,}

if the product extends over all the positive integers $m, m', m'', \ldots$ for which the equation § 114, (8)

\weq{11}{4\,n = y^2 + m\,x^2}

admits proper solutions, and $k, k', k'', \ldots$ denotes in each case the number of these solutions (with the modification indicated there in the two exceptional cases $D = -4$, $D = -3$).

The degree $N$ of the equation $F_n(u, u)$ is to be determined first.

If we choose the representatives in (5) as in § 69, then

\weq{12}{F_n[j(\tau), j(\tau)] = \Pi\left[j(\tau) - j\left(\frac{c + \partial\,\tau}{a}\right)\right].}

Here $a, \partial$ denoted all the pairs of positive integers satisfying the condition $a\,\partial = n$, % [sic] German source prints a singular verb with the plural subject.
and $c$ runs through a system of residues with respect to the modulus $a$, with the exclusion of those values which are not relatively prime to the greatest common divisor $e$ of $a$ and $\partial$, so that the number of values of $c$ belonging to a decomposition of $n$ into the two factors $a$ and $\partial$ is equal to $a\,\varphi(e){:}e$. If now $N$ is the degree of $F_n(u, u)$ and $C$ the coefficient of the highest power of $u$, then the development begins
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 453 =====
% !PRINTED 422
\weberpage{422}
%<<CONT
of $F_n[j(\tau), j(\tau)]$ in powers of $q=e^{\pi i \tau}$ with $Cq^{-2N}$
[§\,69, (4)].

If then we develop the factors of the right-hand side of (12) in the same
way, we can determine both $C$ and $N$.

For a factor of the right-hand side of (1)
\[
j(\tau) - j\left(\frac{c+\partial\tau}{a}\right)
\]
we have the following beginnings of the development
\[
\begin{array}{lll}
1. & -q^{-\frac{2\partial}{a}} e^{-\frac{2\pi i c}{a}}, & \partial > a,\\
2. & q^{-2}, & \partial < a,\\
3. & q^{-2}\left(1-e^{-\frac{2\pi i c}{a}}\right), & \partial = a.
\end{array}
\]

Let us first assume that $n$ is not a square; then case 3. does not occur,
and we have
\[
N = \sum_{\partial > a} \frac{\partial}{e}\varphi(e) + \sum_{\partial < a} \frac{a}{e}\varphi(e),
\]
or, what is the same,
\weq{13}{N = 2\sum_{\partial > a} \frac{\partial}{e}\varphi(e).}

By 1., $C$ is in any case an $n$th root of unity, and since it is at the same
time a rational number, it must be $=\pm 1$.

If then $n$ is a square, $\varphi(\sqrt{n})$ factors of the form 3. occur, and
there results:
\weq{14}{N = 2\sum_{\partial > a} \frac{\partial}{e}\varphi(e) + \varphi(\sqrt{n}).}

Here too $C$ is indeed different from zero, but not equal to $\pm 1$.
In this case we do not need to determine the value of $C$ more closely.
(It is always, as follows from the theory of the division of the circle, a
divisor of $\sqrt{n}$).

If in particular $n$ is a prime, then
\weq{15}{N = 2n.}

One can always dispose of $x$ and $y$ in such a way that, the conditions of
§ 114 being observed, $n = \frac{1}{4}(y^2+mx^2)$ does not become a square.
To this end let $x$ be taken divisible by 4, and $y$ by 2 but not by 4, and
moreover let $y$ have no odd common divisor with $mx^2$. If then
$\frac{1}{4}(y^2+mx^2)$ is a square $M^2$, then
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 454 =====
% !PRINTED 423
\weberpage{423}
%<<CONT
it has an odd square prime divisor $p^2$ which does not divide $y^2$, and
we have
\[
(y+4\lambda p)^2 + m x^2 = 4M^2 + 8\lambda y p + 16\lambda^2 p^2,
\]
and this number, if $\lambda$ is not divisible by $p$, is indeed divisible
by $p$, but not by $p^2$, and so cannot be a square. Moreover, $\lambda$
can still be so disposed of that $y+4\lambda p$ has no odd common divisor
with $x$, so that the conditions of § 114 are satisfied. Accordingly, for
every $m$, $j(\omega)$ satisfies an equation $F_n(u,u)$ in which $C=\pm 1$,
and from this it follows, by Bd. II, § 149:

VI. \gesperrt{The class invariants are integral algebraic numbers.}

\begin{center}
\textbf{\S\,116. \gesperrt{Class Number Relations.}}
\end{center}

If we equate the degree, as it results from what precedes for both parts of
equation (10), § 115, we obtain the formula
\weq{1}{N = hk + h'k' + h''k'' + \cdots,}
\weq{2}{\sum h k = 2\sum \frac{\partial}{e}\varphi(e) + \varphi(\sqrt{n}),}
in which $\varphi(\sqrt{n})=0$ is to be set when $n$ is not a square, and
$N$ is determined by (13), (14) or (15) of the preceding section.
This is the \gesperrt{Kronecker class number relation}, to which we wish to give a
somewhat more convenient form\footnote{The class number relations, of
which the one derived here is only the simplest case, were discovered by
\gesperrt{Kronecker} (Crelles Journal, Bd. 57) and considerably
generalised by \gesperrt{Gierster} (Mathematische Annalen, Bd. 21, 22) and
\gesperrt{Hurwitz} (ibid. Bd. 25).}.

Beside $n$ we consider all the values $n'$ that arise from $n$ by removing
a square factor, form equation (2) for them, and add together all the
results so obtained. Here only the value $n'=1$ is to be excluded, in case
$n$ is a square, because $F_1(u,u)=0$.

Let $\delta^2$, then, be any square factor of $n$ different from $n$
itself, and
\[
n = n'\delta^2.
\]
If we decompose $n'$ into two factors $n' = a'\partial'$ and denote by
$e'$ the greatest common divisor of $\partial'$ and $a'$, then we have
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 455 =====
% !PRINTED 424
\weberpage{424}
%<<CONT
\weq{3}{\Sigma N' = 2\sum_{\partial' > a'}^{\delta}\sum^{\partial'} \frac{\partial'}{e'}\varphi(e') + \sum^{n'} \varphi(\sqrt{n'}),}
if $\delta^2$ runs through all the square factors of $n$ (with the
possible exception of $n$ itself).

If we now set
\[
\partial'\delta = \partial, \quad a'\delta = a, \quad e'\delta = e,
\]
then $a\partial = n$, and $e$ is the greatest common divisor of $a$ and
$\partial$; at the same time $\partial' > a'$ has as its consequence
that $\partial > a$. Conversely, from every decomposition $a\partial$
of $n$ and from every divisor $e'$ of $e$ one obtains a decomposition
$a'\partial'$ of $n'$, where
\[
\delta = \frac{e}{e'}, \quad \partial' = \frac{\partial e'}{e}, \quad a' = \frac{a e'}{e}
\]
holds. Accordingly
\weq{4}{\Sigma N' = 2\sum_{\partial>a} \frac{\partial}{e} \sum \varphi(e') + \sum^{n'} \varphi(\sqrt{n'}).}

In this we now make use of the number-theoretic relation:
$\sum \varphi(\partial) = n$, in which the sum refers to all divisors
of $n$. If we first assume that $n$ is not a square, then none of the
$n'$ are squares either, and $\varphi(\sqrt{n'})=0$. Hence, since
$\sum \varphi(e') = e$, we obtain
\weq{5}{\Sigma N' = 2\sum_{\partial>\sqrt{n}} \partial.}

If on the other hand $n$ is a square, then $e'$ still runs through all
the divisors of $e$, but $\sqrt{n'}$ runs through all the divisors of
$\sqrt{n}$, with the exception of 1; from this there follows for this
case:
\weq{6}{\Sigma N' = 2\sum_{\partial>\sqrt{n}} \partial + \sqrt{n} - 1.}

In both cases $\partial$ runs through all the divisors of $n$ that are
\gesperrt{greater} than $\sqrt{n}$.

We have now still to form the sum of the expressions $\Sigma k h$ for
the various values of $n'$ or $\delta$. But if we set
$n = \delta^2 n'$, then from every proper solution of
\weq{7}{4n' = y'^2 + m x'^2}
we obtain, by multiplication by $\delta^2$, a solution (improper, if
$\delta > 1$) of
\weq{8}{4n = y^2 + m x^2,}
namely
\[
y = \delta y', \quad x = \delta x'.
\]

%% ===== canonical stable idx 456 =====
% !PRINTED 425
\weberpage{425}
If, conversely, any solution $x, y$ of (8) is given, then $4n$ is
divisible by the square of every common divisor of $x$ and $y$. We
denote by $\delta$ the greatest common divisor of $x, y$ whose \gesperrt{square} is
at the same time a divisor of $n$, and which is therefore either equal
to the greatest common divisor of $x, y$ or equal to half of it, and we
set
\[
y = \delta y', \quad n = \delta x', % [sic]
\]
and thus obtain a \gesperrt{proper solution} of (7).

If, then, we put for $-m$ all discriminants for which equation (8) has
solutions at all, and understand by $k$ the \gesperrt{number} of these solutions
(with positive $x$), and further by $h(m)$ the class number of primitive
forms of discriminant $-m$, then the formula results
\weq{9}{\Sigma k\, h(m) = 2\sum \partial,}

if $n$ is not a square,
\[
= 2\sum \partial + \sqrt{n} - 1,
\]
if $n$ is a square.

Here it must still be recalled that in the two exceptional cases $m=3$,
$m=4$ only the third part or the half of the number of proper solutions
of (8) was understood by $k$ in § 115.

We will now do justice to this circumstance by understanding by $k$ the
total number of solutions of (8), but setting
\[
h(3) = \tfrac{1}{3}, \quad h(4) = \tfrac{1}{2}
\]
[instead of $h(3)=1$, $h(4)=1$].

It is further to be observed that in forming the sum (9) the solutions
belonging to the value $n'=1$ have not been counted. This comes into
consideration only in the case where $n$ is a square. Equation (7):
\[
4 = y'^2 + m x'^2
\]
then has only the following proper solutions:
\[
\begin{array}{lllll}
m=3: & x'=1, & y'=\pm 1, & k=2, & h=\tfrac{1}{3},\\
m=4: & x'=1, & y'=0, & k=1, & h=\tfrac{1}{2},
\end{array}
\]
and hence, if one wished to remove this exception, there would still
have to be added to (9):
\[
\Sigma k h, \text{ referred to } n'=1, = \tfrac{1}{2}+\tfrac{2}{3} = \tfrac{7}{6}.
\]

%% ===== canonical stable idx 457 =====
% !PRINTED 426
\weberpage{426}
Accordingly the formula now reads

\weq{10}{\Sigma k\, h(m) = 2\Sigma\partial,}

$n$ not a square,
\[
= 2\Sigma\partial + \sqrt{n} + \tfrac{1}{6},
\]
$n$ a square.

We decompose the sum on the left side of (10) into its individual parts by taking each solution of equation (8) separately. We then obtain a sum of expressions $h(m)$, in which, however, the same $m$ occurs as often as (8) has solutions. One of the solutions, however, gives
\[
m = \frac{4n-y^2}{x^2},
\]
and this occurs \gesperrt{once} if $y=0$, and twice (with $+y$ and $-y$) if $y$ is different from zero. But the number of primitive classes of the discriminant $-m$ is equal to the number of non-primitive classes of the discriminant $-x^2m$ of divisor $x$; and so, if we now understand by $h(m)$ (in distinction from the previous formula) the \gesperrt{total number} of classes of the discriminant $-m$ (primitive and imprimitive), then we obtain from (10):
\weq{11}{\begin{aligned}
&h(4n) + 2h(4n-1) + 2h(4n-4) + 2h(4n-9) + \cdots \\
&= 2\sum_{\partial>\sqrt{n}}\partial, \quad (n \text{ not a square}), \\
&= 2\sum_{\partial>\sqrt{n}}\partial + \sqrt{n} + \tfrac{1}{6}, \quad (n \text{ a square}).
\end{aligned}}

In this, the sum of the $h(4n-y^2)$ on the left is to be continued as long as $4n-y^2$ remains positive, and on the right $\partial$ runs through all divisors of $n$ that are greater than $\sqrt{n}$.

\gesperrt{It is, however, to be observed here that the forms $(x,0,x)$ are to be reckoned only with $\frac{1}{2}$ each, and $(x,x,x)$ with $\frac{1}{3}$,} because they arise from the representations of $4n$ by the discriminant $m=-4,-3$.

\begin{center}
\S\ 117. \textbf{\gesperrt{Arithmetic Nature of the Class Function $H_m(u)$.}}
\end{center}

We now return once more to equation (10), § 115, in order to derive from it the nature of the coefficients of the class equation $H_m(u)=0$. First, however, we consider the two special cases: $m=4$ and $m=3$.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 458 =====
% !PRINTED 427
\weberpage{427}
If we set, as in § 54, (4)
\[
\gamma_2(\omega) = \sqrt[3]{j(\omega)}, \quad \gamma_3(\omega) = \sqrt[2]{j(\omega)-1728},
\]
then it follows from § 54, (14):
\[
\gamma_3(i) = -\gamma_3(i), \quad \text{hence} \quad \gamma_3(i) = 0.
\]
Furthermore, by the same formula, if we set
\[
\varrho = \frac{-1+i\sqrt{3}}{2}, \qquad \varrho+1 = \frac{-1}{\varrho}
\]
then:
\[
\gamma_2(\varrho+1) = e^{-\frac{2\pi i}{3}}\gamma_2(\varrho) = \gamma_2\left(-\frac{1}{\varrho}\right) = \gamma_2(\varrho),
\]
consequently $\gamma_2(\varrho) = 0$, and we obtain
\weq{1}{\begin{aligned}
H_3(u) &= u, & j(\varrho) &= 0, \\
H_4(u) &= u-1728, & j(i) &= 1728.
\end{aligned}}

The two functions $H_3(u)$ and $H_4(u)$ therefore have integral rational numerical coefficients. This property we can now establish in general for all $H_m$ by complete induction.

First we observe that, once it has been proved that $H_m(u)$ has \gesperrt{rational coefficients}, it follows at once that the coefficients are \gesperrt{integral rational numbers} (the first $=1$). For these coefficients are integral algebraic numbers (by § 115, VI.), and consequently, if they are rational, \gesperrt{integral rational numbers}. Now we consider the largest among the values of $m$ that occur in equation (10), § 115; these are
\[
\begin{aligned}
m &= 4n, & x &= 1, & y &= 0, & k &= 1, \\
m &= 4n-1, & x &= 1, & y &= \pm 1, & k &= 2.
\end{aligned}
\]

Accordingly $F_k(u,u)$ contains the two factors $H_{4n}(u)$, $H_{4n-1}(u)^2$, and otherwise nothing but factors $H_m(u)$ in which $m<4n-1$. If we assume that it has already been proved of the latter that they have rational coefficients, it follows that
\[
H_{4n}(u)\, H_{4n-1}(u)^2 = \varPhi(u)
\]
has rational coefficients, and hence, in order to find $H_{4n-1}(u)$, one has to seek the greatest common divisor of $\varPhi(u)$ and $\varPhi'(u)$, which is done by rational calculation. But thereby $H_{4n}(u)$ too is found by rational means, and since $H_3(u)$ and $H_4(u)$ have rational coefficients, it follows in general:

VII. \gesperrt{The class functions $H_m(u)$ have integral rational numerical coefficients.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 459 =====
% !PRINTED 428
\weberpage{428}
\begin{center}
\S\ 118. \textbf{\gesperrt{Composition of the Quadratic Forms.}}
\end{center}

Since in the algebraic theory of the class equation we must rely upon the theory of the composition of the quadratic forms, we preface the following remarks about it:

Two primitive forms $\varphi_1=(a_1,b_1,c_1)$, $\varphi_2=(a_2,b_2,c_2)$ of discriminant $-m$ are called \gesperrt{concordant} (einig, concordantes) if $a_1,a_2,\tfrac{1}{2}(b_1+b_2)$ are without a common divisor; $\varphi_1$ and $\varphi_2$ are therefore certainly concordant if $a_1,a_2$ are already without a common divisor, and since, when only the classes $k_1,k_2$ of $\varphi_1,\varphi_2$ are given, one can always choose $\varphi_1,\varphi_2$ in their classes in this way, it follows that in any two classes (which may also be identical) one can always find two concordant forms. If, then, this assumption holds, it follows from
\[
\tfrac{1}{4}(b_1^2-b_2^2) = \tfrac{1}{2}(b_1-b_2)\cdot\tfrac{1}{2}(b_1+b_2) = a_1c_1-a_2c_2,
\]
that $\tfrac{1}{2}(b_1-b_2)$ is divisible by the greatest common divisor $\delta$ of $a_1,a_2$, and from this, that the two congruences
\weq{1}{b' \equiv b_1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 2a_1), \quad b' \equiv b_2\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 2a_2)}
can always be satisfied.

For from the first of them it follows that $b'=b_1+2\lambda a_1$, and one has therefore to determine $\lambda$ from the congruence
\[
\tfrac{1}{2}(b_1-b_2) + a_1\lambda \equiv 0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ a_2)
\]
which is always solvable. If $\mu$ is the least common multiple of $a_1$ and $a_2$, so that $a_1a_2=\mu\delta$, then by (1) $b'$ may still be replaced by $b=b'+2\mu h$, where $h$ is an arbitrary integer. Now since $\tfrac{1}{4}(b_1^2+m)$ is divisible by $a_1$, and $\tfrac{1}{2}(b_2^2+m)$ by $a_2$, % [sic] printed with 1/4 and 1/2 respectively, inconsistently
$\tfrac{1}{4}(b'^2+m)$ is divisible by $\mu$, and if we determine $h$ from the congruence
\[
\frac{b'^2+m}{4\mu} + b'h \equiv 0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ \delta)
\]
which is always solvable, since $b'$ is by assumption relatively prime to $\delta$, then $b^2+m=4a_1a_2c$ becomes divisible by $4a_1a_2$. The two classes $k_1,k_2$ are then represented by
\[
\varphi_1=(a_1,b,a_2c), \quad \varphi_2=(a_2,b,a_1c),
\]
and the form
\[
\varphi = \varphi_1\varphi_2 = (a_1a_2,b,c)
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 460 =====
% !PRINTED 429
\weberpage{429}
%<<CONT
is compounded from $\varphi_1\varphi_2$. The form $\varphi$ belongs to a class $k$ which is said to be \gesperrt{compounded} from $k_1,k_2$.

Let us assume $\varphi=(a,b,c)$ in such a way that $a$ is relatively prime to $m$; then $b$ is also relatively prime to $a$ (because of $m=4ac-b^2$). If $a=a_1a_2$, then $(a_1,b,ca_2)$, $(a_2,b,ca_1)$ are likewise concordant primitive forms, and one obtains the composition
\[
(a,b,c) = (a_1,b,ca_2),\ (a_2,b,ca), % [sic] German source omits the expected subscript 1 on the final a.
\]
and by repeated application of this theorem one arrives at the result:

I. \gesperrt{The form $\varphi=(a,b,c)$ can, if $a$ is relatively prime to $m$, be composed of forms whose first coefficients are primes, namely the prime factors of $a$.}

One of these components, say
\[
(p,b,acp^{-1}),
\]
can be replaced by an equivalent form $(p,b',c'p^g)$ whose third coefficient $c'p^g$ is divisible by an arbitrarily high power of $p$.

To prove this we need the symbol $\sim$ for equivalence, and we have
\[
(p,b,cp^{g-1}) \sim (p,b+2\lambda p^g,c'p^g),
\]
in which $c'$, on account of the equality of the discriminants, is to be determined from
\[
pc' = c+\lambda b+\lambda^2 p^g
\]
Now since $b$ is not divisible by $p$, $\lambda$ can be determined from the congruence $c+\lambda b \equiv 0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ p)$, and $c'$ turns out to be an integer. With this, having regard to (I.), the following is proved:

II. \gesperrt{In every class $k$ of primitive forms of discriminant $D$ one can find a representative $\varphi$ which can be composed of forms}
\[
P=(p,b,p^gc),
\]
\gesperrt{in which $p$ is a prime not dividing $D$, and $g$ is an arbitrary exponent.}

The form $P$ can easily be composed with itself, for, in the sense of the compositions, when $g>\nu$:
\[
(p^\nu,b,p^{g-\nu}c)(p,b,p^gc) = (p^{\nu+1},b,p^{g-\nu-1}c),
\]
and consequently, by the inference from $\nu-1$ to $\nu$:
\weq{2}{P^\nu = (p^\nu,b,p^{g-\nu}c).}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 461 =====
% !PRINTED 430
\weberpage{430}

In the chain of compositions
\weq{3}{P,\ P^2,\ P^3,\ \ldots}
there may occur a form that belongs to the \gesperrt{principal class}, that is, one equivalent to $(1,\,0,\,\tfrac14 m)$ or $[1,\,1,\,\tfrac14(m+1)]$. If this happens for $P^{\varepsilon}$, then $p^{\varepsilon}$ is representable by the principal form, and there is a \gesperrt{proper} representation
\weq{4}{4\,p^{\varepsilon} = y^2 - D\,x^2.}
If conversely such a representation is possible, then there is a form $(p^{\varepsilon},\,b,\,c)$ in the principal class.

\gesperrt{If $\varepsilon$ is the least positive exponent for which equation (4) is properly solvable, then $\varepsilon$ is called the index of $p$, and $p$ belongs to the exponent $\varepsilon$.}

If
\weq{5}{P = (p,\,b,\,p^{\varepsilon-1}c),}
then
\[
b^2 \equiv D \pmod{4\,p^{\varepsilon}},
\]
and when this condition is satisfied, then in the form $(p,\,b,\,c')$ of discriminant $D$ the third coefficient is divisible by $p^{\varepsilon-1}$. The form (5) is preserved if we replace $b$ by any number $b'$ congruent to it with respect to the modulus $2\,p^{\varepsilon}$. If therefore $a$ is not divisible by $p$, and
\[
\varphi = (a,\,B,\,C)
\]
is any form of discriminant $D$ concordant with $P$, then the two congruences
\[
x \equiv b \pmod{2\,p^{\varepsilon}}, \quad x \equiv B \pmod{2\,a}
\]
can be satisfied at the same time, and if one then puts this $x$ in place of $b$ and $B$, it follows that:

III. \gesperrt{If $l$ is the class of $P$ and $k$ an arbitrary class of discriminant $D$, then in $l$ and $k$ one can choose the representatives:}
\weq{6}{(p,\,b,\,a\,c\,p^{\varepsilon-1}),\quad (a,\,b,\,c\,p^{\varepsilon}),}
and in the compounded class $lk$ one obtains a representative
\weq{7}{(a\,p,\,b,\,p^{\varepsilon-1}c).}
If therefore
\[
\omega = \frac{-b+\sqrt{-m}}{2\,a}
\]
is a root of the class $k$, then $\omega\colon p$ is a root of the class $lk$.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 462 =====
% !PRINTED 431
\weberpage{431}

\S\ 119. \gesperrt{The Discriminant of the Invariant Equation.}

We now raise the question when an invariant equation
\weq{1}{F_p(v,\,u) = 0,}
in which $p$ is a prime, has two or more equal roots $v$ for $u = j(\omega)$, or when among the $p+1$ quantities
\weq{2}{j(p\,\omega),\quad j\!\left(\frac{\omega+c}{p}\right),\quad c = 0,\,1,\,\ldots,\,p-1}
two or more occur that are equal to one another. This takes place then and only then, when among the $p+1$ quantities
\weq{3}{p\,\omega,\quad \frac{\omega+c}{p}}
two equivalent ones occur. Accordingly $\omega$ must in any case satisfy a quadratic equation with integral coefficients and negative discriminant $D=-m$, which we assume in the form:
\weq{4}{A\,\omega^2 + B\,\omega + C = 0,\quad 4\,A\,C - B^2 = m > 0,}
in which $A,\,B,\,C$ are without a common divisor.

If we replace $\omega$ by an equivalent number, and hence (4) by an equivalent equation, the quantities (2) are only interchanged among themselves. The question as to the \gesperrt{number} of equal roots of (1) is therefore not affected by this, and we may accordingly assume that $A$ is not divisible by $p$. If now, in the first place, $p\,\omega$ is equivalent to $\dfrac{\omega+c}{p}$, then:
\weq{5}{\frac{\omega+c}{p} = \frac{\gamma+\delta\,p\,\omega}{\alpha+\beta\,p\,\omega},\quad \alpha\,\delta-\beta\,\gamma = 1.}
If we write this equation thus:
\weq{6}{\beta\,p\,\omega^2 + (\alpha+\beta\,c\,p-\delta\,p^2)\,\omega + c\,\alpha-\gamma\,p = 0,}
then it follows by comparison with (4) (since $A$ was to be indivisible by $p$) that $\alpha$ is divisible by $p$, and must therefore be $=p\,\alpha'$, and that an integer $x$ exists which satisfies the conditions:
\weq{7}{\beta = A\,x,\quad \alpha'+\beta\,c-\delta\,p = B\,x,\quad c\,\alpha'-\gamma = C\,x.}
If we further put
\weq{8}{\alpha'-\beta\,c+\delta\,p = y,}
then it follows:
\weq{9}{\begin{aligned}
2\,\alpha' &= B\,x+y,\\
2\,(\beta\,c-\delta\,p) &= B\,x-y.
\end{aligned}}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 463 =====
% !PRINTED 432
\weberpage{432}
%<<CONT
and from
\weq{10}{p\,\alpha'\,\delta-\beta\,\gamma = 1}
there then follows
\weq{11}{y^2+m\,x^2 = 4.}

The value $x=0$ is to be excluded, because otherwise $\beta=0$ would have to hold, which contradicts equation (10), and we may, without loss of generality, assume $x$ to be positive. Since moreover $m$ must be either $\equiv 0$ or $\equiv 3$ with respect to the modulus 4, there remain for the satisfaction of (11) only the following two possibilities:
\[
1.\quad m=3,\quad x=1,\quad y=\pm 1.
\]

Since for the discriminant $-3$ there is only one class of forms, we may assume $A=1,\,B=1,\,C=1$, that is, we may set for $\omega$ the imaginary third root of unity $e^{\frac{2\pi i}{3}}$, and we then obtain among the quantities (3) three equivalent ones by taking $y=+1$ and $=-1$:
\weq{12}{p\,\omega,\quad \frac{\omega}{p},\quad \frac{\omega+1}{p},}
as is also recognised from the equations
\[
\frac{\omega}{p} = \frac{-1}{p+p\,\omega}, \quad \frac{\omega+1}{p} = \frac{-1}{p\,\omega}
\]
from which the equivalence of the three quantities (12) is evident.
\[
2.\quad m=4,\quad x=1,\quad y=0.
\]

Because here too there is only one class of forms, we may assume $B=0,\,A=C=1$, that is, $\omega=i$, and we find the two equivalent values:
\[
p\,\omega,\quad \frac{\omega}{p},
\]
as also follows from the equation
\[
p\,\omega = \frac{-p}{\omega}
\]

Further, let two of the values (3)
\[
\frac{\omega+c}{p}, \quad \frac{\omega+c'}{p}
\]
be equivalent, so that an equation holds:
\weq{13}{\frac{\omega+c}{p} = \frac{\gamma\,p+\delta\,(\omega+c')}{\alpha\,p+\beta\,(\omega+c')}, \quad \alpha\,\delta-\beta\,\gamma = 1,}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 464 =====
% !PRINTED 433
\weberpage{433}
%<<CONT
or
\weq{14}{\beta\,\omega^2 + (\beta\,c'+\beta\,c+\alpha\,p-\delta\,p)\,\omega + \beta\,c\,c'+\alpha\,c\,p-\delta\,c'\,p-\gamma\,p^2 = 0,}
whence by comparison with (4):
\weq{15}{\begin{aligned}
\beta &= A\,x,\\
\beta\,c'+\beta\,c+\alpha\,p-\delta\,p &= B\,x,\\
\beta\,c\,c'+\alpha\,c\,p-\delta\,c'\,p-\gamma\,p^2 &= C\,x.
\end{aligned}}
and if one again sets
\weq{16}{\beta\,c'-\beta\,c+\alpha\,p+\delta\,p = y}
then:
\weq{17}{\begin{aligned}
2\,(\beta\,c'+\alpha\,p) &= B\,x+y,\\
2\,(\beta\,c-\delta\,p) &= B\,x-y.
\end{aligned}}
From this
\weq{18}{y^2+m\,x^2 = 4\,p^2.}
If $x$ is divisible by $p$, then $y$ must also be divisible by $p$, and by cancellation of the factor $p^2$ we come back to equation (11), which, as we have seen, is solvable only in the cases $m=3$ and $m=4$. We therefore assume further that $x$ is indivisible by $p$.

If $m$ is divisible by $p$, then $y$ is also divisible by $p$, and $\beta$ is, by (15), not divisible by $p$. But then it follows from (16): $c\equiv c' \pmod{p}$, and both therefore correspond to the same root of (1).

So let $p$ now divide neither $x$ nor $m$. Then it does not divide $y$ either, and by (17) $c$ and $c'$ are determined from the congruences
\weq{19}{\beta\,c' \equiv \frac{B\,x+y}{2}, \quad \beta\,c \equiv \frac{B\,x-y}{2} \pmod{p}}
and once $c,\,c'$ are determined, $\alpha$ and $\delta$ result from (17) as \gesperrt{integers}. With this the first two equations (15) are satisfied, and $\gamma$ is obtained from the last equation (15) likewise as an integer.

Indeed we have
\weq{20}{\gamma\,p^2 = \beta\,c\,c'+(\alpha\,c-\delta\,c')\,p-C\,x \equiv 0 \pmod{p^2}.}
For from (17) and (15) we have
\[
\begin{aligned}
\beta^2\,c\,c'+\beta\,(\alpha\,c-\delta\,c')\,p-\alpha\,\delta\,p^2-A\,C\,x^2
&= \beta\,[\beta\,c\,c'+(\alpha\,c-\delta\,c')\,p-C\,x]-\alpha\,\delta\,p^2\\
&= -\frac{y^2+m\,x^2}{4} = -p^2;
\end{aligned}
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 465 =====
% !PRINTED 434
\weberpage{434}
%<<CONT
consequently the second term of (20) is divisible by $p^2$, and if
one substitutes $\gamma p^2$ for it, it follows that
\[
\alpha\delta - \beta\gamma = 1.
\]
We thus arrive at the result:

IV. \gesperrt{The invariant equation $F_p(v,u)$ has multiple roots always
then and only then, when $u=j(\omega)$, where $\omega$
is the root of a quadratic equation whose discriminant
is not divisible by $p$, but which admits a solution of equation (18).}

For a given $p$ there is only a finite number of
values $m$ which meet this requirement, since $m < 4p^2$ must
hold. The values $m=3$, $m=4$ are contained among them as special
cases.

Since by (18) $-m$ is a quadratic residue of $p$, $p$
is representable by a form of discriminant $-m$; but $p^2$ is
representable by the principal form of a discriminant. The
class of forms by which $p$ is representable is therefore itself either
the principal class, or, compounded with itself, it gives the
principal class; it is therefore two-sided. We can therefore also
state Theorem IV. in the following way:

V. \gesperrt{The roots of the discriminant of the invariant equation
$F_p(v,u)$ are the singular invariants $j(\omega)$, where $\omega$
is the root of a quadratic equation of negative discriminant
$D$ for which the prime $p$ has the index 1 or 2.}

\begin{center}\rule{0.18\linewidth}{0.4pt}\end{center}

\begin{center}
\gesperrt{Eighteenth Chapter.}

\gesperrt{Galois Group of the Class Equation.}
\end{center}

\begin{center}\rule{0.18\linewidth}{0.4pt}\end{center}

\begin{center}
\textbf{\S\,120. \gesperrt{Relations between the class invariants of the same
discriminant.}}
\end{center}

For what follows it is convenient to have a notation by which the
dependence of the class invariant on the \gesperrt{class of forms} is expressed
more simply. We therefore set, when $k$ denotes an arbitrary
 primitive class of discriminant $-m$, which
according to § 118, III. is represented by $(a, b, c p^{\varepsilon})$:
\[
(k) = j\left(\frac{-b + \sqrt{-m}}{2a}\right) = j(\omega).
\]
When one or more of the $(k)$ occur under a function
 symbol, we shall also omit the brackets,
writing for example $f(k, k', \ldots)$ for $f[(k), (k'), \ldots]$.

If therefore
\weq{1}{(k) = j(\omega),}
and $l$ is a class represented by $(p, b, a c p^{\varepsilon-1})$, then by
§ 118, III.:
\weq{2}{(lk) = j\left(\frac{\omega}{p}\right),}
and so the two quantities
\[
u = (k), \quad v = (lk)
\]
satisfy the invariant equation
\weq{3}{F_p(v, u) = 0.}
The quantity $v = (lk)$ is, however, in addition a root of the
class equation
\weq{4}{H_m(v) = 0,}
and it is first to be established how many roots equation
(3) has in common with (4).

%% ===== canonical stable idx 467 =====
% !PRINTED 436
\weberpage{436}
But all the roots of (3) are, by § 69:
\weq{5}{j(p\omega), \quad j\left(\frac{\omega + \lambda}{p}\right),}
where $\lambda$ runs through a system of residues with respect to the
modulus $p$. The first of these does not belong to the roots of (4), for
$\omega' = p\omega$ satisfies the equation:
\[
a\omega'^2 + p b \omega' + p^{\varepsilon+2} c = 0,
\]
which is primitive and of discriminant $-mp^2$. If, however, we set
$p\omega' = \omega + \lambda$, we obtain for $\omega'$ the equation:
\weq{6}{a p^2 \omega'^2 + p(b - 2a\lambda)\omega' + (a\lambda^2 - b\lambda + c p^{\varepsilon}) = 0,}
and these equations likewise have the discriminant
$-mp^2$. But there are two among them which are imprimitive with the
divisor $p$, namely those which correspond to the values
\weq{7}{\lambda \equiv 0, \quad a\lambda - b \equiv 0 \pmod{p}}
The first is the root of the form $(a p, b, c p^{\varepsilon-1})$, the
second that of the form
\[
(a p, \; b - 2a\lambda, \; C),
\]
and since $b - 2a\lambda \equiv b \pmod{2a}$ and [by (7)] $\equiv -b \pmod{2p}$,
this form is compounded from $(a, b, c p^{\varepsilon})$ and $(p, -b, a c p^{\varepsilon-1})$,
which belongs to the class $l^{-1}$ reciprocal to $l$. From this it follows:

I. \gesperrt{The equations (3) and (4) have only two roots
 in common with one another, namely the class invariants
$(lk)$ and $(l^{-1}k)$, and if the class $l$
is two-sided, they have only one root
in common.}

If, then, one sets $u = (k)$ in (3), the greatest common
 divisor of (3) and (4) is of the second degree, and if $l$
is two-sided, of the first degree. In the former case $(lk)$ and
$(l^{-1}k)$ are the roots of a quadratic equation whose coefficients
 depend rationally on $u$, and whose form is for the rest
dependent only on the class $l$, not on $k$. To what has thus
been proved we can give the following expression:

II. \gesperrt{We have}
\weq{8}{(lk) + (l^{-1}k) = f_l(k),}
\gesperrt{or, if $l$ is two-sided,}
\weq{9}{(lk) = f_l(k),}
\gesperrt{in which $f_l(k)$ denotes a rational function of $(k)$,
whose rational numerical coefficients depend only
on the class $l$, not on the class $k$.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 468 =====
% !PRINTED 437
\weberpage{437}
We now consider the sequence of class invariants
\weq{10}{\ldots, (l^{-2}k), (l^{-1}k), (k), (lk), (l^2k), (l^3k), \ldots,}
which can be continued arbitrarily forwards and backwards. In this
sequence, if $l$ belongs to the exponent $\varepsilon$, then $(l^{\nu}k)$ is
identical with $(l^{\nu+\varepsilon}k)$, while all the terms lying between
them differ from it and from one another. If $l$ is two-sided, the
sequence (10) contains only two different terms, each of which is
\gesperrt{rationally expressible} by the other. Otherwise we conclude from (8)
that every term of the sequence (10) is rationally expressible by the
two preceding ones (or also by the two following ones) in the form
\weq{11}{(l^{\nu+1}k) = -(l^{\nu-1}k) + f_l(l^{\nu}k).}
By a repeated application of this formula one arrives at the theorem
\gesperrt{that every term of the sequence (10) can be rationally expressed by
any two consecutive terms of the same sequence.}

\gesperrt{But if $l$ is two-sided, then all the terms of the sequence
(10) are rationally expressible by one of them.}

\begin{center}
§ 121. \gesperrt{Separation of the opposite classes.}
\end{center}

It is now a question of separating the two roots of the quadratic
equation from one another in the case of an $l$ that is not two-sided
as well, which is possible by the adjunction of $\sqrt{D}$.

If the class $l$ is not two-sided, the two class invariants
$(lk)$, $(l^{-1}k)$ are different from one another, and therefore
(§ 118, III.)
\[
v = (lk) = j\left(\frac{\omega}{p}\right)
\]
is a \gesperrt{simple} root of the transformation equation
\[
F_p(u, v) = 0
\]
(§ 119, V.). If we therefore put
\weq{1}{M = \left(\frac{\eta\left(\dfrac{\omega}{p}\right)}{\eta(\omega)}\right)^{24},}
then it follows by § 72 that $M$ is \gesperrt{rationally} expressible by
\[
j(\omega) \quad \text{and} \quad j\left(\frac{\omega}{p}\right),
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 469 =====
% !PRINTED 438
\weberpage{438}

%<<CONT
is therefore expressible \gesperrt{rationally} through $(k)$ and $(lk)$, and from § 72
it follows that $M$ is an \gesperrt{integral algebraic number}.

We apply this theorem to each two consecutive
terms of the sequence (7) and obtain, if we set
\[
\omega_1 = \frac{\omega}{p}, \quad \omega_2 = \frac{\omega_1}{p}, \quad \dotsc, \quad \omega_\varepsilon = \frac{\omega_{\varepsilon-1}}{p}
\]
and if $\varphi$ denotes a rational function completely determined by the
class $l$:
\[
\begin{aligned}
M &= \left(\frac{\eta(\omega_1)}{\eta(\omega)}\right)^{24} &&= \varphi(k,\, lk), \\
(2)\quad M_1 &= \left(\frac{\eta(\omega_2)}{\eta(\omega_1)}\right)^{24} &&= \varphi(lk,\, l^2k), \\
&\dotsc\dotsc\dotsc\dotsc\dotsc\dotsc\dotsc\dotsc\dotsc\dotsc\dotsc\dotsc \\
M_{\varepsilon-1} &= \left(\frac{\eta(\omega_\varepsilon)}{\eta(\omega_{\varepsilon-1})}\right)^{24} &&= \varphi(l^{\varepsilon-1}k,\, k).
\end{aligned}
\]
By multiplication of all these equations there follows:
\weq{3}{\left(\frac{\eta(\omega_\varepsilon)}{\eta(\omega)}\right)^{24} = \varphi(k,\, lk)\,\varphi(lk,\, l^2k)\,\dotsc\,\varphi(l^{\varepsilon-1}k,\, k).}
But by § 120 the right-hand side of this equation can be represented as a
rational function $\Phi(k, lk)$ of $(k)$ and $(lk)$ (with rational numerical
coefficients).
On the other hand, since $l$ belongs to the exponent $\varepsilon$, $l^\varepsilon$ is equivalent to
the principal form, and so $l^\varepsilon k$ to $k$ and $\omega_\varepsilon$ to $\omega$; there is therefore
an equation:
\weq{4}{\omega_\varepsilon = \frac{\gamma + \delta\,\omega}{\alpha + \beta\,\omega}, \quad \alpha\delta - \beta\gamma = 1,}
and $\eta(\omega_\varepsilon) : \eta(\omega)$ is to be determined according to § 38. If, as
we have assumed, $\omega$ satisfies the equation
\weq{5}{a\,\omega^2 + b\,\omega + c\,p^\varepsilon = 0,}
then one obtains from (4), since $\omega_\varepsilon = \omega/p^\varepsilon$:
\[
\beta\,\omega^2 + (\alpha - p^\varepsilon\delta)\,\omega + \gamma\,p^\varepsilon = 0,
\]
which by comparison with (5) gives
\[
\beta = a\,x, \quad \alpha - p^\varepsilon\delta = b\,x, \quad \gamma = -c\,x,
\]
and if one sets $\alpha + p^\varepsilon\delta = y$:
\weq{6}{\alpha = \frac{y + b\,x}{2}, \quad \beta = a\,x,}
\[
p^\varepsilon\gamma = -c\,x, \quad p^\varepsilon\delta = \frac{y - b\,x}{2},
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 470 =====
% !PRINTED 439
\weberpage{439}
%<<CONT
hence
\[ 4 p^\varepsilon = y^2 + m x^2. \]

From this $x$ and $y$ are determined up to sign, and $x$ may be assumed positive, and the sign of $y$ follows from the congruence
\weq{7}{y \equiv b x \pmod{p^\varepsilon}.}

If, on the other hand, one considers the composition $l^{-1} k$, then one has to compose the form $(a, b, c p^\varepsilon)$ with $(p, -b, a c p^{\varepsilon - 1})$; one determines $b'$ from the two congruences:
\[ b' \equiv b \pmod{2a}, \qquad b' \equiv -b \pmod{2 p^\varepsilon}, \]
and everything is to be carried out in just the same way, except that in place of (7) the congruence % [sic] German print has the grammatically anomalous dative "der Kongruenz"
\weq{8}{y \equiv -b x \pmod{p^\varepsilon}}
enters, that is, $y$ receives the opposite sign.

But according to (5) and (6)
\weq{9}{\alpha + \beta\omega = \frac{y + (2 a \omega + b) x}{2} = \frac{y + \sqrt{-m}\, x}{2},}
in which, if $a$ and $x$ and consequently $\beta$ are assumed positive, $\sqrt{-m}$ is to be taken positive imaginary.

But by \S\,38, (4)
\[ \left( \frac{\eta(\omega_\varepsilon)}{\eta(\omega)} \right)^{24} = \left( \frac{y + \sqrt{-m}\, x}{2} \right)^{12}, \]
and consequently one obtains by (3)
\weq{10}{\Phi(k, lk) = \left( \frac{y + \sqrt{-m}\, x}{2} \right)^{12}.}

In the same way there follows, on account of (16): % [sic] printed (16); no antecedent equation (16) occurs in this section here
\weq{11}{\Phi(k, l^{-1}k) = \left( \frac{y - \sqrt{-m}\, x}{2} \right)^{12},}
and equation (10) is therefore \gesperrt{not satisfied} when $(lk)$ is replaced by $(l^{-1}k)$, except when
\weq{12}{\left( \frac{y + \sqrt{-m}\, x}{2} \right)^{12} = \left( \frac{y - \sqrt{-m}\, x}{2} \right)^{12}}
holds.

But this is not possible if, as we have assumed, $p$ does not divide $m$. For if one decomposes $p$ in the field $\Omega = \Re(\sqrt{D})$ into the two conjugate prime ideals $\mathfrak{p}, \mathfrak{p}'$, distinct from one another, then the one divides $\frac{1}{2}(y + \sqrt{-m}\, x)$, the other
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 471 =====
% !PRINTED 440
\weberpage{440}
%<<CONT
$\frac{1}{2}(y - \sqrt{-m}\, x)$, and these two quantities must therefore be relatively prime. Consequently equation (12) cannot hold.

The quadratic equation whose two roots are $(lk)$, $(l^{-1}k)$ therefore has % [sic] German print has (18); no antecedent equation (18) occurs in this section here
\gesperrt{only one root} in common with (18), and from this there results the important theorem:

III. \gesperrt{After the adjunction of $\sqrt{D}$, $(lk)$ can be expressed rationally by $(k)$ in the form:}
\weq{13}{(lk) = f_l(k, \sqrt{D}),}
\gesperrt{where $f_l$ is a rational function whose form is determined by the class $l$ alone.}

The change of the sign of $\sqrt{D}$ has the effect that $(lk)$ passes into $(l^{-1}k)$, thus:
\[ f_l(k, \sqrt{D}) = f_{l^{-1}}(k, -\sqrt{D}). \]
If $l$ is two-sided, then by I. the same formula holds, only that $\sqrt{D}$ then does not occur in $f_l$.

If $l'$ is a second class of the same nature as $l$, then one can apply formula (13) to $l'k$ and obtains:
\[ (l\, l' k) = f_l(l' k, \sqrt{D}), \]
which, with the use of
\[ (l' k) = f_{l'}(k, \sqrt{D}) \]
passes into an equation of the form:
\[ (l\, l' k) = f_{l l'}(k, \sqrt{D}) \]
Since on the left side $l$ can be interchanged with $l'$, it follows that
\[ f_{l l'}(k, \sqrt{D}) = f_{l' l}(k, \sqrt{D}), \]
so that $f_{l l'}$ depends only on the composed class $l l'$. In the same way one can derive
\[ (l\, l'\, l'' k) = f_{l l' l''}(k, \sqrt{-m}), \] % [sic] printed \sqrt{-m}; the parallel formulas use \sqrt{D}
and since by \S\,118, II. every arbitrary class $s$ of the discriminant $D$ can be composed out of such classes $l$, formula (13), together with the consequences drawn from it, is no longer bound to the special assumption made about $l$, that the first coefficient be a prime.

\gesperrt{We have then, if $s, k$ denote two arbitrary classes of the discriminant $D$, the formulae:}
\weq{14}{(sk) = f_s(k, \sqrt{D}),}
\weq{15}{(s^{-1}k) = f_s(k, -\sqrt{D}).}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 472 =====
% !PRINTED 441
\weberpage{441}
% running head: § 121. Separation of the opposite classes.

If $k$ is the \gesperrt{principal class}, then
\[
2\omega = \sqrt{D} \text{ or } 2\omega = -1+\sqrt{D},
\]
and since $\sqrt{D}$ is purely imaginary, $k=j(\omega)$ is \gesperrt{real} by § 69 (4). Accordingly there follows from (14) and (15), since we now have $(sk)=(s)$:

\gesperrt{The invariants of opposite classes are conjugate imaginary, the invariants of two-sided classes are real.}

If we return to an arbitrary class $k$ and put $sk$ in place of $k$ in formula (15), it follows that:
\weq{16}{(k) = f_s(sk, -\sqrt{D}),}
or, putting $sk=k'$ and writing $f$ for $f_s$, by (21) % [sic] German print has (21), a forward reference in a passage currently numbered (16)--(17)
\weq{17}{\begin{aligned} (k') &= f(k, \sqrt{D}),\\ (k) &= f(k', -\sqrt{D}), \end{aligned}}
where now $k, k'$ may be any two classes of the determinant $D$.

We are hereby in a position to determine the \gesperrt{Galois} group of the class equation, or at least, to begin with, a group of permutations in which the group of the class equation is contained as a divisor.

Let us assume first that $\sqrt{D}$ has been adjoined to the domain of rationality of the rational numbers, and let $(k), (k'), (k'')\ldots$ denote all the class invariants of the discriminant $D$, while
\[
R(k, k', k'', \ldots)
\]
is any rational function of these quantities. By our theorem this function can be expressed rationally by one of the quantities $(k)$, thus say:
\[
R(k, k', k'', \ldots) = R'(k).
\]
If, further, $(s)$ denotes an arbitrary class invariant of the discriminant $D$, and if the function $R$ has the property of remaining unchanged under all $h$ permutations
\[
\begin{pmatrix} k, & k', & k'', & \ldots \\ sk, & sk', & sk'', & \ldots \end{pmatrix},
\]
whose totality we will denote by $\mathfrak{S}$, then $R'(k)=R'(sk)$, and is therefore \gesperrt{rationally expressible}.

\gesperrt{The Galois group of the class equation after the adjunction of $\sqrt{D}$ is therefore contained in the system $\mathfrak{S}$,}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 473 =====
% !PRINTED 442
\weberpage{442}
% running head: 442  Eighteenth Chapter.  § 122.

%<<CONT
\gesperrt{and since $\mathfrak{S}$ is an Abelian group, the class equation is an Abelian one.}

Let us assume that the function $R$ has real (rational) coefficients; its rational expression will nevertheless have the form $a+b\sqrt{D}$, in which $a, b$ are rational numbers. The imaginary part will drop out then and only then, when $R$ also remains unchanged under the interchange of all the classes $k, k', k'', \ldots$ with their opposites. From this it follows that, without adjunction of $\sqrt{D}$, the \gesperrt{Galois} group of the class equation is contained in the system of $2h$ permutations which one obtains by converting every class in $\mathfrak{S}$ into its opposite. Only in the particular case in which all the classes are two-sided (which occurs only for a finite number of determinants) is this latter system identical with $\mathfrak{S}$, and the class equation is then an \gesperrt{Abelian} one without adjunction of $\sqrt{D}$.

The algebraic field which is formed from the rational functions of a class invariant is therefore, apart from the exceptional case last mentioned, not a \gesperrt{normal field}, but is different from its conjugate fields. One obtains a normal field, on the other hand, if one adjoins the square root $\sqrt{D}$ to the field of the class invariants. For every rational function of all the roots of the equation can be expressed rationally by one of them and $\sqrt{D}$.

\begin{center}
§ 122. \gesperrt{Irreducibility.}
\end{center}

We now consider the algebraic number field
\weq{1}{\mathfrak{K} = \mathfrak{R}(k, \sqrt{D}),}
which is composed of a class invariant $(k)$ of the discriminant $D$ and of $\sqrt{D}$; by the preceding section this field contains all the class invariants $(k), (k'), (k''), \ldots$ belonging to the same discriminant. This field we call the \gesperrt{class field} of the discriminant $D$. The quadratic field $\mathfrak{R}(\sqrt{D})$ we denote, as hitherto, by $\Omega$; if $D=Q^2\Delta$ and $\Delta$ is the stem of $D$, it is identical with $\mathfrak{R}(\sqrt{\Delta})$.
Let $h$ be the \gesperrt{class number} of the discriminant $D$.

1. Let $(k)$ be any one of the $h$ class variants, and let % [sic] German print has "Klassenvarianten"; context requires "Klasseninvarianten"
\weq{2}{\Phi(k) = (k)^\nu + \alpha_1(k)^{\nu-1} + \alpha_2(k)^{\nu-2}\cdots + \alpha_\nu = 0}
be the equation of lowest degree in $\Omega$ whose root is $(k)$. Since $(k)$ is an integer, the $\alpha_i$ must also be integers
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 474 =====
% !PRINTED 443
\weberpage{443}
% running head: § 122.  Irreducibility.  443

%<<CONT
of the field $\Omega$ (Bd.\,II, § 149). If $t$ denotes a variable, then $\Phi(t)$ is a divisor of the class function $H_m(t)$, and consequently the discriminant of $\Phi(t)$ is also a divisor of the discriminant of $H_m(t)$.

If $\xi$ is an arbitrary integer of the field $\mathfrak{R}$, then the relative trace with respect to $\Omega$ (Bd.\,II, § 175):
\[
\mathfrak{S}\left(\frac{\xi}{t-(k)}\,\Phi(t)\right) = \varphi(t)
\]
is an integral function of $t$, of degree at most $\nu-1$, whose coefficients are \gesperrt{integers} of $\Omega$. If we therefore let $t$ pass over into $(k)$, it follows that:
\weq{3}{\xi = \frac{\varphi(k)}{\Phi'(k)},}
and from this:
\weq{4}{b\xi = \beta_0 + \beta_1(k) + \beta_2(k)^2 + \cdots + \beta_{\nu-1}(k)^{\nu-1},}
in which $\beta_0, \beta_1, \ldots, \beta_{\nu-1}$ are \gesperrt{integers} in $\Omega$, and $b$ denotes an integral rational number, for which the discriminant of equation (2):
\[
b = N[\Phi'(k)]
\]
may be taken. The field discriminant then divides $b$, and \gesperrt{none of the primes not dividing $b$ is divisible in $\Omega$ or in $\mathfrak{R}$ by the square of a prime ideal} (Bd.\,II, § 174). The number $b$ does not depend on the particular number $\xi$.

An integer $\xi$ can be represented in the form (4) in only one way, since otherwise $(k)$ would satisfy an equation of lower than the $\nu$th degree, which contradicts the assumption; \gesperrt{and from this it follows that $\xi$ is divisible by an integer $\alpha$ of the field $\Omega$ only if all the coefficients $\beta_0, \beta_1, \ldots, \beta_{\nu-1}$ are divisible by $\alpha$.} For if one represents $\xi/\alpha$ in the form (4), the coefficients in this representation must likewise be integers.

If we replace $(k)$ in (3) by another root of equation (2), then $\xi$ passes over into a conjugate value, which is likewise an integer.

2. By \gesperrt{Fermat's} theorem we have, for every arbitrary prime $p$, when $a$ denotes an integral rational number:
\weq{5}{a^p \equiv a \pmod{p}.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 475 =====
% !PRINTED 444
\weberpage{444}
% running head: 444  Eighteenth Chapter.  § 122.

Furthermore, if $p$ does not divide $2D$, then by § 85
\[
D^{\frac{p-1}{2}} \equiv (D, p) \pmod{p},
\]
and hence:
\weq{6}{\sqrt{D}^p \equiv (D, p)\sqrt{D} \pmod{p}.}
If therefore $\alpha$ denotes, as above, an integer of the field $\Omega$:
\[
\alpha = \frac{x + y\sqrt{\Delta}}{2},
\]
then, if one multiplies by $2Q$, writes $x$ for $Qx$, and denotes by $\alpha'$ the number conjugate to $\alpha$:
\[
2Q\alpha = x + y\sqrt{D}, \quad 2Q\alpha' = x - y\sqrt{D},
\]
and from this it follows by \gesperrt{Fermat}'s theorem and by (6):
\weq{7}{\begin{aligned} \alpha^p &\equiv \alpha, & (D,p) &= +1,\\ \alpha^p &\equiv \alpha', & (D,p) &= -1, \end{aligned} \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ p).}
From this it now follows, if $f(k, \sqrt{-m})$ is any number of the form (4), by application of the polynomial theorem:
\weq{8}{\begin{aligned} f(k,\sqrt{D})^p &\equiv f(k^p, \sqrt{D}), & (D,p) &= +1,\\ f(k,\sqrt{D})^p &\equiv f(k^p, -\sqrt{D}), & (D,p) &= -1, \end{aligned} \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ p),}
in which $k^p$ stands for $(k)^p$, and so has the meaning of an actual power.

3. If $\mathfrak{P}$ is a prime ideal in $\mathfrak{R}$ that divides $p$, then the norm of $\mathfrak{P}$ is a power of $p$:
\weq{9}{N(\mathfrak{P}) = p^f.}

The exponent $f$ is the \gesperrt{degree} of the prime ideal $\mathfrak{P}$. For every arbitrary integer $\xi$ of the field $\mathfrak{R}$ we have
\weq{10}{\xi^{N(\mathfrak{P})} \equiv \xi \pmod{\mathfrak{P}},}
and if conversely $p^f$ is the lowest power of $p$ for which the congruence
\weq{11}{\xi^{p^f} \equiv \xi \pmod{\mathfrak{P}}}
is satisfied by \gesperrt{every} number $\xi$, then $f$ is the degree of the ideal $\mathfrak{P}$ (Bd.\,II, § 167).

The degrees of the prime ideals contained in the prime $p$ are now to be determined.

Since $p$ does not divide the fundamental number of the field $\mathfrak{R}$, $p$ is not divisible by the square of a prime ideal.

\weberpage{445}
4. If $(k), (k'), \ldots, (k^{(h-1)})$ denote all the roots of the
equation
\[
H_m(u) = 0,
\]
then for a variable $t$
\[
H_m(t) = [t - (k)] [t - (k')] \ldots [t - (k^{(h-1)})],
\]
and this function has integral rational coefficients. Hence by (5)
we have:
\[
[H_m(t)]^p \equiv H_m(t^p) \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ p),
\]
and so, if we set $t = (k)$:
\[
[(k)^p - (k)] [(k)^p - (k')] \ldots [(k)^p - (k^{(h-1)})] \equiv 0 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ p).
\]
If, then, $\mathfrak P$ denotes a prime ideal in $\mathfrak K$ that divides $p$,
at least one of the factors of the left side must be divisible by
$\mathfrak P$, and from this there follows a congruence
\weq{12}{(k)^p \equiv (k') \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak P),}
in which $(k')$ is some one of the class invariants, and it may also
be identical with $(k)$.

5. If first
\[
(D, p) = -1,
\]
then $\mathfrak P$ can in no case be of the first degree, since already
\weq{13}{\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{D}^p &\equiv -\sqrt{D}\\
\sqrt{D}^{p^2} &\equiv \sqrt{D}
\end{aligned} \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak P)}
holds. But if in (12) (according to § 121)
% [sic] The German print mixes parenthesized class invariants with bare k in the next three displays.
\[
(k') = f(k, \sqrt{D}), \quad k = f(k', -\sqrt{D}),
\]
then it follows from (13) that
\[
(k')^p \equiv f(k^p, -\sqrt{D}) \equiv f(k', -\sqrt{D}) \equiv k,
\]
\[
(k)^{p^2} \equiv k \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak P),
\]
and consequently, for all integers $\xi$ of the field $\mathfrak K$,
\weq{14}{\xi^{p^2} \equiv \xi \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak P),}
and $\mathfrak P$ is of the \gesperrt{second degree}.

6. If secondly
\[
(D, p) = +1,
\]
then there are, as was proved in § 118, two opposite classes
$l, l^{-1}$ (which, if $l$ is two-sided, are identical with one another),
which can be represented by forms with the first coefficient $p$;
and if $(k)$ is any class invariant, then by § 120 the invariant
equation for the degree of transformation $p$ is:
\weq{15}{F_p(u, v) = 0}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 477 =====
% !PRINTED 446
\weberpage{446}
%<<CONT
is satisfied for
\[
u = (k), \quad v = (lk) \quad \text{and} \quad v = (l^{-1}k).
\]
But from what was proved at the end of § 69 [formula
(32)], the congruence follows from this:
\weq{16}{[(k)^p - (lk)] [(lk)^p - (k)] \equiv 0 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ p).}
If now $\mathfrak P$ is a prime ideal that divides $p$, then one of the
two factors on the left side of (17) % [sic] German print has (17); only (16) has two factors on its left side
must be divisible by $\mathfrak P$.
Which of the two assumptions thus possible we pursue further
is immaterial, since the one passes over into the other when
$k$ is interchanged with $l^{-1}k$ and $l$ with $l^{-1}$. So
let
\weq{17}{(k)^p \equiv (lk) \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak P).}
If the congruence (17) is satisfied for any one of the conjugate
values $(k)$, then it holds for every other one as well.
For by § 121:
\[
(k') = f(k, \sqrt{D}), \quad (lk') = f(lk, \sqrt{D}),
\]
hence
\[
(k')^p \equiv f(k^p, \sqrt{D}) \equiv f(lk, \sqrt{D}) \equiv (lk') \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak P).
\]
It therefore follows from (14), % [sic] German print has (14); the substitution described applies to (17)
if $k$ is replaced by $l^{-1}k$:
\weq{18}{(l^{-1}k)^p \equiv (k) \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak P),}
that is, according as the one or the other of the two classes $l$
belonging to $p$ is put for $l$, the one or the other
factor of (16) is divisible by $\mathfrak P$.
By repeated application of (17) there results, for any
arbitrary positive exponent $\pi$,
\weq{19}{(k)^{p^\pi} \equiv (l^\pi k) \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak P)}
(inference from $\pi$ to $\pi + 1$).
If now $l$ belongs to the exponent $\varepsilon$, or $\varepsilon$ is the index of
$p$, then by (19):
\weq{20}{(k)^{p^\varepsilon} \equiv (k) \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak P),}
and $p^\varepsilon$ is the \gesperrt{lowest} power of $p$ that satisfies this
condition. For if a still lower power of $p$ satisfies the congruence (19), % [sic] German print cites (19) then (20); their logical roles appear interchanged
it follows from (20) that two \gesperrt{different}
class invariants $(k)$, $(k')$ are congruent with respect to the modulus $\mathfrak P$.
Their difference $(k) - (k')$ would then be divisible by $\mathfrak P$, and consequently the
discriminant of $H_m$ divisible by $p$, contrary to the hypothesis.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 478 =====
% !PRINTED 447
\weberpage{447}
From this it now follows again, by (7), that the congruence
\weq{21}{\xi^{p^\varepsilon} \equiv \xi \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak P)}
is satisfied for every integer $\xi$ in $\mathfrak K$, and hence the theorem:

\gesperrt{A prime $p$ splits in the field $\mathfrak K$ into prime ideals all different from one another, whose degree is equal to the index of $p$.}

We wish to prove further that among the different
prime ideals $\mathfrak P$ dividing $p$ there is always one for which,
of the two congruences following from (16), the congruence
(17) holds.

To this end we remark: if we transform all the numbers of the
field $\mathfrak K$ into the conjugate imaginary ones, interchanging
$\sqrt{D}$ with $-\sqrt{D}$ and every class invariant $(k)$ with the opposite one $(k^{-1})$, then all the numbers of an
ideal $\mathfrak A$ pass over into the numbers of a conjugate imaginary ideal $\mathfrak A'$,
which may also be identical with $\mathfrak A$, and the norm of the
ideal $\mathfrak A$ is equal to the norm of the ideal $\mathfrak A'$. If $\mathfrak A$ is a prime ideal,
then $\mathfrak A'$ is a prime ideal too.

If now the congruence (17) is not satisfied, then by (16)
\[
(lk)^p \equiv (k) \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak P)
\]
must hold, and this congruence too remains in force when $k$ is
replaced by another class $k'$. If, then, we put $l^{-1}k^{-1}$ in
place of $k$, it follows that:
\[
(k^{-1})^p \equiv (l^{-1}k^{-1}) \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak P).
\]

Since therefore $(k^{-1})^p - (l^{-1}k^{-1})$ is a number in $\mathfrak P$, $(k)^p - (lk)$
is contained in the ideal $\mathfrak P'$ conjugate to $\mathfrak P$, and we have
\[
(k)^p \equiv (lk) \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak P'),
\]
which arises from (17) by the interchange of $\mathfrak P$ with $\mathfrak P'$.

7. From these theorems the irreducibility of the class equation, even after adjunction of $\sqrt{D}$, is a simple consequence.

If $k, k'$ are any two classes of the discriminant $D$, then
by § 118 we can compose $k'$ in the following manner:
\[
k' = k l l' l'' \ldots,
\]
so that the classes $l, l', l'', \ldots$ represent the primes $p, p', p'', \ldots$.
By what has just been proved, we can therefore choose
the prime divisors $\mathfrak P, \mathfrak P', \mathfrak P''$ of these primes in such a way that
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 479 =====
% !PRINTED 448
\weberpage{448}
%<<CONT
\weq{22}{\begin{aligned}
(k)^p &\equiv (kl) & &(\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak P),\\
(kl)^{p'} &\equiv (kll') & &(\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak P'),\\
(kll')^{p''} &\equiv (kll'l'') & &(\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak P'')
\end{aligned}}
\[
\cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot
\]
Let us now assume that the class equation splits, so that for a
variable $t$
\[
H_m(t) = H_1(t) H_2(t),
\]
then, since $k, k'$ were arbitrary classes, we may choose $(k)$ among
the roots of $H_1(t)$ and $(k')$ among those of $H_2(t)$. In the
chain (22) the initial term $(k)$ therefore belongs to the roots $(k_1)$
of $H_1(t)$, and the final term $(k')$ to the roots $(k_2)$ of $H_2(t)$.
Since the passage from the roots of the one factor to those of
the other must take place at at least one point of the chain (22),
there is a pair of roots $(k_1), (k_2)$ which, for some
prime $p$ and a prime ideal $\mathfrak P$ dividing it, satisfies the
congruence
\[
(k_1)^p \equiv (k_2) \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak P)
\]
Now since $H_1(k_1) = 0$, it follows by the inference often applied that
\[
H_1(k_1)^p \equiv H_1(k_1^p) \equiv H_1(k_2) \equiv 0 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak P).
\]
Since now
\[
H_1(k_2) = \prod^{k_1} [(k_2) - (k_1)]
\]
one of the differences $(k_2) - (k_1)$ must be divisible by $\mathfrak P$,
which is not possible, since $p$ does not divide the discriminant
of $H$.

\gesperrt{With this the irreducibility of the class equation is proved; the degree of the field $\mathfrak K$ is established as equal
to twice the class number $h$, and
the group $\mathfrak S$ found in the preceding section
is recognised as the true group of the class equation.}

8. Accordingly we can decompose all primes $p$, \gesperrt{apart
from a finite number of exceptions} (those which divide $2D$
or the discriminant of $H$) into their prime factors
in the field $\mathfrak K$.

If $(D, p) = +1$, then $p$ splits and field $\Omega$ % [sic] German print has "und Körper"; grammatically and mathematically expected "im Körper"
into two conjugate prime ideals of the first degree. If $p$ is of index $\varepsilon$, then
every prime ideal $\mathfrak p$ dividing $p$ is of degree $\varepsilon$. If therefore
\[
p = \mathfrak P_1 \mathfrak P_2 \ldots \mathfrak P_r,
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 480 =====
% !PRINTED 449
\weberpage{449}
%<<CONT
then by 5. $N(p) = p^{2h}$, and consequently
\[
2h = r\varepsilon.
\]

The number of prime factors into which $p$ splits in the field $\mathfrak{K}$
is therefore equal to $2h/\varepsilon$.

If further $(D, p) = -1$, then the prime factors of $p$ are of the second degree, and their number is therefore $= h$.

9. We draw one further interesting conclusion from these results. Let $(D, p) = +1$ and let $\varepsilon$ be the index of $p$. Then $4p^{\varepsilon}$ is representable by the form $x^2 - Dy^2$, and
\weq{23}{p^{\varepsilon} = \mu\mu',}
if for brevity
\weq{24}{\mu = \frac{x + y\sqrt{D}}{2}, \quad \mu' = \frac{x - y\sqrt{D}}{2}}
is set. We now know that $p$ splits into nothing but distinct prime ideals of degree $\varepsilon$. Since $p$ is odd, and $x, y$ have at most the common divisor 2, $\mu, \mu'$ have no common prime factor in $\mathfrak{K}$. To every prime ideal $\mathfrak{P}$ that divides $\mu$ there corresponds a prime ideal $\mathfrak{P}'$ distinct from it (the conjugate one), which arises from $\mathfrak{P}$ by putting, for all numbers of $\mathfrak{P}$, the conjugate imaginary numbers. Thus $\mu$ is divisible not only by $\mathfrak{P}$, but by $\mathfrak{P}^{\varepsilon}$.

According to \S\,121 we have
\weq{25}{\left(\frac{\eta(\omega_1)}{\eta(\omega)}\right)^2 \left(\frac{\eta(\omega_2)}{\eta(\omega_1)}\right)^2 \cdots \left(\frac{\eta(\omega_{\varepsilon})}{\eta(\omega_{\varepsilon-1})}\right)^2 = \varrho\mu,}
and by \S\,72, 4 the factors $P^2$ on the left side of this expression satisfy an equation $P^2\varphi(P^2, \gamma_2, \gamma_3) = p$, in which $\varphi(P^2, \gamma_2, \gamma_3)$ is an integral algebraic number.

From this it follows, however, that $P^2$ cannot be divisible by a higher than the first power of $\mathfrak{P}$, while $\mu$ is nevertheless divisible by $\mathfrak{P}^{\varepsilon}$. We therefore conclude from (25) that \gesperrt{each} of the numbers $P^2$ must be divisible by the first power of $\mathfrak{P}$, and hence that all these numbers \gesperrt{are associated}. If, then, $\varrho$ denotes any algebraic unit, we have
\[
\frac{x + y\sqrt{-m}}{2} = \varrho P^{2\varepsilon},
\]
so $\mu$ is really represented as the $\varepsilon$th power of a number existing in the field $\mathfrak{K}$, and $P^2$ itself is a representation of a prime ideal in the field $\Omega$ by a \gesperrt{principal ideal} in the field $\mathfrak{K}$.
