\begin{center}
\gesperrt{Twenty-first Chapter.}

\textbf{The Norms of the Class Invariants $f(\omega)$.}

\rule{0.3\linewidth}{0.4pt}
\end{center}

\begin{center}
§ 140. \gesperrt{Convergence of an Infinite Series.}
\end{center}

We consider an arbitrary quadratic form
\weq{1}{\psi(x,y) = Ax + 2Bxy + Cy^2} % [sic] source prints $Ax$; the quadratic form requires $Ax^2$
with negative discriminant
\weq{2}{-m = B^2 - AC,}
in which, for the present, the coefficients $A$, $B$, $C$ are not necessarily to be regarded as integers; they are only required to be real. If we take $x$, $y$ as rectangular coordinates in a plane, then to the integral values of $x$, $y$ there correspond the \gesperrt{lattice points}. The equation
\[\psi(x,y) = t\]
represents, for a constant $t$, an ellipse, and the number $Z(t)$ of those values of $\psi$, for \gesperrt{integral} $x$, $y$, which are smaller than $t$ is equal to the number of lattice points lying in the interior of this ellipse. According to Bd.\,II, § 194, (5), the limiting value of the ratio $Z(t):t$ for an infinitely large $t$ approaches the area of the ellipse $\psi = 1$, namely the value $\pi:\sqrt{m}$. Thus we have
\weq{3}{\mathrm{Lim}\, \frac{Z(t)}{t} = \frac{\pi}{\sqrt{m}}.}
If, then, in the infinite series
\weq{4}{S = \sum^{x,\,y} \frac{1}{\psi(x,y)^s}}
we let the numbers $x$, $y$ run through all integral values, with the exception of the combination $x=0$, $y=0$, then, according to Bd.\,II, § 196, 4, $S$ is convergent for $s>1$, and we have
\weq{5}{\mathrm{Lim}_{s=1}\, (s-1)S = \frac{\pi}{\sqrt{m}}.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 557 =====
% !PRINTED 526
\weberpage{526}
In what follows it shall be shown, by direct transformation of the sum $S$,
that
\[ S - \frac{\pi}{(s-1)\sqrt{m}} \]
has a finite limiting value for $s=1$, and this limiting value
shall be determined.

\begin{center}
\S\ 141.\quad \gesperrt{The Kronecker limit formula.}
\end{center}

We arrange the terms of the series
\[ S = \Sigma^{x,y}\frac{1}{\psi(x,y)^s} \]
first in such a way that we separate off the terms corresponding to the
vanishing $y$, and take together, two at a time, those of the remaining ones
which correspond to opposite values of $x$ and $y$.

Thus we obtain:
\weq{1}{S = M_s + N_s,}
if for brevity
\weq{2}{M_s = 2\Sigma_{1,\infty}^{y}\Sigma_{-\infty,\infty}^{x}\frac{1}{(Ax^2+2Bxy+Cy^2)^s},}
\weq{3}{N_s = 2\Sigma_{1,\infty}^{x}\frac{1}{(Ax^2)^s}}
is set. The value $N$, which $N_s$ takes for $s=1$, can be determined
directly, since the series remains unconditionally convergent for $s=1$,
and it gives:
\weq{4}{N = \frac{2}{A}\Sigma_{1,\infty}^{x}\frac{1}{x^2} = \frac{\pi^2}{3A}.}

In order to ascertain the behaviour of $M_s$ for $s=1$, we decompose
the function $\psi(x,y) = Ax^2 + 2Bxy + Cy^2$ into two conjugate
imaginary linear factors:
\[ Ax^2 + 2Bxy + Cy^2 = A(x+\omega_1y)(x-\omega_2y), \]
if
\weq{5}{\omega_1 = \frac{B+i\sqrt{m}}{A}, \quad \omega_2 = \frac{-B+i\sqrt{m}}{A}}
are so defined that $\sqrt{m}$ is positive.

By this means
\weq{6}{M = \frac{2}{A^s}\Sigma_{1,\infty}^{y}\Sigma_{-\infty,\infty}^{x}\frac{1}{(x+\omega_1y)^s(x-\omega_2y)^s}.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 558 =====
% !PRINTED 527
\weberpage{527}
Now, by a well-known theorem from the theory of the
$\Gamma$-functions, if $k$ denotes an arbitrary quantity with positive
 imaginary part:
\[ \frac{1}{(-ik)^s} = \frac{(2\pi)^s}{\Gamma(s)}\int_0^\infty e^{2\pi ik\xi}\,\xi^{s-1}\,d\xi, \]
in which the power $(-ik)^s$ is uniquely defined by the convention that, when
$-ik = \varrho e^{i\Theta}$ is set, $\varrho$ is taken positive and the angle $\Theta$ between $-\frac{\pi}{2}$
and $+\frac{\pi}{2}$, one is to set $(-ik)^s = \varrho^s e^{i\Theta s}$.

If we here replace $ik$ by the conjugate imaginary
quantity $-ik'$, at the same time choosing a new letter of integration
 $\eta$, and multiply the two equations, there follows:
\weq{7}{\frac{1}{(kk')^s} = \frac{(2\pi)^{2s}}{\Gamma(s)\Gamma(s)}\int_0^\infty\int_0^\infty e^{2\pi i(k\xi-k'\eta)}(\xi\eta)^{s-1}\,d\xi\,d\eta.}
In this we substitute for $k, k'$ the two conjugate factors
$x+\omega_1y$, $x-\omega_2y$ of $\psi$, and introduce the integral expression (7)
into (6).

In this way we obtain:
\weq{8}{M_s = \frac{(2\pi)^{2s}}{A_s\Gamma(s)\Gamma(s)}\Sigma^{x,y}2\int_0^\infty\int_0^\infty e^{2\pi i[x(\xi-\eta)+y(\omega_1\xi+\omega_2\eta)]}(\xi\eta)^{s-1}\,d\xi\,d\eta.}
We now regard the product of the two integrals on the
right-hand side of this expression, which for brevity we denote by
\weq{9}{W = 2\int_0^\infty\int_0^\infty e^{2\pi i[x(\xi-\eta)+y(\omega_1\xi+\omega_2\eta)]}(\xi\eta)^{s-1}\,d\xi\,d\eta}
as a double integral which, if $\xi, \eta$ are interpreted as rectangular
 coordinates in the plane, extends over the positive
quadrant of the coordinate system.

\weberfigure{527}{Fig. 2: Coordinate system with axes $\eta$ (vertical) and $\xi$ (horizontal); a bisector issuing from the origin divides the positive quadrant into regions I (below, at the $\xi$-axis) and II (above, at the $\eta$-axis). The hatched strips lie at the outer boundaries $v=\infty$ and do not touch the origin.}

In order to transform the double integral, we divide the domain of integration
 by a straight line bisecting the angle into the two
parts I, II (see Fig. 2), and substitute in the first part
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 559 =====
% !PRINTED 528
\weberpage{528}
%<<CONT
\[ \xi - \eta = u, \qquad \xi + \eta = v, \]
in the second part:
\[ \xi - \eta = -u, \qquad \xi + \eta = v. \]
If one then integrates, as the figure indicates, first with respect
to $v$ at constant $u$, one obtains:
\[
W = \int_0^\infty e^{2\pi ixu}\,du\int_u^\infty e^{\pi iy[u(\omega_1-\omega_2)+v(\omega_1+\omega_2)]}\left(\frac{v^2-u^2}{4}\right)^{s-1}dv
\]
\[
{}+\int_0^\infty e^{-2\pi ixu}\,du\int_u^\infty e^{\pi iy[-u(\omega_1-\omega_2)+v(\omega_1+\omega_2)]}\left(\frac{v^2-u^2}{4}\right)^{s-1}dv,
\]
or, if one sets, as an abbreviation,
\weq{10}{\varphi_{\pm}(u) = \int_u^\infty e^{\pi iy[v(\omega_1+\omega_2)\pm u(\omega_1-\omega_2)]}\left(\frac{v^2-u^2}{4}\right)^{s-1}dv}
then
\weq{11}{W = \int_0^\infty e^{2\pi ixu}\varphi_+(u)\,du + \int_0^\infty e^{-2\pi ixu}\varphi_-(u)\,du.}
We decompose these integrals taken with respect to $u$ into parts of
such a kind that their limits are the sequence of the integers; we
therefore set, since $x$ is an integer:
\weq{12}{\begin{aligned}
\int_0^\infty e^{\pm2\pi ixu}\varphi_{\pm}(u)\,du &= \Sigma_{0,\infty}^{\nu}\int_\nu^{\nu+1}e^{\pm2\pi ixu}\varphi_{\pm}(u)\,du,\\
&= \Sigma_{0,\infty}^{\nu}\int_0^1 e^{\pm2\pi ixu}\varphi_{\pm}(u+\nu)\,du,\\
&= \int_0^1 e^{\pm2\pi ixu}f(u)\,du,
\end{aligned}}
if again
\weq{13}{f(u) = \Sigma_{0,\infty}^{\nu}\varphi_{\pm}(u+\nu)}
is set.

If we now first carry out the summation with respect to $x$, we can
make use of the fundamental formula from the theory of \gesperrt{Fourier series}:
\weq{14}{\begin{aligned}
\Sigma_{-\infty,\infty}^{x}\int_0^1 e^{\pm2\pi ixu}f(u)\,du &= \tfrac{1}{2}[f(0)+f(1)]\\
&= \tfrac{1}{2}\varphi_{\pm}(0) + \Sigma_{1,\infty}^{\nu}\varphi_{\pm}(\nu),
\end{aligned}}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 560 =====
% !PRINTED 529
\weberpage{529}
%<<CONT
and thus obtain, since by (10)
\weq{15}{\varphi_+(0) = \varphi_-(0) = \varphi(0) = \int_0^\infty e^{\pi iyv(\omega_1+\omega_2)}\left(\frac{v}{2}\right)^{2s-2}dv}
holds, from (11), (12) and (14):
\weq{16}{\Sigma_{-\infty,\infty}^{x}W = \varphi(0) + \Sigma_{1,\infty}^{\nu}[\varphi_+(\nu)+\varphi_-(\nu)].}
If we introduce this into (8), then $M_s$ splits into two parts:
\weq{17}{M_s = P_s + Q_{s,}}
if
\weq{18}{P_s = \frac{(2\pi)^{2s}}{A^s\Gamma(s)\Gamma(s)}\Sigma_{1,\infty}^{y}\varphi(0),}
\weq{19}{Q_s = \frac{(2\pi)^{2s}}{A^s\Gamma(s)\Gamma(s)}\Sigma_{1,\infty}^{y}\Sigma_{1,\infty}^{\nu}[\varphi_+(\nu)+\varphi_-(\nu)]}
are set.

By (15), if for $v$ we introduce a new variable of integration
$t$ by the equation
\[ \pi iv(\omega_1+\omega_2) = -\frac{2\pi v\sqrt{m}}{A} = -t \]
and carry out the summation over $y$, we have:
\[ \Sigma_{1,\infty}^{y}\varphi(0) = \frac{2A^{2s-1}}{(4\pi\sqrt{m})^{2s-1}}\int_0^\infty\frac{t^{2s-2}\,dt}{e^t-1}, \]
and therefore:
\weq{20}{P_s = \frac{(2\pi)^{2s}A^{s-1}}{(4\pi\sqrt{m})^{2s-1}\Gamma(s)^2}\,2\int_0^\infty\frac{t^{2s-2}\,dt}{e^t-1}.}
From this the limiting value $P$ can easily be determined. For
the integral
\weq{21}{\int_0^\infty t^{2s-2}e^{-t}\left(\frac{1}{1-e^{-t}}-\frac{1}{t}\right)dt,}
is continuous up to $s=1$, since the expression standing within the
parenthesis retains a finite value for $t=0$ and $t=\infty$, and it
therefore has the limiting value:
\[ \int_0^\infty e^{-t}\left(\frac{1}{1-e^{-t}}-\frac{1}{t}\right)dt = -\Gamma'(1) = 0{,}5772\ldots \]

%% ===== canonical stable idx 561 =====
% !PRINTED 530
\weberpage{530}

If, then, we decompose the integral (21) into its two parts and set
\[
\int_0^\infty t^{2s-3}e^{-t}\,dt = \Gamma(2s-2) = \frac{\Gamma(2s-1)}{2(s-1)},
\]
there follows:
\[
\mathrm{Lim}_{s=1}\left(\int_0^\infty \frac{t^{2s-2}\,dt}{e^t-1} - \frac{\Gamma(2s-1)}{2(s-1)}\right) = -\Gamma'(1),
\]
and if therefore the development in powers of $s-1$:
\[
\Gamma(2s-1) = 1 + 2\Gamma'(1)(s-1) + \cdots
\]
is substituted,
\weq{22}{\mathrm{Lim}_{s=1}\left\{2\int_0^\infty \frac{t^{2s-2}\,dt}{e^t-1} - \frac{1}{s-1}\right\} = 0.}

One obtains further, by development in powers of $s-1$:
\weq{23}{\begin{aligned}
\frac{(2\pi)^{2s}A^{s-1}}{(4\pi\sqrt m)^{2s-1}\Gamma(s)^2}
&= \frac{\pi}{\sqrt m}\left[1+(s-1)\left(\log\frac{A}{4m}-2\Gamma'(1)\right)+\cdots\right]
\end{aligned}}
so that, by (20):
\weq{24}{\begin{aligned}
P_s &= \frac{(2\pi)^{2s}A^{s-1}}{(4\pi\sqrt m)^{2s-1}\Gamma(s)^2}\left(2\int_0^\infty \frac{t^{2s-2}\,dt}{e_t-1} - \frac{1}{s-1}\right)\\ % [sic] German source prints $e_t-1$; equation (22) and the sense require $e^t-1$
&\quad + \frac{\pi}{\sqrt m(s-1)} + \frac{\pi}{\sqrt m}\left(\log\frac{A}{4m}-2\Gamma'(1)\right)+\cdots,
\end{aligned}}
in which the terms that still follow vanish with $s-1$. From this it follows:
\weq{25}{\mathrm{Lim}\left(P_s' - \frac{\pi}{\sqrt m(s-1)}\right) = \frac{\pi}{\sqrt m}\left(\log\frac{A}{4m}-2\Gamma'(1)\right).}
% [sic] German source prints $P_s'$; equation (24) defines $P_s$ without a prime.

There still remains the part $Q_s$ to be investigated, which for $s=1$ takes a finite limiting value $Q$; this we can determine at once by substituting the value $s=1$.

For in (10), as long as $u$ and $y$ are greater than zero, after substituting the value $s=1$, the integration
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 562 =====
% !PRINTED 531
\weberpage{531}

%<<CONT
carried out, and with regard to the value $2i\sqrt m$ of $A(\omega_1+\omega_2)$ it gives:
\[
\varphi_\pm(\nu) = \frac{A}{2\pi\sqrt m\,y}\,e^{2\pi i y\nu\omega},
\]
in which $\omega=\omega_1$ or $=\omega_2$ is to be set, according as the upper or the lower sign is taken in $\varphi_\pm(\nu)$. By carrying out the summation with respect to $y$ there follows from this:
\[
\sum_{1,\infty}^{\nu}\sum_{1,\infty}^{y}\varphi_\pm(\nu) = -\frac{A}{2\pi\sqrt m}\sum_{1,\infty}^{\nu}\log\left(1-e^{2\pi i\nu\omega}\right),
\]
and the sum with respect to $\nu$ can be reduced to the function $\eta(\omega)$, since by \S\,24, (8):
\[
\eta(\omega) = e^{\frac{\pi i \omega}{12}}\prod_{1,\infty}^{\nu}\left(1-e^{2\pi i\nu\omega}\right)
\]
holds. Accordingly there results, always for $s=1$,
\[
\sum_{1,\infty}^{\nu}\sum_{1,\infty}^{y}\varphi_\pm(\nu) = -\frac{A}{2\pi\sqrt m}\left(\log\eta(\omega) - \frac{\pi i \omega}{12}\right).
\]
If we introduce this result into (19), after having set $s=1$ there, we obtain the limiting value of $Q_s$:
\weq{26}{Q = -\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt m}\log\eta(\omega_1)\eta(\omega_2) - \frac{\pi^2}{3A}.}
Accordingly we obtain from (4), (25), (26) the following limit formula, the derivation of which was the aim of this discussion:
\weq{27}{\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{Lim}_{s=1}\sum^{x,y}\frac{1}{(Ax^2+2Bxy+Cy^2)^s} - \frac{\pi}{(s-1)\sqrt m}\\
= -\frac{2\pi\Gamma'(1)}{\sqrt m} + \frac{\pi}{\sqrt m}\log\frac{A}{4m} - \frac{2\pi}{\sqrt m}\log\eta(\omega_1)\eta(\omega_2).
\end{aligned}}

From (27) there follows, in agreement with \S\,140, (5):
\[
\mathrm{Lim}\,(s-1)\sum^{x,y}\frac{1}{\psi^s} = \frac{\pi}{\sqrt m},
\]
hence depending only on $m$, not on the particular form $\psi$. If we now understand $A, 2B, C$ to be integers and let $\psi$ run through a complete system of representatives of the classes of forms belonging to the discriminant $-4m$, then it follows
\weq{28}{\mathrm{Lim}_{s=1}(s-1)\sum^{\psi}\sum^{x,y}\frac{1}{\psi^s} = \frac{\pi h}{\sqrt m},}
where $h$ is the class number belonging to the discriminant $-4m$.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 563 =====
% !PRINTED 532
\weberpage{532}

From (27) one derives a simpler formula for the function
\[
f(\omega) = e^{-\frac{\pi i}{24}}\,\frac{\eta\!\left(\frac{\omega+1}{2}\right)}{\eta(\omega)} = e^{\frac{\pi i}{24}}\,\frac{\eta\!\left(\frac{\omega-1}{2}\right)}{\eta(\omega)}.
\]

For if one replaces
\[
\begin{aligned}
A &\ \text{by}\ 2A,\\
B &\ \text{\textquotedbl}\ \ A+B,\\
C &\ \text{\textquotedbl}\ \ \tfrac12(A+2B+C),
\end{aligned}
\]
then $m=AC-B^2$ remains unchanged, and $\omega_1,\omega_2$ pass over into
\[
\omega_1' = \frac{\omega_1+1}{2},\quad \omega_2' = \frac{\omega_2-1}{2}.
\]

If one therefore sets
\weq{29}{\begin{aligned}
\psi &= (A,\,2B,\,C),\\
\psi' &= [2A,\,2(A+B),\,\tfrac12(A+2B+C)],
\end{aligned}}
then there results from (27)
\weq{30}{\mathrm{Lim}_{s=1}\left(\sum^{x,y}\frac{1}{\psi^s} - \sum^{x,y}\frac{1}{\psi'^s}\right) = \frac{2\pi}{\sqrt m}\log\frac{f(\omega_1)f(\omega_2)}{\sqrt 2}.}

We now take not only $A, 2B, C$, but also $A, B, C$, to be integers without common divisor, and $A$ odd. Then $\psi$ is a primitive form of discriminant $-4m$, and we consider first the two cases
\[
m\equiv 1,\quad m\equiv 2\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 4).
\]

If we assume, which is no further restriction, that $B\equiv m+1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 2)$, that is, $B$ even or odd according as $m$ is odd or even, then there results from
\[
m = AC-B^2\text{:}
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
A-C&\equiv 0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 4) \quad m\ \text{odd},\\
A+C&\equiv 0\ \text{\textquotedbl} \qquad\ \ m\ \text{even},
\end{aligned}
\]
and the form $\psi'$ is primitive of discriminant $-4m$. By the composition of quadratic forms we have:
\[
\psi' = \psi_0\psi,
\]
if
\[
\begin{aligned}
\psi_0 &= \left(2,\,2,\,\tfrac{m+1}{2}\right) & (m\ \text{odd}),\\
&= \left(2,\,0,\,\tfrac{m}{2}\right) & (m\ \text{even}),
\end{aligned}
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 564 =====
% !PRINTED 533
\weberpage{533}

%<<CONT
and consequently $\psi'$ runs through a system of representatives of the discriminant $-4m$ at the same time as $\psi$. But $\omega_1$ runs through the same sequence of values as $\omega_2$, though in a different order, and accordingly summation of formula (30) gives:
\weq{31}{\Pi\,\frac{f(\omega)}{\sqrt[4]2} = 1,}
if the product $\Pi$ refers to the roots with positive imaginary part of a complete system of forms with the discriminant $-4m$.

\gesperrt{In what follows we shall, for the sake of brevity, call this sequence of values of the $\omega$ a complete system of roots of the discriminant $-4m$.}

\S\,142. \gesperrt{The Norms of the Class Invariants $f(\omega)$.}

We let $\omega$ run through a complete system of roots of the discriminant $-4m$, and we assume that in the form $(A, 2B, C)$, whose root is $\omega$, $A, C$ are odd and $A$ is relatively prime to $m$, which involves no further restriction; then by \S\,126 the 24th powers of $f(\omega)$ are class invariants and their norm is a power of 2.

In a two-sided class there is always a representative of one of the two forms:
\[
(A,\,0,\,C),\quad (A,\,2B,\,A),
\]
in which $A$ may be assumed to be odd. In the first case $\omega$ is purely imaginary and consequently [\S\,24, (11)]:
\[
f(\omega),\quad f_1(\omega),\quad f_2(\omega)
\]
are real and positive; in the second case $\omega$ and $1:\omega$ are conjugate imaginary, and consequently:
\[
f(\omega) = f\!\left(-\frac{1}{\omega}\right)
\]
is real and
\[
f_1(\omega) = f_2\!\left(-\frac{1}{\omega}\right),\quad f_2(\omega) = f_1\!\left(-\frac{1}{\omega}\right)
\]
are conjugate imaginary, and by the formula $f(\omega)f_1(\omega)f_2(\omega)=\sqrt 2$ here too $f(\omega)$ is positive.

We may therefore always assume the representative $(A, 2B, C)$ to be so chosen that $A$ and $C$ are odd and that $f(\omega)$ becomes real and positive for a two-sided class; if
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 565 =====
% !PRINTED 534
\weberpage{534}
%<<CONT
we further denote two opposite classes by $(A, \pm 2B, C)$, then the
corresponding values of $f(\omega)$ are conjugate imaginary, their product
therefore positive, and it follows accordingly from these determinations
that the product
\[
\Pi f(\omega)
\]
has a positive real value which is a power of 2. Denoting the class number
by $h$, we set this power $= 2^{h\tau}$, so that
\weq{1}{\Pi\,\frac{f(\omega)}{2^\tau} = 1.}

It will be our task to determine this exponent $\tau$. But we first premise
the following remark, which lends this task an increased interest.

In consequence of the equation [§ 54, (8)]:
\weq{2}{f(\omega)^{24} - \gamma_2(\omega) f(\omega)^8 - 16 = 0}
it follows that, if $\omega$ is the root of a form of the discriminant
$-4m$ belonging to the class $k$, $f(\omega)$ is an \gesperrt{integral algebraic
number}; and since $f(\omega)^8$ in (2) may also be replaced by
$-f_1(\omega)^8$, $-f_2(\omega)^8$, the quantities $f_1(\omega)$,
$f_2(\omega)$ are likewise integral algebraic numbers. Consequently so is
\[
\frac{\sqrt{2}}{f(\omega)} = f_1(\omega) f_2(\omega).
\]

If $p$ is an odd prime of which $-m$ is a quadratic residue, and if $p$ is
representable by the forms of the class $l$ (of the discriminant $-4m$),
then, upon a suitable determination of $c$ according to § 118,
\[
\frac{c+\omega}{p}
\]
is the root of a form belonging to the compounded class $lk$, and (unless
it happens that $p=3$) $c$ may be assumed divisible by 48. If we therefore
set:
\[
u = f(\omega), \quad v = f\left(\frac{c+\omega}{p}\right),
\]
then $uv$ as well as $2:uv$ is an \gesperrt{integral algebraic number}. If therefore
we set, following § 74,
\[
B = (uv)^s + \left(\frac{2}{p}\right)\frac{2^s}{(uv)^s},
\]
\[
A = \left(\frac{u}{v}\right)^r + \left(\frac{v}{u}\right)^r
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 566 =====
% !PRINTED 535
\weberpage{535}
%<<CONT
set (where now $A$, $B$ are of course not to be confused with the
coefficients of the quadratic form), then $B$ is an integral algebraic
number, and by § 74, (14) $A$ is the root of an algebraic equation whose
coefficients are integral algebraic numbers. Hence $A$ too is an integral
algebraic number.

But since the two quotients $u^r:v^r$ and $v^r:u^r$ are the roots of the
quadratic equation
\[
x^2 - Ax + 1 = 0
\]
it follows that
\[
\frac{u}{v} \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{v}{u}
\]
are integers, and, since they are reciprocal to one another, \gesperrt{units.}

\gesperrt{Thus $u$ and $v$ are associated numbers.}

Since one can now, by § 118, pass by repeated compositions with classes
$l$ (are representable by the primes) from every class $k$ to every other
class $k'$ of the same discriminant, and since two numbers associated with
a third are associated with one another, we have the theorem:
\gesperrt{If one puts for $\omega$ the $h$ roots of the forms of a system
of representatives of the discriminant $-4m$, then the $h$ numbers
$f(\omega)$ are associated with one another}; and from this, by (1), at
once the remarkable theorem, which may easily be confirmed in all the
examples: \gesperrt{$f(\omega):2^\tau$ is an integer, and indeed a unit.}

1. The determination of the exponents $\tau$ is possible by
elementary means, if $m \equiv 1$ or $\equiv 2\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 4)$
or $m \equiv 3\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 8)$.

If in the equation with odd outer coefficients
\weq{3}{A\omega^2 + 2B\omega + C = 0}
with the discriminant $4(B^2 - AC) = -4m$ we make the substitution
\weq{4}{\omega = \frac{\omega'-1}{\omega'+1}, \quad \omega' = -\frac{\omega+1}{\omega-1},}
we obtain the equation
\weq{5}{\frac{A+2B+C}{2}\,\omega'^2 - (A-C)\,\omega' + \frac{A-2B+C}{2} = 0,}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 567 =====
% !PRINTED 536
\weberpage{536}
%<<CONT
which likewise has the discriminant $-4m$, and in which, if $m \equiv 1$
or $\equiv 2\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 4)$, the two outer coefficients are odd; for
we have:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{for } m \equiv 1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 4), \quad B \equiv 0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 2), \quad A+C \equiv 2\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 4),\\
&\text{for } m \equiv 2\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 4), \quad B \equiv 1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 2), \quad A+C \equiv 0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 4).
\end{aligned}
\]

From this it follows that $f(\omega)$ and $f\left(\dfrac{\omega-1}{\omega+1}\right)$,
apart from 24th roots of unity, run through the same sequence of values.
For if one replaces $\omega'$ by an equivalent number, then, if the outer
coefficients are to remain odd, the substitution must belong to the first
or the second class (§ 36), and from (4) it then follows that $\omega$ too
passes into an equivalent number. But if two forms (5) are equivalent,
then the corresponding forms (3) are equivalent as well, and conversely.

Accordingly
\[
\Pi\, f(\omega)\, f\!\left(\frac{\omega-1}{\omega+1}\right) = 2^{2h\tau},
\]
while on the other hand [§ 34, (18)]:
\[
f(\omega)\, f\!\left(\frac{\omega-1}{\omega+1}\right) = \sqrt{2},
\]
from which there results:
\weq{6}{\tau = \frac{1}{4}, \quad m \equiv 1,\, 2\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 4),}
in agreement with the result of the preceding section [§ 141, (31)].

2. If next $m \equiv 3\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 8)$, then to a root
$\omega'$ of a form of discriminant $-m$ there correspond in each case three
roots of forms of discriminant $-4m$:
\[
2\omega', \quad \frac{\omega'}{2}, \quad \frac{\omega'+1}{2},
\]
and the 24th powers of the quantities:
\[
\begin{aligned}
f_1(2\omega') &= \frac{\sqrt{2}}{f_2(\omega')},\\
f_2\!\left(\frac{\omega'}{2}\right) &= \frac{\sqrt{2}}{f_1(\omega')},\\
f_2\!\left(\frac{\omega'+1}{2}\right) &= \frac{\sqrt{2}}{f(\omega')},
\end{aligned}
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 568 =====
% !PRINTED 537
\weberpage{537}
%<<CONT
whose product is $= 2$, a class invariant of the discriminant $-4D$.
Accordingly:
\[
\Pi f(\omega) = 2^{\frac{1}{3}h},
\]
hence
\weq{7}{\tau = \frac{1}{3}, \quad m \equiv 3\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 8).}

3. For the case $m \equiv 7\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 8)$ we cannot
determine the value of $\tau$ in this simple way. For this the limit
formula derived in the preceding section is required. We first treat
the two cases $m \equiv 3\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 4)$ uniformly and set:
\[
\varphi = ax^2 + bxy + cy^2 = (a,b,c),
\]
\weq{8}{b^2 - 4ac = -m,}
\weq{9}{S' = \sum^{x,y}\frac{1}{\varphi(x,y)^s},}
in which $x, y$ run through all integer values, with the exception of
the combination $0, 0$.

We decompose the sum $S$ into four partial sums
\[
S_{00}', \quad S_{01}', \quad S_{10}', \quad S_{11}',
\]
so that $x, y$ run through only even values in $S_{00}'$, and only odd
values in $S_{11}'$. In $S_{10}'$, $x$ runs through the odd numbers and
$y$ the even ones, and conversely in $S_{01}'$. Then
\weq{10}{S' + 2S_{00}' = (S_{01}'+S_{00}') + (S_{10}'+S_{00}') + (S_{11}'+S_{00}').}

If we replace
\[
\begin{array}{l@{\quad}l@{\quad}l}
\text{in } S_{00}' & x, y \text{ by} & 2x,\ 2y,\\
\text{\textquotedbl} & S_{01}'+S_{00}' \ x,y\ \text{\textquotedbl} & 2x,\ y,\\
\text{\textquotedbl} & S_{10}'+S_{00}' \ x,y\ \text{\textquotedbl} & x,\ 2y,\\
\text{\textquotedbl} & S_{00}'+S_{11}' \ x,y\ \text{\textquotedbl} & x-y,\ x+y,
\end{array}
\]
then the new $x, y$ are subject to no further restriction than that they
do not both vanish at the same time. If we therefore set:
\weq{11}{\begin{aligned}
\varphi &= (a,b,c),\\
\varphi_1 &= (4a, 2b, c),\\
\varphi_2 &= (a, 2b, 4c),\\
\varphi_3 &= (a+b+c,\ 2(c-a),\ a-b+c),
\end{aligned}}
then
\weq{12}{\begin{aligned}
4^s S_{00}' &= S',\\
S_{01}' + S_{00}' &= \Sigma^{x,y} \varphi_1^{-s},\\
S_{10}' + S_{00}' &= \Sigma^{x,y} \varphi_2^{-s},\\
S_{00}' + S_{11}' &= \Sigma^{x,y} \varphi_3^{-s}.
\end{aligned}}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 569 =====
% !PRINTED 538
\weberpage{538}

We assume $a$ to be odd and let $\varphi$ run through a complete
system of representatives of the discriminant $-m$. If
then $m \equiv 3 \pmod 8$, then $c$ is odd, and $\varphi_1$, $\varphi_2$, $\varphi_3$
together run through a system of representatives of the discriminant $-4m$. For among the $3h$ roots of these forms
\[
\frac{\omega}{2}, \quad 2\,\omega, \quad 1 - \frac{2}{\omega+1}
\]
there occur, by § 123, no equivalent ones.

If on the other hand $m \equiv 7 \pmod 8$, then $c$ is even, $\frac{1}{2}\varphi_1$, $\frac{1}{2}\varphi_3$ each run through a system of representatives of the discriminant $-m$, while $\varphi_2$
runs through a system of representatives of the discriminant $-4m$.

If then $\psi$ runs through a system of representatives of the discriminant $-4m$, and we set
\weq{13}{S = \overset{x,y}{\Sigma}\, \frac{1}{\psi^s},}
then there results from (10):
\weq{14}{\begin{aligned}
\Bigl(1 + \frac{2}{4^s}\Bigr) \overset{\varphi}{\Sigma} S' &= \overset{\psi}{\Sigma} S, & m &\equiv 3 \\
\Bigl(1 + \frac{2}{4^s} - \frac{2}{2^s}\Bigr) \overset{\varphi}{\Sigma} S' &= \overset{\psi}{\Sigma} S, & m &\equiv 7
\end{aligned} \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ 8).}
If in formulae (29), (30) of the preceding section we set
\[
\psi' = 2\,\varphi, \quad \psi = (A, 2B, C),
\]
thus:
\[
\begin{aligned}
A &= a, \\
B &= b - a, \\
C &= 4c - 2b + a,
\end{aligned}
\]
then there results:
\[
S - \frac{1}{2^s} S' = \frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{m}} \log \frac{f(\omega_1)f(\omega_2)}{\sqrt{2}},
\]
and when $\psi$ runs through a system of representatives of the discriminant $-4m$,
then $\varphi$ runs three times, or only once, through a system of representatives of the discriminant $-m$, according as $m \equiv 3$
or $\equiv 7 \pmod 8$. We therefore obtain, if $\varepsilon$ in these
two cases is 3 or 1:
\weq{15}{\mathrm{Lim}_{s=1} \Bigl(\overset{\psi}{\Sigma} S - \frac{\varepsilon}{2^s} \overset{\varphi}{\Sigma} S'\Bigr) = \frac{4\pi}{\sqrt{m}} \log \Pi \frac{f(\omega)}{\sqrt[4]{2}},}
in which $\omega$ runs through the roots of the forms $\psi$. And from this
there results, by (14):
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 570 =====
% !PRINTED 539
\weberpage{539}

%<<CONT
\weq{16}{\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{Lim}_{s=1} (4^s + 2 - 3.2^s) \overset{\psi}{\Sigma} S &= \frac{24\pi}{\sqrt{m}} \log \Pi \frac{f(\omega)}{\sqrt[4]{2}}, & m &\equiv 3 \pmod 8, \\
\mathrm{Lim}_{s=1} (4^s + 2 - 3.2^s) \overset{\psi}{\Sigma} S &= \frac{8\pi}{\sqrt{m}} \log \Pi \frac{f(\omega)}{\sqrt[4]{2}}, & m &\equiv 7 \pmod 8.
\end{aligned}}
But we have [§ 141, (28)]:
\[
\mathrm{Lim}\,(s-1) \overset{\psi}{\Sigma} S = \frac{\pi h}{\sqrt{m}}, \quad \mathrm{Lim}\,\frac{4^s + 2 - 3.2^s}{s-1} = 2 \log 2,
\]
hence:
\weq{17}{\begin{aligned}
\log \Pi \frac{f(\omega)}{\sqrt[3]{2}} &= 0, & m &\equiv 3 \pmod 8, \\
\log \Pi \frac{f(\omega)}{\sqrt{2}} &= 0, & m &\equiv 7 \pmod 8.
\end{aligned}}
The first of these formulae gives the result already derived in another
way; the second gives the new one:
\weq{18}{\tau = \tfrac{1}{2}, \quad m \equiv 7 \pmod 8.}
4. There still remains the determination of $\tau$ in the case where
$m$ is divisible by a higher power of 2. In order to carry out this
determination as well, let
\weq{19}{m = 4m',}
\weq{20}{\omega' = \frac{-B + i\sqrt{m}}{A}, \quad m' = AC - B^2,}
so that $\omega'$ is the root of the quadratic form $(A, 2B, C)$ of
discriminant $-m$, in which $A$ and $C$ may be assumed to be \gesperrt{odd}. Then
\weq{21}{\omega_1 = 2\,\omega', \quad \omega_2 = \frac{\omega'}{2}}
are roots of the forms
\weq{22}{(A, 4B, 4C), \quad (4A, 4B, C),}
and by § 126, (13) the 24th powers of
\[
f_1(\omega_1) = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{f_2(\omega')}, \quad f_2(\omega_2) = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{f_1(\omega')}
\]
are class invariants of the discriminant $-4m$.

If $\omega'$ runs through a complete system of roots of the discriminant $-m$, then $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ together run through a complete
system of roots of the discriminant $-4m$ (§ 123), and we obtain,
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 571 =====
% !PRINTED 540
\weberpage{540}

%<<CONT
when $\omega$ runs through a complete system of roots of forms with odd
outer coefficients, with the use of the formula:
\[
f_1(\omega')f_2(\omega')f(\omega') = \sqrt{2},
\]
if $h'$ is the class number belonging to the discriminant $-m'$:
\weq{23}{\Pi f(\omega) = \Pi f_1(\omega_1)f_2(\omega_2) = \frac{2^h}{\Pi f_1(\omega')f_2(\omega')} = \sqrt{2}^{\,h'} \Pi f(\omega'),}
in which $h$, $h'$ denote the class numbers for the discriminants $-4m$,
$-m$. We then have (§ 123):
\[
h = 2h'.
\]
If therefore, as above, $\tau$, $\tau'$ are so determined that
\[
\frac{f(\omega)}{2^\tau}, \quad \frac{f(\omega')}{2^{\tau'}}
\]
become units, then
\[
\Pi f(\omega) = 2^{h\tau}, \quad \Pi f(\omega') = 2^{h'\tau'},
\]
and from this, by (23):
\weq{24}{\tau = \frac{\tau'}{2} + \frac{1}{4},}
a formula which holds also for $m' = 1$, where $h' = h$ and
the two values $2\,\omega'$ and $\omega' : 2$ are equivalent.

By repeated application of this formula there results, when
\[
m = 4^\lambda m'
\]
holds, for an arbitrary positive $\lambda$:
\[
\tau = \frac{\tau'}{2^\lambda} + \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2^{\lambda+1}}.
\]
If we summarise what has here been proved, we can
say that the following quantities are \gesperrt{algebraic units}:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{f(\omega)}{\sqrt[4]{2}}, & \quad m \equiv 1, 2 \pmod 4, \\
\frac{f(\omega)}{\sqrt[3]{2}}, & \quad m \equiv 3 \pmod 8, \\
\frac{f(\omega)}{\sqrt{2}}, & \quad m \equiv 7 \pmod 8,
\end{aligned}
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 572 =====
% !PRINTED 541
\weberpage{541}

%<<CONT
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{f(\omega)}{\dfrac{1}{2^{1/2}} - \dfrac{1}{2^{\lambda+2}}}, & \quad m = 4^\lambda m', \quad m' \equiv 1, 2 \pmod 4, \\
\frac{f(\omega)}{\dfrac{1}{2^{1/2}} - \dfrac{1}{3.2^{\lambda+1}}}, & \quad m = 4^\lambda m', \quad m' \equiv 4 \pmod 8, \\
\frac{f(\omega)}{\sqrt{2}}, & \quad m = 4^\lambda m', \quad m' \equiv 7 \pmod 8.
\end{aligned}
\]

\begin{center}
§ 143.\\
\gesperrt{Partial norms of $f(\omega)$.}
\end{center}

We make one further application of the limit formula (30) of § 141 to the
determination of the product
\weq{1}{\Pi f(\omega),}
in which the product sign $\Pi$ extends not over a complete system of
roots, but only over the roots $\omega$ of the classes of forms of one
genus. We restrict ourselves here, however, to the case in which
\weq{2}{\Delta = -4m}
is a \gesperrt{fundamental discriminant}, so that $m$ has no square
divisor and is either $\equiv 1$ or $\equiv 2 \pmod 4$, or, what is the
same thing,
\weq{3}{\Delta \equiv -4 \ \text{or} \ \equiv 8 \pmod{16}.}
Let $\delta$ be a \gesperrt{fundamental divisor} of $\Delta$ different from
$\Delta$ and 1, and let $\chi(\delta, k)$ be the character of the class $k$
corresponding to this fundamental divisor.

If $\delta'$ is the fundamental divisor to $\delta$ that is complementary
to $\delta$, then in this case
\[
\begin{aligned}
\delta\,\delta' &= \Delta, \\
\chi(\delta, k) &= \chi(\delta', k),
\end{aligned}
\]
and we thus obtain all the genera if we put for $\delta$ the \gesperrt{odd
fundamental divisors}, which is what we shall do here. Now let, as in
§ 141, (29), (30):
\[
\psi_0 = \Bigl(2, 2, \frac{m+1}{2}\Bigr), \ \Bigl(2, 0, \frac{m}{2}\Bigr),
\]
\weq{4}{\begin{aligned}
\psi &= (A, 2B, C), \\
\psi' &= \psi_0\,\psi.
\end{aligned}}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 573 =====
% !PRINTED 542
\weberpage{542}
If then $k$, $k_0$, $k'$ are the classes to which $\psi$, $\psi_0$, $\psi'$ belong, then
\[
\chi(\delta, k') = \chi(\delta, k_0)\,\chi(\delta, k),
\]
hence
\weq{5}{\begin{aligned}
\chi(\delta, k) &= (\delta, A), \\
\chi(\delta, k') &= (\delta, 2)(\delta, A).
\end{aligned}}

If $\omega_1$ is a root of the class $k$, then $\omega_2$ is a root of the opposite class $k^{-1}$; but in these two classes the characters $\chi(\delta, k)$ and $\chi(\delta, k^{-1})$ are the same. If we therefore multiply the formula \S\,141, (30) by $\chi(\delta, k)$ and form the sum over all classes $k$, it follows that:
\weq{6}{\overset{k}{\Sigma}\,\chi(\delta,k)\Bigl(\overset{x,y}{\Sigma}\frac{1}{\psi^s} - \overset{x,y}{\Sigma}\frac{1}{\psi'^s}\Bigr) = \frac{4\pi}{\sqrt{m}}\overset{k}{\Sigma}\,\chi(\delta,k)\log\frac{f(\omega)}{\sqrt[4]{2}},}
and on account of (5) one may write for the left-hand side:
\[
[1-(\delta,2)]\overset{k}{\Sigma}\frac{\chi(\delta,k)}{1}\overset{x,y}{\Sigma}\frac{1}{\psi^s}.
\]
Accordingly we have:
\weq{7}{\begin{aligned}
(\delta,2) = +1\colon &\quad \frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{m}}\overset{k}{\Sigma}\,\chi(\delta,k)\log\frac{f(\omega)}{\sqrt[4]{2}} = 0, \\
(\delta,2) = -1\colon &\quad \frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{m}}\overset{k}{\Sigma}\,\chi(\delta,k)\log\frac{f(\omega)}{\sqrt[4]{2}} = \overset{k}{\Sigma}\,\chi(\delta,k)\overset{x,y}{\Sigma}\frac{1}{\psi^s},
\end{aligned}}
where on the right the limiting value for $s=1$ is to be taken.

In \S\,113 we proved the formula:
\weq{8}{\overset{k}{\Sigma}\,\chi(\delta,k)\overset{x,y}{\Sigma}\frac{1}{\psi^s} = \Sigma\frac{(\delta,n)}{n^s}\Sigma\frac{(\delta',n)}{n^s}.}

If we denote by $K(\delta)$ the class number for the discriminant $\delta$, then, as was proved in \S\,112, (8): % faint pre-delta speck is scan/print damage, not a character
\weq{9}{\begin{aligned}
\sum^n \frac{(\delta,n)}{n} &= \frac{\pi}{\sqrt{-\delta}}\,K(\delta) \qquad \delta<0, \\
\sum^n \frac{(\delta,n)}{n} &= \frac{\log\varepsilon}{\sqrt{\delta}}\,K(\delta) \qquad \delta>0,
\end{aligned}}
in which the square roots are to be taken positive, and
\[
\varepsilon = \frac{T+U\sqrt{\delta}}{2}
\]
is the fundamental positive unit of the quadratic field with the fundamental number $\delta$. For the two exceptional cases $\delta=-3$, $\delta=-4$ these formulae hold if by $K$ one understands not the
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 574 =====
% !PRINTED 543
\weberpage{543}
%<<CONT
class number itself, but the third part or the half of it.

Now $\delta'$ is always even and of opposite sign to $\delta$, and $4m=-\delta\delta'$; accordingly there result from (7) the formulae:
\weq{10}{\begin{aligned}
2\overset{k}{\Sigma}\,\chi(\delta,k)\log\frac{f(\omega)}{\sqrt[4]{2}} &= 0, & \delta&\equiv 1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 8), \\
&= K(\delta)K(\delta')\log\varepsilon, & \delta&\equiv 5\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 8),
\end{aligned}}
in which
\weq{11}{\begin{aligned}
\varepsilon &= \frac{T+U\sqrt{\delta}}{2}, & \delta&>0\equiv 1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 8), \\
&= \frac{T+U\sqrt{\delta'}}{2}, & \delta&<0\equiv 5\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 8)
\end{aligned}}
is to be set. The first of the formulae (10) still holds for $\delta=1$ as well.

Since now the character $\chi(\delta,k)$ has the same value for all classes of a genus and for every $\delta$, the products (1) are determined by (10) and (11). For by \S\,113
\[
\overset{\delta}{\Sigma}\,\chi(\delta,k) = 0,
\]
except when $k$ is the principal class, and for this class the sum is equal to the number $g$ of the genera. One obtains, for example, for the roots $\omega$ of the \gesperrt{principal genus}
\[
\left(\Pi\,\frac{f(\omega)}{\sqrt[4]{2}}\right)^{2g} = \Pi\,\varepsilon^{K(\delta)K(\delta')},
\]
in which $g$ denotes the number of the genera, and the product on the left is to be extended over all roots $\omega$ of the principal genus, the product on the right over all fundamental divisors $\delta$ of $\Delta$ which are $\equiv 5\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 8)$.

In order to form the product of the class invariants for a genus other than the principal genus, one has to multiply formula (8), before the summation, by $\chi(\delta,k^{-1})$, if $k$ denotes a class of the genus in question.

The application of formula (10) requires the knowledge of the class numbers of positive and negative discriminants and of the numbers $T$, $U$. The class numbers have been computed to a wide extent by \gesperrt{Gauss} and published from his posthumous papers in the second volume of the Werke, pp.\,450 to 476. For the solutions $T$, $U$ of the \gesperrt{Pell} equation, \gesperrt{Legendre's} \glqq Theorie des nombres\grqq{}, or also the \glqq Canon Pellianus\grqq{} of \gesperrt{Degen}, contains a table.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 575 =====
% !PRINTED 544
\weberpage{544}
There exist 63 negative discriminants with the property that each genus contains only a single class; that there are no more, indeed even that their number is only a finite one, can of course so far only be inferred by induction, not proved. The majority of these discriminants, which have already been collected in \S\,139, are $\equiv 1, 2\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 4)$ and without square divisor, or $\equiv 8\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 16)$.

For the former the \gesperrt{class invariants} can be completely computed by formula (10), and a similar formula, into whose formation we do not wish to enter here, also leads to the goal for the discriminants divisible by 8.

For the isolated discriminants of this kind which do not fit in here, the class invariants $f(\omega)$ can be computed by one of the other methods.\footnote{Cf.\ the author's memoir: \glqq Zur komplexen Multiplikation elliptischer Funktionen\grqq{}. Mathematische Annalen, Bd.\,23. I here call attention to an error in the \gesperrt{Gauss} table which I found on the occasion of these computations: \gesperrt{Gauss'} Werke, Bd.\,II, S.\,475, the positive determinant 136 must have the designation IV, 2, not IV, 1.}

In order to carry out the calculation on a simple example that is easy to survey, we choose $m=105=3.5.7$. If we omit the values of $\delta$ which are $\equiv 1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 8)$, since these give no contribution in the sum of the formulae (10), then we have to put:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\delta &= -3, & 5, & & 21, & & -35, \\
\delta' &= 140, & -84, & & -20, & & 12
\end{aligned}
\]
and obtain, since $g=8$:
\[
\begin{aligned}
16\log\frac{f(\sqrt{-105})}{\sqrt[4]{2}} &= K(-3)\,K(140)\log\frac{T+U\sqrt{140}}{2}, \\
&\quad + K(5)\,K(-84)\log\frac{T+U\sqrt{84}}{2}, \\
&\quad + K(21)\,K(-20)\log\frac{T+U\sqrt{20}}{2}, \\
&\quad + K(-35)\,K(12)\log\frac{T+U\sqrt{12}}{2}.
\end{aligned}
\]

%% ===== canonical stable idx 576 =====
% !PRINTED 545
\weberpage{545}
But we have
\[
\begin{aligned}
K(-3) &= \tfrac{1}{3}, & K(-84) &= 4, & K(-20) &= 2, & K(-35) &= 2, \\
K(+140) &= 4, & K(5) &= 1, & K(21) &= 2, & K(12) &= 2
\end{aligned}
\]
\footnote{According to the notation of \gesperrt{Gauss} the class numbers of the second kind are to be taken.}
as one finds from the tables of \gesperrt{Gauss}, or here also easily by direct enumeration.

Further, according to the tables of \gesperrt{Legendre} or of \gesperrt{Degen}:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\log\left(\frac{T+\sqrt{140}\,U}{2}\right) &= \log(6+\sqrt{35}) = \log\frac{(\sqrt{5}+\sqrt{7})^2}{2}, \\
\log\left(\frac{T+\sqrt{5}\,U}{2}\right) &= \log\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}\right)^2 = \tfrac{2}{3}\log(2+\sqrt{5}), \\
\log\frac{T+\sqrt{21}\,U}{2} &= \log\frac{5+\sqrt{21}}{2} = \tfrac{1}{3}\log(55+12\sqrt{21}) \\
&= \log\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{7}}{2}\right)^2, \\
\log\left(\frac{T+\sqrt{12}\,U}{2}\right) &= \log(2+\sqrt{3}),
\end{aligned}
\]
and from this one obtains:
\[
\left(\frac{f(\sqrt{-105})}{\sqrt[4]{2}}\right)^{12} = (2+\sqrt{5})^2(55+12\sqrt{21})(6+\sqrt{35})(2+\sqrt{3})^3,
\]
or, what means the same thing:
\[
\sqrt{2}^{13}f(\sqrt{-105})^6 = (1+\sqrt{5})^3(\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{7})^3(\sqrt{5}+\sqrt{7})(1+\sqrt{3})^3.
\]

\begin{center}
\S\,144. \gesperrt{Calculation of some further class invariants.}
\end{center}

Next after the discriminants for which only \gesperrt{one} class of forms occurs in each genus, which we considered in the preceding section, the simplest results are given by those which contain two classes of forms in each genus, and among these again by those for which only two genera occur. The class invariants for these discriminants $-4m$ are the roots of quadratic equations whose coefficients contain only one square root. We again assume fundamental discriminants, and obtain from the table of \gesperrt{Gauss} the following values of $m$:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 577 =====
% !PRINTED 546
\weberpage{546}
%<<CONT
\[
\begin{aligned}
m &= 14,\ 34,\ 46,\ 82,\ 142 \equiv \pm2 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ 16),\\
m &= 17,\ 49,\ 73,\ 97,\ 193 \equiv 1 \qquad (\mathrm{mod}\ 8).
\end{aligned}
\]
In these cases the classes of forms of the \gesperrt{principal genus} can be represented, for an even $m$, by

\weq{1}{(1, 0, m), \quad \left(2, 0, \dfrac{m}{2}\right),}

for an odd $m$ by

\weq{2}{(1, 0, m), \quad \left(2, 1, \dfrac{m+1}{2}\right),}

of which the latter is equivalent to

\weq{3}{\left(\dfrac{m+1}{2},\ \dfrac{m-1}{2},\ \dfrac{m+1}{2}\right).}

For the forms (1) the class invariants are, by § 127, 6.,
\[
\frac{f_1(\sqrt{-m})^2}{\sqrt2} \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{1}{\sqrt2} f_2\left(\frac{\sqrt{-m}}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{\sqrt2}{f_1(\sqrt{-m})^2} \qquad (\S\ 34)
\]
and for the forms (2), (3) (§ 127, 3.)
\[
\frac{f(\sqrt{-m})^2}{\sqrt2} \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{1}{\sqrt2} f\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{-m}}{1-\sqrt{-m}}\right)^2 = \frac{\sqrt2}{f(\sqrt{-m})^2},
\]
and by § 142 these are integral algebraic numbers.

If then we set, corresponding to the two cases:

\weq{4}{\sqrt2\, x = f_1(\sqrt{-m})^2, \quad f(\sqrt{-m})^2,}

then
\[
x + \frac{1}{x}
\]
is an integral algebraic number which contains only one square root, and from § 138 we obtain information as to which square root occurs in it.

It is $\sqrt2$ when $m \equiv 6$ $(\mathrm{mod}\ 8)$, hence for $m = 14, 46, 142$; it is $\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{2}}$ when $m \equiv 2$ $(\mathrm{mod}\ 8)$, hence for $m = 34, 82$; and further $\sqrt m$ in the case of an odd $m$ (with the exception of $m = 49$, where $\sqrt7$ takes its place).

If then we set

\weq{5}{x + \frac{1}{x} = a + b\sqrt p,}

then $a, b$ are rational numbers which have at most the denominator 2. But $a$ and $b$ must also be positive. For if in (5) we change the sign of $\sqrt p$, there arises another quadratic
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 578 =====
% !PRINTED 547
\weberpage{547}
%<<CONT
equation whose roots are the class invariants belonging to the second genus, and which are therefore conjugate imaginary, while the roots of (5) are real. From this there follows the determination of quantity:
\[
(a+b\sqrt p)^2 > 4 > (a-b\sqrt p)^2;
\]
and so $a$ and $b$ must have the same sign. But since $x$ is positive by (4), $a$ and $b$ must both be positive.

In order actually to find $a$ and $b$, one needs only to compute the expression on the left-hand side of (5), by (4), to a few decimals, and for this it is amply sufficient to put
\[
f(\sqrt{-m}) = f_1(\sqrt{-m}) = e^{\frac{\pi\sqrt m}{24}}
\]
and to compare the decimals so found with the decimals of $\sqrt p$, in order to obtain $b$ at once and thereupon $a$. The calculation is exceedingly simple and gives the following results:
\[
\begin{aligned}
m &= 14, & x + \frac1x &= 1 + \sqrt2,\\
m &= 17, & x + \frac1x &= \frac{1+\sqrt{17}}{2},\\
m &= 34, & x + \frac1x &= \frac{3+\sqrt{17}}{2},\\
m &= 46, & x + \frac1x &= 3 + \sqrt2,\\
m &= 49, & x + \frac1x &= 2 + \sqrt7,\\
m &= 73, & x + \frac1x &= \frac{5+\sqrt{73}}{2},\\
m &= 82, & x + \frac1x &= \frac{15+\sqrt{41}}{2},\\
m &= 97, & x + \frac1x &= \frac{9+\sqrt{97}}{2},\\
m &= 142, & x + \frac1x &= 9 + 5\sqrt2,\\
m &= 193, & x + \frac1x &= 13 + \sqrt{193}.
\end{aligned}
\]

\begin{center}\rule{3cm}{0.4pt}\end{center}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 579 =====
% !PRINTED none
% part title: Abschnitt-opening page, no printed page number visible in the scan (chapter divider + opening section text; expected sequence puts this at p.548, but no digit is visible anywhere on the page image).
\begin{center}
\gesperrt{Twenty-Second Chapter.}

\textbf{Cayley's Development of the Modular Functions.}

\rule{0.3\textwidth}{0.4pt}

\S\,145. \gesperrt{Limiting values for $s = 1$.}
\end{center}

In this chapter a function-theoretic application of the limit formula is to be given. Here, therefore, $\omega$ does not denote a quadratic irrational number, but a variable with positive imaginary part. The modular functions belong to the functions with \gesperrt{natural boundaries}, that is: as one approaches the boundary of convergence, the singular points lie everywhere dense upon that boundary, here therefore upon the axis of the real $\omega$, so that these functions cannot be continued analytically beyond this boundary. \gesperrt{Cayley} gave, in his last investigations, developments of the modular functions which are remarkable because they make evident the behaviour of the functions on approach to the boundary. The key to these developments is the limit formula § 141, (27)$^1$).

If in this formula:

\weq{1}{\begin{aligned}
&\mathrm{Lim}_{s=1} \sum^{x,y} \frac{1}{(Ax^2+2Bxy+Cy^2)^s} - \frac{\pi}{(s-1)\sqrt m}\\
&= -\frac{2\pi\Gamma'(1)}{\sqrt m} + \frac{\pi}{\sqrt m}\log\frac{A}{4m} - \frac{2\pi}{\sqrt m}\log \eta(\omega_1),\ \eta(\omega_2),
\end{aligned}}
\[
\omega_1 = \frac{B+i\sqrt m}{A}, \quad \omega_2 = \frac{-B+i\sqrt m}{A},
\]

\weq{2}{\omega_1 = \alpha+\beta i, \quad \omega_2 = -\alpha+\beta i, \quad \beta > 0}

$^1$) \gesperrt{Cayley}'s first paper is found in the Comptes Rendus of the Paris Academy of 1893, Bd.\,161. Further matter in a correspondence with the author of this book, which is published in the 47th volume of the Mathematische Annalen.
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 580 =====
% !PRINTED 549
\weberpage{549}
%<<CONT
puts, there results
\[
A = 1, \quad B = \alpha, \quad C = \alpha^2+\beta^2, \quad m = \beta^2,
\]
and formula 1 gives:

\weq{3}{\begin{aligned}
\sum^{x,y} \frac{1}{[(x-\alpha y)^2+\beta^2 y^2]^s} &= \sum^{x,y} \frac{1}{(x+\omega_1 y)^s (x-\omega_2 y)^s}\\
&= \frac{\pi}{(s-1)\beta} - \frac{2\pi\Gamma'(1)}{\beta} - \frac{\pi}{\beta}\log 4\beta^2 - \frac{2\pi}{\beta}\log \eta(\omega_1)\eta(\omega_2).
\end{aligned}}

The symbol Lim has here been omitted for the sake of brevity.

We put

\weq{4}{S = \sum^{x,y} \frac{1}{[(x-\alpha y)^2+\beta^2 y^2]^s},}

in which $x, y$ run through all integer values with the exception of the combination $0,0$. $S$ is an unconditionally convergent series so long as $s > 1$.

Now we divide the terms of $S$ into three kinds, according as the $x, y$ are even or odd, and put

\weq{5}{\begin{aligned}
S_0 &= \sum^{x,y} \frac{1}{[(x-\alpha y)^2+\beta^2 y^2]^s}, & x &\equiv y \pmod2,\\
S_1 &= \sum^{x,y} \frac{1}{[(x-\alpha y)^2+\beta^2 y^2]^s}, & x &\equiv 0 \pmod2,\\
S_2 &= \sum^{x,y} \frac{1}{[(x-\alpha y)^2+\beta^2 y^2]^s}, & y &\equiv 0 \pmod2.
\end{aligned}}

In $S_0$, then, the numbers $x, y$ are either both even or both odd; in $S_1$, $x$ runs through the even numbers and $y$ through all integers; in $S_2$, $y$ is even and $x$ arbitrary. If one considers the sum $S_0+S_1+S_2$, all the terms of $S$ occur in it, and indeed three times over those terms in which $x$ and $y$ are both even. If one takes the factor $4^{-s}$ out of the sum of these terms, then $S$ itself remains, and there results accordingly:

\weq{6}{S_0+S_1+S_2 = \left(1+\frac{2}{4^s}\right) S.}

If one passes to the limit $s = 1$, one has to put

\weq{7}{\frac{1}{4^s} = \frac14 - \frac{s-1}{2}\log2 \ldots,}

and obtains from (3) the formula valid for $s = 1$:

\weq{8}{S_0+S_1+S_2 = \frac32 S - \frac{\pi}{\beta}\log2.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 581 =====
% !PRINTED 550
\weberpage{550}

If we replace $\alpha$ and $\beta$ in $S$ by $2\alpha$ and $2\beta$, this has the
same effect as if we replaced $y$ by $2y$; that is, $S$
passes into $S_2$, and accordingly we obtain from (3):
\weq{9}{
\begin{aligned}
2\,S_2 &= \frac{\pi}{(s-1)\beta} - \frac{2\pi\,\Gamma'(1)}{\beta} - \frac{\pi}{\beta}\log 4\beta^2\\
&\quad - \frac{2\pi}{\beta}\log 2\,\eta(2\omega_1)\,\eta(2\omega_2).
\end{aligned}
}

If one replaces $\alpha$, $\beta$ by $\frac12\alpha$, $\frac12\beta$ and multiplies by $4^{-s}$, the
effect is the same as if one had replaced $x$ by $2x$, and
one obtains $S_1$. Thus from (3), having regard to (7):
\weq{10}{
\begin{aligned}
2\,S_1 &= \frac{\pi}{(s-1)\beta} - \frac{2\pi\,\Gamma'(1)}{\beta} - \frac{\pi}{\beta}\log 4\beta^2\\
&\quad - \frac{2\pi}{\beta}\log \eta\left(\frac{\omega_1}{2}\right)\eta\left(\frac{\omega_2}{2}\right).
\end{aligned}
}

If finally one replaces $\alpha$, $\beta$ by $\frac12(\alpha+1)$, $\frac12\beta$ and then
$2x-y$ by $x$, there results in the same way:
\weq{11}{
\begin{aligned}
2\,S_0 &= \frac{\pi}{(s-1)\beta} - \frac{2\pi\,\Gamma'(1)}{\beta} - \frac{\pi}{\beta}\log 4\beta^2\\
&\quad - \frac{2\pi}{\beta}\log \eta\left(\frac{1+\omega_1}{2}\right)\eta\left(\frac{-1+\omega_2}{2}\right),
\end{aligned}
}
and accordingly, having regard to the formulae [§ 34, (9)]:
\[
f(\omega) = e^{-\frac{\pi i}{24}}\frac{\eta\left(\frac{\omega+1}{2}\right)}{\eta(\omega)}
= e^{\frac{\pi i}{24}}\frac{\eta\left(\frac{\omega-1}{2}\right)}{\eta(\omega)},
\]
\[
f_1(\omega) = \frac{\eta\left(\frac{\omega}{2}\right)}{\eta(\omega)}, \qquad
f_2(\omega) = \sqrt{2}\,\frac{\eta(2\omega)}{\eta(\omega)},
\]
by subtracting the formulae (9), (10), (11) from (3):
\[
S - 2\,S_0 = \frac{2\pi}{\beta}\log f(\omega_1)\ f(\omega_2),
\]
\[
S - 2\,S_1 = \frac{2\pi}{\beta}\log f_1(\omega_1)\ f_1(\omega_2),
\]
\[
S - 2\,S_2 = \frac{2\pi}{\beta}\log f_2(\omega_1)\ f_2(\omega_2),
\]
from which, by addition according to § 34, (11), relation (8) follows
again.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 582 =====
% !PRINTED 551
\weberpage{551}
In the difference $2S_0 - S$ there now occur exactly the same
terms as in $S$; only those in which $x+y$ is odd
receive the negative sign, and we can therefore also write:
\weq{12}{\begin{aligned}
\frac{-2\pi}{\beta}\log f(\omega_1)\,f(\omega_2) &= \mathrm{Lim}_{s=1} \sum \frac{(-1)^{x+y}}{[(x-\alpha y)^2+\beta^2y^2]^s},\\
\frac{-2\pi}{\beta}\log f_1(\omega_1)\,f_1(\omega_2) &= \mathrm{Lim}_{s=1} \sum \frac{(-1)^{x}}{[(x-\alpha y)^2+\beta^2y^2]^s},\\
\frac{-2\pi}{\beta}\log f_2(\omega_1)\,f_2(\omega_2) &= \mathrm{Lim}_{s=1} \sum \frac{(-1)^{y}}{[(x-\alpha y)^2+\beta^2y^2]^s},
\end{aligned}}
in which $x, y$ now assume \gesperrt{all} integral pairs of values with the exception
of $0,0$. These three formulae can be derived from one of them by § 34, (13), (14),
for example by replacing, in the second,
\[
\omega_1, \omega_2 \quad\text{by}\quad \omega_1+1, \quad \omega_2-1,
\]
and by
\[
\frac{-1}{\omega_1}, \quad \frac{-1}{\omega_2},
\]
that is,
\weq{13}{\begin{aligned}
\alpha, \beta &\quad\text{by}\quad \alpha+1, \quad \beta,\\
&\quad\text{and by}\quad \frac{-\alpha}{\alpha^2+\beta^2}, \quad \frac{\beta}{\alpha^2+\beta^2}
\end{aligned}}

§ 146. \gesperrt{A Theorem on the Convergence of Series.}

If one wished to interchange the symbols Lim and $\Sigma$ with one another
in the expressions (12), § 145, that is, to put $s=1$ under the
summation sign without more ado, one would not obtain unconditionally
convergent series, and it must therefore be investigated
in what sense these formulae then still remain valid.

In order to carry out this investigation, we will first
derive a general theorem from the theory of series, which is a
sharpening of the theorem Bd.\,II, § 196, 3. Let
\weq{1}{\mu_1 \leqq \mu_2 \leqq \mu_3 \leqq \mu_4 \ldots}
be a series of \gesperrt{infinitely many} positive numbers, and let $Z(t)$
denote the number of these numbers that are not greater than $t$.
This $Z(t)$ is to have a finite value for every $t$, from which
it then follows that the $\mu_n$ increase to infinity with $n$. But we
will further assume that
\weq{2}{\frac{Z(t)}{t} = a + \frac{\theta}{\sqrt{t}}}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 583 =====
% !PRINTED 552
\weberpage{552}
%<<CONT
be, where $a$ is a constant (independent of $t$), and $\theta$ a function of $t$ which remains enclosed within finite limits.

If we assume first that the $\mu_n$ are all different from one another, then $Z(\mu_n) = n$, and from (2) it follows that:
\weq{3}{\frac{n}{\mu_n} = a + \frac{\theta}{\sqrt{\mu_n}};}
from this it follows that $n:\mu_n$ remains finite, and consequently, with an altered meaning of $\theta$:
\[
\frac{n}{\mu_n} = a + \frac{\theta}{\sqrt{n}},
\]
or, by the binomial theorem, for any positive $s$:
\weq{4}{\frac{n^s}{\mu_n^s} = a^s\left(1 + \frac{\theta}{\sqrt{n}}\right),}
in which all the quantities denoted by $\theta$ have finite values.

But these formulae still hold even when equal ones occur among the $\mu_n$. For let, say (as in Bd.\,II, § 196, 3.)
\[
\mu_{m+1}, \mu_{m+2}, \ldots, \mu_{m+l} = \mu_n
\]
be equal to one another and
\[
m < n \leqq m+l,
\]
then
\[
Z(\mu_n-0) = m, \qquad Z(\mu_n) = m+l,
\]
\[
\frac{Z(\mu_n-0)}{\mu_n} < \frac{n}{\mu_n} \leqq \frac{Z(\mu_n)}{\mu_n},
\]
\[
a + \frac{\theta'}{\sqrt{\mu_n}} < \frac{n}{\mu_n} < a + \frac{\theta}{\sqrt{\mu_n}},
\]
from which (3) follows and (4) can be derived as above.

The theorem we wish to prove runs as follows:

\gesperrt{Let $\varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2, \varepsilon_3, \ldots$ be an infinite sequence of positive or negative, but finite quantities and}
\weq{5}{\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2+\cdots+\varepsilon_n = \gamma_n\sqrt{n},}
\gesperrt{so constituted that $\gamma_n$ remains, in absolute value, below a finite constant.}

\gesperrt{Then}
\weq{6}{\sigma = \frac{\varepsilon_1}{\mu_1^s} + \frac{\varepsilon_2}{\mu_2^s} + \frac{\varepsilon_3}{\mu_3^s} + \cdots}
\gesperrt{is convergent and a continuous function of $s$, so long as}
\[
s > \tfrac{1}{2}
\]
\gesperrt{holds.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 584 =====
% !PRINTED 553
\weberpage{553}
§ 147. \gesperrt{Development of $f, f_1, f_2$.}

Because of (4) this theorem need only be proved for
$\mu_n = n$, since the series $\Sigma\, \varepsilon_n\theta/n^{s+\frac{1}{2}}$ converges unconditionally and
therefore has this property by known elementary theorems.

Let us therefore set
\weq{7}{\sigma = \frac{\varepsilon_1}{1^s} + \frac{\varepsilon_2}{2^s} + \frac{\varepsilon_3}{2^s} + \cdots} % [sic] third denominator printed 2^s, not 3^s
and, by (5), $\varepsilon_n = \gamma_n\sqrt{n} - \gamma_{n-1}\sqrt{n-1}$; then
\weq{8}{\sigma = \frac{\varepsilon_1}{1^s} + \gamma_2\sqrt{2}\left(\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{3^s}\right) + \gamma_3\sqrt{3}\left(\frac{1}{3^s} - \frac{1}{4^s}\right) + \cdots} % [sic] German source prints $2$, not $2^s$, as the first denominator in the parenthesis
Since now, for an infinitely large $n$,
\[
\sqrt{n}\left(\frac{1}{n^s} - \frac{1}{(n+1)^s}\right) = \frac{s}{n^{s+\frac{1}{2}}}
\]
holds, the series (8) is unconditionally convergent as long as $s > \frac{1}{2}$,
and from this our assertion follows for this series also
by the same elementary theorems.

§ 147. \gesperrt{Development of $f, f_1, f_2$.}

The series (12), § 145 are now in this case. Let us consider,
for example, the second of them, from which, as we have
seen, the others can be derived, and let us set for
$\mu_1, \mu_2, \mu_3, \ldots$ the values, arranged in order of magnitude, of the function
\weq{1}{(x-\alpha y)^2 + \beta^2y^2 = n.}
We take $xy$ as rectangular coordinates in the plane
and overlay the plane with two \gesperrt{lattices}, setting in the
one lattice the even integers for the $x$, in the other the odd
ones.

The number of lattice points that lie in the interior of the ellipse (1)
or on its periphery, and for which therefore $\mu_n \leqq n$, we denote for the two kinds by $Z^0(n), Z^1(n)$.

Let us set
\[
x = \xi\sqrt{n}, \qquad y = \eta\sqrt{n},
\]
then (1) goes over into
\weq{2}{(\xi-\alpha\eta)^2 + \beta^2\eta^2 = 1,}
and the area of this ellipse is $\pi/\beta$, and by Bd.\,II,
§ 194, 1.:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 585 =====
% !PRINTED 554
\weberpage{554}

%<<CONT
\weq{3}{\begin{aligned}
\frac{Z^0(t)}{t} &= \frac{\pi}{2\,\beta} + \frac{\gamma^0}{\sqrt{t}}, \\
\frac{Z^1(t)}{t} &= \frac{\pi}{2\,\beta} + \frac{\gamma^1}{\sqrt{t}},
\end{aligned}}

in which $\gamma^0$ and $\gamma^1$ remain finite for $t=\infty$. The factor $\frac{1}{2}$ in
$\pi/2\,\beta$ comes from the fact that here the meshes of the lattice are rectangles of area 2.
This, however, is in agreement with the formula § 146, (2).

From (3) there follows

\weq{4}{Z^0(t) - Z^1(t) = \gamma\sqrt{t},}

in which $\gamma$ likewise remains finite.

Now we can write the sum occurring in formula (12), § 145
\[
\sigma = \sum \frac{(-1)^x}{[(x-\alpha y)^2 + \beta^2 y^2]^s}
\]
in the following way:
\[
\sigma = \frac{\varepsilon_1}{\mu_1^s} + \frac{\varepsilon_2}{\mu_2^s} + \frac{\varepsilon_3}{\mu_3^s} + \cdots,
\]
in which the $\varepsilon_1$, $\varepsilon_2$, $\varepsilon_3$, \dots\ have only the values $\pm 1$ and

\weq{5}{\begin{aligned}
\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2 + \varepsilon_3 + \cdots + \varepsilon_n &= Z^0(n) - Z^1(n), \\
&= \gamma \sqrt{n}.
\end{aligned}}

With this the assumptions of our theorem § 146 are satisfied.

Accordingly $\sigma$ is a continuous function of $s$ for $s > \frac{1}{2}$, and hence in
particular also for $s=1$, and from § 145, (12) we obtain:
\[
-\frac{2\pi}{\beta}\log f(\omega_1)\,f(\omega_2) = \sum \frac{(-1)^{x+y}}{(x-\alpha y)^2 + \beta^2 y^2},
\]

\weq{6}{\begin{aligned}
-\frac{2\pi}{\beta}\log f_1(\omega_1)\,f_1(\omega_2) &= \sum \frac{(-1)^{x}}{(x-\alpha y)^2 + \beta^2 y^2}, \\
-\frac{2\pi}{\beta}\log f_2(\omega_1)\,f_2(\omega_2) &= \sum \frac{(-1)^{y}}{(x-\alpha y)^2 + \beta^2 y^2}.
\end{aligned}}

These formulae can also be represented in yet another way. We introduce the notation:

\weq{7}{\begin{aligned}
\sum \frac{1}{(x-\alpha y)^2 + \beta^2 y^2} &= S_{00} : x \text{ even}, \ y \text{ even}, \\
&= S_{01} : x \text{ even}, \ y \text{ odd}, \\
&= S_{10} : x \text{ odd}, \ y \text{ even}, \\
&= S_{11} : x \text{ odd}, \ y \text{ odd}.
\end{aligned}}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 586 =====
% !PRINTED 555
\weberpage{555}

Then
\[
\frac{2\pi}{\beta}\log f(\omega_1)\cdot f(\omega_2) = -S_{00} + S_{10} + S_{01} - S_{11},
\]

\weq{8}{\begin{aligned}
\frac{2\pi}{\beta}\log f_1(\omega_1)\,f_1(\omega_2) &= -S_{00} + S_{10} - S_{01} + S_{11}, \\
\frac{2\pi}{\beta}\log f_2(\omega_1)\,f_2(\omega_2) &= -S_{00} - S_{10} + S_{01} + S_{11},
\end{aligned}}

from which by addition:
\[
\frac{2\pi}{\beta}\log 2 = -3\,S_{00} + S_{10} + S_{01} + S_{11},
\]
and if one eliminates $S_{00}$ by means of this:
\[
\frac{2\pi}{\beta}\log f(\omega_1)\,f(\omega_2) = \frac{2\pi}{3\,\beta}\log 2 + \tfrac{2}{3}S_{10} + \tfrac{2}{3}S_{01} - \tfrac{4}{3}S_{11},
\]

\weq{9}{\begin{aligned}
\log f_1(\omega_1)\,f_1(\omega_2) &= \frac{2\pi}{3\,\beta}\log 2 + \tfrac{2}{3}S_{10} - \tfrac{4}{3}S_{01} + \tfrac{2}{3}S_{11}, \\
\log f_2(\omega_1)\,f_2(\omega_2) &= \frac{2\pi}{3\,\beta}\log 2 - \tfrac{4}{3}S_{10} + \tfrac{2}{3}S_{01} + \tfrac{2}{3}S_{11}.
\end{aligned}}

These sums, however, are to be understood in such a way that in all of them at once
\[
(x-\alpha y)^2 + \beta^2 y^2 < n
\]
shall hold, and that $n$ then grows to infinity. Each individual sum $S$ thereby becomes
infinite, but their combinations, as they occur in these formulae, receive
finite limiting values.

We wish further to denote by $S'_{01}$, $S'_{10}$, $S'_{11}$ the sums which have the same
expression as $S_{01}$, $S_{10}$, $S_{11}$ according to (6), only with the difference \gesperrt{that $x$
and $y$ are to have no common divisor.}

If we set
\[
S_{10} + S_{01} - 2\,S_{11} = T_n, \qquad (x-\alpha y)^2 + \beta^2 y^2 < n, \qquad
\mathrm{Lim}_{n=\infty} T_n = T
\]
and denote by $T_n^{(p)}$ the sum which arises from $T_n$ when all terms
are removed in which $x$ and $y$ are both divisible by the odd prime $p$, then
there results:
\[
T_n^{(p)} = T_n - \frac{1}{p^2}\,T_{np^{-2}}
\]
and by passage to the limit $n=\infty$:
\[
T^{(p)} = T\left(1 - \frac{1}{p^2}\right).
\]

%% ===== canonical stable idx 587 =====
% !PRINTED 556
\weberpage{556}

If one proceeds in this way with all primes and sets
\[
S'_{10} + S'_{01} - 2\,S'_{11} = T',
\]
then it follows that
\[
T' = T\,\Pi\left(1 - \frac{1}{p^2}\right),
\]
in which the product $\Pi$ extends over \gesperrt{all odd primes} $p$. Now, by development in
ascending powers of $p^{-2}$, one obtains:
\[
\frac{1}{\Pi(1-p^{-2})} = 1 + \frac{1}{3^2} + \frac{1}{5^2} + \frac{1}{7^2} + \frac{1}{9^2} + \cdots,
= \frac{\pi^2}{8},
\]
and consequently
\[
T = \frac{\pi^2}{8}\,T',
\]
and by proceeding in the same way with the two other sums, there follows from (9):
\[
\log f(\omega_1)\,f(\omega_2) = \tfrac{1}{3}\log 2 + \frac{\beta\pi}{24}\left(S'_{10} + S'_{01} - 2\,S'_{11}\right),
\]

\weq{10}{\begin{aligned}
\log f_1(\omega_1)\,f_1(\omega_2) &= \tfrac{1}{3}\log 2 + \frac{\beta\pi}{24}\left(S'_{10} - 2\,S'_{01} + S'_{11}\right), \\
\log f_2(\omega_1)\,f_2(\omega_2) &= \tfrac{1}{3}\log 2 + \frac{\beta\pi}{24}\left(-2\,S'_{10} + S'_{01} + S'_{11}\right).
\end{aligned}}

These formulae simplify essentially if one sets $\alpha = 0$, and hence
\[
\omega_1 = \omega_2 = \omega = i\,\beta
\]
that is, if one assumes a \gesperrt{purely imaginary} $\omega$. Then
\[
S'_{10} = \sum \frac{1}{x^2 - \omega^2 y^2} \qquad x \text{ odd}, \ y \text{ even}, \ xy \text{ relatively prime}.
\]

If one separates off the term $x = \pm 1$, $y = 0$ and takes the remaining ones together four
at a time, then there results
\[
S'_{10} = 2 + 4\sum \frac{1}{x^2 - \omega^2 y^2},
\]
in which $x$, $y$ run through \gesperrt{positive values} only.

One proceeds in the same way with the other sums. If one then sets
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 588 =====
% !PRINTED 557
\weberpage{557}
%<<CONT

\weq{11}{\begin{aligned}
\sum \frac{\omega}{y^2\omega^2 - x^2} &= S_1 \qquad x, y \text{ odd}, \\
&= S_2 \qquad x \text{ odd}, \ y \text{ even}, \\
&= S_3 \qquad x \text{ even}, \ y \text{ odd},
\end{aligned}}

$x$, $y$ positive and relatively prime, then it follows:
\[
\beta\,S'_{10} = -2\,i\,\omega + 4\,i\,S_2,
\]
\[
\beta\,S'_{01} = +\frac{2\,i}{\omega} + 4\,i\,S_3,
\]
\[
\beta\,S'_{11} = 4\,i\,S_1,
\]
and consequently there results from (10), for a purely imaginary $\omega$:
\[
\log f(\omega) = \tfrac{1}{3}\log\sqrt{2} + \frac{\pi i}{24}\left(-\omega + \frac{1}{\omega} - 4\,S_1 + 2\,S_2 + 2\,S_3\right),
\]

\weq{12}{\begin{aligned}
\log f_1(\omega) &= \tfrac{1}{3}\log\sqrt{2} + \frac{\pi i}{24}\left(-\omega - \frac{2}{\omega} + 2\,S_1 + 2\,S_2 - 4\,S_3\right), \\
\log f_2(\omega) &= \tfrac{1}{3}\log\sqrt{2} + \frac{\pi i}{24}\left(2\,\omega + \frac{1}{\omega} + 2\,S_1 - 4\,S_2 + 2\,S_3\right).
\end{aligned}}

§ 148.

\gesperrt{Elementary Derivation of the Developments.}

One can also arrive at the foregoing developments by the following route. By a known
formula of analysis:

\weq{1}{\sum_{1,\infty}^{x} \frac{\omega}{\omega^2 y^2 - x^2} = -\frac{1}{2\,\omega y^2} + \frac{\pi i}{2\,y}\,\frac{q^{2y}+1}{q^{2y}-1},}

if $q = e^{\pi i \omega}$\footnote{From the development:
\[
\mathrm{cotg}\ z = \frac{1}{z} + \frac{2\,z}{z^2-\pi^2} + \frac{2\,z}{z^2-4\pi^2} + \frac{2\,z}{z^2-9\pi^2} + \cdots
\]}. From this, by development in powers of $q$:

\weq{2}{\sum_{1,\infty}^{x} \frac{\omega}{\omega^2 y^2 - x^2} = -\frac{1}{2\,\omega y^2} - \frac{\pi i}{y}\left(\frac{1}{2} + \sum_{1,\infty}^{n} q^{2ny}\right).}

If one here replaces $y$ by $\tfrac{1}{2}y$, it follows:

\weq{3}{\sum_{1,\infty}^{x} \frac{2\,\omega}{\omega^2 y^2 - 4x^2} = -\frac{1}{\omega y^2} - \frac{\pi i}{y}\left(\frac{1}{2} + \sum_{1,\infty} q^{ny}\right),}

and if one subtracts (2) from (3):

\weq{4}{\sum \frac{(-1)^x\,\omega}{\omega^2 y^2 - x^2} = -\frac{1}{2\,\omega y^2} - \frac{\pi i}{y}\sum_{1,\infty}^{x} q^{(2n-1)y}.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 589 =====
% !PRINTED 558
\weberpage{558}

If we sum these formulae once again with respect to $y$ from $1$ to
$\infty$, and make use of the formulae which are partly known and
partly follow from \S\,24, (11):

\[
\sum_{1,\infty}^{y}\frac{1}{y^2}=\frac{\pi^2}{6},\quad
\sum_{1,\infty}^{y}\frac{(-1)^y}{y^2}=-\frac{\pi^2}{12},\quad
\sum_{1,\infty}^{y}\frac{(-1)^y}{y}=-\log 2,\,.
\]

\[
\sum_{1,\infty}^{n}\sum_{1,\infty}^{y}\frac{q^{(2n-1)y}}{y}
=-\log\Pi(1-q^{2n-1})=-\log f_1(\omega)-\frac{\pi i\omega}{24},
\]

\[
\sum_{1,\infty}^{n}\sum_{1,\infty}^{y}\frac{(-1)^y q^{2ny}}{y}
=-\log\Pi(1+q^{2n})=-\log f_2(\omega)+\frac{\pi i\omega}{12}-\tfrac{1}{2}\log 2,
\]

\[
\sum_{1,\infty}^{n}\sum_{1,\infty}^{y}\frac{(-1)^y q^{(2n-1)y}}{y}
=-\log\Pi(1+q^{2n-1})=-\log f(\omega)-\frac{\pi i\omega}{24},
\]

then there results:

\[
\sum_{1,\infty}^{y}\sum_{1,\infty}^{x}\frac{(-1)^{x+y}\omega}{\omega^2y^2-x^2}
=\frac{\pi^2}{24\omega}-\frac{\pi^2\omega}{24}+\pi i\log f(\omega),
\]

\weq{5}{
\begin{aligned}
&\sum_{1,\infty}^{y}\sum_{1,\infty}^{x}\frac{(-1)^x\omega}{\omega^2y^2-x^2}
=-\frac{\pi^2}{12\omega}-\frac{\pi^2\omega}{24}+\pi i\log f_1(\omega),\\[4pt]
&\sum_{1,\infty}^{y}\sum_{1,\infty}^{x}\frac{(-1)^y\omega}{\omega^2y^2-x^2}
=\frac{\pi^2}{24\omega}+\frac{\pi^2\omega}{12}+\pi i\log f_2(\omega)\,.
\end{aligned}
}

The double sums on the left side of these formulae are to be understood
in such a way that the summation with respect to $x$ is to be carried
out first, and then the summation with respect to $y$. But we may also
sum in such a way that we take

\weq{6}{
0<x<m,\quad 0<y<n,\quad n=\infty\,,\quad \frac{m}{n}=\infty
}

and then let $m$ and $n$ grow to infinity so that $m:n$ becomes
infinite. That both give the same can be shown in various ways, for
example by comparing the sums with integrals.

If, then, we set, as in \S\,147, (10), binding $x$, $y$ to the
condition (6):

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum^{x,y}\frac{\omega}{\omega^2y^2-x^2}&=S_0 & x,\,y&\ \text{even,}\\
&=S_1 & x,\,y&\ \text{odd,}\\
&=S_2 & x\ \text{odd,}\ y&\ \text{even,}\\
&=S_3 & x\ \text{even,}\ y&\ \text{odd,}
\end{aligned}
\]

it follows from (5):
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 590 =====
% !PRINTED 559
\weberpage{559}

%<<CONT
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_0+S_1-S_2-S_3&=\phantom{-}\frac{\pi^2}{24\omega}-\frac{\pi^2\omega}{24}+\pi i\log f(\omega),\\[4pt]
S_0-S_1-S_2+S_3&=-\frac{\pi^2}{12\omega}-\frac{\pi^2\omega}{24}+\pi i\log f_1(\omega),\\[4pt]
S_0-S_1+S_2-S_3&=\phantom{-}\frac{\pi^2}{24\omega}+\frac{\pi^2\omega}{12}+\pi i\log f_2(\omega).
\end{aligned}
\]

From this by addition:
\[
3S_0-S_1-S_2-S_3=\pi i\log\sqrt{2},
\]
and if $S_0$ is eliminated:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\tfrac{4}{3}S_1-\tfrac{2}{3}S_2-\tfrac{2}{3}S_3&=\phantom{-}\frac{\pi^2}{24\omega}-\frac{\pi^2\omega}{24}-\frac{\pi i}{3}\log\sqrt{2}+\pi i\log f(\omega),\\[4pt]
-\tfrac{2}{3}S_1-\tfrac{2}{3}S_2+\tfrac{4}{3}S_3&=-\frac{\pi^2}{12\omega}-\frac{\pi^2\omega}{24}-\frac{\pi i}{3}\log\sqrt{2}+\pi i\log f_1(\omega),\\[4pt]
-\tfrac{2}{3}S_1+\tfrac{4}{3}S_2-\tfrac{2}{3}S_3&=\phantom{-}\frac{\pi^2}{24\omega}+\frac{\pi^2\omega}{12}-\frac{\pi i}{3}\log\sqrt{2}+\pi i\log f_2(\omega).
\end{aligned}
\]

One can now pass over, just as before, from the sums $S$ to
the $S'$, in which $x$, $y$ are relatively prime, and finds:

\[
\log f(\omega)=\tfrac{1}{3}\log\sqrt{2}+\frac{\pi i}{24}\Bigl(-\omega+\frac{1}{\omega}-4S_1'+2S_2'+2S_3'\Bigr),
\]

\weq{7}{
\log f_1(\omega)=\tfrac{1}{3}\log\sqrt{2}+\frac{\pi i}{24}\Bigl(-\omega-\frac{2}{\omega}+2S_1'+2S_2'-4S_3'\Bigr),
}

\[
\log f_2(\omega)=\tfrac{1}{3}\log\sqrt{2}+\frac{\pi i}{24}\Bigl(-\omega-\frac{1}{\omega}+2S_1'-4S_2'+2S_3'\Bigr).
\]

These formulae agree in form with \S\,147, (11), which is
remarkable in so far as the manner of the passage to the limit
is a different one in the two cases.

\begin{center}
\S\,149.\quad \gesperrt{Developments for the function $\log\eta(\omega)$.}
\end{center}

Let us consider the sum

\weq{1}{
U=\sum^{x,y}\frac{1}{(x+\omega y)^{2s}},
}

extended over all $x$, $y$ with the exception of the combination $0$, $0$.

By separating off the terms with $y=0$, one may write for
it:

\weq{2}{
U=2\sum_{1,\infty}^{x}\frac{1}{x^{2s}}+2\sum_{1,\infty}^{y}\sum_{-\infty,\infty}^{x}\frac{1}{(x+\omega y)^{2s}};
}

next we have
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 591 =====
% !PRINTED 560
\weberpage{560}

%<<CONT
\[
\frac{\Gamma(2s)}{[-2\pi i(x+\omega y)]^{2s}} = \int_0^\infty e^{2\pi i(x+y\omega)\xi}\xi^{2s-1}\,d\xi,
\]
\[
{}= \int_0^1 e^{2\pi i x\xi}\sum_{0,\infty}^n e^{2\pi i y\omega(\xi+n)}(\xi+n)^{2s-1}\,d\xi.
\]
If one now sums over $x$ and applies the \gesperrt{Fourier} series:
\[
\sum^x \int_0^1 e^{2\pi i x\xi} f(\xi)\,d\xi = \tfrac{1}{2}[f(0)+f(1)],
\]
then it follows:
\[
\frac{\Gamma(2s)}{(-2\pi i)^{2s}} \sum_{-\infty,\infty}^x \frac{1}{(x+\omega y)^{2s}} = \sum_{1,\infty}^n e^{2\pi i y\omega n}\,n^{2s-1},
\]
and by summation over $y$:
\[
\frac{\Gamma(2s)}{(-2\pi i)^{2s}} \sum_{1,\infty}^y \sum_{-\infty,\infty}^x \frac{1}{(x+\omega y)^{2s}} = \sum_{1,\infty}^n \frac{e^{2\pi i\omega n}}{1-e^{2\pi i\omega n}}\,n^{2s-1}
\]
\[
{}= -\frac{1}{2\pi \imath}\sum_{1,\infty}^n \frac{d\log(1-e^{2\pi i\omega n})}{d\omega}\,n^{2s-2}.
\]
Accordingly we obtain, by passing to the limit and having regard to the definition of the function $\eta(\omega)$ [§ 24, (8)]:
\[
\mathrm{Lim}_{s=1}\sum_{1,\infty}^y \sum^x \frac{1}{(x+\omega y)^{2s}} = -2\pi i\,\frac{d\log\eta(\omega)}{d\omega} - \frac{\pi^2}{6}.
\]
Furthermore we have
\[
\mathrm{Lim}\sum \frac{1}{x^{2s}} = \frac{\pi^2}{6},
\]
and accordingly from (1) and (2) it follows:
\weq{3}{\mathrm{Lim}_{s=1}\sum^{x,y} \frac{1}{(x+\omega y)^{2s}} = -4\pi i\,\frac{d\log\eta(\omega)}{d\omega}}
[to be summed as indicated for (1)]. If one wished here to pass to the limit under the summation sign, one would obtain:
\weq{4}{-4\pi i\,\frac{d\log\eta(\omega)}{d\omega} = \sum^{x,y} \frac{1}{(x+\omega y)^2},}
but then one would have a sum that is only conditionally convergent, and a precise manner of passing to the limit would have to be laid down. One would have to assume in the $xy$-plane a closed curve within which the points $x, y$ lie, and then let this curve move out to infinity. The value of the sum will depend on the nature of this curve. Perhaps the ellipse $|x+\omega y| = n$ presents itself for this. In itself formula (4) has no meaning.

\begin{center}
\gesperrt{Twenty-Third Chapter.}

\textbf{The Division Field.}
\end{center}

\begin{center}
\rule{2cm}{0.4pt}
\end{center}

\begin{center}
\S\,150. \textbf{The Homogeneous \gesperrt{Weierstrass} Functions.}
\end{center}

In \S\,114 we set out from the question under what suppositions a doubly
periodic function $\varphi(u)$ with the periods $\omega_1, \omega_2$
admits a multiplication $\varphi(\mu u)$, that is, under what
circumstances $\mu\omega_1, \mu\omega_2$ can be expressed linearly and
with integral coefficients by $\omega_1, \omega_2$; and we had arrived at
the result that, for variable $\omega_1, \omega_2$, this is possible only
when $\mu$ is an integral rational number, and that only when

\weq{1}{\omega = \frac{\omega_2}{\omega_1}}

is an imaginary quadratic irrational number can $\mu$ also be a complex
number of the same field as $\omega$. What now matters is to explore
somewhat more closely the formulae of complex multiplication that follow
from this assumption.

We will first investigate, as the formally simpler case, the complex
multiplication of the Weierstrass elliptic function $\wp(u)$, but we must
then also take into consideration the complex multiplication of the
\gesperrt{Jacobian} elliptic functions.

In \S\,37, (8), \S\,46, (13) we derived the formulae for the
homogeneity of the functions $\sigma(u)$, $\wp(u)$ and of the invariants
$g_2, g_3, 16\,G = g_2^3 - 27\,g_3^2$, which we here collect once more:

\weq{2}{\begin{aligned}
\sigma(\lambda u, \lambda\omega_1, \lambda\omega_2) &= \lambda\ \sigma(u, \omega_1, \omega_2), \\
\wp(\lambda u, \lambda\omega_1, \lambda\omega_2) &= \lambda^{-2}\, \wp(u, \omega_1, \omega_2), \\
g_2(\lambda\omega_1, \lambda\omega_2) &= \lambda^{-4}\, g_2(\omega_1, \omega_2), \\
g_3(\lambda\omega_1, \lambda\omega_2) &= \lambda^{-6}\, g_3(\omega_1, \omega_2), \\
G(\lambda\omega_1, \lambda\omega_2) &= \lambda^{-12}\, G(\omega_1, \omega_2),
\end{aligned}}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 595 =====
% !PRINTED 564
\weberpage{564}

%<<CONT
and the functions \S\,46, (12), (15), (16):

\weq{3}{\begin{aligned}
\frac{4\,.\,27\,g_2^3}{G} &= j(\omega), \\
\frac{4\,.\,27\,.\,27\,g_3^2}{G} &= j(\omega) - 27\,.\,64, \\
\omega_1^{12}\,G &= 2^8\,\pi^{12}\,\eta(\omega)^{24}
\end{aligned}}

depend on the ratio (1).

In \S\,54, (4), (5) the single-valued functions of $\omega$:

\weq{4}{\begin{aligned}
\gamma_2(\omega) &= \sqrt[3]{j(\omega)} = \frac{f(\omega)^{24} - 16}{f(\omega)^8}, \\
\gamma_3(\omega) &= \sqrt{j(\omega) - 27\,.\,64} = \frac{[f(\omega)^{24} + 8]\,[f_1(\omega)^8 - f_2(\omega)^8]}{f(\omega)^8}
\end{aligned}}

are further defined.

From the last equation (3) one recognises [for instance from the
development of $\eta(\omega)$, \S\,24, (8)] that $G$ cannot vanish
so long as $\omega$ has a positive imaginary part, and consequently
$g_2, g_3$ also cannot both vanish at once.

From the series developments of \S\,56 there results:

\weq{5}{\begin{aligned}
\sigma(u) &= \sum^{m,n} a_{m,n}\left(\tfrac{1}{2}g_2\right)^m (2g_3)^n \frac{u^{2\nu+1}}{(2\nu+1)!}, \\
\nu &= 2m + 3n,
\end{aligned}}

in which the rational coefficients $a_{m,n}$ can have only powers of 3
in the denominator (according to \gesperrt{Schwarz-Weierstrass} they are integers,
but that is of no consequence here).

Likewise

\weq{6}{\wp(u) = \sum b_{m,n}\left(\tfrac{1}{2}g_2\right)^m (2g_3)^n \frac{u^{2\nu-2}}{(2\nu+1)!}}

with rational coefficients $b_{m,n}$. In order to obtain functions of
two variables, we make the following substitution:

If neither of the two invariants $g_2, g_3$ vanishes, we put:

\weq{7}{u = \sqrt{\frac{g_2 g_3}{G}}\, w,}

hence

\[
g_2^m g_3^n u^{2\nu+1} = \left(\frac{g_2^3}{G}\right)^{m+n} \left(\frac{g_2^2}{G}\right)^{m+2n} \sqrt{\frac{g_2 g_3}{G}}\, w^{2\nu+1},
\]

and thereby there results from (5):

\weq{8}{\sqrt{\frac{G}{g_2 g_3}}\, \sigma(u) = \sum A_{m,n}\, j^{m+n} (j - 27\,.\,64)^{m+2n} \frac{w^{2\nu+1}}{(2\nu+1)!}}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 596 =====
% !PRINTED 565
\weberpage{565}

%<<CONT
in which the $A_{m,n}$ are rational numbers that can contain in the
denominator only powers of 2 and of 3.

In the same way there results from the series development (6) for
the $\wp$-function:

\weq{9}{\frac{g_2 g_3}{G}\, \wp(u) = \sum_{m,n} B_{m,n}\, j^{m+n} (j - 27\,.\,64)^{m+2n} \frac{w^{2\nu-2}}{(2\nu+1)!},}

in which the $B_{m,n}$ are rational numerical coefficients. That these
too have only powers of 2 and 3 in the denominator is made probable by
the first cases, but does not come into consideration for us now.

If $g_2$ or $g_3$ is equal to zero, the substitution (7) is not
usable. If first

\[
g_3 = 0,
\]

then in the series for $\sigma(u)$ and $\wp(u)$ those terms drop out
in which $n$ is positive. We then have

\[
\sigma(u) = \sum a_{m,0}\, g_2^m\, \frac{u^{4m+1}}{(4m+1)!},
\]
\[
\wp(u) = \sum b_{m,0}\, g_2^m\, \frac{u^{4m-2}}{(2m+1)!}.
\]

We then set

\weq{10}{u = g_2^{-\frac{1}{4}}\, w}

and obtain

\weq{11}{\begin{aligned}
g_2^{\frac{1}{4}}\, \sigma(u) &= \sum_m A_m\, \frac{w^{4m+1}}{(4m+1)!}, \\
g_2^{-\frac{1}{2}}\, \wp(u) &= \sum_m B_m\, \frac{w^{4m-2}}{(4m+1)!},
\end{aligned}}

where $A_m, B_m$ are again rational numbers.

If finally

\[
g_2 = 0,
\]

then we set

\weq{12}{u = g_3^{-\frac{1}{6}}\, w,}

and obtain

\weq{13}{\begin{aligned}
g_3^{\frac{1}{6}}\, \sigma(u) &= \sum_n A_n\, \frac{w^{6n+1}}{(6n+1)!}, \\
g_3^{-\frac{1}{3}}\, \wp(u) &= \sum_n B_n\, \frac{w^{6n-2}}{(6n+1)!}.
\end{aligned}}

In the developments (8), (9), (11), (13) we have

\weq{14}{A_{00} = 1, \quad B_{00} = 1, \quad A_0 = 1, \quad B_0 = 1.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 597 =====
% !PRINTED 566
\weberpage{566}

§ 151. \gesperrt{The complex multiplication of the function $\wp(u)$.}

We now assume that the periods $\omega_1$, $\omega_2$ of the function $\wp(u)$ satisfy a quadratic equation
\weq{1}{A\omega_2^2 + B\omega_2\omega_1 + C\omega_1^2 = 0,}
in which $A$, $B$, $C$ are integral rational numbers without a common divisor. Let $A$ be positive, and let the discriminant of the quadratic form $(A, B, C)$
\weq{2}{B^2 - 4AC = \Delta}
be a \gesperrt{negative fundamental discriminant}, i.\,e. let $\Delta$ contain no square factor after whose separation a discriminant remains (§ 84).

If we set
\weq{3}{\omega = \dfrac{\omega_2}{\omega_1},}
then from (1) there follows:
\weq{4}{2A\omega = -B + \sqrt{\Delta},}
and if we assume $\sqrt{\Delta}$ to be positive imaginary, then $\omega$ receives a positive imaginary part and can serve as the modulus of a $\vartheta$-function. $\Delta$ is the fundamental number of an imaginary quadratic field, which we denote by $\Omega$\footnote{The assumption that $\Delta$ is a fundamental discriminant is made here for the sake of simplification. In my memoir ``Über Zahlgruppen in algebraischen Körpern'' (Mathematische Annalen, Bd. L) this assumption is not made. One then obtains more general fields, which belong to the orders, as in § 124.}.

The class field $\mathfrak{R}(\Delta)$ is determined by the singular invariant $j(\omega)$, and its relative degree with respect to $\Omega$ is equal to the class number of the discriminant $\Delta$. The integers of the quadratic field $\Omega = \mathfrak{R}(\sqrt{\Delta})$ are of the form:
\weq{5}{\mu = \dfrac{x + y\sqrt{\Delta}}{2},}
in which $x$ and $y$ are integral rational numbers that satisfy the condition
\[ x \equiv By \pmod{2} \]
For the number $\mu$ defined by (5) we determine four integral rational numbers $a$, $b$, $c$, $\partial$:
\weq{6}{\begin{aligned} a &= \dfrac{x+By}{2}, & b &= Ay, \\ c &= -Cy, & \partial &= \dfrac{x-By}{2}, \end{aligned}}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 598 =====
% !PRINTED 567
\weberpage{567}

%<<CONT
from which:
\weq{7}{a\partial - bc = \dfrac{x^2 - \Delta y^2}{4} = \mu\mu' = m,}
if
\weq{8}{\mu' = \dfrac{x - y\sqrt{\Delta}}{2}}
is the number of the field $\Omega$ conjugate to $\mu$.

If we take $y$ different from zero, then from (1), by multiplication by $y$, there follows:
\[ b\omega_2^2 + (a-\partial)\omega_2\omega_1 - c\omega_1^2 = 0, \]
and for this one can also write:
\[ (a\omega_1 + b\omega_2)\omega_2 = (c\omega_1 + \partial\omega_2)\omega_1 \]
or
\weq{9}{\omega = \dfrac{c + \partial\omega}{a + b\omega}.}
By (4) and (5) there follows from (6):
\weq{10}{\begin{aligned} a + b\omega &= \dfrac{x + (2A\omega+B)y}{2} = \mu, \\ c + \partial\omega &= \mu\omega, \end{aligned}}
or in homogeneous form:
