\weq{11}{\begin{aligned} \mu\omega_1 &= a\omega_1 + b\omega_2, \\ \mu\omega_2 &= c\omega_1 + \partial\omega_2, \end{aligned}}
and by solving these linear equations:
\weq{12}{\begin{aligned} \mu'\omega_1 &= \partial\omega_1 - b\omega_2, \\ \mu'\omega_2 &= -c\omega_1 + a\omega_2. \end{aligned}}

From this it follows that $\wp(\mu u)$ is a doubly-periodic function with the periods $\omega_1$, $\omega_2$, and since it is moreover an even function of $u$, it can be represented rationally by $\wp(u)$ (§ 21). If, then, we denote by $R$ and $P$ integral rational functions of $\wp(u)$ without common divisor, then
\weq{13}{\wp(\mu u) = \dfrac{R}{P}.}

Since the quotient $\wp(\mu u):\wp(u)$ remains finite for $u=0$, i.\,e. for $\wp(u)=\infty$, the degree of $R$ is higher by one unit than the degree of the denominator.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 599 =====
% !PRINTED 568
\weberpage{568}

\begin{center}
§ 152.\qquad \gesperrt{The Poles of the Function} $\wp(\mu u)$.
\end{center}

In order to establish the degree of the functions $R$ and $P$, we must count the zeros of $P$, that is, the points of infinity of $\wp(\mu u)$ which are not at the same time points of infinity of $\wp(u)$. But $\wp(\mu u):\wp(u)$ becomes infinite then and only then, when
\weq{1}{u = \dfrac{h_1\omega_1 + h_2\omega_2}{\mu}}
holds, where $h_1$, $h_2$ are integers and where $h_1\omega_1 + h_2\omega_2$, but not $(h_1\omega_1+h_2\omega_2):\mu$, is a period. If we therefore set
\weq{2}{\wp(\mu u) = \dfrac{R_\mu[\wp(u)]}{P_\mu[\wp(u)]},}
and denote by $g$ the roots of $P_\mu(x)$, then
\weq{3}{g = \wp\left(\dfrac{h_1\omega_1+h_2\omega_2}{\mu}\right).}
The number $g$ does not change when $h_1$ and $h_2$ are altered by multiples of $m=\mu\mu'$, because by this the argument of the $\wp$-functions is, according to (11), § 151, altered by a period.

Since the functions $\wp(u)$ and $\wp(\mu u)$ are not altered when we subject the period $\omega_1$, $\omega_2$ to a linear transformation with determinant 1, we do not restrict the generality by assuming that $A$ is relatively prime to $m$; and on account of the periodicity of $\wp(u)$ we may therefore also set:
\[ g = \wp\left(\dfrac{h_1\omega_1+h_2 A\omega_2}{\mu}\right). \]
On account of the homogeneity of $\wp(u)$ we may now set $\omega_1=1$, $\omega_2=\omega$, and obtain, according to § 151, (4):
\[ A\omega = \dfrac{-B+\sqrt{\Delta}}{2}, \]
and accordingly we have
\weq{4}{h_1\omega_1 + h_2 A\omega_2 = h_1 + h_2\left(\dfrac{-B+\sqrt{\Delta}}{2}\right).}
If we therefore set
\[ h_1 + h_2\dfrac{-B+\sqrt{\Delta}}{2} = \nu \]
then from (3) there results:
\weq{5}{g = \wp\left(\dfrac{\nu}{\mu}\right),}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 600 =====
% !PRINTED 569
\weberpage{569}

%<<CONT
where $\nu$, like $\mu$, is an integer of the field $\Omega$ that is \gesperrt{not divisible by $\mu$.}

If this condition is fulfilled, then $g$ is a root of $P_\mu(x)$. But since $\wp(\mu u)$ becomes infinite in the second order in the $u$-plane for $u\equiv 0\ (\mathrm{modd}.\ \omega_1,\omega_2)$, $P_\mu(x)$ is divisible by $(x-g)^2$, unless
\[ \wp(u) - g \]
itself vanishes in the second order for $u=\nu:\mu$; on account of § 46, (18) this occurs when
\[ \wp'\left(\dfrac{\nu}{\mu}\right) = 0 \]
holds, that is, when $\nu:\mu$ is a half period, and thus
\weq{6}{g = e_1, e_2, e_3}
results.

\begin{quote}
{\small 1. \gesperrt{By (4), if $\omega_1=1$, $\omega_2=\omega$ is set, every integer of the field $\Omega$ is a period of $\wp(u)$. The converse does not hold; but since $A\omega$ is an integer in $\Omega$, every period must be converted into an integer by multiplication by $A$.}}
\end{quote}

From this it follows that two values
\[ g = \wp\left(\dfrac{\nu}{\mu}\right), \qquad g' = \wp\left(\dfrac{\nu'}{\mu}\right) \]
are equal to one another then and only then, when
\[ \nu \equiv \pm \nu' \pmod{\mu} \]
holds. For if $g=g'$, then either
\[ \dfrac{\nu+\nu'}{\mu} \quad \text{or} \quad \dfrac{\nu-\nu'}{\mu} \]
must be converted into an integer by multiplication by $A$. But $A$ is relatively prime to $\mu$, and consequently one of these two numbers must itself be an integer. The number of incongruent values of $\nu$, however, is equal to $N(\mu) = m$ (Bd.\ II, § 165).

If we therefore let $\nu$ run through a complete system of residues with respect to the modulus $\mu$, excluding zero, we obtain every value of $g$ twice, except when
\weq{7}{2\nu \equiv 0 \pmod{\mu},}
and in this case $\wp\left(\dfrac{\nu}{\mu}\right)$ is one of the values $e$. From this it follows:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 601 =====
% !PRINTED 570
\weberpage{570}

%<<CONT
\weq{8}{P_\mu(x) = \Pi\left[x - \wp\left(\frac{\nu}{\mu}\right)\right],}

and $P_\mu(x)$ is of degree $m - 1$.

In the product $P_\mu(x)$ every factor $x - g$ occurs twice, except when $g$ is equal to one of the $e$, that is, when the congruence (7) can be satisfied for a $\nu$ different from zero.

1) If $\mu$ is relatively prime to 2, and hence if $m$ is \gesperrt{odd}, then the congruence (7) has only the root $\nu = 0$. In that case $P_\mu(x)$ is a square, and if $S(x)$ is a function of degree $\frac{1}{2}(m - 1)$,

\weq{9}{P_\mu(x) = S^2, \quad m \equiv 1 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 2).}

If $\mu$ has a divisor in common with 2, three cases are to be distinguished.

2) If $\mu$ is divisible by 2, then $\nu$, if it is to satisfy the congruence (7), must be a multiple of $\frac{1}{2}\mu$; and since there are in $\Omega$ three numbers different from zero that are incongruent with respect to the modulus 2, (7) has three roots. Accordingly the three values $e_1, e_2, e_3$ occur among the $g$, and we have:

\weq{10}{P_\mu(x) = \wp'(u)^2 S^2, \quad m \equiv 0 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 2),}

where $S$ is an integral function of degree $\frac{1}{2}m - 2$.

3) If 2 splits in the field $\Omega$ into two (equal or different) prime ideals, that is, if $\Delta \equiv 0 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 4)$ or $\equiv 1 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 8)$, then $\mu$ can be divisible by one of these prime factors without being divisible by 2. In that case the congruence (7) has only one root different from zero, and among the numbers $g$ only one of the three numbers (6), say $e$, occurs. In this case

\weq{11}{P_u(x) = [\wp(u) - e]\, S^2,} % [sic] The German source prints P_u, although the surrounding formulas and prose require P_\mu.

where $S$ is a function of degree $\frac{1}{2}m - 1$.

With regard to the two special cases $g_3 = 0$ and $g_2 = 0$ the following is still to be remarked.

4) If $g_3 = 0$, then $\Delta = -4$, $j(\omega) = 0$, and from the differential equation §\,46, (18) there follows:

\[
\wp'(u)^2 = 4\wp(u)^3 - g_2 \wp(u),
\]

by which, having regard to the initial term of the development, the $\wp$-function is uniquely determined.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 602 =====
% !PRINTED 571
\weberpage{571}

If one then replaces $u$ by $iu$, it follows that:

\[
-[\wp'(iu)]^2 = 4\wp^3(iu) - g_2 \wp(iu),
\]

and from this:

\weq{12}{\wp(iu) = -\wp(u).}

The quantities $g$ are therefore opposite to one another in pairs, one of the three quantities $e_1, e_2, e_3$ is equal to zero, and the other two are likewise opposite and equal. From this it follows that in formulae (9) to (11) \gesperrt{the function $S$ can in this case contain only the even powers of $\wp(u)$.}

5) If $g_2 = 0$, then $\Delta = -3$, $j(\omega) = 64.27$, and, when an imaginary third root of unity is denoted by $\varrho$, we have:

\weq{13}{\wp(u) = \varrho\, \wp(\varrho^2 u) = \varrho^2\, \wp(\varrho u),}

and the roots $g$ of $S$ arrange themselves in threes in the manner:

\weq{14}{g, \quad \varrho g, \quad \varrho^2 g.}

Among these three values two are equal to one another only if all three vanish. From (13), however, it follows that this occurs when $u$ becomes congruent to one of the values $\pm 1 : \sqrt{-3}$. For when $\Delta = -3$, $1, \varrho, \varrho^2$ are periods of $\wp(u)$, and since now

\[
\frac{\varrho - \varrho^2}{\sqrt{-3}} = 1
\]

holds, it follows by (13) that:

\[
\wp\left(\frac{\varrho}{\sqrt{-3}}\right) = \wp\left(\frac{\varrho^2}{\sqrt{-3}}\right) = 0,
\]

and the value zero therefore occurs among the $g$ then and only then, when $m$ is divisible by 3.

From this it follows:

If $\Delta = -3$ and $m \equiv 0 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 3)$, then $S : \wp(u)$ is a rational function of $\wp(u)^3$.

If $\Delta = -3$ and $m \equiv 1 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 3)$, then $S$ itself is a rational function of $\wp(u)^3$.

[Since $m$ must have the form $\frac{1}{4}(x^2 + 3y^2)$, $m$ cannot here be $\equiv -1 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 3)$.]

\begin{center}
§\,153. \gesperrt{The Function $\tau(u)$.}
\end{center}

Following §\,150 (6), (8), (9), (10), (12), (13) we now introduce a function $\tau = \tau(u)$ which depends on only two arguments $w, \omega$, by setting:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 603 =====
% !PRINTED 572
\weberpage{572}

%<<CONT
\weq{1}{
\begin{aligned}
&\text{a)} \quad \tau(u) = \frac{g_2 g_3}{G} \wp(u), \quad \text{in general,} \\
&\text{b)} \quad \phantom{\tau(u)} = \frac{\wp(u)^2}{g_2}, \quad \text{if } g_3 = 0, \\
&\text{c)} \quad \phantom{\tau(u)} = \frac{\wp(u)^3}{g_3}, \quad \text{if } g_2 = 0.
\end{aligned}
}

And if then $\mu$ is, as above, an integer of the field $\Omega$, we can set in all three cases:

\weq{2}{\tau(\mu u) = \frac{\Psi(\tau)}{\Phi(\tau)},}

in which $\Phi, \Psi$ are integral functions of $\tau$ which, apart from constant factors, agree in case (1) a) with the $R, P$ of the preceding section, and in the cases (1) b) and (1) c) arise from these by raising to the square or to the cube [§\,152, 4), 5)].

We arrange the fraction (2) so that the highest power of $\tau$ in the denominator $\Phi$ has the coefficient 1.\par\noindent
The remaining coefficients of $\Phi$ are then rationally composed of quantities of the form

\[
\tau\left(\frac{\nu}{\mu}\right) = \tau\left(\frac{\nu \mu'}{m}\right),
\]

and since $\nu\mu'$ is a period of $\tau$, these quantities belong to the roots of the division equation of the periods, and are therefore, since the modulus of the corresponding elliptic functions is an algebraic number, themselves algebraic numbers (§\,58, §\,61).

From this it follows:

2. \gesperrt{The coefficients in $\Phi(\tau)$ are algebraic numbers.}

We extend the fraction $\Psi : \Phi$ by multiplication of numerator and denominator by the product of the conjugate values $\Phi', \Phi'', \Phi''', \ldots$ and obtain:

\weq{3}{\tau(\mu u) = \frac{Z}{N},}

in which now $Z$ and $N$ are integral functions of $\tau$ which may contain a common divisor, while $N$ has rational numerical coefficients.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 604 =====
% !PRINTED 573
\weberpage{573}

By §\,150, (8), (10), (13) the development of $\tau(u)$ in ascending powers of $u$ begins with a negative power of $u$. In the equation

\weq{4}{\tau(\mu u)\, N = Z}

we arrange the function $Z$ in descending powers of $\tau$, develop both sides in ascending powers of $u$, and compare the coefficients of equally high powers of $u$. We then obtain, for the determination of the coefficients of $Z$, a sequence of linear equations, each following one of which contains only one new one of these coefficients, and from this these coefficients can be calculated successively and rationally. If one now attends to the form of the developments of §\,150, it follows that the coefficients of $Z$ are rational functions of $j(\omega)$ and $\sqrt{\Delta}$.

If one frees $N$ and $Z$ from common factors by the Euclidean algorithm, one comes back to the functions $\Psi, \Phi$, and it follows, if by the class field we understand the totality of the rational functions of $\sqrt{\Delta}$ and $j(\omega)$:

3. \gesperrt{The coefficients of the functions $\Phi(\tau)$, $\Psi(\tau)$ in (2) belong to the class field.}

\begin{center}
§\,154. \gesperrt{The Division Field.}
\end{center}

If we free the function $\Phi(x)$ (by rational computation) from all factors occurring in it more than once, there remains an integral function $T_\mu(x)$ of $x$ whose coefficients belong to the class field, and the roots of $T_\mu(x)$ are all those different from one another among the quantities

\weq{1}{\tau\left(\frac{\nu}{\mu}\right).}

Two of these quantities

\[
\tau\left(\frac{\nu}{\mu}\right), \quad \tau\left(\frac{\nu'}{\mu}\right)
\]

are equal to one another,

in case (1) a), when $\dfrac{\nu}{\mu} \equiv \pm\dfrac{\nu'}{\mu}$,

(1) b), when $\dfrac{\nu}{\mu} \equiv \pm\dfrac{\nu'}{\mu} \equiv \pm i\dfrac{\nu'}{\mu}$,

(1) c), when $\dfrac{\nu}{\mu} \equiv \pm\dfrac{\nu'}{\mu}$, $\pm\varrho\dfrac{\nu'}{\mu}$, $\pm\varrho^2\dfrac{\nu'}{\mu}$,
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 605 =====
% !PRINTED 574
\weberpage{574}
%<<CONT
in which the congruence is referred to the periods, and thus (\S\ 152, 1.)
\weq{2}{\begin{aligned}
&\text{in case a)}\text{, when } \nu \equiv \pm\nu', \\
&\text{b)}\text{, when } \nu \equiv \pm\nu', \ \pm i\nu' \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ \mu), \\
&\text{c)}\text{, when } \nu \equiv \pm\nu', \ \pm\varrho\nu', \ \pm\varrho^2\nu'.
\end{aligned}}
Now let
\weq{3}{\mu = \mathfrak{a}\,\mathfrak{m}, \quad \mu_1 = \mathfrak{a}_1\,\mathfrak{m}}
be two integers with the greatest common ideal divisor $\mathfrak{m}$ in the field $\Omega$. Then $T_\mu$ and $T_{\mu_1}$ have a common linear divisor if
\weq{4}{\tau\left(\frac{\nu}{\mu}\right) = \tau\left(\frac{\nu_1}{\mu_1}\right),}
and by (2) this takes place then and only then, when
\weq{5}{\mu\nu_1 \equiv \varepsilon\mu_1\nu \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ \mu\mu_1),}
in which $\varepsilon$ is a \gesperrt{unit} of the field $\Omega$, and thus $\varepsilon = \pm 1$ in general, $\varepsilon = \pm 1, \pm i$ when $\Delta = -4$, and $\varepsilon = \pm 1, \pm\varrho, \pm\varrho^2$ when $\Delta = -3$. But from (5) it follows that $\nu$ must be divisible by $\mathfrak{a}$, and $\nu_1$ by $\mathfrak{a}_1$.

If we think of $\nu$ as given and $\nu_1$ as sought, then the congruence (5) is possible only if $\mu_1\nu$ is divisible by $\mu$; and since $\mathfrak{a}$ and $\mathfrak{a}_1$ are relatively prime, $\nu$ must be divisible by $\mathfrak{a}$. If $\alpha$ is an integer in $\Omega$ divisible by $\mathfrak{a}$, and so constituted that $\alpha : \mathfrak{a}$ is relatively prime to $\mathfrak{m}$, then we may accordingly put
\weq{6}{\nu \equiv \alpha\xi \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ \mu)}
(Bd. II, \S\ 166, 7.), and we obtain all the values $\tau\left(\dfrac{\nu}{\mu}\right)$ that are different from one another, and each of them two, four, or six times, if we let $\xi$ run through a complete system of residues with respect to the modulus $\mathfrak{m}$ (with exclusion of zero). One then obtains all the common roots of $T_\mu$ and $T_{\mu_1}$ in the form
\weq{7}{\tau_\xi = \tau\left(\frac{\alpha\xi}{\mu}\right).}
The greatest common divisor $D_{\mathfrak m}$ of $T_\mu$ and $T_{\mu_1}$ therefore has all the quantities (7) as roots. From $D_{\mathfrak m}$ a divisor $T_{\mathfrak m}$ can still be separated off by rational means, one that has as roots only those among the quantities (7) in which $\xi$ is relatively prime to $\mathfrak{m}$, if one frees $D_{\mathfrak m}$ of all the factors that it has in common with a $D_{\mathfrak m'}$, where $\mathfrak{m}'$ is a divisor of $\mathfrak{m}$. Since in this
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 606 =====
% !PRINTED 575
\weberpage{575}
%<<CONT
consideration in (3) $\mathfrak{m}$ can denote any arbitrary ideal in $\Omega$, we arrive at the following \gesperrt{principal theorem}:

4. \gesperrt{If $\mathfrak{m}$ is an arbitrary ideal of the field $\Omega$, then there exists a function $T_{\mathfrak m}$ in $\Omega$ whose roots are those of the numbers $\tau_\xi$ that are distinct from one another, when $\xi$ runs through a system of incongruent numbers coprime to $\mathfrak{m}$.}

To determine the degree of the function $T_{\mathfrak m}$, we observe that two quantities $\tau_\xi, \tau_{\xi'}$ are equal to one another only when
\weq{8}{\xi \equiv \varepsilon\xi' \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak{m})}
holds. Thus just as many of the $\tau_\xi$ become equal to one another as there are units incongruent modulo $\mathfrak{m}$; in general these are two, for $\Delta = -4$ they are four, and for $\Delta = -3$ they are six. These numbers are, however, reduced still further when different ones among the units $\varepsilon$ are congruent with respect to the modulus $\mathfrak{m}$, that is, when $1 - \varepsilon$ is divisible by $\mathfrak{m}$. But this can occur only when $\mathfrak{m}$ is a divisor of 2 or of 3. Hence:

5. \gesperrt{The degree of the function $T_{\mathfrak m}$ is equal to the number $\psi(\mathfrak{m})$ (Bd. II, \S\ 168) of the numbers in $\Omega$ that are incongruent with respect to the modulus $\mathfrak{m}$ and coprime to $\mathfrak{m}$, divided by the number of units in $\Omega$ that are incongruent with respect to $\mathfrak{m}$.}

The roots of the function $T_{\mathfrak m}$ determine an algebraic field $\mathfrak{T}_{\mathfrak m}$ over the class field, whose relative degree is at most equal to the degree of $T_{\mathfrak m}$, and both degrees are equal when $T_{\mathfrak m}$ is irreducible.

6. \gesperrt{This field $\mathfrak{T}_{\mathfrak m}$ we shall call the division field for the modulus $\mathfrak{m}$.}

These division fields play a similar role for the field $\Omega$ to that played by the cyclotomic fields for the field of rational numbers, except that here the class field is still interposed between them, and to this there is no analogue in the field of rational numbers, just as there is none in any one-class field.

By the multiplication theorem (\S\ 151),
\weq{9}{\tau(\xi u) = \theta_\xi[\tau(u)]}
can be expressed rationally in terms of $\tau(u)$. If we set $u = \xi'\dfrac{\alpha}{\mu}$, then it follows:
\weq{10}{\tau_{\xi\xi'} = \tau\left(\frac{\xi\xi'\alpha}{\mu}\right) = \theta_\xi(\tau_{\xi'}),}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 607 =====
% !PRINTED 576
\weberpage{576}
%<<CONT
and consequently, by interchange of $\xi$ with $\xi'$:
\weq{11}{\theta_\xi(\tau_{\xi'}) = \theta_{\xi'}(\tau_\xi),}
and hence, according to Bd. I, \S\ 169:

7. \gesperrt{The division field is relatively Abelian with respect to the class field.}

The numbers $\xi$, taken with respect to the modulus $\mathfrak{m}$, form a group under multiplication, and the relative group of the division field is isomorphic with this group (or at least with a divisor of this group. The irreducibility of $T_{\mathfrak m}$ will be proved further on, whereby the group of $\mathfrak{T}_{\mathfrak m}$ itself is then established).

\begin{center}
\S\ 155. \gesperrt{Multiplication of the elliptic functions for an}\\
\gesperrt{odd multiplier.}
\end{center}

For the demonstration of the existence of the division field, the use of the \gesperrt{Weierstrass} function and of the $\tau$-function derived from it is very expedient, and it would be most convenient if the further investigation of this field could also be based upon it. But for that the arithmetic nature of the multiplication formulae is not yet sufficiently known, and it is therefore for the present still necessary to consider the complex multiplication and division of the \gesperrt{Jacobi} elliptic functions as well.

Here we wish to give the multiplication formulae which we derived in \S\ 57 yet a somewhat different shape.

We consider throughout, to begin with, the multiplier $m$ as an \gesperrt{odd} number. We set, if
\weq{1}{\varkappa = \frac{\vartheta_{10}}{\vartheta_{00}}}
denotes the modulus of the elliptic functions, following \gesperrt{Kronecker}\footnote{Zur Theorie der elliptischen Funktionen. Sitzungsbericht der Berliner Akademie vom 29. Juli 1886.}:
\weq{2}{\lambda = 4\left(\varkappa + \frac{1}{\varkappa}\right) = 4\,\frac{f(\omega)^4}{f_2(\omega)^4} + 4\,\frac{f_2(\omega)^4}{f(\omega)^4} \quad [\S\ 54, (3)],}
and develop this expression in ascending powers of
\[
q = e^{\pi i \omega}.
\]

%% ===== canonical stable idx 608 =====
% !PRINTED 577
\weberpage{577}
The form of this development can be derived from the product formulae [\S\ 24, (11)]:
\[
\lambda = q^{-\frac{1}{2}} \Pi\left(\frac{1+q^{2\nu-1}}{1+q^{2\nu}}\right)^4 + 16\,q^{\frac{1}{2}}\ \Pi\left(\frac{1+q^{2\nu}}{1+q^{2\nu-1}}\right)^4
\]
and one finds:
\weq{3}{\lambda = q^{-\frac{1}{2}}(1 + \lambda_1 q + \lambda_2 q^2 + \lambda_3 q^3 + \cdots),}
in which the constants $\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \lambda_3, \ldots$ are \gesperrt{integral rational numbers}.

If we further set
\weq{4}{x = \sqrt{\varkappa}\ \operatorname{sn}\left(\frac{w}{\sqrt{\varkappa}},\varkappa\right),}
then, by \S\ 45, (9), (4) remains unchanged when $\varkappa$ is interchanged with $1:\varkappa$. Now $x$ satisfies the differential equation
\weq{5}{\left(\frac{dx}{dw}\right)^2 = 1 - \tfrac{1}{4}\lambda x^2 + x^4.}
If, then, one develops $x$ by \gesperrt{Taylor's} theorem into a series in ascending powers of $w$:
\weq{6}{x = w + X_1 w^3 + X_2 w^5 \ldots,}
then the coefficients $X_1, X_2, \ldots$ are \gesperrt{integral rational functions of $\lambda$ with rational numerical coefficients}, as follows from (5) by the method of indeterminate coefficients.

If one uses the notation of \S\ 42, then
\weq{7}{x = \sqrt{\varkappa}\ \operatorname{sn} v = \frac{\vartheta_{11}(u)}{\vartheta_{01}(u)},}
and, by \S\ 57, IV., with a somewhat modified meaning of the $A, B, C, D$:
\weq{8}{\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{\varkappa}\ \operatorname{sn} mv &= \frac{xA(x)}{D(x)}, \\
\operatorname{cn} mv &= \sqrt{1-\frac{x^2}{\varkappa}}\ \frac{B(x)}{D(x)}, \\
\operatorname{dn} mv &= \sqrt{1-\varkappa x^2}\ \frac{C(x)}{D(x)}.
\end{aligned}}
Here $A(x), B(x), C(x), D(x)$ are integral rational functions of $x$ of degree $\frac{1}{2}(m^2-1)$, and it is to be seen from the recursion formulae \S\ 57, (13), (14) that the functions $A, D$ and the product $BC$ are integral rational functions of $\lambda$, whose
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 609 =====
% !PRINTED 578
\weberpage{578}
%<<CONT
numerical coefficients are rational. That they are integers cannot be
seen, on account of the denominator 2 which appears at first.

In order to investigate this more closely, we consider the roots
of the function $A(x)$: they are, if we set:
\[
\Omega_{h,h'} = \frac{2hK+2h'iK'}{m},
\]
\weq{9}{x_{h,h'} = \sqrt{\varkappa}\,\mathrm{sn}\,\Omega_{h,h'} = \frac{\vartheta_{11}\left(\frac{h+h'\omega}{m},\omega\right)}{\vartheta_{01}\left(\frac{h+h'\omega}{m},\omega\right)},}
in which $h,h'$ may be any integers whatever; only they must not
both be equal to zero. One obtains \gesperrt{all the roots} of
$A(x)$ by letting $h,h'$ each run through a complete system of
residues with respect to the modulus $m$, apart from the combination 0,0.
It is then
\weq{10}{x_{h,h'} = \frac{-i\sum\limits_{-\infty,\infty}^{\nu}(-1)^\nu e^{\frac{\pi i h}{m}(2\nu+1)} q^{\left(\frac{2h+1}{2}+\frac{h'}{m}\right)^2}}{\sum\limits_{-\infty,\infty}^{\nu}(-1)^\nu e^{\frac{2\pi i \nu h}{m}} q^{\left(\nu+\frac{h'}{m}\right)^2}}.}
In order to develop this expression in ascending powers of $q$,
one must first seek out the lowest power of $q$ in the denominator,
that is, the term in which $\nu+\frac{h'}{m}$ becomes as small as
possible. This occurs when $\nu$ is the integer lying nearest to $-h'/m$.
Since $m$ is odd, there is \gesperrt{only one} such
number $\nu$, and formula (10) takes the shape:
\weq{11}{x_{h,h'} = \frac{Q_1}{1+Q_2} = Q_1 - Q_1 Q_2 + Q_1 Q_2^2 - \dots,}
in which $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ are series ordered according to ascending powers of $q$,
whose coefficients are integral algebraic numbers (cyclotomic
numbers).

\gesperrt{Accordingly $x_{h,h'}$ can be developed in ascending powers
of $q$, and the coefficients of this development
are integral algebraic numbers.}

If $S$ is a symmetric function of the $x_{h,h'}$ with rational
integral coefficients, then it too can be developed in the same
way in powers of $q$. On the other hand, by
the fundamental theorem on symmetric functions $S$ is rationally expressible through
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 610 =====
% !PRINTED 579
\weberpage{579}
%<<CONT
expressible in terms of the coefficients of $A(x)$, and is therefore an
integral rational function of $\lambda$ with rational numerical coefficients
of the form:
\weq{12}{S = S_0\lambda^s + S_1\lambda^{s-1} + S_2\lambda^{s-2} + \cdots + S_s,}
in which the $S_0, S_1, S_2, \ldots$, are rational numbers. That they are
\gesperrt{integers} is just what is to be proved. But this follows very simply if in
(12) one substitutes the development (3) for $\lambda$ and then compares
with one another the coefficients of equally high powers of $q$ on both
sides. For one obtains, for the determination of the $S_0, S_1, S_2, \ldots$,
a sequence of linear equations, each following one of which contains only
one new $S_i$, and that with the coefficient 1, while on the other side of
these equations there stand integral algebraic numbers. Accordingly the
$S_0, S_1, S_2, \ldots$, are integral algebraic numbers, and since they are
rational, they are also \gesperrt{integral rational numbers}.

Since we know moreover, by § 57, II and (7), $A(0)$ and $A(\infty)$,
there results for $A(x)$ the expression:
\weq{13}{A(x) = \pm x^{m^2-1} + a_1 x^{m^2-3} + a_2 x^{m^2-5} + \cdots + m,}
\gesperrt{in which the $a_1, a_2, \ldots$, are integral functions of
$\lambda$ with integral coefficients.}

Further, by § 57, (7):
\[
D(x) = \pm x^{m^2-1} A\left(\frac{1}{x}\right),
\]
and consequently:
\weq{14}{\pm D(x) = \pm 1 + a_1 x^2 + a_2 x^4 + \cdots + m x^{m^2-2}.}
\[
\text{[The sign } \pm \text{ in (13) and (14) is determined according to § 57 by}
(-1)^{\frac{m-1}{2}}\text{].}
\]
For the functions $B$ and $C$ the relation holds:
\weq{15}{B(x) = x^{m^2-1} C\left(\frac{1}{x}\right),}
and their roots are therefore reciprocal to one another. The first and
the last coefficient are equal to unity in $B$ and in $C$.

The roots of $B$ are:
\[
y_{h,h'} = \sqrt{\varkappa}\,\mathrm{sn}(\Omega_{h,h'}+K) = \sqrt{\varkappa}\,\frac{\mathrm{cn}\,\Omega_{h,h'}}{\mathrm{dn}\,\Omega_{h,h'}}
\]
\weq{16}{= \frac{\vartheta_{10}\left(\frac{h+h'\omega}{m},\omega\right)}{\vartheta_{00}\left(\frac{h+h'\omega}{m},\omega\right)}}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 611 =====
% !PRINTED 580
\weberpage{580}
%<<CONT
and can be developed in the following way:
\weq{17}{\frac{\sum\limits_{-\infty,\infty}^{\nu} q^{\left(\nu+\frac12+\frac{h'}{m}\right)^2} e^{\frac{(2\nu+1)\pi i}{m}h}}{\sum\limits_{-\infty,\infty}^{\nu} q^{\left(\nu+\frac{h'}{m}\right)^2} e^{\frac{2\nu\pi i}{m}h}}.}
In the denominator of this expression there occurs only one term with
the lowest power of $q$; one obtains it by putting for $\nu$
the integer that lies nearest to the fraction $-h'/m$.

In the numerator too there occurs in general only one lowest
term, whose coefficient is a unit. In the particular
case where $h'/m$ is an integer, however, two
equal lowest terms occur in the numerator, namely (for $h'=0$) $\nu=0,-1$.
Together these give
\[
q^{\frac14}\,2\cos\frac{h\pi}{m}
\]
and $2\cos\dfrac{h\pi}{m}$ is an algebraic unit. [To be inferred from
Bd. I, § 144, (19).]

Accordingly both the expression (17) and \gesperrt{its
reciprocal value} can be developed in ascending powers of $q$ in such a way
that the coefficient of the first term has the value 1
and all the remaining coefficients are integral algebraic numbers.
From this one concludes, just as in regard to $A(x)$, that
$B(x)\,C(x)$ can be represented in the following way:
\weq{18}{B(x)\,C(x) = x^{2m^2-2} + b_1 x^{2m^2-4} + \cdots + 1,}
in which the $b_1, b_2 \ldots$ are integral rational functions of $\lambda$ with integral
rational numerical coefficients. Moreover the coefficients
 $b$ that are equally distant from the beginning and from the end are
equal to one another.

Let us consider further the equation arising from (8):
\weq{19}{x A(x) - \sqrt{\varkappa}\,\mathrm{sn}\,mv\,D(x) = 0,}
which in regard to $x$ is of degree $m^2$. Its roots are the
quantities:
\[
\sqrt{\varkappa}\,\mathrm{sn}\,v, \quad \sqrt{\varkappa}\,\mathrm{sn}(v+\Omega_{h,h'}).
\]
The product of these roots is, apart from the sign,
equal to the independent term in this equation, and hence equal to
\[
\pm \sqrt{\varkappa}\,\mathrm{sn}\,mv,
\]
and from this there results:
\weq{20}{\pm\frac{\sqrt{\varkappa}\,\mathrm{sn}\,mv}{\sqrt{\varkappa}\,\mathrm{sn}\,v} = \prod{}^{h,h'} \sqrt{\varkappa}\,\mathrm{sn}(v+\Omega_{h,h'}).}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 612 =====
% !PRINTED 581
\weberpage{581}
\begin{center}
\textbf{\S\,156.\qquad \gesperrt{Transition to the singular moduli.}}
\end{center}

We now assume that $\omega$ satisfies a quadratic
equation:
\weq{1}{a\omega^2 + b\omega + c = 0}
whose \gesperrt{fundamental discriminant}
\weq{2}{\Delta = b^2 - 4ac}
is negative.

If then $j(\omega)$ is the invariant, the quantity $\lambda$ [§ 155,
(2)] satisfies the equation of degree 6:
\weq{3}{\lambda^6 - 9.16\lambda^4 - [j(\omega)-27.2^8]\lambda^2 + 64[j(\omega)-27.64] = 0,}
whose coefficients are integral algebraic numbers. Consequently
$\lambda$ is itself an \gesperrt{integral algebraic number} (Bd. II, § 154, 11.)\footnote{It is this circumstance that particularly recommends the introduction of $\lambda$ in place of $\varkappa$, because $\varkappa$ is in general not an integer, but only $4\varkappa$ is.}
and in § 135 we have seen that $\lambda$ is a class invariant of the
discriminant $4\Delta$ or $16\Delta$.

We therefore adjoin the number $\lambda$ to the class field $\mathfrak{K}(\Delta)$
and obtain a class field:
\weq{4}{\begin{array}{l}
\mathfrak{L} = \mathfrak{K}(4\Delta), \text{ if } \Delta \equiv 0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 4), \text{ or } \equiv 1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 8).\\
\mathfrak{L} = \mathfrak{K}(16\Delta), \qquad \Delta \equiv 5\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 8).
\end{array}}
If $h$ is the class number of $\Delta$, and therefore the relative degree of $\mathfrak{K}(\Delta)$
with respect to the quadratic field $\Omega = \mathfrak{R}(\sqrt{\Delta})$, and $h'$ the
relative degree of $\mathfrak{L}$ with respect to $\Omega$, then (§ 100, § 123):
\weq{5}{\begin{array}{ll}
h' = h, & \text{if } \Delta \equiv 1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 8),\\
h' = 2h, & \text{,,}\quad \Delta \equiv 0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 4),\\
h' = 6h, & \text{,,}\quad \Delta \equiv 5\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 8).
\end{array}}
In the first of these three cases $\mathfrak{L}$ is therefore identical with $\mathfrak{K}(\Delta)$.

Through the substitution of the singular modulus $\omega$ the
coefficients $a_1, a_2 \ldots, b_1, b_2, \ldots$, in § 155, (13), (18) pass into integral
algebraic numbers, and from this it follows, Bd. II, § 154, 11.,
that the roots of $A(x)$, namely:
\weq{6}{\sqrt{\varkappa}\,\mathrm{sn}\,\Omega_{h,h'}, \text{\gesperrt{integers}}}
and the roots of $B(x)$:
\weq{7}{\sqrt{\varkappa}\,\frac{\mathrm{cn}\,\Omega_{h,h'}}{\mathrm{dn}\,\Omega_{h,h'}}, \text{\gesperrt{units}}}
are.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 613 =====
% !PRINTED 582
\weberpage{582}

Now for variable $\varkappa$ and $v$ we have [\S\,45, (5)]:
\weq{8}{\mathrm{dn}\,(v,\varkappa) = \dfrac{\mathrm{dn}\,(iv,\varkappa')}{\mathrm{cn}\,(iv,\varkappa')}.}
If we here set:
\[
v = \Omega_{h,h'} = \dfrac{2hK + 2h'iK'}{m},
\]
\[
iv = \dfrac{-2h'K' + 2hiK}{m} = \Omega'_{-h',h},
\]
then the $\Omega'$ have the same meaning for $\varkappa'$ as the $\Omega$ have for $\varkappa$, i.\,e. they correspond to the interchange of $(\omega, -1/\omega)$, and it follows from (7) and (8) that also
\[
\dfrac{\mathrm{dn}\,\Omega_{h,h'}}{\sqrt{\varkappa'}} \text{ is a unit.}
\]
Thus also
\[
\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\varkappa'}}\,\mathrm{dn}\,\Omega_{h,h'} = \dfrac{\vartheta_{00}\left(\dfrac{h+h'\omega}{m}\right)}{\vartheta_{01}\left(\dfrac{h+h'\omega}{m}\right)},
\]
\weq{9}{\sqrt{\dfrac{\varkappa}{\varkappa'}}\,\mathrm{cn}\,\Omega_{h,h'} = \dfrac{\vartheta_{10}\left(\dfrac{h+h'\omega}{m}\right)}{\vartheta_{01}\left(\dfrac{h+h'\omega}{m}\right)}\ \text{are algebraic units.}}
From formula \S\,155, (20) there follows for $v=0$:
\weq{10}{\pm m = \overset{h,h'}{\varPi}\ \sqrt{\varkappa}\ \mathrm{sn}\,\Omega_{h,h'} = \varPi\, \varkappa_{h,h'}.}
1. \gesperrt{The integers $\varkappa_{\mu,\mu'}$ are therefore divisors of the number $m$.}

We now set, when $m$ and $n$ are two odd numbers:
\[
\Omega_{h,h'} = \dfrac{2hK + 2h'iK'}{m},
\]
\[
H_{l,l'} = \dfrac{2lK + 2l'iK'}{n},
\]
and substitute in formula \S\,155, (20):
\[
v = H_{l,l'}.
\]
This gives:
\weq{11}{\dfrac{\sqrt{\varkappa}\,\mathrm{sn}\,m\,H_{l,v'}}{\sqrt{\varkappa}\,\mathrm{sn}\,H_{l,v'}} = \overset{h,h'}{\varPi}\ \sqrt{\varkappa}\ \mathrm{sn}\,(H_{l,v'} + \Omega_{h,h'}), % [sic] printed \textquotedbl{}H_{l,v'}\textquotedbl{} here though defined above as H_{l,l'}
}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 614 =====
% !PRINTED 583
\weberpage{583}

%<<CONT
in which
\[
H_{l,v'} + \Omega_{h,h'} = \dfrac{2(lm+hn)K + 2(lm+h'n)iK'}{mn}, % [sic] \textquotedbl{}H_{l,v'}\textquotedbl{} as on preceding page
\]
and consequently the factors of the product (11):
\[
\sqrt{\varkappa}\ \mathrm{sn}\,(H_{l,v'} + \Omega_{h,h'})
\]
are integers [by (6)]. If in (11) one again interchanges $m$ and $n$, it follows that:
\weq{12}{\dfrac{\sqrt{\varkappa}\ \mathrm{sn}\,n\,\Omega_{h,h'}}{\sqrt{\varkappa}\ \mathrm{sn}\,\Omega_{h,h'}} \text{ is an integer.}}
This holds for arbitrary odd $n$, and hence also, when $n$ is relatively prime to $m$, for $n^{-1}$ (mod $m$); and so it is likewise true that
\[
\dfrac{\sqrt{\varkappa}\ \mathrm{sn}\,n^{-1}\,\Omega_{h,h'}}{\sqrt{\varkappa}\ \mathrm{sn}\,\Omega_{h,h'}} \text{ is an integer.}
\]
If here one replaces $h,h'$ by $nh, nh'$, it follows that also
\[
\dfrac{\sqrt{\varkappa}\ \mathrm{sn}\,\Omega_{h,h'}}{\sqrt{\varkappa}\ \mathrm{sn}\,n\,\Omega_{h,h'}} \text{ is an integer,}
\]
and therefore the quotient (12) is a \gesperrt{unit}, or, expressed otherwise:

2. \gesperrt{If $n$ runs through a sequence of odd numbers coprime to $m$, then the integers:}
\weq{13}{\sqrt{\varkappa}\ \mathrm{sn}\,n\,\Omega_{h,h'}}
\gesperrt{are associated with one another.}

\begin{center}
\S\,157. \gesperrt{Complex Multipliers.}
\end{center}

Let $\omega$ satisfy, as in the preceding section, the quadratic equation
\weq{1}{a\omega^2 + b\omega + c = 0}
with negative fundamental discriminant
\[
\varDelta = b^2 - 4ac,
\]
so let:
\weq{2}{\omega = \dfrac{-b + \sqrt{\varDelta}}{2a}.}
As in the preceding section, we base our considerations upon the function
\weq{3}{\sqrt{\varkappa}\ \mathrm{sn}\,v = \dfrac{\vartheta_{11}(u)}{\vartheta_{01}(u)} = \boldsymbol{s}(u)}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 615 =====
% !PRINTED 584
\weberpage{584}

%<<CONT
as our basis, and we denote it, as a function of $u = v/2K$, by $\boldsymbol{S}(u)$. This function then has the double periodicity expressed by
\weq{4}{\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol{S}(u+1) &= -\boldsymbol{S}(u), \\
\boldsymbol{S}(u+\omega) &= \boldsymbol{S}(u)
\end{aligned}}
All periods of $\boldsymbol{S}(u)$ are contained in the form $2m + n\omega$, in which $m, n$ are integral rational numbers, and they therefore pass over into integers on multiplication by $a$.

Two numbers $u, u'$ that differ only by a period are called congruent with respect to the modulus $2, \omega$:
\[
u' \equiv u \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 2, \omega).
\]
\gesperrt{Since the function $\mathrm{sn}\,v$ takes a value only twice in the period parallelogram, we have}
\[
\boldsymbol{S}(u) = \boldsymbol{S}(u'),
\]
\gesperrt{only when either}
\weq{5}{\begin{aligned}
u &\equiv u' \\
u &\equiv 1 - u'
\end{aligned}\quad (\mathrm{mod}\ 2, \omega)}
\gesperrt{holds, and $\boldsymbol{S}(u)$ vanishes only when}
\[
u \equiv 0, 1 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 2, \omega)
\]
\gesperrt{holds.}

Since every fractional number in $\Omega$ can be transformed into an integer by multiplication with an integral rational number, the following theorem results from \S\,156, (6): % [sic] German column prints \textquotedbl{}ergiebt\textquotedbl{}, the older spelling, though the page uses modern spelling elsewhere; reproduced as printed

1. \gesperrt{If $\eta$ is any fractional number of the field $\Omega$, then $\boldsymbol{S}(\eta)$ is an algebraic number, and if in particular $\eta$ can be represented in such a way that its denominator is relatively prime to 2, then $\boldsymbol{S}(\eta)$ is an integral algebraic number.}

Now let
\weq{6}{\mu = y + x\sqrt{\varDelta}}
be an integer in $\Omega$, in which $x, y$ are integral rational numbers\footnote{In the case of an even $\varDelta$, $\mu$ can accordingly be any integer from $\Omega$. In the case of an odd $\varDelta$, $\mu$ is a number of the order [2].}, and
\[
\mu' = y - x\sqrt{\varDelta},
\]
the number conjugate to $\mu$. Further
\weq{7}{m = \mu\mu' = y^2 - \varDelta x^2}
the norm of $\mu$, which we assume to be \gesperrt{odd}.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 616 =====
% !PRINTED 585
\weberpage{585}

It is then, by (2),
\weq{8}{\begin{aligned}
\mu &= y + bx + 2a\omega x, \\
\mu\omega &= -2cx + (y-bx)\omega, \\
m &= (y+bx)(y-bx) + 4acx^2,
\end{aligned}}
from which it follows that
\[
y + bx \text{ and } y - bx
\]
are odd.

From this there results, by (4):
\weq{9}{\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol{S}[\mu(u+1)] &= -\boldsymbol{S}(\mu u), \\
\boldsymbol{S}[\mu(u+\omega)] &= \boldsymbol{S}(\mu u).
\end{aligned}}
The function $\boldsymbol{S}(\mu u)$ therefore has the same periods as $s(u)$, % [sic] printed lower-case \textquotedbl{}s(u)\textquotedbl{} here though the function is elsewhere denoted \boldsymbol{S}(u)
and since $\boldsymbol{S}(\mu u)$ is an odd function of $u$, it can be expressed rationally by $\boldsymbol{S}(u)$. We denote by $A(\boldsymbol{S})$, $D(\boldsymbol{S})$ integral rational functions of $\boldsymbol{S} = \boldsymbol{S}(u)$, which moreover contain only the even powers of $\boldsymbol{S}$, and set:
\weq{10}{\boldsymbol{S}(\mu u) = \mu\,\boldsymbol{S}(u)\,\dfrac{A(\boldsymbol{S})}{D(\boldsymbol{S})}.}
The values of $\boldsymbol{S}(u)$ for which $\boldsymbol{S}(\mu u)$ becomes zero or infinite are, by 3., algebraic numbers, and since the coefficients of $A$ and $D$ can be composed out of these, these too are algebraic numbers. In order to determine their nature more closely, we think of the fraction (10) as first extended in such a way that $D$ receives rational coefficients. This is brought about by multiplying numerator and denominator by the product of all the factors conjugate to the denominator. We can therefore put $A(\boldsymbol{S})$ and $D(\boldsymbol{S})$ into the form:
\weq{11}{\begin{aligned}
A(\boldsymbol{S}) &= A_1 + A_3\boldsymbol{S}^2 + A_5\boldsymbol{S}^4 + \cdots, \\
D(\boldsymbol{S}) &= D_1 + D_3\boldsymbol{S}^2 + D_5\boldsymbol{S}^4 + \cdots,
\end{aligned}}
in which the $D_1, D_3, \dots$, are by our assumption rational numbers, while $A_1, A_3, \dots$, are to be determined. If we set, as in \S\,155, (4), (6):
\[
w = \sqrt{\varkappa}\,v = 2\sqrt{\varkappa}\,Ku,
\]
then $\boldsymbol{S}(u)$ goes over into $\sqrt{\varkappa}\ \mathrm{sn}\left(\dfrac{w}{\sqrt{\varkappa}}\right)$, and equation (10) gives:
\weq{12}{\dfrac{D\left[\sqrt{\varkappa}\ \mathrm{sn}\left(\dfrac{\omega}{\sqrt{\varkappa}}\right)\right]\ \sqrt{\varkappa}\ \mathrm{sn}\left(\dfrac{\mu w}{\sqrt{\varkappa}}\right)}{\mu\ \mathrm{sn}\left(\dfrac{w}{\sqrt{\varkappa}}\right)} = A_1 + A_3\boldsymbol{S}^2 + A_5\boldsymbol{S}^4 + \cdots}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 617 =====
% !PRINTED 586
\weberpage{586}
If one develops the left side in powers of $w$, the coefficients are
rationally expressible through $\lambda$ and $\sqrt{\Delta}$, and hence
belong to the field
\[
\mathfrak{L} = \mathfrak{R}(\lambda, \sqrt{\Delta})
\]
If one develops the right side in the same way and orders it by the
powers of $w$, then $A_\nu$ appears first in the coefficient of
$w^{\nu-1}$, and indeed carrying the factor 1. Accordingly $A_\nu$ can
be determined once the earlier coefficients have already been
determined, and it follows that all these coefficients belong to the
field $\mathfrak{L}$.

Since afterwards the numerator and denominator of the fraction $A/D$
can again be freed from common factors by rational calculation, the
following theorem results:

2. \gesperrt{If in the expression (8) the numerator and denominator
$A(\boldsymbol{s})$, $D(\boldsymbol{s})$ are freed from common factors,
then these functions belong to the field $\mathfrak{L}$.}

In order to represent the function $A(x)$, we take the coefficient of
the highest power of $x$ equal to 1 and investigate for which values of
$u$ the function $\boldsymbol{s}(\mu u)$ vanishes. We denote a value
$u$ for which $\boldsymbol{s}(\mu u)$ vanishes by $2\varrho/\mu$, and
then obtain as the condition for the vanishing, by (5), one of the two
congruences
\[
2\varrho \equiv 0, 1 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ 2, \omega).
\]
Thus $\varrho$ is a number of the field $\Omega$ which may indeed be
fractional, but can have no other denominators than a divisor of $2a$.
On the other hand one may alter $\varrho$ by a multiple of $\mu$
without the value $\boldsymbol{s}(2\varrho/\mu)$ being changed, and
since only the latter is of consequence, and since the congruence
\[
\varrho \equiv \frac{\xi}{2a} \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ \mu),
\]
where $\xi$ is an integer in $\Omega$, can be satisfied by an integer
$\varrho$, we may assume $\varrho$ to be an \gesperrt{integer} if we \gesperrt{presuppose
that the first coefficient $a$ in (1) is odd and relatively prime to
$\mu$.} We hold fast to this assumption from now on.

If, then, we let $\varrho$ run through a complete system of residues
with respect to the modulus $\mu$, with exclusion of zero, we obtain
all the values of $\boldsymbol{s}$ for which $A(\boldsymbol{s})$
vanishes, in the form:
\weq{13}{\boldsymbol{s}\left(\frac{2\varrho}{\mu}\right).}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 618 =====
% !PRINTED 587
\weberpage{587}
It remains to be shown that no two of the numbers (13) are equal to
one another. If we had
\[
\boldsymbol{s}\left(\frac{2\varrho}{\mu}\right) = \boldsymbol{s}\left(\frac{2\varrho'}{\mu}\right),
\]
without $\varrho \equiv \varrho'$ (mod $\mu$) holding, then by (5)
\[
\frac{2(\varrho + \varrho')}{\mu} \equiv 1 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ 2, \omega)
\]
would have to hold. Hence $a(1+\omega)$ would have to be divisible by 2,
and hence also, if $\omega$ is conjugate to $\omega'$, $a(1+\omega')$ divisible by 2,
and consequently
\[
a(\omega - \omega') = \sqrt{\Delta} \equiv 0 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ 2).
\]
Thus $\Delta$ would be divisible by 4, and $\frac{1}{4}\Delta = \frac{1}{4}a^2(\omega - \omega')^2$
would likewise still be a discriminant, which contradicts the assumption
that $\Delta$ is a fundamental discriminant\footnote{$b$ would have to be even and $a-b+c$ divisible by 4, and
$\frac{1}{4}\Delta = \left(\frac{b}{2}-a\right)^2 - a(a-b+c)$ would be a discriminant. For an arbitrary
discriminant $D$ the same end could be attained by adding to the
numerator of the expressions (13) a power of 2 as a factor.}. Accordingly the
quantities (13), whose number amounts to $m-1$ (Bd. II, § 165), are all
different from one another, and there results
\weq{14}{A(x) = \overset{\varrho}{\prod}\left[x - \boldsymbol{s}\left(\frac{2\varrho}{\mu}\right)\right].}

By § 44, (20) the function $\boldsymbol{s}(u)$ satisfies the equation:
\[
\boldsymbol{s}\left(u + \frac{\omega}{2}\right) = \frac{1}{\boldsymbol{s}(u)},
\]
and, because of (8) and (4):
\[
\boldsymbol{s}\left[\mu\left(u + \frac{\omega}{2}\right)\right] = \frac{(-1)^{cx}}{\boldsymbol{s}(\mu u)},
\]
and accordingly there results from (10), if $u$ is replaced by $u + \dfrac{\omega}{2}$
:
\weq{15}{\frac{(-1)^{cx}}{\boldsymbol{s}(\mu u)} = \frac{1}{\boldsymbol{s}(u)}\,\frac{A\left(\dfrac{1}{\boldsymbol{s}}\right)}{D\left(\dfrac{1}{\boldsymbol{s}}\right)} = \frac{(-1)^{cx} D(\boldsymbol{s})}{\boldsymbol{s}(u) A(\boldsymbol{s})},}
\weq{16}{A(\boldsymbol{s}) A\left(\frac{1}{\boldsymbol{s}}\right) = (-1)^{cx} D(\boldsymbol{s}) D\left(\frac{1}{\boldsymbol{s}}\right).}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 619 =====
% !PRINTED 588
\weberpage{588}

Since $A$ and $D$ are without common divisors, we have, for a variable $x$ and a constant $h$:
\[
h\,x^{m-1} A\!\left(\frac{1}{x}\right) = D(x),
\]
and, on replacing $x$ by $1/x$:
\[
h\,A(x) = x^{m-1} D\!\left(\frac{1}{x}\right),
\]
and by (16):
\[
h^2 = (-1)^{cx}.
\]
Thus
\weq{17}{D(x) = \varepsilon\,x^{m-1} A\!\left(\frac{1}{x}\right),}
where $\varepsilon = \pm 1$ or $= \pm i$. By (16) this depends on whether $cx$ is even or odd.\footnote{From § 138 it follows that $i$ is contained in the field $\mathfrak{L}$; (17) is therefore not in contradiction with Theorem 2.}

If we therefore use the notation (10) again, but now under the hypothesis that $A$ and $D$ are without common divisors, we obtain:
\weq{18}{\varepsilon\,\boldsymbol{S}(\mu u) = \frac{A_1\boldsymbol{S} + A_3\boldsymbol{S}^3 + \cdots A_{m-2}\boldsymbol{S}^{m-2} + \boldsymbol{S}^m}{1 + A_{m-2}\boldsymbol{S}^2 + \cdots A_3\boldsymbol{S}^{m-3} + A_1\boldsymbol{S}^{m-1}},}
and the $A_1, A_3, \ldots, A_{m-1}$ are \gesperrt{integers of the field} $\mathfrak{L}$, for they are the symmetric fundamental functions of the integers (13).

In particular, if one sets $u=0$, it follows that:
\weq{19}{A_1 = \varepsilon\mu,}
and from this:
\weq{20}{\varepsilon\mu = \prod\nolimits^{\varrho} \boldsymbol{S}\!\left(\frac{2\varrho}{\mu}\right).}
The $\boldsymbol{S}\!\left(\dfrac{2\varrho}{\mu}\right)$ are therefore divisors of $\mu$.

From (10) it follows that:
\weq{21}{\boldsymbol{S}A(\boldsymbol{S}) - \boldsymbol{S}(\mu u)D(\boldsymbol{S}) = 0,}
and this, when $\boldsymbol{S}(\mu u)$ is regarded as given, is an equation for $\boldsymbol{S}(u)$ of degree $m$, whose roots are:
\[
\boldsymbol{S}(u),\ \boldsymbol{S}\!\left(u+\frac{2\varrho}{\mu}\right).
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 620 =====
% !PRINTED 589
\weberpage{589}
%<<CONT

The product of these roots is therefore, since $\boldsymbol{s}^m$ has the coefficient 1,
equal to the negative independent term, i.\,e. it is:
\weq{22}{\varepsilon\,\frac{\boldsymbol{s}(\mu u)}{\boldsymbol{s}(u)} = \overset{\varrho}{\prod} \boldsymbol{s}\left(u + \frac{2\varrho}{\mu}\right),}
and from this, for $u = 0$, as above:
\weq{23}{\varepsilon\mu = \overset{\varrho}{\prod} \boldsymbol{s}\left(\frac{2\varrho}{\mu}\right).}

Now let $\eta$ be a fractional number in $\Omega$ with the odd
ideal denominator $\mathfrak{a}$; then it follows from (22) that $\boldsymbol{s}(\mu\eta)/\boldsymbol{s}(\eta)$ is an
integer, if $\mu$ is an arbitrary number (6) in $\Omega$. If we take
$\mu$ relatively prime to $\mathfrak{a}$ and set $\mu'\mu \equiv 1$ (mod $\mathfrak{a}$), then we may
replace $\eta$ by $\mu'\eta$ and find that $\boldsymbol{s}(\eta)/\boldsymbol{s}(\mu'\eta)$
is likewise an integer, in which $\mu'$ is just as arbitrary as $\mu$. Consequently
$\boldsymbol{s}(\eta)/\boldsymbol{s}(\mu\eta)$ is also an integer and hence a \gesperrt{unit}.

We have therefore the theorem:

3. \gesperrt{If $\eta$ is a number in $\Omega$ with odd ideal denominator,
and if $\mu$ runs through a sequence of numbers relatively prime
to $\mathfrak{a}$, then the numbers}
\[
\boldsymbol{s}(\mu\eta)
\]
\gesperrt{are associated with one another.}

Yet a further consequence follows from this if one sets
$u = 2\varrho_1/\mu_1$ in (22):
\weq{24}{\frac{\boldsymbol{s}\left(\dfrac{2\mu\varrho_1}{\mu_1}\right)}{\boldsymbol{s}\left(\dfrac{2\varrho_1}{\mu_1}\right)} = \overset{\varrho}{\prod} \boldsymbol{s}\left(\frac{2\varrho_1}{\mu_1} + \frac{2\varrho}{\mu}\right).}

If now $\mu$ and $\varrho_1$ are relatively prime to $\mu_1$, then by 3. the left side
is a unit, and consequently all the factors of the
right side
\weq{25}{\boldsymbol{s}\left(\frac{2\varrho_1}{\mu_1} + \frac{2\varrho}{\mu_2}\right),}
% [sic] The source prints \mu_2 here; equation (24) has \mu.
which are indeed integers, must be units.

But every $\boldsymbol{s}(\eta)$ can be brought into this form if
\[
\eta = \frac{\nu}{\mu}
\]
is a fractional number in $\Omega$ in whose denominator two distinct
prime ideals divide, provided this denominator is odd. For in this case one
can decompose the denominator $\mu$ of $\eta$ into two ideals $\mathfrak{a}_1\mathfrak{a}_2$
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 621 =====
% !PRINTED 590
\weberpage{590}
%<<CONT
which are relatively prime to one another, and one can then
determine two odd integers $\alpha_1, \alpha_2$ in $\Omega$ that are relatively
prime to one another, of which the one is divisible by $\mathfrak{a}_1$, the
other by $\mathfrak{a}_2$. Then $\eta\alpha_1\alpha_2$ is an integer in $\Omega$,
and by Bd.\ II, \S\,166, (4) one can determine two integers $\varrho_1, \varrho_2$
in such a way that
\[
\frac{\nu\,\alpha_1\alpha_2}{\mu} = \varrho_1\alpha_2 + \varrho_2\alpha_1
\]
and therefore
\[
\boldsymbol{S}\!\left(\frac{2\nu}{\mu}\right) = \boldsymbol{S}\!\left(\frac{2\varrho_1}{\alpha_1} + \frac{2\varrho_2}{\alpha_2}\right)
\]
holds. But this is of the form (25). From it we obtain
the theorem:

4. \gesperrt{If a fractional number $\eta$ in $\Omega$ with odd
denominator contains two or more distinct prime factors in the
denominator, then $\boldsymbol{S}(\eta)$ is a unit.}

\begin{center}
\textbf{\S\ 158. \gesperrt{Decomposition of the Function $\boldsymbol{A}(x)$.}}
\end{center}

Now let
\weq{1}{\begin{aligned} \mu &= y + x\sqrt{\Delta}, \\ \mu_1 &= y_1 + x_1\sqrt{\Delta} \end{aligned}}
be two odd integers in $\Omega$ of the form \S\,157, (6). Let
$\mathfrak{m}$ be the greatest common ideal divisor of $\mu$ and $\mu_1$.
If one therefore sets
\weq{2}{\begin{aligned} \mu &= \mathfrak{m}\mathfrak{a}, \\ \mu_1 &= \mathfrak{m}\mathfrak{a}_1 \end{aligned}}
then $\mathfrak{a}$ and $\mathfrak{a}_1$ are two \gesperrt{equivalent ideals} without a common
divisor.

The functions $\boldsymbol{A}(x)$ that correspond to the two numbers $\mu, \mu_1$
we denote by
\[
\boldsymbol{A}_\mu(x), \ \boldsymbol{A}_{\mu_1}(x),
\]
and we ask what common roots these functions
have, that is, when the equation:
\weq{3}{\boldsymbol{S}\!\left(\frac{2\varrho}{\mu}\right) = \boldsymbol{S}\!\left(\frac{2\varrho_1}{\mu_1}\right)}
can be satisfied, when $\varrho$ is taken with respect to the modulus $\mu$, and $\varrho_1$
with respect to the modulus $\mu_1$.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 622 =====
% !PRINTED 591
\weberpage{591}
Since the congruence
\[
\frac{2\varrho}{\mu} + \frac{2\varrho_1}{\mu_1} \equiv 1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 2,\,\omega)
\]
is not possible, as one shows exactly as above (p.\ 589), the following is
necessary and sufficient for equation (3):
\weq{4}{\frac{2(\mu_1\varrho - \mu\varrho_1)}{\mu\mu_1} \equiv 0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 2,\,\omega).}
From this it follows:
\weq{5}{\mu\varrho_1 \equiv \mu_1\varrho\ (\mathrm{mod}\ \mu\mu_1),}
and this is possible only if
\weq{6}{\varrho \equiv 0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak{a}), \quad \varrho_1 \equiv 0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak{a}_1).}
If conversely the conditions (5) and (6) are satisfied, then:
\[
\frac{2\varrho}{\mu} - \frac{2\varrho_1}{\mu_1}
\]
is an integer and equation (3) is satisfied.

Now take an integer in $\Omega$ divisible by $\mathfrak{a}$:
\weq{7}{\alpha = \mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{c},}
in which $\mathfrak{c}$ is relatively prime to $\mu$ and $\mu_1$. If then $\varrho$ is
divisible by $\mathfrak{a}$, one can determine an integer $\xi$ with respect to the
modulus $\mathfrak{m}$ from the congruence
\[
\varrho \equiv \alpha\xi\ (\mathrm{mod}\ \mu)
\]
(Bd.\ II, \S\,166, 7.); then
\weq{8}{\alpha_1 = \frac{\alpha\mu_1}{\mu} = \mathfrak{a}_1\mathfrak{c}}
is an integer divisible by $\mathfrak{a}_1\mathfrak{c}$ and by no other ideal,
and from (5) there results
\[
\varrho_1 \equiv \alpha_1\xi\ (\mathrm{mod}\ \mu_1).
\]
5. \gesperrt{We thus obtain the common roots of
$\boldsymbol{A}_\mu(x), \boldsymbol{A}_{\mu_1}(x)$ in the form:}
\weq{9}{\boldsymbol{s}\!\left(\frac{2\alpha\xi}{\mu}\right) = \boldsymbol{s}\!\left(\frac{2\alpha_1\xi}{\mu_1}\right),}
\gesperrt{where $\xi$ runs through a complete system of residues with respect to the modulus $\mathfrak{m}$.}

\gesperrt{Here $\mathfrak{m}$ can denote any arbitrary odd ideal in $\Omega$.}

For to every such ideal one can choose two numbers $\mu, \mu_1$
of the form (2), and then choose $\omega$ among the equivalent
numbers in such a way that $\mathfrak{a}$ becomes odd and relatively prime to $\mu\mu_1$.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 623 =====
% !PRINTED 592
\weberpage{592}
If one seeks the greatest common divisor of $\boldsymbol{A}_\mu$ and
$\boldsymbol{A}_{\mu_1}$, one obtains an integral function $\boldsymbol{A}_{\mathfrak{m}}$ whose coefficients % [sic] German source prints singular "Koeffizient"
are integers in $\mathfrak{L}$ and whose roots are the quantities (9); and
if one finally frees $\boldsymbol{A}_{\mathfrak{m}}$ of the factors that it has in common
with any $\boldsymbol{A}_{\mathfrak{m}'}$ in which $\mathfrak{m}'$ is a proper divisor of $\mathfrak{m}$, one
obtains an integral function:
\weq{10}{T_{\mathfrak{m}}(x) = x^{\nu} - \tau_{\nu-1}x^{\nu-1} + \tau_{\nu-2}x^{\nu-2} - \cdots \pm \tau_0,}
whose roots are only those among the quantities (8) in which $\xi$
is relatively prime to $\mathfrak{m}$.

The degree $\nu$ of this function is to be determined according to Bd.\ II, \S\,168.
We shall call it the \gesperrt{ideal division function}. Its coefficients
are \gesperrt{integers} of the field $\mathfrak{L}$, and in
particular
\weq{11}{\tau_0 = \overset{\xi}{\Pi}\,\boldsymbol{S}\!\left(\frac{2\alpha\xi}{\mu}\right),}
in which $\xi$ runs through a complete system of numbers incongruent to one
another and coprime to $\mathfrak{m}$.

The roots of $T_{\mathfrak{m}}(x)$ are equal and opposite, and
we obtain an equation of degree $1/2\,\nu$ for the quantity
\[
\boldsymbol{S}\!\left(\frac{2\alpha\xi}{\mu}\right)^{2}.
\]
By adjunction of these quantities to the field $\mathfrak{L}$ there arises
a field $\mathfrak{T}_{\mathfrak{m}}$, which we likewise call a division field. It
results from the division field of \S\,154 by adjunction
of $x$. The group of this field is contained in the group of the numbers
$\xi\ (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak{m})$, as follows easily from the multiplication formulae.

We note further that the general division field
$\mathfrak{T}_{\mathfrak{m}}$ can be reduced, by application of the addition theorem, to
the case where $\mathfrak{m}$ is a power of a prime ideal in $\Omega$.

\begin{center}
\textbf{\S\ 159. Prime Ideals.}
\end{center}

6. \gesperrt{If $\eta$ is a fractional number of the field $\Omega$ which in
reduced form has the odd ideal denominator $\mathfrak{a}$, and if $\mathfrak{m}$
is an ideal relatively prime to $\mathfrak{a}$, then the integer $\boldsymbol{S}(\eta)$ is relatively
prime to $\mathfrak{m}$.}

For let there be taken in $\Omega$ an integer $\mu$ divisible by $\mathfrak{a}$ and
 coprime to $2\mathfrak{m}$. Then $\mu\eta$ is an integer. In the
product \S\,157, (23)
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 624 =====
% !PRINTED 593
\weberpage{593}
%<<CONT
\weq{1}{\mu = \overset{\varrho}{\Pi}\,\boldsymbol{S}\!\left(\frac{2\varrho}{\mu}\right)}
there occurs a number $2\varrho$ which is congruent to $\mu\eta$ with respect to
 the modulus $\mu$. Consequently $\boldsymbol{S}(\eta)$ is a divisor of $\mu$ and
hence relatively prime to $\mathfrak{m}$, as was to be proved.

Let us now assume that in the formula (11), \S\,158
\weq{2}{\tau_0 = \overset{\xi}{\Pi}\,\boldsymbol{S}\!\left(\frac{2\alpha\xi}{\mu}\right)}
$\mathfrak{m}$ is a prime ideal of the field $\Omega$, and let us accordingly set
$\mathfrak{m} = \mathfrak{p}$, so that $\xi$ runs through a complete system of residues with
respect to the modulus $\mathfrak{p}$, with the exclusion of zero.

If we then take $\mu$ so that it is divisible only by the first power
of $\mathfrak{p}$ and is not divisible by some arbitrarily chosen other prime ideal
$\mathfrak{p}'$, then by Theorem 6.\ $\tau_0$ cannot be divisible by $\mathfrak{p}'$.
Now $\tau_0$ depends only on the ideal $\mathfrak{p}$ and is independent
of how the number $\mu$ is otherwise taken.
Consequently by Theorem 6.\ $\tau_0$ is divisible by no prime ideal
different from $\mathfrak{p}$. But neither can $\mathfrak{p}$ divide $\tau_0$ in a higher
than the first power, for the factors of the
product (1) all occur among the factors of the product (2),
and consequently $\mu$ is divisible by $\tau_0$. Accordingly we may
set outright
\weq{3}{\tau_0 = \mathfrak{p}}
and since $\tau_0$ is a number in the field $\mathfrak{L}$, it follows:

7. \gesperrt{Every odd prime ideal of the field $\Omega$ is a
field $\mathfrak{L}$, a principal ideal.}
% [sic] German source prints ``ist ein Körper $\mathfrak L$, ein Hauptideal''; sense requires ``ist im Körper $\mathfrak L$ ein Hauptideal''.

The assumption that $\mu$ should be relatively prime to $\mathfrak{a}$ likewise
involves no restriction of this theorem. For, with $\mathfrak{p}$ given, we can
select from among the equivalent forms $(a, b, c)$, without changing $\lambda$,
one for which this requirement is fulfilled.

This does not, however, yet prove that $\mathfrak{p}$ is also a principal
ideal in the class field $\mathfrak{K}(\Delta)$ itself. At least, this follows
only in the case $\Delta \equiv 1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 8)$, where $\mathfrak{K}$ is identical with
$\mathfrak{L}$\footnote{Cf.\ on this \S\,122, where the case of the prime 2 is also settled.}.

By Theorem 3., \S\,157 the factors of the product (2)
are all associated with one another. The number of these factors is
$N(\mathfrak{p}) - 1$, and accordingly we may also set:
\weq{4}{\mathfrak{p} = \Bigl[\boldsymbol{S}\!\left(\frac{2\alpha}{\mu}\right)\Bigr]^{N(\mathfrak{p})-1}.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 625 =====
% !PRINTED 594
\weberpage{594}
§ 160. \gesperrt{Prime ideals of the first degree in $\mathfrak{T}_{\mathfrak{m}}$.}

What now matters above all is to seek out the primes $p$ that are decomposable in the field $\mathfrak{L}$ into prime ideals of the first degree. By § 122 and § 156 these are the primes $p$ that are representable by the principal form of the discriminant $D = 4\Delta$ or $16\Delta$. These are of the form:
\[
\begin{aligned}
1) \quad & p = y^2 - \Delta x^2, \qquad \Delta \equiv 0 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 4) \text{ or } \equiv 1 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 8),\\
2) \quad & p = y^2 - 4\Delta x^2, \qquad \Delta \equiv 5 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 8).
\end{aligned}
\]
If $\Delta \equiv 1 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 8)$, then the third coefficient of the form $(a, b, c)$ must be even. If $\Delta \equiv 0 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 4)$, then we may assume $c$ even, by passing if necessary to the parallel form $(a, b+2a, a+b+c)$. If therefore $p$ splits into the two prime factors $\pi, \pi'$, then
\weq{1}{\begin{aligned}
1) \quad & \pi = y + x\sqrt{\Delta},\\
2) \quad & \pi = y + 2x\sqrt{\Delta},
\end{aligned}}
and in order to apply the multiplication formula § 157, (10), (17) to $\mu = \pi$, we have in the latter case to replace $x$ by $2x$. We may therefore in all cases assume $cx$ even, and hence $\varepsilon = \pm 1$.

The conditions for the modulus 2 that lie in the representations (1), 1), 2) can be summarised in the single one:
\[
\pi \equiv 1 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 2).
\]
If we set, when $N(\pi) = p$, for the moment by way of abbreviation:
\weq{2}{\begin{aligned}
\varphi(x) &= A_1x + A_3x^3 + \cdots + A_{p-2}x^{p-2} + x^p,\\
\psi(x) &= 1 + A_{p-2}x^2 + \cdots + A_3x^{p-3} + A_1x^{p-1}, % source plus has a small damage tick; no mathematical prime is printed here
\end{aligned}}
then by § 157, (18), (19)
\weq{3}{A_1 = \pm\pi,}
and
\weq{4}{\pm \boldsymbol{S}(\pi u) = \frac{\varphi(\boldsymbol{S})}{\psi(\boldsymbol{S})},}
and from this there follows by differentiation with respect to $u$:
\weq{5}{\pm \frac{\pi \boldsymbol{S}'(\pi u)}{\boldsymbol{S}'(u)} = \frac{\varphi'(\boldsymbol{S})\psi(\boldsymbol{S}) - \varphi(\boldsymbol{S})\psi'(\boldsymbol{S})}{\psi(\boldsymbol{S})^2}.}
But by § 155, (5)
\[
\boldsymbol{S}'(u)^2 = 1 - \tfrac{1}{4}\lambda \boldsymbol{S}^2 + \boldsymbol{S}^4,
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 626 =====
% !PRINTED 595
\weberpage{595}
%<<CONT
and from (5) there results, by squaring and making use of (4):
\[
\pi^2 \frac{4\psi(\boldsymbol{S})^4 - \lambda\varphi(\boldsymbol{S})^2\psi(\boldsymbol{S})^2 + 4\psi(\boldsymbol{S})^4}{4 - \lambda \boldsymbol{S}^2 + 4\boldsymbol{S}^4} = [\varphi'(\boldsymbol{S})\psi(\boldsymbol{S}) - \varphi'(\boldsymbol{S})\psi(\boldsymbol{S})]^2. % [sic] German source prints both the repeated numerator term and repeated right-hand factor; (5) and the next display give the intended complementary terms
\]
Since on the right there stands an integral function of $\boldsymbol{S}$, the numerator on the left-hand side must be divisible by the denominator (which also follows from consideration of the zero points), and it follows:
\[
\pi^2 \Phi = [\varphi'(\boldsymbol{S})\psi(\boldsymbol{S}) - \varphi(\boldsymbol{S})\psi'(\boldsymbol{S})]^2,
\]
where $\Phi$ is an integral function of $\boldsymbol{S}$ whose coefficients are integers in $\mathfrak{L}$. Hence $\Phi$ must be the square of an integral function whose coefficients are likewise integral algebraic numbers (Bd. I, § 2; Bd. II, § 159), and from this there results, for a variable $x$:
\weq{6}{\varphi'(x)\psi(x) - \psi'(x)\varphi(x) \equiv 0 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ \pi).}
From this it can be proved that the coefficients $A_1, A_3, A_5, \ldots, A_{p-2}$ are all divisible by $\pi$.

Of $A_1$ we know this already. Let us then assume that it has been proved for
\[
A_1, A_3, \ldots, A_{2\nu-1} \quad (2\nu+1 < p),
\]
then it follows:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\varphi(x) &\equiv A_{2\nu+1}x^{2\nu+1} + \cdots\\
\varphi'(x) &\equiv (2\nu+1)A_{2\nu+1}x^{2\nu} + \cdots \qquad (\mathrm{mod}\ \pi)\\
\psi(x) &\equiv 1 + A_{p-2}x^2 + \cdots\\
\psi'(x) &\equiv 2A_{p-2}x + \cdots
\end{aligned}
\]
If we now seek in (6) the coefficient of $x^{2\nu}$, it follows:
\[
(2\nu+1)A_{2\nu+1} \equiv 0 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ \pi).
\]
Since $2\nu+1 < p$ and $p$ is a prime, $2\nu+1$ is relatively prime to $\pi$, and it follows:
\weq{7}{A_{2\nu+1} \equiv 0 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ \pi).}
If in (4) we put for $u$ one of the values $2\alpha\xi/\mu$, § 158, (9), then $\boldsymbol{S}(u)$ becomes a root of the ideal division equation § 158, (10), and it follows:
\[
\pm \boldsymbol{S}(\pi u) \equiv [\boldsymbol{S}(u)]^p \ (\mathrm{mod}\ \pi),
\]
and if we raise to a square:
\weq{8}{\boldsymbol{S}(\pi u)^2 \equiv [\boldsymbol{S}(u)]^{2p} \ (\mathrm{mod}\ \pi).}
In particular, therefore, we have
\weq{9}{\boldsymbol{S}(u)^2 \equiv \boldsymbol{S}(u)^{2p} \ (\mathrm{mod}\ \pi),}
if
\weq{10}{\pi \equiv \pm 1 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak{m})}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 627 =====
% !PRINTED 596
\weberpage{596}
%<<CONT
is. The number $\mathbf{S}(u)^2$ generates the field $\mathfrak{T}_{\mathfrak{m}}$. Moreover,
by § 122, for every number $\varrho$ in $\mathfrak{L}$:

\weq{11}{\varrho \equiv \varrho^{p} \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak{P}),}

if $\mathfrak{P}$ is a prime ideal in $\mathfrak{L}$ that divides $\pi$, and consequently,
for every integer $\tau$ in $\mathfrak{T}_{\mathfrak{m}}$, if $\mathfrak{P}'$ is a prime ideal in $\mathfrak{T}_{\mathfrak{m}}$:

\weq{12}{\tau^{p} \equiv \tau \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak{P}'),}

if the conditions (10) and (1) are satisfied.

From this it follows:

8. \gesperrt{In order that a prime $\pi$ existing in $\Omega$ should split in the field $\mathfrak{T}_{\mathfrak{m}}$ into prime ideals of the first degree, it is necessary and sufficient that}
\[
\begin{aligned}
\pi &\equiv 1 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ 2), \\
\pi &\equiv \pm 1 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak{m}).
\end{aligned}
\]

A certain finite number of primes (those which divide the
discriminants of the equations that occur) is here left out of
account.

\begin{center}
§ 161. \gesperrt{Number Groups and Ideal Groups.}
\end{center}

As in § 98 and § 106 I denote by $O$ the totality of the
integral and fractional numbers of the quadratic field $\Omega$,
after the exclusion of all numbers that are not coprime to an
arbitrarily assumed $S$. $S$ may be a rational number, a number
in $\Omega$, or an ideal as well. I will call it the \gesperrt{excludent}.
In the three memoirs \glqq über Zahlgruppen in algebraischen
 Körpern\grqq{}\,\textsuperscript{1)} I have gathered together, under the name \gesperrt{number groups},
certain systems of numbers out of $O$ which were defined by
the requirement that the \gesperrt{product} and the \gesperrt{quotient} of any two
numbers of such a group were contained in the same group.
Such a number group can never contain the number zero,
but certainly contains the number 1\,\textsuperscript{2)}.

In the same sense in which we speak of number groups we
may also speak of \gesperrt{ideal groups}, which likewise may have their
excludent. Here fractional ideals naturally occur as well, and
in dealing with them one makes use, not without advantage, of the mode of representation
 by means of the \gesperrt{functionals} (Bd. II, § 169).

\begingroup
\footnotesize
\noindent\rule{4cm}{0.4pt}\par
\textsuperscript{1)}\, Mathematische Annalen Bd. 48, 49, 50.

\textsuperscript{2)}\, \gesperrt{Fueter} calls these groups \glqq \gesperrt{Zahlstrahlen}\grqq{}. Cf. \gesperrt{Fueter}, Die
Theorie der Zahlstrahlen I, II; \gesperrt{Crelle}, Bd. 130, 132.
\endgroup

%% ===== canonical stable idx 628 =====
% !PRINTED 597
\weberpage{597}

The totality of the integral and fractional numbers of the field $\Omega$, to
which we assign an arbitrary excludent $S$, forms the number group $O$, and the
totality of the ideals $\overline{O}$ in the same sense an \gesperrt{ideal group}.

Likewise the totality of the \gesperrt{numerical units} forms a number group $E$, and the
totality of the \gesperrt{functional units} an ideal group $\overline{E}$.

The multiplication of two groups $A$ and $B$ into the product $AB$ is effected
by multiplying every element of $A$ by every element of $B$. If $A$ is a number
group, then $\overline{E}A$ is an ideal group. But this contains only principal
ideals and can therefore be called a \gesperrt{principal ideal group}.

If the whole group $O$ splits into a \gesperrt{finite number of subsidiary groups} with
respect to $A$:
\weq{1}{O = A\alpha_1 + A\alpha_2 + \cdots + A\alpha_j,}
then the number $j$ is called the index of $A$ and is denoted by
\weq{2}{j = (O, A)}
(as in § 100).

We state the first theorem:

1. \gesperrt{If $A$ is a number group with finite index $j$, and $\eta$ any
number in $O$, then $\eta^j$ is contained in $A$.}

For of the unlimited sequence of powers $1, \eta, \eta^2, \eta^3, \dots$, two
different terms must be contained in the same subsidiary group $A\alpha_i$, and
their quotient, which is of course also a power of $\eta$, is contained in $A$.
The lowest exponent $r$ for which $\eta^r$ is contained in $A$ proves, in the
well-known way, to be a divisor of $j$.

2. \gesperrt{If $A$ is a number group with finite index, then the ideal group
$\overline{O}$ can likewise be decomposed with respect to $\overline{E}A$ into a
finite number of subsidiary groups:}
\weq{3}{\begin{aligned}
\overline{O} &= \overline{A}_1 + \overline{A}_2 + \cdots + \overline{A}_h,\\
&= A\mathfrak{a}_1 + A\mathfrak{a}_2 + \cdots + A\mathfrak{a}_h,
\end{aligned}}
and indeed we can therein choose $\mathfrak{a}_1, \mathfrak{a}_2, \dots,
\mathfrak{a}_h$ as integral ideals in $\overline{O}$, since by 1. we can
convert every fractional ideal in $\overline{O}$ into an integral ideal by
multiplication with a number in $A$. We need only choose for $\eta$ a number
that is divisible by the denominator of the ideal, and multiply by a
sufficiently high power of $\eta$.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 629 =====
% !PRINTED 598
\weberpage{598}
The number
\weq{4}{h = (\overline{O},\, \overline{E}A)}
is called the \gesperrt{class number of the field $\Omega$ with respect to $A$}, and the system
$A\mathfrak{a}_1, A\mathfrak{a}_2, \ldots, A\mathfrak{a}_h$ the \gesperrt{ideal classes with respect to $A$}. We can prove
Theorem 2 by the general theorems on groups in \S\,100, 12.
According to this:
\[
\begin{aligned}
(\overline{O},\, \overline{E}A) &= (\overline{O},\, \overline{E}O)\,(\overline{E}O,\, \overline{E}A), \\
(\overline{E}O,\, \overline{E}A) &= (\overline{E}O,\, \overline{E}EA) = (O,\, EA), \\
(O,\, EA)\,(EA,\, A) &= (O,\, A), \\
(EA,\, A) &= (E,\, E'),
\end{aligned}
\]
if $E'$ denotes the group of numerical units contained in $A$. Consequently
\weq{5}{(\overline{O},\, \overline{E}A) = (\overline{O},\, \overline{E}O)\,\dfrac{(O,\, A)}{(E,\, E')},}
and $(\overline{O},\, \overline{E}O)$ is the number of absolute ideal classes in $\Omega$, hence
a finite number. In the quadratic field with negative discriminant
the number $(E,\, E')$ is equal to 1 if $-1$ occurs in $A$,
equal to 2 if $-1$ does not occur in $A$, and it can rise to 4 or
to 6 only in the two exceptional cases $\Delta = -4$, $\Delta = -3$.

If $\mathfrak{a}_1, \mathfrak{a}_1'$ belong to a class $\overline{A_1}$, and $\mathfrak{a}_2, \mathfrak{a}_2'$ to a class
$\overline{A_2}$, then the products $\mathfrak{a}_1 \mathfrak{a}_2$ and $\mathfrak{a}_1' \mathfrak{a}_2'$ belong to the \gesperrt{same class}, which
we call the class $\overline{A_1}\,\overline{A_2}$. The classes can therefore be composed and
form a finite \gesperrt{Abelian group}, in which the
principal class $\overline{E}A$ is the unit.

A number group $A$ shall be called a \gesperrt{congruence group} if it
consists not merely of individual numbers, but of whole number
classes with respect to a modulus $M$; that is, if $\alpha$ belongs to $A$,
then all numbers congruent to $\alpha$ with respect to the modulus $M$
shall also belong to $A$; $M$ shall be called the \gesperrt{modulus of the congruence group}.
A congruence group always has a finite index, since
the \gesperrt{number classes} with respect to the modulus $M$ are already finite in number.
Instead of $M$ one may also choose any multiple of $M$ as the modulus.
For this reason we also gain no more general concept if
we take an ideal for $M$. We may even assume $M$ to be a natural
number.

If an ideal $\mathfrak{m}$ is relatively prime to $M$, then in
every number class represented by $\alpha$ one can determine a number $\alpha_0$ from the
congruence
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 630 =====
% !PRINTED 599
\weberpage{599}
%<<CONT
\weq{6}{\alpha_0 = \alpha + M\vartheta \equiv 0 \pmod{\mathfrak{m}}}
where $\vartheta$ is an integer in $\Omega$.

From this it follows that every prime ideal $\mathfrak{e}$ dividing the
excludent must divide $M$, since otherwise $\alpha_0$ would be divisible
by $\mathfrak{e}$ for $\mathfrak{m} = \mathfrak{e}$.

If $\alpha$ and $M$ have a common divisor, then all numbers of the form
$\alpha + M\xi$, in which $\xi$ is an arbitrary number, have the same
common divisor with $M$. But in $A$ there are also numbers that are
relatively prime to $M$, e.\,g. the number 1. The following theorem
then holds:

3. \gesperrt{If $\mathfrak{m}$ is relatively prime to $M$, then in $A$
one can determine an integer $\alpha_0 = \mathfrak{m}\mathfrak{n}$
divisible by $\mathfrak{m}$ in such a way that $\mathfrak{n}$ becomes
relatively prime to $M$ and to an arbitrarily given ideal $\mathfrak{c}$.}

For if by (6) one has determined a number divisible by $\mathfrak{m}$,
\[
\alpha_0 = \mathfrak{m}\mathfrak{n}
\]
which is coprime to $M$, then one obtains other such numbers:
\[
\alpha_0' = \alpha_0 + M\xi = \mathfrak{m}\mathfrak{n}',
\]
if
\[
\xi = \mathfrak{m}\mathfrak{r}
\]
is an arbitrary integer divisible by $\mathfrak{m}$. Now if $\mathfrak{q}$ is a prime ideal that divides $\mathfrak{c}$
but not $\alpha_0$, let $\mathfrak{r}$ be assumed divisible by
$\mathfrak{q}$; then $\mathfrak{n}'$ is not divisible by $\mathfrak{q}$. But if $\mathfrak{q}$ divides $\mathfrak{c}$
and $\alpha_0$, let $\mathfrak{r}$ be assumed not divisible by $\mathfrak{q}$; then
$\mathfrak{n}'$ is likewise not divisible by $\mathfrak{q}$.

From this it follows:

4. \gesperrt{If $\mathfrak{m}$ is an arbitrary ideal coprime to $M$,
then in every ideal class $\overline{A_\nu}$ there are ideals that are
relatively prime to $\mathfrak{m}$.}

To prove this, take an ideal $\mathfrak{b}$ in the class
$(\overline{A_\nu})^{-1}$ and determine by 3. a number
\[
\alpha = \mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b},
\]
so that $\mathfrak{a}$ is relatively prime to $\mathfrak{m}$; then $\mathfrak{a}$ belongs to the class $\overline{A_\nu}$
and satisfies the requirement of Theorem 4.

\noindent\textbf{\S\ 162.\qquad \gesperrt{The ideals of the principal class divisible by an ideal.}}

\gesperrt{By $\Omega$ there shall now be understood the quadratic field with
negative fundamental number $\Delta$.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 631 =====
% !PRINTED 600
\weberpage{600}
In this field let $A$ be a congruence group with the modulus
$M$ and the excludent $S$. The group $A$ contains, as we have
 seen, infinitely many \gesperrt{integers}. We ask for the number
$T(t)$ of the integers in $A$ that are divisible by some
given integral ideal $\mathfrak{m}$ coprime to $M$, and whose
norm is not greater than the positive number $t$.

Let $(\alpha_1, \alpha_2)$ be a basis of $\mathfrak{m}$; then by \S\,91, (11):
\weq{1}{\alpha_1 = a_{22}\,a, \quad \alpha_2 = a_{22}\,\dfrac{b + \sqrt{\Delta}}{2}.}

Here let $a_{22}$ denote the greatest integral rational
number dividing $\mathfrak{m}$, and $a_{22}\,a$ the least integral rational number
divisible by $\mathfrak{m}$; $b$ is a root of the congruence:
\[
b^2 \equiv \Delta \pmod{4a},
\]
and we have:
\weq{2}{\Delta = b^2 - 4ac.}
\weq{3}{N(\mathfrak{m}) = a_{22}^2\,a.}
Since $\mathfrak{m}$ has been assumed relatively prime to $M$, we can, by
\S\,161, (6), determine in every number class with respect to $M$
occurring in $A$ a number $\alpha_0$ divisible by $\mathfrak{m}$. This number has the form
\[
\alpha_0 = x_0\alpha_1 + y_0\alpha_2,
\]
and if we set
\weq{4}{\begin{aligned} \alpha &= \alpha_0 + M(x\alpha_1 + y\alpha_2) \\ &= (x_0 + Mx)\alpha_1 + (y_0 + My)\alpha_2 \end{aligned}}
and let $x, y$ run through all positive and negative integral
rational numbers, then $\alpha$ runs through the totality of the
integers of the group $A$ that are divisible by $\mathfrak{m}$ and congruent
to $\alpha_0$ with respect to $M$.

In order to obtain all the integers in $A$ divisible by $\mathfrak{m}$,
we have to seek a complete system of residues with respect to $M$ in $\Omega$
and to select from among them the numbers $\alpha_0$ contained in $A$
that are divisible by $\mathfrak{m}$.

If the norm of this number $\alpha$ is to be not greater than $t$, then,
 if we denote the quadratic form
\[
a x^2 + b x y + c y^2
\]
by $\varphi(x, y)$, the condition for this is:
\[
\varphi(x_0 + Mx, \; y_0 + My) \leqq \dfrac{t}{a_{22}^2\,a}, \qquad [\S\,91, (2), (4)].
\]

%% ===== canonical stable idx 632 =====
% !PRINTED 601
\weberpage{601}
Let us take in a plane a rectangular coordinate system
 $X, Y$, and let us call \gesperrt{lattice points} those points
with the coordinates
\[
X = (x_0 + Mx)\, a_{22}\, \sqrt{\dfrac{a}{t}},
\]
\[
Y = (y_0 + My)\, a_{22}\, \sqrt{\dfrac{a}{t}},
\]
where $x_0, y_0$ are kept fixed and $x, y$ run through all integral
rational numbers; then by this lattice the plane is divided into
squares whose area is
\[
\delta^2 = M^2\, \dfrac{a_{22}^2\, a}{t}
\]
and if $T_0$ is the number of lattice points that lie within
the ellipse
\[
\varphi(X, Y) = 1
\]
or on its boundary, then $T_0\,\delta^2$ is, for an infinite $t$,
equal to the area of this ellipse, and hence equal to $\dfrac{\pi}{\sqrt{-\Delta}}$.

If one takes account further of the elements of area $\delta^2$ that are
cut through by the periphery of the ellipse, from which one obtains a
measure for the error of this determination of area, then
\weq{5}{T_0 = \dfrac{\pi t}{M^2\, a_{22}^2\, a\, \sqrt{-\Delta}} + R_0\sqrt{t},}
where $R_0$ is a quantity that remains finite as $t$ increases
infinitely [Bd.\,II, \S\,194, (6)].

We obtain such an expression for every $\alpha_0$, and if
we add all these expressions together, we obtain, having regard
to (3), the theorem:

\gesperrt{If $A$ is a congruence group with the modulus $M$
and $\mathfrak{m}$ an ideal in $\Omega$ coprime to $M$, and further $T$
the number of integral principal ideals contained in $\overline{E}A$
whose norm is not greater than $t$, then}
\weq{6}{T = \dfrac{g t}{N(\mathfrak{m})} + R\sqrt{t},}
\gesperrt{where $g$ is a number independent of $\mathfrak{m}$ and $t$ and different
from zero, and $R$ is a function of $t$ that is finite as $A$ % [sic]
increases infinitely.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 633 =====
% !PRINTED 602
\weberpage{602}

The constant $g$ is more closely determined by (5):

\weq{7}{g = \frac{\gamma\,\pi}{M^2\sqrt{-\Delta}},}

where $\gamma$ is the number of classes of numbers contained in $A$ with respect to the modulus $M$.

If by $T$ we wish to understand the number of integral ideals of the principal class $\overline{E}A$ whose norm is not greater than $t$, then (6) still holds in that case too; only, if $-1$ occurs in $A$, the number $g$ has to be halved, and in the two exceptional cases $\Delta = -4$, $\Delta = -3$ it may possibly have to be divided further by 4 or by 6.

\begin{center}
\S\,163. \gesperrt{The Dirichlet Sums.}
\end{center}

We now understand by $\overline{O}$ the ideal group of all the ideals in $\Omega$ (with regard to the excludent $S$); let $A$ be a congruence group and

\weq{1}{\overline{A} = \overline{E}A,}

the group of the corresponding principal ideals. We decompose $\overline{O}$ according to \S\,161, (3) into the \gesperrt{classes} with respect to $A$:

\weq{2}{\overline{O} = \overline{A}_1 + \overline{A}_2 + \cdots + \overline{A}_h,}

and consider the sums:

\weq{3}{S_i = \sum^{a_i}\frac{1}{(N a_i)^s},}

in which $s$ denotes a positive variable $> 1$, and $a_i$ runs through all the integral ideals of a class $\overline{A}_i$.

We transform the sums $S_i$ in the following way:

Since $N(a_i)$ must be one of the numbers 1, 2, 3, \dots\ we denote by $a_\nu$ the number of ideals of the class $\overline{A}_i$ whose norm $= \nu$, and obtain

\weq{4}{S_i = a_1 + \frac{a_2}{2^s} + \frac{a_3}{3^s} + \frac{a_4}{4^s} + \cdots}

where, if a number $\nu$ does not occur among the $N(a_i)$, one is to set $a_\nu = 0$.

If we denote by $Z(\nu)$ the number of ideals of the class $\overline{A}_i$ whose norm is not greater than $\nu$, then for $Z(\nu)$ we obtain from formula (6) of the preceding section a limiting value:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 634 =====
% !PRINTED 603
\weberpage{603}
%<<CONT

By \S\,161, 4. we take in the class $(A_i)^{-1}$ an ideal $m$ coprime to $M$, and in

\weq{5}{m\, a_i = \overline{\alpha}}
