we let $a_i$ run through the ideals of the class $\overline{A}_i$, and consequently $\overline{\alpha}$ through the ideals of the principal class divisible by $m$; if then

\[
N(a_i) \leqq \nu,
\]

then

\[
N(m)\,N(a_i) = N(\alpha) \leqq \nu\,N(m).
\]

If, as before, $T$ denotes the number of ideals of the principal class divisible by $m$ whose norm is not greater than $t$, then, if we set $t = \nu N(m)$,

\[
Z(\nu) = T,
\]

and from formula \S\,162, (6) there results

\weq{6}{Z(\nu) = g\nu + R_\nu\sqrt{\nu},}

in which $g$ denotes a number that is the same for all classes $\overline{A}_i$, and $R_\nu$ a function of $\nu$ that does not become infinite as $\nu$ increases to infinity.

By the meaning of $a_\nu$ we have

\weq{7}{a_\nu = Z(\nu) - Z(\nu - 1), \quad Z(0) = 0}

and consequently

\weq{8}{S_i = \sum_{0,\infty}\frac{Z(\nu) - Z(\nu - 1)}{\nu^s}.}

If we substitute the expression (6) for $Z(\nu)$, there follows:

\weq{9}{S_i = g\sum\frac{1}{\nu^s} + \sum R_\nu\sqrt{\nu}\left(\frac{1}{\nu^s} - \frac{1}{(\nu+1)^s}\right).}

The second term of this sum:

\[
\sum R_\nu\sqrt{\nu}\left(\frac{1}{\nu^s} - \frac{1}{(\nu+1)^s}\right)
\]

is unconditionally convergent so long as $s > \frac{1}{2}$, and is therefore a continuous function of $s$ which for $s = 1$ passes into

\[
\sum_{1,\infty}\frac{R_\nu}{\sqrt{\nu}\,(\nu+1)}
\]

; for we have

\[
\operatorname{Lim}_{\nu=\infty} \nu^{s+\frac{1}{2}} R_\nu \sqrt{\nu}\left(\frac{1}{\nu^s} - \frac{1}{(\nu+1)^s}\right) = s\operatorname{Lim} R_\nu
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 635 =====
% !PRINTED 604
\weberpage{604}

%<<CONT
finite. The first sum in (9) is

\weq{10}{\sum\frac{1}{\nu^s} = \frac{1}{s-1} + C_s,}

where $C_s$ remains finite for $s = 1$, passing namely into the \gesperrt{value of Euler's constant} $0{,}5772\dots$ (Bd.\ II, S.\ 723).

If this is taken into account, there follows from (9) the result:

5. \gesperrt{If $S_i$ has the meaning (3), then}

\weq{11}{S_i = \frac{g}{s-1} + C_i,}

\gesperrt{where $g$ is a constant different from zero and independent of the particular class $\overline{A}_i$, and $C_i$ is a function of $s$ depending on $\overline{A}_i$ which remains finite for $s = 1$.}

The group of degree $h$ of the ideal class $\overline{A}_i$ is an \gesperrt{Abelian} one, and there are therefore $h$ characters $\chi_\kappa(\overline{A}_i)$, which are all $h$th roots of unity, among them the \gesperrt{principal character} $\chi_1$, which is $= 1$ for every class. Likewise, for the principal class $\overline{A}_1$ each of the characters has the value $+1$. For these characters the theorems hold:

\weq{12}{\begin{aligned}
&\sum^{i}\chi_\kappa(\overline{A}_i) = 0, \quad \sum^{\kappa}\chi_\kappa(\overline{A}_i) = 0, \\
&\kappa = 2,3,\dots,h, \quad i = 2,3,\dots,h, \\
&\sum^{i}\chi_1(\overline{A}_i) = h, \quad \sum^{\kappa}\chi_\kappa(\overline{A}_1) = h
\end{aligned}}

(Bd.\ II, \S\,13). If \gesperrt{the integral ideal} $a$ in $\overline{O}$ belongs to the class $\overline{A}$, then we set for every $\chi$:

\weq{13}{\chi(a) = \chi(\overline{A}),}

\gesperrt{and have thus determined the characters according to the group $A$ for every ideal in $\overline{O}$}. For any two ideals $a$ and $b$ from $\overline{O}$ the relation holds:

\weq{14}{\chi(a)\,\chi(b) = \chi(ab).}

Now from $S_i$ we form the $h$ sum:

\weq{15}{Q_\kappa = \sum^{i}\chi_\kappa(\overline{A}_i)\,S_i,}

for which, by (3) and (13), we may also write:

\weq{16}{Q = \sum^{a}\frac{\chi(a)}{(Na)^s}.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 636 =====
% !PRINTED 605
\weberpage{605}

In this, $\chi$ may be any of the characters $\chi_\kappa$, and the sum extends over all ideals $a$ of $\overline{O}$. By (11), if we set

\[
G_\kappa = \sum^{i}\chi_\kappa(\overline{A}_i)\,C_i
\]

then

\weq{17}{\begin{aligned}
Q_1 &= \frac{hG}{s-1} + G_1, \\
Q_\kappa &= G_\kappa, \quad \kappa > 1.
\end{aligned}}

where the $G_1, G_2, \dots, G_h$ are \gesperrt{functions of $s$ which retain a finite value for $s = 1$.}

The sums $Q$ can be transformed in the same way that we have already come to know in \S\,197 of the second volume.

Accordingly, if $p$ denotes any prime ideal in $\overline{O}$:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{1 - \chi(p)N(p)^{-s}} &= 1 + \chi(p)N(p)^{-s} + \chi(p)^2 N(p)^{-2s} + \cdots \\
&= 1 + \frac{\chi(p)}{N(p)^s} + \frac{\chi(p^2)}{N(p^2)^s} + \frac{\chi(p^3)}{N(p^3)^s} + \cdots,
\end{aligned}
\]

and since all ideals $a$ can be represented as products of such ideals $p$, it follows that:

\weq{18}{Q = \Pi\,\frac{1}{1 - \chi(p)N(p)^{-s}},}

where the infinite product $\Pi$ extends over all prime ideals $p$ in $\overline{O}$.

To every ideal $a$ in $\overline{O}$ there belongs a certain exponent $\varphi$, that is, there is a certain lowest positive exponent $\varphi$ for which $a^\varphi$ is contained in the principal class $\overline{A}_1$. The number $\varphi$ is always a divisor of the class number $h$. We set:

\weq{19}{h = \varepsilon\varphi.}

If in this sense $a$ belongs to the exponent $\varphi$, then all the characters $\chi_k(a)$ are $\varphi$th roots of unity, and every $\varphi$th root of unity occurs $\varepsilon$ times among them (Bd.\ II, \S\,198, 1.).

If, then, $p$ belongs to the exponent $\varphi$, we have

\[
\begin{aligned}
&[1 - \chi_1(p)N(p)^{-s}][1 - \chi_2(p)N(p)^{-s}]\cdots[1 - \chi_h(p)N(p)^{-s}] \\
&\qquad = [1 - N(p)^{-\varphi s}]^\varepsilon,
\end{aligned}
\]

and from (18) it follows that:

\weq{20}{Q_1 Q_2 \cdots Q_h = \Pi\,\frac{1}{[1 - N(p)^{-\varphi s}]^\varepsilon}.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 637 =====
% !PRINTED 606
\weberpage{606}

The question now concerns the limiting value which these expressions approach when $s=1$.

As regards the left-hand side, it follows from (17) that
\weq{21}{\left\{\begin{aligned}
&\mathrm{Lim}\,(s-1)\,Q_1 = hg \text{ finite and different from zero,}\\
&\mathrm{Lim}\,Q_2\,Q_3\ldots Q_h \text{ finite (perhaps zero)}
\end{aligned}\right.}
To assess the right-hand side we observe that the prime ideals $\mathfrak{p}$ are of the first or of the second degree, and that accordingly $N(\mathfrak{p})$ is equal to a natural prime or to the square of a natural prime. Further, we rely on the well-known theorem of analysis according to which an infinite product
\[
(1-q_1)\,(1-q_2)\,(1-q_3)\ldots
\]
converges unconditionally and has a limiting value different from zero, if
\[
q_1+q_2+q_3+\cdots
\]
is an unconditionally convergent series, and none of the $q_i=1$.

We accordingly divide the prime ideals $\mathfrak{p}$ into two kinds, $\mathfrak{p}_1, \mathfrak{p}_2$, in such a way that the $\mathfrak{p}_1$ are to be of the first degree and to belong to the exponent $\varphi=1$ (hence $\varepsilon=h$). The $\mathfrak{p}_2$ are to be either of the second degree, or to belong to a higher exponent $\varphi$. \gesperrt{Thus the $\mathfrak{p}_1$ are the prime ideals of the first degree belonging to the principal class $\overline{A}_1$.}

Then
\[
N(\mathfrak{p}_1)^{\varphi} = N(\mathfrak{p}_1) = p_1
\]
is a natural prime, and
\[
N(\mathfrak{p}_2)^{\varphi} = p_2^{k}
\]
is at least the 2nd (at most the $2h$th) power of a prime. By the analytic theorem just mentioned, the product
\[
\Pi\bigl[1-N(\mathfrak{p}_2)^{-s\varphi}\bigr]^{\varepsilon}
\]
is then finite and different from zero for $s=1$, and from (20), (21) there follows the theorem:

6. \gesperrt{The limiting value}
\[
\mathop{\mathrm{Lim}}\limits_{s=1} \; \Pi\,\dfrac{s-1}{\Pi\bigl[1-N(\mathfrak{p}_1)^{-s}\bigr]^{h}}
\]
\gesperrt{is finite when $\mathfrak{p}_1$ runs through the prime ideals of the first degree of the principal class $\overline{A}_1$.}

A particular interest attaches to the question whether this limiting value can vanish.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 638 =====
% !PRINTED 607
\weberpage{607}

\begin{center}
§ 164.

\gesperrt{The Class Field.}
\end{center}

To the number group $A$ in the quadratic field $\Omega$ there shall exist an algebraic field over $\Omega$, to be denoted by $\mathfrak{K}$ or $\mathfrak{K}(A)$, of which we shall assume only:

7. \gesperrt{Definition of the class field.}

\gesperrt{The prime ideals $\mathfrak{p}_1$ of the first degree of the principal class $\overline{A}_1$, and only these, shall split again in the field $\mathfrak{K}(A)$ into prime ideals of the first degree.}

Thus it is only the prime ideals in $\Omega$, which we designated earlier by $\mathfrak{p}_1$, that split in $\mathfrak{K}$ into prime ideals of the first degree.

Any finite number of primes may thereby be excepted. They are then taken into the excludents.

If $n$ is the relative degree of the field $\mathfrak{K}$ over $\Omega$, and $p$ a natural prime which the ideals $\mathfrak{p}_1$ and $\mathfrak{P}$ in $\Omega$ and $\mathfrak{K}$ divide, and if one denotes the absolute norms in the fields $\Omega$ and $\mathfrak{K}$ by $N_\Omega, N_\mathfrak{K}$, then
\[
N_\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{P}) = N_\Omega(\mathfrak{p}_1) = p, \quad N_\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{p}_1) = p^n,
\]
and consequently $\mathfrak{p}_1$ must split in the field $\mathfrak{K}$ into $n$ prime ideals $\mathfrak{P}$:
\weq{1}{\mathfrak{p}_1 = \mathfrak{P}_1 \mathfrak{P}_2 \ldots \mathfrak{P}_n.}
The prime ideals which divide the fundamental numbers of the fields $\Omega$ or $\mathfrak{K}$ shall always be excluded. Then the $\mathfrak{P}_1, \mathfrak{P}_2, \ldots, \mathfrak{P}_n$ are distinct from one another.

Whether such a field $\mathfrak{K}$ exists remains for the present undecided. We will investigate what can be concluded from the definition.

Since $n$ ideals $\mathfrak{P}$ divide every ideal $\mathfrak{p}_1$, we have
\weq{2}{\prod\nolimits \left[1 - N_\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{p}_1)^{-s}\right]^n = \prod\nolimits \left[1 - N_\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{P})^{-s}\right],}
in which the first product extends over all ideals $\mathfrak{p}_1$ of the field $\Omega$, the second over all ideals $\mathfrak{P}$ of the first degree of the field $\mathfrak{K}$; and by Theorem I, § 197 of Band II, which holds for any field whatever,
\weq{3}{(s-1)\prod\nolimits \frac{1}{\left[1-N_\mathfrak{K}(\mathfrak{P})^{-s}\right]}}
has for $s=1$ a finite limiting value different from zero, which is there reduced to the class number in the field $\mathfrak{K}$. If we put, for brevity,
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 639 =====
% !PRINTED 608
\weberpage{608}

%<<CONT
\weq{4}{P = \prod\nolimits \frac{1}{\left[1-N(\mathfrak{p}_1)^{-s}\right]},}
then according to (2) and (3), for $s=1$
\weq{5}{(s-1)\,P^n \text{ finite and different from zero,}}
and according to § 163, 6.:
\weq{6}{(s-1)\,P^h \text{ finite,}}
and if one eliminates $P$ from these, it follows that:
\[
(s-1)^{n-h} \text{ finite.}
\]
Therefore
\weq{7}{n \overline{\overline{>}} h.}
From this follows the theorem:

8. \gesperrt{The relative degree $n$ of the class field cannot be smaller than the class number $h$ of the group. If $n=h$, then $(s-1)P^h$ is not zero for $s=1$, and the sums $Q_2, Q_3, \ldots, Q_h$ are likewise different from zero.}

If an equation of degree $h$ can be formed in $\Omega$ from which a field can be derived that exhibits the characteristic properties of the class field, and if the degree of this field is not greater than $h$, then it follows that it cannot be smaller either, and so must be $= h$. With this the irreducibility of the equation in question is established.

On this rests the demonstration of the \gesperrt{irreducibility of the cyclotomic equation} which we gave in § 198 of the II. Band. There the field of rational numbers took the place of $\Omega$. In the next chapter we shall make further applications of this.

Whether there are groups for which the degree of the class field is greater than the class number remains undecided. I consider it improbable.

We prove further that there can be at most \gesperrt{one} class field. Every such field is generated by the adjunction of an algebraic number $\xi$ to $\Omega$.

Let $\xi$ be an \gesperrt{integer} generating the class field $\mathfrak{K} = \Omega(\xi)$, one which therefore satisfies an equation irreducible in $\Omega$
\weq{8}{f(\xi) = \xi^n + \alpha_1 \xi^{n-1} + \alpha_2 \xi^{n-2} + \cdots + \alpha_n = 0}
in which the $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n$ are integers in $\Omega$.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 640 =====
% !PRINTED 609
\weberpage{609}
Every integer $\eta$ of the field $\mathfrak{K}$ can (Bd.\,I, § 151) be represented in
the form:
\[
\eta = \frac{\varphi(\xi)}{f'(\xi)},
\]
where $\varphi(\xi)$ has integral coefficients in $\Omega$. One can put this in the
form:
\weq{9}{\gamma\eta = \gamma_0 + \gamma_1\xi + \gamma_2\xi^2 + \cdots + \gamma_{n-1}\xi^{n-1},}
where $\gamma, \gamma_0, \gamma_1, \ldots, \gamma_{n-1}$ are integers in $\Omega$, and such that the
first, $\gamma$, is a divisor of the discriminant of $f$. The prime factors of
$\gamma$ we exclude by means of the excludent.

Let

$\mathfrak{P}$ be a prime ideal of the first degree in $\mathfrak{K}$,

$\mathfrak{p}_1$ the prime ideal of the first degree in $\Omega$ that is divisible by $\mathfrak{P}$,

$p$ the norm of $\mathfrak{p}_1$ and of $\mathfrak{P}$;

then for every integer $\alpha$ in $\Omega$:
\[
\alpha^p \equiv \alpha \ (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak{p}_1)
\]
and
\weq{10}{\xi^p \equiv \xi \ (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak{P}),}
hence, by (9), for every integer $\eta$ in $\mathfrak{K}$:
\[
\eta^p \equiv \eta \ (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak{P}).
\]

9. \gesperrt{The necessary and sufficient condition for $\mathfrak{K}(\xi)$ to be a class field therefore consists in this, that for every prime ideal $\mathfrak{P}$ dividing a $\mathfrak{p}_1$, and only for this one, the congruence (10) is satisfied.}

Let now
\[
\mathfrak{K} = \Omega(\xi), \quad \mathfrak{K}' = \Omega(\xi')
\]
be two class fields of the same group $A$. First of all, it readily follows that they must be \gesperrt{of the same degree}. For the condition (5) must be satisfied for both. If, then, $n$ and $n'$ are the degrees, $(s-1)^{n'-n}$ must be finite and different from zero for $s=1$, which is only possible if $n=n'$.

By composition of $\mathfrak{K}$ and $\mathfrak{K}'$ we derive a third field:
\[
\mathfrak{K}'' = \Omega(\xi, \xi'),
\]
of which we shall show that it too is a class field.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 641 =====
% !PRINTED 610
\weberpage{610}
We can generate the field $\mathfrak{K}''$ by means of a number:
\weq{11}{\xi'' = \alpha\xi + \alpha'\xi',}
in which $\alpha, \alpha'$ are integers in $\Omega$.

Let $\mathfrak{P}''$ be a prime ideal in $\mathfrak{K}''$ dividing some $\mathfrak{p}_1$, and let
$\mathfrak{P}, \mathfrak{P}'$ be the prime ideals in $\mathfrak{K}, \mathfrak{K}'$ divisible by $\mathfrak{P}''$, and $N(\mathfrak{p}_1) = p$.
Then by 9.:
\weq{12}{\xi^p \equiv \xi \ (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak{P}), \quad \xi'^p \equiv \xi' \ (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak{P}'),}
and consequently, by (11):
\weq{13}{\xi''^p \equiv \alpha^p \xi^p + \alpha'^p \xi'^p \equiv \xi'' \ (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak{P}'').}
If conversely the congruence (13) is satisfied, then the congruences (12)
follow from it again, because $\xi$ and $\xi'$ can be expressed rationally
[in the form (9)] by means of $\xi''$.

Thus $\mathfrak{K}''$ is likewise a class field, and its degree is just as
high as that of $\mathfrak{K}$ and $\mathfrak{K}'$. Hence $\xi$ and $\xi'$ are primitive
numbers of $\mathfrak{K}''$, and consequently all these fields are identical (Bd.\,I,
§ 151, 3.). If $\mathfrak{K}$ is a class field, then the fields conjugate to $\mathfrak{K}$
are also class fields and are therefore identical with $\mathfrak{K}$.

With this the theorem is proved:

10. \gesperrt{For a given number group there is only one class field, and this is a normal field.}

We now wish to become more closely acquainted with the most important properties and
applications of the class field in the cases arising from complex
multiplication.

Let us assume that the number group $A$ contains another group $A'$ as a divisor of
finite index $(A, A')$, and that these two groups
possess class fields:
\weq{14}{\begin{aligned} \mathfrak{K} &= \mathfrak{K}(A) = \Omega(\xi), \\ \mathfrak{K}' &= \mathfrak{K}(A') = \Omega(\xi'), \end{aligned}}
then it can be proved that the field $\mathfrak{K}$ is contained in $\mathfrak{K}'$. For if
$\mathfrak{p}_1, \mathfrak{p}_1'$ are the prime ideals of the first degree in $\Omega$ of the
principal classes $\overline{A}_1, \overline{A}_1'$, then the $\mathfrak{p}_1'$ are contained
among the $\mathfrak{p}_1$. If therefore $p$ is the prime which $\mathfrak{p}_1$ and $\mathfrak{p}_1'$ divide,
then by 9.:
\weq{15}{\begin{aligned} \xi^p &\equiv \xi \ (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak{P}) \text{ for all } \mathfrak{p}_1 \text{ and consequently for all } \mathfrak{p}_1', \\ \xi'^p &\equiv \xi' \ (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak{P}') \text{ for all } \mathfrak{p}_1', \end{aligned}}
if $\mathfrak{P}$ and $\mathfrak{P}'$ are prime ideals of the first degree in $\mathfrak{K}$ and $\mathfrak{K}'$.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 642 =====
% !PRINTED 611
\weberpage{611}
We now form the field:

\weq{16}{\mathfrak{K}'' = \Omega(\xi, \xi') = \Omega(\xi''),}

by setting

\weq{17}{\xi'' = \alpha\xi + \alpha'\xi'}

and we denote by $\mathfrak{P}''$ a prime ideal of the first degree of this field
that divides some $\mathfrak{p}_1'$.

Let $\mathfrak{P}, \mathfrak{P}'$ be, as above, the prime ideals in
$\mathfrak{K}, \mathfrak{K}'$ divisible by $\mathfrak{P}''$. Then by (15) and (17)
\[
\xi''^{p} \equiv \xi'' \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak{P}''),
\]
and consequently $\mathfrak{K}''$ is a class field of $A'$.

Accordingly $\mathfrak{K}''$ is identical with $\mathfrak{K}'$; $\xi'$ is a primitive number
of $\mathfrak{K}''$, and consequently every number in $\mathfrak{K}''$, and hence $\xi$ as well, can be
expressed rationally by $\xi'$.

From this it follows:

11. \gesperrt{If a number group $A$ contains another number
 group $A'$ as a divisor of finite index, and if the
 class fields $\mathfrak{K}(A)$, $\mathfrak{K}(A')$ exist, then $\mathfrak{K}(A)$
is contained in $\mathfrak{K}(A')$.}

\begin{center}
§ 165. \gesperrt{Prime Ideals in the Classes.}
\end{center}

We now return to the functions $Q$ which we represented in
§ 163, (16) by infinite series and in § 163, (18) by
infinite products:

\weq{1}{Q_{\varkappa} = \Pi\, \frac{1}{1 - \chi_{\varkappa}(\mathfrak{p})\,N(\mathfrak{p})^{-s}}}

in which $\chi_{\varkappa}$ denotes one of the characters of the group
and $\mathfrak{p}$ runs through all prime ideals in $\overline{O}$. We develop the logarithm
 of this product in the following way:

\weq{2}{\log Q_{\varkappa} = \sum \frac{\chi_{\varkappa}(\mathfrak{p})}{N(\mathfrak{p})^{s}} + \frac{1}{2}\sum \frac{\chi_{\varkappa}(\mathfrak{p}^2)}{N(\mathfrak{p})^{2s}} + \frac{1}{3}\sum \frac{\chi_{\varkappa}(\mathfrak{p}^3)}{N(\mathfrak{p})^{3s}} + \cdots}

We do not need to know the multiple of $2\pi i$ that is not more closely defined
in the $\log Q$, since it could change with $s$ only discontinuously; and since
continuous functions of $s$ stand on the right and on the left, as long
as $s > 1$, this multiple does not change with $s$ at
 all.

Let $\overline{A}_i$ be one of the classes of the ideal group $\overline{A}$ and $\overline{A}_i'$ the
opposite class. Then by (12), (13), (14), § 163:
\[
\sum_{\varkappa=1}^{k} \chi_{\varkappa}(\overline{A}_i')\,\chi_{\varkappa}(\mathfrak{a}) = h \ \text{or} = 0,
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 643 =====
% !PRINTED 612
\weberpage{612}

%<<CONT
according as the ideal $\mathfrak a$ is contained in the class $A_i$ or in some other
class. If we therefore multiply formula (2) by
$\chi_\varkappa(\overline{A_i'})$ and sum with respect to $\varkappa$, it follows that:

\weq{3}{
\frac{1}{h}\overset{\varkappa}{\sum}\chi_\varkappa(A_i') \log Q_k
= \overset{(1)}{\sum}\frac{1}{N(\mathfrak p)^s} + \frac{1}{2}\overset{(2)}{\sum}\frac{1}{N(\mathfrak p)^{2s}} + \frac{1}{3}\overset{(3)}{\sum}\frac{1}{N(\mathfrak p)^{3s}} + \cdots,
}
in which the sums $\overset{(1)}{\sum}, \overset{(2)}{\sum}, \overset{(3)}{\sum}, \ldots$ extend over all prime ideals $\mathfrak p$
whose first, second, third, $\ldots$ power is contained in the class $\overline{A_i}$.

We pass in (3) to the limit $s = 1$; the sums $\overset{(2)}{\sum}, \overset{(3)}{\sum}, \ldots$
retain a finite value in doing so, since their unconditional convergence does not cease for $s = 1$. The same holds of that part
of the sum $\overset{(1)}{\sum}$ which relates to prime ideals of higher than the
first degree, and so it remains questionable only whether
the sum

\[
\sum \frac{1}{N(\mathfrak p)^s},
\]

extended over all prime ideals of the first degree of the class $\overline{A_i}$, remains
finite or becomes infinite. The former would be the case if
there were in $\overline{A_i}$ no prime ideals of the first degree at all, or only
a finite number of them.

But if we assume the existence of a class field of degree $h$% faint pre-$h$ mark is scan/print damage, not a character
, then from § 164, 8. and § 163, (21) it follows that

\[
\log Q_2,\ \log Q_3,\ \ldots,\ \log Q_h
\]

retain finite limiting values, while $\log Q_1$ becomes infinite. The
left-hand side of (3) therefore becomes infinite, and the right-hand side cannot
remain finite.

Thus it is proved:

12. \gesperrt{If a class field exists whose degree
is not higher than the class number, then every
class contains infinitely many prime ideals of the first degree.}

\begin{center}
§ 166. \textbf{\gesperrt{Prime Ideals in the Ideal Classes.}}
\end{center}

If we take as group first of all the totality of the numbers $O$
of the field $\Omega$ without zero, then the classes are the ideal classes
 of the field $\Omega$, which, as we have seen, are uniquely assigned to the classes
of quadratic forms of the discriminant $\varDelta$
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 644 =====
% !PRINTED 613
\weberpage{613}
%<<CONT
can be represented. If we take as our group the order $O' = [Q]$ with the conductor $Q$, which is defined by the congruence condition that every number in $O'$ shall be congruent to a rational number modulo $Q$, then we have a congruence group whose excludent and modulus is $= Q$. The classes correspond to the classes of forms of the discriminant $D = Q^2\Delta$. The second case includes the first within itself (for $Q = 1$). The class field is here the class field $\mathfrak{K}(D)$, which, to distinguish it from more general ones, we shall call the \gesperrt{order field}.

For if $(k)$ is a class invariant, then (\S\,122)
\[
(k)^p \equiv (k) \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak{P})
\]
is satisfied only when $p$ is representable by the principal class of the discriminant $D$. Then $p$ splits in $\Omega$ into two conjugate prime ideals $\mathfrak{p}$, $\mathfrak{p}'$, which are representable by \gesperrt{numbers} in $O$ or in $O'$, and hence are principal ideals.

The field $\mathfrak{K}(\Delta)$ is the \gesperrt{class field of $\Omega$ in the narrower sense}, the one that corresponds to the ideal classes of this field, and it may also be designated the \gesperrt{principal class field} $\mathfrak{K}(\Omega)$.

In every ideal class, both with respect to $O$ and with respect to $O'$, there are therefore infinitely many prime ideals of the first degree. In other words: if $\mathfrak{a}$ is an arbitrary ideal (coprime to $Q$), then there are infinitely many prime ideals $\mathfrak{p}$ which are equivalent to $\mathfrak{a}$ with respect to $O'$. Then, by \S\,95, the forms corresponding to the ideals $\mathfrak{a}$ and $\mathfrak{p}$ are also equivalent, and $p$ is \gesperrt{representable by the form} belonging to $\mathfrak{a}$. With this the theorem is proved:

1. \gesperrt{By every primitive form of the discriminant $D$ infinitely many primes are representable}\footnote{This theorem, for negative as well as for positive discriminants, was first proved by \gesperrt{Dirichlet}, but the proof was published only in one special case (Bericht der Berliner Akademie 1840, Werke Bd.\ I, S.\ 497). The detailed proof was given by H. \gesperrt{Weber} (Mathematische Annalen XX, 1882). A generalisation likewise originating with \gesperrt{Dirichlet}, to which we shall come back in the next section, was proved by A. \gesperrt{Meyer} (Crelles Journ., Bd.\ 103). The proof given here in the text rests on a different foundation, but for the present it of course applies (so long as the class field for positive discriminants is not known) only to negative discriminants.}.

\begin{center}
\S\,167. \gesperrt{Primes in Linear Forms.}
\end{center}

We now define a number group $A$ in $\Omega$ as follows:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 645 =====
% !PRINTED 614
\weberpage{614}
%<<CONT
Let $\mathfrak{m}$ be an integral ideal in $\Omega$, and let $A$ consist of all integral and fractional numbers $\alpha$ in $\Omega$ that are coprime to $\mathfrak{m}$ and satisfy the condition:
\weq{1}{\alpha \equiv 1 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak{m}).}
If we take the prime divisors of $\mathfrak{m}$ into the excludents, and denote by $O$ the group of the numbers in $\Omega$, then $O$ splits with respect to the modulus $\mathfrak{m}$ into $\psi(\mathfrak{m})$ classes of numbers, in which $\psi(\mathfrak{m})$ has the meaning it has in Bd.\ II, \S\,168, namely, when $\mathfrak{p}$ runs through the prime divisors of $\mathfrak{m}$:
\weq{2}{\psi(\mathfrak{m}) = N(\mathfrak{m})\ \Pi\Bigl(1 - \frac{1}{N(\mathfrak{p})}\Bigr).}
To the group $A$ there belong not merely individual numbers, but classes of numbers with respect to the modulus $\mathfrak{m}$. Accordingly:
\weq{3}{(O, A) = \psi(\mathfrak{m}).}
In order to determine the class number for our group, we apply the theorems of \S\,161.

According to these, if $\overline{E}$ denotes the group of the functional units and $E$ the group of the numerical units:
\[
(\overline{O}, \overline{E}A) = (\overline{O}, \overline{E}O)\,(\overline{E}O, \overline{E}A),
\]
\[
(\overline{E}O, \overline{E}A) = (\overline{E}O, \overline{E}EA) = (O, EA).
\]
Further
\[
(O, EA)\,(EA, A) = (O, A) = \psi(\mathfrak{m}).
\]
$(EA, A) = e$ is the number of the units incongruent with respect to $\mathfrak{m}$, and
\[
(\overline{O}, \overline{E}O) = H
\]
is the class number of the field $\Omega$,
\[
(\overline{O}, \overline{E}A) = h
\]
is the class number with respect to $A$. From this there results:
\weq{4}{h = \frac{H\,\psi(\mathfrak{m})}{e}.}
The number $e$ is in general equal to the number of the units in $\Omega$, hence $= 2$, and in the two exceptional cases $\Delta = -4$, $\Delta = -3$ we have $e = 4$ and $e = 6$. The number $e$ is smaller when among the units there occur congruent ones (modulo $\mathfrak{m}$), which is only possible when $\mathfrak{m}$ is a divisor of 2 or of 3.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 646 =====
% !PRINTED 615
\weberpage{615}
\gesperrt{If $E$ denotes the group of units, or also a group contained in it, then we obtain the same value of the class number and the same class field if we let $EA$ take the place of $A$.}

This holds not only for this particular group, but generally. We could therefore, e.\,g., also have defined the numbers $\alpha$ of the group $A$ by
\[
\alpha \equiv \pm 1 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak{m})
\]
since $E = +1, -1$ is a group also in the exceptional cases $\Delta = -4$, $\Delta = -3$.

Now it can be shown that the division field $\mathfrak{T}_{\mathfrak{m}}$ is the class field for $A$. If we first exclude all prime factors which divide the discriminant of the division field, and denote by $\tau$ any number of the division field, then by \S\,160
\weq{5}{\tau^p \equiv \tau \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak{p})}
is satisfied only when $\mathfrak{p}$ is a \gesperrt{prime ideal of the first degree} in $\Omega$ which belongs to the principal class. But that is the criterion for the class field. By \S\,154, however, the degree of the division field is at most equal to the expression $h$ given in (4); consequently it is exactly equal to $h$, and the division equation is irreducible. Moreover, it is thereby proved that in each of the ideal classes $\overline{A}_\nu$ with respect to $A$ there are infinitely many prime ideals of the first degree.

One can give this theorem the following expression:

If $\beta$ is an arbitrary number in $O$, and $\mathfrak{a}$ an arbitrary ideal in $\overline{O}$, then by
\weq{6}{\overline{A}_\nu = \mathfrak{a}\beta A}
a class with respect to $A$ is determined (\S\,161), and this class contains infinitely many prime ideals of the first degree. By (6) such a prime ideal can be represented in the form:
\weq{7}{\mathfrak{p} = \mathfrak{a}\beta\alpha,}
where $\alpha \equiv 1$ (mod $\mathfrak{m}$). If we therefore set
\[
\alpha\beta = \pi,
\]
then
\[
\pi \equiv \beta \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak{m}).
\]
From this it follows:

2. \gesperrt{If $\beta$ is a number in $O$, $\mathfrak{a}$ an ideal in $\overline{O}$, then there are infinitely many, in general fractional, numbers $\pi$ in $O$ which satisfy the condition}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 647 =====
% !PRINTED 616
\weberpage{616}
%<<CONT
\weq{8}{\pi \equiv \beta \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak{m})}
\gesperrt{holds, and for which}
\weq{9}{\mathfrak{p} = \mathfrak{a}\pi}
\gesperrt{becomes a prime ideal.}

If one takes $\mathfrak{a} = 1$, then $\pi$ becomes an integer, and hence a prime existing in $\Omega$. For this particular case the theorem reads:

3. \gesperrt{In the field $\Omega$ there are infinitely many existing primes $\pi$ whose norm is a natural prime, and which are congruent, with respect to an arbitrary modulus $\mathfrak{m}$, to an arbitrary number $\beta$ coprime to $\mathfrak{m}$.}

If we take for the modulus $\mathfrak{m}$ an integer $\mu$ in $\Omega$, we obtain the following theorem:

4. \gesperrt{If $\mu$ is an integer in $\Omega$, then in the linear form}
\[
\mu\xi + \beta,
\]
\gesperrt{in which $\xi$ runs through the integers of $\Omega$ and $\beta$ is relatively prime to $\mu$, infinitely many primes are contained.}

Here one has a beautiful generalisation of the theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions (Bd.\ II, \S\,198)\footnote{For the case $\Delta = -4$ this proof has been given by \gesperrt{H. Weber}, Crelles Journ., Bd.\ 129 (Dirichlet-Band), for $\Delta = -3$ in a Strasbourg dissertation by \gesperrt{H. Bresslau} (Straßburg 1907).}.

\begin{center}
\S\,168. \gesperrt{Reduction of the class equation in the cyclotomic fields.}
\end{center}

We define a further group $A$ by the following determination:

Let $Q$, $m$ be two integral rational numbers whose prime factors we take up into the excludent $S$. Let $O$ be, as in \S\,98, the group of the numbers in $\Omega$, and $O'$ the group of the numbers of the order $[Q]$, and let $A$ consist of all integral and fractional numbers $\alpha$ in $O'$ for which the congruence condition
\weq{1}{N(\alpha) \equiv 1 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ m)}
holds. First of all we have the class number
\weq{2}{h = (\overline{O}, \overline{E}A) = (\overline{O}, \overline{E}O')\,(\overline{E}O', \overline{E}A)}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 648 =====
% !PRINTED 617
\weberpage{617}
%% [page furniture, not body text -- source-confirmed 2026-08-10]
%% \S\,168\ Reduction of the class equation in the cyclotomic fields.

%<<CONT
to determine. The first factor is the class number of the quadratic forms of the order $O'$ [\S\,100, (3)], which we denote by $H'$. We have therefore
\weq{3}{h = H' (\bar{E} O', \bar{E} A) = H' (O', A)}
(by \S\,100, 13.).

It remains to determine $(O', A)$.

If $\varrho_1, \varrho_2, \dots, \varrho_\mu$ denotes a complete system of representatives of $O'$ with respect to $A$, then the numbers
\weq{4}{N(\varrho_1),\ N(\varrho_2)\dots,\ N(\varrho_\mu)}
must all be different with respect to the modulus $m$, and every norm of a number in $O$ is congruent with respect to $m$ to one of these numbers. If therefore $Z$ is the group of rational numbers, $M$ the group of those numbers $z$ from $Z$ which satisfy the condition
\[
z \equiv 1 \pmod{m}
\]
and $R_m$ the group of norm residues with respect to $m$, then (4) is a complete system of representatives of $R_m$ with respect to $M$, and consequently
\[
\mu = (O', A) = (R_m, M).
\]
For this one may also put (\S\,100, 12.):
\weq{5}{(O', A) = \frac{(Z, M)}{(Z, R_m)}.}
Now we have
\weq{6}{(Z, M) = \varphi(m) = m \Pi\Bigl(1 - \frac{1}{r}\Bigr),}
where $r$ runs through the prime factors of $m$, and consequently
\weq{7}{h = \frac{H'\varphi(m)}{(Z, R_m)}.}

We obtain the class field $\mathfrak{K}(A)$ of our group by adjoining to the class field $\mathfrak{K}(D)$ a primitive $m$th root of unity:
\weq{8}{\mathfrak{K}(A) = \mathfrak{K}(D, \varrho).}
For the condition that a prime ideal $\mathfrak{P}$ of the field $\mathfrak{K}(D,\varrho)$ dividing a prime $p$ be of the first degree is, if $(k)$ denotes a class invariant of the discriminant $D$:
\weq{9}{(k)^p \equiv (k), \quad \varrho^p \equiv \varrho \pmod{\mathfrak{P}},}
provided that all disturbing primes, e.g. those in the discriminants of the equations defining the numbers $(k)$ and $(\varrho)$, have been taken up among the excludents $S$.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 649 =====
% !PRINTED 618
\weberpage{618}
%% [page furniture, not body text -- source-confirmed 2026-08-10]
%% 618 \quad Twenty-Third Chapter. \quad \S\,168.

The first of the conditions (9) requires that $p$ be properly representable by the principal form of the discriminant $D$ (\S\,122), the second that
\weq{10}{p \equiv 1 \pmod{m}}
hold.

In order that a prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}$ of the first degree in $\Omega$, which does not divide $S$, be contained in $\bar{E}A$, it is necessary and sufficient that

1. $\mathfrak{p}$ be a principal ideal, i.\,e. an existing number $\pi$, and that this number $\pi$ be contained in $A$, i.\,e. that
\[
\text{2. } N(\pi) = p \equiv 1 \pmod{m}
\]
hold. These conditions agree exactly with the conditions (9), and consequently $\mathfrak{K}(D, \varrho)$ is \gesperrt{the class field of the group $A$}.

The degree of the field $\mathfrak{K}(A)$ is therefore not merely at most, but exactly equal to $h$.

The number $(Z, R_m)$ is $=1$ if none of the characteristic primes of \S\,108 divides $m$, and then the degree of the field $\mathfrak{K}(A)$ is equal to $H'\varphi(m)$. If, conversely, we include in $m$ all the characteristic primes and prime powers, then $R_m = R$ becomes \gesperrt{the group of absolute norm residues}, and we have
\[
(Z, R) = 2g,
\]
if $g$ is the number of genera of the discriminant $D$ (\S\,113, 7.). If, then, $H'_g$ denotes the number of classes of one genus, then $H' = g H'_g$, and formula (7) gives:
\weq{11}{h = \tfrac{1}{2} H'_g \varphi(m).}

By \S\,138 the class function $H_{-D}(u)$ splits, through the adjunction of square roots, into as many factors as there are genera of classes of forms, and the degree of each of these factors is $H'_g$.

Now if the class equation were still further decomposable, through the adjunction of any roots of unity whatever, than according to the genera, then one could assume $m$ in such a way that these roots of unity too, and also $\sqrt{\Delta}$, were contained in the field $\mathfrak{K}(\varrho)$.

If then $h''$ is the lowest degree to which the class equation can be reduced by the adjunction of roots of unity, then the absolute degree of the field $\mathfrak{K}(D, \varrho)$ is at most equal to $h''\varphi(m)$
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 650 =====
% !PRINTED 619
\weberpage{619}
%% [page furniture, not body text -- source-confirmed 2026-08-10]
%% \S\,169 \quad Relation of the division fields to the class field. \quad 619

%<<CONT
and the relative degree with respect to $\Omega$ at most equal to $\tfrac{1}{2} h''\varphi(m)$, and from this it follows by (11) that $h''$ cannot be smaller than $H'_g$. Thus it is proved:

5. \gesperrt{The class equation $H_{-D}(u)$ is, in the field that contains all roots of unity, not further decomposable than into the factors corresponding to the genera.}

\noindent\textbf{\S\,169.\qquad \gesperrt{Relation of the division fields to the class field.}}

In the last two sections we have considered two kinds of groups, of which the first led to the division fields of the elliptic functions, the second to the order fields in combination with roots of unity. Between these there exists a relation:

The first group $A$ consisted of the numbers $\alpha$ in $O$ which satisfied the condition
\weq{1}{\alpha \equiv \pm 1 \pmod{\mathfrak{m}}}
where $\mathfrak{m}$ is any ideal in $\Omega$; the second group $A'$ consisted of the numbers $\alpha'$ of the order $[Q]$ which satisfied the condition
\weq{2}{N(\alpha') \equiv 1 \pmod{m}}
where $m$ and $Q$ denote natural numbers.

If we assume that $\mathfrak{m}$ is a prime ideal or a power of a prime ideal, then we can choose $Q$ and $m$ in such a way that the group $A'$ is contained in the group $A$.

For if $r$ is a rational number, then, since $\alpha'$ belongs to the order $[Q]$:
\weq{3}{\alpha' \equiv r \pmod{Q}, \quad N(\alpha') \equiv r^2 \pmod{Q},}
and if $Q$ is divisible by $m$:
\weq{4}{\alpha' \equiv r \pmod{m},}
hence by (2) and (3)
\[
r^2 \equiv 1 \pmod{m}
\]
\weq{5}{(r - 1)(r + 1) \equiv 0 \pmod{m},}
we therefore assume $Q$ to be divisible by $m$, and $m$ by $\mathfrak{m}$; then by (5), if $\mathfrak{m}$, as we have assumed, is a prime ideal or a power of such a one, either
\weq{6}{r \equiv 1 \text{ or } r \equiv -1 \pmod{\mathfrak{m}},}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 651 =====
% !PRINTED 620
\weberpage{620}
%% [page furniture, not body text -- source-confirmed 2026-08-10]
%% 620 \quad Twenty-third Chapter. \quad \S\,169.

%<<CONT
and from (4) it follows that:
\weq{7}{\alpha' \equiv \pm 1 \pmod{\mathfrak{m}};}
consequently $A'$ is contained in $A$, and by \S\,164, 11. $\mathfrak{K}(A)$ is therefore contained in $\mathfrak{K}(A')$. Since now, by \S\,158, every division field can be composed of such fields whose divisor is a prime ideal or a power of a prime ideal, it follows that:

6. \gesperrt{The division field of the elliptic functions can be reduced to order fields and cyclotomic fields.}\footnote{A part of this theorem is proved by another route in the Stra\ss burg dissertation of \gesperrt{Daniel Bauer}, ``\"Uber den Teilungsk\"orper der elliptischen Funktionen mit singul\"arem Modul''. Stra\ss burg 1903.}

\begin{center}
\gesperrt{Twenty-fourth Chapter.}

\medskip
{\Large Algebraic Functions of One Variable.}
\end{center}

\rule{5em}{0.4pt}

\begin{center}
§ 170. \gesperrt{Introductory.}
\end{center}

The theory of algebraic functions of one variable is the starting point
of the general investigations of \gesperrt{Abel} on the new
transcendents, which have since received the name \glqq Abelian
functions\grqq{} and which are the highest generalisation of the
elliptic functions. The principal problems of this theory have been
brought to a certain conclusion by the papers of \gesperrt{Riemann},
\gesperrt{Weierstrass}, \gesperrt{Clebsch}, \gesperrt{Brill} and
\gesperrt{Noether}. In particular, in the conception of many-sheeted
(\gesperrt{Riemann}) surfaces \gesperrt{Riemann} has created a means for the
investigation of these functions that is extraordinarily effective
through its intuitive clarity.

All these investigations, however, which rest on the one hand upon the
theory of functions, on the other hand, as with \gesperrt{Clebsch},
\gesperrt{Brill}, \gesperrt{Noether}, upon the methods of rational
algebra (theory of forms and invariants, or of algebraic curves), must
always make certain restrictions; they must exclude certain
\glqq exceptional cases\grqq{} and content themselves with the treatment
of the so-called general cases. Not subject to this restriction is the
theory of algebraic functions worked out on the analogy of number theory
by \gesperrt{Dedekind} and myself, of which a survey is to be given
here\textsuperscript{1)}.

\smallskip
\noindent\rule{5em}{0.4pt}

\noindent\textsuperscript{1)}~On the literature concerning algebraic and
\gesperrt{Abel}ian functions let the following be mentioned here: \gesperrt{Abel},
Mém. sur une propriété générale d'une classe très-étendue de fonctions
transcendentes (presented to the Paris Academy in 1826, Werke, new
edition by \gesperrt{Sylow} and \gesperrt{Lie}, Bd.\,I, S.\,145).
\gesperrt{Riemann}, Theorie der \gesperrt{Abel}schen Funktionen, Crelles Journ.,
Bd.\,54, 1857, Werke 2. Aufl., Nr.\,88. \gesperrt{Weierstrass},
Vorlesungen 1875/76, Werke, Bd.\,IV. \gesperrt{Clebsch}, Über die
%CONT>>
