\begin{center}
§ 171. \gesperrt{Definition of algebraic functions.}
\end{center}

A variable $\theta$ is called an algebraic function of an independent
variable $z$ when the two variables are connected with one another by an
algebraic equation
\weq{1}{F(\theta,z)=0}
In this, $F$ denotes an expression of the form
\weq{2}{F(\theta,z)=a_0\theta^n+a_1\theta^{n-1}+\cdots+a_{n-1}\theta+a_n,}
whose coefficients $a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_n$ are integral rational functions
of $z$ without a common divisor. About the constant coefficients in these
expressions we make no further assumption than that they are real or
complex numbers\textsuperscript{1)}. We assume the function $F(\theta,z)$
to be irreducible in the sense that it shall not split into factors which
are themselves rational functions of $\theta$ and $z$. Every integral
function $G(\theta,z)$ can, according to Bd.\,I, § 20, be decomposed in
only one way into irreducible factors (apart from constant factors). We
say that the function $G(\theta,z)$
%CONT>>
% body text is cut off here by the page break; the sentence continues on the
% next page, which is not included in this scan set.

\smallskip
\noindent Anwendung der \gesperrt{Abelschen} Funktionen in der Geometrie, Crelles
Journ., Bd.\,63, 1864. \gesperrt{Clebsch} and \gesperrt{Gordan},
Theorie der \gesperrt{Abelschen} Funktionen, Leipzig 1866. \gesperrt{Brill} and
\gesperrt{Noether}, Über die algebraischen Funktionen und ihre
Anwendung in der Geometrie, Mathematische Annalen VII, 1874.
\gesperrt{Brill} and \gesperrt{Noether}, Die Entwickelung der Theorie
der algebraischen Funktionen, Bericht der Deutschen
Mathematiker-Vereinigung 1894. \gesperrt{Appell} et \gesperrt{Goursat},
Théorie des fonctions algébriques, Paris 1895. On the
number-theoretic methods: \gesperrt{Kronecker}, Über die
Diskriminante algebraischer Funktionen, Crelles Journ., Bd.\,91, 1881,
and: Festschrift zu \gesperrt{Kummers} Doktor-Jubiläum, Crelles
Journ., Bd.\,92, 1881. \gesperrt{Dedekind} and \gesperrt{Weber},
Theorie der algebraischen Funktionen einer Veränderlichen, Crelles
Journ., Bd.\,92, 1879. \gesperrt{Hensel} and \gesperrt{Landsberg},
Theorie der algebraischen Funktionen einer Variablen, Leipzig 1902.
The form of the theory presented in what follows rests upon the concept
of functionals introduced in Bd.\,II, § 153, which in this form had
already been applied, in a Strassburg dissertation prompted by
\gesperrt{Wellstein} and written by \gesperrt{Rehfeld} (1906), to the
treatment of a special problem of the theory of functions.

\smallskip
\noindent\textsuperscript{1)}~No gap would remain anywhere if we wished
to restrict ourselves here to \gesperrt{algebraic numbers}. If one regards
$\theta, z$ as Cartesian coordinates in the plane, then equation (1)
represents an algebraic curve, and one can apply the theory of these
curves, as \gesperrt{Clebsch} and \gesperrt{Gordan} and \gesperrt{Brill}
and \gesperrt{Noether} have done. To be sure, only the real values of
these variables have a really intuitive meaning here.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 656 =====
% !PRINTED 625
\weberpage{625}
%<<CONT
shall vanish then and only then, when the function $F(\theta,z)$ occurs among its irreducible factors. This is the definition of vanishing, according to which, if one wished to be entirely correct, every equation $G(\theta,z) = 0$ would have to be understood as a congruence with respect to the modulus $F$. In order not to be prolix, however, we shall not employ this mode of expression here.

If we divide equation (1) by $a_0$, it takes the form
\weq{3}{f(\theta,z) = \theta^n + b_1\theta^{n-1} + b_2\theta^{n-2} + \cdots + b_{n-1}\theta + b_n,}
in which the $b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_n$ are integral or fractional rational functions of $z$.

The system of all integral and fractional rational functions $\Phi(\theta,z)$ of $\theta$ and $z$ in which the denominator is not divisible by $F$, and so does not vanish, has the property of reproducing itself by addition, subtraction, multiplication and division (except by 0), and therefore forms a \gesperrt{field of algebraic functions} (Bd.\,I, \S\,146), which I shall denote by $\Omega$.

The degree $n$ of the irreducible equation (2) or (3), that is, of the equation of lowest degree which $\theta$ satisfies, is called \gesperrt{the degree of the algebraic field with respect to} $\theta$, or also the \gesperrt{degree of} $\theta$.

If $\varphi(\theta)$ is an integral function of $\theta$ whose coefficients are integral or fractional rational functions of $z$, then by division one can form an equation:
\[
\varphi(\theta) = f(\theta)q(\theta) + r(\theta),
\]
in which $q(\theta)$ and $r(\theta)$ are functions of the same kind as $\varphi$, but of which $r(\theta)$ is \gesperrt{at most of degree} $n-1$. By reason of (3) we then have
\weq{4}{\varphi(\theta) = r(\theta).}

If $\varphi(\theta)$ is not divisible by $f(\theta)$, then the two functions have no rational divisor in common, and one can determine two functions of the field $f_1(\theta), \varphi_1(\theta)$ in such a way that
\[
f(\theta)f_1(\theta) + \varphi(\theta)\varphi_1(\theta) = 1
\]
holds (Bd.\,I, \S\,6). Since now $f(\theta) = 0$, there follows from this:
\weq{5}{\varphi_1(\theta) = \frac{1}{\varphi(\theta)}.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 657 =====
% !PRINTED 626
\weberpage{626}
One can therefore replace every fractional function of $\theta$ by an integral function of $\theta$, and so obtains the theorem:

1. \gesperrt{Every function $\xi$ of the field $\Omega$ can be put in one single way into the form:}
\weq{6}{\xi = x_0 + x_1\theta + x_2\theta^2 + \cdots + x_{n-1}\theta^{n-1},}
\gesperrt{whose coefficients $x_0, x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{n-1}$ are rational functions of $z$.}

That this is possible at all is inferred from (4) and (5); that it is possible in only one way follows from the irreducibility of $f(\theta)$; for if one had two different representations of one and the same quantity $\xi$ in the form (6), their difference would yield an equation for $\theta$ of a degree lower than $n$.

If one chooses $n$ functions of the field $\Omega$ arbitrarily:
\weq{7}{
\begin{aligned}
\eta_1 &= x_0^{(1)} + x_1^{(1)}\theta + \cdots + x_{n-1}^{(1)}\theta^{n-1}, \\
\eta_2 &= x_0^{(2)} + x_2^{(2)}\theta + \cdots + x_{n-1}^{(2)}\theta^{n-1}, \\% [sic] printed x_2^{(2)}, not x_1^{(2)}
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots \\
\eta_n &= x_0^{(n)} + x_1^{(n)}\theta + \cdots + x_{n-1}^{(n)}\theta^{n-1},
\end{aligned}
}
with the single restriction that the determinant
\[
\Sigma \pm x_0^{(1)} x_1^{(2)} \cdots x_{n-1}^{(n)}
\]
is not identically zero, then by elimination of the powers of $\theta$ from (6) and (7) every function $\xi$ in $\Omega$ can be put into the form:
\weq{8}{\xi = y_1\eta_1 + y_2\eta_2 + \cdots + y_n\eta_n,}
whose coefficients $y_i$ are rational functions of $z$.

Such a system of functions $\eta_1, \eta_2, \ldots, \eta_n$ is called a \gesperrt{basis} of the field $\Omega$.

In order that a system of functions $\eta_1, \eta_2, \ldots, \eta_n$ form a basis of $\Omega$, it is necessary and sufficient that no equation of the form
\[
y_1\eta_1 + y_2\eta_2 + \cdots + y_n\eta_n = 0
\]
subsist in which the coefficients $y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n$ do not all vanish identically.

Thus the functions
\[
1, \theta, \theta^2, \ldots, \theta^{n-1}
\]
form a basis of $\Omega$.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 658 =====
% !PRINTED 627
\weberpage{627}
The transition from one basis $\eta_1, \eta_2, \ldots, \eta_n$ to another $\eta_1', \eta_2', \ldots, \eta_n'$ takes place through a linear substitution:
\weq{9}{(\eta_1', \eta_2', \ldots, \eta_n') = L(\eta_1, \eta_2, \ldots, \eta_n)}
or, written more briefly,
\weq{10}{(\eta_i') = L(\eta_i),}
in which $L$ has the meaning
\weq{11}{
L = \begin{pmatrix}
l_{1,1}, & l_{1,2}, & \ldots, & l_{1,n} \\
l_{2,1}, & l_{2,2}, & \ldots, & l_{2,n} \\
\cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot \\
l_{n,1}, & l_{n,2}, & \ldots, & l_{n,n}
\end{pmatrix} \quad \text{(Bd.\,II, \S\,41).}
}

The elements $l_{i,k}$ of this substitution are rational functions of $z$.

\gesperrt{The system $(\eta')$ is again a basis then and only then, when the determinant $|L|$ of this substitution does not vanish.}

\begin{center}
\S\ 172.

\gesperrt{Norms and Traces.}
\end{center}

If, for the representation of the functions in $\Omega$, one chooses an arbitrary basis $\eta_1, \eta_2, \ldots, \eta_n$, then, $\xi$ being an arbitrary function of the field, one can set, since the products $\xi\eta_i$ are contained in the field:
\weq{1}{
\begin{aligned}
\xi\eta_1 &= y_{1,1}\eta_1 + y_{1,2}\eta_2 + \cdots + y_{1,n}\eta_n, \\
\xi\eta_2 &= y_{2,1}\eta_1 + y_{2,2}\eta_2 + \cdots + y_{2,n}\eta_n, \\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots \\
\xi\eta_n &= y_{n,1}\eta_1 + y_{n,2}\eta_2 + \cdots + y_{n,n}\eta_n,
\end{aligned}
}
and from this one obtains, by elimination of the $\eta$:
\weq{2}{
\begin{vmatrix}
y_{1,1} - \xi, & y_{1,2}, & \ldots, & y_{1,n} \\
y_{2,1}, & y_{2,2} - \xi, & \ldots, & y_{2,n} \\
\cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot \\
y_{n,1}, & y_{n,2}, & \ldots, & y_{n,n} - \xi
\end{vmatrix} = 0,
}
an equation which, ordered according to powers of $\xi$, takes the shape:
\weq{3}{\varphi(\xi) = \xi^n + b_1\xi^{n-1} + \cdots + b_{n-1}\xi + b_n = 0,}
in which $b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_n$ are rational functions of $z$. These coefficients are independent of the choice of the basis $\eta_i$. For the equations (1), by which the transition from the basis $\eta_i$
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 659 =====
% !PRINTED 628
\weberpage{628}
%<<CONT
to the basis $\xi\eta_i$ is effected, we can represent, following the notation (9), (10) of the preceding section, in this way:
\weq{4}{(\xi\eta_i) = Y(\eta_i),}
and accordingly there results, by transition to the basis $\eta_i'$:
\[
(\xi\eta_i') = LYL^{-1}(\eta_i').
\]
The functions $b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_n$ are therefore completely determined by the function $\xi$.

The function
\weq{5}{(-1)^n b_n =
\begin{vmatrix}
y_{1,1}, & y_{1,2}, & \ldots, & y_{1,n} \\
y_{2,1}, & y_{2,2}, & \ldots, & y_{2,n} \\
\cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot \\
y_{n,1}, & y_{n,2}, & \ldots, & y_{n,n}
\end{vmatrix}}
is called the \gesperrt{norm of the function} $\xi$ and is denoted by $N(\xi)$. Concerning it the following theorems hold:

1. \gesperrt{If $\xi$ is not identically zero, then $N(\xi)$ is different from zero.}

For if the determinant of the system (1) vanishes, then rational functions $y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n$, not all of which vanish, can be determined so that
\[
\xi(y_1\eta_1 + y_2\eta_2 + \cdots + y_n\eta_n) = 0
\]
holds, and this requires, since $\eta_1, \eta_2, \ldots, \eta_n$ is a basis, that $\xi = 0$.

2. \gesperrt{If $\xi$ is a rational function of $z$, then its norm is the $n$th power of this function.}

For if $\xi$ is rational, the equations (1) reduce to the identities $\xi\eta_i = \xi\eta_i$. Accordingly all terms in the determinant (5) vanish with the exception of the diagonal terms, and these all become equal to $\xi$. We express this theorem by the formula:
\[
N(a) = a^n.
\]

3. \gesperrt{If $\xi, \xi'$ are two functions in $\Omega$, then the theorem holds}
\weq{6}{N(\xi\xi') = N(\xi)N(\xi').}
For if, according to (4):
\[
(\xi\eta_i) = Y(\eta_i), \quad (\xi'\eta_i) = Y'(\eta_i),
\]
then
\[
(\xi\xi'\eta_i) = YY'(\eta_i),
\]
and from this formula (6) follows, because the determinant of a composed linear substitution, here $YY'$, is equal to the product of the determinant of the components.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 660 =====
% !PRINTED 629
\weberpage{629}
\gesperrt{4. From 2. and 3. it follows, when $\xi$ is different from zero:}
\[
N(\xi)\,N\left(\frac{1}{\xi}\right) = 1,
\]
\gesperrt{and from this, for any two $\xi, \xi'$:}
\weq{7}{N\left(\frac{\xi'}{\xi}\right) = \frac{N(\xi')}{N(\xi)}.}

\gesperrt{5. If $t$ is an indeterminate or variable quantity, and $\varphi(t)$ the function which by (3) becomes zero for $t = \xi$, then}
\weq{8}{\varphi(t) = N(t - \xi).}

This follows from (1) and (2). For if in (1) one replaces $\xi$ by $\xi - t$, this amounts to the same thing as replacing $y_{i,i}$ by $y_{i,i} - t$ and leaving the remaining $y_{i,k}$ unchanged.

If we decompose the function $\varphi(t)$, which is a rational function of $t$ and $z$, into a product of irreducible factors $\varphi_1(t), \varphi_2(t), \dots$ then one of these factors must vanish for $t = \xi$. Let this be $\varphi_1(t)$, and let
\weq{9}{\varphi_1(t) = t^e + b_1' t^{e-1} + \cdots + b_{e-1}' t + b_e'}
be of degree $e$. Then $\varphi_1(\xi) = 0$ is the equation of lowest degree which $\xi$ satisfies, and from $\xi$ one derives a field $\Omega_1$ which is contained in $\Omega$ and has the degree $e$. Every number $\eta$ of the field $\Omega_1$ can be represented, and that in only one way, in the form:
\weq{10}{\eta = x_0 + x_1 \xi + \cdots + x_{e-1} \xi^{e-1}.}

Let further
\weq{11}{\theta^f + \eta_1 \theta^{f-1} + \cdots + \eta_{f-1} \theta^{f-1} + \eta_f = 0} % [sic] exponent on the penultimate term prints \theta^{f-1} again, not a descending power
be the equation of lowest degree with coefficients in $\Omega_1$ which $\theta$ satisfies, so that $f$ is the relative degree of $\Omega$ with respect to $\Omega_1$.

By means of the $ef$ functions
\weq{12}{\xi^h \theta^k \qquad \begin{array}{l} h = 0, 1, \dots, e-1 \\ k = 0, 1, \dots, f-1 \end{array}}
every function of the field can be expressed linearly, and between them there subsists no linear equation with coefficients depending rationally on $z$. For otherwise $\theta$ or $\xi$ would arise from an equation of lower degree than $f$ or $e$. Ac-
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 661 =====
% !PRINTED 630
\weberpage{630}
%<<CONT
accordingly the functions (12) form a basis of the field $\Omega$, and it follows that
\weq{13}{ef = n.}
Thus $e$ and $f$ are divisors of $n$.

If
\weq{14}{\xi_1, \xi_2, \dots, \xi_e}
denotes a basis of the field $\Omega_1$, then the $n$ quantities:
\weq{15}{\xi_1 \theta^k, \xi_2 \theta^k, \dots, \xi_e \theta^k, \qquad k = 0, 1, 2, \dots, f-1}
form a basis of $\Omega$. If one forms the substitution of the $e$ quantities:
\weq{16}{(\xi \xi_i) = Y_1(\xi_i),}
then
\weq{17}{(-1)^e b_e' = |Y_1| = N_1(\xi)}
is the norm of $\xi$ in the field $\Omega_1$, and if one forms the substitution for $(\xi \xi_i \theta_k)$ in the field $\Omega$ with the basis (15), there results
\[
(\xi \xi_i \theta^k) = Y_1(\xi_i)\, Y_1(\xi_i \theta) \dots Y_1(\xi_i \theta^{e-1}),
\]
from which
\weq{18}{N(\xi) = |Y_1|^f.}
From the substitution determinant $|Y_1|$ one derives the function $\varphi_1(t)$ by formula (2), and so it follows from (18):
\weq{19}{N(t - \xi) = [\varphi_1(t)]^f,}
and from this:

6. \gesperrt{The function $\varphi(t) = N(t - \xi)$ is either irreducible or a power of an irreducible function.}

If the exponent $f$ of this power is greater than 1, then the field $\Omega$ is imprimitive, $\Omega_1$ is a subfield, and $\Omega$ is a field of degree $f$ over $\Omega_1$ (Bd. I, \S\ 151).

If $f = 1$, $e = n$, then $\xi$ is called a \gesperrt{primitive function of the field} $\Omega$, and $\Omega_1$ is identical with $\Omega$.

We return to equation (2) or (3), which, as we have seen, is independent of the choice of the basis, and define the coefficient
\weq{20}{-b_1 = y_{1,1} + y_{2,2} + \cdots + y_{n,n} = S(\xi)}
as the \gesperrt{trace of the function} $\xi$. For the trace there result from the definition the following fundamental theorems, in which $\xi, \xi'$ denote any two functions in $\Omega$, and $x$ a rational function:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 662 =====
% !PRINTED 631
\weberpage{631}
%<<CONT
\weq{21}{\begin{aligned}
S(0) &= 0, \\
S(1) &= n, \\
S(x\xi) &= x\,S(\xi), \\
S(\xi + \xi') &= S(\xi) + S(\xi').
\end{aligned}}
All traces are rational functions of $z$.

\S\,173. \gesperrt{Discriminants.}

If $(\eta_1, \eta_2, \dots, \eta_n) = (\eta_i)$ is a system of $n$ functions in the field $\Omega$, then the $n^2$ traces $S(\eta_i \eta_k)$ are rational functions of $z$. We define as the \gesperrt{discriminant of the system} $(\eta_i)$ the determinant
\weq{1}{\Delta(\eta_1, \eta_2, \dots, \eta_n) =
\begin{vmatrix}
S(\eta_1\eta_1), & S(\eta_1\eta_2), & \dots, & S(\eta_1\eta_n) \\
S(\eta_2\eta_1), & S(\eta_2\eta_2), & \dots, & S(\eta_2\eta_n) \\
\cdots & \cdots & \cdots & \cdots \\
S(\eta_n\eta_1), & S(\eta_n\eta_2), & \dots, & S(\eta_n\eta_n)
\end{vmatrix},}
for which we also write, more briefly, $\Delta(\eta_i)$.

We prove the theorem:

7. \gesperrt{The discriminant $\Delta(\eta_i)$ is then and only then different from zero, when $(\eta_i)$ is a basis of the field $\Omega$.}

In order to prove it, let us first assume that $\Delta(\eta_i) = 0$. Then, by an elementary theorem on determinants, the rational functions $y_1, y_2, \dots, y_n$ can be so determined, without their being all zero, that
\weq{2}{y_1 S(\eta_1\eta_k) + y_2 S(\eta_2\eta_k) + \cdots + y_n S(\eta_n\eta_k) = S[\eta_k(y_1\eta_1 + y_2\eta_2 + \cdots + y_n\eta_n)] = 0 \qquad (k = 1, 2, \dots, n)}
holds. If $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ denotes an arbitrary system of rational functions, and one sets
\weq{3}{\begin{aligned}
y_1\eta_1 + y_2\eta_2 + \cdots + y_n\eta_n &= \eta, \\
x_1\eta_1 + x_2\eta_2 + \cdots + x_n\eta_n &= \xi,
\end{aligned}}
then from (2), by multiplication by $x_k$ and summation, there follows:
\weq{4}{S(\xi\eta) = 0.}
Now if $(\eta_i)$ is a basis, then $\xi$ can be any function whatever in $\Omega$, and hence also $1/\eta$, and then formula (4) gives the contradictory result $S(1) = 0$; the discriminant of a basis $(\eta_i)$ can therefore not vanish.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 663 =====
% !PRINTED 632
\weberpage{632}
In order to prove the converse as well, we assume that $(\eta_i)$ is a basis and that
\weq{5}{(\eta_i') = X(\eta_i)}
is a linear substitution. The system $(\eta_i')$ is then and only then likewise a basis, when the determinant $|X|$ of this substitution is different from zero (\S\ 171). If one sets, in accordance with (5),
\[
\eta_h' = x_{h,1}\eta_1 + x_{h,2}\eta_2 + \cdots + x_{h,n}\eta_n,
\]
then
\[
S(\eta_h'\eta_k') = \sum^{i\,i'} x_{h,i} x_{k,i'} S(\eta_i \eta_{i'}),
\]
and by forming the determinant from this:
\weq{6}{\Delta(\eta_1', \eta_2', \dots, \eta_n') = |X|^2 \Delta(\eta_1, \eta_2, \dots, \eta_n).}

If, then, $\Delta(\eta_i')$ is different from zero, $|X|$ cannot vanish, and $(\eta_i')$ is a basis. With this, 7. is proved.

From (6) there follows further, by the definition of the norm in \S\ 172, if one sets $\eta_i' = \xi\eta_i$, where $\xi$ is an arbitrary function in $\Omega$:
\weq{7}{\Delta(\xi\eta_i) = N(\xi)^2 \Delta(\eta_i).}

\S\,174. \gesperrt{The Power Sums.}

The traces of the powers of $\theta$
\weq{1}{s_k = S(\theta^k)}
are nothing other than the \gesperrt{power sums}, which can be calculated by the \gesperrt{Newton} formulae. But since we may not speak here of the \glqq roots\grqq{} of the equation $f(\theta) = 0$, which we do not yet possess, these formulae must be derived directly from the definition of the trace.

If $f(\theta) = 0$ is the equation defining the field $\Omega$, we set
\weq{2}{f(t) = t^n + a_1 t^{n-1} + \cdots + a_{n-1} t + a_n}
and form the quotient:
\weq{3}{\frac{f(t)}{t - \theta} = \eta_0 + \eta_1 t + \eta_2 t^2 + \cdots + \eta_{n-1} t^{n-1},}
in which
\weq{4}{\begin{aligned}
\eta_0 &= a_{n-1} + a_{n-2}\theta + \cdots + a_1\theta^{n-2} + \theta^{n-1}, \\
\eta_1 &= a_{n-2} + a_{n-3}\theta + \cdots + \theta^{n-2}, \\
&\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots \\
\eta_{n-2} &= a_1 + \theta, \\
\eta_{n-1} &= 1.
\end{aligned}}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 664 =====
% !PRINTED 633
\weberpage{633}

Between these functions there hold the relations:

\weq{5}{
\begin{aligned}
\theta\,\eta_0 &= -a_n\eta_{n-1}, \\
\theta\,\eta_1 &= \eta_0 - a_{n-1}\eta_{n-1}, \\
\theta\,\eta_2 &= \eta_1 - a_{n-2}\eta_{n-1}, \\
&\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots \\
\theta\,\eta_{n-1} &= \eta_{n-2} - a_1\eta_{n-1},
\end{aligned}
}

and the $\eta_0, \eta_1, \ldots, \eta_{n-1}$ form a basis of $\Omega$, since by
(4) the powers of $\theta$ can be expressed linearly by the $\eta_i$.

If, then, $\zeta$ is an arbitrary function in $\Omega$, one can set:

\weq{6}{\zeta = y_0\eta_0 + y_1\eta_1 + \cdots + y_{n-1}\eta_{n-1}.}

From $y_0, y_1, \ldots, y_{n-1}$ we derive a continuation of the sequence of these rational
functions $y_n, y_{n+1}, y_{n+2}, \ldots$ by setting:

\weq{7}{a_n y_r + a_{n-1}y_{r+1} + \cdots + a_1 y_{r+n-1} + y_{r+n} = 0
\qquad (r = 0, 1, 2, \ldots).}

Then from (5) and (6) there results:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\zeta\theta &= \eta_0 y_1 + \eta_1 y_2 + \cdots + \eta_{n-2}y_{n-1}, \\
&\quad - \eta_{n-1}(a_n y_0 + a_{n-1}y_1 + \cdots + a_1 y_{n-1}), \\
&= y_1\eta_0 + y_2\eta_1 + \cdots + y_n\eta_{n-1},
\end{aligned}
\]

and in general, for a positive $r$:

\weq{8}{\zeta\theta^r = y_r\eta_0 + y_{r+1}\eta_1 + \cdots + y_{r+n-1}\eta_{n-1},}

as one easily confirms from (5) and (7) by the inference from $r$ to $r+1$.
If one orders this sum according to powers of $\theta$, there results an expression of the
form

\weq{9}{\zeta\theta^r = x_{0,r} + x_{1,r}\theta + x_{2,r}\theta^2 + \cdots + x_{n-1,r}\theta^{n-1},}

wherein

\weq{10}{
\begin{aligned}
x_{0,r} &= y_r a_{n-1} + y_{r+1}a_{n-2} + \cdots + y_{r+n-2}a_1 + y_{r+n-1}, \\
x_{1,r} &= y_r a_{n-2} + y_{r+1}a_{n-3} + \cdots + y_{r+n-1}, \\
&\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots \\
x_{n-2,r} &= y_r a_1 + y_{r+1}, \\
x_{n-1,r} &= y_r.
\end{aligned}
}

But by the definition of the trace [\S\,172, (20)] we have

\weq{11}{
\begin{aligned}
S(\zeta) &= x_{0,0} + x_{1,1} + \cdots + x_{n-1,n-1}, \\
&= y_0 a_{n-1} + 2y_1 a_{n-2} + 3y_2 a_{n-3} + \cdots + n y_{n-1}.
\end{aligned}
}

If one wishes to apply this expression to $\zeta = \eta_r$, one has to set $y_r = 1$ and the
remaining $y = 0$, and obtains

\[
S(\eta_r) = (r+1)a_{n-r-1}, \quad S(\eta_{n-1-r}) = (n-r)a_r,
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 665 =====
% !PRINTED 634
\weberpage{634}
%<<CONT
and consequently, so long as $r \leqq n$, by (4) with the notation (1):

\weq{12}{(n-r)a_r = a_r s_0 + a_{r-1}s_1 + \cdots + a_1 s_{r-1} + s_r,}

and if one takes the trace of $\theta^r f(\theta) = 0$:

\weq{13}{0 = a_n s_r + a_{n-1}s_{r+1} + \cdots + a_1 s_{r+n-1} + s_{r+n}.}

These are the \gesperrt{Newton}ian formulae (Bd.\ I, \S\,46).

If we denote by

\[
f'(t) = n t^{n-1} + (n-1)a_1 t^{n-2} + \cdots + 2a_{n-2}t + a_{n-1}
\]

the derived function of $f(t)$, multiply equation (12) by
$\theta^{n-r-1}$ and sum from $r=0$ to $r=n-1$, then it follows that:

\weq{14}{f'(\theta) = \eta_0 s_0 + \eta_1 s_1 + \cdots + \eta_{n-1}s_{n-1},}

and if, for any positive $k$, one multiplies equations (12) by
$\theta^{n-r+k-1}$ and takes in as many of equations (13) besides as are needed
until $n-r+k-1$ begins to become negative, there results:

\weq{15}{\theta^k f'(\theta) = \eta_0 s_k + \eta_1 s_{k+1} + \cdots + \eta_{n-1}s_{k+n-1}.}

To form the norm of $f'(\theta)$, one would have first to express, in these equations, the
basis $\eta_0, \eta_1, \ldots, \eta_{n-1}$ by means of the substitution (2) in terms of
$(1, \theta, \theta^2, \ldots, \theta^{n-1})$, then to form equation (15) for
$k = 0, 1, \ldots, n-1$ and to take the determinant of this system. Instead of
this one may take the determinant with respect to the $\eta$, and then multiply by the
substitution determinant:

\[
\begin{vmatrix}
a_{n-1}, & a_{n-2}, & \ldots, & a_1, & 1 \\
a_{n-2}, & a_{n-3}, & \ldots, & 1, & 0 \\
\cdots & \cdots & \cdots & \cdots & \cdots \\
1, & 0, & \ldots, & 0, & 0
\end{vmatrix}
= (-1)^{\frac{1}{2}n(n+1)} % [sic] printed exponent; algebraically n(n-1)/2
\]

In this way one obtains

\weq{16}{N[f'(\theta)] = (-1)^{\frac{1}{2}n(n+1)} % [sic] printed exponent; algebraically n(n-1)/2
\begin{vmatrix}
s_0, & s_1, & \ldots, & s_{n-1} \\
s_1, & s_2, & \ldots, & s_n \\
\cdots & \cdots & \cdots & \cdots \\
s_{n-1}, & s_n, & \ldots, & s_{2n-2}
\end{vmatrix}.}

But this determinant is, by the definition of the discriminant (\S\,173):

\[
\Delta(1, \theta, \theta^2, \ldots, \theta^{n-1}),
\]

and so we have:

\weq{17}{Nf'(\theta) = (-1)^{\frac{1}{2}n(n+1)}\Delta(1, \theta, \theta^2, \ldots, \theta^{n-1}). % [sic]
}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 666 =====
% !PRINTED 635
\weberpage{635}

In the discussion of this chapter we have, in accordance with the principal aim of the
investigation, regarded the coefficients $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ \gesperrt{as rational functions of}
$z$. Everything, however, remains entirely unchanged if we fix upon any \gesperrt{domain of
rationality} whatever for these quantities.

\begin{center}
\S\ 175. \gesperrt{Integral Functions of $z$.}
\end{center}

Every function $\omega$ of the field $\Omega$ satisfies, as we have seen, an equation of
lowest degree:

\weq{1}{\omega^e + b_1\omega^{e-1} + b_2\omega^{e-2} + \cdots + b_e = 0,}

whose coefficients $b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_e$ are rational functions of $z$.

1.\ \gesperrt{If these coefficients are integral rational functions of $z$, then $\omega$ is
called an integral algebraic function, or briefly an integral function, of $z$.}

For the integral algebraic functions the same theorems hold as for the integers (Bd.\ II,
\S\,149).

If we set

\weq{2}{\varphi(t) = t^e + b_1 t^{e-1} + b_2 t^{e-2} + \cdots + b_e,}

then, as we have seen in \S\,172,

\weq{3}{N(t - \omega) = \varphi(t)^f \quad (ef = n)}

is an integral power of $\varphi(t)$. If we therefore arrange $N(t-\omega)$ according to
powers of $t$, the coefficients all become integral rational functions again, and hence in
particular:

2.\ \gesperrt{The norm and the trace of an integral function $\omega$ are integral rational
functions of $z$.}

3.\ \gesperrt{A rational function of $z$ is an integral algebraic function only when it is
an integral rational function.}

For if $\omega = -b$ is rational, then $e = 1$ and $\omega + b = 0$ is the equation of
lowest degree for $\omega$, and hence $\omega$ is integral only when $b$ is integral and
rational.

4.\ \gesperrt{Every function $\eta$ in $\Omega$ can be transformed into an integral
algebraic function by multiplication by a rational function of $z$ different from zero.}

For every function $\eta$ satisfies an equation of lowest degree:

\weq{4}{b_0\eta^e + b_1\eta^{e-1} + \cdots + b_{e-1}\eta + b_e = 0,}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 667 =====
% !PRINTED 636
\weberpage{636}
%<<CONT
and if one multiplies by $b_0^{e-1}$ and sets $b_0\eta = \omega$, one obtains an equation
of the form (1).

5.\ \gesperrt{A function $\omega$ of the field $\Omega$ is an integral function if it
satisfies any equation}

\weq{5}{\psi(\omega) = \omega^m + c_1\omega^{m-1} + \cdots + c_{m-1}\omega + c_m = 0}

\gesperrt{in which $c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_m$ are integral rational functions, even if this is
not the equation of lowest degree.}

For if $\varphi(\omega) = 0$ is the equation of lowest degree for $\omega$, then $\psi(t)$
must, for a variable $t$, be divisible by $\varphi(t)$. That is simply the content of
equation (5). We have therefore

\[
\psi(t) = \chi(t)\varphi(t),
\]

in which $\psi(t)$ is likewise an integral function of $t$. % [sic] printed psi; sense calls for chi
If now, as was assumed,
$\psi(t)$ has integral coefficients, then by a theorem of \gesperrt{Gauss} the
coefficients of $\varphi(t)$ and of $\chi(t)$ must also be integral functions. Cf.\ Bd.\ I,
\S\,2, \S\,20, \S\,148\,$^1$).

From this there follows the principal theorem below:

6.\ \gesperrt{Sum, difference, product of two integral functions in $\Omega$ are again
integral functions.}

For if $\omega'$, $\omega''$ are two integral functions in $\Omega$ which satisfy the
equations:

\weq{6}{
\begin{aligned}
\omega'^{\,n'} + b_1'\omega'^{\,n'-1} + \cdots + b_{n'-1}'\omega' + b_{n'}' &= 0, \\
\omega''^{\,n''} + b_1''\omega''^{\,n''-1} + \cdots + b_{n''-1}''\omega'' + b_{n''}'' &= 0,
\end{aligned}
}

then let

\[
\omega_1, \omega_2, \ldots, \omega_m
\]

denote the products

\[
\omega'^{\,\nu'}\omega''^{\,\nu''}; \quad \nu' = 0, 1, \ldots, n'-1, \quad
\nu'' = 0, 1, \ldots, n''-1,
\]

and let $\omega$ denote one of the three functions $\omega' \pm \omega''$,
$\omega'\omega''$; then with the help of equations (6) one may set:

\weq{7}{
\begin{aligned}
\omega\omega_1 &= x_{1,1}\omega_1 + \cdots + x_{1,m}\omega_m, \\
&\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots \\
\omega\omega_m &= x_{m,1}\omega_1 + \cdots + x_{m,m}\omega_m,
\end{aligned}
}

%CONT>>
\begin{quote}
$^1$) In this proof the decomposability of integral rational functions into linear factors
need not be assumed, but only the decomposability into irreducible factors. One may
therefore still stipulate an arbitrary domain of rationality for the numerical
coefficients. In what follows, however, we shall nevertheless have to assume the
decomposability of an integral rational function of $z$ into linear factors, i.\ e.\ the
fundamental theorem of algebra.
\end{quote}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 668 =====
% !PRINTED 637
\weberpage{637}
%<<CONT
where $m = n'n''$, and the $x_{\nu,\nu'}$ are integral rational functions of
$z$. From (7) there results, by elimination of the $\omega_i$:

\[
\begin{vmatrix}
x_{1,1} - \omega, & x_{1,2}, & \ldots, & x_{1,m} \\
x_{2,1}, & x_{2,2} - \omega, & \ldots, & x_{2,m} \\
\hdotsfor{4} \\
x_{m,1}, & x_{m,2}, & \ldots, & x_{m,m} - \omega
\end{vmatrix} = 0,
\]

and this is an equation for $\omega$ of the form (5).

By repeated application of this theorem it follows that every
\gesperrt{integral rational function of integral functions is again
an integral function.}

7. \gesperrt{An integral function $\omega$ is called divisible by an
integral function $\omega'$ if there exists a third integral function
$\omega''$ such that}

\weq{8}{\omega = \omega'\omega''}

\gesperrt{holds.}

From this definition it follows at once:

\gesperrt{If $\omega$ is divisible by $\omega'$ and $\omega'$ is divisible by $\omega''$, then
$\omega$ is also divisible by $\omega''$.}

\gesperrt{If $\omega'$ and $\omega''$ are divisible by $\omega$, then $\omega' \pm \omega''$
is also divisible by $\omega$.}

\gesperrt{If $\omega_1, \omega_2, \omega_3, \ldots$ are divisible by $\omega$ and $\omega_1', \omega_2', \omega_3', \ldots$
are arbitrary integral functions, then}

\[
\omega_1 \omega_1' + \omega_2 \omega_2' + \omega_3 \omega_3' + \cdots
\]

\gesperrt{is also divisible by $\omega$.}

\begin{center}
§ 176. \gesperrt{Minimal basis and field discriminant.}
\end{center}

Since every function of the field $\Omega$ can be converted by multiplication
with an integral rational function into an integral algebraic
function of $z$, there also exist field bases
consisting of \gesperrt{integral functions} (e.g., in the notation
 of § 171, (2), the powers of $a_0 \theta$).

If now

\weq{1}{\omega_1, \ \omega_2, \ \ldots, \ \omega_n}

is such a basis consisting of integral functions, then every one
is of the form

\weq{2}{\omega = x_1 \omega_1 + x_2 \omega_2 + \cdots + x_n \omega_n}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 669 =====
% !PRINTED 638
\weberpage{638}
%<<CONT
contained function, when the $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ are integral rational
functions, an integral function in $\Omega$. But it is not thereby
said that conversely, in the form (2) with \gesperrt{integral coefficients}
 $x_i$, all integral functions in $\Omega$ are contained.

If, then, there are integral functions in the form (2) in which the
$x_i$ are not all integral rational functions, we can find an
integral function:

\[
\frac{x_1 \omega_1 + x_2 \omega_2 + \cdots + x_n \omega_n}{z - c},
\]

in which the $x_i$ are integral and not all divisible by $z - c$.
If we reduce the $x_i$ to their constant residues (with respect to $z - c$),
there results an integral function $\omega$ in the form:

\weq{3}{\omega = \frac{c_1 \omega_1 + c_2 \omega_2 + \cdots + c_n \omega_n}{z - c},}

in which the constants $c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_n$ certainly do not all vanish.

If, say, $c_1$ is different from zero, we can express $\omega_1$
by $\omega, \omega_2, \ldots, \omega_n$ and obtain a new integral
 basis of $\Omega$:

\weq{4}{\omega, \omega_2, \ldots, \omega_n.}

But for the discriminant there results, by § 173, (6), the
relation:

\weq{5}{\varDelta(\omega, \omega_2, \ldots, \omega_n) = \frac{c_1^2}{(z-c)^2} \varDelta(\omega_1, \omega_2, \ldots, \omega_n).}

Both discriminants are integral rational functions of $z$,
but the discriminant of the basis (4) is of \gesperrt{lower degree
than the discriminant of the basis} (1).

If we continue in this way to lower the degree of the
 discriminant, we must finally arrive at a basis $\omega_1, \omega_2, \ldots, \omega_n$
consisting of integral functions and having the property that in the form (2), with
integral rational $x_i$, all and only the integral functions in $\Omega$ are expressed.

8. \gesperrt{Definition: An integral basis $\omega_1, \omega_2, \ldots, \omega_n$
of the field $\Omega$ is called a minimal basis if in the
form}

\weq{6}{\omega = x_1 \omega_1 + x_2 \omega_2 + \cdots + x_n \omega_n}

\gesperrt{all integral functions of the field $\Omega$ can be represented
with integral rational $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$.}

Such a minimal basis therefore always exists.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 670 =====
% !PRINTED 639
\weberpage{639}
9. \gesperrt{A system of integral functions derived from a minimal
 basis $\omega_1, \omega_2, \ldots, \omega_n$}

\weq{7}{\omega_\nu' = x_{\nu,1} \omega_1 + x_{\nu,2} \omega_2 + \cdots + x_{\nu,n} \omega_n,}
\[
\nu = 1, 2, \ldots, n
\]

\gesperrt{is then and only then a minimal basis, when the
determinant}

\weq{8}{X = \Sigma \pm x_{1,1} x_{2,2} \ldots x_{n,n}}

\gesperrt{is a constant different from zero.}

For if this determinant, which is a rational function
of $z$, has a linear factor $z - c$, then the constants
$c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_n$ can be so determined that the $n$ integral rational functions


\[
c_1 x_{1,\nu} + c_2 x_{2,\nu} + \cdots + c_n x_{n,\nu}
\]

become divisible by $z - c$ without all the $c_i$ vanishing.
But then

\[
\frac{c_1 \omega_1' + c_2 \omega_2' + \cdots + c_n \omega_n'}{z - c}
\]

is an integral function, and $\omega_1', \omega_2', \ldots, \omega_n'$ is not a minimal basis.

For the discriminant one obtains from (7), according to § 173, (6)

\weq{9}{\varDelta(\omega_1', \omega_2', \ldots, \omega_n') = X^2 \varDelta(\omega_1, \omega_2, \ldots, \omega_n).}

From this it follows:

10. \gesperrt{The discriminant of a minimal basis is, apart from
a constant factor, independent of the particular
 choice of the basis.}

Among all discriminants of bases formed from integral functions,
 the discriminant of a minimal basis has the \gesperrt{lowest
 degree} (hence the name minimal basis). It is an integral
rational function of $z$ uniquely determined by the field
itself, apart from a constant factor. It is therefore also called
\gesperrt{the discriminant of the field $\Omega$} and is denoted
by $\varDelta(\Omega)$.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 671 =====
% !PRINTED none
\begin{center}
\gesperrt{Twenty-fifth Chapter.}

Functionals.

\rule{4cm}{0.4pt}
\end{center}

\begin{center}
§ 177. \gesperrt{Rational Functionals.}
\end{center}

We now carry over the concept of the functional, which served us in
the 17th chapter of the second volume for the foundation of the theory
of algebraic numbers, to the algebraic functions
.

We therefore adjoin arbitrary variables to the field $\Omega$ and
calculate with them according to the rules of literal calculation. There
thus arises an extended field $\overline{\Omega}$, whose elements are called \gesperrt{functionals}.
 The field $\overline{\Omega}$ itself is called the \gesperrt{functional field}.
 The variables here are not to be taken, in the sense of analysis,
as symbols for variable numbers, but as mere symbols of calculation
, and are to be well distinguished from the
variables $z, \theta$ of the field $\Omega$. We wish to call these auxiliary variables
the \gesperrt{functional variables}.

From the field $Z$ of the rational functions of $z$ there arises,
by adjunction of the variables, the field $\overline{Z}$ of the \gesperrt{rational
functionals}.

An integral rational function of the variables:

\[
\Phi(u, v, w, \ldots)
\]

with integral rational functions of $z$ as coefficients is called
an integral function in $Z$. The greatest common divisor
of the coefficients of $\Phi$ is called \gesperrt{the divisor of the function}, and
the function is called \gesperrt{primitive} if the coefficients have no common
 divisor. The primitive rational functions
 and their quotients are also called \gesperrt{units in the field}
$\overline{Z}$.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 672 =====
% !PRINTED 641
\weberpage{641}

The quotients of integral functions in $Z$ are the functionals in $\overline{Z}$. Every functional $\overline{A}$ in $\overline{Z}$ can be put into the form:
\weq{1}{\overline{A} = \frac{\Phi_1}{\Phi_2} = a\frac{E_1}{E_2} = aE,}
where $\Phi_1$, $\Phi_2$, $E_1$, $E_2$ are integral functions in $Z$, among them the units $E_1$, $E_2$, and $E$ is a unit in $\overline{Z}$ which is represented as a fractional function. $a$ is the quotient of the divisors of $\Phi_1$ and $\Phi_2$, hence an integral or fractional rational function of $z$.

The functions $a$ and $E$ in formula (1) are completely determined by $\overline{A}$, apart from \gesperrt{constant factors}, which here play the role of the \gesperrt{numerical units}. We shall call $a$ the ``\gesperrt{Absolute}'' of $\overline{A}$. The following theorem then holds:

1. \gesperrt{The Absolute of a product is equal to the product of the Absolutes of the factors,}
and we define:

2. \gesperrt{A rational functional is called integral if its Absolute is an integral function of $z$.}

From 1. it follows that the product of two integral functionals in $\overline{Z}$ is again an integral functional. The same follows also for the sum and difference of two integral functionals $\overline{A}_1$, $\overline{A}_2$ in $\overline{Z}$. For if we set:
\[
\overline{A}_1 = a_1\frac{E_1}{E}, \quad \overline{A}_2 = a_2\frac{E_2}{E},
\]
\[
\overline{A}_1 \pm \overline{A}_2 = \frac{a_1E_1 \pm a_2E_2}{E},
\]
where $a_1$, $a_2$ are integral rational functions of $z$, and $E_1$, $E_2$, $E$ integral units, then the Absolute of $\overline{A}_1 \pm \overline{A}_2$ is the divisor of the integral function $a_1E_1 \pm a_2E_2$, hence likewise an integral function of $z$. Thus the theorem holds:

3. \gesperrt{Sum, difference and product of two integral functionals in $\overline{Z}$ are again integral rational functionals.}

By the definition, all units and their reciprocals are to be designated as \gesperrt{integral}. If the Absolute of an integral rational functional $\overline{A}$ is linear ($= z - c$), then $\overline{A}$ is called a \gesperrt{rational prime functional} or a \gesperrt{prime functional} in $\overline{Z}$.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 673 =====
% !PRINTED 642
\weberpage{642}

4. \gesperrt{Every integral rational functional can be decomposed into prime factors, and indeed, apart from unit factors, in only one way.}

\gesperrt{If a product of integral functionals in $\overline{Z}$ is divisible by a prime functional, then at least one of the factors is divisible by this prime functional.}

\begin{center}
§ 178.\\
\gesperrt{Functionals of the field $\overline{\Omega}$.}
\end{center}

A functional of the field $\overline{\Omega}$ is an expression of the form:
\weq{1}{\overline{\omega} = \overline{x}_0 + \overline{x}_1\theta + \cdots + \overline{x}_{n-1}\theta^{n-1},}
where $\theta$ is the algebraic function that generates the field $\Omega$, and $\overline{x}_0, \overline{x}_1, \ldots, \overline{x}_{n-1}$ \gesperrt{are rational functionals}. $\overline{\omega}$ is $= 0$ only when all the coefficients $\overline{x}_0, \overline{x}_1, \ldots, \overline{x}_{n-1}$ vanish.

Every functional which, with respect to $\theta$, is of higher than the $(n-1)$th degree can be replaced by the remainder of the division by $f(\theta)$, and so reduced to the $(n-1)$th degree; and the quotient of two expressions (1), in which the denominator is not $=0$, can be brought into the form (1) as in § 171, 1.

If one takes an arbitrary basis
\[
\omega_1, \omega_2, \ldots, \omega_n
\]
of the field $\Omega$, then $\overline{\omega}$ can also be put into the form
\weq{2}{\overline{\omega} = \overline{x}_1\omega_1 + \overline{x}_2\omega_2 + \cdots + \overline{x}_n\omega_n}
If one applies this to the products $\overline{\omega}\omega_i$ and sets
\weq{3}{\overline{\omega}\omega_i = \overline{x}_{i,1}\omega_1 + \overline{x}_{i,2}\omega_2 + \cdots + \overline{x}_{i,n}\omega_n,}
in which the $\overline{x}_{i,n}$ are rational functionals, then there results for $\overline{\omega}$ an equation:
\weq{4}{\left|\begin{array}{lll}
\overline{x}_{1,1} - \overline{\omega}, & \overline{x}_{1,2}, & \ldots, \overline{x}_{1,n} \\
\overline{x}_{2,1}, & \overline{x}_{2,2} - \overline{\omega}, & \ldots, \overline{x}_{2,n} \\
\cdot & \cdot & \cdots \\
\overline{x}_{n,1}, & \overline{x}_{n,2}, & \ldots, \overline{x}_{n,n} - \overline{\omega}
\end{array}\right| = 0,}
and so:

5. \gesperrt{Every functional in $\overline{\Omega}$ satisfies an equation}
\weq{5}{\varphi(\overline{\omega}) = 0,}
\gesperrt{in which}
\weq{6}{\varphi(t) = t^n + \overline{A}_1 t_2^{n-1} + \overline{A}_2 t^{n-2}, \cdots + \overline{A}_n} % [sic] printed with subscript \textquotedbl{}t_2\textquotedbl{} rather than plain t, reproduced as scanned
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 674 =====
% !PRINTED 643
\weberpage{643}

%<<CONT
\gesperrt{is a rational function of degree $n$ of $t$, whose coefficients $\overline{A}_1, \overline{A}_2, \ldots, \overline{A}_n$ are functionals of the field $\overline{Z}$.}

We define the norm and the trace of the functional as in § 172:
\weq{7}{N(\overline{\omega}) = \left|\begin{array}{llll}
\overline{x}_{1,1}, & \overline{x}_{1,2}, & \ldots, & \overline{x}_{1,n} \\
\overline{x}_{2,1}, & x_{2,2}, & \ldots, & \overline{x}_{2,n} \\
\cdot & \cdot & \cdots & \cdot \\
\overline{x}_{n,1}, & \overline{x}_{n,2}, & \ldots, & \overline{x}_{n,n}
\end{array}\right|} % [sic] second entry of second row printed without overline, reproduced as scanned
\weq{8}{S(\overline{\omega}) = \overline{x}_{1,1} + \overline{x}_{2,2} + \cdots + \overline{x}_{n,n},}
and the theorems § 172, (6) and (21) hold unchanged for the norms and traces of the functionals as well.

Then, as in § 172, (8),
\weq{9}{\varphi(t) = N(t - \overline{\omega}),}
and the discriminant of a system of functionals is defined as in § 173, (1); and if the functional $\overline{\omega}$ is contained in a field $\overline{\Omega}_1$ of degree $e$ that is contained in $\overline{\Omega}$, then $\overline{\omega}$ satisfies an equation of degree $e$, $\varphi_1(t) = 0$. As in § 172, (19) it is proved that
\[
\varphi(t) = [\varphi_1(t)]^f \quad (n = ef)
\]
is a power of $\varphi_1(t)$.

\begin{center}
§ 179.\\
\gesperrt{Integral Functionals of the Field $\overline{\Omega}$.}
\end{center}

6. \gesperrt{Definition. A functional $\overline{\omega}$ in $\overline{\Omega}$ is called integral if it satisfies an equation:}
\weq{1}{F(\overline{\omega}) = \overline{\omega}^m + \overline{A}_1\overline{\omega}^{m-1} + \cdots + \overline{A}_{m-1}\overline{\omega} + \overline{A}_m = 0}
\gesperrt{whose coefficients $\overline{A}_1, \ldots, \overline{A}_m$ are integral rational functionals.}

From \gesperrt{Gauss's} theorem (Bd. I, § 2) it follows, since by § 177 one knows the prime factors in $\overline{Z}$, that if $F(t)$ is reducible in $\overline{Z}$, every function dividing $F(t)$ also has integral coefficients, and in particular therefore also the equation of lowest degree $\varphi(\overline{\omega}) = 0$ which $\overline{\omega}$ satisfies.

The necessary and sufficient condition for a functional $\overline{\omega}$ to be integral is therefore that
\[
N(t - \overline{\omega})
\]
when ordered according to powers of $t$, has integral rational functionals for coefficients.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 675 =====
% !PRINTED 644
\weberpage{644}

As in § 175 one proves the theorems:

7. \gesperrt{Sum, difference, product of integral functionals in $\overline{\Omega}$ are again integral functionals.}

8. \gesperrt{If $\overline{\omega}$ is an integral functional in $\overline{\Omega}$ according to Definition 6. and at the same time rational, then it is an integral functional in $\overline{Z}$ (according to Definition 2.).}

9. \gesperrt{If $\overline{\omega}$ is an integral functional in $\overline{\Omega}$, then $N(\overline{\omega})$ is an integral functional in $\overline{Z}$, and the absolute of $N(\overline{\omega})$ is called the \glqq absolute norm of $\overline{\omega}$\grqq{}.}

The absolute norm of $\overline{\omega}$ is therefore a function in $Z$.

If we denote the absolute norm by $N_a(\overline{\omega})$, then the theorem holds:
\weq{2}{N_a(\overline{\omega}\,\overline{\omega}') = N_a(\overline{\omega})\,N_a(\overline{\omega}').}

\begin{center}
§ 180. \gesperrt{Divisibility of functionals. Units.}
\end{center}

The theorems of Bd. II, § 155 are now to be repeated, with quite slight modifications, to which attention is drawn in what follows. To simplify the expression, integral functionals in $\overline{\Omega}$ shall here be denoted by the small Greek letters, integral functionals in $\overline{Z}$ by the small Latin letters. Then we have:

1. \gesperrt{Definition: If $\beta$ is different from zero, then $\alpha$ is called divisible by $\beta$ if $\alpha/\beta = \gamma$ is an integral functional in $\overline{\Omega}$.}

2. \gesperrt{If $\xi, \eta, \ldots$ are arbitrary integral functionals in $\overline{\Omega}$ and $\alpha, \beta, \ldots$ are divisible by $\delta$, then}
\[
\xi\alpha + \eta\beta + \cdots
\]
\gesperrt{is also divisible by $\delta$.}

3. \gesperrt{Definition: An integral functional $\varepsilon$ whose reciprocal $1/\varepsilon$ is integral, i.\,e. a divisor of the number 1, is called a unit in $\overline{\Omega}$. A unit is a divisor of every integral functional. Product and quotient of two units are again units.}

4. \gesperrt{Two integral functionals $\alpha$, $\beta$ which are mutually divisible by one another are called associated. Their quotient $\alpha/\beta = \varepsilon$ is a unit. Two functionals $\alpha$ and $\alpha\varepsilon$ are associated.}

5. \gesperrt{If $\alpha$ is divisible by $\beta$, then every functional associated with $\alpha$ is divisible by every functional associated with $\beta$.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 676 =====
% !PRINTED 645
\weberpage{645}
6. \gesperrt{If two integral functionals are associated with a third, then they are also associated with one another.}

7. \gesperrt{The norm $N(\alpha)$ is divisible by $\alpha$.}

This follows from equation (6), \S\,178: $\varphi(\alpha)=0$, whose last coefficient is $\overline{A}_n=\pm N(\alpha)$. For according to this:
\[
\pm N(\alpha) = \alpha(\alpha^{n-1}+\overline{A}_1\alpha^{n-2}+\cdots+\overline{A}_{n-1}).
\]
8. \gesperrt{An integral functional whose absolute norm is a constant is a unit, and conversely the absolute norm of a unit $\varepsilon$ is a constant different from zero.}

For if $\varepsilon$ is a unit, then
\[
N(\varepsilon) \text{ and } N\left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\right) = \frac{1}{N(\varepsilon)}
\]
are integral functionals in $\overline{Z}$; consequently $N(\varepsilon)$ is a unit in $\overline{Z}$. Conversely $N(\varepsilon)$ is divisible by $\varepsilon$; hence, if $N(\varepsilon)$ is a unit in $\overline{Z}$, $\varepsilon$ is a divisor of 1, that is, a unit.

9. \gesperrt{There are integral rational functions of $z$, for example the absolute norm of $\alpha$, that are divisible by $\alpha$. If $a$ is an integral rational function of $z$ divisible by $\alpha$ and of the lowest possible degree, then every other integral rational function of $z$ divisible by $\alpha$ is divisible by $a$.}

\begin{center}
\S\,181. \gesperrt{Greatest common divisor.}
\end{center}

If $\alpha, \beta, \ldots$ are integral functionals in $\overline{\Omega}$ and $x, y, \ldots$ are variables that do not occur in $\alpha, \beta, \ldots$, then
\weq{1}{\delta = \alpha x + \beta y + \cdots}
is, by \S\,180, 2., likewise an integral functional, and indeed $\delta$ is \gesperrt{divisible by every common divisor of $\alpha, \beta, \ldots$} If $x_0, y_0, \ldots$ are arbitrary integral functions or functionals in $\overline{Z}$, then, as is now to be proved,
\weq{2}{\delta_0 = \alpha x_0 + \beta y_0 + \cdots}
is divisible by $\delta$. For if we denote the absolute norm of $\delta$ by $D$, then
\weq{3}{N(\delta) = D E(x, y, \ldots) = D E,}
and $E(x, y, \ldots)$ is a unit in $\overline{Z}$, but at the same time an integral homogeneous function of the variables $x, y, \ldots$

%% ===== canonical stable idx 677 =====
% !PRINTED 646
\weberpage{646}
If $t$ denotes a new variable, then
\[
N(\delta t - \delta_0) = D E(x t - x_0,\ y t - y_0, \ldots),
\]
and hence, if we arrange in descending powers of $t$ and cancel the factor $N(\delta) = D E$ on both sides:
\weq{4}{N\left(t - \frac{\delta_0}{\delta}\right) = t^n + \overline{C}_1 t^{n-1} + \overline{C}_2 t^{n-2} + \cdots,}
in which $\overline{C}_1, \overline{C}_2 \ldots$ have no denominator other than $E$, and consequently are integral functionals in $\overline{Z}$. Accordingly, by the definition of \S\,179, 6., $\delta_0 : \delta$ is likewise an integral functional, as was to be proved.

Accordingly we obtain the following definitions:

1. \gesperrt{The functional $\delta = \alpha x + \beta y + \cdots$, and every functional associated with $\delta$, is the greatest common divisor of $\alpha, \beta, \ldots$}

2. \gesperrt{If $\alpha x + \beta y$ is a unit, then $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are called coprime or relatively prime. If there are functionals $\xi, \eta$ for which $\alpha \xi + \beta \eta$ is a unit, then $\alpha, \beta$ are relatively prime.}

3. \gesperrt{If $\alpha$ is relatively prime to $\beta$ and to $\gamma$, then it is also relatively prime to $\beta\gamma$.}

For by assumption
\[
\varepsilon = \alpha x + \beta y,\quad \varepsilon_1 = \alpha u + \beta v % [sic] printed beta; argument requires gamma
\]
are units ($x, y, u, v$ new variables).
\[
\alpha(\alpha u x + \gamma v x + \beta u y) + \beta \gamma v y = \varepsilon \varepsilon_1,
\]
and hence, by 3., $\alpha$ and $\beta\gamma$ are relatively prime. % [sic] printed self-reference; argument invokes 2.

4. \gesperrt{If $\alpha$ is relatively prime to $\beta$ and $\alpha\mu$ is divisible by $\beta$, then $\mu$ is divisible by $\beta$.}

For from the assumption it follows that
\[
\alpha \mu x + \beta \mu y = \varepsilon \mu,
\]
from which, since $\varepsilon$ is a unit, the proof results.

\begin{center}
\S\,182. \textbf{Prime functionals in $\overline{\Omega}$.}
\end{center}

1. \gesperrt{Definition. An integral functional $\pi$ in $\overline{\Omega}$ is called a prime functional if it is not a unit and, apart from by the units, is divisible only by the functionals associated with it.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 678 =====
% !PRINTED 647
\weberpage{647}
From this it follows:

2. \gesperrt{If a product $\alpha\beta$ is divisible by $\pi$, then at least one of the two factors, $\alpha$ or $\beta$, is divisible by $\pi$.}

For if neither $\alpha$ nor $\beta$ is divisible by $\pi$, then both are relatively prime to $\pi$, and by \S\,181, 3. $\pi$ is also relatively prime to $\alpha\beta$.

3. \gesperrt{Every integral functional $\overline{\omega}$ different from zero is divisible by a prime functional.}

For if $\overline{\omega}$ is not itself a prime functional, then it is divisible by a functional $\alpha$ different from $\omega$. % [sic] printed without the expected bar over omega
If
\[
\overline{\omega} = \alpha \overline{\omega}',
\]
then $\overline{\omega}'$ is not a unit, and
\[
N_a(\overline{\omega}) = N_a(\alpha)\, N_a(\overline{\omega}').
\]
The absolute norms occurring here are integral functions in $z$, and the degree of $N_a(\overline{\omega}')$ is smaller than the degree of $N_a(\omega)$. % [sic] printed without the expected bar over omega
If $\overline{\omega}'$ is still not a prime functional, one can continue in this way and must finally arrive at a prime factor $\pi$ of $\overline{\omega}$.

In this way one argues further as in Bd.\,II, \S\,158, except that here the \gesperrt{height of the degree} of integral rational functions of the variable $z$ takes the place of the \gesperrt{quantity} of the integral rational numbers used there. Thus one also obtains the theorems:

4. \gesperrt{Every integral functional $\overline{\omega}$ in $\overline{\Omega}$ that is not a unit can be decomposed into a finite number of prime factors, and indeed in only one way, if associated functionals are regarded as not different.}

In what follows we must make use of the theorem that an integral rational function of $z$ with numerical coefficients is decomposable into linear factors; in other words, we must presuppose the fundamental theorem of algebra on the existence of roots. From this there follows first of all:

5. \gesperrt{The integral rational function of $z$ of lowest degree that is divisible by a prime functional $\pi$ is a linear function $z - c$.}

By \S\,180, 9. there do exist integral % [sic] printed singular form
rational functions of $z$ that are divisible by $\pi$. If one decomposes such a func-
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 679 =====
% !PRINTED 648
\weberpage{648}
%<<CONT
tion into linear factors, then by 2. one of these linear factors must be divisible by $\pi$. Two different linear functions $z - c$ and $z - c'$ cannot be divisible by the same $\pi$, since otherwise the constant $c - c'$, which is different from zero, would be divisible by $\pi$.

6. \gesperrt{Every integral function $\omega$ in $\Omega$ is congruent to a constant $b$ with respect to the modulus $\pi$, i.\,e. the constant $b$ can be so chosen that
$\omega - b$ becomes divisible by $\pi$.}
% [sic] German source prints unbarred $\Omega$ here; statement 7 below prints $\overline{\Omega}$.
% [sic] German source prints "das" for "daß".

For by \S\,175 the function $\omega$ satisfies an equation:
\[
\omega^n + a_1 \omega^{n-1} + \cdots + a_{n-1}\omega + a_n = 0,
\]
in which the $a_1, \ldots, a_n$ are integral rational functions of $z$. If $a_1^0, \ldots, a_n^0$ are the residues of these functions on division by $z - c$, and hence constants, it follows that:
\[
\omega^n + a_1^0 \omega^{n-1} + \cdots + a_{n-1}^0 \omega + a_n^0 \equiv 0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ \pi),
\]
and if the function on the left side is decomposed into linear factors:
\weq{1}{(\omega - b)(\omega - b')(\omega - b'') \cdots \equiv 0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ \pi).}
At least one of these linear factors must therefore be divisible by $\pi$, which was to be proved.

From the one-valued decomposability of the functionals into prime factors that has now been established there follow far-reaching consequences, of which the most important shall be adduced here.

If in a functional $\varphi$ of the field $\Omega$ a certain number of the auxiliary variables, $x, y, \ldots$, occur only in the numerator, then
% [sic] German source prints unbarred $\Omega$ here; statement 7 below prints $\overline{\Omega}$.
\[
\varphi = \varphi(x, y, \ldots)
\]
shall be called a \gesperrt{holomorphic function} of $x, y, \ldots$. Of these the theorem holds:

7. \gesperrt{A holomorphic function is an integral functional in $\overline{\Omega}$ only when the coefficients of the ordered function $\varphi$ are integral functionals.}

It is evidently sufficient to establish the theorem for holomorphic functions of one variable
\weq{2}{\varphi = x^m \varphi_0 + x^{m-1}\varphi_1 + \cdots + x \varphi_{m-1} + \varphi_m}
since from this it can be proved in general by complete induction.

This proof, however, follows from the \gesperrt{Gauss} theorem:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 680 =====
% !PRINTED 649
\weberpage{649}
%<<CONT
If two holomorphic functions
\[
\begin{aligned}
\alpha &= \alpha_0 x^h + \alpha_1 x^{h-1} + \cdots + \alpha_h, \\
\beta &= \beta_0 x^k + \beta_1 x^{k-1} + \cdots + \beta_k
\end{aligned}
\]
have a product
\[
\gamma = \gamma_0 x^{h+k} + \gamma_1 x^{h+k-1} + \cdots + \gamma_{h+k},
\]
whose coefficients are integral functionals, then the $\gamma_0$,
$\gamma_1, \ldots, \gamma_{h+k}$ can all be divisible by a prime functional $\pi$
only if either all of $\alpha_0, \alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_h$, or all of $\beta_0, \beta_1, \ldots, \beta_k$
are divisible by $\pi$, which is proved in exactly the same way as in Bd. I, § 2.

If now (2) is an integral functional without $\varphi_0, \varphi_1, \ldots, \varphi_m$
being integral, then one can determine an integral functional $\mu$, and in it a
prime factor $\pi$, in such a way that
\weq{3}{\chi = \mu\varphi = \alpha_0 x^m + \alpha_1 x^{m-1} + \cdots + \alpha_m,}
is divisible by $\pi$, while $\alpha_0, \alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n$ are not all divisible by $\pi$. % [sic] printed $\alpha_n$; the sum in (3) runs to $\alpha_m$

If now $\varphi$ is integral, then it satisfies an equation:
\weq{4}{E\varphi^m = a_1 E_1 \varphi^{m-1} + a_2 E_2 \varphi^{m-2} + \cdots + a_m E_m}
and from this, by multiplication by $\mu^m$:
\weq{5}{E\chi^m = \mu(a_1 E_1 \chi^{m-1} + a_2 E_2 \mu \chi^{m-2} + a_m E_m),}
in which the $a_1, a_2, \ldots$ are integral functions in $Z$, and the $E, E_1, \ldots, E_m$
are units in $\bar{Z}$. The units $E, E_1, \ldots, E_m$ may indeed still
contain $x$, but they may be assumed to be holomorphic.
If we arrange the right-hand and the left-hand side of (5) according to $x$, then
the coefficients of $E$ are not all divisible by $\pi$. Likewise,
by the theorem mentioned, the coefficients of $\chi^m$ are not
all divisible by $\pi$, while on the right-hand side all coefficients
have the factor $\mu$, and hence also the factor $\pi$. That is
impossible, and with this our theorem is proved (Bd. II, § 159).

8. \gesperrt{A holomorphic integral functional $\varphi$ is the
greatest common divisor of all its coefficients.}

If $\alpha, \beta, \ldots$ are the coefficients of $\varphi$, then $\varphi$ is in any case
divisible by the greatest common divisor of $\alpha, \beta, \ldots$.
If we decompose a linear function $z - c$ into its functional prime
factors, then in these prime functionals $\pi$ we may denote the variables
as we please, and since every prime functional must divide some $z - c$,
we may assume that the variables in it are different from the
variables $x, y, \ldots$ in $\varphi$. Accordingly we can
%CONT>>

we determine a functional $\psi = \varepsilon\varphi$ that is free of the $x, y, \ldots$ and
associated with $\varphi$. Since $\varphi/\psi$ is then integral, the coefficients of
$\varphi$ must, by 7., all be divisible by $\psi$, and consequently all be divisible
by $\varphi$ as well. Which was to be proved.

At the same time this proves:

9. \gesperrt{A holomorphic integral functional passes over into
an associated one when the variables are denoted
differently.}

10. \gesperrt{Every functional $\bar\omega$ in $\bar\Omega$ passes over, by multiplication
 with a unit in $\bar Z$, into a holomorphic
functional.}

\[
\omega = \frac{\psi}{\varphi} % [sic] printed without the expected bar
\]

\weq{6}{E_m \bar\omega = \frac{\psi \varphi'}{a_m}.}

\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots

12. \gesperrt{Every integral functional $\bar\omega$ is the greatest common

To prove this, we take $\alpha = \bar\omega \mu$, divisible by $\bar\omega$,

\bar\omega = \alpha x + \beta y
