is the greatest common divisor of $\alpha$ and $\beta$.

\begin{center}
\textbf{§ 183.\qquad \gesperrt{Bases and Basis Forms of the Functionals.}}
\end{center}

Now let
\weq{1}{\omega_1, \omega_2, \ldots, \omega_n}
be a minimal basis of the field $\Omega$ (§ 176) and
\weq{2}{\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n}
another basis of $\Omega$. Let the linear substitution by which
the $\alpha$ are connected with the $\omega$ be:
\weq{3}{\alpha_s = \overset{i}{\Sigma} a_{s,i} \omega_i,}
in which the $a_{s,i}$ are integral functions in $Z$, whose determinant
\weq{4}{A = \Sigma \pm a_{1,1} a_{2,2} \ldots a_{n,n}}
does not vanish identically. If $t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_n$ are variables, then
\weq{5}{\lambda = \alpha_1 t_1 + \alpha_2 t_2 + \cdots + \alpha_n t_n}
is the greatest common divisor of $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n$.

If one substitutes integral functions in $Z$ for $t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_n$, there arise
 from $\lambda$ integral functions in $\Omega$, all of which are divisible by $\lambda$.

1. \gesperrt{One calls $\lambda$ a basis form and $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n$
a basis of the functional $\lambda$, if one obtains all numbers
in $\Omega$ divisible by $\lambda$ by putting
integral functions in $Z$ for $t_i$.}

If the $\alpha_i$ form such a basis, then one can determine integral functions,
$g_{r,s}^{(i)}$ in $Z$, so that
\weq{6}{\alpha_r \omega_s = \overset{i}{\Sigma} g_{r,s}^{(i)} \alpha_i}
holds.

From this it follows:
\weq{7}{\lambda \omega_s = \overset{i}{\Sigma} \alpha_i t_{i,s},}
if
\weq{8}{t_{i,s} = \overset{r}{\Sigma} g_{r,s}^{(i)} t_r}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 683 =====
% !PRINTED 652
\weberpage{652}
%<<CONT
is set, and by substituting the expressions (3) for $\alpha_i$ in (7)
:
\weq{9}{\lambda \omega_r = \overset{i}{\Sigma} \omega_i \overset{s}{\Sigma} a_{s,i} t_{s,r}.}

By the definition of the norm (§ 172), $N(\lambda)$ is therefore the
determinant formed from the coefficients
\[
\overset{s}{\Sigma} a_{s,i} t_{s,r},
\]
and by the multiplication theorem for determinants one can decompose
 it into
\weq{10}{N(\lambda) = A T}
where $A$ has the meaning (4), and $T$ is the determinant:
\weq{11}{T = \Sigma \pm t_{1,1} t_{2,2} \ldots t_{n,n}.}

Here $T$ is a homogeneous function of degree $n$ in the $t_i$,
whose coefficients are integral functions in $Z$. $A$ is itself
an integral function in $z$. One now proves, as in Bd. II, § 164,
that $T$ is a unit. For if this were not the case, then
$T$ would have some linear factor $z - c$, and by an elementary
theorem on determinants one could determine holomorphic integral
functionals $y_i$ in $z$, not all of them divisible by $z - c$, in
such a way that
\[
u_s = y_1 t_{s1} + \cdots + y_n t_{sn}
\]
becomes divisible by $z - c$ (one can even give the $y_i$ constant
coefficients, since they can be reduced to their residues with respect
 to $z - c$).

If one now sets
\[
\omega = \omega_1 y_1 + \omega_2 y_2 + \cdots + \omega_n y_n,
\]
then it follows from (7)
\[
\lambda \omega = \alpha_1 u_1 + \alpha_2 u_2 + \cdots + \alpha_n u_n,
\]
and from this it follows, since the $\alpha_i$ are divisible by $\lambda$ and the $u_i$ by $z - c$,
that $\omega$ is divisible by $z - c$, which contradicts the definition of the
minimal basis. Accordingly it follows from (10) that $A$
is the absolute norm of the functional $\lambda$:
\weq{12}{N_a(\lambda) = \Sigma \pm a_{11} a_{22} \ldots a_{nn}.}

For a prime functional $\pi$ we can easily find a basis.
Not all the elements $\omega_1, \omega_2, \ldots, \omega_n$ of a minimal basis
can be divisible by $\pi$, since by the linear form
\weq{13}{\omega = x_1 \omega_1 + x_2 \omega_2 + \cdots + x_n \omega_n}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 684 =====
% !PRINTED 653
\weberpage{653}
%<<CONT
the function ``1'' must also be representable. Let us assume that
$\omega_1$ is not divisible by $\pi$. By \S\ 182, 6. there are constants
$c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_n$, the first of which may, without prejudice to generality, be
assumed $= 1$, and which satisfy the conditions:
\[
\omega_1 \equiv 1, \ \omega_2 \equiv c_2, \ \ldots, \ \omega_n = c_n \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ \pi) % [sic] last relation printed with = rather than \equiv
\]
We set:
\weq{14}{
\begin{aligned}
\alpha_1 &= (z - c)\,\omega_1,\\
\alpha_2 &= \omega_2 - c_2\,\omega_1,\\
&\cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot\\
\alpha_n &= \omega_n - c_n\,\omega_1.
\end{aligned}
}
That this is a basis of $\pi$ one sees at once if one represents
the function (13) in this way:
\weq{15}{
\omega = x_2\alpha_2 + \cdots + x_n\alpha_n + (x_1 + c_2x_2 + \cdots + c_nx_n)\,\omega_1\,;
}
since $\alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n$ are divisible by $\pi$, $\omega$ can be divisible by
$\pi$ only if the integral function in $Z$:
\[
x_1 + c_2x_2 + \cdots + c_nx_n
\]
is divisible by $(z - c)$, and consequently $\omega$ is representable by formula (5).
Hence formulae (10) and (14) give:
\weq{16}{
N_a(\pi) = z - c\,,
}
and thus the theorem:

2. \gesperrt{The absolute norm of a prime functional is a linear function of $z$.}

This theorem marks an essential difference between
the theories of numbers and of functions. In number theory
 there are prime ideals of various degrees whose norm is a
power of a prime. In the theory of functions we have
only prime functionals of the first degree. This comes about because
by virtue of the fundamental theorem of algebra we can decompose every integral
function of one variable, with respect to the modulus $\pi$, into linear
factors.

The number of prime factors into which $(z - c)$ splits is accordingly
 $n$, since $N(z-c) = (z-c)^n$.

If we collect the mutually equal prime factors into
powers, then
\weq{17}{
z - c = \varepsilon\,\pi_1^{e_1}\pi_2^{e_2}\pi_3^{e_3}\ldots\,,
}
in which
\weq{18}{
n = e_1 + e_2 + e_3 + \cdots\,,
}
where $\varepsilon$ is a unit.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 685 =====
% !PRINTED 654
\weberpage{654}
\begin{center}
\S\ 184. \gesperrt{Basis Form and Ramification Functional.}
\end{center}

By the basis form of the field $\Omega$ we shall understand the linear
 form:
\weq{1}{
\tau = \omega_1t_1 + \omega_2t_2 + \cdots + \omega_nt_n\,,
}
in which $t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_n$ are the functional variables, and whose coefficients
 $\omega_1, \omega_2, \ldots, \omega_n$ form a minimal basis of $\Omega$. This
form is the greatest common divisor of $\omega_1, \omega_2, \ldots, \omega_n$
and consequently a \gesperrt{unit.} From $\tau$ one can derive all integral
functions in $\Omega$ by putting for the variables $t_1,
t_2, \ldots, t_n$ integral functions in $Z$.

If we put
\weq{2}{
F(t) = N(t - \tau) = t^n + A_1t^{n-1} + \cdots + A_{n-1}t + A_n\,,
}
then the $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n$ are holomorphic integral functionals in
$\overline{Z}$, and $\tau$ satisfies the equation of degree $n$:
\weq{3}{
F(\tau) = 0.
}
If $\pi$ is a prime functional and
\[
N_a(\pi) = z - c\,,
\]
then by \S\ 182, 6. one can determine the \gesperrt{constants} $c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_n$ from
the congruences
\weq{4}{
\omega_1 \equiv c_1, \ \omega_2 \equiv c_2, \ \ldots, \ \omega_n \equiv c_n \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ \pi)
}
and if one puts
\weq{5}{\tau_0 = c_1t_1 + c_2t_2 + \cdots + c_nt_n}
then $\tau_0$ is a \gesperrt{constant functional}, and $\tau - \tau_0$ is
divisible by $\pi$. It is now to be proved:

3. \gesperrt{The prime functional $\pi$ is the greatest common
 divisor of $\tau - \tau_0$ and $z - c$:}
\weq{6}{
\pi = u(\tau - \tau_0) + v(z - c)\,,
}
\gesperrt{and if therefore $(z - c)$ is divisible by a higher than the
first power of $\pi$, then $\tau - \tau_0$ is divisible only by
the first power of $\pi$.}

First of all it follows from the definition \S\ 181 that
\weq{7}{
\tau - \tau_0 = t_1(\omega_1 - c_1) + t_2(\omega_2 - c_2) + \cdots + t_n(\omega_n - c_n)
}
is the greatest common divisor of $(\omega_1 - c_1), (\omega_2 - c_2), \ldots,
(\omega_n - c_n)$. If now
\weq{8}{
\omega = x_1\omega_1 + x_2\omega_2 + \cdots x_n\omega_n \equiv 0 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ \pi)\,, % [sic] missing \textquotedbl{}+\textquotedbl{} before x_n\omega_n as printed
}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 686 =====
% !PRINTED 655
\weberpage{655}
%<<CONT
then $x_1c_1 + x_2c_2 + \cdots + x_nc_n$ is divisible by $\pi$, and, since it is a
function in $Z$, by $(z - c)$. We set:
\[
x_1c_1 + x_2c_2 + \cdots + x_nc_n = (z - c)y
\]
and obtain from (8)
\weq{9}{
\begin{aligned}
\omega &= x_1(\omega_1 - c_1) + x_2(\omega_2 - c_2) + \cdots + x_n(\omega_n - c_n) + (z - c)y\\
&= (\tau - \tau_0) + (z - c)y.
\end{aligned}
}

If now $(\tau - \tau_0)$ and $(z - c)$ had the common divisor
$\pi\delta$, then by \S\ 182, 11. one could find a function $\omega$ in $\Omega$ that is
divisible by $\pi$ and coprime to $\delta$. But equation (9) contradicts
this, and with that our theorem is proved.

Let
\weq{10}{
\Phi(t) = B_0t^m + B_1t^{m-1} + \cdots + B_{m-1}t + B_m
}
be a function of degree $m$ in $t$, and let $B_0, B_1, \ldots, B_m$ be integral
holomorphic functionals in $\overline{Z}$ with the functional variables $t_1,
t_2, \ldots, t_n$, the function satisfying the congruence condition
\weq{11}{
\Phi(\tau) \equiv 0 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ z - c)
}
[as, for example, the function $F(t) = N(t - \tau)$ does]. Then
\[
\Phi(\tau_0) \equiv 0 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ \pi)\,,
\]
and if we divide $\Phi(t)$ by $\tau - \tau_0$, there results
\weq{12}{
\Phi(t) \equiv (t - \tau_0)\Phi_1(t) \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ \pi)\,,
}
in which $\Phi_1(t)$ is a holomorphic integral functional in $\overline{Z}$ (because
$\tau_0$ is contained in $\overline{Z}$ as a \gesperrt{constant} functional). Since now in (12)
only rational functions of $z$ occur besides the functional variables,
this congruence must also be valid for the modulus $z - c$:
\weq{13}{
\Phi(t) \equiv (t - \tau_0)\Phi_1(t) \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ z - c).
}

If $\pi'$ is a second prime functional, which may also be identical
with $\pi$, and if $z - c$ is divisible by $\pi\pi'$, and $\tau \equiv \tau_0' \ (\mathrm{mod}\ \pi')$,
then $(\tau - \tau_0)\!: \pi$ is relatively prime to $\pi'$ (by 3.), and because of (11)
we have $\Phi_1(\tau_0') \equiv 0 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ \pi')$. From this one concludes
\[
\Phi_1(t) \equiv (t - \tau_0')\Phi_2(t)
\]
first for the modulus $\pi'$, but then, since the functionals
lie in $\overline{Z}$, also for the modulus $(z - c)$. We therefore have:
\weq{14}{
\Phi(t) \equiv (t - \tau_0)(t - \tau_0')\Phi_2(t) \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ z - c).
}

From this we infer the following important theorem:

4. \gesperrt{Let, according to \S\ 183, (17)}
\weq{15}{
z - c = \pi_1\pi_2\ldots\pi_n
}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 687 =====
% !PRINTED 656
\weberpage{656}
%<<CONT
\gesperrt{into $n$ (equal or different) prime factors
, and let}
\weq{16}{\tau_1, \tau_2, \ldots, \tau_n}
\gesperrt{be the constant functionals to which $\tau$, with respect to the
moduli}
\weq{17}{\pi_1, \pi_2, \ldots, \pi_n}
\gesperrt{becomes congruent.}

\gesperrt{Let $\Phi(t)$ be an integral holomorphic functional in $z$
of degree $m$ with respect to $t$, which satisfies the condition}
\weq{18}{
\Phi(\tau) \equiv 0 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ z - c)
}
\gesperrt{Then:}
\weq{19}{
\Phi(t) \equiv (t - \tau_1)(t - \tau_2)\ldots(t - \tau_n)\,\Psi(t) \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ z - c)\,,
}
\gesperrt{where $\Psi$ is a functional of the same kind of degree $m - n$.}

From this it follows:

5. \gesperrt{A functional $\Phi$ that satisfies the condition (18)
cannot be of lower than degree
$n$.}

And applied to the function $F(t)$, the formula follows:
\weq{20}{
F(t) = N(t - \tau) \equiv (t - \tau_1)(t - \tau_2)\ldots(t - \tau_n) \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ z - c).
}
We can replace the congruence (20) by an equation in the
following way:

As in (17) of the preceding section, we collect in the
decomposition of $z - c$ into prime factors the equal factors
 together, and set:
\weq{21}{
\begin{aligned}
z - c &= \pi_1^{e_1}\pi_2^{e_2}\ldots\pi_m^{e_m}\\
e_1 + e_2 + \cdots + e_m &= n\,,
\end{aligned}
}
then by (20):
\weq{22}{
F(t) = (t - \tau_1)^{e_1}(t - \tau_2)^{e_2}\ldots(t - \tau_m)^{e_m} + (z - c)R(t)\,,
}
where $R(t)$ is an integral functional, in the first place in $\Omega$. But
formula (22) itself says that $R(t)$ is contained in $\overline{Z}$, and
that it is an integral function of the functional variables $t, t_1, t_2,
\ldots, t_n$.

We can therefore also form the derivative of equation (12)
with respect to $t$, and obtain:
\weq{23}{
\begin{aligned}
F'(t) = {}& e_1(t - \tau_1)^{e_1-1}(t - \tau_2)^{e_2}\ldots(t - \tau_m)^{e_m}\\
+ {}& e_2(t - \tau_1)^{e_1}(t - \tau_2)^{e_2-1}\ldots(t - \tau_m)^{e_m}\\
& \cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot\\
+ {}& e_m(t - \tau_2)^{e_1}(t - \tau_2)^{e_2}\ldots(t - \tau_m)^{e_m-1} + (z - c)R'(t) % [sic] first factor of last row printed (t-\tau_2) twice, apparently for (t-\tau_1)
\end{aligned}
}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 688 =====
% !PRINTED 657
\weberpage{657}
%<<CONT

and herein lies the proof of the following principal theorem, which
one obtains by setting $t = \tau_1$.

6. \gesperrt{If $e_1 = 1$, then $F'(\tau)$ is not divisible by
$\pi_1$. Otherwise $F'(\tau)$ is divisible by $\pi_1^{e_1-1}$, but not
by $\pi_1^{e_1}$. The same holds of the remaining prime factors of
$(z-c)$, and consequently $F'(\tau)$ is coprime to all prime factors
$z-c$ in $Z$ which are not divisible by the square of a prime factor
in $\Omega$.}

There is therefore only a finite number of prime factors $(z-c)$ that
are divisible by a higher than the first power of a prime factor in
$\Omega$, and $F'(\tau)$, decomposed into prime factors, is the
product of all the factors $\pi^{e-1}$, when $\pi^e$ is the highest
power of $\pi$ dividing $N(\pi) = z - c$.

The functional $F'(\tau)$ is called the \gesperrt{ramification functional} of the
field $\Omega$.

For the absolute norm of the ramification functional we obtain:

\weq{24}{N_a F'(\tau) = \Pi (z-c)^{e_1-1+e_2-1+\cdots},}

in which the product $\Pi$ extends over all linear factors $(z-c)$
that are divisible by a higher than the first power of a prime
factor.

We can show further that this absolute norm is nothing other than the
\gesperrt{field discriminant} $D$.

In order to prove this, we set:

\weq{25}{\tau^k = u_{k,1}\omega_1 + u_{k,2}\omega_2 + \cdots + u_{k,n}\omega_n,}

in which the $u_{k,1}, u_{k,2}, \ldots, u_{k,n}$ are homogeneous
functions of degree $k$ in $t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_n$, and the
determinant

\weq{26}{U =
\begin{vmatrix}
u_{1,0}, & u_{2,0}, & \ldots, & u_{n,0} \\
u_{1,1}, & u_{2,1}, & \ldots, & u_{n,1} \\
\cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot \\
u_{1,n-1}, & u_{2,n-1}, & \ldots, & u_{n,n-1}
\end{vmatrix}}

is a unit.

For if $U$ were not a unit, it would have at least one linear factor
$z-c$, and one could determine the integral rational holomorphic
functionals $y_0, y_1, \ldots, y_{n-1}$ in such a way that

\[ u_{r,0}y_0 + u_{r,1}y_1 + \cdots + u_{r,n-1}y_{n-1} \equiv 0 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ z-c) \]

would hold without all the $y_s$ being divisible by $z-c$.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 689 =====
% !PRINTED 658
\weberpage{658}

Then from (20) a congruence would follow:

\[ y_0 + y_1\tau + y_2\tau^2 + \cdots + y_{n-1}\tau^{n-1} \equiv 0 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ z-c), \]

which by Theorem 5. is not possible.

By § 174, (17) and § 176, (9) we have

\weq{27}{\begin{aligned}
N F'(\tau) &= \pm \Delta(1, \tau, \tau^2, \ldots, \tau^{n-1}) \\
&= \pm U^2 \Delta(\omega_1, \omega_2, \ldots, \omega_n) \\
&= \pm U^2 \Delta;
\end{aligned}}

thus

\weq{28}{N_a F'(\tau) = \Delta}

is \gesperrt{the field discriminant, which is accordingly decomposed by (24) into
linear factors.}

We use the results obtained for the proof of the following theorem as
well:

7. \gesperrt{If an integral function in $\Omega$}

\weq{29}{\omega = x_1\omega_1 + x_2\omega_2 + \cdots + x_n\omega_n}

\gesperrt{is divisible by every prime functional that divides $z-c$, then
$S(\omega)$ is divisible by $z-c$.}

Here $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ are integral functions in $Z$. The function
$\omega$ arises from $\tau$ through the substitution

\weq{30}{t_1 = x_1,\ t_2 = x_2,\ \ldots,\ t_n = x_n.}

If therefore $\omega$ is divisible by $\pi$, and $\omega_1 \equiv c_1,
\ldots, \omega_n \equiv c_n \pmod{\pi}$, then

\[ x_1c_1 + x_2c_2 + \cdots + x_nc_n \equiv 0 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ \pi) \]

and consequently it is also, as a function in $Z$, divisible by $z-c$. If
therefore $\tau_1, \tau_2, \ldots, \tau_m$ are the constant functionals
to which $\tau$ is congruent with respect to the prime factors $\pi_1,
\pi_2, \ldots, \pi_m$ of $(z-c)$, and if these pass by the substitution
(30) into $\tau_1^0, \tau_2^0, \ldots, \tau_m^0$, then all these
functions are divisible by $(z-c)$ [because by hypothesis they are
divisible by a prime divisor of $(z-c)$]. Now by (22)

\weq{31}{-S(\tau) \equiv e_1\tau_1 + e_2\tau_2 + \cdots + e_m\tau_m,}

and hence

\[ -S(\omega) \equiv e_1\tau_1^0 + e_2\tau_2^0 + \cdots + e_m\tau_m^0 \equiv 0 \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ z-c), \]

as was to be proved.

\begin{center}
§ 185. \textbf{\gesperrt{The Fractional Functions in $\Omega$ and the
Taylor Development.}}
\end{center}

A fractional function $\eta$ in the field $\Omega$ can be transformed in
infinitely many ways into an integral function $\mu$ by multiplication
with an integral function $\nu$. It is then
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 690 =====
% !PRINTED 659
\weberpage{659}

%<<CONT
\weq{1}{\eta = \frac{\mu}{\nu},}

and $\mu$ is called the numerator, $\nu$ the denominator of $\eta$. These
two functions are not completely determined by $\eta$; what is determined,
however, are the functionals that remain when all common functional factors
are removed from numerator and denominator. For if

\weq{2}{\frac{\mu}{\nu} = \frac{\mu'}{\nu'}; \quad \mu\nu' = \nu\mu',}

then every prime functional that divides $\nu$ but not $\mu$ must divide
$\nu'$. The functionals $\bar\alpha$ and $\bar\beta$ thus determined from
$\eta$ we call the numerator functional and denominator functional of $\eta$.
In order to represent $\eta$ by functions, one first takes a function $\nu$
divisible by $\bar\beta$ but otherwise arbitrary, and sets
$\nu = \bar\beta\bar\gamma$; in this $\bar\gamma$ may be assumed relatively
prime to any functional one pleases. Then $\eta\nu$ is an integral function
divisible by $\bar\gamma$, and one sets

\[ \eta\nu = \mu = \bar\alpha\bar\gamma. \]

The functional $\bar\alpha$ cannot, however, as we shall prove later on, be
chosen arbitrarily any longer once $\bar\beta$ is given.

The functionals $\bar\alpha, \bar\beta$ we shall also call, for short, \gesperrt{the
numerator and the denominator} of $\eta$.

If $\pi$ is a prime functional, then there are \gesperrt{numbers} (constants) $a, b,
a', b'$ which satisfy the congruences

\[ \mu \equiv a,\ \ \nu \equiv b,\ \ \mu' \equiv a',\ \ \nu' \equiv b' \quad (\mathrm{mod}\ \pi) \]

and from (2) it follows that

\[ ab' = ba', \quad \frac{a}{b} = \frac{a'}{b'} = c, \]

provided that $\nu$ and $\nu'$ are not divisible by $\pi$. Then $\eta - c$ is
a function in $\Omega$ in which the numerator, but not the denominator, is
divisible by $\pi$. If $\varrho$ is an integral or fractional function in
which the numerator is divisible by $\pi$ but not by $\pi^2$, and the
denominator is likewise not divisible by $\pi$, then $(\eta - c) : \varrho$
is a function whose denominator is not divisible by $\pi$ and whose numerator
contains the factor $\pi$ one time fewer than $(\eta - c)$. We set:

\[ \eta - c = \varrho\eta_1. \]

We apply the same consideration to $\eta_1$, and so obtain a sequence of
equations that may be continued as far as we please:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 691 =====
% !PRINTED 660
\weberpage{660}

%<<CONT
\weq{3}{\begin{aligned}
\eta &= c + \varrho\eta_1, \\
\eta_1 &= c_1 + \varrho\eta_2, \\
&\;\cdots \\
\eta_{r-1} &= c_{r-1} + \varrho\eta_r,
\end{aligned}}

from which it follows:

\weq{4}{\eta = c + c_1\varrho + c_2\varrho^2 + \cdots + c_{r-1}\varrho^{r-1} + \eta_r\varrho^r.}

The sequence of the constants $c, c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_{r-1}$ is
completely determined by $\eta$, and $\eta_1, \eta_2, \ldots, \eta_r$
is a sequence of functions in $\Omega$ whose denominator is not
divisible by $\pi$.

One might call this expression the \gesperrt{Taylor development} of the function
$\eta$ in powers of $\varrho$. A similar development can also be given
for a function $\eta$ whose denominator is divisible by $\pi$, only
that negative powers then occur as well: one can namely determine a
power $\varrho^s$ in such a way that the denominator of
$\varrho^s\eta$ is no longer divisible by $\pi$, and if one applies
the development (4) to this product, there follows:

\weq{5}{\eta = c\varrho^{-s} + c_1\varrho^{-s+1} + \cdots + c_{r-1}\varrho^{r-s-1} + \eta_r\varrho^{r-s}.}

\begin{center}
§ 186. \textbf{\gesperrt{Birational Transformation.}}
\end{center}

We now come to a subject which distinguishes the region of algebraic
functions above all else from that of algebraic numbers, and the
reason for this is that the theory of integral functions and
functionals has for functions by no means the character of invariance
that it has for numbers; this is birational transformation.

If $z_1$ is any non-constant function of the field $\Omega$, and
$N(t - z_1)$ is the $f$th power of an irreducible function of degree
$e$ (§ 172, 6.), then there subsists between $z$ and $z_1$ an
equation which with respect to $z_1$ is of degree $e$, and whose
degree with respect to $z$, once denominators and superfluous factors
have been cleared away, shall be denoted by $e_1$. Let this equation
be

\weq{1}{G\bigl(\overset{e}{z_1},\, \overset{e_1}{z}\bigr) = 0.}

Among the various equations of this form there is only one
irreducible one, and this is of the lowest possible degree both with
respect to $z$ and with respect to $z_1$ (Bd. I, § 20).

If $\theta$ is a primitive function of the field $\Omega$, then by
§ 172, (12)

\weq{2}{z_1^h\theta^k \qquad
\begin{aligned}
h &= 0, 1, \ldots, e-1 \\
k &= 0, 1, \ldots, f-1
\end{aligned}}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 692 =====
% !PRINTED 661
\weberpage{661}
%<<CONT
a basis of the field $\Omega$, and consequently every function $\omega$
in $\Omega$ can be represented in the form:

\weq{3}{\omega = \xi_0 + \xi_1\theta + \cdots + \xi_{f-1}\theta^{f-1},}
in which the $\xi_0, \xi_1, \ldots, \xi_{f-1}$ are rational functions of $z$ and
$z_1$, hence numbers of the field determined by (1). If we set

\weq{4}{n = ef, \quad n_1 = e_1 f,}
then the functions $\xi_i$ can be represented in each of the two
forms:

\weq{5}{\begin{aligned}
\xi &= x_0 + x_1 z_1 + x_2 z^2 + \cdots + x_{e-1} z_1^{e-1}, \\ % [sic] printed without subscript 1 on the third $z$; mathematically $z_1^2$ is intended
&= y_0 + y_1 z + y_2 z^2 + \cdots + y_{e_1-1} z^{e_1-1},
\end{aligned}}
in which the $x$ are rational functions of $z$, the $y$ rational functions
of $z_1$.

1. \gesperrt{Accordingly every function $\omega$ can be represented linearly with
rational coefficients in $z_1$ by the $n_1$ functions:}

\weq{6}{z^r\theta^s \quad \begin{aligned} r &= 0, 1, \ldots, e_1-1 \\ s &= 0, 1, \ldots, f-1 \end{aligned},}
\gesperrt{which we denote, in some order, by}

\weq{7}{\eta_1, \eta_2, \ldots, \eta_{n_1}}
\gesperrt{and these functions are linearly independent, i.\,e. there
exists between them no linear relation with rational
coefficients in $z_1$:}
\[
x_1\eta_1 + x_2\eta_2 + \cdots + x_{n_1}\eta_{n_1} = 0,
\]
\gesperrt{except when the $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{n_1}$ all vanish.}

For $f$ is the lowest degree of an equation for $\theta$ with
rational coefficients in $z$ and $z_1$ (\S\ 172).

Let us now consider the functional

\weq{8}{\tau_1 = t_1\eta_1 + t_2\eta_2 + \cdots + t_{n_1}\eta_{n_1}}
with the functional variables $t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_{n_1}$; there then results
a system of equations:

\weq{9}{\tau_1^r = x_{1,r}\eta_1 + x_{2,r}\eta_2 + \cdots + x_{n_1,r}\eta_{n_1},}
in which $r$ may be any natural number, including 0, and the $x_{i,r}$
are rational holomorphic functionals in $z_1$. From this there results,
by elimination of the $\eta$, an equation

\weq{10}{\Phi(\tau_1) = \tau_1^m + A_1\tau_1^{m-1} + \cdots + A_{m-1}\tau_1 + A_m = 0}
of degree at most $n_1$, with rational functionals in $z_1$ as
coefficients.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 693 =====
% !PRINTED 662
\weberpage{662}
It is to be proved that this degree \gesperrt{cannot be less than $n_1$}, or, what
means the same thing, that $\eta_1, \eta_2, \ldots, \eta_{n_1}$ admit of
a rational representation by $\tau_1$. This follows if one
differentiates (10) partially with respect to one of the $t_\nu$:
\[
\Phi'(\tau_1)\,\eta_\nu + \frac{\partial A_1}{\partial t_\nu}\tau_1^{m-1}
+ \cdots + \frac{\partial A_{m-1}}{\partial t_\nu}\tau_1
+ \frac{\partial A_m}{\partial t_\nu} = 0.
\]

Now since $\Phi'(\tau_1)$ does not vanish when $m$ is the lowest
possible degree of the equation (10), one obtains from this at once the
required representation of $\eta_\nu$. Hence $m = n_1$ must hold. With
this it is proved:

2. \gesperrt{The functional $\tau_1$ satisfies an irreducible equation
of degree $n_1$ in $z_1$.}

If therefore we put $r = 0, 1, 2, \ldots, n_1-1$ in (9), there results a
system of linear equations for $\eta_1, \eta_2, \ldots, \eta_{n_1}$
whose determinant is a non-vanishing functional in $z_1$, and one can
therefore assign to the variable $t_i$ such constant values that the
determinant does not vanish even then. If $\tau_1$ passes by this
substitution into $\theta_1$, then from the system (9) one can express
$\eta_1, \eta_2, \ldots, \eta_{n_1}$ rationally by $z_1$ and $\theta_1$.

With this, however, it is proved:

3. \gesperrt{If $z_1$ is an arbitrary, non-constant function in
$\Omega$, and $\theta_1$ a second function of the same field which
satisfies no equation of lower degree than $n_1$ in $z_1$, then all
functions of the field $\Omega$, and hence also $z$ and $\theta$, are
rationally expressible by $z_1$ and $\theta_1$.}

Between any two functions $\alpha, \beta$ of the field $\Omega$ there
always subsists an equation with constant coefficients

\weq{11}{F(\alpha, \beta) = 0,}
and among all possible equations of this form there is one of the lowest
possible degree, both with respect to $\alpha$ and with respect to
$\beta$.

\begin{center}
\rule{4cm}{0.4pt}
\end{center}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 694 =====
% !PRINTED none
% Chapter-opening page: no running head / page number visible in the
