\begin{center}
\gesperrt{Twenty-sixth Chapter.}

\textbf{Numerical Values of the Algebraic Functions.}

\rule{4cm}{0.4pt}

\textbf{§ 187. \gesperrt{The Point.}}
\end{center}

The question now arises how a meaning can be assigned to the algebraic
functions in the region of \gesperrt{numbers}. In doing so we presuppose as given
the region of the real and imaginary rational and irrational numbers,
and within this region the reckoning with the four species. We extend
this region by the addition of a number symbol ``Infinity'': $\infty$,
and we reckon with this symbol too in the well-known manner, so that

\weq{1}{\frac{1}{\infty} = 0, \quad \frac{1}{0} = \infty, \quad \infty \cdot \infty = \infty}

holds, while to the symbols
\[
\infty \pm \infty, \quad 0 \cdot \infty, \quad \frac{0}{0}, \quad \frac{\infty}{\infty}
\]
\gesperrt{no meaning attaches} (or else, in each individual case as required, an
arbitrary numerical value is assigned to them).

The field $\Omega$ now consists of all possible algebraic
functions $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \dots$, which by § 186 can be represented
as rational functions of two among them with numerical coefficients. The
kind of this representation is at first of no consequence.

We now set up the following definition:

1. \gesperrt{If all individuals $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \dots$ of the field $\Omega$
are replaced by definite numerical values $\alpha_0, \beta_0, \gamma_0, \dots$
in such a way that}

\begin{center}
\begin{minipage}{0.7\linewidth}
1. \quad $\alpha = \alpha_0$, if $\alpha$ is constant,

2. \quad $(\alpha + \beta)_0 = \alpha_0 + \beta_0$,

3. \quad $(\alpha - \beta)_0 = \alpha_0 - \beta_0$,

4. \quad $(\alpha\beta)_0 = \alpha_0\beta_0$,

5. \quad $\left(\dfrac{\alpha}{\beta}\right)_0 = \dfrac{\alpha_0}{\beta_0}$,
\end{minipage}
\end{center}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 695 =====
% !PRINTED 664
\weberpage{664}
%<<CONT
\gesperrt{so we assign to such a coincidence of values
a point $\mathfrak{P}$.} We say: $\alpha = \alpha_0$, or $\alpha$ has the value $\alpha_0$
at the point $\mathfrak{P}$. Two points $\mathfrak{P}$ and $\mathfrak{P}'$ are called different then and only
then, when there is at least one function in $\Omega$ that has
different values at $\mathfrak{P}$ and $\mathfrak{P}'$.

Rules 2. to 5. fail in the exceptional cases, namely
2. and 3., when $\alpha_0$ and $\beta_0 = \infty$; 4., when $\alpha_0 = 0$, $\beta_0 = \infty$
or $\alpha_0 = \infty$, $\beta_0 = 0$; and 5., when $\alpha_0$ and $\beta_0$ are both $= 0$
or both $= \infty$.

Nevertheless the functions $(\alpha \pm \beta)_0$, $(\alpha\beta)_0$ and $(\alpha : \beta)_0$
must have determinate values in these cases too; these values, however, are not
 determined directly from prescriptions 2. to 5., but in an indirect
way.

\gesperrt{The point is accordingly an invariant concept belonging
 to the field $\Omega$}, one that has nothing to do with the accidental
circumstance of which of the functions of $\Omega$ we regard as the
independent variable.

To find all points, one proceeds as follows. If $\mathfrak{P}$ is a point,
then there are functions that have a finite value at it,
for if a function $\alpha$ is infinite at $\mathfrak{P}$, then $1 : \alpha$ is finite
. Such a function is to be taken as the independent variable $z$
and its value at the point $\mathfrak{P}$ denoted by $c$. All integral functions
 of $z$ are then likewise finite at $\mathfrak{P}$, for if $\omega$ is an
integral function that satisfies the equation
\[
\omega^{n} + a_1\omega^{n-1} + \cdots + a_n = 0
\]
then
\[
1 + \frac{a_1}{\omega} + \frac{a_2}{\omega^2} + \cdots + \frac{a_n}{\omega^n} = 0
\]
must be satisfied at $\mathfrak{P}$, and since the $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$, as integral rational
functions of $z$, are finite at $\mathfrak{P}$, $\omega$ cannot be $= \infty$.

Every congruence with respect to the modulus $z - c$ must therefore pass over at the
point $\mathfrak{P}$ into a correct equation, even when this
congruence subsists between holomorphic integral functionals.
If, then, $\tau$ is the basis form of $\Omega$ in $Z$, the
equation must hold, by § 184, (20):
\[
(\tau - \tau_1)(\tau - \tau_2)\dots(\tau - \tau_n) = 0.
\]
One of the factors of the left side must therefore vanish in $\mathfrak{P}$
. If this is $\tau - \tau_1$, then to this factor there corresponds a
prime factor $\pi$ of $z - c$. Thus in $\mathfrak{P}$ there will be

\weq{2}{\omega_1 = c_1, \quad \omega_2 = c_2, \dots, \omega_n = c_n,}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 696 =====
% !PRINTED 665
\weberpage{665}
%<<CONT
if $c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_n$ are the numerical values determined by the congruences

\weq{3}{\omega_1 \equiv c_1,\ \omega_2 \equiv c_2,\ \ldots,\ \omega_n \equiv c_n\ (\mathrm{mod}\ \pi)}

By this the values of all integral functions of $z$ at the point $\mathfrak{P}$ are determined. Every integral function $\omega$ is congruent, with respect to the modulus $z - c$, to an expression
\[
a_1\omega_1 + a_2\omega_2 + \cdots + a_n\omega_n
\]
with constant coefficient $a$, and it is then and only then divisible by $\pi$, when
\[
a_1c_1 + a_2c_2 + \cdots + a_nc_n = 0
\]
holds. Accordingly it follows:

2. \gesperrt{Among the integral functions of $z$, only those divisible by $\pi$ have the value 0 at $\mathfrak{P}$.}

Since every fractional function in $\Omega$ can be represented in such a way that numerator and denominator are not both divisible by $\pi$, the value of every function at $\mathfrak{P}$ is thereby determined.

3. \gesperrt{The prime factor $\pi$ is said to be generated by the point $\mathfrak{P}$. It cannot be generated by a point different from $\mathfrak{P}$.}

Conversely, one can also generate a point from every prime factor $\pi$ in $z$.

If $z - c$ is the linear function divisible by $\pi$, then let the function $z$ be given the value $c$. Then take a function $\varrho$ that is divisible by $\pi$, but not by $\pi^2$, and set, in accordance with § 185, (5), for every function $\eta$:

\weq{4}{\eta = a\varrho^m + \eta_1\varrho^{m+1},}

where $m$ is an integral rational number and $\eta_1$ a function whose denominator is not divisible by $\pi$. To the function $\varrho$ let the value 0 be assigned, and to the function $\eta$ the value
\[
\begin{aligned}
\eta_0 &= \infty, \text{ if } m < 0,\\
\eta_0 &= a, \text{ if } m = 0,\\
\eta_0 &= 0, \text{ if } m > 0.
\end{aligned}
\]
4. \gesperrt{The values of all functions $\eta$ so determined satisfy the conditions 1. to 5. and therefore constitute a point, which is said to be generated by the prime functional $\pi$.}

Thus from a single function $z$ and the prime factors of the linear forms $z - c$ one can derive all points at which
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 697 =====
% !PRINTED 666
\weberpage{666}
%<<CONT
$z$ has a finite value. In order to determine the others as well, one must further make use of a second function, say $z_1 = 1 : z$, which has the finite value 0 at the still missing points, which are present in finite number.

\gesperrt{The totality of the points form the absolute Riemann surface\textsuperscript{1)}.}

\begin{center}
\textbf{§ 188. \gesperrt{Order Numbers.}}
\end{center}

1. \gesperrt{If $\mathfrak{P}$ is a point, then to every function $\eta$ that receives at this point a finite value different from zero we assign the order 0 in $\mathfrak{P}$.}

2. \gesperrt{If $\omega$ runs through the totality of the functions vanishing in $\mathfrak{P}$, and $\varrho$ is one of these functions for which all}
\[
\frac{\omega}{\varrho}
\]
\gesperrt{have finite values, then $\varrho$ has the order 1.}

One also says that $\varrho$ becomes infinitely small in $\mathfrak{P}$ in the first order.

If $\dfrac{\varrho'}{\varrho}$ is neither zero nor infinity, then by this $\varrho'$ likewise has the order 1. Conversely, if $\varrho$ and $\varrho'$ both have the order number 1, then $\varrho : \varrho'$ and $\varrho' : \varrho$ are neither zero nor infinity.

3. \gesperrt{If $\varrho$ is of the first order and $\omega$ is any function in $\Omega$, then $\omega$ has the order number $n$ when $\varrho^{-n}\omega$ becomes neither zero nor infinite in $\mathfrak{P}$.}

This determination of the order $n$ is independent of which function of the first order we have taken. If $n$ is positive, $\omega$ becomes zero; if $n$ is negative, $\omega$ becomes infinite; and if $n = 0$, then $\omega$ has in $\mathfrak{P}$ a finite value different from zero.

\medskip\noindent\rule{4cm}{0.4pt}\par
\textsuperscript{1)} According to \gesperrt{Riemann's} theory of algebraic functions, every point of the closed many-sheeted surface corresponds to a point in our sense. If $z$ is the independent variable, then the \gesperrt{Riemann} surface is spread out in $n$ sheets over the $z$-plane.
As an absolute \gesperrt{Riemann} surface one may regard any surface to which the totality of those many-sheeted surfaces can be referred in a one-to-one and continuous manner.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 698 =====
% !PRINTED 667
\weberpage{667}
The definition of the order number is therefore attached to the point $\mathfrak{P}$. It is invariant for the field $\Omega$.

That every function receives at every point $\mathfrak{P}$ a definite \gesperrt{integer $n$} as its order number now follows from § 185, (5).

Take a function $z$ which remains finite at $\mathfrak{P}$ as independent variable, determine the prime functional $\pi$ belonging to $\mathfrak{P}$, and choose a function $\varrho$ whose numerator is divisible by $\pi$, but not by $\pi^2$. This function is of the first order.

Then every function $\omega$ can be put into the form:

\weq{1}{\omega = a\varrho^n + \eta_1\varrho^{n+1},}

in which $a$ is a constant different from zero, and $n$ is the \gesperrt{order number} of $\omega$.

If $\varrho$ has the order 1, then $\varrho^n$ has the order $n$.

The following theorems hold for the order numbers, and all of them follow easily from (1):

4. \gesperrt{The order of a product of two functions is equal to the sum of the orders of the factors. The order of a quotient is equal to the difference of the orders of numerator and denominator.}

\gesperrt{The order of a sum is equal to the lowest among the orders of the summands. If several summands of the same lowest order number occur, then the order of the sum can be greater, but not smaller.}

\gesperrt{Of a function which becomes zero at $\mathfrak{P}$ in the $n$th order one also says that it becomes zero in the first order at $n$ coincident points.}

\begin{center}
\textbf{§ 189. \gesperrt{Polygons.}}
\end{center}

1. \gesperrt{Definition. Complexes of points, which may also contain the same point several times, are called polygons or many-sided figures (of the field $\Omega$).}

The number of points of a polygon is called its order, and a polygon of the $m$th order is also called briefly an $m$-gon.

As designation for the polygons the letters of the capital German alphabet $\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{C}, \ldots$ shall serve.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 699 =====
% !PRINTED 668
\weberpage{668}
2. \gesperrt{By the product $\mathfrak{A}\mathfrak{B}$ of two polygons one understands the polygon that contains the points of $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ together, and indeed contains a point $\mathfrak{P}$ that occurs $r$ times in $\mathfrak{A}$ and $s$ times in $\mathfrak{B}$, $r+s$ times. The order of a product is equal to the sum of the orders of the factors.}

If, then, we denote distinct points by $\mathfrak{P}_1, \mathfrak{P}_2, \ldots$, we can put every polygon $\mathfrak{A}$ in one way into the form:

\weq{1}{\mathfrak{A} = \mathfrak{P}_1^{r_1}\mathfrak{P}_2^{r_2}\cdots}

The points are therefore the prime elements in the calculation with polygons. In order to have a representative for the unit as well, the \glqq zero-gon\grqq{} $\mathfrak{O}$, which contains no point at all, must be named along with them.

\gesperrt{The greatest common divisor of two polygons} $\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{B}$ contains every point that occurs in $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$, and indeed as often as it occurs in each of the two.

\gesperrt{The least common multiple} contains every point of $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$, and indeed in the highest of the orders in which it occurs in $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$.

3. \gesperrt{If $z$ is a variable of the field $\Omega$ and $n$ the degree of the field with respect to $z$, then $z$ takes every value $c$ at $n$ points.}

For if one decomposes $z - c$ into its prime factors [§ 183, (17)]:
\[
z - c = \pi_1^{e_1}\pi_2^{e_2}\cdots, \quad e_1 + e_2 + \cdots = n,
\]
then each of these prime factors generates a point, e.\,g. $\pi_1$ the point $\mathfrak{P}_1$, at which the function $z - c$ becomes zero in the $e_1$th order. If one counts this point $e_1$-fold, one obtains a polygon
\[
\mathfrak{P}_1^{e_1}\mathfrak{P}_2^{e_2}\cdots
\]
of order $n$, at whose points the function $z - c$ vanishes.

But the same theorem holds also for the value $c = \infty$, as one concludes from the fact that the degree of the field $\Omega$ with respect to $1 : z$ is the same as with respect to $z$.

4. \gesperrt{The $n$ points at which $z$ takes a value $c$ are called conjugate with respect to $z$, and the values $\eta_1, \eta_2, \ldots, \eta_n$ that a function $\eta$ in $\Omega$ takes at $n$ conjugate points are likewise called conjugate with respect to $z$, and $z$ is said to be of order $n$. The constants, and only these, have the order 0.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 700 =====
% !PRINTED 669
\weberpage{669}
\begin{center}
§ 190. \gesperrt{Branch Points and Branch Numbers.}
\end{center}

According to § 184 there is only a finite number of points at which $z-c$ becomes zero in an order higher than the first. These are called the branch points of $\Omega$ in $z$.

We construct a polygon $\mathfrak{Z}_z$ which contains $(e-1)$ times every point $\mathfrak{P}$ at which $z-c$ or $1:z$ becomes zero in the $e$th order. This polygon is called the \gesperrt{branch polygon of $\Omega$ with respect to $z$}, and its order

\weq{2}{w_z = \Sigma(e-1)}

is called the \gesperrt{branch number with respect to $z$}\footnote{If one spreads the \gesperrt{Riemann} surface over the $z$-plane, then $n$ is the number of sheets lying one above another, and $w_z$ is the number of branch points of this surface.}.

In § 184, (20) we obtained the formula:

\weq{3}{N(t-\tau) \equiv (t-\tau_1)(t-\tau_2)\ldots(t-\tau_n) \ (\mathrm{mod}\ z-c),}

in which $\tau$ denotes the basis form of the field $\Omega$ with respect to $z$, and $\tau_1, \tau_2, \ldots, \tau_n$ the equal or different constant functionals to which $\tau$ becomes congruent with respect to the prime factors of $z-c$, that is to say, the values which $\tau$ takes at the points $\mathfrak{P}_1, \mathfrak{P}_2, \ldots, \mathfrak{P}_n$ conjugate with respect to $z$. At each of these points (3) must pass over into a correct equation, and from this there follow, for example:

\weq{4}{N(\tau) = \tau_1 \tau_2 \ldots \tau_n \,,}

\weq{5}{S(\tau) = \tau_1 + \tau_2 + \cdots + \tau_n}

as the values of the rational functionals $N(\tau)$ and $S(\tau)$ for $z=c$. If one substitutes rational functions of $z$ for the functional variables, then corresponding formulae hold for the functions in $\Omega$, provided that none of the exceptional cases $0\,.\,\infty$, $\infty+\infty$ occurs.

If, therefore, $\eta_1, \eta_2, \ldots, \eta_n$ is a basis of $\Omega$, and if $\eta_{i,1}, \eta_{i,2}, \ldots, \eta_{i,n}$ are values of $\eta_i$ conjugate with respect to $z$, then by (5) and by the definition of the discriminant in § 173

\weq{6}{\Delta(\eta_1, \eta_2, \ldots, \eta_n) = (\Sigma \pm \eta_{1,1}\eta_{2,2}\ldots\eta_{n,n})^2.}

If two functions $z$ and $z'$ in $\Omega$ stand in a linear relation:

\weq{7}{z' = \dfrac{az+b}{cz+d},}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 701 =====
% !PRINTED 670
\weberpage{670}
%<<CONT
in which $a, b, c, d$ are constants whose determinant $ad - bc$ is different from zero, then the branch polygons $\mathfrak{Z}_z$ and $\mathfrak{Z}_{z'}$ are identical, and hence $w_z = w_{z'}$ also; for if at a point $z-z_0$ or $1:z$ becomes zero in the $e$th order, then at the same point

\[
z' - z_0' = \dfrac{(ad-bc)(z-z_0)}{(cz+d)(cz_0+d)}
\]

or, when $z_0$ is infinite, so that $z_0' = a:c$:

\[
z' - z_0' = \dfrac{-(ad-bc)}{c(cz+d)},
\]

and when $z_0' = \infty$, so that $cz_0+d = 0$:

\[
\dfrac{1}{z'} = \dfrac{cz+d}{az+b}
\]

is likewise infinitely small in the $e$th order.

If we apply this to $z' = 1:z$, we obtain the branch points at which $z$ has a finite value from the field discriminant $D_z$ according to § 184, (24), (28). There are then still lacking the branch points at which $z=\infty$, and hence $z'=0$, and these follow in the same way from the vanishing roots of the field discriminant $D_{z'}$. Accordingly we have the theorem:

5. \gesperrt{The branching number $w_z$ is equal to the degree of the field discriminant $D_z$, increased by the number of the vanishing roots of $D_{z'}$. ($z' = 1:z$).}

\begin{center}
§ 191. \gesperrt{Polygon quotients and polygon classes.}
\end{center}

A function $\eta$ in $\Omega$ has an order number different from zero only at a finite number of points. The sum of the positive order numbers is just as great as the sum of the negative ones, namely equal to the order of the function $\eta$ (§ 189, 4.). If the order numbers of $\eta$ are known for every point $\mathfrak{P}$, then the function $\eta$ is thereby determined up to a constant factor. For if a second function $\eta'$ has the same order numbers everywhere, then $\eta:\eta'$ has the order number $0$ everywhere and is therefore constant (§ 189, 4.).

We form a polygon $\mathfrak{A}$, into which we take up every point at which $\eta$ has a positive order number as often as this order number indicates, and a second polygon $\mathfrak{B}$, into which we
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 702 =====
% !PRINTED 671
\weberpage{671}
%<<CONT
corresponding fashion take up the points at which $\eta$ has a negative order number. Then the polygons $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ are of equal order, namely of the order of the function $\eta$, and by these polygons the function $\eta$ is determined up to a constant factor.

We can therefore introduce the symbolic notation:

\weq{1}{\eta = \dfrac{\mathfrak{A}}{\mathfrak{B}}\,,}

and call $\mathfrak{A}$ the \gesperrt{numerator} or the \gesperrt{upper polygon}, $\mathfrak{B}$ the \gesperrt{denominator} or the \gesperrt{lower polygon} of $\eta$. According to this definition, $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ are in the first instance relatively prime to one another. But we wish to extend this notation still further by setting, when $\mathfrak{M}$ is an arbitrary polygon:

\weq{2}{\dfrac{\mathfrak{M}\mathfrak{A}}{\mathfrak{M}\mathfrak{B}} = \dfrac{\mathfrak{A}}{\mathfrak{B}}}

Then the notation (1) is free of the restriction that $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ are to be relatively prime. Both polygons are still of equal order, but this order can be greater than the order of $\eta$.

With this representation of the functions $\eta$ the same rules then hold for multiplication and division as in reckoning with numerical fractions in the region of the natural numbers.

In (1) $\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{B}$ cannot be arbitrary $m$-gons, and the investigation of the relation between them is the great question which, in another way, is answered by \gesperrt{Abel's theorem}.

We set up the following definition:

1. \gesperrt{If two $n$-gons $\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{A}'$ can be the upper polygon and the lower polygon of a function $\eta$ in $\Omega$, then $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{A}'$ are called equivalent.}

In symbols: if there is a function $\eta$ to which the notation

\[
\eta = \dfrac{\mathfrak{A}}{\mathfrak{A}'}
\]

belongs, then

\weq{3}{\mathfrak{A} \sim \mathfrak{A}'.}

From the formula

\[
\eta = \dfrac{\mathfrak{A}}{\mathfrak{A}'}\,, \quad \eta' = \dfrac{\mathfrak{A}}{\mathfrak{A}''}\,, \quad \dfrac{\eta'}{\eta} = \dfrac{\mathfrak{A}'}{\mathfrak{A}''}
\]

there results the theorem:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 703 =====
% !PRINTED 672
\weberpage{672}
%<<CONT
2. \gesperrt{If two $n$-gons are equivalent to a third, then they are also equivalent to one another. Accordingly one unites equivalent polygons $\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{A}', \ldots$ into a polygon class $A$. Every polygon is contained in one class, and in only one class.}

There also exist polygons that are equivalent to no other, and that therefore each form a separate class by themselves. These are called \gesperrt{isolated polygons}.

3. \gesperrt{If $\mathfrak{A} \sim \mathfrak{A}'$, $\mathfrak{B} \sim \mathfrak{B}'$, then $\mathfrak{A}\mathfrak{B} \sim \mathfrak{A}'\mathfrak{B}'$.}

This follows from

\weq{4}{\eta = \dfrac{\mathfrak{A}}{\mathfrak{A}'}\,, \quad \eta_1 = \dfrac{\mathfrak{B}}{\mathfrak{B}'}\,, \quad \eta\eta_1 = \dfrac{\mathfrak{A}\mathfrak{B}}{\mathfrak{A}'\mathfrak{B}'}.}

The class $C$ to which the product $\mathfrak{A}\mathfrak{B}$ of the classes $A, B$ belongs therefore contains all products of a polygon of the class $A$ with a polygon of the class $B$ (in certain circumstances still others as well), and is therefore completely determined by the classes $A$ and $B$. On this rests the multiplication (composition) of the classes, which is expressed in the formula:

\weq{5}{C = AB = BA.}

From an equation between three classes $A, B, M$

\[
MA = MB
\]

it follows accordingly that $A = B$. For if $\mathfrak{M}\mathfrak{A} \sim \mathfrak{M}\mathfrak{B}$, then by (2) it follows that $\mathfrak{A} \sim \mathfrak{B}$. If $\mathfrak{A} \sim \mathfrak{A}'$ and

\[
\mathfrak{A}\mathfrak{B} = \mathfrak{C} \quad \text{and} \quad \mathfrak{A}'\mathfrak{B} = \mathfrak{C}'\,,
\]

then $\mathfrak{C} \sim \mathfrak{C}'$ as well. If, then, $\mathfrak{A}$ is contained in $\mathfrak{C}$, every polygon equivalent to $\mathfrak{A}$ is contained in a polygon $\mathfrak{C}'$ equivalent to $\mathfrak{C}$.

4. \gesperrt{We call a class $C$ divisible by a class $A$ if a polygon of $A$ is contained in a polygon of $C$, and we set}

\weq{6}{AB = C.}

\gesperrt{The class $B$ is completely determined by $A$ and $C$.}

\begin{center}
\textbf{§ 192. Families of Polygons.}
\end{center}

If $\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{A}_1, \mathfrak{A}_2, \ldots, \mathfrak{A}_s$ are polygons of a class $A$, then there are $s$ functions in $\Omega$:

\weq{1}{\eta_1 = \dfrac{\mathfrak{A}_1}{\mathfrak{A}}\,, \quad \eta_2 = \dfrac{\mathfrak{A}_2}{\mathfrak{A}}\,, \quad \cdots, \quad \eta_s = \dfrac{\mathfrak{A}_s}{\mathfrak{A}}\,.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 704 =====
% !PRINTED 673
\weberpage{673}

If $\mathfrak{P}$ is any point and $\varrho$ a function which has order 1 at this
point, then following § 185 we set

\weq{2}{\begin{aligned}
\eta_1 &= e_1\varrho^m + \sigma_1\varrho^{m+1},\\
\eta_2 &= e_2\varrho^m + \sigma_2\varrho^{m+1},\\
&\text{\quad$\cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot$}\\
\eta_s &= e_s\varrho^m + \sigma_s\varrho^{m+1},
\end{aligned}}

in which $e_1, e_2, \ldots, e_s$ are constants that do not all vanish,
and $\sigma_1, \sigma_2, \ldots, \sigma_s$ are functions that are finite at $\mathfrak{P}$;
$m$ is the lowest order number at $\mathfrak{P}$ that occurs among the functions $\eta_i$.

The totality of the functions

\weq{3}{\eta = c_1\eta_1 + c_2\eta_2 + \cdots + c_s\eta_s}

with constants $c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_s$ is called a \gesperrt{family}. We denote it by

\weq{4}{(\eta_1, \eta_2, \ldots, \eta_s),}

and call $\eta_1, \eta_2, \ldots, \eta_s$ a \gesperrt{basis of the family}. The order
of $\eta$ at $\mathfrak{P}$ is not smaller than $m$ (it is greater when
$e_1c_1 + e_2c_2 + \cdots + e_sc_s = 0$). But $\eta$ can become infinite at no
point $\mathfrak{P}$ which is not contained in $\mathfrak{A}$, and
also not to a higher order than that to which the point $\mathfrak{P}$ enters into $\mathfrak{A}$.

We can therefore set:

\weq{5}{\eta = \frac{\mathfrak{A}'}{\mathfrak{A}},}

in which $\mathfrak{A}'$ likewise belongs to the class $A$.

If instead of $\mathfrak{A}$ one takes another polygon $\mathfrak{B}$ of the class $A$
and sets

\weq{6}{\xi = \frac{\mathfrak{A}}{\mathfrak{B}},}

then from 1. it follows that:

\weq{7}{\begin{aligned}
\xi\eta_1 &= \eta_1' = \frac{\mathfrak{A}_1}{\mathfrak{B}},\\
\xi\eta_2 &= \eta_2' = \frac{\mathfrak{A}_2}{\mathfrak{B}},\\
&\text{\quad$\cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot\ \cdot$}\\
\xi\eta_s &= \eta_s' = \frac{\mathfrak{A}_s}{\mathfrak{B}}
\end{aligned}}

and

\weq{8}{\xi\eta = \eta' = c_1\eta_1' + c_2\eta_2' + \cdots + c_s\eta_s' = \frac{\mathfrak{A}'}{\mathfrak{B}}.}

Every polygon $\mathfrak{A}'$ generated by the denominator $\mathfrak{A}$ and a system
of constants $c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_s$ is therefore also generated by every
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 705 =====
% !PRINTED 674
\weberpage{674}

%<<CONT
$\mathfrak{A}$ and the same system of constants, and this polygon $\mathfrak{A}'$ is
therefore dependent only on the constants and on the polygons
$\mathfrak{A}_1, \mathfrak{A}_2, \ldots, \mathfrak{A}_s$. The totality of these polygons is called a
\gesperrt{family of polygons with the basis} $\mathfrak{A}_1, \mathfrak{A}_2, \ldots, \mathfrak{A}_s$,
and the designation

\weq{9}{(\mathfrak{A}_1, \mathfrak{A}_2, \ldots, \mathfrak{A}_s)}

is used for it.

If the polygons $\mathfrak{A}_1, \mathfrak{A}_2, \ldots, \mathfrak{A}_s$ have the greatest common
 divisor $\mathfrak{M}$, then this divisor is contained in all the polygons
of the family, and is called the \gesperrt{divisor of the family}. But
in the family one can determine a polygon $\mathfrak{A}' = \mathfrak{M}\mathfrak{B}$ in such a way
that $\mathfrak{B}$ does not contain arbitrarily given points.

For if a point $\mathfrak{P}$ is contained $\mu$ times in $\mathfrak{M}$ and $\nu$ times in $\mathfrak{A}$,
and $\varrho$ is a function that vanishes at $\mathfrak{P}$ to the first order
, then in the developments (2):

\[
m = \mu - \nu,
\]

and the development of $\eta = \mathfrak{A}' : \mathfrak{A} = \mathfrak{M}\mathfrak{B} : \mathfrak{A}$ reads

\[
\eta = e\varrho^m + \sigma\varrho^{m+1},
\]

in which

\[
e = e_1c_1 + e_2c_2 + \cdots + e_sc_s.
\]

If, then, one chooses the $c_i$ so that $e$ does not vanish, then
$\mathfrak{P}$ is not contained in $\mathfrak{B}$.

A family that has a divisor $\mathfrak{M}$ is called an \gesperrt{improper
 family}.

If among the functions $\eta_1, \eta_2, \ldots, \eta_s$ there subsists a relation
of the form:

\weq{10}{c_1\eta_1 + c_2\eta_2 + \cdots + c_s\eta_s = 0,}

in which the constants $c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_s$ are not all $= 0$, then the
 same relation

\weq{11}{c_1\eta_1' + c_2\eta_1' + \cdots + c_s\eta_s' = 0} % [sic] second term repeats \eta_1' rather than \eta_2' as printed

subsists between the functions (7). We then call these functions
\gesperrt{linearly dependent}. Correspondingly, the polygons
of the family $\mathfrak{A}_1, \mathfrak{A}_2, \ldots, \mathfrak{A}_s$ are also called linearly dependent. One can then express one
of the functions, say $\eta_s$, linearly by the others,
and the family $(\eta_1, \eta_2, \ldots, \eta_s)$ is identical with $(\eta_1, \eta_2, \ldots, \eta_{s-1})$.
The same holds for the families of polygons $(\mathfrak{A}_1, \mathfrak{A}_2, \ldots, \mathfrak{A}_s)$ and $(\mathfrak{A}_1,
\mathfrak{A}_2, \ldots, \mathfrak{A}_{s-1})$. By repeated application of this reduction
one can represent every family by a \gesperrt{linearly independent or
irreducible basis}. Two irreducible bases of one
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 706 =====
% !PRINTED 675
\weberpage{675}

%<<CONT
family have the same number of elements, and this number is called the
\gesperrt{dimension of the family}, and the family is called an \gesperrt{$s$-fold} one.
If $\mathfrak{A}_1, \mathfrak{A}_2, \ldots, \mathfrak{A}_s$ are linearly dependent or independent, the same
holds of $\mathfrak{M}\mathfrak{A}_1, \mathfrak{M}\mathfrak{A}_2, \ldots, \mathfrak{M}\mathfrak{A}_s$.

In a family of dimension $s > 1$

\weq{12}{S = (\mathfrak{A}_1, \mathfrak{A}_2, \ldots, \mathfrak{A}_s)}

one can find a polygon that contains an arbitrary point $\mathfrak{P}$ at least
once more often than the divisor $\mathfrak{M}$ of this family does.

This purpose is attained by setting up the development (2) for this
point and then determining one of the constants $c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_s$
from the equation

\weq{13}{c_1e_1 + c_2e_2 + \cdots + c_se_s = 0}

These polygons then form a family of the $(s-1)$th
dimension, whose divisor is divisible by $\mathfrak{M}\mathfrak{P}$.

This theorem can be extended as follows:

5. \gesperrt{The polygons of an $s$-fold family that are divisible
by an $r$-gon $\mathfrak{R}$ form an at least
$(s-r)$-fold family.}

If this theorem has already been proved for an $r$-gon, it follows
for an $(r+1)$-gon $\mathfrak{R}\mathfrak{P}$ from the preceding one.
For by the
addition of the point $\mathfrak{P}$ the dimension is either not
changed, if $\mathfrak{P}$ divides the divisor of the family reduced by $\mathfrak{R}$,
or it is diminished by 1.

The polygon $\mathfrak{R}$ can be so chosen that the dimension of
$S$ is reduced exactly to $(s-r)$. For this purpose the
points of $\mathfrak{R}$ have to be chosen successively so that each following one
is not contained in the divisor of the family reduced by the
preceding one. From this it follows:

6. \gesperrt{In an $s$-fold family there is at least
one polygon that is divisible by a given $(s-1)$-gon.}

If the class $A$, to which all polygons of the family $S$ belong,
is of the $m$th order, then the dimension $s$ of the family cannot
be greater than $m+1$. For otherwise one could, by 6., find
a polygon in $S$ that would be divisible by an $(m+1)$-gon,
which is absurd, since $S$ contains only $m$-gons. Hence the
dimension $s$ of the family has a \gesperrt{maximum} for a given class $A$.
If this maximum is reached, then all polygons of the class $A$
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 707 =====
% !PRINTED 676
\weberpage{676}

%<<CONT
contained in $S$. For if there is a polygon $\mathfrak{A}_{s+1}$ in $A$
that is not contained in $S$, then

\[
(\mathfrak{A}_1, \mathfrak{A}_2, \ldots, \mathfrak{A}_s, \mathfrak{A}_{s+1})
\]

is a family of dimension $s+1$. Thus it is proved:

7. \gesperrt{The polygons of a class form a family
of a finite dimension $s$. This number shall
be called the dimension of the class.}

If in a class $C$ there are polygons that are divisible by a
polygon $\mathfrak{A}$ of a class $A$, then $C$ is divisible by $A$.

If

\[
C = AB,
\]

then one obtains the dimension of $B$ by selecting from $C$ the
family that is divisible by some polygon $\mathfrak{A}$ in $A$. This
dimension therefore depends only on the two classes $A$ and $C$,
and shall be denoted by $(A, C)$. The symbol for the dimension of
a class $A$ is accordingly $(O, A)$, if $O$ is the class of the
null polygon. We then have

\weq{14}{(A, C) = (A, AB) = (O, B),}

and if $a$ is the order of the class $A$, then by 5.:

\weq{15}{(A, C) \geqq (O, C) - a.}

If we denote by $A$ the proper class which one obtains
when one cancels $\mathfrak{M}$ away everywhere, then the improper class
with the divisor $\mathfrak{M}$ shall be denoted by $\mathfrak{M}A$.

8. \gesperrt{The divisor of an improper class is an
isolated polygon.}

For if $\mathfrak{M}A$ is an improper class, then a polygon $\mathfrak{A}$
can be found in $A$ that is relatively prime to $\mathfrak{M}$. If $\mathfrak{M}'$ is
equivalent to $\mathfrak{M}$, then $\mathfrak{M}'\mathfrak{A}$ is contained in $\mathfrak{M}A$ and consequently
divisible by $\mathfrak{M}$. Hence $\mathfrak{M}'$ too is divisible by $\mathfrak{M}$, and therefore
identical with $\mathfrak{M}$. There is therefore in the class of $\mathfrak{M}$ only the
single polygon $\mathfrak{M}$.

\begin{center}
§ 193. \gesperrt{Normal bases.}
\end{center}

According to the foregoing we can represent a function $z$ of the field
$\Omega$ of the $n$th order in the form

\weq{1}{z = \frac{\mathfrak{U}'}{\mathfrak{U}}}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 708 =====
% !PRINTED 677
\weberpage{677}
%<<CONT
represented, in which $\mathfrak{U}$ and $\mathfrak{U}'$ are equivalent $n$-gons without common divisor. An integral function $\omega$ of $z$ is characterised by the fact that it becomes infinite at no point which is not contained in $\mathfrak{U}$. Consequently such a function $\omega$ can be represented in the following way:
\weq{2}{\omega = \dfrac{\mathfrak{A}}{\mathfrak{U}^r},}
in which $r$ is a positive exponent. In (2) the numerator and the denominator may have common divisors. We may, however, assume that $\mathfrak{A}$ is not divisible by $\mathfrak{U}$. Then in (2) the exponent $r$ has the least possible value. \gesperrt{This number $r$ shall be called the exponent of $\omega$ in $z$.}

1. \gesperrt{If we set $z' = 1:z$, then by (1), (2):}
\[
z' = \frac{\mathfrak{U}}{\mathfrak{U}'}, \quad \omega' = \omega z'^r = \frac{\mathfrak{A}}{\mathfrak{U}'^r},
\]
and if $\mathfrak{A}$ is not divisible by $\mathfrak{U}'$, then $r$ is the exponent of $\omega'$ with respect to $z'$. The assumption that $\mathfrak{A}$ is not divisible by $\mathfrak{U}'$ means that $\omega$ is not divisible by $z$, and from this it follows that $\omega'$ too is not divisible by $z'$.

2. The exponent of an integral rational function of $z$ of degree $m$
\[
x = a_0 + a_1 z + \cdots + a_m z^m
\]
is equal to $m$. For this function becomes infinite of the $m$th order at every point contained in $\mathfrak{U}$. The exponent of the product $x\omega$ is equal to $r + m$.

3. The exponent of a sum
\[
\omega = c_1\omega_1 + c_2\omega_2 + \cdots + c_s\omega_s
\]
is at most equal to the greatest of the exponents of $\omega_1, \omega_2, \ldots, \omega_s$.

4. We determine a sequence of integral functions of $z$
\[
\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \lambda_3, \ldots
\]
by the following recurrent determination:
\begin{itemize}
\item[1)] $\lambda_1$ constant (exponent $r_1 = 0$),
\item[2)] $\lambda_2$ a non-rational integral function of $z$ with the smallest possible exponent $r_2$,
\item[3)] $\lambda_s$ an integral function of $z$ not contained in the form
\weq{3}{x_1\lambda_1 + x_2\lambda_2 + \cdots + x_{s-1}\lambda_{s-1}}
with the smallest possible exponent $r_s$,
\end{itemize}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 709 =====
% !PRINTED 678
\weberpage{678}
%<<CONT
and continue this sequence as long as one can still find functions $\lambda_s$ that are not contained in the form (3).

By 4., 3) the functions $\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \ldots, \lambda_s$ are linearly independent in the sense that no linear equation with rational coefficients in $z$ subsists between them. Since there are not more than $n$ linearly independent functions, $s$ cannot be greater than $n$. On the other hand, as long as $s \leqq n$, there are always still integral functions that are not linearly dependent on $\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \ldots, \lambda_{s-1}$, and among them also ones of least exponent. We therefore obtain $n$ functions
\weq{4}{L = (\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \ldots, \lambda_n),}
and these form a basis of the field $\Omega$ with respect to $z$. They form a minimal basis; for if this were not the case, then for some $s \leqq n$ a function $x_1\lambda_1 + x_2\lambda_2 + \cdots + x_s\lambda_s$ would have to be divisible by a linear function $z - c$ without $x_s$ being divisible by $z - c$. If one reduces $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_s$ to their residues with respect to $z - c$, an equation results:
\[
c_1\lambda_1 + c_2\lambda_2 + \cdots + c_s\lambda_s = (z - c)\mu,
\]
in which the $c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_s$ are constant, $c_s$ different from zero, and $\mu$ an integral function. Now $\mu$ is not contained in the form (3), and by 2. and 3. its exponent is smaller than the exponent of $\lambda_s$, which contradicts the determination 4. 3). Hence:

5. \gesperrt{The functions $\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \ldots, \lambda_n$ form a minimal basis of $\Omega$ with respect to $z$. It is called a normal basis.}

The exponents $r_1, r_2, r_3, \ldots, r_n$ of these functions satisfy the condition:
\weq{5}{r_1 = 0, \quad 1 \leqq r_2 \leqq r_3 \ldots \leqq r_n.}
For if $r_s < r_{s-1}$, then by 3. 3) one would have had to take $\lambda_s$ in place of $\lambda_{s-1}$.

Of the functions $\lambda_i$ none is divisible by $z$; for if $\lambda_s = z\mu$, then $\mu$ would have a smaller exponent than $\lambda_s$ and would not be contained in the form (3). Thus $\mu$ would have to take the place of $\lambda_s$.

6. Accordingly (by 1.)
\[
r_1, r_2, \ldots, r_n
\]
are the exponents of
\weq{6}{\lambda_1' = z'^{r_1}\lambda_1, \quad \lambda_2' = z'^{r_2}\lambda_2, \ldots, \lambda_n' = z'^{r_n}\lambda_n}
in regard to $z' = 1:z$, and these functions are the elements of a normal basis of $\Omega$ with respect to $z'$.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 710 =====
% !PRINTED 679
\weberpage{679}
For if we denote by $x_i'$ integral rational functions of $z'$, of degree at most $m$, then
\weq{7}{x_i = z^m x_i'}
is an integral rational function of $z$. Now if we had
\[
\lambda_s' = \sum_{0,\,s-1}^{i} x_i'\lambda_i',
\]
then from (6) and (7) it would follow:
\[
z^m\lambda_s = \sum_{0,\,s-1}^{i} x_i z^{r_s-r_i}\lambda_i,
\]
and this is impossible, because the $\lambda_i$ are linearly independent; and there can also be no function $\lambda_s'$ of lower exponent than $r_s$, because from it one could derive a function $\lambda_s$ of lower exponent.

The field discriminants $D_z, D_{z'}$ with respect to the variable $z$ and $z'$ are
\[
\begin{aligned}
D_z &= \Delta(\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \ldots, \lambda_n), \\
D_{z'} &= \Delta(\lambda_1', \lambda_2', \ldots, \lambda_n'),
\end{aligned}
\]
and from this it follows by (6):
\weq{8}{D_{z'} = z'^{2(r_1+r_2+\cdots+r_n)}D_z.}

If, then, $\delta$ is the degree of $D_z$, then
\[
2(r_1+r_2+\cdots+r_n) - \delta
\]
is the number of the vanishing roots of $D_{z'}$, and from \S\,190, 5. it follows:
\weq{9}{w_z = 2(r_1+r_2+\cdots+r_n).}

7. \gesperrt{The branching number $w_z$ is therefore always an even number.}

\begin{center}
\S\,194. \gesperrt{Differential quotients.}
\end{center}

Where we make no use of continuity, we cannot introduce the differential quotients in the ordinary way. We take two functions $\alpha, \beta$ from $\Omega$, between which the irreducible equation
\weq{1}{F(\alpha, \beta) = 0}
holds; we denote by $F'(\alpha), F'(\beta)$ the derived functions and define the differential quotient as a function of the field $\Omega$ by the formula:
\weq{2}{\left(\frac{d\alpha}{d\beta}\right) = -\frac{F'(\beta)}{F'(\alpha)}.}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 711 =====
% !PRINTED 680
\weberpage{680}
%<<CONT
Let $\alpha_0, \beta_0$ be the finite values of the functions $\alpha, \beta$ at a point $\mathfrak{P}$. Then $F(\alpha_0, \beta_0) = 0$, and we can represent equation (1) in the following way:
\weq{3}{
\begin{aligned}
0 = {} & (\alpha - \alpha_0)F'(\alpha_0) + (\beta - \beta_0)F'(\beta_0) \\
& + \tfrac{1}{2}\left[(\alpha-\alpha_0)^2 F''(\alpha_0,\alpha_0) + 2(\alpha-\alpha_0)(\beta-\beta_0)F''(\alpha_0,\beta_0) \right. \\
& \left. \quad + (\beta-\beta_0)^2 F''(\beta_0,\beta_0)\right] + \cdots
\end{aligned}
}
The two mutually reciprocal functions
\[
\frac{\alpha - \alpha_0}{\beta - \beta_0}, \quad \frac{\beta - \beta_0}{\alpha - \alpha_0}
\]
cannot both be infinite at the point $\mathfrak{P}$. Let therefore:
\[
\left(\frac{\alpha - \alpha_0}{\beta - \beta_0}\right)_0
\]
be the finite value of the first of these quotients. Then it follows from (3), if $F'(\alpha_0)$ is not zero:
\weq{4}{\left(\frac{\alpha - \alpha_0}{\beta - \beta_0}\right)_0 = -\frac{F'(\beta_0)}{F'(\alpha_0)} = -\left(\frac{F'(\beta)}{F'(\alpha)}\right)_0 = \left(\frac{d\alpha}{d\beta}\right)_0.}
This equation holds for all points $\mathfrak{P}$, with the possible exception of a finite number\footnote{Among the points to be excepted are in any case those in which $\alpha_0$ or $\beta_0$ becomes infinite. For at these points the functions $\alpha - \alpha_0$, $\beta - \beta_0$ are not defined at all.}.

1. \gesperrt{A function $\eta$ in $\Omega$ which at all points, with the exception of a finite number, satisfies the condition:}
\weq{5}{\eta_0 = \left(\frac{\alpha-\alpha_0}{\beta-\beta_0}\right)_0}
\gesperrt{is identical with $\left(\dfrac{d\alpha}{d\beta}\right)$.}

For from (4) and (5) it follows that the function
\[
\left(\frac{d\alpha}{d\beta}\right) - \eta
\]
has infinitely many zero points and must therefore vanish identically.

Formula (5) can accordingly likewise serve as the definition of the differential quotient.

From this the principal theorems on the differential quotients follow simply:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 712 =====
% !PRINTED 681
\weberpage{681}
%<<CONT

2. \gesperrt{Let $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ be three functions in $\Omega$; then}
\weq{6}{\left(\frac{d\alpha}{d\beta}\right)\left(\frac{d\beta}{d\gamma}\right) = \left(\frac{d\alpha}{d\gamma}\right).}
For, for infinitely many points,
\[
\left(\frac{\alpha-\alpha_0}{\beta-\beta_0}\right)_0 \left(\frac{\beta-\beta_0}{\gamma-\gamma_0}\right)_0 = \left(\frac{\alpha-\alpha_0}{\gamma-\gamma_0}\right)_0,
\]
and from this Theorem 2 follows as in 1.

Accordingly, to every function $\alpha$ in $\Omega$ one can assign a function $d\alpha$ in such a way that, for any two of these functions:
\weq{7}{\left(\frac{d\alpha}{d\beta}\right) = \frac{d\alpha}{d\beta}}
becomes an actual quotient of two functions $d\alpha, d\beta$. These functions we call the \gesperrt{differentials} of $\alpha, \beta$. The differentials of the constants, and only these, are equal to zero. The other differentials are all completely determined as soon as one of them has been assumed arbitrarily (for example, constant).

3. \gesperrt{If $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \ldots$, are arbitrary functions in $\Omega$ which satisfy an equation}
\weq{8}{F(\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \ldots) = 0}
\gesperrt{then}
\weq{9}{F'(\alpha)\,d\alpha + F'(\beta)\,d\beta + F'(\gamma)\,d\gamma + \cdots = 0.}
To prove this theorem, take a point $\mathfrak{P}$ at which none of the functions $\alpha, \beta, \gamma \ldots$ or $d\alpha, d\beta, d\gamma, \ldots$ becomes infinite or zero and at which the derived functions $F'(\alpha), F'(\beta), F'(\gamma)$ also do not vanish, and arrange, as in (3), the function $F$ according to powers and products of $\alpha - \alpha_0, \beta - \beta_0, \gamma - \gamma_0, \ldots$ It then turns out that equation (9) is satisfied for infinitely many points, and hence identically. As special cases of (9) there result: % [sic] German source shifts from singular ``nehme man'' to plural ``ordnen''
\weq{10}{\begin{aligned}
d(\alpha+\beta) &= d\alpha + d\beta,\\
d(\alpha\beta) &= \beta\,d\alpha + \alpha\,d\beta,\\
d\left(\frac{\alpha}{\beta}\right) &= \frac{\beta\,d\alpha - \alpha\,d\beta}{\beta^2}.
\end{aligned}}
The concept of the differential can be carried over without further ado to \gesperrt{holomorphic functionals}, provided the functional variables are regarded as constants. Theorem 3. and the formulae (10) which follow from it then still hold when $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \ldots$ are holomorphic functionals and $F(\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \ldots)$ is an integral rational function of $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \ldots$.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 713 =====
% !PRINTED 682
\weberpage{682}

If $\alpha$ is an integral rational function of $z$, then $d\alpha/dz$ is likewise an integral rational function, namely the derivative of $\alpha$ with respect to $z$.

\begin{center}
\S\,195. \textbf{\gesperrt{Representation of the Differential Quotients by Polygon Quotients.}}
\end{center}

We take any function $z$ of the $n$th order in $\Omega$ and a minimal basis $\omega_1, \omega_2, \ldots, \omega_n$ with respect to $z$. All integral functions of $z$ of the field $\Omega$ are then representable in the form:
\weq{1}{\omega = x_1\omega_1 + x_2\omega_2 + \cdots + x_n\omega_n}
and arise from the basis functional
\weq{2}{\tau = t_1\omega_1 + t_2\omega_2 + \cdots + t_n\omega_n}
when integral rational functions $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ of $z$ are put for the functional variables $t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_n$.

If we put, as in \S\,184,
\[
N(t - \tau) = F(t, z),
\]
then $\tau$ satisfies the irreducible rational equation:
\[
F(\tau, z) = 0,
\]
and one obtains, by \S\,194, 3.:
\weq{3}{F'(\tau)\,d\tau + F'(z)\,dz = 0,}
and here $F'(\tau)$ is the \gesperrt{branching functional} (\S\,184).

By (1) and (2),
\weq{4}{d\omega = d\tau + \omega_1\,dx_1 + \omega_2\,dx_2 + \cdots + \omega_n\,dx_n,}
where in $d\tau$ the $t_i$ are to be replaced by the $x_i$, and from (3) there follows therefore the theorem:

4. \gesperrt{If $\omega$ is an integral function of $z$, then}
\weq{5}{F'(\tau)\frac{d\omega}{dz} = -F'(z) + \omega_1\frac{dx_1}{dz} + \cdots + \omega_n\frac{dx_n}{dz}}
\gesperrt{is an integral functional.}

On the other hand, $F'(\omega)$ is divisible by $F'(\tau)$, by \S\,182, 8. If we therefore put:
\weq{6}{F'(\omega) = \varrho\,F'(\tau),}
then $\varrho$ is an integral functional, and from (4), when one replaces the $t_i$ by the $x_i$, there results:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 714 =====
% !PRINTED 683
\weberpage{683}
%<<CONT
\weq{7}{\begin{aligned}
-F'(z) &= F'(\omega)\left(\frac{d\omega}{dz} - \omega_1\frac{dx_1}{dz} - \cdots - \omega_n\frac{dx_n}{dz}\right)\\
&= \varrho\,F'(\tau)\left(\frac{d\omega}{dz} - \omega_1\frac{dx_1}{dz} - \cdots - \omega_n\frac{dx_n}{dz}\right),
\end{aligned}}
and from this it follows that $F'(z)$ too (after replacing the $t_i$ by the $x_i$) is divisible by $\varrho$.

Accordingly, with regard to the geometric analogy, we call $\varrho$ the \gesperrt{functional of the double points} in $\omega, z$.

If $\mathfrak{P}$ is a point at which $z$ is finite and $F'(\tau)$ is different from zero, so that it is not a branch point in $z$, then by 4. an integral function $\omega$ of $z$ has a finite differential quotient at $\mathfrak{P}$. A fractional function $\eta$ of $z$ which is finite at $\mathfrak{P}$ can be represented as a quotient of two integral functions $\omega' : \omega$ whose denominator $\omega$ does not vanish at $\mathfrak{P}$.

From this it follows:
\[
\frac{d\eta}{dz} = \frac{1}{\omega^2}\left(\omega'\frac{d\omega}{dz} - \omega\frac{d\omega'}{dz}\right),
\]
and consequently $d\eta : dz$ is likewise finite at the point $\mathfrak{P}$.

In order to recognise the behaviour of an arbitrary differential quotient $d\alpha : d\beta$ at any point $\mathfrak{P}$, take a function $z$ which becomes zero of the first order at $\mathfrak{P}$, and denote by $r, s$ the order numbers of $\alpha - \alpha_0, \beta - \beta_0$ at the point $\mathfrak{P}$. For the case that $\alpha$ becomes infinite at $\mathfrak{P}$, one sets $\alpha_0 = 0$ and obtains a negative order number $r$. The corresponding statement holds when $\beta$ becomes infinite.

Then by \S\,185:
\weq{8}{\begin{aligned}
\alpha - \alpha_0 &= z^r\alpha',\\
\beta - \beta_0 &= z^s\beta',
\end{aligned}}
where $\alpha'$ and $\beta'$ are functions in $\Omega$ which become neither zero nor infinite at $\mathfrak{P}$.

From this there results, by \S\,194:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d\alpha}{dz} &= r z^{r-1}\alpha' + z^r\frac{d\alpha'}{dz},\\
\frac{d\beta}{dz} &= s z^{s-1}\beta' + z^s\frac{d\beta'}{dz},
\end{aligned}
\]
\weq{9}{\frac{\beta-\beta_0}{\alpha-\alpha_0}\frac{d\alpha}{d\beta} = \frac{r + z\dfrac{d\alpha'}{\alpha'\,dz}}{s + z\dfrac{d\beta'}{\beta'\,dz}},}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 715 =====
% !PRINTED 684
\weberpage{684}
%<<CONT
and if one passes to the point $\mathfrak{P}$:
\weq{10}{\left(\frac{\beta-\beta_0}{\alpha-\alpha_0}\frac{d\alpha}{d\beta}\right)_0 = \frac{r}{s},}
which is a finite value different from zero.

From this it follows:

5. \gesperrt{The order number of the differential quotient $d\alpha : d\beta$ at any point $\mathfrak{P}$ is equal to the difference of the order numbers of $\alpha - \alpha_0$ and $\beta - \beta_0$.}

If $r > s$, or $r < s$, then
\[
\left(\frac{\alpha-\alpha_0}{\beta-\beta_0}\right)_0 = 0 \text{ or} = \infty,
\]
and consequently, by (10), also
\[
\left(\frac{d\alpha}{d\beta}\right)_0 = 0 \text{ or} = \infty.
\]
If $r = s$, then from (10) there follows
\weq{11}{\left(\frac{d\alpha}{d\beta}\right)_0 = \left(\frac{\alpha-\alpha_0}{\beta-\beta_0}\right)_0.}
\gesperrt{Here every trace of the variable $z$ has dropped out, and this formula holds for every point $\mathfrak{P}$ without exception.}

Accordingly the zero points and the points of infinity of the differential quotients can be determined exactly, and these functions can thereby be represented as \gesperrt{polygon quotients}.

If $a$ is the order number of $\alpha - \alpha_0$ at a point $\mathfrak{P}$ according to \S\,188, then the branch polygon $\mathfrak{Z}_\alpha$ contains the point $\mathfrak{P}$ $a - 1$ times or $-a-1$ times, according as $a$ is positive or negative. If $a$ is negative, then the denominator polygon $\mathfrak{A}$ of $\alpha$ contains the point $\mathfrak{P}$ $(-a)$ times, and consequently in both cases the point $\mathfrak{P}$ is contained $(a-1)$ times in $\mathfrak{Z}_\alpha : \mathfrak{A}^2$. If $\mathfrak{Z}_\beta, \mathfrak{B}, b$ have the corresponding meaning for $\beta$, then the quotient:
\[
\frac{\mathfrak{Z}_\alpha \mathfrak{B}^2}{\mathfrak{Z}_\beta \mathfrak{A}^2}
\]
contains the point $\mathfrak{P}$ $(a-b)$ times.

But by 5. the order number of $d\alpha : d\beta$ at $\mathfrak{P}$ is just as great, and from this there results the representation:
\weq{12}{\frac{d\alpha}{d\beta} = \frac{\mathfrak{Z}_\alpha \mathfrak{B}^2}{\mathfrak{Z}_\beta \mathfrak{A}^2},}
in which, to repeat it, $\mathfrak{Z}_\alpha, \mathfrak{Z}_\beta$ are the branch polygons, $\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{B}$ the denominators of $\alpha, \beta$.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 716 =====
% !PRINTED 685
\weberpage{685}
\S\ 196. \gesperrt{Genus of the field $\Omega$.}

Since in a polygon quotient numerator and denominator are of the same order, it follows from the last formula [\S\ 195, (12)]:
\weq{1}{w_\alpha - 2a = w_\beta - 2b.}
If, then, we denote by $n$ the order and by $w$ the branching number for an arbitrary variable, which, as we have seen in \S\ 193, is an even number, then the integer:
\weq{2}{p = \tfrac{1}{2}w - n + 1,}
is an invariant integer belonging to the field $\Omega$, and it is called the \gesperrt{genus of the field}. That this number cannot be negative follows from \S\ 193, (5) and (9), according to which
\weq{3}{p = (r_2-1)+(r_3-1)+\cdots+(r_{n_1}-1)}
% [sic] German source prints final subscript $n_1$; formulas §193 (5), (9) require $n$.
holds, so that it consists entirely of summands of which none is negative.

Two functions $\alpha$, $\beta$ we call a \gesperrt{primitive pair} of the field $\Omega$ if all functions in $\Omega$ can be expressed rationally by $\alpha$ and $\beta$. If $\alpha$ is of order $m$ and $\beta$ of order $n$, then by \S\ 171 it is necessary and sufficient for a primitive pair that the irreducible equation subsisting between $\alpha$ and $\beta$:
\weq{4}{F(\overset{n}{\alpha},\overset{m}{\beta}) = 0}
be of degree $n$ in $\alpha$ and of degree $m$ in $\beta$.

The functions $F'(\alpha)$, $F'(\beta)$ are now to be represented by polygon quotients. We set:
\weq{5}{\alpha = \dfrac{\mathfrak{M}}{\mathfrak{A}}, \quad \beta = \dfrac{\mathfrak{N}}{\mathfrak{B}},}
in which $\mathfrak{A}$, $\mathfrak{M}$ are of order $m$, and $\mathfrak{B}$, $\mathfrak{N}$ of order $n$. $\mathfrak{A}$ then has no point in common with $\mathfrak{M}$, nor $\mathfrak{B}$ with $\mathfrak{N}$. We set:
\weq{6}{\begin{aligned}
F(\alpha,\beta) &= a_0\alpha^n + a_1\alpha^{n-1} + \cdots + a_n,\\
F'(\alpha) &= na_0\alpha^{n-1} + (n-1)a_1\alpha^{n-2} + \cdots + a_{n-1},\\
\alpha F'(\alpha) &= -a_1\alpha^{n-1} - 2a_2\alpha^{n-2} - \cdots - na_n.
\end{aligned}}
From the second of these equations one concludes that in the denominator of $F'(\alpha)$ there occur no points that are not contained in $\mathfrak{A}$ or in $\mathfrak{B}$, and from the third it follows that this denominator can at most be $= \mathfrak{A}^{n-2}\mathfrak{B}^m$. We therefore set:
\weq{7}{F'(\alpha) = \dfrac{\mathfrak{L}}{\mathfrak{A}^{n-2}\mathfrak{B}^m}.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 717 =====
% !PRINTED 686
\weberpage{686}
It is now to be proved that $\mathfrak{L}$ is divisible by the branch polygon $\mathfrak{Z}_\beta$.

Let us first assume that $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ are relatively prime to $\mathfrak{Z}_\beta$; then there is an integral rational function $x$ of $\beta$ which vanishes at no point of $\mathfrak{Z}_\beta$ and for which $\omega = x\alpha$ becomes an integral function of $\beta$. If we set
\[
f(\omega) = x^n F(\alpha,\beta),
\]
then:
\[
f'(\omega) = x^{n-1}F'(\alpha).
\]
If $\tau$ is the basis form of $\Omega$ with respect to $\beta$, then by \S\ 182 $f'(\omega)$ is divisible by $f'(\tau)$; and since by assumption $\beta$ becomes infinite at no branch point, $f'(\tau)$, and consequently $F'(\alpha)$ also, is divisible by the branch polygon $\mathfrak{Z}_\beta$, and our assertion is proved. We set:
\[
\mathfrak{L} = \mathfrak{R}\mathfrak{Z}_\beta,
\]
\weq{8}{F'(\alpha) = \dfrac{\mathfrak{R}\mathfrak{Z}_\beta}{\mathfrak{A}^{n-2}\mathfrak{B}^m}.}
This formula is thereby proved only under the assumption that neither $\alpha$ nor $\beta$ becomes infinite at one of the branch points.

But if we make the linear substitution:
\weq{9}{\begin{aligned}
\alpha(\alpha_1+1) &= a\alpha_1,\\
\beta(\beta_1+1) &= b\beta_1,
\end{aligned}}
then by \S\ 190
\[
\mathfrak{Z}_\beta = \mathfrak{Z}_{\beta_1},
\]
and we can choose the constants $a$, $b$ so that $\alpha_1$ and $\beta_1$ become infinite at no point of $\mathfrak{Z}_\beta$. We have only to take for $a$ and $b$ any constant values that $\alpha$ and $\beta$ do not assume at any point of $\mathfrak{Z}_\beta$.

If $F_1(\alpha_1,\beta_1)=0$ is the rational equation subsisting between $\alpha_1$, $\beta_1$, then:
\[
F_1(\alpha_1,\beta_1) = (\alpha_1+1)^n(\beta_1+1)^m F(\alpha,\beta),
\]
or also, by (9):
\[
\alpha^n\beta^m F_1(\alpha_1,\beta_1) = a^n b^m \alpha_1^n \beta_1^m F(\alpha,\beta);
\]
further $d\alpha : d\alpha_1 = \alpha^2 : a\alpha_1^2$, and consequently, having regard to $F=0$, $F_1=0$:
\weq{10}{\alpha^{n-2}\beta^m F_1'(\alpha_1) = a^{n-1}b^m \alpha_1^{n-2}\beta_1^m F'(\alpha).}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 718 =====
% !PRINTED 687
\weberpage{687}
By (9), $\alpha_1$, $\beta_1$ vanish at the same points and with the same order numbers as $\alpha$, $\beta$, and from this there follow, corresponding to the representations (2) and (4), the polygon representations:
\weq{11}{\alpha_1 = \dfrac{\mathfrak{M}}{\mathfrak{A}_1}, \quad \beta_1 = \dfrac{\mathfrak{N}}{\mathfrak{B}_1},}
and from (5), (7) and (10):
\weq{12}{F_1'(\alpha_1) = \dfrac{\mathfrak{L}}{\mathfrak{A}_1^{n-2}\mathfrak{B}_1^m}.}
With this, formula (8) is proved \gesperrt{in general}.

If one sets, following \S\ 194, (9):
\[
F'(\alpha)\,d\alpha + F'(\beta)\,d\beta = 0,
\]
then from (8) and \S\ 195, (12) it follows that:
\weq{13}{F'(\beta) = \dfrac{\mathfrak{R}\mathfrak{Z}_\alpha}{\mathfrak{A}^n\mathfrak{B}^{m-2}}.}
Both derivatives $F'(\alpha)$, $F'(\beta)$ therefore vanish at the points of $\mathfrak{R}$, and $\mathfrak{R}$ is called the polygon of the double points in $(\alpha,\beta)$.

The order of $\mathfrak{A}^n\mathfrak{B}^{m-2}$ is $2n(m-1)$, and from this there results for the order $2r$ of $\mathfrak{R}$ an even number, namely:
\[
2r = 2n(m-1) - w_\alpha = 2m(n-1) - w_\beta,
\]
and for the genus $p$ there results, by (2):
\weq{14}{p = (n-1)(m-1) - r.}
