\rule{4cm}{0.4pt}
\end{center}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 719 =====
% !PRINTED none
% Part-title / new-Abschnitt opening page: "Siebenundzwanzigster Abschnitt. Algebraische und
% Abelsche Differentiale." followed directly (same page) by the heading "§ 197. Differentiale
% in Ω." and the opening paragraphs and formulas of that section. No running-head page number
% is visible on this page in the scan.
\begin{center}
\gesperrt{Twenty-seventh Chapter.}

\textbf{Algebraic and Abelian Differentials.}

\rule{0.3\linewidth}{0.4pt}

\textbf{\S\,197. \gesperrt{Differentials in $\Omega$.}}
\end{center}

If $z$ and $z_1$ are two variables in $\Omega$ of the orders $n$, $n_1$ with the lower vertices $\mathfrak{U}$, $\mathfrak{U}_1$, with the branching vertices: $\mathfrak{Z}$, $\mathfrak{Z}_1$, and the branching numbers $w$, $w_1$, then by \S\ 195, (12)
\[
\dfrac{dz}{dz_1} = \dfrac{\mathfrak{Z}\mathfrak{U}_1^2}{\mathfrak{Z}_1\mathfrak{U}^2}.
\]
If one sets
\weq{1}{\omega = \dfrac{\mathfrak{A}\mathfrak{U}^2}{\mathfrak{B}\mathfrak{Z}}, \quad \omega_1 = \dfrac{\mathfrak{A}\mathfrak{U}_1^2}{\mathfrak{B}\mathfrak{Z}_1},}
then it follows from this that
\weq{2}{\omega\,dz = \omega_1\,dz_1.}
If $\mathfrak{A}\mathfrak{U}^2$ is equivalent to $\mathfrak{B}\mathfrak{Z}$, then $\omega$ is a function in $\Omega$, and $\omega_1$ is likewise a function in $\Omega$. If $a$, $b$ are the orders of $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$, then [\S\ 196, (2)]
\weq{3}{\begin{aligned}
b+w &= a+2n,\\
a &= b+2p-2,
\end{aligned}}
where $p$ is the genus of the field $\Omega$. We now set, in a new symbolic notation,
\weq{4}{dz = \dfrac{\mathfrak{Z}}{\mathfrak{U}^2},}
\weq{5}{\omega\,dz = dJ = \dfrac{\mathfrak{A}}{\mathfrak{B}},}
and we call these expressions the \gesperrt{differentials} belonging to the field $\Omega$.

In the numerator and denominator $\mathfrak{A}$, $\mathfrak{B}$ of a differential, common factors may be added or omitted. If $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ have no common divisor, then $\mathfrak{A}$ is called the \gesperrt{upper vertex}, $\mathfrak{B}$ the \gesperrt{lower vertex} of the differential $dJ$.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 720 =====
% !PRINTED 689
\weberpage{689}

The notation (5) for a differential differs from the similar notation for
the \gesperrt{functions} in $\Omega$ in that the degree of the numerator is higher by
$(2p - 2)$ than that of the denominator.

The differentials $d\alpha$ of the functions in $\Omega$ defined in § 194 % [sic] German source has singular `Differentiale`

are special cases of the general differentials (5). For not all of these
$dJ$ are differentials of functions in $\Omega$. We distinguish \gesperrt{proper
differentials} $d\alpha$, i.e. those which are differentials of functions
in $\Omega$, and \gesperrt{improper} or \gesperrt{Abelian differentials} $dJ$, which are not.
For the latter, $J$ itself has no meaning; it acquires one only in the
integral calculus, which is not accessible to the purely arithmetical
method.

If $z$ is any variable in $\Omega$ and $dJ$ a differential, then $dJ:dz$
is a function in $\alpha$, % [sic] printed alpha for Omega
and $dJ:dz$ is a \gesperrt{differential quotient}. Here
too we distinguish \gesperrt{proper and improper} differential quotients. The
quotient of two differentials $dJ:dJ'$ is likewise always a function in
$\Omega$, and can likewise be called a differential quotient.

In order that a polygon quotient $\mathfrak{A}:\mathfrak{B}$ can be the
symbol for a differential, it is necessary that the difference $(a - b)$
of the orders of $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ be equal to $(2p - 2)$.
But this condition is not sufficient; there is the further requirement
that a variable $z$ must exist in $\Omega$ for which
\weq{6}{\mathfrak{U}^2\mathfrak{A} \sim \mathfrak{Z}\mathfrak{B}}
holds. If this requirement is satisfied, it remains satisfied when
$z$ is replaced by any other variable in $\Omega$, and $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ by
equivalent polygons. Thus if $\mathfrak{A}'$, $\mathfrak{A}''$, \dots{} are polygons
of the class $A$ determined by $\mathfrak{A}$, then $\mathfrak{A}':\mathfrak{B}$, $\mathfrak{A}'':\mathfrak{B}$, \dots{}
are likewise differentials.

If
\[ A = (\mathfrak{A}_1,\ \mathfrak{A}_2,\ \mathfrak{A}_3,\ \dots) \]
and $\mathfrak{A}_1$, $\mathfrak{A}_2$, $\mathfrak{A}_3$, \dots{} is a basis of $A$, then the corresponding
differential quotients
\[ \frac{dJ_1}{dz},\ \frac{dJ_2}{dz},\ \frac{dJ_3}{dz},\ \dots \]
are the basis of a family of functions of finite dimension, and we can
call
\[ (dJ_1,\ dJ_2,\ dJ_3,\ \dots) \]
the basis of a family of differentials of the same dimension.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 721 =====
% !PRINTED 690
\weberpage{690}

Every differential $dJ$ whose lower polygon is $\mathfrak{B}$, or a divisor
of $\mathfrak{B}$, can then be represented in the form:
\weq{7}{dJ = c_1dJ_1 + c_2dJ_2 + c_3dJ_3 + \cdots}
with constant coefficients.

The simplest differentials are those whose lower polygon is the
null polygon, and whose upper polygons $\mathfrak{W}$ are accordingly of order
$(2p - 2)$. These are called \gesperrt{differentials of the first kind}
and are denoted by $dW$. They are characterized by the fact
that for every variable $z$ the polygons $\mathfrak{U}^2\mathfrak{W}$ and $\mathfrak{Z}$ must be
equivalent, and the $\mathfrak{W}$ accordingly form, assuming their existence, a
class of polygons $W$ whose dimension is to be determined.

The polygon $\mathfrak{W}$ is called the fundamental polygon of the differential $dW$
and is named a \gesperrt{complete polygon of the first kind}. If
$\mathfrak{W} = \mathfrak{A}\mathfrak{B}$, then $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ too are called polygons of the first
kind, and indeed \gesperrt{complementary polygons} of one another.

Every polygon that is not a divisor of a complete polygon
of the first kind is said to be \gesperrt{of the second kind}.

If $\mathfrak{A}$ is a polygon of the first kind, then every polygon $\mathfrak{A}'$
equivalent to $\mathfrak{A}$ is also of the first kind, and we call
the class $A$ of $\mathfrak{A}$ a \gesperrt{class of the first kind}. For if
$\mathfrak{A}\mathfrak{B} = \mathfrak{W}$, then $AB = W$, where $B$ is the class of $\mathfrak{B}$, and
$\mathfrak{A}'\mathfrak{B} = \mathfrak{W}'$ is equivalent to $\mathfrak{W}$, hence of the first kind.

If, then, $q$ is the number of linearly independent polygons
of the first kind that are divisible by a polygon of the class $A$,
then by § 192, (14)
\weq{8}{q = (A,\ W) = (O,\ B),}
that is, equal to the dimension of the complementary class.

If $A$ is a class of the second kind, then there is no polygon
of the first kind divisible by $\mathfrak{A}$, and
\[ (A,\ W) = 0. \]

\begin{center}
§ 198. \textbf{\gesperrt{The Family of Polygons of the First Kind.}}
\end{center}

In order to determine the dimension $(O, W)$ of the family of polygons of the first kind and
thereby at the same time to establish its existence, we take
an arbitrary variable $z$ in $\Omega$ with the branch polygon
$\mathfrak{Z}$ and the lower polygon $\mathfrak{U}$. If $dW$ is a differential of the first kind,
then
\weq{1}{w = \frac{dW}{dz} = \frac{\mathfrak{W}\mathfrak{U}^2}{\mathfrak{Z}}}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 722 =====
% !PRINTED 691
\weberpage{691}

%<<CONT
a function in $\Omega$, which we call a \gesperrt{differential quotient}
of the first kind.

If $\mathfrak{P}$ is a point at which $(z - z_0)$ becomes infinitely small of
order $e$, then this point occurs $(e - 1)$ times in $\mathfrak{Z}$,
and consequently $[w(z - z_0)]_0 = 0$. If $z$ becomes infinite in
another point $\mathfrak{P}$ in the $e$th order, then this point occurs
$e$ times in $\mathfrak{U}$ and $(e - 1)$ times in $\mathfrak{Z}$, hence once in the
numerator of $wz$, and consequently at this point too $(wz)_0 = 0$,
and these two requirements, namely:

a) At every point at which $z$ has a finite value $z_0$,
$[w(z - z_0)]_0 = 0$;

b) At a point at which $z$ becomes infinite, $(wz)_0 = 0$,

are also sufficient to define a differential quotient of the first kind
$w$.

In order to satisfy the first condition, we take a
minimal basis with respect to $z$:
\weq{2}{\omega_1,\ \omega_2,\ \dots,\ \omega_n,}
put
\weq{3}{a_{r,\,s} = S(\omega_r\omega_s),}
so that
\weq{4}{\Delta = \Sigma \pm a_{1,1}a_{2,2}\dots a_{n,n}}
is the field discriminant (with respect to $z$), and determine a basis
\weq{5}{\varepsilon_1,\ \varepsilon_2,\ \dots,\ \varepsilon_n}
from the equations:
\weq{6}{\omega_r = \Sigma a_{r,\,i}\varepsilon_i.}

If $(r, s)$ is a symbol which is $= 0$ when $r$ and $s$ are different,
and $= 1$ when $r = s$, then one can determine the rational
functions $a'_{r,\,s}$ of $z$ in such a way that
\weq{7}{\sideset{^i}{}\sum a_{i,\,r}a'_{i,\,s} = (r,\ s)}
holds, and one obtains from (6):
\weq{8}{\varepsilon_r = \sideset{^i}{}\sum a'_{i,\,r}\omega_i,}
and the quantities $a'_{r,\,s}$ have no denominator other than $\Delta$.
From this there follows, by reason of (3) and (7):
\weq{9}{\begin{aligned}
S(\varepsilon_r\omega_s) &= (r,\ s), \\
a'_{r,\,s} &= S(\varepsilon_r\varepsilon_s).
\end{aligned}}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 723 =====
% !PRINTED 692
\weberpage{692}

If, conversely, for a system of functions $\eta_1$, $\eta_2$, \dots, $\eta_n$ the
condition
\weq{10}{S(\eta_r\omega_s) = (r,\ s)}
is satisfied, then $\eta_r = \varepsilon_r$; for if one sets
\[ \eta_r = \sideset{^i}{}\sum x_{i,\,r}\varepsilon_i, \]
it follows from (9) and (10) that $x_{r,\,s} = (r,\ s)$. Accordingly the conditions
(9) and (6) are completely equivalent.

The quantities $\varepsilon_i$ form a basis of $\Omega$, but are not
integral functions. The bases (5) and (2) are called \gesperrt{complementary
to one another}.

The quantities
\weq{11}{\Delta\varepsilon_1,\ \Delta\varepsilon_2,\ \dots,\ \Delta\varepsilon_n}
are integral functions, and if $t_1$, $t_2$, \dots, $t_n$ are functional variables,
then
\weq{12}{\Delta(\varepsilon_1t_1 + \varepsilon_2t_2 + \cdots + \varepsilon_nt_n) = \Delta\varepsilon}
is the greatest common divisor of the functions (11).

If
\weq{13}{r = (z - c_1)(z - c_2)(z - c_3)\dots}
is the product of all the linear factors of $\Delta$ that are distinct from
one another, and
\weq{14}{\varkappa = \pi_1\pi_2\pi_3\dots}
the product of the distinct prime functionals dividing $\Delta$,
then we can put every integral function $\varrho$ of $z$ in $\Omega$ that is
divisible by $r$ into the form:
\[ \varrho = r(x_1\varepsilon_1 + x_2\varepsilon_2 + \cdots + x_n\varepsilon_n), \]
in which $x_1$, $x_2$, \dots, $x_n$ are rational functions of $z$. Then
one obtains by (9)
\[ rx_i = S(\varrho\omega_i), \]
and since $\varrho\omega_i$ is divisible by every prime factor of $r$, by the
theorem of § 184, 7. $S(\varrho\omega_i)$ is an integral function in $Z$ % [sic] printed capital Z; sense requires lowercase z
divisible by $r$, and consequently $x_i$ an integral rational function.

From this it follows that
\[ \Delta\varrho = r(x_1\Delta\varepsilon_1 + x_2\Delta\varepsilon_2 + \cdots + x_n\Delta\varepsilon_n) \]
is divisible by $r\varepsilon\Delta$, and that accordingly $r\varepsilon$ is an integral
functional dividing $\varrho$.

If $\pi$ were a prime factor of $r\varepsilon$ not contained in $\varkappa$, then
one could assume $\varrho$ to be such that it is not divisible by $\pi$,
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 724 =====
% !PRINTED 693
\weberpage{693}
%<<CONT
and $\varrho$ could not be divisible by $r\varepsilon$. In the same way one concludes
that each of the prime factors $\pi_1, \pi_2, \ldots$ divides $r\varepsilon$, but none
of them more than once; hence, apart from unit factors,

\weq{15}{r\varepsilon = \varkappa.}

Thus each of the functions $\varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2, \ldots, \varepsilon_n$ satisfies condition a).
Conversely, every function $w$ that satisfies this condition is also
contained in the form:

\weq{16}{w = x_1\varepsilon_1 + x_2\varepsilon_2 + \cdots + x_n\varepsilon_n,}

in which the $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ are integral rational functions of $z$.

For $rw$ is an integral function divisible by $\varkappa$, and
consequently, by (9), (16) and § 184, 7.:
\[
S(rw\omega_i) = rx_i
\]
is an integral function of $z$ divisible by $r$; consequently

\weq{17}{x_i = S(w\omega_i).}

In order, then, to obtain the differential quotients of the first
kind, one has to select, among the functions (16), those that
satisfy condition b).

To this end we take for (2) the normal basis considered in § 193,
\[
\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \ldots, \lambda_n
\]
and denote the basis complementary to it by
\[
\mu_1, \mu_2, \ldots, \mu_n,
\]
which is defined by

\weq{18}{S(\lambda_r\mu_s) = (r, s)}

If we then set

\weq{19}{w = y_1\mu_1 + y_2\mu_2 + \cdots + y_n\mu_n,}

then, if $r_i$ is the exponent of $\lambda_i$, it follows by (17) that
\[
\frac{y_i}{z^{r_i-1}} = S\!\left(wz\frac{\lambda_i}{z^{r_i}}\right)\!.
\]

By the definition of $r_i$, $\lambda_i:z^{r_i}$ is finite for $z=\infty$, and
$wz$ vanishes on account of b). Consequently $y_i:z^{r_i-1}$ must vanish
for $z=\infty$, that is, $y_i$ can be at most of degree $(r_i-2)$
and therefore contains at most $r_i-1$ constant coefficients.

Since $\mu_1=1$, $r_1=0$ and the degree of $y_1$ cannot be
negative, $y_1$ must be identically zero, and it follows that
\[
S(w) = 0.
\]

%% ===== canonical stable idx 725 =====
% !PRINTED 694
\weberpage{694}
\gesperrt{This is Abel's theorem for the differential
 quotients of the first kind.}

To show that this requirement on the $y_i$ is also sufficient for the
 fulfilment of b), we regard the functions in $\Omega$
as functions of $z' = 1:z$. For these,
\[
\lambda_1' = z'^{r_1}\lambda_1,\quad \lambda_2' = z'^{r_2}\lambda_2,\quad \ldots,\quad \lambda_n' = z'^{r_n}\lambda_n
\]
form a minimal basis by § 193, 6., and
\[
\mu_1' = z^{r_1}\mu_1,\quad \mu_2' = z^{r_2}\mu_2,\quad \ldots,\quad \mu_n' = z^{r_n}\mu_n
\]
is by (10) the basis complementary to it. Consequently $z'\mu' = 0$
for $z' = 0$ [by a), applied to $z'$], and hence
\[
z^{r_i-1}\mu_i = 0,
\]
\[
zy_i\mu_i = \frac{y_i}{z^{i-2}}z^{r_i-1}\mu_i = 0 \text{ for } z = \infty, % [sic] printed with dropped r in denominator exponent; expected r_i-2
\]

if the degree of $y_i$ is not higher than $(r_i-1)$. % [sic] German source prints $r_i-1$; the preceding and following derivation require $r_i-2$

It has thereby been shown that all functions contained in the
 form (19), in which the $y_i$ are integral rational functions
of $z$ of degree at most $r_i-2$, are differential quotients
of the first kind, and that conversely all differential quotients
of the first kind can be represented in this form, and
the principal theorem follows:

1. \gesperrt{The class of differentials of the first kind
is of the dimension}
\[
(O,W) = (r_2-1)+(r_3-1)+\cdots+(r_n-1) = p.
\]

From this the following further results: if $A$ is any
class of polygons of order $a$ and $W$ the principal class of the
first kind, then by § 192, (14):
\[
(A, W) \mathrel{\underset{>}{=}} (O, W) - a = p - a, % source prints equality bars over a greater-than wedge
\]
hence, if $a \mathrel{\underset{<}{=}} p - 1$: % source prints equality bars over a less-than wedge
\[
(A, W) \mathrel{\underset{>}{=}} 1. % source prints equality bars over a greater-than wedge
\]

Hence, if $a$ is less than $p$, there are always polygons of the first
kind that are divisible by $\mathfrak{A}$, and from this it follows:

2. \gesperrt{Every polygon of the $(p-1)$th and lower
order is of the first kind.}

By § 192, 5., if $m$ is not greater than $p$, one can choose
an $m$-gon $\mathfrak{M}$ so that, if $M$ is the class determined by $\mathfrak{M}$,
\[
(M, W) = p - m
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 726 =====
% !PRINTED 695
\weberpage{695}
%<<CONT
is obtained, and if one here sets $m=p$, it follows that there are
classes of order $p$ of the second kind.

\begin{center}
§ 199. \gesperrt{The Riemann-Roch Theorem.}
\end{center}

The theorem known under the name of the \gesperrt{Riemann-Roch theorem}
has the purpose of determining the dimensions of polygon
 classes.

We consider first a \gesperrt{proper polygon class}
 $A$ of order $n$, take in it two coprime
polygons $\mathfrak{A}$, $\mathfrak{A}'$ and set:
\[
z = \frac{\mathfrak{A}'}{\mathfrak{A}}.
\]

If then $\mathfrak{A}''$ is another polygon of the same class, we
set
\[
\omega = \frac{\mathfrak{A}''}{\mathfrak{A}},\quad \frac{\omega}{z} = \frac{\mathfrak{A}''}{\mathfrak{A}'}.
\]

Thus $\omega$ is an integral function of $z$, and $\omega:z$ an
integral function of $1:z$. If then $\omega$ is not constant, the
exponent $r$ of $\omega$ is equal to 1. Conversely, every integral
function $\omega$ of $z$ of exponent 0 or 1 is likewise representable in the form
$\mathfrak{A}'':\mathfrak{A}$.

We thus obtain the whole class $A$ from the totality
of the integral functions of $z$ whose exponent is $\leqq 1$. These
we obtain easily from the normal basis $(\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \ldots, \lambda_n)$ in $z$,
with the sequence of exponents $r_1, r_2, \ldots, r_n$ (§ 193). If $\lambda_s$ is the
last of these functions whose exponent is equal to 1 or 0, then
every integral function whose exponent is $\leqq 1$ is representable in the form

\weq{1}{\omega = c_0 z + c_1\lambda_1 + c_2\lambda_2 + \cdots + c_s\lambda_s}

($c_0$ must be constant, because by the definition
of the normal basis it must be an integral function, and if its
exponent were positive, the exponent of $\omega$ would be greater than
one). Accordingly

\weq{2}{(O, A) = s + 1,}

and this number is therefore always $\leqq n + 1$.

The upper limit $n+1$ is reached only when all
$r_2, r_3, \ldots, r_n = 1$ and consequently $p = 0$.

Since at least two polygons are contained in a proper class,
so that $(O, A) \geqq 2$ must hold, $n = 1$ can occur only
in the case $p = 0$.

%% ===== canonical stable idx 727 =====
% !PRINTED 696
\weberpage{696}
A function $z$ which becomes 0 and $\infty$ at only a single point each,
and so has order 1, therefore exists only in the case $p = 0$.
\gesperrt{Every function in $\Omega$ can be rationally represented by such a $z$}
\footnote{This function field leads to what the geometers call
\glqq \gesperrt{unicursal curves}\grqq{}.}.

If $r_i > 2$, then by § 198 $\mu_i$ and $z\mu_i$ are differential
quotients of the first kind. By (1) there are therefore polygons $\mathfrak{W}$, $\mathfrak{W}'$
of the first kind which satisfy the condition:
\[
\mu_i = \frac{\mathfrak{A}^2\mathfrak{W}}{\mathfrak{Z}},\quad \mu_i z = \frac{\mathfrak{A}^2\mathfrak{W}'}{\mathfrak{Z}},\quad z = \frac{\mathfrak{W}'}{\mathfrak{W}} = \frac{\mathfrak{A}'}{\mathfrak{A}},
\]
and since $\mathfrak{A}$, $\mathfrak{A}'$ are coprime, $\mathfrak{A}$ must divide $\mathfrak{W}$, and $\mathfrak{A}'$ must divide $\mathfrak{W}'$.
Hence $A$ is a class of the first kind.

If $A$ is a class of the second kind, then all the exponents
$r_1, r_2, \ldots, r_n$ are equal to 2 or less than 2, and in
particular $r_{s+1}=2, r_{s+2}=2, \ldots, r_n=2$. Consequently
\[
p = (r_2-1)+(r_3-1)+\cdots+(r_n-1) = n-s,
\]
and by (2) we have the theorem:

3. \gesperrt{The dimension of a proper class $A$ of
the second kind is}

\weq{3}{(O,A) = n - p + 1.}

If, further, $A$ is a proper class of the first kind and

\weq{4}{AB = W}

is the complete class of the first kind, then take a polygon $\mathfrak{B}$
in $B$ and form the differential quotients of the first kind:
\[
w = \frac{\mathfrak{A}^3\mathfrak{B}}{\mathfrak{Z}},\quad zw = \frac{\mathfrak{A}^2\mathfrak{A}'\mathfrak{B}}{\mathfrak{Z}},
\]
and this form is preserved when $\mathfrak{B}$ is replaced by an equivalent
polygon $\mathfrak{B}'$. The dimension $(O, B)$ is therefore as great
as the dimension of the family of differential quotients of the first
kind $w$ which have the property that $zw$ too is still of
the first kind. For this to be the case, in the
expression:
\[
w = y_1\mu_1 + y_2\mu_2 + \cdots + y_n\mu_n
\]
the degrees of the functions $y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n$ may rise only to the height
$r_1-2, r_2-2, \ldots, r_n-2$, and from this it follows:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 728 =====
% !PRINTED 697
\weberpage{697}
%<<CONT
\[
(O, B) = (r_{s+1} - 2) + (r_{s+2} - 2) + \cdots + (r_n - 2),
\]
\weq{5}{p = (r_{s+1} - 1) + (r_{s+2} - 1) + \cdots + (r_n - 1),}
\[
(O, B) = p - n + s,
\]
and by (2):
\[
(O, A) - (O, B) = n - p + 1.
\]
Now by \S\,192, (14) $(O, B) = (A, W)$, and we have
the \gesperrt{Riemann-Roch} theorem for classes of the first kind:

4. \gesperrt{The dimension of a proper class $A$
of the first kind is}
\weq{6}{(O, A) = n - p + 1 + (A, W).}
This formula contains (3) within itself, because for polygons of the
second kind $(A, W) = 0$.

Since the dimension of a proper class is at least equal
to 2, it follows for a class of the second kind that
\[
n \geqq p + 1,
\]
and herein is contained the proof of a theorem of \gesperrt{Riemann}:

5. \gesperrt{A function whose order is less than
$(p + 1)$ is of the first kind.}

It follows further from this that the class $W$ of the polygons
of the first kind is a proper one. For suppose $W$ had
the divisor $\mathfrak{M}$, and let $W = \mathfrak{M} A$; then $(O, W) = (O, A) = p$.
If one takes $\mathfrak{A}$ in $A$ relatively prime to $\mathfrak{M}$, then in $W$ there is only
one polygon divisible by $\mathfrak{A}$, namely $\mathfrak{A}\mathfrak{M}$, and consequently
$(A, W) = 1$. Accordingly formula (6) gives:
\[
n = 2p - 2,
\]
hence equal to the order of $W$. The order of $A$ is therefore
just as great as that of $W$, and consequently $\mathfrak{M} = \mathfrak{O}$.

Theorem 4. holds unchanged for improper classes as well.
In order to prove this, let $A$ first be of the first kind
and of divisor $\mathfrak{M}$:
\weq{7}{
\begin{aligned}
A &= \mathfrak{M} A', \\
AB &= W, \\
A'B' &= W, \\
B' &= \mathfrak{M} B, \quad (\S\,192,\,8.) \\
(A', W) &= (O, B').
\end{aligned}
}
Let the orders of $\mathfrak{M}, A, B$ be $m, a, b$, so that $a + b$ is the
order of $W$, i.e.
\weq{8}{a + b = 2(p - 1).}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 729 =====
% !PRINTED 698
\weberpage{698}
By (7) and \S\,192 we have
\weq{9}{(O, B) \geqq (O, B') - m,
}
and by (6), applied to $A'$:
\[
(O, A) = (O, A') = a - m - p + 1 + (O, B'),
\]
hence by (8):
\[
(O, A) - \tfrac{1}{2} a \leqq (O, B) - \tfrac{1}{2} b.
\]
But since we can interchange $A$ and $B$, there results from
this
\[
(O, A) - \tfrac{1}{2} a = (O, B) - \tfrac{1}{2} b,
\]
and if one puts
\[
(O, B) = (A, W),
\]
\[
\tfrac{1}{2}(a - b) = a - p + 1
\]
then:
\[
(O, A) = a - p + 1 + (A, W)
\]
in exact agreement with (6).

In order to derive the corresponding theorem for improper
classes of the second kind as well, let
\weq{10}{A = \mathfrak{M} A'}
be an improper class of the second kind with the divisor $\mathfrak{M}$.

In a proper class of the second kind, $C$, whose
dimension is greater than the order $a$ of $A$, there are by
\S\,192, 5. always polygons that are divisible by a polygon of the class $A$,
and $C$ is therefore also divisible by $A$.

From \S\,192, (15) it follows:
\[
(O, A) \geqq (O, C) - c + a,
\]
and from (3):
\[
(O, C) = c - p + 1,
\]
hence
\weq{11}{(O, A) \geqq a - p + 1.
}
Now $A'$ is a proper class of the same dimension
as $A$, and hence, if $m$ is the order of $\mathfrak{M}$, by (6):
\weq{12}{(O, A) = (O, A') = a - m - p + 1 + (A', W),}
hence by (11):
\weq{13}{(A', W) \geqq m.
}
\gesperrt{From this it follows that $A'$ must be of the first kind.}

If $W = A'B'$, then from (13) it follows:
\weq{14}{(A', W) = (O, B') \geqq m.
}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 730 =====
% !PRINTED 699
\weberpage{699}
If now $(O, B') > m$, then in $B'$ one could find a polygon
$\mathfrak{M}\mathfrak{B}$ divisible by $\mathfrak{M}$ (\S\,192, 5.), and then
\[
\mathfrak{A}' \mathfrak{M} \mathfrak{B} = \mathfrak{A} \mathfrak{B} = \mathfrak{W}
\]
would be a complete polygon of the first kind; $\mathfrak{A}$ itself would
therefore be of the first kind, contrary to the assumption. Hence
$(O, B') = (A', W) = m$ and
\weq{15}{(O, A) = a - p + 1.}
So here too the \gesperrt{Riemann-Roch theorem} holds in the
form 3.

If $A$ consists of an isolated polygon $\mathfrak{M}$, then $(O, A) = 1$,
hence $a = p$, and from this it follows:

6. \gesperrt{An isolated polygon of the second kind must\
be a $p$-gon, and conversely every $p$-gon
of the second kind is an isolated polygon.}

7. \gesperrt{If a point $\mathfrak{P}$ divides the divisor of an improper
 class $A$ of the second kind, and if $A = \mathfrak{P} A'$,
then $A'$ must be of the first kind.}

For by the theorem (6) and (15) we have:
\[
\begin{aligned}
(O, A) &= a - p + 1, \\
(O, A') &= a - p + (A', W), \\
(O, A) &= (O, A'),
\end{aligned}
\]
hence $(A', W) = 1$.

\begin{center}
\textbf{\S\,200. Differentials of the second and third kind.}
\end{center}
We can now represent invariantly the condition for a differential:
\weq{1}{dJ = \frac{\mathfrak{A}}{\mathfrak{B}},}
which we expressed in \S\,197, (6) with reference to a variable $z$ in the
form:
\[
\mathfrak{U}^2 \mathfrak{A} \sim \mathfrak{Z} \mathfrak{B},
\]
by using the complete polygons of the first kind, according to
which
\[
\mathfrak{U}^2 \mathfrak{W} \sim \mathfrak{Z}
\]
holds:
\[
\mathfrak{A} \sim \mathfrak{W} \mathfrak{B},
\]
or, by introducing the classes:
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 731 =====
% !PRINTED 700
\weberpage{700}
%<<CONT
1. \gesperrt{The polygon quotient (1) is a differential,
if the classes $A$, $B$ of $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ are relatively prime
and satisfy the condition:}
\weq{2}{A = WB.}
If $a$ and $b$ are the order numbers of $A$ and $B$, then:
\weq{3}{a - b = 2p - 2,}
and since $A$ is in any case of the second kind, by \S\,199, (15):
\weq{4}{(O, A) = b + p - 1.}
If $B$ consists of a single point $\mathfrak{P}$, then $(O, A) = p$,
and the dimension of $A$ is just as great as that of $W$; if therefore
\[
(\mathfrak{W}_1, \mathfrak{W}_2, \ldots, \mathfrak{W}_p)
\]
is a basis of $W$, then
\[
(\mathfrak{P} \mathfrak{W}_1, \mathfrak{P} \mathfrak{W}_2, \ldots, \mathfrak{P} \mathfrak{W}_p)
\]
is a basis of $A$. Hence $A$ is an improper class with
the divisor $\mathfrak{P}$, and it follows:

2. \gesperrt{A single point $\mathfrak{P}$ cannot be the lower
vertex of a differential.}

If the class $A$ has a divisor $\mathfrak{M}$ of degree $m$, then $\mathfrak{M}$ must
be contained in the divisor of $B$; for $\mathfrak{M}$ must divide each of the
polygons $\mathfrak{W}\mathfrak{B}$, and consequently, since $W$ is a proper class,
each of the $\mathfrak{B}$. If
\[
\mathfrak{M} A' = A, \quad \mathfrak{M} B' = B,
\]
then
\weq{5}{(O, A) = (O, A')}
must hold. But by (3) and (4), applied to $A$ and $A'$,
if $A'$ is of the second kind:
\[
(O, A) = (O, A') + m,
\]
hence $(O, A) > (O, A')$; consequently $m = 0$ must hold.

But $A'$ can be of the first kind only if
$B$ is an isolated polygon and $B = \mathfrak{M}$. Then:
\[
A' = W, \quad (O, A') = p,
\]
so that $(O, A) = p$, $b = 1$ must hold, and we come to the
case of theorem 2. Consequently:

3. \gesperrt{Every polygon of more than one point can
be the lower vertex of a differential.}

By a \gesperrt{differential of the second kind} one understands
one whose lower vertex is a power of a single point $\mathfrak{P}$
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 732 =====
% !PRINTED 701
\weberpage{701}
%<<CONT
is. A differential whose lower polygon consists of only two simple points is called a differential of the third kind. We prove the theorem:

4. \gesperrt{Every differential $dJ$ can be composed linearly and with constant coefficients out of differentials of the first, second and third kind.}

This theorem can also be stated, in accordance with (4), by saying that the class $A$ has a basis
\weq{6}{\mathfrak{A}_1, \mathfrak{A}_2', \ldots, \mathfrak{A}_{b+p-1}}
of such a kind that the quotients
\weq{7}{dJ_r = \frac{\mathfrak{A}_r}{\mathfrak{B}}}
are differentials of one of the three kinds.

In order to prove it by complete induction, we assume that for some $\mathfrak{B}$ such a basis has been found, and we seek one of the same sort for the lower polygon $\mathfrak{P}\mathfrak{B}$, where $\mathfrak{P}$ is an arbitrary point. Such a basis we may assume in the form:
\weq{8}{\mathfrak{P}\mathfrak{A}_1, \mathfrak{P}\mathfrak{A}_2, \ldots, \mathfrak{P}\mathfrak{A}_{b+p-1}, \mathfrak{A}_{b+p},}
in which $\mathfrak{A}_{b+p}$ must be a polygon equivalent to $\mathfrak{W}\mathfrak{B}\mathfrak{P}$ that does not contain the point $\mathfrak{P}$.

If the point $\mathfrak{P}$ divides $\mathfrak{B}$, we put:
\[
\mathfrak{B} = \mathfrak{M}\mathfrak{P}^m,
\]
so that $\mathfrak{P}$ no longer divides $\mathfrak{M}$. The polygon $\mathfrak{W}\mathfrak{P}^{m+1}$ then belongs to a proper class, in which therefore a polygon $\mathfrak{N}$ not divisible by $\mathfrak{P}$ exists.

We then put:
\[
\mathfrak{A}_{b+p} = \mathfrak{M}\mathfrak{N},
\]
and from this we obtain a differential of the second kind:
\weq{9}{dJ_{b+p} = \frac{\mathfrak{A}_{b+p}}{\mathfrak{B}\mathfrak{P}} = \frac{\mathfrak{N}}{\mathfrak{P}^{m+1}}.}

If $\mathfrak{P}$ does not divide $\mathfrak{B}$, then one takes a point $\mathfrak{P}_0$ which divides $\mathfrak{B}$. Then $\mathfrak{W}\mathfrak{P}_0\mathfrak{P}$ belongs to a proper class and contains a polygon $\mathfrak{N}$ not divisible by $\mathfrak{P}$. If then
\[
\mathfrak{B} = \mathfrak{P}_0\mathfrak{M}, \quad \mathfrak{A}_{b+p} = \mathfrak{M}\mathfrak{N},
\]
then
\weq{10}{dJ_{b+p} = \frac{\mathfrak{A}_{b+p}}{\mathfrak{B}\mathfrak{P}} = \frac{\mathfrak{N}}{\mathfrak{P}_0\mathfrak{P}}}
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 733 =====
% !PRINTED 702
\weberpage{702}
%<<CONT
a differential of the third kind. With this Theorem 4. is proved, and even with the sharpening that the differentials of the third kind occurring in it contain an arbitrary fixed point $\mathfrak{P}_0$ in the lower polygon.

\begin{center}
\textbf{§ 201. The Residues.}
\end{center}

If $\mathfrak{P}$ is a point which divides $m$ times into the lower polygon $\mathfrak{B}$ of a differential $dJ$ ($m \mathrel{\underset{>}{=}} 0$),
then one takes a function $z$ in $\Omega$ which becomes infinitely large in the first order at $\mathfrak{P}$. Then, by § 197, (1) and § 185, (5), one may put:
\weq{1}{\frac{dJ}{dz} = a_{m-2}z^{m-2} + a_{m-3}z^{m-3} + \cdots + a_0 + a_{-1}z^{-1} + \eta z^{-2},}
in which the $a$ are constants, and $\eta$ is a function in $\Omega$ that is finite at $\mathfrak{P}$.

\gesperrt{The coefficient $-a_{-1}$ of $-z^{-1}$ is called the residue of the differential $dJ$ with respect to the point $\mathfrak{P}$.}

The residue of $dJ$ at the point $\mathfrak{P}$ can be different from zero only if $m>0$, that is, if the point $\mathfrak{P}$ occurs in the lower polygon of $dJ$. Such points shall be called poles of $dJ$.

1. \gesperrt{The residue of a proper differential is equal to zero. For by differentiation of a power of $z$, $z^{-1}$ can never arise.}

If for $z$ one takes a function $z_1$ which likewise becomes infinite of the first order at $\mathfrak{P}$, then one may put:
\[
z = cz_1 + \eta_1, \quad z^{-1} = c^{-1}z_1^{-1} + \eta_2,
\]
\weq{2}{\frac{dz}{dz_1} = c + z_1^{-2}\eta_3,}
in which the $c$ are constants, and $\eta_1, \eta_2, \eta_3$ are finite at $\mathfrak{P}$.

If one puts
\[
\frac{a_{m-2}z^{m-1}}{m-1} + \frac{a_{m-3}z^{m-2}}{m-2} + \cdots + a_0 = \omega,
\]
then from (1) there results:
\[
\frac{dJ}{dz_1} = \frac{d\omega}{dz_1} + a_{-1}z^{-1}\frac{dz}{dz_1} + z^{-2}\eta',
\]
where $\eta'$ remains finite at $\mathfrak{P}$, and in it, by 1., only the part
\[
a_{-1}z^{-1}\frac{dz}{dz_1}
\]
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 734 =====
% !PRINTED 703
\weberpage{703}
%<<CONT
a contribution to the term with $z_1^{-1}$, and by (2) this has the coefficient $a_{-1}$. From this it follows:

2. \gesperrt{The residue of $dJ$ is independent of the choice of the function $z$.}

The following theorem holds further:

3. \gesperrt{The sum of all residues of a differential is equal to zero.}

We extend the expression $\mathfrak{A}/\mathfrak{B}$ of the differential $dJ$, if necessary, by the addition of points in the numerator and denominator, so that the mutually distinct points of the lower polygon
\weq{3}{\mathfrak{P}_1 \mathfrak{P}_2 \ldots \mathfrak{P}_n}
form a polygon of a proper class. The poles of $dJ$ are then contained among these $\mathfrak{P}$, and possibly other points as well, for which the residue of $dJ$ is equal to zero.

As denominator of $dJ$ we may then take
\weq{4}{\mathfrak{B} = \mathfrak{P}_1^{m_1} \mathfrak{P}_2^{m_2} \ldots \mathfrak{P}_n^{m_n}}
if we add the points taken in excess back again in the numerator.

We take a function $z$ in $\Omega$ of the $n$th order, which becomes infinite at each of the points $\mathfrak{P}_i$ and at each of them only to the first order, and form the development for the point $\mathfrak{P}_i$:
\weq{5}{\frac{dJ}{dz} = a_{m-2}^{(i)}z^{m-2} + \cdots + a_0^{(i)} + a_{-1}^{(i)}z^{-1} + \eta^{(i)}z^{-2}.}

If we admit the value 0 for the coefficient $a_r^{(i)}$, we can begin at all the points $\mathfrak{P}_i$ with the same power $z^{m-2}$. The sum of the residues of $dJ$ is
\[
-\overset{i}{\sum} a_{-1}^{(i)}.
\]

According to § 182, 11. a system of functions $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n$ can be determined in such a way that $\alpha_r$ becomes infinitely small in the first order at the point $\mathfrak{P}_r$, while at the remaining points $\mathfrak{P}_i$ it remains finite and different from zero.

If one then puts
\[
\alpha_1^m \alpha_2^m \ldots \alpha_n^m = \alpha_i^m \varrho_i,
\]
there results
\weq{6}{\begin{aligned}
\varrho_1 &= 0^m \text{ in } \mathfrak{P}_2, \mathfrak{P}_3, \ldots, \mathfrak{P}_n, & \text{finite and not} &= 0 \text{ in } \mathfrak{P}_1, \\
\varrho_2 &= 0^m \text{ ,, } \mathfrak{P}_1, \mathfrak{P}_3, \ldots, \mathfrak{P}_n, & \text{,, ,, ,,} &= 0 \text{ ,, } \mathfrak{P}_2, \\
&\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots \\
\varrho_n &= 0^m \text{ ,, } \mathfrak{P}_1, \mathfrak{P}_2, \ldots, \mathfrak{P}_{n-1} & \text{,, ,, ,,} &= 0 \text{ in } \mathfrak{P}_n.
\end{aligned}}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 735 =====
% !PRINTED 704
\weberpage{704}
If we now understand by $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ rational functions of $z$ that are not all identically $=0$, and set:
\weq{7}{\eta = x_1\varrho_1 + x_2\varrho_2 + \cdots + x_n\varrho_n,}
then $\eta$ can be finite for $z=\infty$, i.\,e. at the points $\mathfrak{P}_1, \mathfrak{P}_2, \ldots, \mathfrak{P}_n$, only if the $x_i$ remain finite for $z=\infty$, that is, are fractions whose numerator is not of higher degree than the denominator.

For if the $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ are not all finite for $z=\infty$, then there is a positive exponent $r$ such that the products $x_1z^{-r}, x_2z^{-r}, \ldots, x_nz^{-r}$ are finite for $z=\infty$, and at least one of these products, say $x_1z^{-r}$, is different from zero. Then
\[
z^{-r}\eta = x_1z^{-r}\varrho_1 + x_2z^{-r}\varrho_2 + \cdots + x_nz^{-r}\varrho_n
\]
is finite and different from zero at the point $\mathfrak{P}_1$, and $\eta$ can therefore not be finite at $\mathfrak{P}_1$. In the same way one sees that no relation of the form
\[
x_1\varrho_1 + x_2\varrho_2 + \cdots + x_n\varrho_n = 0
\]
can subsist, i.\,e. the $\varrho_1, \varrho_2, \ldots, \varrho_n$ form a basis with respect to $z$.

If therefore we set
\weq{8}{\varrho_i \frac{dJ}{dz} = x_{i,1}\varrho_1 + x_{i,2}\varrho_2 + \cdots + x_{i,n}\varrho_n,}
then
\weq{9}{S\left(\frac{dJ}{dz}\right) = x_{1,1} + x_{2,2} + \cdots + x_{n,n}.}

According to (5),
\[
z^{-m+2}\frac{dJ}{dz}\varrho_i
\]
is finite for $z=\infty$, and consequently the same holds of
\weq{10}{z^{-m+2}x_{i,1}, \quad x^{-m+2}x_{i,2}, \quad \ldots, \quad z^{-m+2}x_{i,n}.} % [sic] source prints $x^{-m+2}$ in the second term, where $z^{-m+2}$ is required; reproduced as printed

The functions $zx_{r,s}$ therefore contain each of the points $\mathfrak{P}$ at most $m-1$ times in the denominator, and
\[
z\frac{dJ}{dz}\varrho_1
\]
contains each of the points $\mathfrak{P}_2, \mathfrak{P}_3, \ldots$ in the numerator. ($\mathfrak{P}_1$ in general not.)

Now by (8):
\[
z\frac{dJ}{dz}\varrho_1 = zx_{1,1}\varrho_1 + zx_{1,2}\varrho_2 + \cdots + zx_{1,n}\varrho_n.
\]

%% ===== canonical stable idx 736 =====
% !PRINTED 705
\weberpage{705}
This function must therefore vanish in $\mathfrak P_2,\allowbreak \mathfrak P_3,\allowbreak \ldots$. At the point $\mathfrak P_2$, however, $z\,x_{1,1}\varrho_1,\allowbreak z\,x_{1,3}\varrho_3,\allowbreak \ldots,\allowbreak z\,x_{1,n}\varrho_n$ vanish, while $\varrho_2$ does not vanish. Consequently $z\,x_{1,2}$ must vanish in $\mathfrak P_2$, that is, for $z=\infty$, and $z^2 x_{1,2}$ must remain finite. We have therefore:

\gesperrt{If $r$ is not equal to $s$, then $z^2 x_{r,s}$ is finite for $z=\infty$.}

We now define the rational function $u^{(i)}$ by:
\weq{11}{x_{i,i} = a^{(i)}_{m-2} z^{m-2} + a^{(i)}_{m-3} z^{m-3} + \cdots + a^{(i)}_{-1} z^{-1} + u^{(i)} z^{-2},}
in which the constant $a^{(i)}_\nu$ is to be the same as in (5), and we obtain:
\weq{12}{\frac{dJ}{dz} - x_{i,i} = z^{-2}\bigl[\eta^{(i)} - u^{(i)}\bigr],}
and by (8):
\[
\bigl[\eta^{(i)} - u^{(i)}\bigr]\varrho_i = z^2 x_{i,1}\varrho_1 + \cdots + z^2 x_{i,i-1}\varrho_{i-1} + z^2 x_{i,i+1}\varrho_{i+1} + \cdots + z^2 x_{i,n}\varrho_n.
\]
At the point $\mathfrak P_i$, $\eta^{(i)}$ is finite and $\varrho_i$ different from zero, while on the right-hand side everything vanishes in $\mathfrak P_i$. Consequently $u^{(i)}$ too must be finite in $\mathfrak P_i$, and, since it is rational, also for $z=\infty$; and from (9) and (11) it follows that:
\weq{13}{S\left(\frac{dJ}{dz}\right) = \overset{i}{\Sigma} a^{(i)}_{m-2} z^{m-2} + \cdots + \overset{i}{\Sigma} a^{(i)}_{-1} z^{-1} + \overset{i}{\Sigma} u^{(i)} z^{-2}.}

By our assumption about $z$, the lower polygon $\mathfrak B$ of $dJ$ contains no point at which $z$ has a finite value.

If $\mathfrak P$ is a point at which $z$ has the finite value $z_0$, then
\weq{14}{(z - z_0) = \frac{\mathfrak N}{\mathfrak U}, \quad \frac{dJ}{dz} = \frac{\mathfrak A \mathfrak U^2}{\mathfrak Z\mathfrak B}, \quad (z-z_0)\frac{dJ}{dz} = \frac{\mathfrak U \mathfrak N \mathfrak A}{\mathfrak Z\mathfrak B},}
and the point $\mathfrak P$ is contained once more often in $\mathfrak N$ than in $\mathfrak Z$; consequently:
\weq{15}{\left[(z-z_0)\frac{dJ}{dz}\right]_0 = 0 \quad \text{(in $\mathfrak P$).}}

This is requirement a) in \S\,198.

If therefore $\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \ldots, \lambda_n$ is the normal basis in $z$, and $\mu_1, \mu_2, \ldots, \mu_n$ the complementary basis, then:
\weq{16}{\frac{dJ}{dz} = y_1 \mu_1 + y_2 \mu_2 + \cdots + y_n \mu_n,}
in which the $y_i$ are integral rational functions of $z$, from which it follows that
\weq{17}{S\left(\frac{dJ}{dz}\right) = y_1 \quad [\S\,198, (18)]}
\gesperrt{is an integral rational function of $z$.}

%% ===== canonical stable idx 737 =====
% !PRINTED 706
\weberpage{706}
Since this function can accordingly contain no negative powers of $z$, the theorem to be proved follows from (13):
\[
\overset{i}{\Sigma} a^{(i)}_{-1} = 0,
\]
which no longer has anything to do with the particular assumption about the variable $z$.

As a special application it follows from this that a differential of the second kind has no residue, and that the two residues of the differentials of the third kind are equal and opposite.

\gesperrt{A proper differential $d\sigma$, as we have already seen, has no residue, and the residues of the \glqq logarithmic differential\grqq{}} $d\sigma:\sigma$ are integers, namely the order numbers in $z$.

We will conclude these considerations with the proof of the following theorem:

4. \gesperrt{If we call differentials of the second kind linearly dependent when a linear combination of them and of differentials of the first kind with constant coefficients is equal to a proper differential, then at most $p+1$ differentials of the second kind are always linearly dependent.}

To prove this, we take a $p$-gon of the second kind:
\weq{18}{\mathfrak P_1 \mathfrak P_2 \ldots \mathfrak P_p}
with $p$ distinct points. If then $\mathfrak P$ is a given point, we set:
\weq{19}{\mathfrak U = \mathfrak P \mathfrak P_1 \mathfrak P_2 \ldots \mathfrak P_r} % [sic] printed r; sequence defined through p
and obtain a class $B$ whose divisor $\mathfrak P$ in any case does not divide, since otherwise $\mathfrak P_1 \mathfrak P_2 \ldots \mathfrak P_n$ % [sic] printed n; sequence defined through p
would have to be of the first kind by $\S\,199$, 7. We can therefore determine a function in $\Omega$:
\weq{20}{z = \frac{\mathfrak A}{\mathfrak U}}
in whose lower polygon the point $\mathfrak P$ is in any case contained. We now form the proper differential
\weq{21}{dz = \frac{\mathfrak Z}{\mathfrak U^2},}
whose numerator $\mathfrak Z$ (the branch polygon with respect to $z$) the point $\mathfrak P$ does not divide, because it divides $\mathfrak U$ only simply, and if we express $dz$, according to $\S\,200$, 4., by differentials of the first, second and third
%CONT>>

%% ===== canonical stable idx 738 =====
% !PRINTED 707
\weberpage{707}
%<<CONT
kind, then the third kind cannot occur in this expression, since otherwise the residues could not be $=0$. This expression therefore gives a linear dependence among the differentials of the second kind, whose lower polygon is $\mathfrak P^2, \mathfrak P_1^2, \mathfrak P_2^2, \ldots, \mathfrak P_p^2$.

If one takes, for any positive exponent $m$:
\[
\mathfrak U = \mathfrak P^{m-1}\mathfrak P_1\mathfrak P_2\ldots\mathfrak P_p,
\]
and sets
\[
z = \frac{\mathfrak A}{\mathfrak U}, \quad dz = \frac{\mathfrak Z}{\mathfrak U^2},
\]
then $\mathfrak Z$ is divisible by $\mathfrak P^{m-2}$, $\mathfrak U^2$ by $\mathfrak P^{2m-2}$, and consequently the lower polygon of $dz$ by $\mathfrak P^m$. One then obtains a linear dependence among the differentials with the lower polygons
\[
\mathfrak P^m, \mathfrak P^{m-1}, \ldots, \mathfrak P^2, \mathfrak P_1^2, \mathfrak P_2^2, \ldots, \mathfrak P_p^2,
\]
and with that Theorem 4 is proved in general.

\weq{1}{\begin{aligned}
\frac{2\varkappa K}{\pi}\operatorname{sn}2Ku &= 4\sin\pi v \sum \frac{(1+q^n)q^{\frac{n}{2}}}{1-2q^n\cos2\pi u+q^{2n}} \\
&= 4\sum \frac{q^{\frac{n}{2}}}{1-q^n}\sin n\pi u.
\end{aligned}} % [sic] printed v in the leading factor; the remaining table uses u

\weq{2}{\begin{aligned}
\frac{2\varkappa K}{\pi}\operatorname{cn}2Ku &= 4\cos\pi v \sum (-1)^{\frac{n-1}{2}} \frac{(1-q^n)q^{\frac{n}{2}}}{1-2q^n\cos2\pi u+q^{2n}} \\
&= 4\sum \frac{q^{\frac{n}{2}}}{1+q^n}\cos n\pi u.
\end{aligned}} % [sic] printed v in the leading factor; the remaining table uses u

\weq{3}{\begin{aligned}
\frac{2K}{\pi}\operatorname{dn}2Ku &= 1+4\sum \frac{(-1)^{\frac{n-1}{2}} q^n(\cos2\pi u-q^n)}{1-2q^n\cos2\pi u+q^{2n}} \\
&= 1+4\sum \frac{q^{\frac{m}{2}}}{1+q^m}\cos m\pi u.
\end{aligned}}

\weq{4}{\begin{aligned}
\frac{2K}{\pi}\frac{1}{\operatorname{sn}2Ku} &= \frac{1}{\sin\pi u} + 4\sin\pi n \sum \frac{q^{\frac{m}{2}}(1+q^m)}{1-q^m\cos2\pi u+q^{2m}} \\
&= \frac{1}{\sin\pi u} + 4\sum \frac{q^n}{1-q^n}\sin\pi n u.
\end{aligned}} % [sic] printed \textquotedbl{}4\sin\pi n\textquotedbl{} and omits the coefficient 2 in the denominator

\weq{5}{\begin{aligned}
\frac{2K}{\pi}\frac{\operatorname{cn}2Ku}{\operatorname{sn}2Ku} &= \operatorname{cotg}\pi u + 4\sin2\pi u \sum \frac{q^{\frac{m}{2}}}{1-q^m\cos2\pi u+q^m} \\
&= \operatorname{cotg}\pi u - 4\sum \frac{q^m}{1+q^m}\sin\pi m u.
\end{aligned}} % [sic] denominator omits the coefficient 2 and prints the final term q^m rather than q^{2m}

\weq{6}{\begin{aligned}
\frac{2K}{\pi}\frac{\operatorname{dn}2Ku}{\operatorname{sn}2Ku} &= \frac{1}{\sin\pi u} + 4\sin\pi u \sum \frac{(-1)^{\frac{m}{2}} q^{\frac{m}{2}}(1-q^m)}{1-q^m\cos2\pi u+q^{2m}} \\
&= \frac{1}{\sin\pi u} - 4\sum \frac{q^n}{1+q^n}\sin n\pi u.
\end{aligned}} % [sic] printed denominator omits the coefficient 2

\weq{1}{\begin{aligned}
\frac{d\log H(2Ku)}{\pi\,du} &= \frac{2K}{\pi} Z(2Ku) + \frac{d\log \operatorname{sn}2Ku}{\pi\,du} \\
&= \operatorname{cotg}\pi u + 4\sin2\pi u \sum \frac{q^m}{1-2q^m\cos2\pi u+q^{2m}}, \\
&= \operatorname{cotg}\pi u + 4\sum \frac{q^m}{1-q^m}\sin m\pi u.
\end{aligned}}

\weq{2}{\begin{aligned}
\frac{d\log H(2Ku+K)}{\pi\,du} &= \frac{2K}{\pi} Z(2Ku) + \frac{d\log \operatorname{cn}2Ku}{\pi\,du}, \\
&= -\operatorname{tg}\pi u - 4\sin2\pi u \sum \frac{q^m}{1+2q^m\cos2\pi u+q^m}, \\
&= -\operatorname{tg}\pi u + 4\sum \frac{(-1)^{\frac{m}{2}} q^m}{1-q^m}\sin m\pi u.
\end{aligned}} % [sic] denominator's last term printed q^m, not q^{2m} as in the neighbouring formulas

\weq{3}{\begin{aligned}
\frac{d\log \Theta(2Ku)}{\pi\,du} &= \frac{2K}{\pi} Z(2Ku), \\
&= 4\sin2\pi u \sum \frac{q^n}{1-2q^n\cos2\pi u+q^{2n}}, \\
&= 4\sum \frac{q^{\frac{m}{2}}\sin\pi m u}{1-q^m}.
\end{aligned}}

\weq{4}{\begin{aligned}
\frac{d\log \Theta(2Ku+K)}{\pi\,du} &= \frac{2K}{\pi} Z(2Ku) + \frac{d\log \operatorname{dn}2Ku}{\pi\,du}, \\
&= -4\sin2\pi u \sum \frac{q^n}{1+2q^n\cos2\pi u+q^{2n}}, \\
&= 4\sum (-1)^{\frac{m}{2}} \frac{q^{\frac{m}{2}}}{1-q^m}\sin m\pi u.
\end{aligned}}

\bigskip
\noindent Pages 231, 232. In the application that is here made of Theorem 4,
it was overlooked that the invariants themselves belong to the domain of
 rationality, and hence that the representation of $J$ as a rational
function of $\theta$ is a pure identity ($J = J$). Accordingly
the paragraph from ``From this theorem'' at the foot of page 231 to ``remain
undecided'' at the top of page 232 is to be deleted.\\
\glqq{} 640, line 14 from the top, read $F'(\tau)$ instead of $F'(\tau')$.\\
\glqq{} 697, \glqq{} 13 from the bottom: The mode of reasoning that follows here must be
altered as follows:

\bigskip
\noindent From (13) there results, by multiplication by $g_s$ and summation:

\[
-n\varkappa \Sigma \delta_s g_s + \alpha u < \Sigma g_s \lambda_s < \Sigma \delta_s g_s + \alpha u.
\]

%% ===== canonical stable idx 764 =====
% !PRINTED 733
\weberpage{733}
If one sets
\[
n\varkappa\Sigma\delta_s|g_s| = g,
\]
then all the more, since the sum of the absolute values is not smaller than the absolute value of the sum:

\weq{14}{-g + \alpha u < \Sigma g_s\lambda_s < g + \alpha u.}
Now set
\[
-g + \alpha u = a, \qquad g + \alpha u = a'
\]
\[
\alpha\delta = a' - a = 2g
\]
and one obtains:

\weq{15}{a < \Sigma g_s\lambda_s < a'.}
If one replaces $u$ by $u' = u + \delta$, then $a$ passes over into $a'$ (which would not be the case with the formulation given in the text), and if one sets $a'' = a' + \alpha\delta = g + \alpha u'$, and if $\lambda_s'$ depends on $u'$ in the same way as $\lambda_s$ does on $u$, then there results
\[
a' < \Sigma g_s\lambda_s' < a''.
\]
By continuing this procedure a sequence of integers
\[
\eta, \eta', \eta'', \eta''', \ldots
\]
is determined in accordance with the following conditions.

From here one can proceed as in the text, page 698 above. The text on p. 697 becomes correct through the following four corrections:

Page 697, line 13 from the bottom read $nk\Sigma\delta_s|g_s|$ instead of $k\Sigma\delta_s\gamma_s$.

\glqq{} 11 from the bottom \glqq{} $-g$ instead of $-ng$.

\glqq{} 3 from the bottom \glqq{} $-g$ \glqq{} $-ng$.

\glqq{} 1 from the bottom \glqq{} $2g$ \glqq{} $(n+1)g$.
